    Smooth reduced equations on an open profile domain reconstruct a slice-wise pressure
satisfying the physical momentum equation on each selected open convex spatial slice.

The stream equation supplies the curl, and the two evolution equations supply its
transport. The time set may exclude a singular endpoint. The pressure is constructed separately
on each time slice.

    The Cartesian velocity has finite kinetic energy when the reduced
swirl, streamfunction, and its two physical derivatives have finite
`r³ dr dz` moments. The streamfunction moment fixes the decay normalization;
the independent swirl moment is not replaced by a bound on its derivatives.

The energy formula follows by applying the radial cancellation on almost
every axial slice, then the cylindrical change of variables. No trace at
infinity or integrability of the velocity is an input.

    Reduced viscous equations on an open profile domain `D` give the Cartesian vorticity equation
at every spacetime point whose `(t, s, z)` image lies in `D`. Axis points are covered exactly when
`D` contains a neighbourhood of `s = 0`, so the profiles must be smooth for slightly negative
squared radius as well; this is the even-in-`r` condition of classical axisymmetric flow. The
stream equation identifying this vorticity with curl is a separate condition. Setting viscosity
to zero gives the Euler transport equation.

rate is `2 θ_xx(0)/ω_x(0)`, the vorticity amplitude rate is half of it plus `u_x(0)`, and

    theorem BurgersEquation.ColeHopf.coleHopf_jet_residual_eq_zero
  (ν a b c d e f : ℝ) (ha : a ≠ 0) (hheat : e = ν * c)
  (hheatx : f = ν * d) :
  have k := -2 * ν;
  have u := k * b / a;
  have ut := k * (f * a - b * e) / a ^ 2;
  have ux := k * (c * a - b ^ 2) / a ^ 2;
  have uxx :=
    k * ((d * a - b * c) * a ^ 2 - (c * a - b ^ 2) * (2 * a * b)) /
      a ^ 4;
  ut + u * ux - ν * uxx = 0

  have u := k * b / a;
  have ut := k * (f * a - b * e) / a ^ 2;
  have ux := k * (c * a - b ^ 2) / a ^ 2;
  have uxx :=
    k *
        ((d * a - b * c) * a ^ 2 -
          (c * a - b ^ 2) * (2 * a * b)) /
      a ^ 4;
  ut + u * ux - ν * uxx = 0

Here `a,b,c,d,e,f` stand respectively for `v,vₓ,vₓₓ,vₓₓₓ,vₜ,vₓₜ` at one
spacetime point.  The two hypotheses are the heat equation `vₜ = νvₓₓ` and
its spatial derivative `vₓₜ = νvₓₓₓ`.  The displayed expressions are exactly
the quotient-rule jets of `u = -2νvₓ/v`; their Burgers residual cancels, a
rational identity in `a ≠ 0` checked by `cas`.

This is the purely algebraic step. The six jet values are derived from a smooth
nonvanishing profile in `coleHopfTransform_solvesViscousBurgersOn`.

    structure CAS.Continuum.GaussianRule (a b : ℝ)
  (w : ℝ → ℝ)
  (hw : ContinuousOn w (Set.uIcc a b))
  (n : ℕ) : Type
    A Gaussian rule on `[a, b]` for the weight `w`: `n` distinct nodes in `(a, b)`, positive
weights, and exactness against `w` for every polynomial of degree below `2n`.

    Fields

    nodes : Fin n → ℝ
    The points where the rule evaluates its integrand. 
    weights : Fin n → ℝ
    The coefficient multiplying the integrand at each node. 
    injective : Function.Injective self.nodes
    The nodes are pairwise distinct, so the Lagrange basis and the Hermite interpolant on
them exist. 
    interior : ∀ (i : Fin n), self.nodes i ∈ Set.Ioo a b
    Every node lies in the open interval `(a, b)`, where the integrand is sampled. 
    positive : ∀ (i : Fin n), 0 < self.weights i
    Every weight is strictly positive, which makes the rule stable under uniform
perturbation of the integrand. 
    exact : ∀ (p : Polynomial ℝ),
  p.natDegree < 2 * n →
    ∑ i, self.weights i * Polynomial.eval (self.nodes i) p = (CAS.Continuum.polynomialIntegral a b w hw) p
    The rule integrates every polynomial of degree below `2n` exactly against `w`:
`∑ i, weights i * p (nodes i) = ∫_a^b p w`.

vanishing moments `shiftedMoment p k = 0` for `k < n`, which give orthogonality of the nodal

If the rule is exact to degree `d` against a continuous weight `w`, its nodes lie in `[a,b]`,
and a polynomial of degree at most `d` is within `δ` of `f` on `[a,b]`, then the error on `f` is

    structure CAS.Continuum.RationalInterval.Precision :
  Type

The defaults use exponential Taylor order 8, square-root refinement with 12
binary digits, 10 logarithm series terms, and subdivision depth 2.

    Fields

    expOrder : ℕ

    sqrtDigits : ℕ
    Binary digits for square-root brackets (`sqrtRangeInterval`). 
    logTerms : ℕ

    depth : ℕ
    Number of checked bisection levels used by subdivided enclosures. 
    digits : Option ℕ
    Requested decimal digits. When set, box enclosures first try the precision-parametric

    class CAS.Continuum.RealIntervalBackend.{u} (ι : Type u) : Type u
    class CAS.Continuum.RealIntervalBackend.{u}
  (ι : Type u) : Type u
    A CEGA-facing real interval backend.

The backend chooses the interval representation.  CEGA only asks for lower
and upper real endpoints plus sound projections from backend membership to real
inequalities, so any representation with these projections fits the same API;
`RationalInterval` is the one instance.

The interface permits empty enclosures: it does not require `lo I ≤ hi I`.
Any inhabited enclosure has ordered endpoints by `lower_mem` and `upper_mem`.

    Methods

    lo : ι → ℝ
    Lower real endpoint. 
    hi : ι → ℝ
    Upper real endpoint. 
    MemReal : ι → ℝ → Prop
    Backend membership predicate, interpreted over real values. 
    lower_mem : ∀ {I : ι} {x : ℝ}, CAS.Continuum.RealIntervalBackend.MemReal I x → CAS.Continuum.RealIntervalBackend.lo I ≤ x
    Membership implies the lower endpoint bound. 
    upper_mem : ∀ {I : ι} {x : ℝ}, CAS.Continuum.RealIntervalBackend.MemReal I x → x ≤ CAS.Continuum.RealIntervalBackend.hi I
    Membership implies the upper endpoint bound.

    theorem CAS.Continuum.hermite_remainder {a b : ℝ} (hab : a < b) {n : ℕ}
  (hn : 0 < n) (F : ℕ → ℝ → ℝ)
  (hcontinuous : ∀ k < 2 * n, ContinuousOn (F k) (Set.Icc a b))
  (hderiv :

  ∃ ξ ∈ Set.Icc a b,
    F 0 x -
        Polynomial.eval x
          (CAS.Continuum.hermiteInterpolant nodes
            (fun i ↦ F 0 (nodes i)) fun i ↦ F 1 (nodes i)) =
      F (2 * n) ξ / ↑(2 * n).factorial *
        Polynomial.eval x (Lagrange.nodal Finset.univ nodes) ^ 2
    theorem CAS.Continuum.hermite_remainder {a b : ℝ}
  (hab : a < b) {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n)
  (F : ℕ → ℝ → ℝ)
  (hcontinuous :
    ∀ k < 2 * n,
      ContinuousOn (F k) (Set.Icc a b))
  (hderiv :
    ∀ k < 2 * n,
      ∀ z ∈ Set.Ioo a b,
        HasDerivAt (F k) (F (k + 1) z) z)
  (nodes : Fin n → ℝ)
  (hnodes : Function.Injective nodes)
  (hmem :
    ∀ (i : Fin n), nodes i ∈ Set.Icc a b)
  (x : ℝ) (hx : x ∈ Set.Icc a b) :
  ∃ ξ ∈ Set.Icc a b,
    F 0 x -
        Polynomial.eval x
          (CAS.Continuum.hermiteInterpolant
            nodes (fun i ↦ F 0 (nodes i))
            fun i ↦ F 1 (nodes i)) =
      F (2 * n) ξ / ↑(2 * n).factorial *
        Polynomial.eval x
            (Lagrange.nodal Finset.univ
              nodes) ^
          2
    Pointwise Hermite remainder for a derivative chain `F` on `[a, b]` and `n` distinct nodes
there. At every `x ∈ [a, b]` some `ξ ∈ [a, b]` satisfies
`F 0 x - H x = F (2n) ξ / (2n)! * P x ^ 2`, with `H` the Hermite interpolant of `F 0`, `F 1`
at the nodes and `P` the nodal polynomial. At a node both sides vanish. Otherwise
`G = F 0 - H - c P ^ 2` with `c = (F 0 x - H x) / P x ^ 2` has double zeros at the nodes and
a zero at `x`, so `exists_derivative_chain_zero_of_double_zeros` gives `ξ` with
`G^(2n) ξ = 0`, and `H^(2n) = 0`, `(P ^ 2)^(2n) = (2n)!` unwind this to the claim.

    Positive diagonal pivots. 
    upper : Matrix (Fin count) (Fin count) 𝕜

    Exact checked factorization. 
    lower_triangular : self.lower.IsLowerTriangular
    Entries above the lower factor's diagonal vanish. 
    lower_diagonal : ∀ (index : Fin count), self.lower index index = 1
    The lower factor has unit diagonal. 
    upper_triangular : self.upper.IsUpperTriangular
    Entries below the upper factor's diagonal vanish.

    The upper factor has unit diagonal.

            Bornology.IsBounded (v '' HamiltonJacobi.closedTimeSlab T) ∧

              (∀ (x : E), v (x, T) = g x) →
                (∀ z ∈ HamiltonJacobi.openTimeSlab T,

                            (HamiltonJacobi.openTimeSlab T) z →

                                (gradient (fun x ↦ φ (x, z.2)) z.1)

                            (HamiltonJacobi.openTimeSlab T) →

    structure HeatEquation.IsPointwiseInitialValueSolution
  {n : ℕ} (f : ℝ^n → ℝ → ℝ) (g : ℝ^n → ℝ)
  (u : ℝ^n → ℝ → ℝ) : Prop
    A pointwise solution of the forced heat Cauchy problem on positive time.

Unlike the residual-and-assigned-value `PDEProblem` interface, this structure
records enough regularity for every derivative in the equation to have its
analytic meaning. It also distinguishes the assigned value at `t = 0` from
the limit `u(x, t) → g(x₀)` as `(x, t) → (x₀, 0)` with `t > 0`.

    Fields

    differentiableAt_time : ∀ (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t → DifferentiableAt ℝ (u x) t
    At every positive time, the solution is differentiable in the time variable. 
    differentiableAt_space : ∀ (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t → DifferentiableAt ℝ (fun y ↦ u y t) x
    At every positive time, the spatial slice of the solution is differentiable. 
    differentiableAt_spatialPartial : ∀ (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t → ∀ (i : Fin n), DifferentiableAt ℝ (fun y ↦ (∂[i] fun z ↦ u z t) y) x
    Each first spatial partial is spatially differentiable at positive time. 
    residual_eq : ∀ (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t → HeatEquation.heatParabolicOperator u x t = f x t
    The pointwise forced heat-equation residual vanishes at positive time. 
    initial_value : ∀ (x : ℝ^n), u x 0 = g x
    The explicitly assigned value at time zero is the initial datum. 
    continuousAt_initialBoundary : ∀ (x₀ : ℝ^n) (ε : ℝ), 0 < ε → ∃ δ, 0 < δ ∧ ∀ (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ), ‖x - x₀‖ < δ → 0 < t → t < δ → |u x t - g x₀| < ε
    The spacetime solution extends continuously to each point `(x₀, 0)` of the initial
boundary, with boundary value `g x₀`.

    **Kaplan's lifespan bound.** Let `w ≥ 0` be a Dirichlet eigenfunction of `-Δ` on `Ω` with
eigenvalue `λ > 0`, normalized by `∫ w = 1`, and let `g ≥ 0` have `η₀ = ∫ w g > λ`. A solution of
`uₜ - Δu = u²` on `[0, T]` that is `C²` in the open cylinder, continuous on its closure, zero on
the lateral boundary and equal to `g` at time zero has `T ≤ λ⁻¹ log (η₀ / (η₀ - λ))`. This is the
time at which the solution of `η' = η² - λ η` from `η₀` blows up.

  {n : ℕ} (g : ℝ^n → ℝ) {M : ℝ}

    The heat-kernel evolution preserves uniform bounds.

If the continuous initial datum satisfies `|g| ≤ M`, then its heat evolution
satisfies the same pointwise bound at every time; taking the optimal `M`, this
is the `L∞` contraction property of the heat semigroup. For `t ≤ 0` this is the bound
on `g` itself. For `t > 0`, positivity of the Gaussian
kernel, its unit mass, and the Bochner integral triangle inequality give

`|Γ_t * g| ≤ Γ_t * |g| ≤ M Γ_t * 1 = M`.

Evans obtains the same bound for solutions with the growth bound (24) from his §2.3.3(a),
Theorem 6 (Maximum principle for the Cauchy problem), applied to `u` and `-u`. Continuity of
`g` is used only for measurability.

parabolic boundary, then `u ≤ v` throughout the closed cylinder. The proof
applies the weak maximum principle (Evans's §7.1.4, Theorem 8, with `L = -Δ`) to `u - v`.

the approximate-identity limit at the singular corner. `hsecond` and `hsecond_integrable` state
that both spatial derivatives pass through the source-time integral. Under exactly these
calculus hypotheses, every interior source slice solves the homogeneous heat equation by
`deriv_initialValueSolution_time_eq_laplacian`, so the Duhamel term satisfies
`u_t - Δu = f`.

    An order-`m` time jet whose successive derivatives take values in

`H^m(Omega), H^{m-1}(Omega), ..., H^0(Omega)`.

Each time derivative spends one spatial derivative in this regularity budget;
see Evans, §7.2.3, Theorem 6 for its use in the wave equation. The recursive core
requires adjacent entries to be weak time derivatives, so the entries
describe one trajectory and its derivatives.

representatives from an order-`m` Sobolev time jet.

Compatible problem data and the higher elliptic Dirichlet lift produce a
weak wave with the prescribed initial values and an essentially bounded
order-`m+1` Sobolev time jet representing its displacement and velocity.

The spatial operator is symmetric and coercive, and the stable Galerkin scheme,
Ritz orthogonality, and elliptic lift are explicit hypotheses.

    Evans, §7.2.3: the elliptic step in Theorem 5(ii).

Assume the divergence-form weak wave identity holds almost everywhere in
time and that both `f(t)` and `u_{tt}(t)` are essentially bounded in
`L²(Omega)`. On a domain carrying the operational `C2BoundaryAtlas`, assume
uniformly elliptic `W¹,∞` principal coefficients with global `C¹` representatives.
The wave trajectory then has a canonical `L∞_t H²_x` representative. Constructing
the atlas from an ordinary geometric `C²` boundary is not part of this theorem.

The pointwise estimate retained by the theorem is

`‖u(t)‖_{H²} ≤ ‖S₂‖ (C_f + C_tt)`,

where `S₂ : L²(Omega) → H²(Omega)` is the global elliptic solution operator.
This is the operator form of Evans's estimates (59)-(60). In particular,
the constant is independent of the Galerkin dimension and of time.

    Evans Section 7.2.3: differentiated Galerkin limit with bounded
nonsymmetric lower-order terms.

Let the autonomous wave operator split as `B = A + R`.  The principal part
`A` is symmetric and coercive on the energy space, while `R` is allowed to
be nonsymmetric and is controlled in the mixed `V x H` norm. Stable dense
trial projections, compatible ambient initial data, a coherent forcing chain,
and the uniform forcing budget generate a finite chain of ambient weak-wave
solutions for the full operator `A + R`, provided `hRitz` holds:

`(A + R) (q r.succ - P_k (q r.succ)) w = 0`

for every trial level `k`, adjacent jet index `r`, and test `w` in that trial
space. Here `P_k` is the restriction of the stable pivot projection to `V`.
This full-operator condition is separate from stability and density.

All finite-dimensional trajectories, their uniform bounds, and their common
weak limit are constructed in the proof.  In particular, no limiting weak
wave or higher-regularity conclusion is included among the hypotheses.

    Evans's weak solution of the abstract wave equation

`u_tt(t) + B(t)u(t) = ell(t)`

on `(a,b)`, with initial displacement `q₀ ∈ V` and initial velocity
`p₀ ∈ H`.

The first clause is the integrated equation `u_t = velocity`, viewed through
the pivot embedding `H ↪ V*`; it carries `u(a)=Jq₀`.  The second clause is
the integrated equation `velocity_t = acceleration`; it carries
`u_t(a)=p₀`.  The final clause is the spatial weak equation in `V*` almost
everywhere.

At level `n`, the acceleration is only the residual precomposed with the
trial projection:

`accelerationₙ = (ell - B(·)uₙ) ∘ Pₙ`.

This is the finite-dimensional statement: in general a Galerkin approximation
does not solve the ambient equation in all of `V*`.  Uniform energy stability
and `Pₙv → v` imply strong convergence of the lifted projections on `L²(V)`.
Pairing the weakly convergent residuals against those strongly convergent
tests identifies the acceleration limit with `ell - B(·)u`, and hence recovers
the full ambient equation only at the limit.

Canonical-representative uniqueness shows that the endpoint norm is

nonexistential form is the one used by the Grönwall and interval-restart
arguments.

    Evans, §7.2.3, Theorem 5(i): abstract Galerkin form.

Assume a bounded projected Galerkin family with the same exact initial
displacement `q₀` and velocity `p₀` at every index. Suppose in addition that
estimate (52) has supplied dimension-independent essential bounds

`‖uₘ(t)‖_V ≤ Cᵤ` and `‖uₘ'(t)‖_H ≤ Cᵥ`.

Then the compactness construction produces a weak solution satisfying

`u ∈ L∞(a,b;V)` and `u_t ∈ L∞(a,b;H)`,

with the same almost-everywhere bounds.  In concrete divergence-form wave
problems, `ae_norm_displacementLp_le_of_gelfandWaveEnergy_le` and
`ae_norm_velocityLp_le_of_gelfandWaveEnergy_le` supply these two additional
hypotheses from the coercive Galerkin energy estimate.

The proof uses the same common ultrafilter for displacement, velocity, and
acceleration.  The weak-wave equations are passed to the limit exactly as
in `exists_of_bounded_projected_galerkin_family`, while
`improvedRegularity_of_weak_L2_limits` preserves the closed convex
essential norm balls.  Thus the regularity conclusion is proved rather than
stored as extra data in the definition of a weak solution.

    Evans, §7.2.3, Theorem 5(ii): identification of the differentiated Galerkin limits.

Suppose one common filter gives weak limits for an original Galerkin family
and its differentiated family.  The exact finite-dimensional identities

`J (duₘ) = velocityₘ`,

`J* (dvelocityₘ) = accelerationₘ`

then survive weak convergence.  If the coefficient derivative identity
`d uₘ/dt = duₘ` is also retained in the identity Gelfand triple, the limit
`du` is the `V`-valued weak derivative of `u`.

Uniform essential bounds on `duₘ` in `V` and `dvelocityₘ` in `H` pass to the
same limits by weak closedness of the almost-everywhere norm balls.  Finally,
for an autonomous operator and weakly differentiable forcing, the theorem
constructs `u_{ttt}` in `L²(a,b;V*)`.

This is the compactness/identification step that cannot be justified by
extracting unrelated subnets for the original and differentiated systems.

data.

Unlike `of_projected_galerkin_weak_limits`, the finite-dimensional
displacement and velocity may start from trial-space projections depending
on the Galerkin index.  Strong convergence of those initial values identifies
the two endpoint terms in the limiting weak-wave equations.

    Weak sequential/net closure of Evans's weak-wave solution predicate.

Suppose a family of weak-wave solutions has a common weak limit in the three
natural Bochner spaces:

* displacement in `L²(a,b;V)`,
* velocity in `L²(a,b;H)`, and
* acceleration in `L²(a,b;V*)`.

The acceleration convergence is stated after Riesz transport, matching the
Hilbert weak topology used by the compactness theorem.  Then the three limit
objects again satisfy the weak-wave predicate with the same initial data and
forcing.

The proof follows the Evans limit passage:

1. bounded linearity of `H → V*` passes the displacement identity;
2. fixed space-time testing passes the velocity identity; and
3. bounded operator-valued multiplication passes `B(t)u` weakly, so
   uniqueness of weak limits yields `u_tt + B(t)u = ell` in `L²(V*)`.

pointwise equality without the regularity and neighborhood hypotheses that
such a step requires.

    structure NavierStokes.LerayHopfSolution {n : ℕ} (nse : NavierStokes.Problem n) :
  Type
    structure NavierStokes.LerayHopfSolution {n : ℕ}
  (nse : NavierStokes.Problem n) : Type
    Pressure-free Leray-Hopf solution on `[0,T]`.

The weak momentum equation and incompressibility come from `WeakSolution`. The additional fields
give velocity and gradient Bochner bounds, continuity into the weak topology of `L²`, the
initial trace as equality of `L²` classes, force-work integrability, and the all-time energy
inequality measured from the prescribed datum.

The initial datum is required only in `L²`. Spatial-gradient membership and its weak derivative
identity are imposed on `(0,T]`, while the velocity and its initial trace are defined on `[0,T]`.
These representative requirements at every positive time are stronger than an almost-everywhere
formulation.

  (nse : NavierStokes.Problem n) : Type
    Pressure-retaining weak solution to the Navier-Stokes equations on `[0,T]`.

This is a distributional solution notion in its own right, not a regularity
extension of `PointwiseResidualSolution`. The velocity carries a
distributional spatial-gradient witness. The momentum identity uses test fields
that may be nonzero at the initial time and therefore contains the prescribed
initial datum as a boundary term. This avoids identifying initial data through
an arbitrary value assigned to a representative at the measure-zero slice
`t = 0`.

This is a pressure-retaining, strong-data interface: pressure and forcing have `L²` spatial slices
at every time, while `weak_momentum_integrable_on` separately gives integrability of the summed
iterated integrand.

Pressure is retained, so the test field is a general compactly supported vector field. The
separate `distributionallyDivergenceFree_at` field records distributional
incompressibility.
With the sign convention
`u_t + div(u ⊗ u) + ∇p - ν Δu - f = 0`, integrating by parts against
terminal-time-vanishing test fields gives the displayed integrand:
`-u · φ_t - (u ⊗ u) : ∇φ - p div φ + ν Du : ∇φ - f · φ`.

The initial boundary term appears on the right-hand side. Consequently, the equation cannot be
satisfied by deleting nonzero initial data immediately after `t = 0`.

    abbrev NavierStokes.SmoothSolution {n : ℕ}
  (nse : NavierStokes.Problem n) : Type
    A positive-time classical solution on `(0,T) × ℝ^n` with a continuous initial trace.

This extends a `PointwiseResidualSolution` by the regularity missing from the
residual layer. The velocity and pressure are ambient-smooth at every
positive-time point. Relative continuity of velocity at `t = 0` makes the stored
initial value a one-sided trace rather than an arbitrary value assigned
on a measure-zero slice. Neither a pressure trace nor smoothness up to `t = 0` is
required.

    The integrability obligations behind the iterated weak momentum integral.

Lean's Bochner integral is totalized, so an identity between bare integral expressions would not by
itself assert that the displayed pairings are analytic integrals. This predicate records spatial
integrability at every physical time and outer time integrability. The initial boundary pairing is
integrable automatically from the stored `L²` initial datum and compact support of the test
field.

    structure NavierStokes.WeakSolution {n : ℕ}
  (nse : NavierStokes.Problem n) : Type
    Pressure-free weak Navier-Stokes solution on the closed slab `[0,T]`.

The momentum equation is imposed only against smooth compactly supported solenoidal tests, so
pressure does not occur. The raw fields
retain representatives because the weak-derivative and nonlinear-pairing definitions are
representative based. In particular, the per-time `L²` hypotheses are stronger than a formulation
stated solely as equivalence classes almost everywhere in time.

  (U V : SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.ZeroBoundaryVectorSpace n n Ω) :
  ((NavierStokes.similarityPrincipalForm hΩ hb b Q) U) V =
    ∑ k,
        (∑ i,
              inner ℝ
                ((SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.derivCoordCLM i) (U.ofLp k))
                ((SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.derivCoordCLM i) (V.ofLp k)) +
            ∑ i,
              inner ℝ
                ((↑(b i)).ofLp (SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.baseIndex n 1) •
                  (SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.derivCoordCLM i) (U.ofLp k))
                (SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.baseCoordCLM (V.ofLp k)) -

                inner ℝ

                            i)).ofLp
                      (SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.baseIndex n 1) •
                    (SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.derivCoordCLM i)
                      (U.ofLp k))
                  (SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.baseCoordCLM (V.ofLp k)) +
              inner ℝ (SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.baseCoordCLM (U.ofLp k))
                (SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.baseCoordCLM (V.ofLp k)))) +
      ∑ k,

                Q k j) •

    A regular local characteristic flow box for Evans's system (11),
repeated as (31) in the boundary-data construction.

The fields `xmap`, `pmap`, and `zmap` are defined on all of `ℝ^k × ℝ`,
as is customary for total Lean functions, while every analytic assertion
is restricted to the open box `W × (-ε,ε)`.

`contact_evolution` is not the desired gradient identity.  It is the
homogeneous linearized characteristic ODE

`d/ds (z_y - p · x_y) = -F_z (z_y - p · x_y)`,

for a characteristic family whose initial residual vanishes throughout the
boundary-parameter neighborhood.  The constructor
`ofContDiffOneCharacteristicFamily` proves it from compatible data,
residual preservation, and the boundary variation's ODE. The uniform
coefficient bound is the local boundedness needed by ODE uniqueness; the
main theorem obtains it automatically after shrinking the box.

the regular characteristic flow of (31), there are open neighborhoods
`W₀` of the boundary parameter and `V` of the boundary point together with
a `C²` function `u` such that

identity `Du = p ∘ coords` then gives a `C¹` derivative, hence the `C²` regularity in Evans's

constructs that flow from boundary and value data.

    Quantitative Hilbert-valued one-dimensional `H¹` estimate.

If `u, du ∈ L²(a,b;H)` and `du` is the weak time derivative of `u`, then
the Lions–Magenes representative is continuous on `[a,b]` and satisfies

`‖u(t)‖ ≤ sqrt (‖u‖² / (b-a) + 2 ‖u‖ ‖du‖)`

at every time in the closed interval.  It agrees almost everywhere with
the original Bochner trajectory, so the same explicit estimate holds
almost everywhere for that trajectory.

The constant is the standard non-sharp one-dimensional Sobolev estimate:
choose an interior time where the squared norm equals its interval average,
then apply the exact Hilbert-space energy identity and `L²` Hölder on the
subinterval joining that time to `t`.

Gårding lower bound

`theta ‖v‖_V² ≤ B(t)(v,v) + gamma ‖Jv‖_H²`.

The mass-shifted form is measurable and uniformly coercive.
`existsUnique_of_measurable_galerkin_L2` solves the exponentially rescaled problem, and the
weak exponential change of variables returns the solution of the original equation.
Uniqueness uses the Lions–Magenes energy identity and Grönwall's inequality.

continuous, bounded and uniformly coercive on `[a, b]`.

The Galerkin theorem is first applied to bounded continuous loads. Such loads are dense in
Bochner `L²`, so choose `ellₙ → ell`. The coercive continuous-dependence estimate

`‖uₙ-uₘ‖_{L²(V)} ≤ C⁻¹ ‖ellₙ-ellₘ‖_{L²(V*)}`

makes the corresponding solutions Cauchy. Completeness produces a strong
`L²(V)` limit, and `IsGelfandIntegratedWeakSolution.tendsto_L2` passes the
integrated equation to that limit.

its time derivative.

the original initial values are the Ritz projections of `g`. The
compatibility identity

    The full initial-value theorem for a measurable form satisfying a
Gårding inequality and an arbitrary forcing in `L²(a,b;V*)`.

`existsUnique_of_measurable_galerkin_garding_L2` constructs the unique Bochner class solving
the integrated weak equation. This theorem adds the data that Evans uses to define the
parabolic weak solution and its a priori theory:

* the weak time derivative belongs to `L²(a,b;V*)`;
* `u_t = ell - B(·)u` almost everywhere;
* the state has a representative continuous from `[a,b]` into the pivot
  Hilbert space `H`, with left trace equal to `uInit`;
* the representative satisfies the Gårding energy estimate on every prefix
  `[a,t]`.

Thus the measurable Galerkin construction produces a weak solution in the sense of
Evans §7.1.1, with the continuity into `H` that Evans obtains from §5.9.2, Theorem 3.

    Time regularity for an arbitrary Bochner `L²(H)` forcing.

For bounded continuous pivot loads the measurable Carathéodory solver
constructs the Galerkin family internally. The improved Galerkin estimate
uses only the load's `L²` norm, so density and coercive completion pass both
the solution and its `L²(H)` time derivative to an arbitrary Bochner load.
The functions `A`, `Adot`, and `R` are fixed across these forcing approximations,
and `A` remains time-dependent in the limiting equation.
The derivative bound `N` of the principal form contributes `N/2` beside the
remainder's coefficient `L²` in the energy budget. Principal coercivity gives
the `L∞(V)` bound; coercivity of the full form supplies the basic `L²(V)`
estimate and continuous dependence on the load.

For two solutions with the same initial datum, uniform coercivity gives the
dimension-free estimate

`‖u₁ - u₂‖_{L²(a,b;V)} ≤ C⁻¹ ‖ell₁ - ell₂‖_{L²(a,b;V*)}`.

This is the completion estimate used to extend the Galerkin construction
from continuous loads to arbitrary `L²(a,b;V*)` loads.  In particular, no
pointwise representative or uniform bound on either forcing appears in the
statement.

`theta ‖v‖_V² ≤ B(t)(v,v) + gamma ‖v‖_H²`

is the abstract form of the estimate (22) that Evans uses for parabolic operators
with lower-order terms (§7.1.2). For the difference `w` of two solutions, the

`PDE.Analysis.Evolution` then forces `e = 0`. This avoids the stronger,
generally false requirement that the unshifted form itself be nonnegative.

converge to zero and are dominated by `(C + 1)² ‖u(t)‖²`.

    An order-indexed multivariate formal jet with coefficients in `R`.

The implementation is reducible to Mathlib's `MvPowerSeries`, so all algebraic laws and
coefficient convolution theorems are inherited rather than reproved. The order index is erased:

    A mixed density with positive `p`-coercivity and no upper growth bound attains a
finite extended-energy minimum in every prescribed affine `W¹ᵖ` class containing one
finite-energy competitor. Here `1 < p < ∞`, the domain is bounded and measurable, and
its dimension is positive. On open domains this is the usual affine `W¹ᵖ₀` boundary class;
on measurable sets the condition means the supported smooth-core closure.

Convexity and differentiability concern only the gradient. The density and gradient
supporting field are measurable and continuous in the value variable almost everywhere.
The displayed functional adds the spatial lower bound `b`; if `b` is integrable, this is

special case on these bounded domains.

are the value and gradient derivatives of the density. Their joint continuity
in the two state variables supplies the full derivative, and conjugate power growth
makes its action on every zero-boundary Sobolev variation integrable.

Each a.e. hypothesis holds simultaneously for every state. The endpoint `p = 1, q = ∞`

    structure PDE.Hyperbolic.ConservationLaw.Scalar.IsWeakSolution
  (flux : ℝ → ℝ)
  (U : TopologicalSpace.Opens ℝ^2)
  (u : ℝ^2 → ℝ) : Prop
    Weak solution in the standard test-function formulation.

The domain is open, both `u` and `flux ∘ u` are locally integrable there, and the distributional
identity

`∫ (u φ_t + flux(u) φ_x) = 0`

holds for every compactly supported `C¹` test function. The displayed integrand is integrable
because both coefficients are locally integrable and the derivatives of the test function are
continuous and compactly supported in the domain.

This is the interior distributional equation on `U`. It is not the weak
half-space initial-value formulation: no initial datum or boundary term at
`t = 0` is part of this structure.

    Local integrability of the conserved quantity. 
    flux_locallyIntegrable : MeasureTheory.LocallyIntegrableOn (fun x ↦ flux (u x)) (↑U) MeasureTheory.volume
    Local integrability of the flux.

    A wave transformation for every characteristic family, with the strict
derivative required at zero strength for states in a specified local domain.

At zero strength the transformation fixes the base state. Its derivative
adds the strength variation in the right-eigenvector direction and passes
state variations through unchanged. The carrier functions are globally
defined for convenience; the local inverse theorem uses only their germs at
zero strength. Physical admissibility is recorded separately by
`LocalWaveFamily.IsElementary`. The identity carrier may be totalized outside
the state domain without asserting any regularity there.

entropy-admissible p-system solution with a strong local `L¹` initial trace.

is supplied. The witness is the explicit elementary two-wave solution. Local

on all positive times. The conclusion is the mechanical-entropy inequality.

    structure PDE.LinearPDE.{u𝕜, uE, uF} (𝕜 : Type u𝕜)
  [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]
  (E : Type uE) [NormedAddCommGroup E]
  [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] (F : Type uF)
  [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F]
  (k : ℕ) : Type (max uE uF)
    A linear PDE `L u = f` of order at most `k`.

The operator laws are asserted only for `C^k` functions. The last law says the operator is local
in the order-`k` jet, so it cannot depend on higher derivatives or on global data.

    Fields

    operator : (E → F) → E → F
    The differential operator `L`, defined on every field. Its laws are the fields below. 
    map_zero : ∀ (x : E), self.operator 0 x = 0
    `L 0 = 0`. 
    map_add : ∀ (u v : E → F),
  ContDiff 𝕜 (↑k) u → ContDiff 𝕜 (↑k) v → ∀ (x : E), self.operator (u + v) x = self.operator u x + self.operator v x
    Additivity on fields with the regularity required by an order-`k` equation. 
    map_smul : ∀ (c : 𝕜) (u : E → F), ContDiff 𝕜 (↑k) u → ∀ (x : E), self.operator (c • u) x = c • self.operator u x
    Homogeneity on fields with the regularity required by an order-`k` equation. 
    congr_jet : ∀ (u v : E → F) (x : E),
  ContDiffAt 𝕜 (↑k) u x → ContDiffAt 𝕜 (↑k) v x → PDE.SameJetUpTo 𝕜 k u v x → self.operator u x = self.operator v x
    On `C^k` fields the operator depends only on derivatives through order `k`. 
    rhs : E → F
    Right-hand side `f`. 
    domain : Set E
    Domain where `L u = f` is imposed.

the forcing and pivot-valued time derivative lie in `L²_t L²_x`, so the
elliptic residual `f - u_t` is a Bochner `L²` family. Applying the bounded
global elliptic solution operator pointwise gives an element of `L²_t H²_x`.

order-zero `H¹` slice with the original parabolic trajectory almost
everywhere.

`‖u‖_{L²_t H²_x} ≤ C ‖f - u_t‖_{L²_t L²_x}`,

with `C` the norm of `globalH2SolveCLM`; Evans's pointwise estimate (49) also
carries `‖u‖_{L²(U)}`.

norm and the forcing trace bound. Restricting the spatial lift to `H¹`
agrees almost everywhere with the energy-space solution.

corresponding residual problem, it must depend continuously on the data, and all admissible
solutions must be unique in `Sol`. Equality in `Sol` should therefore encode the intended

    A nonnegative pointwise classical solution of the parabolic–elliptic Keller–Segel system on
an open time domain.

Joint spacetime `C¹` regularity of the density supplies its time derivative. The elliptic
potential needs only joint continuity in spacetime and `C²` spatial slices, since no time
derivative of the potential appears in the equations. None of this gives joint `C^{2,1}`
regularity.

endpoint of its interval by the virial horizon.

`ℝ^n`; only time is restricted. The regularity fields say
that the spacetime function is jointly `C¹` and that every admitted spatial slice is globally

not claim joint `C^{2,1}` regularity.

instead: a closed cylinder `[0, T] × ℝⁿ` with initial data and continuity up to `t = 0`.

    structure SobolevSpace.Approximation.Mollifier
  (n : ℕ) : Type
    A mollifier on `ℝ^n`: a smooth, compactly supported, nonnegative kernel of integral `1`
(Evans §5.3 uses one such kernel, the standard mollifier).

    Fields

    ρ : ℝ^n → ℝ
    The smooth nonnegative kernel, normalized below to have integral one. 
    smooth : ContDiff ℝ (↑⊤) self.ρ
    The kernel is smooth to every finite order. 
    compactSupport : HasCompactSupport self.ρ
    The kernel vanishes outside a compact subset of `ℝ^n`. 
    nonneg : ∀ (x : ℝ^n), 0 ≤ self.ρ x
    The kernel is pointwise nonnegative. 
    integral_one : ∫ (x : ℝ^n), self.ρ x = 1
    The kernel has total mass one with respect to Lebesgue measure.

    class SobolevSpace.Boundary.C1ExtensionAtlas
  (n : ℕ) [Fact (0 < n)] (Ω : Set ℝ^n) :
  Type
    Operational atlas for the extension construction on a bounded `C¹` domain.

It includes the specific charts and cutoffs needed to build an extension operator
by reducing to the half-space construction and summing via a partition of unity.

This structure is stronger than the geometric predicate that `Ω` has `C¹`
boundary; `Boundary.Atlas.Geometric.GraphConstruction` constructs it from local graph
charts.

    Methods

    isOpen : IsOpen Ω
    `Ω` is open. 
    bounded : Bornology.IsBounded Ω

    N : ℕ
    Number of boundary charts (finite). 
    chart : Fin (SobolevSpace.Boundary.C1ExtensionAtlas.N Ω) → OpenPartialHomeomorph (ℝ^n) ℝ^n
    Boundary charts (partial homeomorphisms) that flatten `Ω` to the half-space. 
    chart_contDiff : ∀ (i : Fin (SobolevSpace.Boundary.C1ExtensionAtlas.N Ω)),
  ContDiff ℝ 1 fun x ↦ ↑(SobolevSpace.Boundary.C1ExtensionAtlas.chart i) x
    `C¹` regularity of the (total) chart maps.

We work with charts as total functions `ℝ^n → ℝ^n` which are `C¹` globally, and only later
restrict them to an open source where they are invertible.

The weak chain rule below uses globally defined maps. Obtaining such representatives from the
standard local definition of a bounded `C¹` boundary requires shrinking the chart
neighborhoods.

    def SobolevSpace.Boundary.HasC1GraphBoundary {n : ℕ} (Ω : Set ℝ^n) : Prop
    def SobolevSpace.Boundary.HasC1GraphBoundary
  {n : ℕ} (Ω : Set ℝ^n) : Prop
    A set has C1 graph boundary if, near each boundary point, linear coordinates identify

    Localize a bounded extension of any finite Sobolev order to an arbitrary open
neighborhood of `closure Ω`.

This gives condition (ii) of Evans §5.4, Theorem 1, "`Eu` has support within `V`", which Evans
arranges in step 6 of the proof. We choose a smooth cutoff with support in `V` and equal to one
on `closure Ω`, multiply the original extension by it, and retain both a.e. agreement on `Ω` and
bounded linearity. The domain need only be measurable; the cutoff acts on the whole-space
extension. This includes order zero and `p = ∞`.

On a domain equipped with the operational `C2BoundaryAtlas`, a homogeneous
Dirichlet weak solution of

`-∂ᵢ(aᵢⱼ ∂ⱼu) + bᵢ ∂ᵢu + c u + λu = f`

has an `H²(Ω)` representative when the principal coefficients are
`W^{1,∞}` with global ambient `C¹` representatives, the lower-order
coefficients are `L∞`, and `f ∈ L²(Ω)`. The lower-order terms are absorbed
into the `L²` effective forcing using the given `H¹₀` solution.

Setting `λ = 0` gives the full operator of Evans's Theorem 4.
`Boundary.HasContDiffGraphBoundary.exists_c2BoundaryAtlas` derives the operational
atlas from a `C²` graph boundary.

    **Rellich compactness** for `H¹(Ω) → L²(Ω)` under the operational
`Boundary.C1ExtensionAtlas` hypothesis.
The order-zero inclusion

`H¹(Ω) → L²(Ω)`

is compact when `Ω` carries the operational chart-and-cutoff data used by the
extension theorem.  Deriving this hypothesis from the standard assertion that
`Ω` has `C¹` boundary is a separate geometric step.

The proof factors the inclusion in four steps.  `Extension.C1.extensionCLM`
sends `H¹(Ω)` boundedly into `H¹(ℝ^n)` and agrees with the original base
function almost everywhere on `Ω`.  Multiplying by a smooth compactly supported
cutoff equal to one on `closure Ω` and restricting to a ball `B` containing its
support lands continuously in `H¹₀(B)`.  The bounded-domain Rellich theorem for
`H¹₀(B)` makes zero extension followed by the base-coordinate map compact, and
precomposition keeps it compact.  Finally restriction `L²(ℝ^n) → L²(Ω)` is
bounded, and since the cutoff is one on `Ω` the composite is the order-zero
inclusion.

Assume `W^{1,p}(Ω) → L^s(Ω)` is compact for one exponent
`1 ≤ s ≤ p*`.  Then the inclusion into `L^q(Ω)` is compact for every
`1 ≤ q < p*`.

The proof is the standard Rellich-Kondrachov upgrade.  A bounded Sobolev
sequence has an `L^s`-convergent subsequence by the compactness hypothesis.
Sobolev embedding bounds that subsequence in `L^{p*}`.  Since `q < p*`,
the preceding uniform-integrability estimate and Vitali's theorem improve
convergence in measure to convergence in `L^q`.

  (Ω : Set ℝ^n) (α : List (Fin n))
  (f g : ℝ^n → ℝ) : Prop
    A weak-derivative relation on a set `Ω`, tested against globally smooth functions whose
closed support lies in `Ω`.

We use Mathlib's test-function type `𝓓((⊤ : Opens (ℝ^n)), ℝ)` and require its `tsupport`
(closed support) to lie in `Ω`. When `Ω` is open, this is the test class `C_c^∞(Ω)` of Evans §5.2.1.

Both `f` and its proposed weak derivative `g` are required to lie in `L¹_loc(Ω)`, and the sign is
`(-1)^|α|`, exactly as in Evans §5.2.1, (3).
For an arbitrary set the predicate is still a well-formed test-function relation, but it is not
automatically the standard Sobolev weak derivative: the test class can be too small (and can be
trivial when `Ω` has empty interior), so uniqueness may fail.  Results identifying this relation
with the usual weak derivative therefore require openness or another explicit test-function
density hypothesis.

    The base function belongs to `L¹_loc(Ω)`. 
    locallyIntegrable_g : MeasureTheory.LocallyIntegrableOn g Ω MeasureTheory.volume
    The proposed weak derivative belongs to `L¹_loc(Ω)`.

    structure SobolevSpace.SobolevSpaceOn (n k : ℕ) (p : ENNReal) (Ω : Set ℝ^n) : Type
    structure SobolevSpace.SobolevSpaceOn (n k : ℕ)
  (p : ENNReal) (Ω : Set ℝ^n) : Type
    A representative-level package of `Lᵖ` functions and weak-derivative witnesses on `Ω`.

This stores a concrete representative `toFun` and existential weak-derivative data. It does not
identify functions modulo almost-everywhere equality; use `SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.WkpSpaceOn`
for the `Lp`-quotient normed-space packaging.

For `1 ≤ p ≤ ∞` and open `Ω`, this is the representative-level condition defining
`W^{k,p}(Ω)` in Evans §5.2.2. The order-zero witness is then redundant, but retaining it makes local
integrability explicit when this structure is used at other exponents and prevents nonintegrable
functions from entering through the totalized Bochner integral. On a nonopen set the structure
uses the generalized test-function relation documented by `HasWeakDerivativeOn`, so the usual
uniqueness theorem need not apply.

    Fields

    toFun : ℝ^n → ℝ

    `u ∈ L^p(Ω)` 
    weak_derivs_inLp : ∀ (α : List (Fin n)), α.length ≤ k → SobolevSpace.HasWeakDerivativeInLpOn Ω α p self.toFun

    def SobolevSpace.Weighted.HasLocallyComparableExhaustion {n k : ℕ}
  (w : SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.DerivIndex n k → ℝ^n → ENNReal) : Prop
    def SobolevSpace.Weighted.HasLocallyComparableExhaustion
  {n k : ℕ}
  (w :
    SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.DerivIndex n
        k →
      ℝ^n → ENNReal) :
  Prop
    For every realizable weighted graph `U` and accuracy `ε` there are: a graph `V` within `ε/3`
of `U` in the `w`-norm, a bounded reference weight `v` with a dominated weight `q`, and a
sequence of test functions converging to `V` in the `v`-norm whose `w`-distance to `V` is
eventually at most the `q`-distance plus `ε/3` (`EventuallyDistLeWeightedDistAdd`).

All witnesses, including the comparison constants `B` and `C`, are chosen per `U` and `ε`. Since
`q = v = 0` and `V = U` are admissible, the predicate is equivalent to approximation of every
realizable weighted graph by eligible test functions in the `w`-norm, arranged in the shape
of the localize-compare-mollify argument.

    def SobolevSpace.Weighted.aggregateYoungInterpolationConstant
  (j k η : ℝ) : ℝ
    Additive interpolation constant for the unweighted aggregate of all
two-dimensional order-`j` multiindex derivatives.  The extra power of two is
the explicit conversion from the homogeneous `|D|^m` norm to that aggregate,
raised to the exponent `1/(1-θ)` with `θ = j/k` that the Young step produces.
It is positive for `0 < j < k` and `0 < η` (`aggregateYoungInterpolationConstant_pos`), and
`aggregateYoungInterpolationConstant_eq` gives its explicit product formula. The aggregate
Fourier-norm inequality is `SobolevSpace.wholePlane_aggregateYoungInterpolation`
in `PDE.Spaces.Sobolev.Inequalities.PlanarInterpolation`.

uses radial integration by parts with its order-`n` predecessor. The
successor identities identify both derivatives without commuting
mixed partials. Local C² regularity is required only along these predecessor
slices in `r > 0`, and the middle weight is differentiable there.

measurabilities. The cross-term integrabilities and the two endpoint limits
of each boundary product remain explicit. Neither compact support, a zero
value trace on the axis, nor any row inequality is assumed.

Weight comparisons hold almost everywhere for the open-half-plane product
measure. Zero extension supplies globally nonnegative weights to the Cauchy
estimate without imposing conditions at the singular origin. The conclusion
is one adjacent-order interpolation step.

`|u(y) - u(x)| ≤ ‖u'‖_{Lᵖ(ℝ)} |y - x|^(1 - 1/p)`.

assumption on the global `Lᵖ` seminorm.  When that seminorm is finite, the estimate gives the
usual `(1 - 1/p)`-Hölder bound.

vector-valued unknowns, and systems.  It is expressed as the Fréchet derivative
in the spacetime direction `(1, b)`; `transportOperator_eq` gives the familiar
coordinate formula.  Like `fderiv`, this is a total expression and represents a
classical derivative only under the regularity hypotheses of the surrounding

Schauder's theorem for real or complex Hilbert spaces states

K:H_1\to H_2\ \text{compact} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad K^*:H_2\to H_1\ \text{compact}.

Here K^* is Mathlib's Hilbert adjoint of the bounded linear map K.

If the eigenvalues converged to a nonzero limit, compactness of K would give a convergent subsequence after reciprocal rescaling, contradicting the separation estimate.

Let K be compact on a real Hilbert space. If (\lambda_j) is an injective sequence of nonzero real eigenvalues and \lambda_j\to\lambda, then

\lambda=0.

This is the sequential accumulation statement in Evans's compact-spectrum theorem.
Write the nonzero spectrum as the countable union of the finite sets on which the absolute value is at least 1/(k+1).

For a compact operator K, the nonzero real point spectrum

\sigma_{\mathrm p}(K)\setminus\{0\} =\left\{\lambda\ne0:\exists v\ne0,\ Kv=\lambda v\right\}

is countable.

Every eigenvalue lies in the closed interval determined by the operator norm. An infinite set bounded away from zero would therefore have a convergent injective subsequence whose limit is nonzero, contradicting the preceding accumulation theorem.

For every \varepsilon>0, a compact operator K has only finitely many real eigenvalues away from zero:

\left\{\lambda\in\mathbb R: |\lambda|\geq\varepsilon,\ \exists v\ne0,\ Kv=\lambda v\right\} \quad\text{is finite}.

Let B:V\times V\to\mathbb R be a continuous weak form that becomes coercive after adding a compact mass term, and let F\in V^*. Then

\bigl[\exists u\in V,\ \forall v\in V,\ B(u,v)=F(v)\bigr] \iff \bigl[\forall w\in V,\ (\forall v\in V,\ B(v,w)=0)\Rightarrow F(w)=0\bigr].

Thus solvability is exactly orthogonality of the load to every homogeneous solution of the adjoint weak problem.

The zero-index theorem gives \dim\ker T=\dim\ker T^*. If the kernel is trivial, bijectivity of the continuous Fredholm map follows from surjectivity (range is closed plus trivial cokernel). If the kernel is nontrivial, uniqueness fails. The two cases are mutually exclusive because a nontrivial kernel element is a nonzero homogeneous solution.

\exists u\ne0,\ \forall v,\ B(u,v)=0,

or

\forall F\in V^*,\ \exists!\,u\in V,\ \forall v,\ B(u,v)=F(v).

The two branches are mutually exclusive.

Thus x\in N and A_0x=0, so injectivity of A_0 gives x=0.

The operator K+A is compact, so the compact Fredholm alternative makes T=I-(K+A)=S-A surjective. Choose y\in M outside the range of A_0 and solve Tx=y. Then Sx=Ax+y lies in both \operatorname{range}S and M, hence is zero. It follows that x\in N and y=-Ax=A_0(-x), contradicting the choice of y. Therefore \dim M\leq\dim N. Applying the same argument to K^* gives the reverse inequality.

For a compact operator K:H\to H on a real Hilbert space H,

\dim\ker(K-I)=\dim\ker(K^*-I).

Both kernels are finite-dimensional eigenspaces at the nonzero eigenvalue 1. The equality is the index-zero assertion for a compact perturbation of the identity.

Compose the weak operator on the left with the shifted inverse to obtain I-K, with K compact. This preserves the primal kernel. After Riesz identification, the Hilbert-space representative of B factors as T=Q(I-K) with Q invertible. Then T^*=(I-K)^*Q^*, so the invertible map Q^* identifies \ker T^* with \ker((I-K)^*). If B_\gamma is coercive and M is compact, then the primal and adjoint homogeneous spaces

The Lean theorem is stated for Mathlib's weak-space topology and proves topological compactness.

Weak convergence in a real normed space gives convergence against each continuous functional:

Finally, intersecting with a weakly closed bounded set preserves closedness and boundedness, so Hilbert weak compactness applies.
