It contains the first-variation condition and gives the minimization argument directly.
Apply the energy identity at the named weak solution. The remaining Dirichlet quadratic form is a sum of squared L^2 derivative norms and is therefore nonnegative.

On a bounded domain of positive dimension, let f\in L^2(\Omega) and set

J(v)=\frac12B_\Omega(v,v)-\ell_f(v).

The named Lax–Milgram solution u=Sf satisfies J(u)\le J(v) for every v\in H^1_0(\Omega).

For any set \Omega and f\in L^2(\Omega), the concrete Dirichlet functional on H^1_0(\Omega) is

J(v)=\frac12 B(v,v)-\ell_f(v).

This is the quadratic Poisson specialization of Evans's generalized Dirichlet principle.

On any set \Omega, the Dirichlet form on H^1_0(\Omega) is

B_\Omega(u,v)=\sum_{i=1}^n \int_\Omega D_i u(x)\,D_i v(x)\,dx.

The derivatives are the canonical weak coordinate derivatives in the graph-space model of H^1_0(\Omega).

The solver is defined by applying the inverse Lax–Milgram equivalence to the L^2 load v\mapsto\int_\Omega fv. The defining inverse identity says precisely that its value satisfies the displayed weak equation for every test vector.

If n\ge1 and \Omega is bounded, then for every f\in L^2(\Omega) the named Dirichlet solver S f satisfies

B_\Omega(Sf,v)=\int_\Omega f(x)v(x)\,dx \qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1_0(\Omega).

For positive dimension and a bounded domain, Lax–Milgram gives a continuous linear solution operator

S:L^2(\Omega)\longrightarrow H^1_0(\Omega).

The named pointwise solver is evaluation of this operator at the forcing datum.

The completion of the square identity reduces equality of energies to vanishing Dirichlet energy of the difference. Poincaré coercivity forces that difference to be zero, and the weak equation identifies the minimizer in both directions.

On a bounded domain of positive dimension, coercivity gives

J(v)-J(u)=\frac12B(v-u,v-u)\ge0,

with equality exactly when v=u. Thus the named weak solution is the unique minimizer of the Dirichlet functional. More generally, minimizing J is equivalent to the weak Euler–Lagrange equation B(u,w)=\ell(w) for every test direction w.

For a measurable L^\infty matrix field a, Evans's pointwise condition requires a single \alpha>0 such that, for almost every x and every \xi\in\mathbb R^n, one has

\alpha |\xi|^2\le \sum_{i,j}a_{ij}(x)\xi_j\xi_i.

The matrix need not be symmetric: only its symmetric part contributes to this quadratic inequality, and the coercivity result below applies to nonsymmetric coefficients satisfying the same condition.
Apply the pointwise matrix inequality to the measurable vector of weak derivatives and integrate. Hölder integrability of each coefficient-gradient product justifies the finite sums and integrals.
Almost-everywhere pointwise ellipticity of an L^\infty matrix field implies integrated ellipticity of its multiplication-operator realization.

The signed-trace comparison argument constructs a weak zero-boundary solution between the barriers. Its bounded range controls the derivatives of the reaction needed at each stage of Sobolev composition. Global elliptic regularity then bootstraps the solution through every finite Sobolev order. Morrey regularity supplies one smooth representative on the closure. The trace-kernel identity makes that representative zero at every boundary point. Finally, the weak equation gives the full divergence-form identity almost everywhere; continuity promotes it to a pointwise equation in the interior.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n>0, be bounded and open with smooth boundary. Suppose the coefficients a^{ij},b^i,c are smooth up to the boundary and a is uniformly elliptic. Let f be smooth on an open neighborhood of [\ell,r]. Assume ordered weak barriers \underline u,\overline u\in H^1(\Omega) satisfy

\ell\leq\underline u\leq\overline u\leq r \quad\text{almost everywhere},\qquad \operatorname{Tr}\underline u\leq0\leq\operatorname{Tr}\overline u \quad\text{surface-almost everywhere},

and the subsolution and supersolution inequalities for every nonnegative H^1_0 test function, using the full divergence-form operator below. Then there are u\in H^1_0(\Omega) and a representative z=u almost everywhere, smooth on \overline\Omega, such that

-\sum_{i,j}\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_jz) +\sum_i b^i\partial_i z+cz=f(z)\quad\text{in }\Omega, \qquad z=0\quad\text{on }\partial\Omega.

The representative lies in [\ell,r] at every interior point and between the two Sobolev barriers almost everywhere. The principal matrix need not be symmetric, and the potential need not have a fixed sign.

We choose the explicit mass shift

\mu_0=\frac{n\beta^2}{2\alpha}+\gamma+\frac\alpha2.

This choice records exactly which estimates were used and leaves coercivity constant \alpha/2.

Integrated ellipticity bounds the operator-valued principal form below by \alpha times the Dirichlet form. The bounded-domain Poincaré estimate makes the Dirichlet form coercive for the full graph-space norm, and multiplication of the two positive constants gives the result.

Let A=(A_{ij}) be a matrix of bounded operators on L^2(\Omega). On a bounded measurable domain in positive dimension, suppose A is integrated-uniformly elliptic: for some \alpha>0,

\alpha B_\Omega(u,u)\le B_A(u,u) \qquad\text{for every }u\in H^1_0(\Omega).

Then the variable-coefficient form satisfies B_A(u,u)\ge c\lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0}^2 for some c>0. For a pointwise L^\infty coefficient matrix, the preceding almost-everywhere-to-integrated theorem supplies this hypothesis from Evans's pointwise ellipticity condition.

Represent the coefficient field by its bounded multiplication operators, deduce coercivity from almost-everywhere ellipticity, apply Lax–Milgram, and translate the Hilbert-space equation back to the concrete weak integral identity.

Let \Omega be open, measurable, and bounded with n\ge1. If a\in L^\infty is uniformly elliptic almost everywhere, then every f\in L^2(\Omega) admits exactly one u\in H^1_0(\Omega) satisfying

-D_i(a^{ij}D_j u)=f\quad\text{weakly on }\Omega.

The principal divergence-form bilinear form contracts the weak gradients of the trial and test functions against a matrix of bounded operators on L^2(\Omega). Pointwise multiplication operators give an L^\infty coefficient matrix; arbitrary bounded operators give nonlocal coefficients.

The full bounded divergence-form bilinear form adds the first-order terms \sum_i (b_iD_i u,v)_{L^2} and the zeroth-order term (cu,v)_{L^2} to the principal form. At the operator-valued level the coefficients are bounded maps on L^2; multiplication operators give the local L^\infty coefficient fields.
Bound each first-order pairing by Cauchy–Schwarz and Young's inequality, sum over coordinates, bound the zeroth-order pairing by its operator norm, and combine the result with principal ellipticity.

If the principal form has ellipticity constant \alpha>0, the constants \beta,\gamma are nonnegative, each first-order operator has norm at most \beta, and the zeroth-order operator has norm at most \gamma, then

\frac{\alpha}{2}B_0(u,u) \le B(u,u)+\left(\frac{n\beta^2}{2\alpha}+\gamma\right) \lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2.

Here B_0(u,u)=\sum_i\lVert D_i u\rVert_2^2 is the Dirichlet form. This is Gårding's estimate (Evans, 2010, pp. 318–319) for operator-valued coefficients.

Extend the functional isometrically to the ambient base-gradient product, take its Riesz representative, and read the base and first-derivative coordinates as f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_n. The product-space norm decomposition gives the squared-norm identity.

Every continuous functional on our H^1_0(\Omega) graph space has a representation f_0-\sum_iD_i f_i with all components in L^2(\Omega). The chosen components additionally satisfy an exact squared-norm identity with the dual norm. The components are coordinates of a Riesz representative and need not be derivatives of one another.

Data f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_n\in L^2(\Omega) define the continuous functional

v\longmapsto (f_0,v)_{L^2}+\sum_i(f_i,D_i v)_{L^2},

which represents the distribution f_0-\sum_iD_i f_i in H^{-1}(\Omega).

An operator-valued coefficient matrix is integrated-uniformly elliptic with constant \alpha>0 when its principal quadratic form dominates \alpha times the Dirichlet form on every H^1_0 field. This is exactly the energy inequality needed by the abstract coercivity argument.
Add the mass shift to Gårding's inequality, decompose the graph-space norm into its L^2 and gradient components, and use monotonicity in \mu.
Every \mu\ge\mu_0 makes the shifted full form coercive on the graph-space H^1_0(\Omega), with coercivity constant \alpha/2.

The Gårding estimate at the explicit threshold is strengthened by the nonnegative extra mass term when \mu is larger. Lax–Milgram then gives the unique Hilbert-space solution, and the smooth-test density bridge identifies it with the concrete shifted divergence-form weak equation.

Let \Omega be open and measurable. Suppose the principal L^\infty coefficient matrix has ellipticity constant \alpha>0, while \beta,\gamma\ge0, every coordinate satisfies \lVert b^i\rVert_{L^\infty}\le\beta, and \lVert c\rVert_{L^\infty}\le\gamma. For

\mu\ge\mu_0= \frac{n\beta^2}{2\alpha}+\gamma+\frac{\alpha}{2},

every standard H^{-1} load f_0-D_i f^i has a unique weak solution u\in H^1_0(\Omega).
Apply the weak equation for the named Lax–Milgram solver to v, then expand the generalized load. This gives the mass-shifted bilinear form on the left and (f_0,v)+\sum_i(f^i,D_i v) on the right.

For every v\in H^1_0(\Omega), the named solution satisfies the full shifted variational identity, with right-hand side (f_0,v)+\sum_i(f^i,D_i v). The identity explicitly expands the graph-space load but still permits bounded, possibly nonlocal coefficient operators. After specialization to multiplication operators on an open domain, the smooth-test bridge gives Evans's local distributional equation.

Test the solver equation with v=u. Coercivity at the canonical shift gives (\alpha/2)\lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0}^2 on the left, while Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the generalized load by (\lVert f_0\rVert_2+\sum_i\lVert f^i\rVert_2) \lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0}. Cancel the solution norm to obtain the displayed factor 2/\alpha.

Under integrated ellipticity with constant \alpha>0 and the stated nonnegative lower-order operator bounds, the canonical operator-valued solution obeys the explicit estimate

\lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0}\le \frac{2}{\alpha}\left(\lVert f_0\rVert_2+ \sum_i\lVert f^i\rVert_2\right).

The constant is explicit for the chosen graph-space norm.

Let A_{ij}, b_i, and c be bounded operators on L^2(\Omega). Given integrated ellipticity for A and the nonnegative lower-order bounds used above, the canonical coercive shift determines a named Lax–Milgram solution in H^1_0(\Omega) for every standard graph-space load f_0-D_i f^i. This definition is operator-valued and needs only measurability of \Omega; the pointwise multiplication specialization and openness enter in the distributional-PDE theorem.

For a measurable domain, L^\infty coefficients a, b, and c, a shift \mu, standard H^{-1} data (f_0,f^1,\ldots,f^n), and u\in H^1_0(\Omega), the predicate requires \Omega to be open and records

\int_\Omega a^{ij}D_j uD_i\varphi +\int_\Omega b^iD_i u\,\varphi +\int_\Omega(c+\mu)u\varphi =\int_\Omega f_0\varphi+\int_\Omega f^iD_i\varphi

for every \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega). This is the weak form of -D_i(a^{ij}D_j u)+b^iD_i u+cu+\mu u=f_0-D_i f^i.

For an open measurable domain, a^{ij}\in L^\infty(\Omega), f\in L^2(\Omega), and u\in H^1_0(\Omega), the weak-solution predicate stores the openness of \Omega and records

\sum_{i,j=1}^n\int_\Omega a^{ij}(x)D_j u(x)D_i\varphi(x)\,dx =\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx

for every \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega). This is the concrete distributional equation for -D_i(a^{ij}D_j u)=f. A separate density theorem identifies it with the operator-valued variational identity tested against every v\in H^1_0(\Omega).

Subtract the functions. Green's first identity and the zero face data force the Dirichlet energy to vanish. Continuity then makes every first derivative zero in the interior; convexity gives constancy, and the boundary value fixes that constant to zero.

Let Q=[a,b] have strictly positive side lengths. If u,v\in C^2 satisfy

\Delta u=\Delta v\quad\text{on }Q,\qquad u=v\quad\text{on }\partial Q,

then u=v throughout the closed box.

For \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n and f,g\colon\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R, the classical energy of w is the integral I[w] above. The admissible class \mathcal A_g consists of the functions w that are C^2 on \Omega with derivatives through order two uniformly continuous there, continuous on \overline\Omega, and equal to g on \partial\Omega. The finite-energy class \mathcal A_g^f\subseteq\mathcal A_g consists of those w for which \frac12|Dw|^2-fw is integrable on \Omega.

Suppose -\Delta u=f. The second derivatives of u are bounded on the bounded set \Omega, so f is square integrable there and every member of \mathcal A_g has finite energy. A competitor differs from u by a function v vanishing on \partial\Omega. On the C^1 graph domain such a v has zero trace and so lies in H^1_0(\Omega), which justifies the integration by parts in the expansion above; hence the competitor's energy is at least I[u].

Conversely, let u minimize over \mathcal A_g^f and let \varphi be smooth with compact support in \Omega. Interior continuity of f makes f\varphi integrable, so u+t\varphi stays in \mathcal A_g^f for every real t. The function t\mapsto I[u+t\varphi] is a quadratic polynomial with a minimum at t=0, and its derivative there is \int_\Omega(-\Delta u-f)\varphi\,dx. This vanishes for every \varphi, and the residual -\Delta u-f is continuous, so it is zero in \Omega.

Let n\ge1, let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be a bounded open set with C^1 graph boundary, let f be continuous on \Omega, and let u\in\mathcal A_g. Then

-\Delta u=f\ \text{in }\Omega \iff u\in\mathcal A_g^f\ \text{and}\ I[u]\le I[w]\ \text{for every } w\in\mathcal A_g^f.

If u\in\mathcal A_g^f minimizes I over \mathcal A_g^f, then \mathcal A_g^f=\mathcal A_g and u minimizes I over all of \mathcal A_g. When f is continuous on \overline\Omega, every member of \mathcal A_g has finite energy, and u solves -\Delta u=f exactly when I[u]\le I[w] for every w\in\mathcal A_g.

Apply the divergence theorem on the box to u grad v, expand div(u grad v), and rearrange the two integrals. Both summands are continuous on the compact box, so their Bochner integrability follows from the stated regularity.

For a coordinate box Q=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R^{m+1} with a\le b coordinatewise, globally C^1 u, and globally C^2 v,

\int_Q u\,\Delta v =-\int_Q\nabla u\cdot\nabla v +\int_{\partial Q}u\,\partial_\nu v\,dS.

The linked theorem expands the boundary term into the signed integrals over the upper and lower coordinate faces.
Apply Green's first identity to (u,v) and (v,u), then subtract. Equivalently, apply the box divergence theorem directly to u grad v - v grad u; the mixed gradient terms cancel pointwise.

For globally C^2 functions on a coordinate box Q=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R^{m+1} with a\le b coordinatewise,

\int_Q(u\Delta v-v\Delta u) =\int_{\partial Q} (u\,\partial_\nu v-v\,\partial_\nu u)\,dS.

As in the first identity, the formal statement represents the boundary flux as a finite signed sum over coordinate faces.

Invert the shifted coercive form by Lax–Milgram. The unshifted equation becomes identity minus a compact mass perturbation. The abstract Fredholm alternative gives the mutually exclusive kernel-or-surjectivity dichotomy, while bounded-domain Rellich compactness supplies the required compact mass operator.

Let \Omega be measurable and bounded, and let B be the full operator-valued divergence form on H_0^1(\Omega), assembled from bounded operators A_{ij}, b_i, and c on the derivative-coordinate L^2 space. Assume that for some \lambda\in\mathbb R,

B(u,u)+\lambda\lVert u\rVert_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 \geq c_0\lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0(\Omega)}^2

with c_0>0. Then exactly one branch holds: either

\exists u\ne0,\quad B(u,v)=0\quad\text{for every }v\in H_0^1(\Omega),

or every F\in H^{-1}(\Omega) admits a unique u\in H_0^1(\Omega) with B(u,v)=F(v) for all test fields v.

Openness of \Omega is not needed. Local L^\infty coefficients are the case in which A_{ij}, b_i, and c are multiplication operators.

The mass form is the square-integrable inner product restricted to the zero-trace Sobolev space. Its associated operator factors through the canonical inclusion into square-integrable functions, which is compact by the Rellich–Kondrachov theorem on bounded domains. A bounded sequence in the Sobolev graph norm therefore has a subsequence converging in the square-integrable norm, making the mass operator compact.
For a measurable bounded domain, the Sobolev mass operator on H^1_0(\Omega) is compact. This is the operator form of the bounded-domain Rellich embedding into L^2.

Write M(r) for the spherical mean of \varphi and B(r) for the integral of \Delta\varphi over B(0,r). The ball divergence theorem expresses B(r) through M'(r). The normalized kernel flux then makes the spherical integral of \Phi_n\Delta\varphi the derivative of rM'(r)/(n-2)+M(r). This primitive tends to \varphi(0) as r\to0 and vanishes beyond the support of \varphi. Coarea and the fundamental theorem of calculus give the displayed identity. Applying it to smooth test functions identifies the negative distributional Laplacian with \delta_0.

Let n\ge3. For every compactly supported C^2 test function \varphi\colon\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R,

\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi_n(x)\Delta\varphi(x)\,dx=-\varphi(0).

Consequently the regular distribution induced by the Newtonian kernel is a fundamental solution of the negative Laplacian:

-\Delta T_{\Phi_n}=\delta_0.

Split the integral into the two half-lines. On each half-line the absolute value becomes affine, and two compact-support integration-by-parts identities reduce the integral to the value of the test function at the origin. The two half-line contributions each supply one half of the required negative sign.

For every compactly supported C^2 test function \varphi on the real line, the scalar kernel \Phi(x)=-|x|/2 satisfies

\int_{\mathbb R}\Phi(x)\varphi''(x)\,dx=-\varphi(0).

It is the one-dimensional case of the normalization -\Delta\Phi=\delta_0. The test function is Mathlib's bundled finite-order test function. The result holds both for the scalar presentation and for the canonical \mathbb R^1 kernel pulled back along the standard embedding.

Differentiate \Phi_\varepsilon explicitly to obtain -\Delta\Phi_\varepsilon=K_\varepsilon. Polar integration gives \int K_\varepsilon=1, and scaling shows that K_\varepsilon is an approximate identity. Integration by parts moves the Laplacian from the test function onto the smooth regularization.

For 0<\varepsilon\leq1 and x\ne0, monotonicity of the logarithm places \Phi_\varepsilon(x) between \Phi_{\varepsilon=1}(x) and \Phi_2(x). Thus the absolute value of the left integrand is bounded by (|\Phi_{\varepsilon=1}|+|\Phi_2|)|\Delta\varphi|. This bound is integrable: the first kernel is smooth, the second is locally integrable, and \Delta\varphi is continuous with compact support. The excluded origin has measure zero. Dominated convergence therefore handles the logarithmic kernel, while approximate-identity convergence sends the right side to -\varphi(0).

For every compactly supported C^2 test function \varphi on \mathbb R^2, the logarithmic kernel satisfies

\int_{\mathbb R^2}\Phi_2(x)\,\Delta\varphi(x)\,dx =-\varphi(0).

Equivalently, -\Delta\Phi_2=\delta_0 in the distributional sense.

On a unit ray, the logarithmic branch in dimension two and the Newtonian power-law branch in dimensions at least three are differentiated separately. The resulting radial derivative is -1/(r^{n-1}|S^{n-1}|). The identity |S^{n-1}|=n\alpha_n and integration of this constant over the unit sphere give the asserted flux.

In every dimension n\geq2, the total outward radial flux of \Phi_n through every sphere centered at the pole is -1. More precisely, for r>0,

r^{n-1}\int_{S^{n-1}} \frac{d}{d\rho}\Phi_n(\rho\omega)\big|_{\rho=r}\,dS(\omega)=-1.

Here dS is Mathlib's measure on the unit sphere; the factor r^{n-1} transports it to the sphere of radius r.

The two-dimensional logarithmic branch and the power-law branches are reduced to the radial Laplacian formula. Smoothness away from the pole justifies the second derivatives, and the radial first- and second-derivative terms cancel with the dimension coefficient.

For every n\ge1 and every x\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\},

\Delta\Phi_n(x)=0.

The proof treats neighborhoods away from the origin by continuity. Near the origin, the logarithmic kernel in dimension two is bounded by a multiple of |x|^{-1}, while in higher dimensions the kernel is a multiple of |x|^{-(n-2)}. Mathlib's radial-power estimates apply because 1<2 and n-2<n, respectively.

For every n\ge1,

\Phi_n\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n).
In one Euclidean dimension, the norm of the embedded scalar coordinate is |x|. Substituting n=1 into the canonical kernel selects its one-dimensional branch, so evaluation reduces to -|x|/2.
Under the standard scalar embedding x \mapsto (x) \in \mathbb R^1, the canonical dimension-one Euclidean kernel is exactly the scalar function -|x|/2.

The locally integrable kernel \Phi(x)=-|x|/2 defines the ordinary distribution

T_\Phi(\varphi) =\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(x)\Phi(x)\,dx.

This is the canonical regular-distribution realization of the scalar kernel.

Lower a smooth test function to Mathlib's bundled compactly supported C^2 function. Its two directional derivatives in direction one agree pointwise with the ordinary second derivative. The finite-order integration identity therefore evaluates -D^2T_\Phi as \varphi(0). Extensionality against all test functions identifies the resulting distribution with \delta_0, which is exactly the generic fundamental-solution predicate.

The regular distribution associated with \Phi(x)=-|x|/2 is a fundamental solution for the one-dimensional negative second derivative:

-D^2T_\Phi=\delta_0.

Equivalently, for every smooth compactly supported test function \varphi,

\langle-D^2T_\Phi,\varphi\rangle=\varphi(0).

The operator -D^2 is bundled as a continuous linear endomorphism of ordinary distributions:

T\longmapsto-D(DT).
On the scalar real line, the normalized fundamental solution is \Phi(x)=-|x|/2. This scalar presentation is convenient for the one-dimensional integration-by-parts proof.

The canonical locally integrable kernel defines a regular distribution T_{\Phi_n} in every positive dimension. The dimension-independent operator -\Delta is bundled as the negative sum of the second coordinate distributional derivatives; here both constructions are specialized to n=2.

The generic action formula for the negative distributional Laplacian reduces the claim to the test-function identity \int\Phi_2\Delta\varphi=-\varphi(0). The fundamental-solution predicate then combines the interior pole and the resulting equality with \delta_0; its general action theorem recovers evaluation on every test function.

The regular distribution induced by the logarithmic kernel is a fundamental solution for the planar negative Laplacian:

-\Delta T_{\Phi_2}=\delta_0.

The equality is extensional against every smooth compactly supported test function and therefore holds in Mathlib's distribution space.

For \varepsilon>0, set

\Phi_\varepsilon(x) =-\frac{1}{4\pi}\log\bigl(|x|^2+\varepsilon^2\bigr), \qquad K_\varepsilon(x) =\frac{\varepsilon^2} {\pi\bigl(|x|^2+\varepsilon^2\bigr)^2}.

The exact classical identity is -\Delta\Phi_\varepsilon=K_\varepsilon. Each K_\varepsilon is nonnegative, integrable, and has total mass one.

Substitute \lVert\rho\omega\rVert=\rho for a unit vector and differentiate the logarithmic branch when n=2 and the Newtonian power branch when n\geq3. In both cases the coefficient simplifies using |S^{n-1}|=n\alpha(n), giving -1/(r^{n-1}|S^{n-1}|).

In dimension n\ge2, along every unit ray and at every radius r>0,

\frac{d}{d\rho}\Phi_n(\rho\omega)\big|_{\rho=r} =-\frac{1}{r^{n-1}|S^{n-1}|}.

The right-hand side is independent of the chosen unit direction.

On a neighborhood avoiding the origin, the norm is smooth and strictly positive. The one-dimensional profiles r\mapsto r, \log r, and the relevant real powers are smooth on positive radii. Composing the appropriate profile with the norm proves smoothness of every dimensional branch.

For every n\ge1 and x\ne0, the fundamental solution is smooth at x:

\Phi_n\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}).
The sphere of radius r has area r^{n-1}|S^{n-1}|. Multiplying this by the radial derivative -1/(r^{n-1}|S^{n-1}|) cancels both positive factors and leaves -1.

For n\ge2, r>0, and every unit vector \omega, the radial derivative \frac{d}{d\rho}\Phi_n(\rho\omega)\big|_{\rho=r} times the area of the radius-r sphere equals -1. This is the pointwise normalization from which the integrated flux identity follows.

With \alpha(n)=|B(0,1)\subset\mathbb R^n|, the total kernel is

\Phi_n(x)= \begin{cases} -\frac12|x|, & n=1,\\ -\frac{1}{2\pi}\log |x|, & n=2,\\ \frac{1}{(n-2)n\alpha(n)|x|^{n-2}}, & n\ge3, \end{cases}

The coefficients give outward radial flux -1, the normalization required for -\Delta\Phi_n=\delta_0. The Lean function sets \Phi_n(0)=0; a single point is irrelevant for almost-everywhere and distributional statements.

For r>0, dilation by r carries the unit ball to B(0,r) and scales Lebesgue measure by r^n. At r=0, both sides vanish because n>0. The formal proof specializes Mathlib's Euclidean-ball volume formula and converts the measure to a real number.
In positive dimension, for r\ge0, the Lebesgue volume of B(0,r) is \alpha(n)r^n.

Translate the center to zero, apply Mathlib's polar integration formula with the radial Jacobian measure, identify the inner integral with the defined sphere integral, and translate back. The annulus formula follows by subtracting the nested ball integrals and splitting the radial interval.

In positive dimension, if u is integrable on B(x,r) and r\ge 0, then

\int_{B(x,r)}u(y)\,dy =\int_0^r\left(\int_{\partial B(x,\rho)}u\,dS\right)d\rho.

Subtracting two ball formulas gives the corresponding identity on a concentric annulus, with radial integrability stated explicitly. These are the radial specialization of Evans's polar-coordinate/coarea theorem.
Both (\sqrt{\pi})^n and \Gamma(n/2+1) are strictly positive. Their quotient is therefore positive, which proves positivity of the explicit volume normalization.
For every natural-number dimension n, \alpha(n)>0.

The constant \alpha(n) is the Euclidean volume of the unit ball in \mathbb R^n. The Lean definition is the exact real expression (\sqrt{\pi})^n/\Gamma(n/2+1), which is the usual \pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(n/2+1) formula.

Mathlib's sphere-area identity identifies the total mass of the induced sphere measure with n times the real volume of the unit ball. The ball-volume theorem at radius one identifies that real volume with \alpha(n), yielding |S^{n-1}|=n\alpha(n).
The Mathlib-induced area of the Euclidean unit sphere is n\alpha(n). This identity connects radial derivatives to the surface normalization used in Evans's punctured-ball calculations.

Write x^*=x/\lVert x\rVert^2 for the Kelvin image of a nonzero pole. For \lVert y\rVert=1, the inversion identity gives

\lVert y-x\rVert =\lVert x\rVert\,\lVert y-x^*\rVert =\bigl\|\lVert x\rVert(y-x^*)\bigr\|.

Thus the physical and image arguments of the fundamental solution have the same norm, so the two terms in the Green kernel cancel. The proof treats dimension two and dimensions at least three separately because the fundamental solution is logarithmic in the former and a negative power in the latter. If x=0, both formulas reduce directly using \lVert y\rVert=1.

For n\geq2, an interior pole and a boundary field point satisfy

\lVert x\rVert<1,\quad \lVert y\rVert=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad G_B(x,y)=0.

Expand the Kelvin-inversion formula. Each fundamental-solution term is harmonic away from its pole, and the geometric hypotheses keep both relevant poles outside the point where the field-variable Laplacian is evaluated.

For n\geq2, x,y\in B(0,1), and y\ne x, the field-variable Laplacian vanishes:

\Delta_yG_B(x,y)=0.

In positive dimension, write x^*=x/\lVert x\rVert^2 when x\ne0. The unit-ball Green kernel is the total function

G_B(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{(1-\max\{x_0,y_0\})(1+\min\{x_0,y_0\})}{2},&n=1,\\[4pt] \Phi_n(y-x)-\Phi_n\!\left(\lVert x\rVert(y-x^*)\right),&n\geq2,\ x\ne0, \end{cases}

with the continuous x=0 branch written explicitly in Lean. The first variable is the physical pole and the second is the field point; in the one-dimensional branch, x_0 and y_0 denote their sole coordinates. For n\geq2 the kernel is the Kelvin construction of Evans §2.2.4; for n=1 it is the Dirichlet kernel of -d^2/dx^2 on (-1,1).

Change \Phi_n(\cdot-x) inside a small ball around the pole to get a smooth compactly supported function A with the right boundary values. Solve the Dirichlet problem with data A in H^1: its solution U is weakly harmonic, has a harmonic representative, and the barrier theorem for C^1 domains shows that this representative is continuous up to the boundary with the values of A. Uniqueness is the weak maximum principle on \overline\Omega, applied to the difference of two such functions.

Let n\ge2 and let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be a bounded open set with C^1 boundary, given by local graphs. For every x\in\Omega there is a function \phi^x that is harmonic in \Omega, continuous on \overline\Omega, equal to \Phi_n(\cdot-x) on \partial\Omega, and a.e. equal to an H^1(\Omega) field whose gradient is orthogonal to the gradients of H^1_0(\Omega). Any other function harmonic in \Omega, continuous on \overline\Omega, with the same boundary values equals \phi^x on \overline\Omega.

The domain need not be connected, and n=2, with its logarithmic kernel, is included.

For a pole x and a function \phi, the domain Green kernel is

G_\phi(x,y)=\Phi_n(y-x)-\phi(y).

Its gradient field is \nabla_y\Phi_n(y-x) minus the continuous extension of \nabla\phi to \overline\Omega, so the same field gives the interior gradient and the boundary flux. The definition imposes no conditions on \phi; each theorem states the ones it uses.

Green's second identity on \Omega minus a small ball around x, applied to u and \Phi_n(\cdot-x), gives the Newton representation of u(x), which still contains \partial_\nu u on the boundary. The same identity for u and the harmonic \phi, which has no pole, has no interior point term. Subtracting it cancels \partial_\nu u, because \phi=\Phi_n(\cdot-x) on \partial\Omega. On a C^{n+3} boundary the constructed corrector is C^2 up to the boundary by the boundary regularity theory, and the formula applies to it.

Let n\ge2 and let \Omega be a bounded open set with C^1 boundary. Let u\in C^2(\overline\Omega) solve -\Delta u=f in \Omega with u=g on \partial\Omega, and let x\in\Omega. If \phi is harmonic in \Omega, lies in C^2(\overline\Omega), and equals \Phi_n(\cdot-x) on \partial\Omega, then f\,G_\phi(x,\cdot) is integrable on \Omega, g\,\partial_\nu G_\phi(x,\cdot) is integrable on \partial\Omega, and

u(x)=-\int_{\partial\Omega}g(y)\,\frac{\partial G_\phi}{\partial\nu_y}(x,y)\,dS(y) +\int_\Omega f(y)\,G_\phi(x,y)\,dy.

If the boundary is C^{n+3}, a corrector with these properties exists, and the formula holds with it.

By uniqueness, \phi^x and \phi^y are the constructed correctors, which come with H^1 representatives, and the weak argument with regularized poles applies. For C^2 correctors the second proof writes the Green representation of each corrector at the other pole. The two expressions differ by a boundary flux of the antisymmetric pairing of \Phi_n(\cdot-x) and \Phi_n(\cdot-y), and by Green's identity for the two regular correctors. Both integrals vanish.

Let n\ge2 and let \Omega be a bounded open set with C^1 boundary. If \phi^x and \phi^y are harmonic in \Omega, continuous on \overline\Omega, and equal to \Phi_n(\cdot-x) and \Phi_n(\cdot-y) on \partial\Omega, then

\Phi_n(y-x)-\phi^x(y)=\Phi_n(x-y)-\phi^y(x),

that is, G(x,y)=G(y,x). When the correctors are also C^2 up to the boundary, a second proof goes through Green's identity, as in Evans.

Reflection fixes every boundary point y=(y',0) and changes only the sign of the pole's normal coordinate. Hence \lVert y-x\rVert=\lVert y-Rx\rVert. The fundamental solution is radial, so the two image terms agree and their difference is zero.

In positive dimension, for every pole x and every boundary point y=(y',0),

G_{\mathbb H}(x,y)=0.

The pole x is arbitrary; the cancellation uses only \lVert y-x\rVert=\lVert y-Rx\rVert.
Both image terms are smooth and harmonic away from their poles. Reflection places the image pole outside the upper half-space, while the physical pole is removed from the asserted domain.

In positive dimension, for x\in\mathbb H, the field y\mapsto G_{\mathbb H}(x,y) is C^2 on \mathbb H\setminus\{x\} and satisfies

\Delta_yG_{\mathbb H}(x,y)=0 \qquad(y\in\mathbb H\setminus\{x\}).

In positive dimension, let R(x',x_n)=(x',-x_n) be reflection across the boundary hyperplane. The upper-half-space Green kernel is

G_{\mathbb H}(x,y)=\Phi_n(y-x)-\Phi_n(y-Rx).

The first pole is physical; the reflected image pole lies outside \mathbb H=\{z:z_n>0\} whenever x\in\mathbb H.

Split the whole-space integral into the upper and lower half-planes; their common boundary has Lebesgue measure zero. Reflect the lower integral into the upper half-plane. Reflection preserves Lebesgue measure, while oddness of f changes its sign. The reflected lower term is therefore exactly the negative image term in the half-space Green kernel. For the sufficient logarithmic-moment criterion, continuity controls the locally integrable pole. Outside |y|\le |x|+1, use

|\log|x-y|| \le (1+\log(1+|x|))(1+\log(1+|y|))

and dominate by the two L^1 hypotheses.

Let f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R be odd under reflection across the horizontal boundary. Suppose that, for every field point x,

y\longmapsto \Phi_2(x-y)f(y)

is integrable on \mathbb R^2. Then the method-of-images integrand is integrable on the upper half-plane and

\mathcal G_{\mathbb R^2_+}f(x)=(\Phi_2*f)(x).

No compact support is assumed; the hypothesis is the tail condition for the logarithmic kernel. A concrete sufficient condition is that f be continuous and

f\in L^1(\mathbb R^2),\qquad \log(1+|\cdot|)f\in L^1(\mathbb R^2).

These assumptions make the displayed convolution integrable at every x, so odd data in this class have a well-defined half-space Green potential equal to \Phi_2*f.

Split the whole-space convolution into upper- and lower-half-plane integrals; the separating boundary hyperplane is Lebesgue null. Reflect the lower-half integral into the upper half-plane. Measure preservation and oddness of f turn it into the negative image term, giving exactly the Green potential. The planar whole-space convolution theorem then supplies the equation -\Delta u=f.

Let f\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^2) be odd under reflection across the horizontal boundary, so its restriction to \mathbb R^2_+ is represented by an odd whole-space extension. Then the method-of-images integral is integrable at every field point and

\mathcal G_{\mathbb R^2_+}f=\Phi_2*f, \qquad -\Delta\mathcal G_{\mathbb R^2_+}f=f.

Together with boundary cancellation, this is a classical Dirichlet Poisson solution for this source class.

Boundary vanishing follows pointwise from the image-kernel cancellation. For parity, change variables y=R_i z. Tangential reflection preserves the upper half-space and Lebesgue measure, the Green kernel is invariant when both arguments are reflected, and oddness of f supplies the remaining minus sign.

In positive dimension, for every boundary point x, the potential satisfies \mathcal G_{\mathbb R^n_+}f(x)=0. Let R_i reflect a tangential coordinate. If f(R_i y)=-f(y) for y in the upper half-space and the Green integrand is integrable at one field point x, then it is also integrable at R_i x and

\mathcal G_{\mathbb R^n_+}f(R_i x) =-\mathcal G_{\mathbb R^n_+}f(x).

In positive dimension, for a source f, the method-of-images Green potential is

\mathcal G_{\mathbb R^n_+}f(x) =\int_{\mathbb R^n_+}G_{\mathbb H}(y,x)f(y)\,dy.

The argument order follows the Lean kernel: y is the pole and x is the field point. The integral is a total Mathlib definition, while the Green-potential integrability condition records the analytic domain condition that the displayed integrand is integrable for every x.

Translate the ball to the origin, extend the boundary trace, and identify the translated function locally with its Poisson extension. Differentiating the Poisson kernel at the center and estimating the resulting spherical integral by Cauchy–Schwarz gives the explicit constant nM/r.
In positive dimension, suppose r>0, M\ge0, u is harmonic on a set containing the closed ball of radius r about x, and |u| \le M on the boundary sphere. Then \lVert Du(x)\rVert \le nM/r.

Apply the boundary-supremum estimate on the half-radius ball. At each point of its boundary sphere, apply the ball mean-value formula on the ball of radius r/2 centered there. These smaller open balls lie in B(x,r); the triangle inequality, monotonicity of the integral of |u|, and |B(0,r/2)|=\alpha(n)(r/2)^n give Evans's constant.

In positive dimension, if r>0 and u is harmonic on a set containing \overline{B(x,r)}, then

\lVert Du(x)\rVert \le \frac{C_1}{r^{n+1}}\int_{B(x,r)} |u(y)|\,dy,\qquad C_1=\frac{2^{n+1}n}{\alpha(n)},

where \alpha(n) is the volume of the unit ball. The bound is for the operator norm of the Fréchet derivative, so it bounds each coordinate derivative.

First derive harmonicity of the evaluated derivatives from harmonicity of u on the open domain. Then induct on k, spending the head radius in the final first-derivative estimate. On its boundary sphere, the induction hypothesis controls the preceding iterated derivative using the tail radii. Apply the first-order estimate to each multilinear evaluation and use the operator norm to reassemble the directional bounds. Constant radius budgets give the uniform theorem; replacing k by k+1 gives the successor form.

In positive dimension, let u be harmonic on an open set U, let k be any natural number, and assign a positive radius budget r_i to each derivative step. If

\overline{B\left(x,\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}r_i\right)}\subseteq U, \qquad |u|\le M \quad\text{on this ball},

then

\lVert D^k u(x)\rVert\le \frac{n^kM}{\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}r_i}.

Taking every r_i=r gives the uniform estimate on \overline{B(x,kr)} with denominator r^k. In particular, k=2 and k=3 recover the usual second- and third-derivative nested-ball estimates. The order-zero case is included.

Apply the boundary-supremum derivative estimate on arbitrarily large balls. If the derivative norm were positive, choosing a radius larger than its bound would give a strict contradiction. Mathlib's zero-derivative constancy theorem then identifies every value with the value at the origin.

In positive dimension, if u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is harmonic and globally bounded, then

\exists c\in\mathbb R,\qquad u(x)=c\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n.
A scalar function is harmonic on U\subseteq\mathbb R^n when it is C^2 on U and its Euclidean Laplacian vanishes at every point of U.

Join points of the connected domain by chains of overlapping admissible balls. Each link contributes the local factor 2^n. Compactness gives a finite subcover of K and hence a uniform bound on the number of links needed from a fixed base point. Comparing both x and y with that base point produces one constant valid for every pair in K.

Let n\ge 1, let U\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open and preconnected, and let K\subseteq U be compact. There is a constant C>0, depending only on n, K, and U, such that every nonnegative harmonic function on U satisfies

u(x)\leq C\,u(y)\qquad(x,y\in K).

Slide each paraboloid with vertex y\in\overline B(x^0,\tfrac18) up until it touches u from below on \overline B(0,\tfrac{15}{16}). Because u(x^0)\le1 and u\ge0 on the unit ball, the touching happens at an interior point where u\le\tfrac54. The contact set is compact and the map sending a contact point to its vertex covers the vertex ball. At a contact point the contact Jacobian J is positive semidefinite, and Lu\ge0 together with the gradient identity at contact gives \alpha\operatorname{tr}J\le\operatorname{tr}(aJ)\le\tau+2B. This bounds \det J by ((\tau+2B)/\alpha)^n, and the area formula gives the estimate.

Suppose that on B(0,1) the quadratic form of a is at least \alpha|v|^2 with \alpha>0, \operatorname{tr}a\le\tau, and \lVert b\rVert\le B. Let u\ge0 be continuous on \overline B(0,1), C^2 in B(0,1), and satisfy Lu\ge0 there with c=0. If u(x^0)\le1 for some x^0\in\overline B(0,\tfrac12), then

\bigl|\overline B(x^0,\tfrac18)\bigr| \le\Bigl(\frac{\tau+2B}{\alpha}\Bigr)^n\,\bigl|B(0,1)\cap\{u\le\tfrac54\}\bigr|.

The contact estimate, rescaled to cubes, says that u\le M on a fixed fraction \eta of a cube whenever u\le1 at a point of a slightly larger cube. Apply it to u/M^k. A dyadic child in which \{u>M^{k+1}\} has density above 1-\eta cannot contain a point of its parent where u\le M^k. Mathlib's subbox partition theorem turns this into the induction that loses the factor \delta=1-\eta at each level.

Let \alpha>0, \tau\ge0, and B\ge0. There are M\ge2 and 0<\delta<1 such that the following holds for all coefficients with ellipticity \alpha, \operatorname{tr}a\le\tau, and \lVert b\rVert\le B on the ball of radius 16(n+1). If u\ge0 is C^2 there, satisfies Lu\ge0 with c=0, and u(x^0)\le1 at some point of the closed unit cube Q, then for every k\ge0

\bigl|\{x\in Q:\ u(x)>M^k\}\bigr|\le\delta^k\,|Q|.

The ball B(y,r) lies inside B(x,2r). Nonnegativity makes the integral over the smaller ball no larger than the integral over the larger one. Applying the ball mean-value formula at y and x, then using |B(x,2r)|=2^n|B(y,r)|, gives the stated factor.

Let n>0, r>0, and suppose u is nonnegative and harmonic on a set containing \overline B(x,2r). If \lVert x-y\rVert\leq r, then

u(y)\leq 2^n u(x).

The ambient harmonicity set need not be open: the explicit closed-ball containment supplies every mean-value ball used in the proof.

Continuity turns the almost-everywhere bounds and ellipticity into pointwise ones on the open set U. Compactness of \overline V and connectedness of V give a finite chain of small balls in U. On each ball the level decay bounds the infimum from below and the upper estimate bounds the supremum, with constants fixed by \alpha, the coefficient bounds, and the radius. Multiplying along the chain gives one constant for all pairs of points of V.

Let U be open and bounded and let V be preconnected with \overline V\subseteq U. Let a, b, c be continuous on U with bounded ranges, with a symmetric and \sum_{i,j}a_{ij}(x)v_iv_j\ge\alpha|v|^2 for almost every x\in U, where \alpha>0. There is C>0 such that every u\in C^2(U) with u\ge0 and Lu=0 in U satisfies

\sup_V u\le C\,\inf_V u.

The potential c may have either sign. The second Lean statement replaces the bounded ranges by essential bounds.

For every dimension n, the Laplace equation is the order-two linear PDE record with operator u\mapsto\Delta u, right-hand side 0, and domain \mathbb R^n, representing

\Delta u=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_i^2u=0\qquad\text{on }\mathbb R^n.

Additivity is the sum rule for the iterated coordinate derivatives of two fields that are C^2 at the point, homogeneity is the scalar rule and needs no regularity, and the second-order locality law demanded by the record is proved for C^2 fields by identifying the coordinate Laplacian with the second Fréchet derivative evaluated on the coordinate vectors. For n=0 the coordinate sum is empty and the operator vanishes identically, so analytic applications assume 0<n.
The load is transferred to its Riesz representative. Mathlib's Lax–Milgram continuous linear equivalence for the coercive form is then inverted, and injectivity of that equivalence gives uniqueness.

If H is a real Hilbert space and, for some c>0,

B(v,v)\ge c\lVert v\rVert_H^2\qquad(v\in H),

then every \ell\in H^* has a unique weak solution u\in H satisfying B(u,v)=\ell(v) for all v\in H.
The difference u-v is harmonic and continuous on the closed ball. Apply the weak maximum principle with boundary upper bound zero.

In positive dimension, let u and v be harmonic in the same ball B(x_0,r), with r>0, and continuous on its closure. If u\le v on the sphere, then

u(x)\le v(x)\qquad(x\in\overline{B(x_0,r)}).

Set v(x)=e^{-\lambda\lVert x-z\rVert^2}-e^{-\lambda R^2}. For \lambda large, depending on \kappa, A, B, C, and R, the barrier satisfies Lv\le0 on the annulus. On the inner sphere u<u(x^0) holds with a positive gap by compactness, so for small \varepsilon the function u+\varepsilon v-u(x^0) is at most 0 on both boundary spheres. The weak principle on the annulus gives u(x^0)-u\ge\varepsilon v. Differentiating this at x^0 along the inward radius yields a derivative at most \varepsilon\,\partial_\nu v(x^0)<0.

Let R>0 and \lVert x^0-z\rVert=R. On the annulus R/2<\lVert x-z\rVert<R assume the quadratic form of a is at least \kappa|v|^2 with \kappa>0, \operatorname{tr}a\le A, \lVert b\rVert\le B, 0\le c\le C, c\,u(x^0)\ge0, and Lu\le0. Let u be continuous on \overline B(z,R), C^2 in B(z,R), differentiable at x^0, and suppose u(x)<u(x^0) for every x\in B(z,R). Then

Du(x^0)\,\nu>0,\qquad \nu=\frac{x^0-z}{R}.

The second Lean statement gives the same conclusion as a one-sided inward derivative along the segment from x^0 to z, and does not need differentiability of u at x^0.

For a:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{n\times n}, b:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n, and c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R, the operator in nondivergence form is

Lu(x)=-\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}(x)\,\partial_i\partial_j u(x)+Du(x)\,b(x)+c(x)\,u(x).

The second derivatives are those of the Fréchet derivative, so the formula is defined for every function and is meaningful where u is C^2.

Replace a by its symmetric part. The set where u=u(x^0) is closed in \Omega and nonempty. If it were not all of \Omega, there would be a point of the complement closer to the maximum set than to \partial\Omega, and a ball around it, inside \Omega and in the set u<u(x^0), touching the maximum set at a boundary point y. At y the derivative vanishes, since y is an interior maximum. The Hopf lemma on this ball, with the local constants, says a normal derivative is positive. The contradiction shows the maximum set is open as well.

Let \Omega be open and preconnected. Assume that each point of \Omega has a closed ball in \Omega on which the quadratic form of a is at least \kappa|v|^2 with \kappa>0, and \operatorname{tr}a, \lVert b\rVert, and c\ge0 are bounded above. If u is C^2 in \Omega, Lu\le0, u attains its maximum over \Omega at x^0\in\Omega, and c\,u(x^0)\ge0, then u\equiv u(x^0) on \Omega.

The constants may change from ball to ball; bounded continuous coefficients on a connected domain, with c\ge0 and a nonnegative maximum, are a special case.

Replace a by its symmetric part. Put e(x)=e^{\lambda x_i} and let E be its maximum over the compact set \overline\Omega. Without the potential, e has residual (-\lambda^2a_{ii}+\lambda b^i)e\le(-\lambda^2\alpha+\lambda B)e, which is negative once \lambda\alpha>B. The shifted barrier e-E is nonpositive, so the potential adds c(e-E)\le0 and L(e-E)<0. For \varepsilon>0 the function u_\varepsilon=u+\varepsilon(e-E) is a strict subsolution with u_\varepsilon\le M on the boundary. At an interior maximum above M its gradient would vanish, its Hessian would be negative semidefinite, and c\,u_\varepsilon\ge cM\ge0, which together give Lu_\varepsilon\ge0. Hence u_\varepsilon\le M, and letting \varepsilon\to0 gives the claim.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open with compact closure. Suppose that on \Omega the quadratic form of a(x) is nonnegative, that for one fixed index i we have a_{ii}\ge\alpha>0 and b^i\le B, and that c\ge0. Let u be continuous on \overline\Omega, C^2 in \Omega, with Lu\le0 in \Omega and u\le M on \partial\Omega, where cM\ge0. Then

u\le M\qquad\text{on }\overline\Omega.

When c=0 the bound M may have either sign. When c\ge0 is nonzero somewhere, M must be nonnegative there, which is the form u\le\max_{\partial\Omega}u^+ of Evans's statement.

At a maximum point, the spherical mean-value identity says that the continuous nonnegative gap u(x_0)-u has integral zero on every sufficiently small centered sphere. Positivity of surface measure on open patches forces the gap to vanish on each sphere. Varying the radius fills a ball, so the maximum set is open in U. It is also relatively closed by continuity and contains x_0; preconnectedness makes it all of U.

In positive dimension, let U be open and preconnected. If a harmonic function u attains a domain-wide maximum at some x_0\in U, then

u(x)=u(x_0)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.

Because the two harmonic functions agree on the boundary, the comparison principle applied to u and v gives u\leq v on the closed ball. Applying it again with the functions exchanged gives v\leq u; pointwise antisymmetry then gives u=v.

In positive dimension, let r>0. If u and v are harmonic in B(x_0,r), continuous on \overline{B(x_0,r)}, and satisfy u=v on the sphere, then

u=v\qquad\text{on }\overline{B(x_0,r)}.

This is the homogeneous, ball-domain case of Evans's Dirichlet uniqueness theorem.

Add a small positive quadratic perturbation to make the Laplacian strictly positive. Compactness supplies a maximum on the closed ball, while the second-derivative test rules out an interior maximum above the boundary bound. Letting the perturbation vanish gives the weak inequality.

In positive dimension, let r>0. If u is harmonic in B(x_0,r), continuous on its closure, and u\le M on \partial B(x_0,r), then

u(x)\le M\qquad(x\in\overline{B(x_0,r)}).

This is the harmonic case on a ball. The variable-coefficient weak principle holds on every open set with compact closure.

Compactness gives a maximizer on the closed ball. If it lies on the boundary, the conclusion is immediate. If it lies in the interior, mean-value rigidity makes the function constant on the ball and continuity extends that equality to the boundary. The minimum statement follows by applying the maximum statement to -u.

In positive dimension, let u be continuous on \overline{B(c,r)} and have the spherical mean-value property in B(c,r), where r>0. An upper or lower bound for u on the boundary sphere holds throughout the closed ball.

For an admissible ball, translate its center to the origin, extend the continuous boundary trace, solve the ball Dirichlet problem by the Poisson kernel, and use the maximum-principle uniqueness theorem to identify the original function with the Poisson solution. Evaluation at the center gives the spherical average.

In positive dimension, if u\in C^2(U) and \Delta u=0 on U, then every closed ball \overline{B(x,r)}\subseteq U with r>0 satisfies

u(x)=\frac{1}{|\partial B(x,r)|} \int_{\partial B(x,r)}u(y)\,dS(y).

Sphere integrals are defined by pulling the Euclidean surface measure on the unit sphere through \omega\mapsto x+r\omega and including the Jacobian |r|^{n-1}. Ball integrals are ordinary restricted Lebesgue integrals. Division by the corresponding surface area or volume gives the normalized averages at positive radius; at radius zero both averages are totalized to u(x). The mean-value theorems therefore assume a positive radius.

The first derivative has zero derivative on the interior interval and is therefore constant. Subtracting the corresponding affine function leaves a function with zero first derivative. Continuity extends the resulting identity from the open interval to both endpoints.

If u\in C^2(U), u''=0 on U, and [a,b]\subseteq U with a<b, then there are constants A,B\in\mathbb R such that

u(x)=Ax+B\qquad(a\le x\le b).

This is the complete local classification of one-dimensional harmonic functions.
Insert the affine representation into the interval integral. The odd part around the center cancels, while the constant part contributes exactly the interval length times the value at the center.

If u\in C^2(U), u''=0 on U, and [x-r,x+r]\subseteq U with r>0, then

u(x)=\frac{1}{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r}u(y)\,dy.

This is the one-dimensional ball mean-value identity.

Rewrite the normalized sphere average on radius r as an integral over the fixed unit sphere; the Jacobian and surface-area factors cancel. Global C^1 regularity permits differentiation under this finite measure, and the chain rule differentiates u(x+r\omega) to Du(x+r\omega)\,\omega.

In positive dimension and at positive radii, the normalized geometric sphere average equals the average over the fixed unit sphere, because the radial Jacobian cancels the surface-area scaling. If u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is globally C^1, then differentiation under this fixed finite measure gives

\frac{d}{dr}\left( \frac{1}{|\partial B(x,r)|}\int_{\partial B(x,r)}u\,dS \right) =\frac1{|\partial B(0,1)|} \int_{\partial B(0,1)}Du(x+r\omega)\,\omega\,dS(\omega).

For a function defined only on an open domain, the formula applies after a C^1 extension from a neighborhood of the closed ball.

The spherical identity is the defining property. The ball identity follows by the coarea formula: substitute the spherical identity at every intermediate radius and integrate the surface areas from 0 to r.

In positive dimension, if u has the spherical mean-value property, x\in U, r>0, \overline{B(x,r)}\subseteq U, and u is integrable on B(x,r), then

u(x)=\frac{1}{|B(x,r)|}\int_{B(x,r)}u(y)\,dy.

The spherical mean-value property on U requires

u(x)=\frac{1}{|\partial B(x,r)|} \int_{\partial B(x,r)}u\,dS

for every x\in U, every r>0, and every closed ball \overline{B(x,r)}\subseteq U. The closed-ball containment is essential: the spherical integral evaluates the function on the boundary itself.

Openness of U gives a small closed ball around each point. Continuously extend the boundary trace and form its Poisson solution. The difference from u has the mean-value property and zero boundary values, so the mean-value boundary principle makes it vanish throughout the ball. Local equality with the smooth Poisson solution supplies both C^2 regularity and the vanishing Laplacian.

Conversely, in positive dimension, let U\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open. If u is continuous on U and has the spherical mean-value property on every closed ball contained in U, then u is C^2 on U and satisfies \Delta u=0 there. Together with the forward implication, this characterizes classical harmonic functions by their spherical averages.

The gradient is C^1, and the squared norm, positive square root, and reciprocal preserve the required regularity. Apply the quotient rule to each component. Symmetry of the actual second derivatives combines the two mixed terms; s^2=1+u_0^2+u_1^2 gives the displayed numerator. Since s^3>0, division preserves the zero equation.

If u:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R is C^2 at x, its normalized gradient is C^1 there and

\operatorname{div}\left(\frac{\nabla u}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla u|^2}}\right)(x) =\frac{(1+u_1^2)u_{00}-2u_0u_1u_{01}+(1+u_0^2)u_{11}} {\bigl(\sqrt{1+|\nabla u|^2}\bigr)^3}(x).

The divergence vanishes exactly when the numerator vanishes. The C^1 regularity assertion also holds in every finite dimension.
The right side is |\xi|^2+(p\cdot\xi)^2. Subtract |\xi|^2 and use nonnegativity of the remaining square.

For every p,\xi\in\mathbb R^2,

|\xi|^2\le (1+p_0^2)\xi_0^2+2p_0p_1\xi_0\xi_1+(1+p_1^2)\xi_1^2.

The lower bound is global in p; the coefficients themselves need not have a global upper bound.

The divergence identity gives the nondivergence equation throughout \Omega. Apply local Legendre linearization with the coefficients a=1+p_1^2, b=-p_0p_1, c=1+p_0^2. It constructs the chart and the dual; exchanging the diagonal coefficients and negating the mixed one gives the displayed equation. The lower bound for the dual principal form gives the last assertion.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2 be open, x_*\in\Omega, and u\in C^2(\Omega). Suppose

\operatorname{div}\left(\frac{\nabla u}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla u|^2}}\right)=0 \quad\text{on }\Omega,\qquad \det D^2u(x_*)\ne0.

There is a local inverse chart \nabla u:U\to V through x_*, with U\subseteq\Omega and a C^1 inverse X. Its explicit local dual v(p)=p\cdot X(p)-u(X(p)) is C^2 on V, has gradient X, and satisfies the linear equation

(1+p_0^2)v_{00}+2p_0p_1v_{01}+(1+p_1^2)v_{11}=0 \qquad(p\in V).

Its principal quadratic form is at least |\xi|^2 in every direction \xi\in\mathbb R^2.

Negation preserves harmonicity. If u attains its minimum at x_0, then -u attains its maximum there. The strong maximum principle makes -u constant on the preconnected domain, and multiplying the resulting identity by -1 makes u constant as well.

In positive dimension, let U be open and preconnected. If a harmonic function u attains a domain-wide minimum at some x_0\in U, then

u(x)=u(x_0)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.

The function -u is harmonic whenever u is. The boundary inequality m\leq u is equivalent to -u\leq-m, so the weak maximum principle gives -u(x)\leq-m throughout the closed ball. Negating this inequality yields m\leq u(x).

In positive dimension, let r>0. If u is harmonic in B(x_0,r), continuous on its closure, and m\le u on \partial B(x_0,r), then

m\le u(x)\qquad(x\in\overline{B(x_0,r)}).

Expanding B_\lambda(u,u) gives the squared gradient norm plus \lambda times the squared base L^2 norm. Each coefficient is bounded below by \min(1,\lambda)>0, so their sum controls that constant times the full graph-space norm squared; c=\min(1,\lambda) is the constant the proof supplies.

For \lambda>0, on every set \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n and in every dimension, the form B_\lambda is coercive on H^1_0(\Omega): there is a constant c>0 with

B_\lambda(u,u)\ge c\,\lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0(\Omega)}^2 \qquad\text{for all } u\in H^1_0(\Omega).

The distributional equivalence turns the PDE predicate into the variational weak equation. The solver characterization and uniqueness of the coercive problem then identify u with S_\lambda f. For zero forcing, combine this equivalence with the solver's zero-data identity.

On an open domain with \lambda>0, a distributional solution is the named variational solution:

(-\Delta+\lambda)u=f \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u=S_\lambda f.

For zero forcing this specializes to u=0.

One direction evaluates the Hilbert-space identity on canonical smooth tests. For the reverse direction, density of smooth compactly supported tests in H^1_0 and continuity of both sides extend equality to every Sobolev test.

On an open domain,

B_\lambda(u,v)=\int_\Omega fv\quad(\forall v\in H^1_0(\Omega)) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (-\Delta+\lambda)u=f\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Omega).

The right-hand side is the compactly supported smooth-test formulation.

On an open domain, the distributional predicate requires

\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla\varphi +\lambda\int_\Omega u\varphi =\int_\Omega f\varphi \qquad(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)).

Symmetry and nonnegativity expand the energy difference around a weak solution into one half of B_\lambda(v-u,v-u). For nonnegative \lambda this proves minimality. For positive \lambda, coercivity makes the difference vanish only when v=u, giving the converse, strictness, and uniqueness.

If \lambda\geq0, every weak solution minimizes J_{\lambda,f}. If \lambda>0, coercivity makes the characterization exact:

u\text{ is a global minimizer of }J_{\lambda,f} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B_\lambda(u,v)=\int_\Omega fv\quad(\forall v\in H^1_0(\Omega)).

The named solution S_\lambda f is the unique minimizer, and every other field has strictly larger energy.

For any \Omega, define

J_{\lambda,f}(v) =\frac12 B_\lambda(v,v)-\int_\Omega fv.

Construct the coercive Lax–Milgram solution, transfer its weak equation to the distributional predicate, and use the same equivalence plus uniqueness of the coercive Hilbert-space problem for any competing solution.

On every open domain, if \lambda>0, each f\in L^2(\Omega) admits exactly one u\in H^1_0(\Omega) satisfying

-\Delta u+\lambda u=f\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Omega).

On H^1_0(\Omega), the modified Helmholtz form is

B_\lambda(u,v)= \int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v +\lambda\int_\Omega uv.

It is defined for every set \Omega, measurable or not.

Write \lambda=\lambda^+-\lambda^-. The positive part can be discarded. The base-coordinate norm is bounded by the full graph-space norm, so the negative mass contribution is bounded below by -\lambda^-\lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0}^2. Subtracting this from the Dirichlet lower bound leaves the positive coefficient c-\lambda^-.

Suppose the Dirichlet form has a coercivity modulus c:

c\lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0(\Omega)}^2 \leq\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2 \qquad(u\in H^1_0(\Omega)).

If the negative part of the mass coefficient satisfies \lambda^-<c, then

B_\lambda(u,u)\geq (c-\lambda^-)\lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0(\Omega)}^2.

For \lambda>0 and f\in L^2(\Omega), the named solver is the unique u\in H^1_0(\Omega) satisfying

B_\lambda(u,v)=\int_\Omega fv \qquad(v\in H^1_0(\Omega)).

Satisfying this weak equation is equivalent to equality with the named solver.

The zero-data identity follows from uniqueness. Boundedness of the Lax–Milgram solution operator gives the first estimate for some positive constant depending only on the fixed form. Apply the same estimate to f-g and use linearity of the solver to obtain the Lipschitz bound.

On every domain and for \lambda>0, the solver sends zero data to zero. Moreover, there is a constant C>0, depending on the fixed form, such that for all f,g\in L^2(\Omega),

\lVert S_\lambda f\rVert_{H^1_0} \leq C\lVert f\rVert_{L^2}, \qquad \lVert S_\lambda f-S_\lambda g\rVert_{H^1_0} \leq C\lVert f-g\rVert_{L^2}.

Linearity of the integral and gradient identities proves closure of the distributional predicate under the listed operations. When \lambda>0, the characterization by the unique named solver turns those closure results into the two displayed solver identities.

Distributional modified Helmholtz solutions are closed under addition, negation, subtraction, and real scalar multiplication, with the forcing data transformed by the same operation. Consequently, for \lambda>0,

S_\lambda(f+g)=S_\lambda f+S_\lambda g, \qquad S_\lambda(c f)=cS_\lambda f.

For \lambda\ge1 the cap is empty. Closedness of the good set of parameters follows from continuity of u. For openness at a good \lambda>0, strict comparison gives w_\lambda>0 in the cap and the Hopf lemma gives \partial_eu<0 on the flat face. Near the sphere, a separate argument shows that u decreases along every outward-pointing direction. By the Hopf lemma \partial_\nu u can vanish on the sphere only when f(0)<0, and there the Hessian supplies the sign. Compactness makes these neighbourhoods uniform, so every nearby plane is good. The interval is connected, and the case \lambda=0 is a limit.

Let u be C^2 on \mathbb R^n, positive in B(0,1), zero on the sphere, and a solution of -\Delta u=f(u) in the ball with f Lipschitz. For every unit vector e, every \lambda\ge0, and every x\in B(0,1) with x\cdot e>\lambda,

u(x)\le u(x^\lambda).

Extend u from the closed ball to a C^2 function on \mathbb R^n; the equation only involves the open ball, so it is unchanged. Continuation at \lambda=0 in the directions \pm e gives u(x)=u(x^0). For |x|=|y| and x\ne y, take e=(x-y)/|x-y|; the reflection with \lambda=0 sends x to y, so u(x)=u(y). Define v(r)=u(re_1). For 0\le r<s\le1, strict comparison at \lambda=(r+s)/2 in the direction e_1 compares se_1 with its mirror image re_1 and gives v(s)<v(r). Dimension zero is handled separately.

Let f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be Lipschitz, and let u be C^2 up to the boundary of B(0,1), with

-\Delta u=f(u)\ \text{ and }\ u>0\ \text{ in }B(0,1),\qquad u=0\ \text{ on }\partial B(0,1).

Then there is a continuous v:[0,1]\to[0,\infty) that is strictly decreasing on [0,1], with v(1)=0 and

u(x)=v(|x|)\qquad(x\in\overline B(0,1)).

The Laplacian commutes with reflection, so -\Delta w_\lambda=f(u(x^\lambda))-f(u(x))\ge-L\,w_\lambda when w_\lambda\ge0. The cap is convex and so connected. On its spherical face u=0 while u(x^\lambda)>0, because \lambda>0 puts x^\lambda inside the ball. So w_\lambda is positive somewhere, and the strong principle for -\Delta+L rules out an interior zero.

Let u be C^2 on \mathbb R^n, positive in B(0,1), zero on the sphere, and a solution of -\Delta u=f(u) in the ball, with f Lipschitz with constant L. Let e be a unit vector and \lambda>0. Wherever w_\lambda\ge0 in the cap,

-\Delta w_\lambda+L\,w_\lambda\ge0.

If w_\lambda\ge0 on all of \Sigma_\lambda, then w_\lambda(x)>0 at every x of the closed ball with x\cdot e>\lambda.

Subtract g(x_0) inside the Poisson integral and use that the kernel has mass one. Continuity makes this difference uniformly small near x_0, while positivity and concentration of the kernel control the complementary part. This proves the interior limit; the piecewise definition supplies exact boundary values and glues the two continuous pieces on the closed ball.

In positive dimension, if r>0 and g is continuous, then

u_{r,g}\in C\!\left(\overline{B(0,r)}\right),\qquad u_{r,g}|_{\partial B(0,r)}=g|_{\partial B(0,r)}.

The proof first shows P_rg(x)\to g(x_0) as x\to x_0 through B(0,r) for every x_0\in\partial B(0,r); the attached total solution then gives exact boundary equality.

The Poisson extension integrates the prescribed boundary datum over the radius-r sphere with the normalization used by the ball Poisson kernel. Analytic theorems about this total function supply positivity of r, continuity of the data, and the appropriate interior or boundary hypotheses.
The three clauses are the interior Laplacian identity, interior C^2 regularity, and pointwise boundary convergence of the Poisson integral.

In positive dimension, for r>0 and continuous g, the Poisson formula gives a field P_rg such that

P_rg\in C^2(B(0,r)),\qquad \Delta(P_rg)=0\ \text{in }B(0,r),\qquad \lim_{\substack{x\to x_0\\x\in B(0,r)}}P_rg(x)=g(x_0)

for every x_0\in\partial B(0,r).

Inside the ball, the boundary-attached solution is definitionally the Poisson extension. Apply its interior C^2 theorem and its pointwise Laplacian-zero theorem; together these are exactly the classical harmonicity predicate on B(0,r).

In positive dimension, for r>0 and continuous ambient data g, the boundary-attached solution satisfies

u_{r,g}\in C^2\!\left(B(0,r)\right), \qquad \Delta u_{r,g}=0\quad\text{in }B(0,r).

Interior C^\infty regularity holds as well, by the smoothness theorem.

Fix an interior point and choose a smaller neighborhood whose distance from the boundary sphere is positive. The differences between points in this neighborhood and points on the sphere lie in a compact annulus away from zero. Replace the inverse-distance kernel by a smooth compactly supported kernel that agrees on this annulus. Its convolution with the boundary datum is smooth and agrees locally with the original potential. Multiplying by the smooth Poisson prefactor preserves every derivative order.

In positive dimension, for a positive radius and a continuous ambient representative of the boundary datum, differentiation under the sphere integral gives a C^\infty extension on the open ball. The linked theorems allow every regularity order m\in\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}, both at individual interior points and throughout the ball. The choice m=2 supplies the regularity needed by the classical Laplacian statement.

Insert the explicit formula for K_r(x,y) into the sphere integral. The factor (r^2-\lVert x\rVert^2)/(n\alpha(n)r) is independent of y and can be pulled outside, leaving exactly the prefactor definition of the Poisson extension.
The prefactor form of the ball extension is algebraically equal to the sphere integral of K_r(x,y)g(y).

For a positive radius r, the ball Poisson kernel is

K_r(x,y)=\frac{r^2-\lVert x\rVert^2} {n\alpha(n)r\lVert x-y\rVert^n}.

Its boundary-value interpretation uses x\in B(0,r) and y\in\partial B(0,r); the Lean definition is total.

Use the two derivative formulas justified by interior regularity and sum their diagonal terms. After writing all denominators over \lVert x-y\rVert^{n+4}, the norm-square identities for boundary points \lVert y\rVert=r make the numerator cancel. Integrating the zero kernel Laplacian yields \Delta(P_rg)(x)=0.

In positive dimension, if r>0, g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is continuous, and x\in B(0,r), then the coordinate Laplacian of the Poisson extension vanishes:

\Delta\!\left(P_rg\right)(x)=0.

The proof differentiates the kernel twice, uses the common norm-square identities, and performs the resulting sphere-integral cancellation.

The boundary-attached Dirichlet candidate is the total function

u_{r,g}(x)= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\int_{\partial B(0,r)}K_r(x,y)g(y)\,dS(y), &\lVert x\rVert<r,\\[6pt] g(x),&\lVert x\rVert\geq r. \end{cases}

Thus it is the Poisson extension in the open ball and agrees definitionally with the prescribed ambient datum outside it.

Subtract the two harmonic functions. Their difference is continuous up to the boundary and vanishes there, so the weak maximum principle applied to the difference and its negative forces it to vanish on the ball.

In positive dimension, let r>0, let g be continuous, and let u\in C^2(B(0,r)). If

\Delta u=0\ \text{in }B(0,r),\qquad u\in C\!\left(\overline{B(0,r)}\right),\qquad u=g\ \text{on }\partial B(0,r),

then

u(x)=u_{r,g}(x)\qquad(x\in\overline{B(0,r)}).

Compact support confines every translated derivative of the right factor to a fixed compact set locally in the field variable. Local integrability of the left factor supplies an integrable dominator there. Differentiation under the integral transfers one coordinate derivative to the right factor, and induction repeats this for any finite derivative list.

For a locally integrable left factor and a right factor in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n), every finite iterated coordinate derivative transfers to the right factor. For the datum f\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^n) used in the Poisson construction, the separate one- and two-derivative transfer lemmas give the required identities without assuming infinite smoothness.

Mathlib's convolution regularity theorem gives global C^2 regularity from local integrability of \Phi_n and the compactly supported C^2 datum. Apply the two-derivative transfer lemma in each coordinate and sum the pure second derivatives under the integral to obtain \Phi_n*(\Delta f).

In positive dimension, for f\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^n), the convolution candidate is globally C^2 and

\Delta(\Phi_n*f)(x) =\bigl(\Phi_n*(\Delta f)\bigr)(x) \qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n).

For n=2 this is the planar theorem. For n\ge3, fix x and apply the Newtonian pole identity \int\Phi_n\Delta\varphi=-\varphi(0) to the translated datum \varphi(y)=f(x+y). Reflecting the integration variable and using \Phi_n(-y)=\Phi_n(y) identify this integral with \bigl(\Phi_n*(\Delta f)\bigr)(x), so the Laplacian transfer gives \Delta(\Phi_n*f)(x)=-f(x). Global C^2 regularity is part of the transfer theorem.

Let n\ge2 and f\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^n). The fundamental-solution convolution is a classical solution of the Poisson equation on \mathbb R^n:

u=\Phi_n*f \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u\in C^2(\mathbb R^n), \qquad -\Delta u(x)=f(x)\quad(x\in\mathbb R^n).

Equivalently, the residual of the Poisson equation record vanishes at u on all of \mathbb R^n.
Construct the named Lax–Milgram solution for the coercive Dirichlet form and transport existence and uniqueness across the equivalence between the variational and smooth-test formulations.

If n\ge1 and \Omega is open and bounded, then every f\in L^2(\Omega) admits exactly one u\in H^1_0(\Omega) such that

-\Delta u=f\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Omega).

One implication evaluates the variational equation on the canonical image of each smooth test function. Conversely, equality on smooth tests extends to all of H^1_0(\Omega) because that image has dense range and both sides are continuous linear functionals.

On an open domain, for u\in H^1_0(\Omega) and f\in L^2(\Omega),

B_\Omega(u,v)=\int_\Omega fv\quad(\forall v\in H^1_0(\Omega)) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sum_i\int_\Omega D_i u\,D_i\varphi=\int_\Omega f\varphi \quad(\forall\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)).

Let \Omega be any set, f\in L^2(\Omega), and u\in H^1_0(\Omega). The distributional Poisson predicate requires \Omega to be open and

\sum_{i=1}^n\int_\Omega D_i u\,D_i\varphi =\int_\Omega f\varphi \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).

This is the weak test form of -\Delta u=f.

Derivatives through order three are in L^2, so Cauchy–Schwarz makes every product in the two global integrations by parts integrable. Commuting derivatives gives \int(\partial_i\partial_j u)^2=\int(\partial_i^2u)(\partial_j^2u). Summing over i,j yields the squared Laplacian norm. The proved Poisson equation -\Delta u=f identifies that norm with the source norm. No compact support of u or separately prescribed flux at infinity is needed.

For the half constant, put a=\Delta_yu, b=\partial_z^2u, and let M be the sum of the four axial/transverse squared L^2 norms. The same integration by parts gives M=\int ab. Since a+b=\Delta u,

4M=\int_{\mathbb R^5}(a+b)^2-\int_{\mathbb R^5}(a-b)^2 \le\int_{\mathbb R^5}|f|^2.

Taking square roots gives the factor 1/2 in norm.

Let f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^5) and u=\Phi_5*f. Then -\Delta u=f, and global integration by parts gives

\begin{aligned} \sum_{i,j=1}^5\int_{\mathbb R^5}|\partial_i\partial_j u|^2 &=\int_{\mathbb R^5}|f|^2,\\ \left(\sum_{a=1}^4\int_{\mathbb R^5} |\partial_{y_a}\partial_z u|^2\right)^{1/2} &\le\tfrac12\lVert f\rVert_{L^2(\mathbb R^5)}. \end{aligned}

The full Hessian sum counts both orders of each mixed derivative. The second sum contains just the four axial/transverse entries. These estimates use ordinary five-dimensional volume and the full classical Hessian, including its diagonal local term.

Split \Phi_5 at unit radius. Its near part is in L^1 by local integrability of the kernel. Its far part decays as \lVert X\rVert^{-3} and belongs to L^2: five-dimensional shells have volume proportional to r^4\,dr, so

\int_1^\infty r^4(r^{-3})^2\,dr =\int_1^\infty r^{-2}\,dr<\infty.

Convolution of an L^1 kernel with an L^2 function belongs to L^2 and converges absolutely almost everywhere. Apply this first to the near kernel and f\in L^2, then to f\in L^1 and the far kernel, swapping the convolution variables in the second term. Adding the two absolutely convergent integrals recovers \Phi_5*f and proves its L^2 membership. If an L^2 source vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact set, Cauchy–Schwarz and finite volume give f\in L^1. Continuous compact sources satisfy both hypotheses as well.

Transfer the derivatives onto f and apply the same estimate to each continuous compactly supported source derivative.

In dimension five, let f\in L^1(\mathbb R^5)\cap L^2(\mathbb R^5) and u=\Phi_5*f. The defining integral converges absolutely for almost every field point, and u\in L^2(\mathbb R^5). This also applies to any L^2 source that vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact set. No continuity or radial symmetry is needed. If f\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^5), each Cartesian Hessian entry is also in L^2. If f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^5), then for every finite word \alpha of coordinate directions, including the empty word,

\partial^\alpha u=\Phi_5*(\partial^\alpha f)\in L^2(\mathbb R^5).

The linked theorems prove the L^2 membership; the identity itself is the derivative transfer for a locally integrable kernel.

For a bundled test function f\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^n), the classical whole-space candidate is

(\Phi_n*f)(x) =\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi_n(y)f(x-y)\,dy.
Lebesgue measure on \mathbb R^{n-1} is pushed forward through the canonical embedding into the boundary hyperplane. This measure realizes the boundary integral in Evans's formula.

At an interior point x_0, the ball of radius (x_0)_n/2 remains inside the upper half-space.
