This boundary-coordinate majorant is integrable, so parametric dominated differentiation applies. The scalar prefactor 2x_n/(n\alpha_n) is differentiable by the coordinate projection rule, and the product rule gives the result.

In every positive dimension, if g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is measurable and uniformly bounded on the boundary hyperplane, then its half-space Poisson extension is Fréchet differentiable at every point of \mathbb R^n_+.

Writing \iota(y')=(y',0) for the boundary embedding, the half-space Poisson extension is

(P_{\mathbb H}g)(x) =\frac{2x_n}{n\alpha(n)} \int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}} \frac{g(\iota(y'))}{\lVert x-\iota(y')\rVert^n}\,dy'.

In Lean this is first defined against the pushforward of Lebesgue measure under \iota; the displayed formula is its coordinate realization.

Let t=x_n>0 and let a be the tangential projection of x. Both t and \lVert y'-a\rVert are bounded by d=\lVert x-\iota(y')\rVert, hence

1+\lVert y'-a\rVert\leq(1+t^{-1})d.

After taking nth powers and reciprocals, the inverse-distance kernel is dominated by a constant multiple of the translated integrable weight (1+\lVert y'-a\rVert)^{-n}.

For every interior point x\in\mathbb R^n_+, the boundary-coordinate function

y'\longmapsto\lVert x-\iota(y')\rVert^{-n}

is integrable on \mathbb R^{n-1}. Consequently, bounded measurable boundary data give an integrable Poisson integrand.

Unfold the boundary measure as the pushforward of Lebesgue measure under the canonical embedding \iota(y')=(y',0). The pushforward integration formula turns the boundary integral into an integral over \mathbb R^{n-1}; expanding the Poisson kernel produces the displayed constant and denominator.

In every positive dimension, for measurable ambient data g and every field point x\in\mathbb R^n, the half-space Poisson extension equals the coordinate integral \frac{2x_n}{n\alpha(n)}\int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}g(\iota(y'))\,\lVert x-\iota(y')\rVert^{-n}\,dy'.

For a positive-dimensional upper half-space, the Poisson kernel is

K(x,y)=\frac{2x_n}{n\alpha(n)\lVert x-y\rVert^n}.

The definition is total in the field and boundary variables; its analytic interpretation requires an interior field point and a boundary point.

Translation and positive scaling reduce the boundary-distance integral to unit height. For n\geq2, polar coordinates and the substitution u=r^2 turn its radial part into \frac12 B((n-1)/2,1/2). The Beta–Gamma identity, the sphere-area formula, and \Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi give exactly n\alpha_n/2, which cancels the kernel constant. The case n=1 is the integral over the zero-dimensional boundary.

In every positive dimension, each point x of the upper half-space \mathbb R^n_+ satisfies

(P_{\mathbb H}1)(x)=1.

Equivalently, the half-space Poisson kernel has boundary mass one.

Translate and rescale the boundary variable by y=a+tz. The extension then has a fixed integrable kernel K_n(z)=|e_n-\iota(z)|^{-n}. Continuity gives pointwise convergence of the rescaled boundary data, while boundedness supplies a constant multiple of K_n as an integrable dominator. Dominated convergence and the exact kernel mass from the normalization calculation give the stated limit.

In every positive dimension, let g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R be continuous and bounded on the boundary hyperplane. For each a\in\mathbb R^{n-1},

\lim_{t\downarrow0} (P_{\mathbb H}g)(\iota(a)+t e_n)=g(\iota(a)),

where \iota(a)=(a,0). The linked theorem expresses t\downarrow0 through the positive-height neighborhood filter.

Smooth compactly supported sources are dense in L^2(\mathbb R^5). The energy identity bounds every Hessian component by the source norm, so each component extends continuously to the completion. The full energy identity and the mixed bound pass to the limit. Two such continuous maps agree on the dense class and therefore on every L^2 source.

For the weak-derivative identification, approximate a compactly carried L^2 source by smooth sources supported in a fixed compact set. The potentials converge in L^2, the extended Hessian entries converge in L^2, and the integration-by-parts identity against each test function passes to the limit. A C^2_c source has a C^2 potential, whose classical Hessian is also a weak derivative, so uniqueness of weak derivatives gives the almost-everywhere agreement.

By density, the full classical Hessian extends uniquely to bounded linear maps on all of L^2(\mathbb R^5), retaining the energy identity and mixed 1/2 bound. For an L^2 source vanishing almost everywhere outside a compact set, the extended entry T_{ij}f is the weak derivative \partial_i\partial_j of \Phi_5*f. For a C^2_c source it agrees almost everywhere with the classical Hessian entry.

u=\Phi_2*f \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u\in C^2(\mathbb R^2), \qquad -\Delta u=f.

The residual of a linear PDE record is the operator value minus the right-hand side, so both identities are the definitions of the records unfolded at x. A difference vanishes exactly when its two terms agree, which gives the pointwise characterization. The domain of the Poisson record is all of \mathbb R^n, so quantifying over domain points is quantifying over every x, which gives the global form.

For every field u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R and every point x, the residuals unfold to the pointwise coordinate expressions

\mathcal R_{\mathrm{Poisson}}(u)(x)=-\Delta u(x)-f(x), \qquad \mathcal R_{\mathrm{Laplace}}(u)(x)=\Delta u(x).

Hence the Poisson residual vanishes at x exactly when -\Delta u(x)=f(x), and it vanishes at every point of the domain exactly when -\Delta u=f holds on all of \mathbb R^n.

For a source term f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R, the Poisson equation is the order-two linear PDE record with operator u\mapsto-\Delta u, right-hand side f, and domain \mathbb R^n, representing

-\Delta u=f\qquad\text{on }\mathbb R^n.

The minus sign is the textbook convention; it matches the normalization -\Delta\Phi_n=\delta_0 of the fundamental solution below. The record is built from the same coordinate Laplacian and the same locality proof as the Laplace record.

The all-order principal data fix one pointwise coefficient matrix and one pointwise forcing function. Every forward and inverse boundary chart is smooth; the coefficient matrix has a globally smooth representative; for each k, a W^{k+1,\infty}(\Omega) coefficient bundle represents that same matrix; and a W^{k,2}(\Omega) forcing bundle represents that same forcing. Fixing the underlying functions ensures that the Sobolev data at different orders describe the same coefficients and forcing.

Strong induction begins with global H^2. At a successor order, the previous representative supplies the lower regularity needed to differentiate the localized equation. Interior differentiated equations and flattened boundary equations produce the next localized Sobolev pieces; tangential derivatives, normal-flux recovery, coefficient reciprocals, and pure-normal assembly recover all derivative directions. A finite partition of unity closes the global step.

For every k\in\mathbb N, assume \Omega carries the operational C^2 boundary atlas, with forward charts of class C^{k+2} and inverse charts of class C^{k+1}. Then

f\in W^{k,2}(\Omega),\quad a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}(\Omega),\quad -\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u)=f \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u\in W^{k+2,2}(\Omega),

for every u\in H^1_0(\Omega), provided the coefficients have global C^{k+1} representatives and are uniformly elliptic on \Omega.
A C^2 boundary atlas consists of a finite extension atlas whose flattening charts and inverse charts are twice continuously differentiable.

For n=1, restrict the derivative order once. For n\geq2, lower the exponent to one, perform n-1 subcritical steps to reach exponent n, and apply the critical embedding with finite target exponent 2n. Since 2n>n, higher-order Morrey embedding supplies continuous representatives for the weak derivatives. The closure weak-to-classical theorem reconstructs their Fréchet derivatives within \overline\Omega.

Let n\geq1 and let \Omega carry the operational C^2 boundary atlas. Then every finite-order Sobolev field has a classical representative:

W^{m+n+1,2}(\Omega)\longrightarrow C^m(\overline\Omega)

for every finite m.

Continuity extends the ellipticity lower bound from \Omega to its closure and preserves half of it on an open neighborhood. A smooth cutoff equal to one on the compact closure glues a there to the scalar matrix (\alpha/2)I outside that neighborhood. Entrywise compact support of the deviation from (\alpha/2)I gives global Lipschitz bounds and bounded L^\infty representatives, while convexity of the quadratic-form lower bound preserves ellipticity through the transition region.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be bounded with the operational C^1 extension atlas. If the entries of a are globally C^1 and

\xi^\mathsf{T}a(x)\xi\geq\alpha|\xi|^2 \qquad (x\in\Omega,\ \alpha>0),

then there exist one globally defined extension, entrywise Lipschitz constants, and compatible L^\infty(\mathbb R^n) coefficient classes. The pointwise field agrees with a on \Omega, each entry is globally Lipschitz, the L^\infty classes represent those entries almost everywhere, and the resulting matrix is uniformly elliptic with constant \alpha/2.

For \Omega=(-1,1), the affine endpoint maps \Phi_-(x)=x+1 and \Phi_+(x)=1-x identify neighborhoods of the two boundary points with neighborhoods in the upper half-line (0,\infty). Both maps are affine with affine inverses, hence smooth to every finite order. Together with an interior patch and a finite subordinate partition of unity, they furnish the operational C^2 boundary atlas used by the global elliptic and parabolic regularity theorems.

For every n\geq1, quantitative signed caps, coordinate permutations, globally smooth extensions of x'\mapsto\sqrt{1-\lVert x'\rVert^2}, and triangular graph-flattening maps assemble into a finite operational C^2 boundary atlas for B^n\subset\mathbb R^n.

A finite boundary cover consists of bounded open neighborhoods U_i whose union contains the frontier \partial\Omega of a bounded open domain. Adding \Omega as the interior member gives a finite open cover of \overline\Omega. Mathlib's smooth partition-of-unity theorem then canonically supplies compactly supported interior and boundary test functions subordinate to those sets and summing to one on \Omega.

After the subordinate cutoffs are fixed, one attaches a flattening chart to each boundary neighborhood. Only the compact support of the corresponding cutoff must lie in the chart source. Globally represented C^1 charts produce an extension atlas, while C^2 charts produce the operational boundary atlas used by elliptic regularity.

Use strong induction on k. The base case is full-operator global H^2 regularity. At a successor order, the induction hypothesis supplies the preceding Sobolev representative. The higher-order multiplier estimates then put b\cdot Du, cu, and \lambda u in the required Sobolev space, so the effective forcing belongs to W^{k,2}. Apply the arbitrary-order principal theorem to the rewritten divergence equation.

For every k\in\mathbb N, assume the same operational boundary atlas, with forward charts of class C^{k+2} and inverse charts of class C^{k+1}. Let a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}, let b^i,c\in W^{k,\infty}, and let f\in W^{k,2}. Then every H^1_0 weak solution of

Lu=-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u)+b^i\partial_i u+cu+\lambda u=f

has a W^{k+2,2}(\Omega) representative, provided the principal coefficients have global C^{k+1} representatives and satisfy the same positive uniform ellipticity condition. No regularity above H^1_0 is assumed for the supplied weak solution.

The flattening maps preserve every tangential coordinate and replace the normal coordinate by g(x')-x_n or g(x')+x_n. Direct coordinate calculations give their inverses. The inequalities x_n<g(x') and x_n>-g(x'), respectively, are equivalent to positivity of the flattened normal coordinate. Componentwise calculus proves the required differentiability. Restricting each global homeomorphism to a bounded open source gives a bounded partial chart because the image of the compact source closure is bounded. For the sphere, the local height \sqrt{1-\lVert x'\rVert^2} is smooth on the region where its radicand is positive; Mathlib's relative smooth-extension theorem produces a globally smooth function agreeing with it on any strictly smaller closed tangential cylinder.

For a globally smooth height g:\mathbb R^{n-1}\to\mathbb R, the triangular maps

\Psi_+(x',x_n)=(x',g(x')-x_n),\qquad \Psi_-(x',x_n)=(x',g(x')+x_n)

flatten the region below the graph of g and the region above the graph of -g, respectively, to the standard upper half-space. Their forward and inverse maps retain every finite differentiability order, and restriction to a bounded open source gives the bounded partial charts required by the operational atlas. On every smaller tangential cylinder of the unit sphere, we also construct a global C^\infty height agreeing with g(x')=\sqrt{1-\lVert x'\rVert^2}.

Flatten the boundary chart, transport the weak equation and ellipticity, estimate tangential difference quotients, recover the normal derivative from the normal flux, oddly reflect the zero-trace field, pull it back through the C^2 chart, and restrict it to the physical domain.

Assume \Omega carries the operational C^2 boundary atlas, including its finite charts and partition of unity. For a uniformly elliptic weak equation

-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u)=f,\qquad u\in H^1_0(\Omega),\quad f\in L^2(\Omega),

with global C^1 coefficient representatives, every boundary cutoff \eta_i satisfies \eta_i u\in H^2(\Omega) in the representative sense.

Move b\cdot Du, cu, and \lambda u to the right. Since the supplied weak solution lies in H^1_0 and the coefficients are essentially bounded, the effective forcing remains in L^2. Apply principal-part global H^2 regularity to that equation.

Under the same operational atlas, principal-coefficient, and ellipticity hypotheses, let the first- and zeroth-order coefficients be in L^\infty. Every H^1_0 weak solution of

-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u)+b^i\partial_i u+cu+\lambda u=f

with f\in L^2(\Omega) has an H^2(\Omega) representative. Setting \lambda=0 gives the full lower-order operator in Evans Theorem 4.

A compactly supported cutoff localizes the weak equation away from the boundary. Difference quotients give a uniform weighted L^2 estimate for the first derivatives, weak compactness produces the second weak derivatives, and the coordinate derivatives are assembled into the localized H^2 field.

Assume \Omega carries an operational bounded C^1 extension atlas and

-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u)=f,\qquad u\in H^1_0(\Omega),\quad f\in L^2(\Omega),

where the principal coefficients have global C^1 representatives and are uniformly elliptic on \Omega. If \eta_0 is the atlas's interior cutoff, then \eta_0u has an H^2(\Omega) representative.

Choose an outer cutoff equal to one near K. Its product with u belongs to H^1_0(\Omega) and satisfies a divergence-form equation whose commutator forcing lies in L^2. Choose a second cutoff inside the region where the first equals one and apply the quantitative zero-trace difference-quotient theorem. On the second cutoff region the localized field and u agree almost everywhere, so the resulting H^2 field represents the original weak solution near K.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be open and let u\in H^1(\Omega) solve

-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u)=f

weakly against every H^1_0(\Omega) test function. Assume f\in L^2(\Omega). The theorem takes a selected coefficient field with entries in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n) admitting globally Lipschitz representatives. The selected matrix field is almost-everywhere uniformly elliptic on all of \mathbb R^n with a positive lower bound. For every compact K\subset\Omega, there is an open set V with

K\subset V\subset\Omega

such that the restriction of u has an H^2(V) representative. No boundary condition on u is assumed.

The weak Poisson identity says directly that the first weak derivative of u has weak derivative -f. The second-derivative assembly theorem then combines the base value, first derivative, and second derivative into one W^{2,2} representative.

On an open subset of the real line, let u\in H^1_0 satisfy the weak Poisson identity with forcing f\in L^2. (The openness assumption is carried by the weak Poisson solution predicate.) Then u has a W^{2,2} representative whose first coordinate derivative agrees with the weak first derivative of u and whose second weak derivative is -f almost everywhere. This one-dimensional Dirichlet analogue of the difference-quotient theorem needs no boundary atlas.

Construct the interior piece and every boundary-chart piece, then assemble their finite partition of unity in H^2. Equality of each Sobolev base coordinate with its localized weak solution makes the assembled base coordinate equal to the original H^1_0 function almost everywhere.

On a domain carrying the operational C^2 boundary atlas,

-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u)=f,\qquad u\in H^1_0(\Omega),\quad f\in L^2(\Omega),\quad a^{ij}\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega),

with global C^1 coefficient representatives and a positive uniform ellipticity constant, implies u\in H^2(\Omega) in the representative sense. The representative equals the original weak solution almost everywhere. This is the principal case b=c=0.

Apply first-order cutoff localization to obtain the weak equation for \rho u. Its forcing is the original forcing multiplied by \rho together with the two coefficient-cutoff commutators. Repeated weak Leibniz rules, finite derivative-word sums, and the general W^{k,\infty}\times W^{k,2}\to W^{k,2} multiplier theorem put every term in W^{k,2}. The cutoff factors also show that the assembled forcing vanishes almost everywhere off the support of \rho.

Let k>0 and let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be open. Suppose a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}(\Omega), f\in W^{k,2}(\Omega), and u\in W^{k+1,2}(\Omega) represents an H^1_0(\Omega) weak solution of

-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u)=f.

For every smooth compactly supported cutoff \rho on \mathbb R^n, the product w=\rho u has an H^1_0(\Omega) representative and there is a forcing G\in W^{k,2}(\Omega), supported where \rho is supported, such that

-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j w)=G

weakly on \Omega.

The case m=0 is the compact-set H^2 theorem. For the successor step, first apply the induction hypothesis on an intermediate neighborhood of K, then restrict the weak equation and all Sobolev coefficient and forcing data to that neighborhood. A cutoff equal to one near K localizes the equation, with commutator forcing at the required Sobolev order. Apply the preceding-order regularity theorem to each differentiated localized field, then assemble those first derivatives to gain one order for the localized solution. Restricting once more to the cutoff-one region removes the cutoff and yields the claimed W^{m+3,2} representative of the original solution.

Let m\geq0, let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be open, and suppose u\in H^1(\Omega) is a weak solution of

-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u)=f.

Assume the coefficient matrix has globally Lipschitz representatives for the H^2 base step. More precisely, the theorem takes a coefficient field with entries in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n), requires its almost-everywhere ellipticity hypothesis on all of \mathbb R^n, and requires its restriction to \Omega to agree with one coherent W^{m+1,\infty}(\Omega) bundle. If f\in W^{m,2}(\Omega), then every compact K\subset\Omega has an open neighborhood V with K\subset V\subset\Omega on which u has a W^{m+2,2}(V) representative. No trace or boundary condition is imposed on u.

The all-order elliptic bootstrap supplies a representative in every finite Sobolev order. For requested classical order m, Sobolev iteration gives a W^{m+1,2n} representative. Higher-order Morrey embedding produces continuous representatives for the weak derivatives, and the weak-to-classical reconstruction theorem identifies adjacent representatives as Fréchet derivatives on \Omega. Almost-everywhere agreement and continuity identify the representatives pointwise, so one function belongs to C^m(\Omega) for every finite m.

Let n\geq1. Assume an operationally smooth boundary, coherent principal coefficients and forcing data at every Sobolev order, and a positive ellipticity lower bound. Let u\in H^1_0(\Omega) be a homogeneous Dirichlet weak solution of -\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u)=f with these data. Then u has a representative v satisfying

v\in C^\infty(\Omega), \qquad v=u\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega.

Apply arbitrary-order elliptic regularity at every finite order. The completed-space embedding theorem gives a C^m(\overline\Omega) representative for each m. Any two representatives agree almost everywhere with the same solution; continuity first upgrades this to pointwise equality on \Omega and then on its closure. One representative therefore has every finite derivative order on \overline\Omega.

Let n\geq1. Assume smooth compatible boundary charts, principal coefficients represented coherently at every Sobolev order, compatible forcing data at every order, and uniform ellipticity. Let u\in H^1_0(\Omega) be a homogeneous Dirichlet weak solution of -\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u)=f with these data. Then u has a single representative v such that

v\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega), \qquad v=u\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega.

In every positive dimension, the Euclidean unit ball has a finite cover by 2n signed coordinate caps together with a smooth subordinate partition of unity. The interior and boundary cutoffs have compact support in their assigned sets and sum exactly to one on the ball. Its global defining function \rho(x)=1-\lVert x\rVert^2 is smooth, is positive exactly in the ball, and has nonzero radial differential on the unit sphere.

The caps cover the sphere: a point of the unit sphere is nonzero, so at least one coordinate is either positive or negative, and the identity \sum_j x_j^2=1 shows that the remaining tangential coordinates have squared norm strictly less than one, placing the point in the corresponding signed cap. Together with the open ball, these finitely many caps cover the closed ball. Mathlib's smooth partition-of-unity theorem supplies the cutoffs, and boundedness of the cover sets makes their supports compact.

Qualitative regularity gives a unique higher-order representative for each forcing. Linearity follows from uniqueness of the base weak solution, and a closed-graph argument upgrades the resulting linear map to a continuous linear map. Its standard operator-norm inequality is the asserted estimate.

The all-orders solution map satisfies, for every f\in H^m(\Omega),

\lVert S_{m+2}f\rVert_{H^{m+2}(\Omega)} \le\lVert S_{m+2}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\, \lVert f\rVert_{H^m(\Omega)}.

For every m\in\mathbb N, the all-orders qualitative theorem and uniqueness of the weak solution produce a bounded linear map

S_{m+2}:H^m(\Omega)\longrightarrow H^{m+2}(\Omega)

under the corresponding chart, coefficient, and ellipticity assumptions. The weak H^1_0 solver uses the canonical order-one restriction of the W^{m+1,\infty} coefficient bundle, while the unreduced bundle supplies the derivatives used by the regularity theorem. The base-coordinate identity characterizes the result without unfolding either restriction or the closed-graph construction.

Lift the stationary continuous linear map pointwise to Bochner L^2. The standard functorial construction gives boundedness and almost-everywhere agreement with pointwise application. Composing with the base-coordinate map yields the weak solution identity. Finally, the stationary operator-norm bound applied almost everywhere preserves the assumed L^\infty envelope.

For any measure \mu on time, the generic higher-order solver acts on Bochner trajectories as a bounded linear map

L^2(\mu;H^m(\Omega)) \longrightarrow L^2(\mu;H^{m+2}(\Omega)).

It agrees almost everywhere with pointwise application of the stationary solver, and its Sobolev base coordinate is almost everywhere the corresponding weak solution. If \lVert r(t)\rVert_{H^m}\leq C almost everywhere, then the lifted trajectory belongs to L^\infty(\mu;H^{m+2}) and satisfies

\lVert S_{m+2}r(t)\rVert_{H^{m+2}} \leq \lVert S_{m+2}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\,C

almost everywhere.

Let \Omega be open, let S:L^2(\Omega)\to H^1_0(\Omega) be a bounded linear weak solver, and suppose every H^m datum has an H^{m+2} representative whose base coordinate is the weak solution Sf. Uniqueness of Sobolev fields from their base coordinate makes this qualitative lift linear. Its graph is closed because both the Sobolev base-coordinate map and the weak solver are continuous. The closed graph theorem therefore gives a canonical bounded linear map

S_{m+2}:H^m(\Omega)\longrightarrow H^{m+2}(\Omega),

whose base coordinate is exactly the original weak solution and whose norm obeys the usual operator-norm estimate. The construction uses nothing about the coefficients, which enter only through the lift hypothesis.

The regularity and uniqueness argument has already bundled the solver as a continuous linear map S_2:L^2(\Omega)\to H^2(\Omega). The conclusion is exactly the defining operator-norm inequality \lVert S_2f\rVert\leq\lVert S_2\rVert\lVert f\rVert.

For every f\in L^2(\Omega), the canonical solution satisfies

\lVert S_2f\rVert_{H^2(\Omega)} \le\lVert S_2\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\, \lVert f\rVert_{L^2(\Omega)}.

The constant is independent of the forcing datum.

Under the hypotheses of the global H^2 theorem, the canonical weak Dirichlet solver lifts to a bounded linear map

S_2:L^2(\Omega)\longrightarrow H^2(\Omega).

Its value is the unique H^2 representative of the weak solution.

For an open domain and a bounded weak Dirichlet solver, the higher-order lift condition means that every H^m forcing has an H^{m+2} representative whose base coordinate is the weak solution S f. Concrete elliptic regularity theorems prove this predicate, and the generic functional-analytic construction takes it as input.

Apply the stationary higher-order solution operator at almost every time. The weak-solution identity and uniqueness identify its base coordinate with the original trajectory. Measurability of the lifted map and the stationary operator-norm bound give the Bochner representative, its essential-supremum estimate, and the asserted almost-everywhere compatibility.

Let the right-hand side belong to L^2(\mu;H^m)\cap L^\infty(\mu;H^m) and the given weak-solution trajectory belong to L^2(\mu;H^1_0). Assume the generic higher-order solver is available and the weak-solution identity holds almost everywhere. Then there exists a trajectory in L^2(\mu;H^{m+2})\cap L^\infty(\mu;H^{m+2}) whose base coordinate agrees almost everywhere with the original weak solution and which obeys the operator-norm estimate. The L^2 memberships are separate hypotheses because the time measure may be infinite.

The coercive Lax–Milgram inverse is bounded, so composing it with the compact mass operator gives a compact map. Expanding B_\gamma=B+\gamma M converts the weak eigenvalue identity into B_\gamma u=(\gamma+\lambda)Mu; uniqueness of the shifted solve then gives the displayed eigenvector equation, and the same calculation reverses.

Suppose

B_\gamma=B+\gamma M

is coercive and M is compact. The single shifted solution operator

R=B_\gamma^{-1}M:V\to V

is compact. Coercivity excludes \gamma+\lambda=0 for every weak eigenvalue. For parameters satisfying \gamma+\lambda\ne0, the reciprocal substitution gives the equivalence

u\text{ is a weak eigenfunction at }\lambda \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Ru=(\gamma+\lambda)^{-1}u,\quad u\ne0.

Translate each weak spectral parameter by the coercive shift and take its reciprocal. This gives an injection into the nonzero eigenvalues of the compact shifted solution operator, whose nonzero spectrum is countable.

For an abstract real weak form admitting a coercive shift and compact mass operator, the exceptional set

\sigma_{\mathrm w}(B,M) =\left\{\lambda\in\mathbb R:E_\lambda\ne\{0\}\right\}

is countable.
Rewrite the eigenspace as the kernel of a compact perturbation of the coercive shifted operator. Fredholm theory makes that kernel finite-dimensional.

For the weak pencil B-\lambda M, define

E_\lambda =\left\{u\in V:\forall v\in V,\ B(u,v)=\lambda M(u,v)\right\}.

If B admits a coercive shift and the mass operator M is compact, then \dim E_\lambda<\infty for every \lambda\in\mathbb R.

Compactness of H^1_0\to L^2 gives a unit minimizer of the Rayleigh quotient, and the minimizer is a weak eigenfunction. Replace it by |u|, which has the same energy and mass and so is again a minimizer. Interior regularity gives a C^2 representative f\ge0 with -\Delta f=\lambda f\ge0, and the strong maximum principle for superharmonic functions on the connected set \Omega makes f>0. To show that \lambda is simple, apply the same argument to |w|: every nonzero eigenfunction w has a representative with no zeros in \Omega. Given eigenfunctions u and v, pick a point x_0 and a constant c with v(x_0)=c\,u(x_0). Then v-cu is an eigenfunction or zero, and it vanishes at x_0, so it is zero.

Let n\ge1 and let \Omega be a nonempty, bounded, open, connected set. There are \lambda>0, u\in H^1_0(\Omega) with \lVert u\rVert_{L^2}=1, and a function f equal to u almost everywhere, such that u is a weak Dirichlet eigenfunction of -\Delta with eigenvalue \lambda, the number \lambda is the least value of \int|\nabla v|^2/\int v^2 over v\in H^1_0(\Omega)\setminus\{0\}, and

f\in C^2(\Omega),\qquad -\Delta f=\lambda f\ \text{ and }\ f>0\ \text{ in }\Omega.

Any two weak eigenfunctions for this least Rayleigh value are multiples of each other.
The argument of the Laplacian case applies with the matrix operator in place of -\Delta, after the interior bootstrap and the expansion of the divergence into the matrix operator with drift.

Let \Omega be nonempty, bounded, open, and connected in \mathbb R^n, n\ge1, and let a_{ij} be globally Lipschitz, C^1 at points of \Omega, a.e. symmetric and uniformly elliptic, with restrictions in W^{m+1,\infty}(\Omega) for some m with 3+\lfloor n/2\rfloor\le m+2. Then the least Rayleigh value \lambda>0 of \int a_{ij}\partial_iv\,\partial_jv/\int v^2 over H^1_0(\Omega) is attained by a unit eigenfunction u. It has a representative f that is C^2 and positive in \Omega, and satisfies

-\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\partial_{ij}f-\sum_j\Bigl(\sum_i\partial_ia_{ij}\Bigr)\partial_jf =\lambda f\quad\text{in }\Omega.

A strictly increasing real sequence that failed to tend to +\infty would be bounded above. Monotone convergence would then give a finite limit, in contradiction with the absence of finite injective spectral accumulation.

Under the same shifted-coercive and compact-mass hypotheses, every strictly increasing sequence of weak eigenvalues satisfies

\lambda_j\longrightarrow+\infty.

For every weak eigenvalue, the compact-reduction equation gives the norm bound

1\leq |\gamma+\lambda_j|\,\lVert R\rVert.

Passing to a hypothetical limit first rules out the singular value \lambda=-\gamma. The reciprocals (\gamma+\lambda_j)^{-1} then form an injective convergent sequence of nonzero eigenvalues of the compact operator R. Compact spectral theory forces their limit to be zero, contradicting the fact that the finite non-singular limit has a nonzero reciprocal.

Under the same hypotheses, if \lambda_j\in\sigma_{\mathrm w}(B,M) are pairwise distinct, there is no \lambda\in\mathbb R for which

\lambda_j\longrightarrow\lambda.

Thus the weak spectrum has no finite accumulation point.

Since \Omega is open and nonempty it has positive measure, so L^2(\Omega) is infinite-dimensional. Poincaré's inequality makes B coercive, Rellich's theorem makes H^1_0\to L^2 compact, and the embedding has dense range. An abstract theorem for a symmetric coercive form with a compact dense embedding produces the ordered basis. Its eigenvalues increase to infinity, and the k-th is the least uniform Rayleigh bound on (k+1)-dimensional subspaces, attained on the span of the first k+1 eigenfunctions. For L^\infty coefficients the weak eigenvalue equation is rewritten as the divergence-form equation with load \lambda_kw_k.

Let n\ge1 and let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be nonempty, open, and bounded. Let B be the Dirichlet form of symmetric, uniformly elliptic coefficients (bounded operators on L^2, or measurable L^\infty functions). There are an orthonormal basis (w_k)_{k\ge0} of L^2(\Omega), functions u_k\in H^1_0(\Omega) with u_k=w_k in L^2, and numbers

0<\lambda_0\le\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\cdots\to\infty,

such that each u_k is a weak Dirichlet eigenfunction with eigenvalue \lambda_k, and

\lambda_k=\min\Bigl\{\,r:\ \exists W\subseteq H^1_0(\Omega),\ \dim W=k+1, \ B(v,v)\le r\lVert v\rVert_{L^2}^2\ \ \forall v\in W\Bigr\}.

No regularity of \partial\Omega and no connectedness is assumed. The indexing starts at 0, so \lambda_0 is the first eigenvalue.

Since c\ge0, the Dirichlet problem for L has a compact inverse on L^2 that maps nonnegative functions to nonnegative functions. An interior subeigenvector and Schaefer's fixed point theorem give a normalized nonnegative eigenvector. Elliptic regularity up to the smooth boundary makes it smooth on \overline\Omega with zero boundary values, and the strong maximum principle makes it positive inside. Shifting the potential, the same construction gives a positive eigenfunction of the formal adjoint with the same eigenvalue r. Testing a complex eigenfunction against this positive weight and comparing moduli gives r+s\le|\lambda+s| for every s\ge0, and letting s\to\infty gives r\le\operatorname{Re}\lambda. Every nonzero real eigenfunction for r has a representative with no zeros, so a combination vanishing at one point vanishes identically, which is geometric simplicity. A complex eigenfunction for the real value r splits into two real ones.

Let \Omega be bounded, open, and connected with C^k graph boundary for every k. Let L have smooth coefficients, a symmetric principal part with ellipticity constant \alpha>0, a drift, and a potential c\ge0. There are r>0 and z\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega) with z=0 on \partial\Omega, z>0 in \Omega, Lz=rz in \Omega, and \lVert z\rVert_{L^2}=1, such that:

  • z represents a weak Dirichlet eigenfunction u\in H^1_0\cap H^2 for r;

  • every real weak eigenfunction for r is a multiple of u, and every complex one is a complex multiple of u;

  • every complex weak eigenvalue \lambda of L satisfies r\le\operatorname{Re}\lambda.

Apply the Fredholm dichotomy to the shifted pencil. Absence from the weak spectrum is exactly triviality of the homogeneous kernel; the alternative then gives existence and uniqueness for every load, and the converse follows by testing the zero load.

Under the shifted-coercive and compact-mass hypotheses,

\lambda\notin\sigma_{\mathrm w}(B,M) \iff \forall F\in V^*,\ \exists!\,u\in V,\ \forall v\in V,\ B(u,v)-\lambda M(u,v)=F(v).

So absence of a homogeneous weak eigenfunction is equivalent to unique solvability of the inhomogeneous pencil for every continuous dual load.

For continuous forms B,M:V\to V^*, the pencil at the real parameter \lambda is

P_\lambda=B-\lambda M.

A weak eigenfunction is a nonzero u\in V satisfying

B(u,v)=\lambda M(u,v)\qquad(\forall v\in V).

The weak spectrum \sigma_{\mathrm w}(B,M) is the set of parameters admitting such a field, while the weak eigenspace is the full kernel E_\lambda=\ker P_\lambda, including zero.

For a bounded bilinear form B:H\times H\to\mathbb R and a continuous dual load \ell\in H^*, a weak solution is an element u\in H satisfying

B(u,v)=\ell(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H.

This is Evans's variational definition for a bounded bilinear form B, which need not come from a differential operator.

Suppose x_n\to x and Ax_n\to y. Integrating the orbit derivative gives T(t)x_n-x_n=\int_0^tT(s)Ax_n\,ds. Continuity of T(s) and Bochner integration passes this identity to the limit. Dividing by t and sending t\downarrow0 shows that x\in D(A) and Ax=y.

For every strongly continuous semigroup on a Banach space, the infinitesimal generator has a closed graph in X\times X. The local operator bounds needed to pass to the limit follow from strong continuity and completeness.

A contraction semigroup satisfies \lVert T(t)\rVert\leq1 for every nonnegative time. Consequently each evolution map is nonexpansive, and the norm of an orbit and the distance between two orbits are nonincreasing in time.

Average the orbit over [0,\varepsilon] and divide by \varepsilon. The semigroup law computes the generator of this average from its endpoint difference, so each average lies in D(A). Strong continuity at zero makes the averages converge to the original vector, proving density.

For every strongly continuous semigroup on a Banach space,

\overline{D(A)}=X.

No contractivity bound is needed.
The difference quotient at T(t)x is, by the semigroup law, T(t) applied to the difference quotient at x. Passing to the strong limit through the bounded linear operator T(t) gives A(T(t)x)=T(t)Ax.

For x in the generator domain,

A(T(t)x)=T(t)(Ax).

As with invariance, neither contractivity nor completeness is needed.
The restrictions T(t)|_{D(A)} themselves form a strongly continuous semigroup on D(A) with its inherited norm.

If Ax is the strong derivative of T(h)x at zero, the semigroup law rewrites the difference quotient at T(t)x as T(t) applied to the difference quotient at x. Continuity and linearity of T(t) pass the limit through, giving generator value T(t)Ax and hence T(t)x\in D(A).

Every semigroup operator preserves the generator domain:

x\in D(A)\Longrightarrow T(t)x\in D(A) \qquad(t\geq0).

This holds for every strongly continuous semigroup, with neither contractivity nor completeness.
Generator commutation rewrites the map as the ordinary semigroup orbit of Ax. Strong continuity of the semigroup then gives continuity directly.
For x\in D(A), the map t\mapsto A(T(t)x)=T(t)(Ax) is continuous.

The infinitesimal generator is the strong derivative at zero within [0,\infty). Its natural domain and values form Mathlib's partial linear map A\colon X\to_{\mathrm{lin}}X; uniqueness of one-sided derivatives makes the value Ax well-defined.

Contractivity gives \lVert e^{-\lambda t}T(t)x\rVert\leq e^{-\lambda t}\lVert x\rVert. The norm estimate for the Bochner integral and \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}\,dt=\lambda^{-1} yield the operator bound.

The Laplace transform satisfies Evans's sharp contraction estimate

\lVert R_\lambda\rVert\leq\lambda^{-1}.

For x\in D(A), differentiate e^{-\lambda t}T(t)x and integrate from zero to infinity; exponential decay removes the boundary term at infinity and gives R_\lambda(\lambda-A)x=x. Applying the same integrated difference-quotient calculation to arbitrary y shows R_\lambda y\in D(A) and (\lambda-A)R_\lambda y=y. The two identities give bijectivity.

The Laplace operator maps X into D(A) and is the two-sided inverse of \lambda-A:

R_\lambda(\lambda-A)x=x\quad(x\in D(A)),

(\lambda-A)R_\lambda y=y\quad(y\in X).

In particular, every positive \lambda lies in the resolvent set in the concrete sense that \lambda-A maps the generator domain bijectively onto X.

For a contraction semigroup on a Banach space and \lambda>0, the Bochner integral

R_\lambda x=\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}T(t)x\,dt

defines a bounded linear operator on X.

At zero the generator definition gives the right derivative. The semigroup law transports it to every nonnegative time, and strong continuity makes s\mapsto T(s)Ax continuous. On a Banach space, the fundamental theorem for right derivatives gives T(s)x=x+\int_0^sT(r)Ax\,dr. Near a positive time, the orbit therefore agrees with a differentiable Bochner primitive. Its ordinary derivative is T(t)Ax, continuous in t by strong continuity.

Every orbit starting in the generator domain solves the abstract homogeneous Cauchy problem. At time zero the derivative is taken within [0,\infty). This one-sided statement holds on a normed space. If the ambient space is Banach, then at every positive real time the orbit has the ordinary two-sided derivative T(t)(Ax), and the resulting orbit is C^1 on (0,\infty).

A strongly continuous semigroup consists of bounded linear evolution operators T(t) for nonnegative time, with T(0)=I, T(s+t)=T(s)T(t), and a continuous orbit t\mapsto T(t)x for every vector x. This definition requires only a real normed space; completeness enters when the orbits are integrated.

The global weak subgradient-flow theorem gives unique trajectories on D. Monotonicity of the subdifferential makes the distance between two trajectories nonincreasing. At each fixed time the solution map is therefore 1-Lipschitz, so it extends uniquely from the dense set D to the complete space \overline D. The identity and composition laws pass to the closure by continuity. Contraction controls changes of initial data uniformly in time, while continuity of each orbit controls changes of time; together they give joint continuity. Any other flow agreeing on D agrees everywhere by density.

Let H be a real Hilbert space and I:H\to(-\infty,+\infty] be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. There is a unique jointly continuous flow S:[0,\infty)\times\overline{\operatorname{dom}\partial I} \to\overline{\operatorname{dom}\partial I} which is contractive and agrees with every weak subgradient trajectory starting in \operatorname{dom}\partial I. In particular,

S(0)x=x,\qquad S(s+t)x=S(s)(S(t)x),\qquad \|S(t)x-S(t)y\|\le\|x-y\|.

For initial values in the closure the orbit is continuous and contractive; the weak velocity and the subgradient inclusion are part of the domain theorem for initial values in \operatorname{dom}\partial I.

The Yosida approximations have a common speed bound supplied by an initial subgradient and converge uniformly on each bounded time interval. Their limit has a weak velocity satisfying the subgradient inclusion; countable exhaustion of the positive half-line gives one global velocity. Choosing the least-norm initial subgradient sharpens the speed bound. Monotonicity gives contraction between weak trajectories, hence uniqueness for equal initial data; uniqueness of the weak derivative identifies their velocities almost everywhere.

Let H be a real Hilbert space, I:H\to(-\infty,+\infty] proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and x_0\in D=\operatorname{dom}\partial I. There is a continuous trajectory u:[0,\infty)\to H with u(0)=x_0 and a Bochner velocity g\in L^\infty((0,\infty);H) such that

u'=g\quad\text{in distributions},\qquad -g(t)\in\partial I(u(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t>0.

The trajectory is unique in this continuous weak class, and the velocity is unique almost everywhere. Every u(t) belongs to D. If p_0 is the least-norm element of \partial I(x_0), then

\|u(t)-u(s)\|\le\|p_0\||t-s|,\qquad \|g(t)\|\le\|p_0\|\quad\text{for almost every }t>0.

No density of D or separability of H is required.

Annihilation of V_\sigma=\ker D is precisely the kernel inclusion \ker D\subseteq\ker\ell. Factor \ell through the closed range of D and apply Fréchet–Riesz representation there. The representative belongs to \operatorname{range}D, satisfies the displayed pairing identity, and is unique because the difference of two such representatives is both in the range and orthogonal to it. The adjoint identity is the same equality tested against every v\in V.

Assume now that V and Q are real Hilbert spaces and that D has closed range. If \ell\in V^* annihilates every solenoidal vector, then there is a unique p\in\operatorname{range}D such that

\ell(v)=\langle p,Dv\rangle_Q\qquad(v\in V).

The chosen pressure satisfies the equivalent adjoint equation

D^*p=R_V^{-1}\ell.

The range condition fixes the otherwise possible pressure gauge. A concrete Sobolev divergence operator still requires its own closed-range or inf-sup theorem; given that input, this result reconstructs the pressure.

Rotation through \theta around the third coordinate axis preserves the cylindrical variables r=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2} and z=x_3. Scalar fields may therefore be represented by meridian profiles g(r,z), while vector fields use the corresponding equivariance condition.

Expand the first two coordinates using the angle-addition formulas for sine and cosine. Their squared sum is unchanged, the third coordinate is fixed, and invariance of a meridian lift follows because its two inputs are unchanged.

The rotations form an additive action,

R_{\theta+\phi}x=R_\theta(R_\phi x),

preserve r and z, and every meridian lift x\mapsto g(r(x),z(x)) is rotation invariant.

The divergence cancellation is equality of mixed partial derivatives. The velocity identities cancel the nonzero radius in the reconstruction formulas. For the radial lift, apply the product rule twice to r^2\phi, substitute into L, and collect the radial terms.

A C^2 streamfunction generates conservative meridian flux with zero divergence. Away from r=0, the reconstructed velocities satisfy the two displayed flux identities, and for \psi=r^2\phi,

L(r^2\phi) =r^2\left(\partial_{rr}\phi+\frac3r\partial_r\phi+\partial_{zz}\phi\right).

For a meridian streamfunction \psi(r,z), we use

r u_r=-\partial_z\psi,\qquad r u_z=\partial_r\psi, \qquad L\psi=\partial_{rr}\psi-r^{-1}\partial_r\psi+\partial_{zz}\psi.

Division by r is totalized in Lean, so velocity and vorticity statements that use it retain an explicit off-axis hypothesis r\ne0.

The swirl part is divergence free because \partial_1(-x_2U)+\partial_2(x_1U) equals -2x_1x_2U_s+2x_1x_2U_s=0. For the meridional part, the chain rule through s=x_1^2+x_2^2 gives

\partial_1(-x_1\Psi_z)+\partial_2(-x_2\Psi_z)=-2\Psi_z-2s\Psi_{sz}, \qquad \partial_3(2\Psi+2s\Psi_s)=2\Psi_z+2s\Psi_{sz},

which cancel. Equivariance follows because s and x_3 are rotation invariant while (-x_1,-x_2) and (-x_2,x_1) rotate with the point.

If U is C^1 and \Psi is C^2 on the whole (s,z)-plane, the reconstructed velocity is divergence free on all of \mathbb R^3, the axis included. It is equivariant under rotations about the x_3-axis, and on the axis its first two components vanish. Smooth profiles give a smooth velocity.

For profiles U,\Psi of (s,z) and x=(x_1,x_2,x_3) with s=x_1^2+x_2^2, the reconstructed velocity is the sum of

\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{mer}}(x)&=\bigl(-x_1\Psi_z,\;-x_2\Psi_z,\;2\Psi+2s\,\Psi_s\bigr),\\ u_{\mathrm{swirl}}(x)&=\bigl(-x_2U,\;x_1U,\;0\bigr), \end{aligned}

with every profile evaluated at (s,x_3). In cylindrical components these are u_r=-r\Psi_z, u_z=2\Psi+2r^2\Psi_s and u_\theta=rU.

The curl is linear, so the meridional and swirl parts are treated separately. Each component is a product of a coordinate with a lifted profile; the chain rule for s produces the factors 2x_1 and 2x_2, and collecting terms gives the displayed coefficients.

For C^1 swirl and C^2 streamfunction profiles,

\nabla\times u=\bigl(x_2M-x_1U_z,\;-x_1M-x_2U_z,\;2U+2s\,U_s\bigr), \qquad M=\Psi_{zz}+8\Psi_s+4s\Psi_{ss}.

The vorticity of the swirl has the same shape as the meridional velocity of a streamfunction, with U in place of \Psi. The azimuthal part is \omega_\theta=-rM, so \omega_1=-M, and M is the operator L of the reduced system rewritten in the variable s.

In cylindrical coordinates |u|^2=r^2u_1^2+r^2(\partial_z\psi_1)^2 +(2\psi_1+r\partial_r\psi_1)^2. Expanding the last square gives 4\psi_1^2+4r\psi_1\partial_r\psi_1+r^2(\partial_r\psi_1)^2. Against the weight r, the first two terms are \partial_r(2r^2\psi_1^2), which integrates to zero on almost every axial line because the moment of \psi_1^2 is finite. The cylindrical change of variables then gives the factor 2\pi.

Let U be continuous and \Psi be C^1, and write u_1=U(r^2,z), \psi_1=\Psi(r^2,z). If r^2u_1^2, r^2\psi_1^2, r^2(\partial_r\psi_1)^2 and r^2(\partial_z\psi_1)^2 are integrable for the meridian measure r\,dr\,dz, then u\in L^2(\mathbb R^3) and

\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u|^2\,dx =2\pi\int_0^\infty\!\!\int_{\mathbb R} r^2\bigl(u_1^2+(\partial_r\psi_1)^2+(\partial_z\psi_1)^2\bigr)\,r\,dz\,dr.

The stream equation identifies \omega with \nabla\times u near each point of D, after replacing the profiles by compactly supported smooth ones that agree nearby. The vorticity equation then says that the vector field \nu\Delta u-D_tu has zero curl on each slice. On a convex open set a curl-free smooth field is a gradient, which is the Navier–Stokes pressure theorem for the vorticity form.

Let U,\Omega,\Psi be smooth on an open set D of profile arguments and satisfy \Omega=-L_s\Psi, R_U=0 and R_\Omega=0 there. On every open convex spatial set S and every time set I whose points map into D, there is a pressure p(t,\cdot) with

\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p=\nu\Delta u \qquad\text{on }I\times S.

The pressure is chosen independently on each time slice.

Off the axis, the reduced Navier–Stokes system for (u_1,\omega_1,\psi_1) with viscosity \nu is

\begin{aligned} \partial_tu_1+u_r\partial_ru_1+u_z\partial_zu_1 &=2u_1\,\partial_z\psi_1+\nu\,L u_1,\\ \partial_t\omega_1+u_r\partial_r\omega_1+u_z\partial_z\omega_1 &=2u_1\,\partial_zu_1+\nu\,L\omega_1,\\ -L\psi_1&=\omega_1, \end{aligned} \qquad L=\partial_r^2+\tfrac3r\partial_r+\partial_z^2.

The source terms describe stretching and vorticity production: swirl is stretched by axial variation of the streamfunction, and the centrifugal term \partial_z(u_1^2) creates azimuthal vorticity. Lean records each equation as a pointwise residual in the meridian coordinates, and the reduced system asks all three to vanish on a chosen domain and time set.

The squared-radius residuals are

R_U=D_tU-2U\Psi_z-\nu L_sU,\qquad R_\Omega=D_t\Omega-2UU_z-\nu L_s\Omega,

and \nu=0 gives the Euler versions. The vorticity reconstructed from the coefficients is

\omega=\bigl(-x_1U_z-x_2\Omega,\;-x_2U_z+x_1\Omega,\;2U+2sU_s\bigr),

in which \Omega is a separate unknown. It becomes the curl of the velocity only once the stream equation \Omega=-L_s\Psi holds.

Each Cartesian component of the transport residual is computed explicitly and turns out to be a combination of the lifted reduced residuals with polynomial coefficients in x. The stretching term (\omega\cdot\nabla)u supplies the sources 2U\Psi_z and 2UU_z, and the lifted viscous term reproduces L_s. When both reduced residuals vanish, every component vanishes.

If U,\Omega,\Psi are smooth and R_U=R_\Omega=0, the Cartesian velocity u and the reconstructed vorticity \omega satisfy the three-dimensional vorticity equation

\partial_t\omega+(u\cdot\nabla)\omega-(\omega\cdot\nabla)u-\nu\Delta\omega=0

everywhere in spacetime. For Euler, C^2 swirl and streamfunction and a C^1 vorticity coefficient suffice. Local versions hold on an open set of profile arguments, where the profiles need not extend past its boundary.

Differentiate the two integrals by the fundamental theorem of calculus. The terms involving g cancel in the first derivative and combine to -g in the second, giving the forced equation. At the left endpoint both integrals vanish; the chosen amplitude cancels the value at the right endpoint. Bounding sine and cosine by one bounds each integral by M\beta and gives the displayed estimate. The homogeneous polar identity then supplies the radial factor.

Let g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be continuous, set L=\pi/2, and suppose -2<\alpha<0. With a=2+\alpha, there is a classical solution

-f''-a^2f=g,\qquad f(0)=f(L)=0.

The construction keeps the resonance condition explicit. Define

\begin{aligned} C(\beta)&=\int_0^\beta\cos(as)g(s)\,ds,\\ S(\beta)&=\int_0^\beta\sin(as)g(s)\,ds. \end{aligned}

Then

\begin{aligned} f(\beta)&=A\sin(a\beta)\\ &\quad+\frac{\cos(a\beta)S(\beta)-\sin(a\beta)C(\beta)}{a},\\ A&=\frac{\sin(aL)C(L)-\cos(aL)S(L)}{a\sin(aL)}. \end{aligned}

Here 0<a<2, so 0<aL<\pi and the denominator is nonzero. Continuous forcing gives f\in C^2. If |g|\leq M on [0,L], with M\geq0, the formula also gives the explicit sufficient bound for 0\leq\beta\leq L:

|f(\beta)|\leq\frac{2ML}{a} \left(1+\frac1{|\sin(aL)|}\right).

On the same interval, its first derivative satisfies

|f'(\beta)|\leq2ML\left(1+\frac1{|\sin(aL)|}\right).

The homogeneous streamfunction r^{2+\alpha}f(\beta) therefore has negative polar Laplacian r^\alpha g(\beta) for r>0. A certified residual gives a quantitative correction as well. Let q\in C^2 have exact zero endpoint values and suppose

|g+q''+a^2q|\leq\delta\quad\text{on }[0,L].

Apply the same inverse to this residual and add the correction to q. The result satisfies the exact forced equation and boundary values, with value error at most 2\delta L(1+1/|\sin(aL)|)/a and first-derivative error at most 2\delta L(1+1/|\sin(aL)|). Thus a tighter residual certificate improves both error bounds through the same theorem.

The inverse also gives a Cartesian field. For positive radius and -\pi<\beta<\pi, the inverse polar Jacobian proves C^2 regularity of the reconstructed streamfunction. The local chart round trip then gives

-\Delta U(r\cos\beta,r\sin\beta)=r^\alpha g(\beta).

This excludes the origin and the chart's negative horizontal cut. If the forcing is odd about L, then the solution is odd there too: f(2L-\beta)=-f(\beta) and f''(L)=0. Uniqueness follows from the conserved energy of the difference of two oscillator solutions with the same initial value and slope. These are tangential angular identities; the normal extension of the source vorticity can jump at the physical boundary and needs a separate weak argument.

The moving-endpoint integral rule gives the initial-response term and the integral of the response derivative. Subtract the spatial evolution inside the integral and retain the difference in R. Adding the complementary equation cancels the forcing and error. The norm estimate follows from the operator bounds and the Bochner integral inequality.

For a continuously differentiable response and continuous coefficients, \widehat W_2'=L\widehat W_2+\chi a+R. If the complementary trajectory satisfies W_1'=LW_1-\chi a-R, their sum solves W'=LW exactly and has the initial value of W_1.

The general statement evaluates values and spatial evolution through bounded maps from a regularity space into the equation space. It does not assume that L is bounded on the equation space. A bound \eta on the initial mismatch and a time-dependent bound \varepsilon on the response residual give

\|R(t)\|\leq\eta\|a(t)\| +\int_0^t\|a(s)\|\varepsilon(t-s)\,ds,\qquad t\geq0.

A classical Boussinesq field consists of velocity u, temperature \theta, and pressure p. On the chosen set of times all three fields are jointly C^1, their relevant slices are classically differentiable, and the three displayed equations hold pointwise. The impermeable boundary condition is a separate predicate, not part of the whole-space model. Velocity is an unknown here, not reconstructed from vorticity or a half-plane streamfunction.

Parametrize the segment by \gamma(t)=tx, 0\leq t\leq1. Compare the operator-valued derivative with the quadratic majorant to obtain \|D(tx)\|\leq K\|x\|^2t^2/2. A second mean value comparison gives \|f(tx)\|\leq K\|x\|^3t^3/6. Both comparisons use derivatives within the segment, including its endpoints. For the smooth version, the third derivative bound and the zero Hessian at the origin supply the required Hessian envelope. Set t=1 and divide by the positive factor \|x\|^3. For the Hölder fields, assemble the derivatives by finite coordinate sums and apply these same comparisons. The Riesz isometry identifies the curried Hessian with the Euclidean matrix operator and preserves its norm.

Suppose a field's value, gradient, and Hessian vanish at the origin, it is C^3 near every point of the segment from 0 to x, and its third derivative has operator norm at most K along that segment. Then, for x\neq0,

\frac{\|f(x)\|}{\|x\|^3}\leq\frac K6.

A more general variant uses supplied derivative fields D and H within the segment. If f(0)=D(0)=0 and

\|H(y)\|\leq K\|y\|,\qquad y\in[0,x],

the same cubic bound holds. Here D is the derivative of f and H is the derivative of D within the segment. This allows a segment that starts on or lies along the domain boundary; no smooth extension across that boundary is needed. The Hessian envelope can be verified directly, without differentiating H.

These estimates apply to vector-valued fields on any real normed space and retain the factor 1/6 for numerical error budgets.

For a scalar field in the bounded C^{k,\gamma} space on an open convex domain, apply the estimate to D^\alpha f whenever |\alpha|+2\leq k. Its gradient and Hessian are already supplied by the derivative graph, even at the boundary. The Hessian's coordinate matrix satisfies

\begin{aligned} A_\alpha(y)_{ij}&=D^{\alpha+e_i+e_j}f(y),\\ \|H_\alpha(y)\|&=\|A_\alpha(y)\|_{2\to2}. \end{aligned}

Thus a certified Euclidean matrix norm bound supplies the required Hessian envelope with its original constant. This is the Euclidean operator norm, rather than an entrywise or row-sum norm. The value and first-derivative traces of D^\alpha f must vanish exactly at the base point. Tighter numerical envelopes can be supplied to the same analytic theorem.

Project each derivative field and evaluate its continuous extension at x. Each value is bounded by the corresponding uniform norm, which is bounded by the graph norm. Taking the maximum preserves that bound. For the boundary derivative, use the interior derivative relation and the continuity of its assembled gradient on the closure. The mean value estimate on a convex domain extends differentiability to the boundary with that limiting gradient. Differentiate the finite coordinate sum to obtain the Hessian relation. For the construction, bundle the bounded continuous fields and their top-order Hölder representatives. Each zero extension agrees locally with its ordinary formula at interior points, so the supplied derivative identities give graph compatibility. Taking maxima or summing the supplied budgets gives the two norm bounds. Interpolate the range bound 2C_\alpha at exponent zero with the Lipschitz bound at exponent one to obtain the stated Hölder constant.

For a field in the bounded C^{k,\gamma} space on \Omega, evaluation of all derivatives through order k at a point x\in\overline\Omega is a bounded linear map into the finite coefficient space with its maximum norm:

Q_x f=(D^\alpha f(x))_{|\alpha|\leq k},\qquad \|Q_x\|\leq1.

The bound uses the Hölder graph norm. At a boundary point, the derivative values are the continuous extensions of the interior derivatives. Selecting the required coordinates gives a trace map for the correction; constructing its right inverse still requires the chosen spatial correction fields. If \Omega is open and convex, the fields of order below k have the prescribed derivatives within \overline\Omega. This also identifies the traces with boundary derivatives, without extending the function across the boundary. For a field with two further derivatives available, differentiating its assembled gradient within the closure gives its assembled Hessian.

Ordinary formulas v_\alpha can define a field in this space directly. On an open \Omega, require continuity on the closure, the successor derivative identities in the interior, uniform bounds \|v_\alpha\|_\infty\leq C_\alpha, and top-order Hölder bounds [v_\alpha]_\gamma\leq H_\alpha. The construction preserves the given interior derivatives and boundary traces. Its graph norm is at most B when every C_\alpha\leq B and every top-order C_\alpha+H_\alpha\leq B. Evans's derivative-sum norm satisfies

\begin{aligned} \|f\|_{\mathrm{Evans}}&\leq\sum_{|\alpha|\leq k}C_\alpha\\ &\quad+\sum_{|\alpha|=k}H_\alpha. \end{aligned}

For a top-order field with Lipschitz constant L_\alpha, interpolation supplies the bound

H_\alpha=(2C_\alpha)^{1-\gamma}L_\alpha^\gamma.

The value and Lipschitz bounds are uniform on the closure; the domain may be unbounded. These per-field constants are inputs, so improving their certificates does not change the construction or the norm comparison.

Differentiate the three pullbacks. The derivative of C_lx contributes -c_l C_lx, which cancels advection by c_lx. The reconstructed velocity has scale C_\omega C_l^{-1}. Vorticity advection and the physical vorticity time-derivative term both carry C_\omega^2; temperature advection carries C_\omega C_\theta. The source derivative carries C_\theta C_l, equal to C_\omega^2 by compatibility. The streamfunction scale contributes C_\omega C_l^{-2}C_l^2=C_\omega, preserving the Poisson equation. Positive C_l preserves the upper half-plane, and the boundary trace remains zero under tangential dilation.

A classical upper-half-plane solution on an open physical-time set satisfies the following transformed system at every rescaled time whose physical-time image belongs to that set and at which the scale laws hold:

\partial_\tau\widetilde\omega+ (c_lx+\widetilde u)\cdot\nabla\widetilde\omega =c_\omega\widetilde\omega+\partial_1\widetilde\theta,

\partial_\tau\widetilde\theta+ (c_lx+\widetilde u)\cdot\nabla\widetilde\theta =c_\theta\widetilde\theta, \qquad -\Delta\widetilde\phi=\widetilde\omega,

with the zero streamfunction boundary trace preserved.

At rescaled time \tau, set

\widetilde\omega(x,\tau)=C_\omega\omega(C_lx,t(\tau)),\qquad \widetilde\theta(x,\tau)=C_\theta\theta(C_lx,t(\tau)),

\widetilde\phi(x,\tau)=C_\omega C_l^{-2}\phi(C_lx,t(\tau)).

The scale laws are C_\omega'=c_\omega C_\omega, C_l'=-c_lC_l, C_\theta'=c_\theta C_\theta, and t'=C_\omega, together with C_\theta C_l=C_\omega^2 and c_\theta=c_l+2c_\omega, with C_l>0 so dilation preserves the upper half-plane. The complete transformed-system predicate reuses the canonical pair of rescaled scalar equations and adds the streamfunction Poisson equation and zero boundary trace.

Differentiate the backward ansatz using the common similarity chain rule. Velocity time differentiation, convection, pressure gradient, and buoyancy all carry the factor (1-t)^{\lambda-1}. Temperature time differentiation and temperature advection both carry (1-t)^{\lambda-2}, while divergence carries (1-t)^{-1}. The three physical residuals are therefore these nonzero factors times the three reduced residuals. The regularity part follows by composing the C^1 profiles with the smooth positive backward power scales on t<1.
Every classical profile satisfying the reduced equations generates a classical solution of the physical Boussinesq system on any time set contained in (-\infty,1).

The coordinate residual has norm below one, so its geometric series converges and inverts Q\Phi. Composing with \Phi gives the exact right inverse. The geometric-series norm bound gives the reconstruction estimates; applying L before taking the norm retains the sharper bound on L\Phi. Use variation of constants for the bounded coefficient operator M, integrating only over the prescribed time interval. The fundamental theorem of calculus within a closed interval gives the derivative at its endpoints as well. Differentiate g+\Psi a, substitute the coefficient equation, and apply Q\Psi=\mathrm{id}. This cancels the extracted traces while leaving the full residual explicit. Apply the propagator formula and the integral norm inequality to bound the coefficients. Apply the projection bound to the full corrected residual to bound its remaining spatial error.

A proposed spatial reconstruction \Phi can first be made exact. Suppose its coordinate residual satisfies

\|\mathrm{id}-Q\Phi\|\leq\delta<1.

The Neumann inverse defines \Psi=\Phi(Q\Phi)^{-1} and gives Q\Psi=\mathrm{id}. The correction retains quantitative bounds:

\begin{aligned} \|\Psi\|&\leq\frac{\|\Phi\|}{1-\delta},\\ \|\Psi-\Phi\|&\leq\frac{\|\Phi\|\delta}{1-\delta},\\ \|L\Psi\|&\leq\frac{\|L\Phi\|}{1-\delta}. \end{aligned}

Only the coefficient space must be complete. A finite-dimensional application therefore needs a certified residual bound, rather than an exact inverse matrix. The residual must use the coefficient space's operator norm; for the full derivative trace map above, the coefficient norm is the maximum norm.

On a closed time interval [0,T], suppose the approximate trajectory is differentiable within the interval and its extracted residual is continuous. With this exact reconstruction, the coefficient equation has an exact solution. The corrected trajectory \widetilde g=g+\Psi a has zero extracted initial error, and

\begin{aligned} \widetilde g'&=L\widetilde g+\widetilde R,\\ \widetilde R&=(\mathrm{id}-\Psi Q)(g'-L\widetilde g),\\ Q\widetilde R&=0. \end{aligned}

The general version includes the value map between the two regularity spaces. It allows any complete normed coefficient space. The spatial correction fields need not be eigenfunctions: their remaining evolution error stays in \widetilde R. Only data on [0,T] are required; at its endpoints the evolution equation uses the corresponding one-sided time derivative.

The same exact coefficient solution has quantitative bounds. Let U(t,s) be the propagator of a'=Ma. For a fixed 0\leq t\leq T, suppose

\begin{aligned} \|U(t,s)\|&\leq C_t(s),\\ \|Q(g'(s)-Lg(s))\|&\leq\varepsilon(s),\\ 0&\leq s\leq t, \end{aligned}

and C_t\varepsilon is integrable. Then

\begin{aligned} \|a(t)\|&\leq C_t(0)\|Q(g(0)-\chi)\|\\ &\quad+\int_0^t C_t(s)\varepsilon(s)\,ds. \end{aligned}

Keeping the envelopes inside the integral preserves their time dependence. The remaining spatial error obeys

\begin{aligned} \|\widetilde R(t)\|&\leq\|\mathrm{id}-\Psi Q\|\\ &\quad\cdot\bigl(\|g'(t)-Lg(t)\|\\ &\qquad+\|L\Psi\|\|a(t)\|\bigr). \end{aligned}

These estimates keep the correction's contribution explicit. Sharper bounds on the propagator, extracted residual, or spatial correction can be supplied to the same analytic theorem.

Apply the generic half-space potential theorem to reflection in coordinate zero. This reflection preserves x_2>0; kernel invariance and the measure-preserving change of variables transfer oddness of \omega to \phi. Boundary cancellation is pointwise in the source variable before integration. Under the normal odd-extension hypothesis, the planar method-of-images theorem identifies the potential with \Phi_2*\omega whenever that convolution is integrable. The compact C^2 inversion theorem then proves the pointwise Poisson equation.

If \omega is odd under R(x_1,x_2)=(-x_1,x_2) and its method-of-images Green integrand is integrable at every field point, then

\phi(x)=\int_{\mathbb H}G_{\mathbb H}(y,x)\omega(y)\,dy

is odd under R and has zero horizontal boundary trace. These conclusions are proved from kernel geometry. Normal oddness together with integrability of \Phi_2(x-\cdot)\omega identifies the same integral with the whole-space convolution, without compact support. If, in addition, \omega is a compactly supported C^2 whole-space function, then the integral is C^2 and satisfies -\Delta\phi=\omega on the upper half-plane. The approximate profile of the paper has a nonintegrable r^{\bar\alpha_1}\simeq r^{-1/3} far field, which Section 7.2.1 treats by a semi-analytic homogeneous streamfunction and an angular Dirichlet ODE before estimating a faster-decaying numerical remainder.

The first normalization identity implies c_l\omega_x(0)=2\theta_{xx}(0). Together with the formulas for c_\omega and c_\theta, elementary algebra cancels both ODE right-hand sides. A differentiable real-valued function whose derivative vanishes on an open connected set is constant there.

Substitution of the three normalization identities makes both trace-ODE right-hand sides zero. Hence, on an open connected time domain where the regularity, upper-half-plane equations, symmetries, and normalization hold at every time,

\omega_x(0,\tau)=\omega_x(0,\tau_0),\qquad \theta_{xx}(0,\tau)=\theta_{xx}(0,\tau_0).

Differentiate the vorticity equation once and the temperature equation twice in the tangential variable. At the origin, parity and the two zero traces remove the normal and undifferentiated transport terms. Expanding the remaining advection products gives the two displayed scalar ODEs.

For sufficiently smooth space-time fields satisfying the rescaled equations on the open upper half-plane and the stated symmetries,

\frac{d}{d\tau}\omega_x(0)= (c_\omega-c_l-u_x(0))\omega_x(0)+\theta_{xx}(0),

\frac{d}{d\tau}\theta_{xx}(0)= \bigl(c_\theta-2(c_l+u_x(0))\bigr)\theta_{xx}(0).

These are derived from equation (2.8) by differentiating in the tangential direction, extending the differentiated identities continuously to the origin, and commuting space and time derivatives. The fields are represented by smooth extensions across the boundary, but the equations are assumed only on the open upper half-plane.

At the origin write \omega_x=\partial_1\omega, \theta_{xx}=\partial_1^2\theta, and u_x=\partial_1u_1. The normalization is

c_l=\frac{2\theta_{xx}(0)}{\omega_x(0)},\qquad c_\omega=\frac12c_l+u_x(0),\qquad c_\theta=c_l+2c_\omega,

with the necessary condition \omega_x(0)\ne0. The accompanying symmetry predicates distinguish the minimal cancellations used at the origin from the streamfunction-level assumptions that imply them.

Expand the two velocity components. The divergence is -\partial_1\partial_2\phi+\partial_2\partial_1\phi, which vanishes by the C^2 mixed-partial theorem. Expanding either scalar curl leaves the two diagonal second derivatives with the corresponding sign.
For a C^2 streamfunction, the velocity is incompressible, its standard scalar curl is \Delta\phi, and its clockwise scalar curl is -\Delta\phi.

For a planar streamfunction \phi, define

u=(-\partial_2\phi,\partial_1\phi).

The counterclockwise scalar curl of a planar velocity is \partial_1u_2-\partial_2u_1; the clockwise curl \partial_2u_1-\partial_1u_2 is the convention of the paper.

The Laplacian is invariant under R, so -\phi\circ R solves the same Poisson equation as \phi. It has the same zero boundary trace and remains in \mathcal A by reflection stability. Uniqueness in \mathcal A gives -\phi\circ R=\phi.

Let R(x_1,x_2)=(-x_1,x_2) and let \mathcal A be an admissible class of whole-plane streamfunctions, closed under \phi\mapsto-\phi\circ R. Suppose \phi\in\mathcal A is C^2 on the whole plane and the Dirichlet problem is unique in \mathcal A. Then

-\Delta\phi=\omega\text{ in }\mathbb H,\qquad \phi|_{\partial\mathbb H}=0,\qquad \omega\circ R=-\omega \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \phi\circ R=-\phi.

The theorem keeps \mathcal A explicit. Uniqueness among all smooth functions on the unbounded half-plane would be false without a decay, energy, or representation condition.

Take clockwise curl locally inside the open spatial domain. Equality on a neighborhood gives equality of the required coordinate derivatives, while mixed derivatives cancel the pressure curl. For a divergence-free planar velocity, the curl of the convective term is u\cdot\nabla\omega; the vertical force contributes -\kappa\partial_1\theta. The streamfunction identities then provide incompressibility and -\Delta\phi=\omega, while the primitive scalar transport equation and zero trace give the remaining solution fields and boundary condition.

Assume u is jointly C^2 on spacetime and, at the time considered, p and \theta are respectively C^2 and C^1 on the whole plane. If the primitive momentum force is \kappa\theta e_2 and clockwise vorticity is \omega=\partial_2u_1-\partial_1u_2, then on every open spatial domain where the primitive momentum equation and incompressibility hold,

\partial_t\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega=-\kappa\,\partial_1\theta.

Thus the paper's positive source is the downward-buoyancy choice \kappa=-1. Under that convention, with a supplied C^2 streamfunction satisfying u=(-\partial_2\phi,\partial_1\phi) and the zero boundary trace, a primitive solution with jointly continuously differentiable temperature solving both the momentum equation with force -\theta e_2 and the temperature transport equation induces the full upper-half-plane vorticity–streamfunction solution predicate.

The stationary profile equations are

\nabla\cdot U=0,

-\lambda U+(1+\lambda)(y\cdot\nabla)U +(U\cdot\nabla)U+\nabla P-\Theta e_2=0,

(1-\lambda)\Theta+(1+\lambda)y\cdot\nabla\Theta +U\cdot\nabla\Theta=0.

The profile predicate also requires global first-order classical regularity; the residual equalities alone would otherwise use totalized derivatives.

Both sides of each interior identity are continuous. Equality therefore passes to the closure. On an open domain, the differentiated statements follow by first differentiating the equality and then applying the same closure argument to the continuous derivative fields.

For globally continuously differentiable representatives, either rescaled scalar equation holding on a spatial domain also holds on its closure. If the domain is open, then with one further degree of regularity for each spatial differentiation, the once-differentiated vorticity equation and twice-differentiated temperature equation extend to the closure as well. This applies in particular to the open upper half-plane.

Writing L_\omega=\partial_\tau\omega+V\cdot\nabla\omega, R_\omega=c_\omega\omega+\partial_1\theta, L_\theta=\partial_\tau\theta+V\cdot\nabla\theta, and R_\theta=c_\theta\theta, the conclusions are

L_\omega=R_\omega\text{ on }\Omega \Longrightarrow L_\omega=R_\omega\text{ and }\partial_iL_\omega=\partial_iR_\omega \text{ on }\overline{\Omega},

L_\theta=R_\theta\text{ on }\Omega \Longrightarrow L_\theta=R_\theta\text{ and } \partial_i\partial_jL_\theta=\partial_i\partial_jR_\theta \text{ on }\overline{\Omega}.
Expand the residual as the left side minus the right side and rearrange.

Each rescaled scalar equation holds on a domain exactly when its pointwise residual vanishes throughout that domain.

L_\omega=R_\omega\text{ on }\Omega \Longleftrightarrow \mathcal R_\omega=0\text{ on }\Omega, \qquad L_\theta=R_\theta\text{ on }\Omega \Longleftrightarrow \mathcal R_\theta=0\text{ on }\Omega.

For rate functions c_l,c_\omega,c_\theta, the rescaled transport velocity is

V(x,\tau)=c_l(\tau)x+u(x,\tau).

The scalar part of the rescaled system is the pair of pointwise equations

\partial_\tau\omega+V\cdot\nabla\omega =c_\omega\omega+\partial_1\theta, \qquad \partial_\tau\theta+V\cdot\nabla\theta=c_\theta\theta.

The equations are stated for arbitrary rate functions, independently of any particular scaling data, and may be imposed either at one time or on a specified space-time domain. The two residual functions are the left side minus the right side of the corresponding equation.

For an exponent \lambda and profiles U,\Theta,P, set

y=\frac{x}{(1-t)^{1+\lambda}},\qquad u=(1-t)^\lambda U(y),\qquad \theta=(1-t)^{\lambda-1}\Theta(y),\qquad p=(1-t)^{2\lambda}P(y).

The ansatz is an instance of the common backward-similarity transformation. The quotient formula is used analytically only for t<1, where the real-power base is positive.

Differentiate \phi\circ R=-\phi. Tangential differentiation introduces one sign from R and one from oddness, while normal differentiation introduces only the sign from oddness. The boundary identity follows by differentiating the zero trace tangentially.

Let R(x_1,x_2)=(-x_1,x_2) and u=(-\partial_2\phi,\partial_1\phi). If a C^1 streamfunction is odd under R, then

\partial_2\phi(Rx)=-\partial_2\phi(x),\qquad \partial_1\phi(Rx)=\partial_1\phi(x),

and therefore u_1(Rx)=-u_1(x) while u_2(Rx)=u_2(x). If in addition \phi(x_1,0)=0, then u_2(x_1,0)=0. Thus the scalar symmetries together with odd streamfunction parity and the Dirichlet trace imply all velocity conditions used by the normalization calculation.

The first two claims are the planar streamfunction identities. For the boundary claim, restrict \phi to the horizontal coordinate line. Its trace is the constant zero function, so its tangential derivative \partial_1\phi vanishes. This derivative is precisely the normal velocity component.

The streamfunction equation identifies \omega with the clockwise curl of u; the reconstructed velocity is incompressible; and a differentiable zero streamfunction trace implies zero normal velocity at x_2=0.

On \mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2>0\}, the physical equations are

\partial_t\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega=\partial_1\theta, \qquad \partial_t\theta+u\cdot\nabla\theta=0, \qquad -\Delta\phi=\omega.

The boundary trace is \phi(x_1,0,t)=0. The fields are defined on the whole plane. Vorticity and temperature are jointly C^1 on the admitted times, with ambient time differentiability there; every streamfunction slice is spatially C^2. No joint time regularity of the streamfunction is required. The equations are imposed only in the open upper half-plane.
All profile derivatives and nonlinear terms vanish. Applying the exact reduction theorem gives the physical solution.
The zero velocity, temperature, and pressure profiles satisfy the reduced equations and generate the zero classical solution for every t<1.
Substitute \nabla\cdot\sigma=-\nabla p+\mu\Delta u into D_t^u u-\nabla\cdot\sigma-f. Distributing the minus sign gives D_t^u u+\nabla p-\mu\Delta u-f, component by component.

At unit density, the Cauchy momentum residual is

R_C=D_t^u u-\nabla\cdot\sigma-f.

For a divergence-free Newtonian velocity field with the stated differentiability, it is exactly the Navier–Stokes residual:

R_C =D_t^u u+\nabla p-\mu\Delta u-f =R_{NS}.

Thus the Cauchy momentum balance and the reduced Navier–Stokes equation are the same pointwise equation under these hypotheses.

The time derivative of a constant vanishes, and constant scalar multiplication passes through every spatial partial derivative. Thus the continuity residual is \rho_0 times the divergence. If \rho_0 is nonzero, their product vanishes exactly when the divergence vanishes.

If \rho=\rho_0 is constant, then

R_\rho=\rho_0\,\nabla\cdot u.

Every divergence-free flow therefore conserves constant density. When \rho_0\ne0, the continuity equation and incompressibility are equivalent.
Apply the product rule to each component \partial_j(\rho u_j), sum over the spatial coordinates, and collect the terms u_j\partial_j\rho. The remaining sum is \rho\sum_j\partial_ju_j.

For differentiable density and velocity components, the product rule gives

R_\rho=D_t^u\rho+\rho\,\nabla\cdot u.

The mass flux is \rho u, and the continuity residual is

R_\rho=\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho u).

The material derivative of density is D_t^u\rho=\partial_t\rho+u\cdot\nabla\rho.
Add and subtract \partial_i u_j. Half of their sum is the strain rate, and half of their difference is \Omega_{ij}/2, the antisymmetric part. Exchanging the two indices leaves the sum unchanged.

The velocity gradient splits into its symmetric and antisymmetric parts:

\partial_j u_i=D_{ij}(u)+\frac12\Omega_{ij}(u), \qquad D_{ji}(u)=D_{ij}(u).

Here \Omega_{ij}(u)=\partial_j u_i-\partial_i u_j is twice the antisymmetric part of the velocity gradient, developed as vorticity in the Euler section.

Write spacetime as \mathbb R^{n+1}, with coordinate zero reserved for time. The material derivative is

(D_t^u v)_i =\partial_t v_i+\sum_{j=1}^n u_j\partial_jv_i,

and incompressibility sums only the spatial derivatives. The global condition requires this sum to vanish everywhere; its pointwise form imposes the same identity at one spacetime point.

An incompressible solution pairs an equation-specific momentum predicate with incompressibility and initial data. A residual solution requires only those equations; a classical solution adds the regularity that makes the totalized derivatives analytic derivatives and the assigned initial value a one-sided trace. Global solutions restrict canonically to any positive finite horizon. Euler and Navier–Stokes are both instances of these definitions.
