Evaluate both sides in a velocity component. The definitions have the same time partial and the same finite sum of spatial directional derivatives, so the componentwise equality is immediate.

The material derivative decomposes exactly as

D_t^u v=\partial_t v+(u\cdot\nabla_x)v.

The operators distinguish \partial_tu, (u\cdot\nabla_x)v, \nu\Delta_xu, and \nabla_xp. Every spatial operator uses only coordinates 1,\ldots,n; coordinate zero remains time. This matters because the ambient fields live on spacetime, where an unqualified Laplacian would also differentiate twice in time.

Write the spacetime trajectory as the sum of its time coordinate and the zero-time embedding of X. Their derivatives are respectively the time basis vector and the embedded spatial velocity. The ordinary Fréchet chain rule gives the directional derivative, and expansion in the Euclidean coordinate basis separates its time coordinate from the spatial sum.

If X is a particle path, the associated spacetime curve t\mapsto(t,X(t)) has velocity (1,u(t,X(t))). Therefore every differentiable spacetime field v satisfies

\frac{d}{dt}v(t,X(t)) =Dv(t,X(t))[1,u(t,X(t))].

For scalar v, expanding the Fréchet derivative gives the checked identity

\frac{d}{dt}v(t,X(t)) =\partial_t v(t,X(t)) +\sum_{j=1}^n u_j(t,X(t))\,\partial_jv(t,X(t)).

A particle path is represented by the local identity

X'(t)=u(t,X(t)).

The pointwise predicate is useful when only a local calculation is needed. Its setwise form requires the same identity throughout a time interval.

On the diagonal, D_{ii}=(\partial_i u_i+\partial_i u_i)/2=\partial_i u_i. Summing gives the divergence, which vanishes under incompressibility. Symmetry of the stress follows componentwise from \delta_{ij}=\delta_{ji} and D_{ij}=D_{ji}.

The strain trace is the divergence:

\operatorname{tr}D(u)=\sum_i\partial_i u_i=\nabla\cdot u.

Consequently, incompressible strain is trace free. The Newtonian stress is symmetric because both the pressure tensor and D(u) are symmetric.

Differentiate \sigma_{ij}=-p\delta_{ij}+\mu(\partial_j u_i+\partial_i u_j) with respect to x_j and sum over j. The pressure terms select -\partial_i p; the first viscous sum is \mu\Delta u_i. Commuting the mixed derivatives in the second viscous sum gives \mu\partial_i\sum_j\partial_j u_j. This is \mu\partial_i(\nabla\cdot u), which is zero when the divergence vanishes identically.

For constant dynamic viscosity \mu, taking the spatial divergence of the Newtonian constitutive law gives

(\nabla\cdot\sigma)_i =-\partial_i p+\mu\Delta u_i+\mu\,\partial_i(\nabla\cdot u).

For a divergence-free velocity, the final term vanishes and therefore

\nabla\cdot\sigma=-\nabla p+\mu\Delta u.

The formal statement assumes differentiability of pressure and componentwise C^2 regularity of velocity at the point, so that mixed spatial derivatives commute. Its incompressible conclusion assumes divergence-freeness on the whole field, since the gradient of the divergence must vanish at the point.

The spatial velocity gradient has components (\nabla u)_{ij}=\partial_j u_i. Its symmetric part is the strain rate

D_{ij}(u)=\frac{\partial_j u_i+\partial_i u_j}{2},

and the Newtonian constitutive law is

\sigma_{ij}=-p\,\delta_{ij}+2\mu D_{ij}(u).

On a finite horizon [0,T], a momentum test field is a smooth compactly supported spacetime vector field \varphi satisfying \varphi(T,x)=0. It may be nonzero at t=0, which exposes the initial boundary term after integration by parts. The velocity and initial pairings are

\langle u(t),\psi\rangle =\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(t,x)\cdot\psi(x)\,dx, \qquad \langle u_0,\psi\rangle =\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_0(x)\cdot\psi(x)\,dx.

These are shared test data and pairings; the Euler and Navier–Stokes weak formulations supply their own momentum integrands.

Pair the steady momentum balance (u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p=0 with u. The convective-power identity gives u\cdot((u\cdot\nabla)u)=u\cdot\nabla e, hence u\cdot\nabla(e+p)=0.

For the irrotational strengthening, expand the vorticity contraction:

\partial_i e+\sum_j u_j(\partial_ju_i-\partial_i u_j).

The derivative of e is \sum_j u_j\partial_i u_j, so those terms cancel and leave \sum_j u_j\partial_j u_i. If the vorticity components vanish, the steady Euler component ((u\cdot\nabla)u)_i+\partial_i p=0 becomes \partial_i(e+p)=0.

Set B=p+e. At a point where the velocity components and pressure are differentiable, the steady, unforced balance (u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p=0 gives

u\cdot\nabla B=0.

Thus the Bernoulli function is constant along streamlines on which these hypotheses hold. If the flow is also irrotational at the point, then

((u\cdot\nabla)u)_i=\partial_i e.

The Euler balance then gives the stronger vector identity

\nabla\left(p+\frac12|u|^2\right)=0.

The theorem is pointwise; constancy of the Bernoulli function on a connected region follows when these derivatives vanish throughout that region.

Initial-value data consist of a force f, a prescribed velocity u_0, and distributional incompressibility of u_0. A finite-time residual solution stores u, p, a positive horizon T, the Euler momentum equation and pointwise incompressibility on (0,T)\times\mathbb R^n, and the exact value u(0,x)=u_0(x).

A residual solution carries no differentiability. A smooth solution also requires ambient smoothness at every positive-time point and one-sided continuity of velocity at t=0. A global smooth solution has these properties at all positive times and relative smoothness on [0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^n. Every global smooth solution restricts, with the same fields and data, to every positive finite horizon. Smoothness alone on the whole space does not imply the L^2 bounds, decay, and spacetime integrability required by a weak solution, so a smooth solution is weak only once those bounds are proved.

The antisymmetric velocity derivative is zero because its two terms are mixed second derivatives of v. The irrotational convective-acceleration identity therefore turns (u\cdot\nabla_x)u into the kinetic-energy gradient. Commute time and space derivatives, then combine the four gradients in the momentum residual. Substituting the displayed pressure makes their scalar potential identically zero. Taking the divergence of \nabla_xv gives the spatial Laplacian directly.

In any spatial dimension, let v be C^2 at a spacetime point and let h be differentiable there. Define

u=\nabla_xv,\qquad p=h-v_t-\frac12|\nabla_xv|^2.

Then u is irrotational and satisfies the pointwise momentum equation

u_t+(u\cdot\nabla_x)u+\nabla_xp=\nabla_xh.

Moreover, \nabla_x\cdot u=0 exactly when \Delta_xv=0. On an open region with v\in C^2 and h\in C^1, the constructed velocity and pressure are C^1, so spatial harmonicity gives a classical Euler flow throughout that region.

Differentiating a smooth potential preserves smoothness of the velocity; the time derivative and squared norm in the pressure do the same for pressure. The pointwise reduction supplies momentum balance and incompressibility at every positive time. Restriction of the smooth velocity to the initial slice gives the prescribed trace. At time zero, the classical-to-distributional divergence theorem turns the vanishing Laplacian into the initial data's weak incompressibility condition.

Let v,h\in C^\infty(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n) and suppose \Delta_xv(t,x)=0 for t>0. Given Euler initial-value data with force \nabla_xh and initial velocity g(x)=\nabla_xv(0,x), the velocity u=\nabla_xv and pressure p=h-v_t-\frac12|\nabla_xv|^2 form a global smooth solution. In particular,

\lim_{\substack{(t,y)\to(0,x)\\t>0}}u(t,y)=g(x).

If spatial harmonicity is supplied at time zero as well, the data constructor derives distributional incompressibility of g from the classical divergence identity. The harmonic potential is part of the input.

The pressure Poisson source and residual are

S_p=\nabla_x\cdot((u\cdot\nabla_x)u)-\nabla_x\cdot f, \qquad R_p=-\Delta_xp-S_p.

The spatial subscript distinguishes these operators from derivatives in the time coordinate.

Taking spatial divergence gives \nabla_x\cdot\partial_tu+\nabla_x\cdot((u\cdot\nabla_x)u) +\Delta_xp=\nabla_x\cdot f. The first term vanishes for a sufficiently regular divergence-free flow. Rearranging the remaining scalar identity gives the stated Poisson equation.

If the spatial divergence of the differentiated Euler momentum balance holds and \nabla_x\cdot\partial_tu=0, then

-\Delta_xp =\nabla_x\cdot((u\cdot\nabla_x)u)-\nabla_x\cdot f.
Move the force term across the equality. This is an identity in the additive group of velocity vectors.

The residual vanishes exactly when

D_t^u u+\nabla p=f.

The Euler momentum residual is the vector field

R_E=D_t^u u+\nabla p-f.

The pointwise momentum balance is the equation R_E=0.

The zero-error certificates make each evaluated symbolic residual vanish. The bridge lemmas identify those evaluations with the corresponding analytic operators. Since the certified vorticity is the constant 2, all of its spacetime derivatives vanish, giving the transport equation as well.

The symbolic certificate yields the analytic statements

\nabla_x\cdot u=0,\qquad \omega=2,\qquad D_t^u\omega=0,\qquad D_t^u u+\nabla_xp=0.

These conclusions use the ordinary analytic operators partialDeriv, materialDerivative, and spatialGradient.

The four spatial derivatives are 0,-1,1,0. In each strain component the off-diagonal derivatives cancel and the diagonal derivative is zero. The certified energy expression is therefore a sum of zero squares.

The same rigid rotation has zero strain:

D(u)=0.

Thus the velocity gradient is antisymmetric, every strain entry vanishes, and the symmetric-gradient energy density is zero.

The divergence is \partial_x(-y)+\partial_yx=0. Direct differentiation gives

(u\cdot\nabla)u =(-y\partial_x+x\partial_y)(-y,x)=(-x,-y),

which cancels \nabla p=(x,y). The checked proof reflects these polynomial expressions, differentiates them symbolically, and closes the normalized identities with cas. It also verifies -\Delta p=-2 and \nabla\cdot((u\cdot\nabla)u)=-2.

The verified CAS proves

\nabla\cdot(-y,x)=0,\qquad (u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p=0,\qquad -\Delta p=\nabla\cdot((u\cdot\nabla)u).

The symbolic calculation produces the differentiated residual, while the generated theorem proves that the momentum and pressure residuals vanish on all of \mathbb R^2.
On the diagonal the two derivatives are identical and cancel. Exchanging i and j reverses the order of the same difference, hence changes its sign.

The vorticity tensor is antisymmetric:

\Omega_{ii}=0,\qquad \Omega_{ji}=-\Omega_{ij}.

Differentiate the two momentum components in the transverse spatial directions and subtract. Joint C^2 regularity commutes the time and spatial derivatives. The pressure contribution vanishes because mixed derivatives commute. For a divergence-free planar velocity, the clockwise curl of (u\cdot\nabla)u is u\cdot\nabla\omega_{\mathrm{cw}}. What remains is exactly the clockwise curl of the force. Lean proves the clockwise form first; negating it gives the counterclockwise statement.

Let u be jointly C^2 in space and time, let the pressure slice be C^2, and let the force slice be C^1. Suppose the momentum equation and \nabla\cdot u=0 hold on an open spatial neighborhood of x. For standard counterclockwise vorticity \omega=\partial_xu_2-\partial_yu_1,

\partial_t\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega =\partial_x f_2-\partial_y f_1.

The clockwise-sign counterpart \omega_{\mathrm{cw}}=\partial_yu_1-\partial_xu_2=-\omega, used by the Boussinesq system, satisfies the same identity with the clockwise curl of the force on the right; the two statements differ by an overall sign, and the auxiliary commutation identities are proved in both conventions. In particular, either right-hand side vanishes for unforced planar Euler flow.
Both statements are rearrangements in the additive group of vector fields: A-B-C=0 holds exactly when A=B+C, and the scalar multiple 0\cdot\Delta_x\omega vanishes.

The residual vanishes exactly when

D_t^u\omega=(\omega\cdot\nabla)u+\nu\Delta_x\omega,

and at zero viscosity it reduces to the transport-stretching difference R_\omega(0)=D_t^u\omega-(\omega\cdot\nabla)u.

For spacetime fields u,\omega:\mathbb R^{n+1}\to\mathbb R^n, with time in coordinate zero, the vortex-stretching term is the convective derivative of the velocity along \omega,

\bigl((\omega\cdot\nabla)u\bigr)_i=\sum_{j=1}^n\omega_j\,\partial_ju_i,

and the vorticity transport residual with viscosity \nu is the vector

R_\omega(\nu)=D_t^u\omega-(\omega\cdot\nabla)u-\nu\Delta_x\omega.

When n=3, \omega=\nabla\times u, and u is divergence free, R_\omega(0)=0 is the unforced Euler vorticity equation and R_\omega(\nu)=0 with \nu>0 is the Navier–Stokes vorticity equation. In the definition \omega is an independent vector field in any dimension; for Navier–Stokes flow its identification with the curl and with the two-form vorticity equation is a theorem.

For planar flow, the vorticity-transport residual is

R_\omega =\partial_t\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega.

For unforced planar Euler flow, the vorticity equation is R_\omega=0.

For a flow in n space dimensions, define the antisymmetric velocity-gradient components

\Omega_{ij}=\partial_j u_i-\partial_i u_j.

For a planar spacetime field, scalar vorticity is \omega=\Omega_{21}=\partial_xu_2-\partial_yu_1.

A weak Euler solution on [0,T]\times\mathbb R^n consists of velocity u, pressure p, and a positive horizon T. For every smooth compactly supported vector field \varphi that vanishes at t=T, it satisfies

\int_0^T\!\int_{\mathbb R^n} \left[-u\cdot\partial_t\varphi -(u\otimes u):\nabla\varphi -p\,\nabla\cdot\varphi -f\cdot\varphi\right]dx\,dt =\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_0\cdot\varphi(0)\,dx.

At every t\in[0,T], the velocity slice is distributionally divergence-free, and the velocity, pressure, and forcing slices belong to spatial L^2. The prescribed initial velocity also belongs to L^2. The definition requires spatial integrability of the combined momentum integrand at every such time and time integrability of its spatial integral. The initial pairing is integrable by the L^2 datum and the compactly supported smooth test. It specifies the initial condition through the weak equation, without requiring u(0,\cdot)=u_0 for the chosen representative.

The definition is posed on a whole-space finite slab, allows general tests, keeps the pressure, and uses the initial-boundary and convection signs of Wiedemann's formulation.

Every time derivative, convective term, pressure gradient, and divergence is zero. Constant zero fields are smooth on the closed physical half-space, and their initial value is the prescribed zero datum. Restricting the global solution gives the finite-time result.
For zero initial velocity and zero forcing, u=0 and p=0 give a smooth Euler solution globally and on every positive finite horizon.

All four terms in the momentum integrand vanish pointwise, hence their space and time integrals are integrals of zero. The initial pairing is zero, every zero velocity slice belongs to L^2, and its distributional divergence is zero.
For zero force and zero initial velocity, u=0 and p=0 form a weak Euler solution on every positive finite time slab.

Construct the regular inverse chart. The cofactor identities give the linear mass equation and preserve zero curl, with the signed determinant. Choose a positive-radius ball around w(x_*) inside the open target. The C^1 inverse field has symmetric derivative on this convex ball, so the potential theorem constructs z\in C^2 with \nabla z=X. Substitution and symmetry of the second derivatives give the scalar equation.

Suppose \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2 is open, x_*\in\Omega, w\in C^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^2), and \det Dw(x_*)\ne0. Let \sigma:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R be arbitrary, and suppose w satisfies both displayed compressible-flow equations throughout \Omega. There are a local inverse chart X:V\to U, with x_*\in U\subseteq\Omega, and r>0 such that B(w(x_*),r)\subseteq V. On this ball there is a C^2 function z with \nabla z=X and

(\sigma(q)^2-q_0^2)z_{11} +2q_0q_1z_{01} +(\sigma(q)^2-q_1^2)z_{00}=0.

Here z_{ij}=\partial_{q_i}\partial_{q_j}z.

Split on whether an eventual finite norm bound exists. In the bounded case, the assumed continuation criterion gives extension. In the unbounded case, the negation of every eventual bound is exactly norm unboundedness near the finite horizon. If extension is known to fail, norm-unboundedness remains.

Let u:\mathbb R\to E be a trajectory in a normed space and let T be a candidate terminal time. Suppose a model-specific theorem says that an eventual bound

\|u(t)\|\leq C\qquad(t<T,\ t\ \text{near }T)

implies that the solution extends through T. Then either u is norm-unbounded as t\uparrow T, or the solution extends. In particular, failure of extension forces norm-unboundedness.

The conclusion is weaker than \|u(t)\|\to\infty: an unbounded trajectory may repeatedly return to a bounded region. Upgrading unboundedness to norm blow-up requires an additional persistence property.

An admissible initial velocity on \mathbb R^3 is smooth, divergence free, and rapidly decreasing together with all its derivatives. An admissible force is smooth and rapidly decreasing in space and time together with all its spacetime derivatives. A datum has a global smooth finite-energy solution when its Navier–Stokes problem has a global classical solution whose kinetic energy is bounded uniformly in t\geq0.

Alternative (A) is the statement that for every positive viscosity and every admissible initial velocity, the unforced problem has a global smooth finite-energy solution. Alternative (C) is the statement that for every positive viscosity there are an admissible initial velocity and an admissible force with no global smooth finite-energy solution. The Clay problem on \mathbb R^3 asks for a proof of (A) or a proof of (C). Their disjunction alone follows classically: if (A) fails at some viscosity \nu, the scaling v(x,t)=a\,u(x,at) with a>0 maps solutions at viscosity \nu to solutions at viscosity a\nu and keeps zero force zero, so (C) holds at every viscosity. We therefore state the two alternatives separately.

The force is a smooth function on all of spacetime, and only its restriction to t\geq0 enters the problem. A global classical solution satisfies the momentum equation and incompressibility for t>0, with relative smoothness of velocity and pressure and the initial trace on t\geq0, so no totalized ambient derivative at the initial-time boundary is read as a one-sided physical derivative.

The global zero classical solution supplies smooth velocity and pressure on the physical half-space. The initial velocity is divergence free, and it and the force are smooth and rapidly decreasing because they vanish identically. Every term in the momentum equation is zero, and the kinetic energy is zero at every time. Any positive constant therefore gives the strict uniform energy bound required by alternative (A) for this datum.

For every positive viscosity, the zero initial velocity with zero forcing has a global smooth finite-energy solution:

u_0=0,\qquad f=0,\qquad u(t,x)=0,\qquad p(t,x)=0.

Its kinetic energy vanishes for every nonnegative time, so the existence predicate of alternative (A) holds for this datum.

A finite-time smooth solution adds ambient smoothness at positive times and one-sided continuity at the initial surface. A global pointwise residual solution is posed on (0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^n; it restricts to every finite positive horizon. Global smoothness is relative to the physical closed half-space [0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^n, so nothing is assumed at negative times. Restricting a global smooth solution to a positive finite horizon gives a finite-time smooth solution, smoothness included. As for Euler, a smooth solution is a weak solution only once the L^2 bounds, weak-gradient integrability, decay, and spacetime integrability of the weak class are proved.

A Navier–Stokes problem consists of a positive viscosity \nu, forcing f, and initial velocity u_0. Incompressibility of u_0 is stated in distributions:

\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_0\mathbin\cdot\nabla\psi=0

for every smooth compactly supported scalar test function. Smooth classically divergence-free fields satisfy this definition by integration by parts, so the same datum can be used by both classical and weak theories.

The squared L^2 norm is the L^2 inner product of the class with itself, which Mathlib expresses as the integral of the pointwise inner product. The class agrees almost everywhere with the chosen slice, so the integrands coincide almost everywhere with the kinetic-energy and squared-gradient densities, up to the constant one half. For time integrability, membership of the slice map in Bochner L^2 makes its squared norm integrable, and the pointwise identity transfers integrability to the dissipation.

For a weak solution, the physical energy quantities are the squared Hilbert norms of the corresponding L^2 classes:

E(t)=\frac12\lVert u(t)\rVert_{L^2}^2\quad(0\le t\le T),\qquad E_0=\frac12\lVert u_0\rVert_{L^2}^2,

\int_{\mathbb R^n}|Du(t,x)|^2\,dx=\lVert Du(t)\rVert_{L^2}^2\quad(0<t\le T).

If moreover t\mapsto Du(t) belongs to L^2(0,T;L^2), that is, the gradient slice map is square integrable in time on [0,T], then the weak dissipation t\mapsto\int|Du(t,x)|^2\,dx is integrable on [0,T]. These identities let the energy inequality of a Leray–Hopf solution be read either as a statement about integrals of the representative or as a statement in the Hilbert space L^2.

A pressure-free weak solution on [0,T] stores L^2 membership of every velocity slice and of every weak-gradient slice at positive times. The corresponding Hilbert-space classes are

u(t)\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^n)\quad(0\le t\le T),\qquad Du(t)\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^{n\times n})\quad(0<t\le T),

the classes of x\mapsto u(t,x) and x\mapsto Du(t,x), extended by the zero class outside [0,T] and (0,T] respectively, together with the class u_0\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^n) of the prescribed initial velocity. The velocity slice is also recorded as an element of L^2 carrying the weak topology, which is the topology in which Leray–Hopf solutions are continuous in time.

The kinetic energy is

E(t)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^n}|u(t,x)|^2\,dx,

and we also define the initial-data energy, enstrophy, and two forms of viscous dissipation. The classical dissipation differentiates u pointwise; the weak quantity integrates the square of a separately supplied distributional-gradient witness. Keeping these definitions distinct avoids applying totalized classical derivatives to an energy-class velocity.

The Leray–Hopf definition adds to the pressure-free weak solution L^\infty_tL^2_x velocity, L^2_tL^2_x weak gradient, continuity in the weak L^2 topology, the prescribed L^2 initial trace, force-work integrability, and the energy inequality measured from the initial datum. It uses a chosen representative: velocity slices and the initial trace are imposed at every time in [0,T] and the weak gradient at every time in (0,T], while the initial datum is required only to lie in L^2.

A Leray–Hopf solution with a pressure representative supplies the separate pressure-retaining refinement and projects to this pressure-free class.

For this representative, the energy inequality holds for every t\in[0,T]:

\frac12\|u(t)\|_{L^2}^2+\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u(s)\|_{L^2}^2\,ds \leq\frac12\|u_0\|_{L^2}^2+\int_0^t\langle f(s),u(s)\rangle\,ds.

The force-work term measures external energy input. At zero forcing, the inequality bounds kinetic energy plus accumulated weak-gradient dissipation by the initial kinetic energy. Equality would require the additional regularity needed to justify the smooth integrations by parts.
Use D_t^u u=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u and collect the vector terms. The zero-residual equivalences are the corresponding rearrangements of A-B=0 into A=B.

The residuals recover the Stokes and Navier–Stokes equations and satisfy

R_{NS}=R_E-\nu\Delta u, \qquad R_{NS}=R_S+(u\cdot\nabla)u.

Thus zero viscosity recovers Euler. At a point where convection vanishes, the Navier–Stokes and Stokes residuals agree.

Differentiate e=\frac12\sum_i u_i^2 componentwise and apply the product rule. Multiplication by u_j and summation over j gives the convective identity. Applying the product rule to each \partial_j(eu_j) and \partial_j(pu_j) gives the two flux identities; their compressibility terms vanish when \nabla\cdot u=0.

For a differentiable velocity field, the convective power is transport of the specific kinetic energy e=\frac12|u|^2:

\bigl((u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr)\cdot u=u\cdot\nabla e.

Where pressure is also differentiable, pressure work satisfies

u\cdot\nabla p=\nabla\cdot(pu)-p\,\nabla\cdot u.

Under incompressibility, the pressure contribution is a spatial divergence. The kinetic-energy flux obeys

\nabla\cdot(eu)=u\cdot\nabla e+e\,\nabla\cdot u.

Thus incompressibility also turns the convective power into \nabla\cdot(eu).

A finite-time pointwise solution consists of velocity and pressure on (0,T)\times\mathbb R^n, the momentum equation, incompressibility, and the prescribed value at t=0. The equation is imposed on the open positive-time domain using totalized ambient derivatives, so a residual solution carries no differentiability.

Expand D_t^uu componentwise and differentiate. The antisymmetrised derivative of \partial_tu is \partial_t\Omega_{ij}, that of the Laplacian is \Delta_x\Omega_{ij}, and the convective term \sum_ku_k\partial_ku_j contributes \sum_ku_k\partial_k\Omega_{ij} plus the deformation sum \sum_k(\partial_iu_k\Omega_{kj}+\partial_ju_k\Omega_{ik}) after commuting the mixed derivatives, which is where third derivatives are used. Collecting terms gives minus the two-form residual. Since F(u) is built from finitely many partial derivatives at each point, it is determined by the germ of u; the local statements follow by replacing u with a compactly supported C^3 field that agrees with it near x.

Write F(u)=\nu\Delta_xu-D_t^uu for the pressure-gradient candidate: the force-free Navier–Stokes momentum equation is \nabla_xp=F(u). If u is C^3, or merely C^3 at the spacetime point x, then at x

\partial_iF(u)_j-\partial_jF(u)_i=-R_{ij}.

The candidate depends only on the velocity germ: if u=v on a neighborhood of x, then F(u)=F(v) on a neighborhood of x. It is C^1 near every point at which u is C^3.

At each selected time the candidate F(u)(t,\cdot) is C^1 on s, and by the antisymmetry identity its Jacobian is symmetric exactly because the vorticity residual vanishes. On an open convex set, a C^1 field with symmetric derivative is a gradient: integrating along segments from a base point produces a potential whose gradient is the field. Choosing such a potential for every t\in I defines p, and rewriting \nabla_xp=\nu\Delta_xu-D_t^uu gives the momentum equation. The three-dimensional statements first convert the vector vorticity equation into the two-form equation using incompressibility.

Let s\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open and convex, let I\subseteq\mathbb R be any set of times, and let u:\mathbb R^{n+1}\to\mathbb R^n be C^3 at every point (t,x) with t\in I and x\in s, satisfying the two-form vorticity equation R_{ij}(t,x)=0 there. Then there is a pressure p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R such that for all t\in I and x\in s, the slice p(t,\cdot) has gradient F(u)(t,x) at x and

D_t^uu+\nabla_xp=\nu\Delta_xu\qquad\text{at }(t,x).

For \nu=0 this reconstructs the force-free Euler pressure, D_t^uu+\nabla_xp=0. In three dimensions the two-form hypothesis may be replaced by \nabla\cdot u=0 together with the vector vorticity equation D_t^u\omega=(\omega\cdot\nabla)u+\nu\Delta_x\omega for \omega=\nabla\times u, again for Navier–Stokes and for Euler.

The pressure is selected slice by slice, with no condition in time, and I may exclude a blow-up time: only local regularity at the selected points is used. The reconstructed momentum equation is force free because the vorticity equation carries no forcing term.

Take the spatial divergence of momentum. Local incompressibility makes the divergence of \partial_tu vanish. Commutation of the spatial divergence with the vector Laplacian makes the viscous contribution vanish as well. The remaining identity is exactly the pressure Poisson residual equation.

At every positive-time point of a smooth Navier–Stokes solution,

-\Delta_xp =\nabla_x\cdot((u\cdot\nabla_x)u)-\nabla_x\cdot f.

The viscosity does not alter this pressure source. For a componentwise C^3 incompressible velocity,

\nabla_x\cdot(\nu\Delta_xu) =\nu\Delta_x(\nabla_x\cdot u)=0.

The result is available for both finite-time and global smooth solutions.

The pointwise residuals are

\begin{aligned} R_S&=\partial_tu+\nabla p-\nu\Delta u-f,\\ R_{NS}&=D_t^u u+\nabla p-\nu\Delta u-f. \end{aligned}

Each momentum equation is the assertion that its residual vanishes.
The semantic bridge identifies the analytic integrand with the evaluated symbolic residual. That residual vanishes at every point, so its integral over the chosen domain is zero.

For every integration domain and every velocity component,

\int_\Omega \bigl((u\cdot\nabla)u_i+\partial_i p-\Delta u_i-f_i\bigr)\,dx=0.

The integrand is the combined analytic residual, which vanishes identically, so the identity needs no integrability of the separate terms.

The divergence is \partial_x(\sin y)+\partial_y0=0, and \partial_xu=0 makes convection vanish. Finally, -\Delta u=(\sin y,0)=f. The reflected expressions therefore normalize to zero componentwise, which is exactly the proposition proved by cas.

The verified CAS proves the exact identities

\nabla\cdot u=0,\qquad (u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p-\Delta u-f=0

on all of \mathbb R^2. The momentum theorem is also stored as a zero-error residual certificate. CEGA projects that checked object into the ordinary residual goal. Here cega selects the certificate's proved sound field and checks that its residual, domain, and error budget match the target; no derivative is recomputed and no external solver is called.

Apply integration by parts to |u|^2 and the identity spatial field. Its divergence is three, giving the one-quarter drift coefficient. The same argument with b gives zero transport energy. The Laplacian supplies the sum of squared coordinate derivatives, and the certified compensation inequality bounds the remaining zeroth-order pairing. The positive mass and Dirichlet coefficients control the full Sobolev norm. The divergence kernel is closed because divergence is a continuous linear map; Lax–Milgram applied to the restricted form gives the principal solve.

Let u\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3) and let b be a divergence-free C^1 transporting field. The dilation identity gives

\int\left(-\frac12u-\frac12(x\cdot\nabla)u\right)\cdot u =\frac14\int|u|^2.

\int (b\cdot\nabla)u\cdot u=0.

Suppose a continuous matrix field Q satisfies the compensation inequality

v\cdot(Db(x)+Q(x))v\geq-\eta|v|^2

for every x and v. Define the unprojected principal expression

\begin{aligned} A_Qu={}&-\frac12u-\frac12(x\cdot\nabla)u-\Delta u\\ &+(b\cdot\nabla)u+(u\cdot\nabla)b+Qu. \end{aligned}

Then

\begin{aligned} \int A_Qu\cdot u &\geq\left(\frac14-\eta\right)\int|u|^2\\ &\quad+\sum_{i=1}^3\int|\partial_i u|^2. \end{aligned}

The same lower bound holds on any bounded open domain for u\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^3), with weakly divergence-free background b\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb R^3) and Q\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^{3\times3}). Here divergence and Db are weak Sobolev derivatives, and compensation is required almost everywhere. In this setting the left side is the weak pairing \langle A_Qu,u\rangle_{H^{-1},H^1_0}. The viscous term is the Dirichlet pairing \int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2; no second weak derivative of u is assumed. The bounded coordinate functions supply the dilation pairing. Weak integration by parts proves transport cancellation directly on the completed space.

When \eta<1/4, the constructed bounded-domain form is coercive in the full H^1 norm, with modulus

c=\min\{1/4-\eta,1\}>0.

Restricting both arguments to the closed weak-divergence kernel preserves coercivity. Thus, for every continuous dual load \ell, there is a unique u\in H^1_{0,\sigma}(\Omega) satisfying

\begin{aligned} \langle A_Qu,v\rangle&=\ell(v),\\ &\quad v\in H^1_{0,\sigma}(\Omega). \end{aligned}

This solves the compensated principal linear variational equation. The operator is built from the bounded weak coefficients and coordinate multipliers, and its evaluation formula is proved from that construction. The compensation inequality is accepted directly, so a certified Q can be used without an exact spectral negative-part formula. An application must still certify the actual Q, remove pressure or the Leray projection against divergence-free tests, and pass from bounded domains to the required whole-space limit. PDEAtlas constructs distinct suitable Leray–Hopf solutions from any unstable profile (NavierStokes.Nonuniqueness.of_unstableProfile). The certificates for the paper's numerical profile and unstable eigenpair, and with them the nonuniqueness theorem NavierStokes.nonuniqueness, are formalized in the companion repository BlowupZoo, at its level 8.

Each cyclic component of the two-form residual equals the corresponding component of the vector residual plus the correction (\nabla\cdot u)\,\omega_k; this is an exact identity obtained by expanding the deformation sum and regrouping it in terms of the curl components. At a point where the divergence vanishes, the correction disappears and the three cyclic components of R are the three components of the vector residual. The remaining components of R follow from the antisymmetry of \Omega.

Let u:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^3 be C^3 and let (t,x) be a spacetime point at which \nabla\cdot u=0. Then the two-form residual vanishes at (t,x) if and only if the vector residual does:

R_{ij}=0\ \text{for all }i,j \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D_t^u\omega-(\omega\cdot\nabla)u-\nu\Delta_x\omega=0, \qquad\omega=\nabla\times u.

The implication from the two-form equation to the vector equation needs only C^1 regularity.

For a spacetime velocity u:\mathbb R^{n+1}\to\mathbb R^n, the spatial vorticity two-form has components

\Omega_{ij}=\partial_iu_j-\partial_ju_i,

the transpose, equivalently the negative, of the antisymmetric velocity-gradient convention used for the Euler vorticity tensor. Its transport-diffusion residual with viscosity \nu is

R_{ij}=D_t^u\Omega_{ij} +\sum_{k=1}^n\bigl(\partial_iu_k\,\Omega_{kj}+\partial_ju_k\,\Omega_{ik}\bigr) -\nu\Delta_x\Omega_{ij},

where the deformation sum is the coordinate form of the Lie derivative of a two-form along u. In three dimensions the vector vorticity is the curl of each time slice, \omega(t,x)=\nabla\times u(t,\cdot)(x); for a C^1 velocity its components are the cyclic two-form entries \omega_1=\Omega_{23}, \omega_2=\Omega_{31}, \omega_3=\Omega_{12}. No incompressibility is built into these definitions.

Momentum test fields are smooth and compactly supported and vanish at the terminal time, but they may be nonzero at t=0. Integration by parts then gives

\int_0^T\!\!\int_{\mathbb R^n} \left[-u\mathbin\cdot\phi_t-(u\otimes u):\nabla\phi -p\,\nabla\mathbin\cdot\phi+\nu Du:\nabla\phi-f\mathbin\cdot\phi\right] =\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_0\mathbin\cdot\phi(0).

The integrability predicate requires spatial integrability of the combined momentum integrand at every physical time, and time integrability of its spatial integral rather than of each summand. The initial pairing is integrable by the L^2 initial datum and compactly supported smooth test. This pressure-retaining identity is used by a weak solution with a pressure representative; solenoidal tests remove its pressure term.

A pressure-free weak solution tests momentum only against solenoidal fields. It stores a velocity with L^2 slices at every time in [0,T], an explicit distributional spatial gradient D u with L^2 slices and weak-derivative identities at every time in (0,T], the combined iterated integrability of the momentum integrand, weak incompressibility of every velocity slice, and the initial datum as a boundary functional. The initial datum is required only to lie in L^2, and forcing has L^2 spatial slices at every physical time. The viscous term uses D u, never a classical derivative of the weak velocity.

A weak solution with a pressure representative additionally supplies an L^2 pressure slice at every physical time and the pressure-retaining identity for all momentum tests. Restricting to solenoidal tests gives its checked projection to a pressure-free weak solution; the converse would require pressure reconstruction.

Choose u(t,x)\equiv0 and p(t,x)\equiv0. Every derivative, nonlinear term, pressure gradient, and divergence vanishes, and the initial trace equals the zero datum. Constant zero fields are smooth on every finite horizon and on the full nonnegative-time domain, which gives both forms of the result.

For zero initial velocity and zero forcing, the zero velocity and pressure give

u(t,x)\equiv0,\qquad p(t,x)\equiv0,\qquad \partial_tu-\nu\Delta u+(u\!\cdot\!\nabla)u+\nabla p=0

on every finite horizon and globally for every \nu>0.

Use zero velocity, weak gradient, pressure, forcing, and initial data. Every weak momentum and incompressibility pairing is zero. The zero representative belongs to both energy spaces, all test-function pairings are constantly zero, and the energy inequality reduces to 0\leq0.

For every positive viscosity and every positive finite horizon, zero velocity, zero pressure, zero forcing, and zero initial data give a checked Leray–Hopf solution. In particular,

u\equiv0,\qquad \frac12\|u(t)\|_{L^2}^2 +\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u(s)\|_{L^2}^2\,ds=0

for 0\leq t\leq T.

The Bochner lift agrees almost everywhere with pointwise composition by D. Equality of Bochner classes identifies its kernel with almost-everywhere vanishing, after which weak closedness of a continuous linear kernel gives the limit theorem. The weak compactness theorem for closed norm-bounded Hilbert-space families remains valid after intersecting with this closed constraint set.

For u\in L^2(\mu;V), almost-everywhere incompressibility,

Du(t)=0\quad\text{for almost every }t,

is equivalent to vanishing of the lifted continuous map D_{L^2}:L^2(\mu;V)\to L^2(\mu;Q). Hence the solenoidal trajectory space is weakly closed, and weak L^2 limits of eventually solenoidal trajectories remain solenoidal. If additionally V is a real Hilbert space, intersecting this constraint set with any weakly closed, norm-bounded family is weakly compact.

Compose each slot of the ambient form with the continuous inclusion V_\sigma\hookrightarrow V. Subtype norms equal ambient norms, so the product estimate is unchanged. The first restricted argument is solenoidal, so the assumed integration-by-parts skew identity applies; diagonal skew-symmetry then gives the cubic cancellation.

Restriction of b to V_\sigma^3 is again a continuous trilinear form. Every ambient product bound

|b(u,v,w)|\leq C\|u\|_V\|v\|_V\|w\|_V

passes to the restricted form with the same constant. Skew-symmetry for solenoidal transport fields becomes global skew-symmetry on V_\sigma^3, and therefore

b_\sigma(u,u,u)=0.

The nonlinear energy cancellation holds without choosing a particular domain or a Navier–Stokes solution predicate.

The solenoidal energy space is the closed linear subspace

V_\sigma=\ker D=\{v\in V:Dv=0\}.

It comes with its canonical continuous inclusion V_\sigma\hookrightarrow V. Representing incompressibility as a kernel makes the constraint available to the general theory of submodules, weak limits, and restricted forms.

Regard D as the one-member family of constraints in the abstract weak constraint theorem. Its lifted weak-space kernel is closed, and every limit of an eventually kernel-valued net lies in that kernel.

The set V_\sigma is closed in the weak topology of V. Consequently, if

u_j\rightharpoonup u\quad\text{in }V

and Du_j=0 eventually, then Du=0.

For a domain \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, a force f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^n) and u\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^n), the Stokes energy is

E_f(u)=\frac12\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,dx-\int_\Omega f\cdot u\,dx,

with |\nabla u| the Frobenius norm of the full gradient matrix. The Stokes residual of u is the vector of distributions \Delta u_j+f_j, defined through the weak first derivatives of u.

The divergence is a bounded linear map on H^1_0, so its kernel is a closed subspace and therefore a Hilbert space. On a bounded domain the Poincaré inequality makes the Dirichlet form coercive there, and the direct method for a coercive symmetric form on a closed subspace gives a unique minimizer. The weak equation is the derivative of t\mapsto E_f(u+tv) at t=0, which is admissible because u+tv stays divergence free.

Let n>0 and let \Omega be bounded. For every f\in L^2, there is exactly one u\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^n) with \nabla\cdot u=0 that minimizes E_f among all divergence-free fields in H^1_0. The minimizer satisfies

\int_\Omega\nabla u:\nabla v\,dx=\int_\Omega f\cdot v\,dx \qquad\text{for all }v\in H^1_0\text{ with }\nabla\cdot v=0.

The residual is a locally L^2 field with zero weak curl, so it has weak potentials on balls. To make these potentials agree, use the algebraic functional obtained by factoring the first variation through divergence. On a smaller coordinate box, the difference between that functional and integration against a local potential annihilates all coordinate derivatives. It is therefore a constant times the integral. Adding this constant to the potential makes it represent the prescribed functional.

The adjusted potentials represent the same functional on overlaps and hence agree almost everywhere there. A countable open subcover gives a measurable gluing. Compact-local L^2 bounds for both the pressure and its weak gradient give its H^1 representatives on relatively compact open subsets. The identity for smooth compactly supported tests is the definition of the distributional gradient. It extends to compactly supported H^1 tests by localizing the stress \nabla u-p\,I with a cutoff equal to one near the support of the test, so that every integral involves only local L^2 bounds.

Let n>0, let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be any open set, and let f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^n). Suppose u\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^n) is divergence free and minimizes E_f against every divergence-free H^1_0 competitor. There is a measurable pressure p that is square integrable on every compact subset of \Omega, whose distributional gradient is \Delta u+f, and for which

\int_\Omega\nabla u:\nabla v\,dx =\int_\Omega p\,\nabla\cdot v\,dx+\int_\Omega f\cdot v\,dx

for every v\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^n) that vanishes outside a compact subset of \Omega. The test field need not be divergence free. The same pressure has an H^1(V) representative on every open V with compact closure contained in \Omega. Neither connectedness nor simple connectedness is required.

Testing the weak equation against \partial_i\varphi\,e_j-\partial_j\varphi\,e_i, which is divergence free, shows that the residual is weakly curl free. Each vorticity component then satisfies \Delta\omega_{ij}=\partial_jf_i-\partial_if_j in distributions, a Poisson equation whose right-hand side is a derivative of an L^2 field, and the interior estimate for such equations gives locally square integrable first derivatives. Because \nabla\cdot u=0, the Laplacian of u is the divergence of the vorticity tensor, which gives the local L^2 representative of the residual.

Let u be a divergence-free minimizer of E_f on an open set \Omega. Then the residual \Delta u+f is represented by a function that is square integrable on every compact subset of \Omega, and every component \partial_ju_i-\partial_iu_j of the vorticity has weak first derivatives that are locally square integrable. No second derivative of u is assumed.
The Bochner integral of an integrable function against a countable sum of measures is the sum of the component integrals. Unfold the atlas measure and use finiteness of the chart index type.

If f:\mathbb R^{m+1}\to E is Bochner integrable with respect to \sigma_{\mathcal A}, then

\int_{\mathbb R^{m+1}} f\,d\sigma_{\mathcal A} = \sum_i \int_{C_i} f\,d\sigma_i^\partial.

Replace the restriction of \sigma_{\mathcal A} to the chart source by \sigma_i^\partial using the local restriction theorem. The result is exactly the Bochner integral formula for the physical chart measure.

For a real normed vector space E, let f:\mathbb R^{m+1}\to E be almost everywhere strongly measurable with respect to the restriction of \sigma_{\mathcal A} to the source of \kappa_i. Then

\int_{\operatorname{source}(\kappa_i)} f(x)\,d\sigma_{\mathcal A}(x) = \int_{U_i^\partial} J_i^\partial(y)\, f(\Phi_i(y))\,dy.

Unfold \sigma_{\mathcal A}. The Lebesgue integral of a nonnegative function against a sum of measures is the sum of its integrals against the individual measures. The atlas index type is finite, so the resulting infinite sum is the displayed finite sum.

For every f:\mathbb R^{m+1}\to[0,\infty],

\int_{\mathbb R^{m+1}}^- f\,d\sigma_{\mathcal A} = \sum_i \int_{C_i}^- f\,d\sigma_i^\partial.

Every cell contribution is a restriction of a chart measure, hence is absolutely continuous with respect to intrinsic surface measure by the local result. Absolute continuity is preserved by the finite sum defining \sigma_{\mathcal A}.

The assembled atlas measure is absolutely continuous with respect to intrinsic surface measure:

\sigma_{\mathcal A} \ll \mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega.

The reverse Radon–Nikodym density is

\eta_{\mathcal A} := \frac{ d\sigma_{\mathcal A} }{ d\left(\mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega\right) }.

For each chart, boundedness of the physical chart target and the isometric flat embedding imply that the tangential parameter domain is bounded. The continuous tangential Jacobian is bounded on the compact closure of that domain, so its integral against Lebesgue measure is finite. Mapping this finite parameter measure into physical space preserves its total mass. Finally, the atlas contains only finitely many restricted chart measures, and a finite sum of finite masses is finite.

The operational atlas measure has finite total mass:

\sigma_{\mathcal A}\!\left(\mathbb R^{m+1}\right)<\infty.

Restrict the defining sum to the source of chart i. For each cell C_j, commute the two restrictions and use compatibility of the chart measures on the i,j overlap. The resulting sum is

\sum_j \sigma_i^\partial\restriction C_j.

Pairwise disjointness and \bigsqcup_jC_j=\partial\Omega identify this sum with \sigma_i^\partial\restriction\partial\Omega. The chart measure is already concentrated on its physical boundary patch, so the final restriction changes nothing.

On every chart source, the global measure recovers the full measure of that chart:

\sigma_{\mathcal A} \restriction\operatorname{source}(\kappa_i) = \sigma_i^\partial.
Every summand in the definition is restricted to a cell C_i\subseteq\partial\Omega. Restricting the finite measure sum to the frontier therefore leaves every summand unchanged.

The global atlas measure is concentrated on the frontier:

\sigma_{\mathcal A}\restriction\partial\Omega = \sigma_{\mathcal A}.

The forward implication follows by restricting the global equality to each chart source and applying the local theorem. Conversely, intrinsic surface measure is concentrated on the frontier by definition, so the uniqueness theorem applies to the family of assumed local equalities.

The atlas measure equals intrinsic codimension-one Euclidean Hausdorff surface measure exactly when the equality holds in every chart:

\sigma_{\mathcal A} = \mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall i,\; \left( \mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega \right) \restriction\operatorname{source}(\kappa_i) = \sigma_i^\partial.

Restrict both measures to every disjoint cell C_i. Since C_i\subseteq\operatorname{source}(\kappa_i), the assumed chart equality and the local theorem give equal cell restrictions. Glue those equalities over the disjoint cell cover and use that both measures are concentrated on the frontier.

Let \mu be a measure concentrated on \partial\Omega. If

\mu\restriction\operatorname{source}(\kappa_i) = \sigma_i^\partial

for every boundary chart i, then \mu=\sigma_{\mathcal A}.

The global boundary measure associated with the operational atlas is

\sigma_{\mathcal A} := \sum_i \left( \sigma_i^\partial\restriction C_i \right).
Apply the reciprocal Radon–Nikodym theorem and transfer its exceptional set between the mutually absolutely continuous measures.

The two densities are reciprocal \sigma_{\mathcal A}-almost everywhere:

\rho_{\mathcal A}^{-1} = \eta_{\mathcal A}.
The exceptional set \{x:f(x)\ne g(x)\} is null for one measure exactly when it is null for the other.

For arbitrary functions f,g:\mathbb R^{m+1}\to X,

f=g\quad\sigma_{\mathcal A}\text{-a.e.} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f=g\quad \left( \mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega \right)\text{-a.e.}
Apply the two absolute-continuity directions to the set A.

The atlas and intrinsic surface measures have exactly the same null sets:

\sigma_{\mathcal A}(A)=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \left( \mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega \right)(A)=0.
The atlas trace is the intrinsic trace followed by the density-root linear isometry, so its norm is preserved definitionally by the isometry API.

For every Sobolev input u,

\lVert \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal A,p}u \rVert_{L^p(\sigma_{\mathcal A})} = \lVert \operatorname{Tr}_p u \rVert_{ L^p(\mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega) }.

For 1\le p, the finite-exponent boundary trace in operational atlas coordinates is

\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal A,p} := T_p\circ\operatorname{Tr}_p.

Its representatives are expressed against the atlas measure used by the chartwise boundary calculus.
Apply the Radon–Nikodym reconstruction theorem to the already proved absolute continuity \mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega\ll\sigma_{\mathcal A}.

Weighting the operational atlas measure by \rho_{\mathcal A} recovers intrinsic surface measure exactly:

\rho_{\mathcal A}\,\sigma_{\mathcal A} = \mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega.

Expand the Euclidean-space inner product as the finite sum of coordinate inner products. Over \mathbb R, each scalar inner product is ordinary multiplication. Each gradient coordinate is the corresponding partial derivative.

The coordinate definition agrees everywhere with the Euclidean gradient pairing:

\partial_{\nu_c}v(x) = \left\langle \nabla v(x), \operatorname{normalize}(x-c) \right\rangle.

No differentiability hypothesis is needed for this equality because both sides use the same totalized Fréchet derivative.

For a center c\in\mathbb R^n, a scalar function v, and any x\in\mathbb R^n, define

\partial_{\nu_c}v(x) := \sum_{i=1}^n \partial_i v(x)\, \operatorname{normalize}(x-c)_i.

On a positive-radius sphere \lVert x-c\rVert=r, this is the derivative in the outward radial unit direction. The definition remains total at x=c because Mathlib defines normalize 0 = 0.

Let F=(F_1,\ldots,F_{m+1}) and let [a,b] be a coordinate box. The quantity boxFlux a b F is the explicit oriented sum of its coordinate-face integrals:

\operatorname{boxFlux}_{[a,b]}(F) := \sum_{i=1}^{m+1} \left( \int_{\{x\in[a,b]:x_i=b_i\}}F_i(x)\,dS_i - \int_{\{x\in[a,b]:x_i=a_i\}}F_i(x)\,dS_i \right).

The upper face has normal +e_i and the lower face has normal -e_i. Each face integral is a Lebesgue integral over the m-dimensional box of the remaining coordinates.

A set \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n has C^1 graph boundary if for each x\in\partial\Omega there are a linear isomorphism e:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{n-1}\times\mathbb R and a function \gamma:\mathbb R^{n-1}\to\mathbb R, C^1 near the first component of e(x), such that e(x) lies on the graph of \gamma and, for y near x,

y\in\Omega\iff \gamma\bigl(e(y)_1\bigr)<e(y)_2 .

The isomorphism need not be orthogonal. For a vector field F on a domain with a C^1 boundary atlas, the normal flux is \langle F(x),\nu(x)\rangle at boundary points, with \nu the outward unit normal, and zero elsewhere.
Each physical chart patch is the intersection of an open chart source with the closed frontier. A cell is obtained from that measurable patch by subtracting finitely many earlier measurable patches.
Every cell C_i is measurable.

Disjointization preserves the union of the original finite family. Every chart patch lies in the frontier, and the boundary partition of unity proves that every frontier point belongs to at least one chart source.

The cells cover the whole frontier:

\bigsqcup_i C_i=\partial\Omega.
If i<j, the definition of C_j removes the entire patch assigned to chart i, and C_i is a subset of that patch. The opposite ordering is symmetric.
If i\ne j, then C_i\cap C_j=\varnothing.

Fix the order already carried by the finite atlas. The cell assigned to chart i is

C_i := \left( \operatorname{source}(\kappa_i)\cap\partial\Omega \right) \setminus \bigcup_{j<i} \left( \operatorname{source}(\kappa_j)\cap\partial\Omega \right).
Use the Bochner integral formula for a mapped measure to pull the integral back through \Phi_i. Then apply the parameter-measure integral formula to g=f\circ\Phi_i.

Let E be a real normed vector space and let f:\mathbb R^{m+1}\to E. If f is almost everywhere strongly measurable with respect to the specific chart measure \sigma_i^\partial, then

\int_{\mathbb R^{m+1}}f(x)\,d\sigma_i^\partial(x) = \int_{U_i^\partial} J_i^\partial(y)\, f(\Phi_i(y))\,dy.

Choose the standard orthonormal basis of \mathbb R^m. Every entry of the Gram matrix \langle T_i(y)e_p,T_i(y)e_q\rangle varies continuously with y. Determinant and square root are continuous, and normDet is the nonnegative square root of the Gram determinant.
The function J_i^\partial:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R is continuous.

Injectivity of T_i(y) says its kernel is trivial. Mathlib's criterion for LinearMap.normDet states that zero norm determinant is equivalent to a nontrivial kernel in this finite-dimensional setting. Hence the norm determinant is nonzero. Its general nonnegativity upgrades nonzero to strict positivity.

For y\in U_i^\partial,

J_i^\partial(y)>0.

The chart surface Jacobian is

J_i^\partial(y) := \operatorname{normDet}(T_i(y)).

Here LinearMap.normDet is the generalized determinant norm for the rectangular map \mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^{m+1}. Equivalently,

\left(J_i^\partial(y)\right)^2 = \det\!\left( \bigl[\langle T_i(y)e_p,T_i(y)e_q\rangle\bigr]_{p,q} \right).

The positive Jacobian density makes \sigma_i^\partial absolutely continuous with respect to \nu_i^\partial. On the bounded physical chart patch, the forward chart is Lipschitz. Its codimension-one Hausdorff distortion estimate sends intrinsic surface-null sets to flat null sets, which are exactly the parameter-null sets defining \nu_i^\partial.

The Jacobian-weighted chart measure is absolutely continuous with respect to intrinsic surface measure:

\sigma_i^\partial \ll \mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega.

Use measure extensionality. For a measurable set A, represent its measure as the lintegral of the indicator of A. Rewrite each restricted chart measure by its parameter-overlap formula. The transition integral theorem identifies the two Jacobian-weighted parameter integrals.

The two chart measures agree on their common physical patch:

\sigma_i^\partial \restriction\operatorname{source}(\kappa_j) = \sigma_j^\partial \restriction\operatorname{source}(\kappa_i).

The physical surface measure contributed by chart i is the pushforward

\sigma_i^\partial := (\Phi_i)_\#\mu_i^\partial.

This measure is concentrated on the physical chart boundary piece \operatorname{source}(\kappa_i)\cap\partial\Omega: almost every point belongs to that piece. Its topological support can also contain limit points outside the open chart source.
It is the preimage of the open chart target under the continuous linear isometric flat embedding y\mapsto(y,0).
The set U_i^\partial is open in \mathbb R^m.

Let flatEmbedding insert a zero last coordinate. The parameter domain of chart i is

U_i^\partial := \left\{ y\in\mathbb R^m: (y,0)\in\operatorname{target}(\kappa_i) \right\}.

Unfold the restricted measure and withDensity. The Bochner integral against an extended-nonnegative density uses its real value. Since normDet is nonnegative, toReal (ofReal J_i^\partial)=J_i^\partial, yielding the stated weighted set integral.

For a function g:\mathbb R^m\to E into a real normed vector space,

\int_{\mathbb R^m}g(y)\,d\mu_i^\partial(y) = \int_{U_i^\partial} J_i^\partial(y)\,g(y)\,dy.

In Lean, multiplication of the real Jacobian with a vector-valued integrand is scalar multiplication.

The Jacobian-weighted measure on the flat parameter space is

\mu_i^\partial := \left( \mathcal L^m\!\restriction U_i^\partial \right) \mathbin{\mathrm{withDensity}} \operatorname{ofReal}(J_i^\partial).

The ofReal conversion turns the nonnegative real Jacobian into an extended-nonnegative density.

For injectivity, apply \kappa_i to an equality of two parametrized points. The chart right-inverse identity recovers the two flat embeddings, and the flat embedding itself is injective.

For the image identity, a parameter in U_i^\partial maps to the chart source, and its chart image has zero last coordinate, so it lies on the frontier. Conversely, if x is a boundary point in the chart source, its chart image has last coordinate zero. Project away that coordinate to obtain y, re-embed it, and use the chart inverse identity to recover x=\Phi_i(y).

The restriction of \Phi_i to U_i^\partial is injective, and

\Phi_i(U_i^\partial) = \operatorname{source}(\kappa_i)\cap\partial\Omega.
Compose the globally C^1 inverse chart with the continuous linear flat embedding.
The map \Phi_i:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^{m+1} is globally C^1.

The physical boundary parametrization associated with chart i is

\Phi_i(y) := \kappa_i^{-1}(y,0).

It is defined on all of \mathbb R^m as a Lean function, while its geometric boundary interpretation is used on U_i^\partial.

The unweighted parametrized reference measure of chart i is

\nu_i^\partial := (\Phi_i)_\# \left( \mathcal L^m\restriction U_i^\partial \right).

It separates the geometric transport through \Phi_i from the positive Jacobian density used to define \sigma_i^\partial.

Unfold the pushforward measure and pull the restricted lintegral back through \Phi_i. The preimage of chart j's source inside U_i^\partial is precisely U_{ij}^\partial. Unfold the parameter measure's Jacobian density to obtain the right-hand side.

If g:\mathbb R^{m+1}\to[0,\infty] is measurable, then restricting chart i's physical measure to chart j's source gives

\int g(x)\, d\!\left( \sigma_i^\partial \restriction\operatorname{source}(\kappa_j) \right)(x) = \int_{U_{ij}^\partial} J_i^\partial(y)\, g(\Phi_i(y))\,dy.

Continuity follows from continuity of the Fréchet derivative of the globally C^1 inverse chart, composed with the flat embedding. The derivative formula is the Fréchet chain rule for \Phi_i=\kappa_i^{-1}\circ\operatorname{flatEmbedding}.

The map y\mapsto T_i(y) is continuous, and

D\Phi_i(y)=T_i(y)

for every y\in\mathbb R^m.

Differentiate \kappa_i\circ\kappa_i^{-1}=\operatorname{id} at the flat point (y,0). The derivative of \kappa_i is a left inverse for the derivative of the inverse chart. If T_i(y)v=T_i(y)w, apply this left inverse to deduce that the flat embeddings of v and w agree. Injectivity of the flat embedding then gives v=w.

For y\in U_i^\partial, the linear map

T_i(y):\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^{m+1}

is injective.

The tangential derivative of \Phi_i is the rectangular continuous linear map

T_i(y) := D\kappa_i^{-1}(y,0) \circ \operatorname{flatEmbedding}, \qquad T_i(y):\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^{m+1}.

Apply the same-dimensional change-of-variables theorem to the injective C^1 map

\tau_{ij}:U_{ij}^\partial\to U_{ji}^\partial.

The image theorem identifies its image exactly with the reverse overlap. The chain rule and \Phi_j\circ\tau_{ij}=\Phi_i identify the derivative of the composite. Multiplicativity of normDet converts the transition Jacobian times J_j^\partial into J_i^\partial. Substitute these identities into the change-of-variables formula.

For any extended-nonnegative integrand g:\mathbb R^{m+1}\to[0,\infty],

\int_{U_{ji}^\partial} J_j^\partial(z)\, g(\Phi_j(z))\,dz = \int_{U_{ij}^\partial} J_i^\partial(y)\, g(\Phi_i(y))\,dy.

The formal statement uses ENNReal.ofReal on each Jacobian and lintegral, so it does not need an integrability assumption.

Both y and \tau_{ji}(\tau_{ij}(y)) parametrize the same physical boundary point through \Phi_i. Injectivity of \Phi_i on its parameter domain proves the inverse identity. That identity gives injectivity. Applying the same result with i and j exchanged gives surjectivity onto the reverse overlap.

The transition sends U_{ij}^\partial into U_{ji}^\partial, and the reverse transition is its inverse there:

\tau_{ji}(\tau_{ij}(y))=y \qquad(y\in U_{ij}^\partial).

Consequently, \tau_{ij} is injective on U_{ij}^\partial and

\tau_{ij}(U_{ij}^\partial)=U_{ji}^\partial.

The point \Phi_i(y) lies on the physical frontier. Its image under chart j therefore has last coordinate zero. Re-embedding its tangential projection recovers the full flattened point. The chart right-inverse identity then gives the parametrization equality.

For y\in U_{ij}^\partial,

\tau_{ij}(y)\in U_j^\partial

and

\Phi_j(\tau_{ij}(y))=\Phi_i(y).

The overlap is the intersection of the open parameter domain with the preimage of the open source of chart j under the continuous map \Phi_i. The transition is a composition of \Phi_i, chart \kappa_j, and the continuous linear flat projection, all globally C^1.
The overlap U_{ij}^\partial is open, and \tau_{ij}:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m is globally C^1.

For two charts, define the overlap parameter domain

U_{ij}^\partial := \left\{ y\in U_i^\partial: \Phi_i(y)\in\operatorname{source}(\kappa_j) \right\}.

The tangential coordinate transition is

\tau_{ij}(y) := \operatorname{flatProjection} \left(\kappa_j(\Phi_i(y))\right).

First show that the two chart-height differentials vanish on exactly the same physical vectors. A vector in the kernel of one height differential generates, to first order, a curve in that chart's flat boundary; chart overlap and the boundary-characterization theorem force the other height differential to vanish as well.

Two nonzero linear functionals to \mathbb R with the same kernel are scalar multiples. To determine the sign, move from the boundary point along the positive last-coordinate ray in chart i. Its inverse image lies inside \Omega, so chart j also assigns positive height. Passing to the right-hand derivative shows that the scalar is nonnegative. Nonvanishing of both functionals rules out zero, hence the scalar is positive. Transport the functional equality through the Riesz equivalence.

Suppose x\in\partial\Omega lies in the sources of charts i and j. Then there is a strictly positive scalar a such that

c_j(x)=a\,c_i(x), \qquad a>0.

Thus the atlas gives not just a common tangent hyperplane but a coherent choice of its outward side.

Differentiate the local identity \kappa_i\circ\kappa_i^{-1}=\operatorname{id} at \kappa_i(x). Hence D\kappa_i(x) has a right inverse. Apply this identity to the last basis vector e_{\mathrm{last}}. If

w=D\kappa_i^{-1}(\kappa_i(x))[e_{\mathrm{last}}],

then L_i(x)[w]=1. Therefore L_i(x) is not the zero functional, and its Riesz representative c_i(x) is nonzero.

If x belongs to the source of chart i, then

c_i(x)\ne0.

Let e_{\mathrm{last}}^* be last-coordinate projection. The differential of chart height at x is the continuous linear functional

L_i(x) := e_{\mathrm{last}}^*\circ D\kappa_i(x).

The physical chart conormal is its Riesz representative:

c_i(x) := \mathcal R^{-1}(L_i(x)).

Thus L_i(x)[v]=\langle c_i(x),v\rangle for physical tangent vectors v.

The atlas axioms identify the part of \Omega inside the chart source with the preimage of the upper half-space, and identify the frontier there with the preimage of its boundary hyperplane. The upper half-space is characterized by strict positivity of the last coordinate, while its boundary is characterized by vanishing of that coordinate. Specializing these two identifications at x gives the claimed equivalences.

For x in the source of \kappa_i,

(\kappa_i(x))_{\mathrm{last}}>0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\Omega,

and

(\kappa_i(x))_{\mathrm{last}}=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\partial\Omega.

Here \partial\Omega is represented by frontier Ω. These equivalences fix the inward/outward sign convention used in every subsequent normal definition.

Write c_j=a\,c_i with a>0. Then \lVert c_j\rVert=a\lVert c_i\rVert. The positive factor cancels in

-\frac{c_j}{\lVert c_j\rVert} = -\frac{a c_i}{a\lVert c_i\rVert}.

At a common boundary point of two chart sources,

\nu_i(x)=\nu_j(x).

By the Riesz identity,

L_i(x)[c_i(x)] = \langle c_i(x),c_i(x)\rangle = \lVert c_i(x)\rVert^2.

Apply linearity to -\lVert c_i(x)\rVert^{-1}c_i(x) and cancel one norm factor using c_i(x)\ne0.

On the source of chart i, the chart-height differential evaluates on the outward normal as

L_i(x)[\nu_i(x)] = -\lVert c_i(x)\rVert.
Use L_i(x)[\nu_i(x)]=-\lVert c_i(x)\rVert. Nonvanishing of c_i(x) gives \lVert c_i(x)\rVert>0, so its negative is strictly below zero.

The chart height decreases strictly in the chartwise outward direction:

L_i(x)[\nu_i(x)]<0.

Norm homogeneity gives

\lVert\nu_i(x)\rVert = \lVert c_i(x)\rVert^{-1}\lVert c_i(x)\rVert.

The conormal is nonzero, so its norm is nonzero and the product is one.

On the source of chart i,

\lVert\nu_i(x)\rVert=1.

The chartwise outward unit normal is

\nu_i(x) := -\lVert c_i(x)\rVert^{-1}c_i(x).

The chart models \Omega by positive height. At a boundary point, chart height is zero, so the negative conormal points toward the exterior side of the model half-space.

Write

D(x)=\sum_i\partial_iF_i(x), \qquad H(x)=\sum_iF_i(x)(x-c)_i.

First prove, for positive s near r, the compactly supported weighted identity

\int_{\mathbb R^n} \max\!\left(s^2-\lVert x-c\rVert^2,0\right)D(x)\,dx = 2\int_{B(c,s)}H(x)\,dx.

This is the integration-by-parts step; the positive-part quadratic cutoff removes any boundary-at-infinity term.

Differentiate this identity once with respect to s. The derivative of the left side is 2s\int_{B(c,s)}D, while the radial differentiation formula for the right side gives 2\int_{\partial B(c,s)}H. On \partial B(c,r), write

H(x) = r\sum_iF_i(x)\operatorname{normalize}(x-c)_i.

Substitute this identity and cancel the nonzero factor r. This yields the normal-flux formula.

Assume n>0, r>0, and let every component F_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R be globally C^1. Then

\int_{B(c,r)} \sum_{i=1}^n\partial_iF_i(x)\,dx = \int_{\partial B(c,r)} \sum_{i=1}^n F_i(x)\operatorname{normalize}(x-c)_i\,dS(x).

Equivalently, on the sphere where x\ne c,

\int_{B(c,r)}\operatorname{div}F\,dx = \int_{\partial B(c,r)} F(x)\mathbin{\cdot}\frac{x-c}{\lVert x-c\rVert}\,dS(x).

Identify Euclidean space with Mathlib's finite coordinate-product model by the canonical continuous linear equivalence. The identification preserves the coordinate order, so it carries Set.Icc a b to the corresponding product interval. A separate measure-preservation theorem transports Lebesgue volume; the Euclidean norm and the coordinate-product maximum norm need not agree.

Apply Mathlib's box divergence theorem component by component. Under the equivalence, the Fréchet derivative in the ith basis direction is exactly partialDeriv i. Transport the volume integral and every oriented face integral back through the measure-preserving equivalence. The resulting face sum is definitionally boxFlux.

Fix a,b\in\mathbb R^{m+1} with a\le b. Suppose every scalar component F_i:\mathbb R^{m+1}\to\mathbb R is globally C^1. Then

\int_{[a,b]} \sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\partial_iF_i(x)\,dx = \operatorname{boxFlux}_{[a,b]}(F).

Integrability of the coordinate divergence follows from continuity on the compact box and is not a hypothesis.

First let F be globally C^1 and treat one component and one direction at a time. Cover \overline\Omega by finitely many graph charts and one open set compactly inside \Omega, and split the component with a smooth partition of unity subordinate to that cover. The interior piece has compact support in \Omega, so the integral of its derivative vanishes. On a graph piece, integrate first along the vertical coordinate of the chart; the fundamental theorem of calculus leaves the value on the graph, and the factor produced by the change to graph coordinates is exactly the chart surface element times the corresponding component of \nu. Summing the pieces gives \int_\Omega\partial_iF_i=\int_{\partial\Omega}F_i\nu_i\,d\sigma, and summing over i gives the vector identity.

For a field that is only regular up to the boundary, uniform continuity of the derivatives and the graph structure give a globally C^1 field U equal to F on \overline\Omega. The divergences agree on the open set \Omega and the normal fluxes agree on \partial\Omega, so the identity for U is the identity for F. Integrability comes from the same extension: \operatorname{div}U is continuous on a compact set, and the flux is bounded on a boundary of finite surface measure.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+1} be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary, and write \sigma for the m-dimensional Hausdorff measure on \partial\Omega. Let F:\mathbb R^{m+1}\to\mathbb R^{m+1} be continuous on \overline\Omega, with each component C^1 on \Omega and with the component and its first partial derivatives uniformly continuous on \Omega. Then \operatorname{div}F is integrable on \Omega, the normal flux is \sigma-integrable, and

\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,d\sigma .

The graph hypothesis alone builds the boundary atlas that defines \nu. A second form takes the atlas as given, and a third assumes F is C^1 on all of \mathbb R^{m+1}.

Define F=(Q,-P). Its coordinate divergence is \partial_xQ-\partial_yP. Global C^1 regularity of P and Q gives global C^1 regularity of both components of F, and continuity of the curl gives integrability on the compact rectangle. Apply the box Gauss theorem and unfold rectangleCirculation.

Let a,b\in\mathbb R^2 satisfy a\le b, and let P,Q:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R be globally C^1. Then

\int_{[a,b]} \left( \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} \right)\,dA = \operatorname{rectangleCirculation}_{[a,b]}(P,Q).

Apply the ball Gauss formula to the vector field with components F_i=u\,\partial_i v. The product rule gives

\sum_i\partial_i(u\,\partial_i v) = \sum_i\partial_i u\,\partial_i v+u\,\Delta v.

Global C^1 and C^2 regularity makes the gradient pairing and Laplacian term continuous, hence integrable on the bounded ball. The boundary flux factors as u\,\partial_{\nu_c}v. Split the volume integral and rearrange.

Assume n>0 and r>0. If u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is globally C^1 and v:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is globally C^2, then

\int_{B(c,r)}u\,\Delta v\,dx = -\int_{B(c,r)} \sum_{i=1}^n\partial_i u\,\partial_i v\,dx + \int_{\partial B(c,r)} u\,\partial_{\nu_c}v\,dS.

The gradient pairing is represented in the theorem by its finite coordinate sum. The regularity is assumed on the whole space, which avoids an extension theorem.

Extend u to a globally C^1 function and \nabla v to a globally C^1 field, both agreeing with the originals on the closure. Their product is a globally C^1 field whose divergence on \Omega is \langle\nabla u,\nabla v\rangle+u\,\Delta v. The divergence theorem for globally C^1 fields turns its integral into the flux of u\,\overline{\nabla v}.

Let \Omega be as in the divergence theorem, with its boundary atlas. Let u be C^1 up to the boundary and continuous on \overline\Omega, and let v be C^2 up to the boundary, with continuously extended gradient \overline{\nabla v}. Then u\,\Delta v and \langle\nabla u,\nabla v\rangle are integrable on \Omega, u\,\partial_\nu v is \sigma-integrable, and

\int_\Omega u\,\Delta v\,dx+\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\,dx =\int_{\partial\Omega}u\,\overline{\nabla v}\cdot\nu\,d\sigma .
Apply the two-dimensional box Gauss theorem directly to F=(P,Q). The coordinate divergence is the displayed integrand, and the explicit face sum is rectangleOutwardFlux.

Under the same hypotheses a\le b and global C^1 regularity of P,Q,

\int_{[a,b]} \left( \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \right)\,dA = \operatorname{rectangleOutwardFlux}_{[a,b]}(P,Q).

Apply the ball Gauss theorem to F_i=u\,\partial_i v-v\,\partial_i u. Expanding its divergence produces two mixed terms \partial_i u\,\partial_i v and -\partial_i v\,\partial_i u, which cancel pointwise. The remaining volume term is u\Delta v-v\Delta u, and the radial flux is the displayed antisymmetric combination of normal derivatives.

Assume n>0, r>0, and let u,v:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R be globally C^2. Then

\int_{B(c,r)} \left(u\,\Delta v-v\,\Delta u\right)\,dx = \int_{\partial B(c,r)} \left( u\,\partial_{\nu_c}v - v\,\partial_{\nu_c}u \right)\,dS.
Apply the first identity to (u,v) and to (v,u) and subtract. The gradient terms cancel by symmetry of the inner product.

If u and v are both C^2 up to the boundary and continuous on \overline\Omega, then

\int_\Omega\bigl(u\,\Delta v-v\,\Delta u\bigr)\,dx =\int_{\partial\Omega}\bigl(u\,\overline{\nabla v}\cdot\nu -v\,\overline{\nabla u}\cdot\nu\bigr)\,d\sigma ,

with both integrands integrable.

Each bounded chart target intersects the flat boundary in a bounded measurable set of finite flat Hausdorff measure. The inverse chart is Lipschitz on its target, so its physical boundary patch also has finite Hausdorff measure. The finite chart family covers the frontier.

Intrinsic codimension-one Hausdorff surface measure has finite total mass on the boundary of a bounded operational C¹ domain:

\left( \mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega \right) \left(\mathbb R^{m+1}\right) <\infty.
Compare the chart chosen in the definition of \nu(x) with chart i and apply chartwise overlap compatibility at x.

If chart i contains the boundary point x, then the intrinsic normal agrees with the chartwise normal:

\nu(x)=\nu_i(x).
Choose a chart containing x, replace the intrinsic normal by its chartwise representative, and use the chartwise unit-norm theorem.

For every x\in\partial\Omega,

\lVert\nu(x)\rVert=1.

For x\in\partial\Omega, choose a chart source containing x and define

\nu(x):=\nu_i(x).

The finite atlas covers the frontier, and overlap compatibility proves that the result does not depend on the chosen chart.

Green's first identity with u=0 on the boundary gives \int u\,\Delta u=-\int\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2, and the equation turns this into the energy identity. For the second identity, extend u to a C^1 function on \mathbb R^n and apply the divergence theorem to V(u)\,(x-c). Its flux vanishes because V(u)=0 on \partial\Omega, and its divergence is nV(u)+((x-c)\cdot\nabla u)V'(u), so \int((x-c)\cdot\nabla u)V'(u)=-n\int V(u). By the equation the left side is -\int((x-c)\cdot\nabla u)\Delta u. Substituting into the Rellich identity gives the result.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n, n=m+1, be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary, and let V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be C^1 with V(0)=0. Let u be C^2 up to the boundary, continuous on \overline\Omega, zero on \partial\Omega, with -\Delta u=V'(u) in \Omega. Then for every c, all integrands in the two identities are integrable, and

\int_\Omega\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2\,dx=\int_\Omega u\,V'(u)\,dx,

\frac{n-2}2\int_\Omega\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2\,dx +\frac12\int_{\partial\Omega}\lvert\overline{\nabla u}\rvert^2\,(x-c)\cdot\nu\,d\sigma =n\int_\Omega V(u)\,dx .

For a planar field (P,Q), rectangleCirculation a b P Q is the counterclockwise coordinate-face sum

\oint_{\partial[a,b]} P\,dx+Q\,dy.

Formally it is boxFlux applied to the rotated field (Q,-P). This choice turns outward flux of the rotated field into positive counterclockwise circulation of (P,Q).

For a planar field (P,Q), rectangleOutwardFlux a b P Q is the oriented face sum representing

\oint_{\partial[a,b]}(P,Q)\mathbin{\cdot}\nu\,ds.

It is boxFlux applied directly to the two coordinate components.

The regularity of u up to the boundary gives a C^1 vector field G on all of \mathbb R^{m+1} that equals \nabla u in \Omega and \overline{\nabla u} on the closure. Apply the divergence theorem to R_c(G). Inside \Omega, G is the gradient of u near every point, so the divergence formula of the Rellich field turns the volume side into the left side. On the boundary, u vanishes identically, so all tangential derivatives vanish and \overline{\nabla u} is a multiple of \nu. The normal component of R_c(G) is then \tfrac12\lvert\overline{\nabla u}\rvert^2\,(x-c)\cdot\nu.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+1} be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary, let u be C^2 up to the boundary and continuous on \overline\Omega with u=0 on \partial\Omega, and let c be any point. Write n=m+1 and \overline{\nabla u} for the continuous extension of the gradient to \overline\Omega. Then \lvert\nabla u\rvert^2 and ((x-c)\cdot\nabla u)\,\Delta u are integrable on \Omega, the boundary integrand is \sigma-integrable, and

\int_\Omega\bigl((x-c)\cdot\nabla u\bigr)\,\Delta u\,dx +\Bigl(1-\frac n2\Bigr)\int_\Omega\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2\,dx =\frac12\int_{\partial\Omega}\lvert\overline{\nabla u}\rvert^2\,(x-c)\cdot\nu\,d\sigma .

For a vector field X and a vector field G on \mathbb R^n, the Rellich field is

R_X(G)=(X\cdot G)\,G-\tfrac12\lvert G\rvert^2X ,

and R_c(G) denotes the case X(x)=x-c. If G agrees with \nabla u near x for a function u that is C^2 at x, then

\operatorname{div}R_c(G)(x) =\bigl((x-c)\cdot G(x)\bigr)\,\Delta u(x) +\Bigl(1-\frac n2\Bigr)\lvert G(x)\rvert^2 .

If G(x) is a multiple of a unit vector \nu, then R_c(G)(x)\cdot\nu=\tfrac12\lvert G(x)\rvert^2\,(x-c)\cdot\nu.

The divergence theorem for R_X(G), with G the C^1 extension of the gradient, gives

\int_\Omega\Bigl((X\cdot\nabla u)\Delta u+DX\,\nabla u\cdot\nabla u -\tfrac12\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2\operatorname{div}X\Bigr)dx =\frac12\int_{\partial\Omega}(\partial_\nu u)^2\,X\cdot\nu\,d\sigma .

The right side is at least \tfrac\delta2\int(\partial_\nu u)^2. On the left, 2\lvert(X\cdot\nabla u)\Delta u\rvert\le(\Delta u)^2+M^2\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2, and the other two terms are bounded by K and D/2 times \lvert\nabla u\rvert^2. For the constant, the graph structure provides a smooth field X with X\cdot\nu\ge\tfrac12 on the boundary, built before u is chosen.

Let \Omega be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary. There is a constant C>0 such that every u that is C^2 up to the boundary, continuous on \overline\Omega and zero on \partial\Omega satisfies

\int_{\partial\Omega}(\partial_\nu u)^2\,d\sigma \le C\Bigl(\int_\Omega(\Delta u)^2\,dx+\int_\Omega\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2\,dx\Bigr).

More precisely, if X is C^1 with X\cdot\nu\ge\delta>0 on \partial\Omega, and \lvert X\rvert\le M, \lVert DX\rVert\le K and \lvert\operatorname{div}X\rvert\le D in \Omega, one may take the constant \delta^{-1} in front of \int(\Delta u)^2+(M^2+2K+D)\int\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2.

The segment from x\in\partial\Omega to c lies in \overline\Omega. In a boundary chart at x, the flattened height coordinate is positive in \Omega and zero on the boundary, so on \overline\Omega it has a local minimum at x.
