Its derivative in the direction c-x of the segment is therefore nonnegative. The gradient of the height is a positive multiple of -\nu(x), so (c-x)\cdot\nu(x)\le0.

If \overline\Omega is star-shaped about c, then (x-c)\cdot\nu(x)\ge0 at every boundary point. Consequently \int_{\partial\Omega}w\,(x-c)\cdot\nu\,d\sigma\ge0 for every weight w that is nonnegative on \partial\Omega.

Take V(s)=\lvert s\rvert^{p+1}/(p+1), which is C^1 with V'(s)=\lvert s\rvert^{p-1}s because p\ge1. Write P=\int_\Omega\lvert u\rvert^{p+1}. The energy identity gives \int\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2=P, and by star-shapedness the boundary term of the Pohozaev identity is nonnegative, so

\Bigl(\frac{n-2}2-\frac n{p+1}\Bigr)P\le0 .

The bracket is positive exactly when p+1>2n/(n-2), that is, p>(n+2)/(n-2). Hence P=0, so u=0 almost everywhere in \Omega, everywhere in \Omega by continuity, and on the closure by continuity again.

Let n\ge3 and p>(n+2)/(n-2). Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary, with \overline\Omega star-shaped about some point. If u is C^2 up to the boundary, continuous on \overline\Omega, zero on \partial\Omega, and

-\Delta u=\lvert u\rvert^{p-1}u\quad\text{in }\Omega ,

then u=0 on \overline\Omega.
Apply the finite-exponent density-root change-of-measure equivalence with \sigma_{\mathcal A} as the reference measure and \rho_{\mathcal A}\sigma_{\mathcal A} as intrinsic surface measure.
The atlas-measure representative of T_p f is \rho_{\mathcal A}^{1/p}f almost everywhere.
Use positivity and almost everywhere finiteness of the density to multiply by the reciprocal density root.
The intrinsic-surface representative of T_p^{-1}g is \rho_{\mathcal A}^{-1/p}g almost everywhere.

For a finite real exponent p\ge 1, density-root rescaling gives the canonical linear isometric equivalence

T_p: L^p( \mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega ) \simeq_{\mathrm{iso}} L^p(\sigma_{\mathcal A}).

Its forward map and inverse change representatives by

T_p f=\rho_{\mathcal A}^{1/p}f, \qquad T_p^{-1}g=\rho_{\mathcal A}^{-1/p}g almost everywhere with respect to the corresponding measures. In particular, \lVert T_p f\rVert_{L^p(\sigma_{\mathcal A})} equals the intrinsic surface Lᵖ norm of f.

Intrinsic surface measure is finite on a bounded operational C¹ domain and therefore sigma-finite. The Radon–Nikodym derivative of a sigma-finite measure is finite almost everywhere for its reference measure.
The density \rho_{\mathcal A} is finite \sigma_{\mathcal A}-almost everywhere.
The Radon–Nikodym derivative is positive almost everywhere for intrinsic surface measure. Mutual absolute continuity transfers that statement to the atlas measure.
The density \rho_{\mathcal A} is strictly positive \sigma_{\mathcal A}-almost everywhere.
Apply the Bochner integral change-of-measure theorem for the Radon–Nikodym derivative. In Lean the scalar weight is the real value of the almost everywhere finite extended-nonnegative density.

For every function f into a normed real vector space, Bochner integration against intrinsic surface measure is weighted Bochner integration against the atlas measure:

\int_{\partial\Omega} f\, d\left(\mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega\right) = \int_{\partial\Omega} \rho_{\mathcal A} f\,d\sigma_{\mathcal A}.
Use the nonnegative integral formula for a measure reconstructed from its Radon–Nikodym density.

For every nonnegative almost everywhere measurable f,

\int_{\partial\Omega}^{-} f\, d\left(\mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega\right) = \int_{\partial\Omega}^{-} \rho_{\mathcal A} f\,d\sigma_{\mathcal A}.

Restrict the local reverse absolute-continuity theorem to each disjoint cell C_i. The corresponding chart contribution is one summand of the atlas measure. Summing the restricted intrinsic measures over the disjoint cell cover recovers all intrinsic surface measure.

Intrinsic surface measure is absolutely continuous with respect to the assembled atlas measure:

\mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega \ll \sigma_{\mathcal A}.

The intrinsic surface-measure density relative to the operational atlas measure is the Radon–Nikodym derivative

\rho_{\mathcal A} := \frac{ d\left(\mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega\right) }{ d\sigma_{\mathcal A} }.

Strict positivity of J_i^\partial shows that weighted and unweighted parameter measures have the same null sets. The inverse chart is Lipschitz on its bounded target, so flat parameter-null sets map to intrinsic Hausdorff-null subsets of the physical boundary patch.

On the physical patch covered by chart i, intrinsic surface measure is absolutely continuous with respect to the chart measure:

\left( \mathcal H^m\restriction\partial\Omega \right) \restriction \left( \operatorname{source}(\kappa_i)\cap\partial\Omega \right) \ll \sigma_i^\partial.

Take the Taylor series of the coefficients and apply the convergence theorem. The sum of the formal solution is analytic on its ball of convergence, its trace at t=0 vanishes because the t^0 coefficient does, and the power-series identities for the equation hold after summation. For uniqueness, the Taylor series at the origin of any analytic solution with zero trace solves the formal system, so by the uniqueness of formal solutions both Taylor series coincide, and analytic functions with the same Taylor series agree near their center.

Suppose every B_{jik} and c_i is a real function of (z,x) analytic at the origin. Then for some r>0 there is a field u analytic on the ball of radius r about the origin in \mathbb R^{1+d} with u(0,x)=0 for |x|<r and

\partial_tu_i=\sum_{j,k}B_{jik}(u,x)\,\partial_{x_j}u_k+c_i(u,x)

on that ball. Two fields analytic at the origin that satisfy the equation and have zero initial trace near the origin agree on a neighborhood of the origin.

Finitely many series of positive radius admit one common geometric majorant \alpha/(\rho-\sum_iz_i-\sum_jx_j). Take \kappa=m(d+1)/2. The comparison theorem bounds each component of the formal solution by the scalar majorant, which converges, and a series dominated coefficientwise by a convergent one converges on the same polydisc.

If every coefficient series B_{jik} and c_i has positive radius of convergence, the formal solution of the reduced system has zero coefficient of t^0 and each component has positive radius of convergence. More precisely, whenever all coefficients are majorized by the coefficient majorant with \rho>0 and \alpha\ge0, the formal solution converges.

Write \partial^\alpha(u\circ c) by the finite chain rule for compositions. The derivatives of u of order k appear linearly, with coefficients built from first derivatives of c, and everything else depends only on lower derivatives of u. Collecting terms defines the transformed coefficients and the forcing. The coefficient of the pure derivative \partial_i^k collects the products of the i-th component of the first derivative of c in each slot. That component is \nabla\varphi=\lvert\nabla\varphi\rvert\,\nu, so the coefficient is \lvert\nabla\varphi\rvert^k times the principal symbol at \nu.

Let c be analytic with inverse \psi. Pulling back by c gives transformed coefficients and forcing, analytic where the originals are, such that u\circ c solves the original equation at \psi(y) exactly when u solves the transformed equation at y. If the i-th component of c is \varphi near \psi(y) and \nabla\varphi\ne0 there, the transformed coefficient of \partial_i^k is

\lvert\nabla\varphi\rvert^k\sum_{\lvert\alpha\rvert=k}a_\alpha\,\nu^\alpha, \qquad \nu=\frac{\nabla\varphi}{\lvert\nabla\varphi\rvert},

with the original coefficients evaluated at the transported lower jet. It is nonzero exactly when \Gamma is noncharacteristic at that point.

Group the coefficients of a series by their power of t. Since the unknowns vanish at t=0, substitution into the coefficient series is admissible, and the coefficient of t^n on the right depends only on the coefficients of u of time degree at most n, spatial derivatives included, because \partial_{x_j} does not change the power of t. The equation therefore defines the coefficient of t^{n+1} in u from those already chosen. Strong induction on the time degree gives existence, and the same induction shows that any two solutions agree degree by degree.

Over any commutative ring R containing \mathbb Q, and for any formal coefficient series B_{jik} and c_i, there is exactly one tuple of formal series u_i\in R[[t,x_1,\ldots,x_d]] with zero coefficient of t^0 and

\partial_tu_i=\sum_{j,k}B_{jik}(u,x)\,\partial_{x_j}u_k+c_i(u,x) \qquad(1\le i\le m),

where B_{jik}(u,x) substitutes the series u for the state variables. The underlying recursion is stated for any order k and any index set: if the coefficients of G(u) up to time degree n depend only on the coefficients of u below time degree n+k, then \partial_t^ku=G(u) has a unique solution whose first k time coefficients vanish.

Differentiating the equal normal data tangentially gives equal lower jets on the hypersurface, as in the first step of the jet theorem. Transport these through the chart to equal lower jets on \{y_0=0\}. The transformed equation has a nonzero pure transverse coefficient by the coordinate-change theorem, so flat uniqueness applies to the two pulled-back solutions.

Let c be an analytic chart at p with analytic inverse, c(p)=0, and first component \varphi, with \nabla\varphi(p)\ne0. Suppose the coefficients are analytic at the lower jet of u at p, and the principal symbol at the unit normal is nonzero there. Two solutions analytic at p with the same normal derivatives D_\nu^ju for j<k on \{\varphi=0\} near p agree near p.

Induct on the time degree. At degree zero both solutions vanish. Majorization is preserved by sums, products, substitution into a majorized series, and spatial differentiation, all on sets of multi-indices closed under going down in the time degree. So a bound through degree n for the unknowns gives one for the right-hand sides, and the equation \partial_tu=\text{right-hand side} moves it up to degree n+1.

Let u solve the formal system with coefficients (B,c) and v solve it with coefficients (D,e), both with zero coefficient of t^0. If B_{jik} is majorized by D_{jik} and c_i by e_i for all indices, then every u_i is majorized by v_i. The comparison of right-hand sides holds degree by degree: if u is majorized by v through time degree n, the two right-hand sides are majorized through the same degree.

Below order k, differentiate the equal normal data along the parametrizations of \Gamma. Tangential derivatives of an identity on \Gamma give equality of D^ju and D^jv on any list of j vectors, each tangent to \Gamma or equal to \nu, and for j<k such lists span all of D^ju. In particular J_{<k}u=J_{<k}v on \Gamma, so the two equations have the same coefficients there.

At order k+i induct on i. Tangential differentiation of the previous step fixes every component of D^{k+i}u except the one with all k+i slots filled by \nu. Differentiating the equation i times along \nu produces that component multiplied by the principal symbol, plus terms already known to agree. Since the symbol is nonzero, the pure normal derivative agrees as well. The Lean proof carries out this argument once, for conormal tensors, and the quasilinear statement instantiates it with the coordinate monomials \nu^\alpha; their mixed-partial multiplicities are part of the coordinate expansion and not of the coefficients.

Let k>0, let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open and \Gamma\subseteq\Omega, and let the coefficients a_\alpha(x,p) and b(x,p) be C^\infty on \Omega times the space of lower jets. Let \nu be nonzero along \Gamma, and let \Gamma have local parametrizations whose differential at each point has image \ker\langle\nu(x),\cdot\rangle. Suppose u,v\in C^\infty(\Omega) both solve the equation in \Omega, their lower normal data agree,

D_\nu^ju=D_\nu^jv\quad\text{on }\Gamma\text{ for }0\le j<k,

and the principal symbol at the jet of u does not vanish:

\sum_{|\alpha|=k}a_\alpha\bigl(x,J_{<k}u(x)\bigr)\,\nu(x)^\alpha\ne0 \qquad(x\in\Gamma).

Then D^ju=D^jv on \Gamma for every j\ge0. The first Lean form asks instead that the symbol be nonzero at every lower jet p, which is how the condition is usually stated for linear equations; the second evaluates it only at the jet of u.

Shift by G and divide by the pure time coefficient, which stays nonzero on a neighbourhood by continuity. The normalized coefficients are analytic, and the zero-data theorem solves the shifted equation. Adding G back gives u on a ball small enough for the division to be valid. For uniqueness, use the solution u itself as the data extension. Then 0 and v-u solve the same normalized equation, both with zero pure time traces, and zero-data uniqueness gives v-u=0 near the origin.

Let G be analytic at the origin, let a_\alpha and b be analytic at (0,J_{<k}G(0)), and suppose a_{(0,\ldots,0)}(0,J_{<k}G(0))\ne0. Then on some ball about the origin there is an analytic solution u of the equation with J_{<k}u=J_{<k}G on \{x_0=0\}. Two analytic solutions with the same lower jet on \{x_0=0\} near the origin agree near the origin, provided the pure time coefficient is nonzero at their common initial jet.

The time-degree recursion of the formal solution theorem applies with one unknown and order k. The coefficient of t^n on the right uses only time coefficients of u below n+k, because every term has fewer than k time derivatives. For convergence, the lower jet U=(\partial^\beta u)_{\lvert\beta\rvert<k} satisfies a first-order system. The time derivative of a component of order below k-1 is another component. A top-order derivative with a spatial index i is \partial_{x_i} of a lower component, and the pure time derivative of top order is given by the equation. One extra clock component absorbs the explicit dependence on x_0. The system is in the normal form of the convergence theorem, so its formal solution converges. By formal uniqueness, its first component is the scalar formal solution.

Over any commutative \mathbb Q-algebra and for any formal coefficient series, the normal form has exactly one formal solution whose first k time coefficients vanish. Over \mathbb R, if every coefficient series has positive radius of convergence, this formal solution has positive radius of convergence.

Differentiating the quadratic identity in t and in each x_j gives equations for \partial_tv and \partial_{x_j}v with the common invertible factor \rho-\sum_jx_j-2\kappa v. Substituting v into the coefficient majorant turns its denominator into \rho-\sum_jx_j-mv, and the choice 2\kappa=m(d+1) makes the two sides of the system agree after cancelling that factor. For convergence, collapse all variables to one: the coefficients are nonnegative, so the radius of the multivariable series is controlled by that of a one-variable quadratic root with nonzero constant term in its denominator, and such a root is analytic near zero.

If \rho\ne0 and 2\kappa=m(d+1), the tuple whose m components all equal the scalar majorant solves the formal Cauchy system in which every matrix entry and every forcing component is the coefficient majorant. If \rho>0 and \alpha,\kappa\ge0, the scalar majorant has nonnegative coefficients and a positive radius of convergence.

For \rho,\alpha,\kappa\in\mathbb R, the spatial denominator is \rho-\sum_{j=1}^dx_j and the scalar majorant is the root of (\rho-\sum_jx_j)v=\alpha t+\kappa v^2 with zero trace at t=0,

v=\operatorname{root}\Bigl(\frac{\alpha t}{\rho-\sum_jx_j},\ \frac{\kappa}{\rho-\sum_jx_j}\Bigr),

where \operatorname{root}(a,b) is the formal series solving w=a+bw^2 built from the Catalan numbers, w=\sum_{n\ge0}C_n\,b^n a^{n+1}. The coefficient majorant is \alpha/(\rho-\sum_iz_i-\sum_jx_j) in the m state and d spatial variables.

The sum of the convergent formal solution is analytic on its ball, and the power-series form of the equation turns into the pointwise equation after summation. The vanishing time coefficients give the zero lower jet on the initial plane. For uniqueness, the Taylor series of either solution satisfies the formal equation with zero initial coefficients, so both Taylor series equal the unique formal solution.

If the coefficients a_\alpha and b are analytic at the origin, the normal form has a solution analytic on a ball about the origin in \mathbb R^{1+d} whose whole lower jet vanishes on \{x_0=0\}. Two solutions analytic at the origin whose pure time derivatives of order below k vanish on \{x_0=0\} near the origin agree near the origin.

The coordinate functions are bundled as continuous linear maps

\pi_t\in\mathcal L(\mathbb R^{n+1},\mathbb R), \qquad \pi_x\in\mathcal L(\mathbb R^{n+1},\mathbb R^n),

with exact coordinate laws

\pi_t(z)=z_0, \qquad \pi_x(z)_i=z_{i+1}.

The bundled spatial projection has the same coordinate values as the plain projection.

The map

\iota_x\in\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n,\mathbb R^{n+1}), \qquad \iota_x(v)=(0,v),

is the derivative of every fixed-time embedding x\mapsto(t,x). Its coordinate laws are (\iota_xv)_0=0 and (\iota_xv)_{i+1}=v_i.

Construction. The time map is Mathlib's continuous-linear coordinate projection at 0:\operatorname{Fin}(n+1). For the spatial map, take the family of coordinate projections indexed by i:\operatorname{Fin}(n), using i+1 in spacetime, assemble the family into a continuous linear map to a function space, and transport it through the continuous-linear equivalence between that function space and Euclidean \ell^2 coordinates. Extensional equality with spatialPart follows by evaluating both sides at every i. The embedding is verified in coordinate zero and in every successor coordinate.

Compose f with the jointly smooth assembly map (t,x)\mapsto(t,x). The product of a closed interval and a closed ball in finite-dimensional Euclidean space is compact. A continuous norm-valued function is bounded on that compact set. Replacing the resulting bound by its maximum with zero gives the stated nonnegative constant.

Let f:\mathbb R^{n+1}\to E be continuous, where E is a normed additive group. For every closed time interval [a,b] and closed spatial ball \overline B(c,r), there is a nonnegative C such that

\lVert f(t,x)\rVert\le C \qquad (t\in[a,b],\ x\in\overline B(c,r)).

No assumption that a\le b or r\ge0 is needed. If either set is empty, the conclusion is vacuous; otherwise it is the ordinary compact-cylinder bound.

Differentiate \cos\beta\,f by the product rule and use \sin^2\beta+\cos^2\beta=1 to obtain the weighted-derivative identity. CAS checks the derivatives of the sine and cosine modes. Double-angle and addition formulas then give the two neighboring frequencies. Finite-sum differentiation and linearity yield the expansion formula.

Define

\mathcal Df=(1+\cos^2\beta)f +\sin\beta\cos\beta\,f'.

At each point where f is differentiable,

\begin{aligned} \cos\beta\,\mathcal Df & = \sin\beta\cos\beta\,u' + 2u,\\ u&=\cos\beta\,f. \end{aligned}

For either m_k(\beta)=\sin(k\beta) or m_k(\beta)=\cos(k\beta), with any real frequency k,

\begin{aligned} \mathcal Dm_k &=\frac32m_k+\frac{k+1}{4}m_{k+2}\\ &\quad+\frac{1-k}{4}m_{k-2}. \end{aligned}

The identity extends termwise to any finite expansion with real coefficients and frequencies. It gives an exact transformation of the radial coefficients; the finite index set, its coefficients, and its frequencies are arbitrary. A spherical divergence-free reconstruction also needs the angular basis and the physical coordinate change, which are separate from this one-variable identity.

For any codomain type E, with no topology or algebraic structure required, the coordinate round trip induces

(\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\to E) \;\longleftrightarrow\; (\mathbb R^{n+1}\to E).

Explicitly,

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{uncurry}(u)(z) &=u(\pi_xz)(\pi_tz),\\ \operatorname{curry}(U)(x)(t) &=U(t,x). \end{aligned}

Both composites are identity functions. Since this is a coordinate reindexing, scalar fields, vector fields, predicates, solution records, and symbolic objects can all use the same interface.

Verification. For a curried u, evaluate at arbitrary x,t and use the two projection laws for (t,x). For a spacetime field U, evaluate at arbitrary z and use the reconstruction identity (\pi_tz,\pi_xz)=z. Function extensionality then gives both global equalities.

First split the coordinates into the two blocks equipped with the \ell^2 product norm, represented in Lean by WithLp 2. This is a linear isometry and preserves canonically normalized Euclidean volume. Forgetting the WithLp structure also preserves product volume, by a separate measure-preservation theorem. The composite therefore gives the required product measure, although the ordinary product carries the maximum norm and the composite need not be an isometry.

Orthogonally splitting \mathbb R^{m+n} into its first m and last n coordinates preserves the canonically normalized Euclidean volume measure. This is a measure-theoretic coordinate change, so Fubini's theorem applies to it.

Represent the left side using the constant spatial direction (e_i,0) and the time direction (0,1). Both directions are constant, so differentiating again gives the second differential on the pair, and its symmetry exchanges their order, proving the C^2 identity. For two spatial derivatives, first view the inner spatial derivative as a new C^2 field; one derivative has already been spent from the original C^3 hypothesis. Apply the first commutation theorem and then commute time past the remaining spatial direction.

For a globally C^2 field F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\to E, one spatial derivative commutes with the derivative of a fixed-space time trace:

\frac d{dt}\,\partial_i^xF(x,t) =\partial_i^x\frac d{dt}F(x,t).

For a globally C^3 field, the same is true after two spatial derivatives:

\frac d{dt}\,\partial_i^x\partial_j^xF(x,t) =\partial_i^x\partial_j^x\frac d{dt}F(x,t).

The codomain E is any real normed space. After slice derivatives are rewritten as joint derivatives, the C^2 and C^3 hypotheses provide the symmetric second differentials of the field and of its spatial derivatives that move time past one or two spatial directions.

The radial-power formula with dimension two gives (\partial_r^2+r^{-1}\partial_r)r^m=m^2r^{m-2}. The angular derivative contributes r^{m-2}f''(\beta). Set m=2+\alpha, negate, and collect the common factor r^\alpha. The radial product rule then expands \Delta_{\mathrm{pol}}(\chi r^m f) and isolates the two terms containing \chi' or \chi''. For the coordinate bridge, apply the second-order chain rule to U\circ\Phi; the first-order terms cancel, the mixed Hessian terms cancel, and \sin^2\beta+\cos^2\beta=1 leaves the Cartesian trace.

For a two-variable profile u(r,\beta), define the polar differential expression

\Delta_{\mathrm{pol}}u =\partial_r^2u+\frac1r\partial_ru+\frac1{r^2}\partial_\beta^2u.

At every r>0, a homogeneous angular mode satisfies

-\Delta_{\mathrm{pol}}\bigl(r^{2+\alpha}f(\beta)\bigr) =r^\alpha\left(-f''(\beta)-(2+\alpha)^2f(\beta)\right).

Consequently, the angular equation (-\partial_\beta^2-(2+\alpha)^2)f=g produces the polar source r^\alpha g(\beta). More generally, if (-\partial_\beta^2-m^2)f=g and \chi is a radial C^2 cutoff, Lean proves the product rule with every cutoff error explicit:

-\Delta_{\mathrm{pol}}(\chi r^m f) =\chi r^{m-2}g-r^m f\,\Delta_{\mathrm{rad}}\chi -2m r^{m-1}\chi'f.

For a Cartesian C^2 field U, Lean additionally proves, at every r\ne0,

\Delta U\bigl(r\cos\beta,r\sin\beta\bigr) =\Delta_{\mathrm{pol}}(U\circ\Phi)(r,\beta), \qquad \Phi(r,\beta)=(r\cos\beta,r\sin\beta).

The parameter-plane operator is proved equal to the curried operator \Delta_{\mathrm{pol}}, and a germ-local theorem permits replacing U\circ\Phi by a locally equal polar profile. Thus the homogeneous and cutoff calculations become Euclidean Laplacian identities once their C^2 pullback hypotheses hold.

Start from the measure-preserving polar-coordinate formula. Fubini's theorem then separates the product integral into an angular integral followed by a radial integral. Expanding the radial measure contributes the density r^{\dim E-1} and gives the displayed iterated expression.

On the same positive-dimensional space, for every integrable Banach-valued function, Fubini exposes the familiar iterated formula

\int_E g(x)\,d\mu(x) =\int_0^\infty r^{\dim E-1} \left(\int_{S(E)} g(r\omega)\,d\mu_S(\omega)\right)dr.

Here \mu_S is the canonical sphere measure induced by the chosen additive Haar measure \mu.

Remove the origin, which has Haar measure zero, and integrate over its complement. The polar homeomorphism identifies that complement with the unit sphere times the positive radii and is measure preserving for the sphere measure times volumeIoiPow. Pulling the integrand across this equivalence gives the formula; the radial measure already contains the Jacobian.

For a positive-dimensional real normed space of finite dimension carrying an additive Haar measure, a whole-space Bochner integral equals its angular-times-radial pullback. The radial measure already contains the Jacobian r^{n-1}, and the origin is discarded as a null set before the measure-preserving equivalence is applied.
Differentiate on the positive half-line: (\log r)'=1/r and (\log r)''=-1/r^2. Substitution into the two-dimensional radial Laplacian gives -1/r^2+(1/r)(1/r)=0.

On the positive radial branch,

\left(\frac{d^2}{dr^2}+\frac1r\frac d{dr}\right)\log r=0 \qquad(r>0).

This one-variable identity underlies the two-dimensional logarithmic fundamental solution away from its singularity.

Canonical spacetime has two explicit product views:

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{split}(z)&=(\pi_xz,\pi_tz) \in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R,\\ \operatorname{join}(x,t)&=(t,x) \in\mathbb R^{n+1}. \end{aligned}

They are inverse:

\operatorname{split}(\operatorname{join}(x,t))=(x,t), \qquad \operatorname{join}(\operatorname{split}z)=z.

Both directions are continuous linear maps, and together they define

\mathbb R^{n+1} \xrightarrow[\sim]{\text{continuous linear}} \mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R.

Composing with the product swap gives the equally useful equivalence

\mathbb R^{n+1} \xrightarrow[\sim]{\text{continuous linear}} \mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n.

The names encode the order: spaceTimeContinuousLinearEquiv returns (x,t), while timeSpaceContinuousLinearEquiv returns (t,x), so one pair is never read in both orders.

Verification. For the first round trip, compare the spatial and time components: spatialPart (timeSpaceCons t x) = x and the zeroth coordinate of timeSpaceCons t x is t. For the reverse round trip, use coordinate extensionality. Coordinate zero is reconstructed from z_0; every successor coordinate is reconstructed from the corresponding entry of spatialPart z.

The bundled equivalence is a composite of four Mathlib equivalences: Euclidean coordinates to plain functions, splitting coordinate zero off the tail, returning the tail to Euclidean coordinates, and swapping the two factors. Its forward and inverse maps unfold to the split and join maps by definition, and the time-first equivalence adds one more swap.

In dimension n, the radial expression is f''(r) + (n-1)f'(r)/r. It specializes to the familiar polar and spherical formulas in dimensions two and three. Real division is total in Lean, so the definition itself also has a value at zero; analytic theorems interpreting it as a coordinate Laplacian assume that the radius is positive or nonzero.

By the radial Laplacian theorem, this expression is the Cartesian Laplacian of x\mapsto f(\lVert x\rVert) at x\ne0, provided the profile is twice continuously differentiable at that radius.
On r>0, the first two derivatives of r^p are pr^{p-1} and p(p-1)r^{p-2}. Adding the radial correction (n-1)r^{-1}pr^{p-1} and collecting coefficients yields p(p+n-2)r^{p-2}.

At every positive radius, the dimension-n radial Laplacian sends the power profile r^p to p(p+n-2)r^{p-2}. For n>2, the choice p=2-n gives the harmonic inverse-power profile. In dimension two this choice gives only the constant profile; the nonconstant logarithmic profile is covered by the preceding theorem.

Apply the Fréchet chain rule to the affine inclusions s\mapsto(x,s) and y\mapsto(y,t). Their derivatives are respectively a\mapsto(0,a) and v\mapsto(v,0). Evaluating at 1 or e_i gives the two product formulas.

For canonical spacetime, the fixed-time embedding has derivative \iota_x:v\mapsto(0,v), and \iota_x(e_i)=e_{i+1}. The fixed-space time curve has velocity e_0. Substitution into the same chain rule yields the coordinate formulas. Finally, joinSpaceTime is the inverse continuous linear map from (x,t) coordinates, so the pullback statements are these identities in the product representation.

Let E be a real normed vector space. At a point where the joint field is differentiable, derivatives of fixed-space and fixed-time slices are the corresponding joint directional derivatives.

For a product field F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\to E,

\frac d{ds}F(x,s)\bigg|_{s=t} =DF(x,t)[(0,1)]

and

\partial_i\bigl(y\mapsto F(y,t)\bigr)(x) =DF(x,t)[(e_i,0)].

For a canonical spacetime field U:\mathbb R^{n+1}\to E,

\begin{aligned} \partial_i\bigl(y\mapsto U(t,y)\bigr)(x) &=\partial_{i+1}U(t,x),\\ \frac d{ds}U(s,x)\bigg|_{s=t} &=\partial_0U(t,x). \end{aligned}

The same facts are also stated after pulling U back through joinSpaceTime: the product direction (0,1) becomes spacetime coordinate 0, and (e_i,0) becomes coordinate i+1.

Rewrite each slice derivative using the preceding slice chain rules as fderiv of F evaluated on a constant direction. The derivative field of a C^{m+1} map is C^m; evaluation of a continuous-linear map on a constant vector preserves that regularity. Composing with the smooth paths x\mapsto(x,t) or t\mapsto(x,t) gives the trace statements. Iterate the argument for two spatial derivatives. On an open cylinder, joint ContDiffOn upgrades to ContDiffAt at each interior point, after which the fixed-space chain rule supplies differentiability of the time curve.

The slice operations use exactly the expected number of derivatives. If F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\to E is globally C^{m+1}, then:

  • for every fixed t, the map x\mapsto \frac d{ds}F(x,s)|_{s=t} is C^m;

  • the jointly varying spatial derivative (x,t)\mapsto\partial_i^xF(x,t) is C^m;

  • consequently, for every fixed x, the time trace

t\longmapsto \partial_i\bigl(y\mapsto F(y,t)\bigr)(x)

is C^m.

If F is C^{m+2}, then a fixed-point time trace of two spatial derivatives is C^m. These are the exact variable dependencies of the Lean theorems.

There is also a local cylinder statement. If I\subseteq\mathbb R is open and F is jointly C^1 on \mathbb R^n\times I, then every curve t\mapsto F(x,t) is differentiable at every t\in I. Thus a classical solution predicate that already stores joint C^1 regularity should not store time differentiability again as independent data.

Both directions are composition with one side of the continuous-linear equivalence \mathbb R^{n+1}\cong\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R. Continuous linear maps are C^\infty, so composition preserves every requested order m. The inverse laws identify the resulting composites with the original fields. The curried statement is the same theorem after unfolding spaceTimeUncurry.

Let E be a real normed vector space and let m\in\mathbb N_\infty. Smoothness is invariant under the spacetime coordinate equivalence:

U:\mathbb R^{n+1}\to E\text{ is }C^m \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad ((x,t)\mapsto U(t,x))\text{ is }C^m.

Equivalently, a curried field u(x)(t) is jointly C^m after spaceTimeUncurry exactly when the ordinary product function (x,t)\mapsto u(x)(t) is C^m. This is joint regularity; it is stronger than assuming separate smoothness in x and t.

For a scalar spacetime field u:\mathbb R^{n+1}\to\mathbb R, the spatial gradient discards the time component of the full Euclidean gradient:

\nabla_xu(z):=\pi_x(\nabla u(z)).

Its exact component formula is

(\nabla_xu(z))_i=\partial_{i+1}u(z).

Coordinate zero never appears. As with the full gradient and partialDeriv, this is an equality of totalized expressions; interpreting the components as classical derivatives requires differentiability of u at the point.

Verification. Evaluate the spatial projection at i, which selects coordinate i+1 of the full gradient. The gradient-coordinate theorem attached to the gradient definition identifies that coordinate with \partial_{i+1}u.

Differentiate the composition of f with the affine coordinate line. The line has derivative equal to the ith Euclidean basis vector and passes through x at parameter x_i, so the chain rule gives exactly the Fréchet derivative of f applied to that basis vector.

If f is differentiable at x, the coordinate derivative is the ordinary derivative along the ith coordinate line:

\partial_i f(x) =\left.\frac{d}{dt}f\bigl(x+(t-x_i)e_i\bigr)\right|_{t=x_i}.

This connects the Fréchet definition with one-variable directional calculations.

Equality of f and g near x gives equality of their Fréchet derivatives near x, hence of each coordinate derivative. Induction on the number of derivatives gives the first claim, and applying it to the j-block and then to the i-block gives the second.

Repeated coordinate derivatives are local operators. Suppose f,g:\mathbb R^n\to E agree on a neighborhood of x.

  • The repeated derivatives D_i^m f and D_i^m g agree on a neighborhood of x, and in particular D_i^m f(x)=D_i^m g(x).

  • The same holds after a block of b derivatives in coordinate j followed by a block of a derivatives in coordinate i.

No differentiability hypothesis enters, because the coordinate derivatives are those of the totalized Fréchet derivative.

Induct on the list \alpha. For the empty list, both sides reduce to \partial_i f. For \alpha=j::\beta, unfold one recursive layer on each side. Both expressions become \partial_j applied to the induction hypothesis for \beta, so they agree definitionally after rewriting.

Appending a coordinate to the right of a derivative word means that this new coordinate derivative acts on the original field first:

D_{\alpha\mathbin{+\!\!+}[i]}f =D_\alpha(\partial_i f).

This theorem pins down the list-order convention. It holds for fields with arbitrary real normed-space codomain and is an identity between totalized derivative expressions, with no smoothness assumption.

Induct on \alpha. The empty word reduces to the corresponding pointwise algebra identity. At a successor word, unfold the outer coordinate derivative. Zero and scalar multiplication use their unconditional single-derivative rules. For addition and subtraction, global C^m regularity makes every derivative along a proper tail of the word differentiable, so the single-coordinate sum or difference rule applies at the next step.

For a derivative word \alpha and fields f,g:\mathbb R^n\to E,

D_\alpha 0=0,\qquad D_\alpha(cf)=cD_\alpha f.

These two identities are unconditional because the total Fréchet derivative commutes with zero and constant scalar multiplication even at nondifferentiability points. If f and g are globally C^m, where m is the length of \alpha, then

D_\alpha(f+g)=D_\alpha f+D_\alpha g,\qquad D_\alpha(f-g)=D_\alpha f-D_\alpha g.

All four statements allow an arbitrary real normed-space codomain E.

A derivative word \alpha=[i_1,\ldots,i_m] and a field f:\mathbb R^n\to E, where E is any real normed vector space, determine the recursion

D_{[]}f:=f,\qquad D_{i::\alpha}f:=\partial_i(D_\alpha f).

Consequently,

D_{[i_1,\ldots,i_m]}f =\partial_{i_1}\bigl(\partial_{i_2}(\cdots\partial_{i_m}f)\bigr).

The head of the Lean list is the outermost derivative, while the final list entry is the derivative applied to f first.

The construction does not require a scalar codomain. Every recursive stage still maps \mathbb R^n to the same normed space E, so coordinate differentiation can be iterated for vector-, matrix-, or function-space-valued fields without introducing a second definition. Statements that interpret the totalized expression analytically supply the regularity needed at every iteration.

Unfold partialDeriv as the total Fréchet derivative evaluated on a basis vector. Apply Mathlib's derivative rules for addition, subtraction, negation, and constant scalar multiplication, then evaluate the resulting continuous linear maps on that vector. The sum and difference rules use the stated differentiability hypotheses.

Coordinate differentiation obeys the usual linearity identities:

\partial_i(f+g)=\partial_i f+\partial_i g,\qquad \partial_i(cf)=c\,\partial_i f,

and hence \partial_i(-f)=-\partial_i f and \partial_i(f-g)=\partial_i f-\partial_i g. The sum and difference identities assume that f and g are differentiable at the point; constant scaling and negation hold for the totalized derivative with no hypothesis.

The C^2 hypothesis gives symmetry of the second Fréchet derivative. Evaluate that symmetric bilinear map on the two coordinate basis vectors, identify the evaluations with the two iterated partial derivatives, and use function extensionality for the global form. For finite blocks, induct on one block length, commute one outer derivative past the other block, and use the regularity-budget theorem to retain the smoothness needed by the induction hypothesis.

For a C^2 field f:\mathbb R^n\to E with arbitrary real normed-space codomain, mixed coordinate derivatives commute:

\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f.

The pointwise theorem requires only ContDiffAt ℝ 2 f x; its global function-valued form assumes ContDiff ℝ 2 f. For a globally C^{a+b} field we also have the finite-block law

D_i^a(D_j^b f)=D_j^b(D_i^a f).

For the ith Euclidean basis vector e_i, the coordinate derivative is

\partial_i f(x):=Df(x)[e_i].

The implementation partialDeriv i f x evaluates Mathlib's total Fréchet derivative on e_i. It is therefore a total expression even when f is not differentiable, and denotes the classical partial derivative only under the corresponding differentiability hypothesis.

Induct on k. The zero case is the original regularity hypothesis. For a successor, view one coordinate derivative as evaluation of fderiv on the constant vector e_i. Taking fderiv lowers the differentiability order by one, and continuous-linear-map evaluation preserves the remaining order. Apply the induction hypothesis to the resulting field.

Coordinate differentiation uses exactly the expected finite regularity budget. If f:\mathbb R^n\to E is C^{m+k} at x, then

D_i^k f\quad\text{is }C^m\text{ at }x.

The statement is vector-valued and point-local. Setting m=0 says that D_i^kf is C^0 at x, while larger m keeps smoothness in reserve for later chain or product rules.

Induct on m. At order zero both sides are f(x). At the successor step, apply the induction hypothesis to the first coordinate derivative. Evaluation of a continuous linear map at e_i is itself a continuous linear map, so it can be moved through the iterated Fréchet derivative. Mathlib's successor formula for iteratedFDeriv then identifies the result with the next multilinear derivative evaluated on one additional copy of e_i.

Let D_i denote coordinate differentiation in direction e_i. If f:\mathbb R^n\to E is C^m at x, then

(D_i^m f)(x) =D^m f(x)[e_i,\ldots,e_i].

Here the right side is Mathlib's m-linear iterated Fréchet derivative evaluated on m copies of the same coordinate vector. The codomain E is an arbitrary real normed vector space. The theorem is local: ContDiffAt at x suffices, and no global smoothness is required.

All slices and their parameter derivatives lie in one compact-support Fréchet stage, obtained by projecting \operatorname{supp}\Phi to F. The finite-order distribution bound reduces the Taylor remainder to finitely many fiber-derivative seminorms. Compact-uniform differentiation makes each remainder little-o, yielding smoothness by induction. Outside the first-coordinate support projection every slice vanishes, and the derivative formula follows by differentiating \Phi in its first coordinate before applying T.

The applied slice family is supported in the first-coordinate projection of the original support,

\operatorname{supp}\bigl(x\mapsto\langle T,\Phi_x\rangle\bigr) \subseteq \pi_E(\operatorname{supp}\Phi),

and differentiation in the retained coordinate passes through T:

D_h\bigl(x\mapsto\langle T,\Phi_x\rangle\bigr) = x\mapsto\langle T,(D_{(h,0)}\Phi)_x\rangle.

For fixed T\in\mathcal D'(F;G), the applied-slice assignment is a continuous linear map for the canonical LF topologies,

\mathcal D(E\times F) \longrightarrow \mathcal D(E;G), \qquad \Phi\longmapsto \bigl(x\longmapsto\langle T,\Phi_x\rangle\bigr).

Let T\in\mathcal D'(F;G) and \Phi\in\mathcal D(E\times F), with E finite-dimensional. Applying T to the moving right slices defines a G-valued test function

x\longmapsto \langle T,\Phi_x\rangle \in\mathcal D(E;G).

Iterate the one-direction commutation law, using preservation of the same compact carrier at each derivative. Expand P(D) as its defining finite linear combination. Present every convolution using the same carrier cutoffs; linearity of tensor products and localized pushforward then moves the finite sum through convolution in either factor.

Arbitrary iterated directional derivatives preserve compact carriers and commute with compact-carrier convolution in either factor. Consequently, every finite constant-coefficient differential operator P(D) satisfies

P(D)(S*T)=(P(D)S)*T=S*(P(D)T).

Use compact carriers K,L and product cutoffs equal to one near K\times L. Differentiating the localized pullback along addition gives the pullback of D_v\varphi plus a term where the cutoff is differentiated. The tensor product kills the latter term because the cutoff derivative vanishes near K\times L. The coordinate derivative laws for S\otimes T identify the remaining term with differentiation of either factor.

For every direction v\in E, distributional differentiation commutes with compact-carrier convolution in either factor:

D_v(S*T)=(D_vS)*T=S*(D_vT).

The product K\times L is a compact carrier of S\otimes T. Localized pushforward along the continuous addition map sends this carrier to its compact image, the Minkowski sum of K and L. Cutoff independence identifies that presentation with the canonical convolution.

If compact sets K and L carry S and T, respectively, then S*T has a compact carrier and

\operatorname{supp}(S*T) \subseteq \{x+y:x\in K,\ y\in L\}.

Let S,T\in\mathcal D'(E) have compact carriers, where E is a finite-dimensional real normed space. Their convolution is the cutoff-localized pushforward of S\otimes T along addition:

\langle S*T,\varphi\rangle = \left\langle S\otimes T,\, \chi_1(x)\chi_2(y)\varphi(x+y)\right\rangle,

where \chi_1 and \chi_2 equal one near compact carriers of S and T, respectively. Thus \chi_1\otimes\chi_2 equals one near their product. The resulting distribution is independent of the chosen carrier witnesses and of the cutoffs \chi_1,\chi_2; the cutoff on E\times E is always of this product form.
Commute P(D) through convolution in the left factor, substitute the fundamental-solution equation P(D)G=\delta_0, and use \delta_0*T=T.

Let P(D) be a finite constant-coefficient differential operator. If G and T have compact carriers and P(D)G=\delta_0, then

P(D)(G*T)=T.

The compact carrier of G forces P(D) to have order zero. The Fourier–Laplace transform of a compactly carried G is entire by Paley–Wiener–Schwartz, so p(\zeta)\hat G(\zeta)=1 makes the symbol p a polynomial without complex zeros, hence a nonzero constant, and then G is a multiple of \delta_0. The Newtonian and logarithmic fundamental solutions are supported on all of space; their solution formula is a convolution in which only one factor, normally the datum T, has compact support.

A target test function supported outside f(K) vanishes on a neighborhood of f(K). Its pullback therefore vanishes on a neighborhood of K, as does its product with the cutoff. The localized action formula therefore transports the carrier to f(K), which is compact by continuity of f. For cutoff independence, the difference (\chi-\psi)(\varphi\circ f) vanishes on a neighborhood of K, so the carrier hypothesis makes its pairing with T zero.

Suppose T vanishes outside a compact set K. Then f_{\#,\chi}T vanishes outside f(K), and

\operatorname{supp}(f_{\#,\chi}T)\subseteq f(K).

It therefore has a compact carrier. Moreover, if both \chi and \psi equal one near K, then

f_{\#,\chi}T=f_{\#,\psi}T.

Thus compactly carried distributions have a cutoff-independent pushforward along arbitrary smooth maps.
The distributional support lies in every closed carrier. For a compact carrier, the intrinsic support is therefore a closed subset of a compact set and is compact.

If T vanishes outside a closed set K, then

\operatorname{supp}T\subseteq K.

Consequently, a compact carrier makes the intrinsic distributional support compact.
A distribution T has a compact carrier if there is a compact set K such that T vanishes on every test function supported in K^c.

Joint continuity of D is uniform on a compact fiber near the base parameter. The Banach-space mean-value estimate therefore bounds the first-order remainder simultaneously for every y\in K; taking the supremum gives the required little-o estimate in C(K,G).

Let K\subseteq F be compact. Suppose that f:E\times F\to G is continuous, that for every x\in E and y\in F the map z\mapsto f(z,y) has Fréchet derivative D(x,y) at x, and that D:E\times F\to(E\to_{\mathrm{cont}}G) is jointly continuous. Then the compactly indexed family

x\longmapsto \bigl(y\mapsto f(x,y)\bigr)\big|_K

is Fréchet differentiable as a map from E into the supremum-norm space C(K,G), with derivative h\mapsto(y\mapsto D(x,y)h).

Choose a compact set L with K in its interior and L\subseteq U. Mathlib's smooth separation theorem gives a smooth function with values in [0,1] that equals one on a neighborhood of K and vanishes outside L. Its support lies in the compact set L\subseteq U, so it is a test function with the stated properties.

If K\subset U\subset E, where E is a finite-dimensional real normed space, K is compact, and U is open, then there is a test function \chi such that

0\leq\chi\leq1,\qquad \operatorname{supp}\chi\subseteq U,

and \chi=1 on a neighborhood of every point of K.

Mathlib provides each iterated directional derivative as LineDeriv.iteratedLineDerivOpCLM. Fixed scalar multiplication and finite sums of continuous linear maps assemble these terms into P(D). Evaluation of the finite sum gives the displayed action formula.

For every admissible x,

P(D)x =\sum_{i\in I}a_iD_{v_{i,1}}\cdots D_{v_{i,k_i}}x.

Mathlib proves that every iterated directional derivative preserves a vanishing region. Scalar multiples and finite sums preserve the same property, so the finite operator does as well. The support inclusion follows from the vanishing characterization of distributional support, and a compact carrier can be reused unchanged.

For ordinary distributions, P(D) preserves every vanishing region. Hence

\operatorname{supp}(P(D)T)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}T.

If T has a compact carrier, then P(D)T has the same compact carrier.

Mathlib's tempered iterated-derivative support theorem applies term by term. The vanishing identity is stable under complex scalar multiplication and finite sums, and the intrinsic support inclusion follows from the same vanishing characterization.

For tempered distributions and complex coefficients, P(D) preserves every vanishing region and cannot enlarge support:

\operatorname{supp}(P(D)T)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}T.

Let I be a finite index set. For each i\in I, choose a coefficient a_i, an order k_i, and directions m_i=(v_{i,1},\ldots,v_{i,k_i}). The associated constant-coefficient operator is

P(D)=\sum_{i\in I}a_iD_{v_{i,1}}\cdots D_{v_{i,k_i}}.

Whenever the ambient topological module carries continuous line derivatives, P(D) is a continuous linear endomorphism.

For the left identity, choose a cutoff equal to one near \{0\} and another equal to one near a compact carrier of T. Evaluation by \delta_0 reduces the localized tensor pairing to T applied to the second cutoff times the test function; their difference vanishes near the carrier. For two Dirac masses, the tensor product is \delta_{(x,y)}, so localized pushforward along addition evaluates every test function at x+y.

The Dirac mass at the origin is a left identity for compact-carrier convolution, and Dirac masses convolve by addition:

\delta_0*T=T, \qquad \delta_x*\delta_y=\delta_{x+y}.

Distributional differentiation is defined as the negative transpose of the continuous derivative operator on test functions. Applying this transpose to \varphi gives exactly -\langle T,D_v\varphi\rangle.

For a distribution T, test function \varphi, and direction v,

\langle D_vT,\varphi\rangle =-\langle T,D_v\varphi\rangle.

At v=e_i, this is the integration-by-parts identity \langle\partial_iT,\varphi\rangle =-\langle T,\partial_i\varphi\rangle used to define weak derivatives.

If T vanishes on an open set, then it annihilates the derivative of every test function supported there because differentiation preserves the support inclusion. The derivative distribution therefore vanishes on every open set where T vanishes, which gives the support inclusion.

For T\in\mathcal S'(E;F) with F a complex normed space, distributional differentiation cannot enlarge support:

\operatorname{supp}_{\mathcal S'}(D_mT) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_{\mathcal S'}T.

Pair both sides with a test function \varphi. The two minus signs from the definition cancel, leaving T(D_wD_v\varphi) and T(D_vD_w\varphi), which agree because \varphi is smooth. For the value map, A is linear, so it passes through the minus sign and the evaluation.

On an open subset of a real normed space, the directional derivatives D_v and D_w of distributions commute for any constant directions v and w. Composing a distribution with a continuous linear map A of its values commutes with every D_v.

Write x\cdot\nabla v=\sum_ix_i\,\partial_iv. For each i, integrate by parts with the coordinate function x_i as the second factor. It is smooth everywhere, and compact support of v removes the boundary term, so \int x_i\,\partial_iv=-\int v\,\partial_ix_i=-\int v. There are n coordinates. The same result follows from the change of variables \int v(\lambda x)\,dx=\lambda^{-n}\int v by differentiating at \lambda=1.

If v:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is C^1 with compact support, then

\int_{\mathbb R^n}x\cdot\nabla v(x)\,dx=-n\int_{\mathbb R^n}v(x)\,dx .
The Dirac distribution is the continuous evaluation functional at a. Evaluating that functional on \varphi therefore reduces definitionally to \varphi(a).

For every test function \varphi,

\langle\delta_a,\varphi\rangle=\varphi(a).

By basis independence, the distributional Laplacian equals \Delta T=\sum_i\partial_i^2 T. For the Dirac mass at a, apply the derivative action formula twice in each coordinate:

\langle\partial_i^2\delta_a,\varphi\rangle =-\langle\partial_i\delta_a,\partial_i\varphi\rangle =\langle\delta_a,\partial_i^2\varphi\rangle =\partial_i^2\varphi(a).

The two minus signs cancel, leaving point evaluation of the second derivative. Summing over i=1,\ldots,n gives \langle\Delta\delta_a,\varphi\rangle=\sum_i\partial_i^2\varphi(a)=\Delta\varphi(a). The operators act on \delta_a although it has no pointwise representative to differentiate.

The distributional Laplacian of the Dirac mass acts by

\langle\Delta\delta_a,\varphi\rangle =(\Delta\varphi)(a).

The Dirac distribution at a\in\mathbb R^n is evaluation at that point:

\delta_a:\varphi\longmapsto\varphi(a).

Mathlib defines it as the continuous evaluation functional.
Integrate u\,\partial_i^2u by parts once in each coordinate and sum.
If u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is C^2 with compact support, then \int u\,\Delta u\,dx=-\int\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2\,dx.

For the first identity, transpose the parameter derivative formula for the applied-slice family. For the second, commute the fiber derivative with slicing. In each case the negative sign from distributional differentiation appears on both sides and the defining pairings agree.

Distributional differentiation acts on the corresponding tensor factor:

D_{(v,0)}(S\otimes T)=(D_vS)\otimes T, \qquad D_{(0,w)}(S\otimes T)=S\otimes(D_wT).

Slicing \varphi\otimes\psi at x gives \varphi(x)\psi. Linearity of T therefore turns the applied-slice family into \langle T,\psi\rangle\varphi, and applying S gives the product of the two pairings. For two point masses, unfolding the definition on any test function gives evaluation at (x,y).

On elementary test functions the pairing factors,

\langle S\otimes T,\varphi\otimes\psi\rangle = \langle S,\varphi\rangle\langle T,\psi\rangle.

In particular,

\delta_x\otimes\delta_y=\delta_{(x,y)}.

If S vanishes on U, then S\otimes T vanishes on U\times F because the applied-slice family is supported in the first projection of the original test-function support. If T vanishes on V, then every right slice of a test function supported in E\times V lies in V, so the applied-slice family is zero. A point outside the product of the factor supports has one coordinate in such an open vanishing neighborhood, which gives an open product neighborhood on which S\otimes T vanishes. For compact carriers, the generalized tube lemma enlarges K and L to product neighborhoods disjoint from the support of a given test function. The same slicing argument then proves vanishing outside K\times L.

The distributional support of a tensor product is contained in the product of the factor supports:

\operatorname{supp}(S\otimes T) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}(S)\times\operatorname{supp}(T).

Moreover, if K and L are compact carriers of S and T, then K\times L is a compact carrier of S\otimes T.

Let S\in\mathcal D'(E) and T\in\mathcal D'(F), with E finite-dimensional. Their tensor product is the distribution on E\times F defined by

\langle S\otimes T,\Phi\rangle = \left\langle S,\, x\longmapsto\langle T,\Phi_x\rangle \right\rangle.

For fixed T, the map S\mapsto S\otimes T is continuous linear for the compact-convergence distribution topologies.

A distribution is a continuous linear functional

T:\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)\longrightarrow\mathbb R, \qquad \mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n):=\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)'.

Mathlib's 𝓓'((⊤ : Opens (ℝ^n)), ℝ) is this compact-convergence dual. For the smooth test-function space, compact convergence agrees with bounded convergence, but it is stronger than mere pointwise convergence for general filters. Distributional differentiation is the negative transpose of test-function differentiation.

Compose the continuous functional T with the canonical inclusion of the fixed-support Fréchet stage into the LF test-function space. Pulling back the norm seminorm gives a continuous seminorm, hence a bound by finitely many defining derivative seminorms. Their largest order is dominated by the cumulative derivative seminorm in the statement.

Let K\subseteq E be compact and let T\in\mathcal D'(E;G). Restriction to test functions supported in K is a continuous linear map

T_K:\mathcal D_K(E)\longrightarrow G.

There are an order k and a constant C>0 such that

\lVert T_K\varphi\rVert \leq C\max_{0\leq i\leq k} \sup_{x\in K}\lVert D^i\varphi(x)\rVert

for every \varphi\in\mathcal D_K(E).

The forward implication projects the interiority condition and applies the distribution equality to an arbitrary test function. The Dirac action formula reduces the right side to \varphi(x). Conversely, retain the supplied proof that x\in\Omega and use extensionality: continuous linear functionals are equal when they agree on every test function.

The fundamental-solution predicate is equivalent to the conjunction

x\in\Omega \qquad\text{and}\qquad \langle P T,\varphi\rangle=\varphi(x) \quad\text{for every }\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega).

Thus a proved fundamental-solution predicate supplies both a valid interior pole and the action formula. Conversely, interiority together with the family of test-function identities determines the distribution equality.

Let \Omega\subseteq E be open, let P:\mathcal D'(\Omega)\to \mathcal D'(\Omega) be continuous and linear, and let T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega). The distribution T is a fundamental solution for P at x precisely when

x\in\Omega \qquad\text{and}\qquad P T=\delta_x \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Omega).

The membership condition is mathematically essential. Mathlib defines \delta_x on \Omega by evaluation of test functions at x; because every such test function vanishes off \Omega, this functional is zero when x\notin\Omega. This is an identity between totalized expressions, because both sides use the same Fréchet derivative.

The Euclidean gradient is the vector characterized by

\bigl(\nabla f(x)\bigr)_i=\partial_i f(x) \qquad(0\leq i<n).

Mathlib constructs it as the Riesz representative of the totalized Fréchet derivative, so it carries the same regularity caveat as partialDeriv.

By definition, \operatorname{div}(\nabla f)=\sum_i\partial_i(\nabla f)_i. The gradient agreement theorem identifies (\nabla f)_i=\partial_i f, so each summand becomes \partial_i(\partial_i f)=\partial_i^2 f. The resulting sum \sum_i\partial_i^2 f is the coordinate definition of \Delta f. The identity is purely algebraic in the totalized expressions; no differentiability hypothesis is used.

The coordinate Laplacian agrees with the divergence of the canonical gradient:

\Delta f=\operatorname{div}(\nabla f).

Both sides use the same totalized Fréchet-calculus convention.

For every coordinate i, the first chain rule gives

\partial_i(f\circ q)(y)=2y_i f'(q(y))

on a neighborhood of x where the local C^2 hypothesis propagates. Differentiate this product once more in coordinate i:

\partial_i^2(f\circ q)(x) =2f'(q(x))+4x_i^2 f''(q(x)).

Sum over i. The constant term contributes 2n f'(q(x)), while \sum_i x_i^2=\lVert x\rVert^2 converts the second term to 4\lVert x\rVert^2f''(q(x)).

Let q(x)=\lVert x\rVert^2. If f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R is C^2 at q(x), then

\Delta(f\circ q)(x) =4\lVert x\rVert^2 f''(\lVert x\rVert^2) +2n f'(\lVert x\rVert^2).

In Lean, f' and f'' are written deriv f and deriv (deriv f). This squared-radius formulation is valid at x=0; there is no division by \lVert x\rVert. It is therefore the preferred chain rule for Gaussian profiles, heat kernels, and other radial expressions that are naturally smooth functions of \lVert x\rVert^2.

Write r=\lvert x-y\rvert. Away from the pole, \partial_i r^{-k}=-k\,r^{-k-2}(x-y)_i, and differentiating again in the same coordinate gives

\partial_i^2r^{-k}=-k\,r^{-k-2}+k(k+2)\,r^{-k-4}(x-y)_i^2 .

Summing over i and using \sum_i(x-y)_i^2=r^2 gives -nk\,r^{-k-2}+k(k+2)\,r^{-k-2}. The derivative formulas come from a closed-form Fréchet derivative of z\mapsto\operatorname{dist}(z,y)^{-k}, valid on the open set z\ne y.

Let y\in\mathbb R^n, k\in\mathbb N and x\ne y. Then

\Delta_x\,\lvert x-y\rvert^{-k}=k\,(k+2-n)\,\lvert x-y\rvert^{-k-2}.

Mathlib's Laplacian is the trace of the second derivative, and that trace can be computed in any orthonormal basis. Computing \Delta(f\circ A) in the standard basis (e_i) is the same as computing \Delta f at Ax in the orthonormal basis (Ae_i). Where f is C^2, the coordinate Laplacian agrees with Mathlib's, which gives the linear case, and the translation y\mapsto y+b does not change second derivatives.

Let A be a linear isometry of \mathbb R^n, let b\in\mathbb R^n, and let f be C^2 at Ax+b. Then

\Delta\bigl(f(A\,\cdot+b)\bigr)(x)=(\Delta f)(Ax+b).

For Mathlib's basis-free Laplacian on finite-dimensional inner product spaces the identity \Delta(f\circ A)=(\Delta f)\circ A holds for any linear isometric equivalence and needs no regularity.

Unfold the Laplacian as a finite sum of same-coordinate second derivatives. Neighborhood equality is preserved by the first coordinate derivative on a possibly smaller neighborhood, and locality of the second derivative gives equality of each summand at x. Sum these coordinatewise equalities.

The Laplacian depends only on the germ of a field with values in a real normed space. If f=g throughout a neighborhood of x, then

\Delta f(x)=\Delta g(x).

The theorem is stated for the totalized coordinate Laplacian and has no differentiability hypothesis; its content is locality of the totalized Fréchet derivatives.

Differentiate the squared norm using the inner-product formula to obtain \partial_i\lVert x\rVert^2=2x_i. Differentiating once more gives 2 in each coordinate. The Laplacian is therefore the sum of n copies of 2, namely 2n.
For every x\in\mathbb R^n, \partial_i\lVert x\rVert^2=2x_i, \qquad \Delta\lVert x\rVert^2=2n.

Apply the product rule to \partial_j(fg)=\partial_jf\,g+f\,\partial_jg on a neighbourhood of x, where both factors are differentiable, and differentiate once more in direction i. Setting i=j and summing over i collects the two cross terms into 2\sum_i\partial_if\,\partial_ig.

If f and g are C^2 at x, then

\Delta(fg)(x)=\Delta f(x)\,g(x)+2\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_if(x)\,\partial_ig(x)+f(x)\,\Delta g(x),

and each mixed second derivative satisfies \partial_i\partial_j(fg)=\partial_i\partial_jf\,g+\partial_jf\,\partial_ig +\partial_if\,\partial_jg+f\,\partial_i\partial_jg at x.

Away from zero, the derivative of the norm is the linear functional v\mapsto\langle x/r,v\rangle, hence

\partial_i(f\circ\lVert\cdot\rVert)(x) =f'(r)\frac{x_i}{r}.

Use neighborhood locality so that this first-derivative identity may be differentiated at x. The product and quotient rules give

\partial_i^2(f\circ\lVert\cdot\rVert)(x) =\frac{f'(r)}r-\frac{f'(r)x_i^2}{r^3} +\frac{f''(r)x_i^2}{r^2}.

After summing, use \sum_i x_i^2=r^2. The second sum becomes f'(r)/r, the third becomes f''(r), and the first consists of n copies of f'(r)/r; collecting terms yields the stated f''(r)+(n-1)f'(r)/r.

Let x\ne0 and let f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be C^2 at r=\lVert x\rVert. Then the Laplacian of the radial field y\mapsto f(\lVert y\rVert) is

\Delta(f\circ\lVert\cdot\rVert)(x) =f''(r)+\frac{n-1}{r}f'(r).

The formal coefficient in Lean is ((n:\mathbb R)-1)/r. The nonzero hypothesis is essential: the norm is not Fréchet differentiable at the origin, and the displayed formula contains 1/r. At the origin one should instead use a theorem tailored to the profile's parity or rewrite the field through the squared radius when possible.

The Euclidean Laplacian is the coordinate trace of the second derivative:

\Delta f(x):=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_i^2f(x).

For scalar fields this gives the operator in the classical Laplace and Poisson equations of Evans Chapter 2. The same sum makes sense for vector fields and complex-valued functions, so we use one definition, PDE.laplacian, for all of them. Mathlib's canonical Laplacian.laplacian instead traces the totalized second Fréchet derivative. The two agree under local C^2 regularity; for a nonsmooth function, their totalized expressions can differ.

Unfold advection as Df(x)[u(x)] and apply the scalar coordinate expansion of the Fréchet derivative with direction u(x). Commutativity of real multiplication puts each summand in the conventional order u_i(x)\partial_i f(x).

For a scalar field, the Fréchet definition expands exactly to the familiar coordinate expression (u\mathbin{\cdot}D)f(x)=\sum_i u_i(x)\,\partial_i f(x). This equality is algebraic in the totalized Fréchet derivative.

A field u:E\to F satisfies an equation e exactly when

\forall x\in\Omega_e,\qquad \mathcal P_e[u](x)=g_e(x).

Lean expresses this directly as Set.EqOn (e.operator u) e.rhs e.domain, a pointwise residual identity on the stored set. In particular, it does not say that u is differentiable, even when \mathcal P_e was written using Mathlib's totalized derivative operators; any required differentiability must appear in a stronger solution class or in a separate hypothesis.

An equation over fields u:E\to F stores a residual type G, an operator \mathcal P:(E\to F)\to E\to G, a right-hand side g:E\to G, and a set \Omega\subseteq E. Its intended assertion is

\mathcal P[u](x)=g(x)\qquad(x\in\Omega).

The residual type is stored inside each PDEEquation. Consequently one problem can combine scalar, vector, tensor, and proposition-valued residuals without forcing them into a common codomain.

Two fields have the same k-jet at x precisely when

u\sim_x^k v \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D^j u(x)=D^j v(x)\ \text{ for every }0\leq j\leq k.

The predicate SameJetUpTo is this relation. It lets an operator state finite-order locality without choosing coordinates or expanding derivatives into multi-indices.

For normed spaces E and F over \mathbb K, a formal Fréchet jet is a sequence

J=(J_j)_{j\geq0}, \qquad J_j\in\mathcal L^j_{\mathbb K}(E;F),

where \mathcal L^j_{\mathbb K}(E;F) denotes the continuous j-linear maps from E^j to F. Mathlib represents this sequence by FormalMultilinearSeries. The totalized jet of u:E\to F at x is ftaylorSeries 𝕜 u x, with

J_j=D^j u(x).

A linear PDE of order at most k consists of an operator L, a right-hand side f, and a domain \Omega, representing

Lu=f\qquad\text{on }\Omega.

For C^k fields it records the linearity laws

L(u+v)=Lu+Lv, \qquad L(cu)=c\,Lu,

and, for fields that are C^k at x, the locality law

u\sim_x^k v\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Lu(x)=Lv(x).

The regularity qualification is essential: Mathlib's totalized derivatives are not linear on arbitrary nondifferentiable functions.

The stored operator and LinearPDE.residual are nevertheless total Lean expressions. Evaluating them does not certify regularity or domain membership; those hypotheses belong to the classical or weak solution theorem that uses the expression.

The forward implication projects the sole interior equation and sole boundary condition from SatisfiesPDEProblem. Conversely, the two pointwise hypotheses discharge the sole member of each singleton list through the generic satisfaction constructor.

A field u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R satisfies the bundled problem exactly when it satisfies both pointwise clauses:

\operatorname{Satisfies}(P_f,u) \iff \left(\forall x\in B_1(0),\ -\Delta u(x)=f(x)\right) \land \left(\forall x\in\partial B_1(0),\ u(x)=0\right).

For f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R, the unit-ball homogeneous Dirichlet problem is the bundled PDEProblem

-\Delta u=f\quad\text{in }B_1(0), \qquad u=0\quad\text{on }\partial B_1(0).

The equation list contains the residual -\Delta u=f on the open unit ball. The boundary-condition list contains the identity equation u=0 on the unit sphere.

A bundled problem is a finite system

\mathcal P_r[u](x)=g_r(x) \quad(x\in\Omega_r,\ 1\leq r\leq m),

together with a second finite system of side conditions. PDEProblem stores these systems in the lists eqns and sideConditions. Write \mathcal E_P for all the equations in these two lists.

The designation of the second list is organizational rather than semantic. The same typed equation record occurs in both lists, and its domain need not literally be a topological boundary or a time slice. Weak, variational, trace-based, and almost-everywhere interpretations are introduced separately in the analytic chapters whose solution spaces support them.

Unfolding the solution predicate says that every equation in the concatenated equation and boundary-condition lists is satisfied. Membership in this concatenation splits into membership in either list, yielding the two universal conditions; conversely the two conditions cover every member of the concatenation.

The solution predicate splits exactly along the two stored lists:

\operatorname{Solves}(P,u) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \left(\forall e\in P_{\mathrm{eq}},\ u\models e\right) \land \left(\forall e\in P_{\mathrm{side}},\ u\models e\right).

Pointwise PDE examples use this equivalence to establish or to use satisfaction one list at a time.

A field u:E\to F satisfies a bundled problem when every stored equation holds on its own domain:

\operatorname{Solves}(P,u) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall e\in\mathcal E_P,\qquad u\models e.

Expanding the equation predicate gives

\forall e\in\mathcal E_P,\ \forall x\in\Omega_e,\qquad \mathcal P_e[u](x)=g_e(x).

This is exactly SatisfiesPDEProblem P u.
Unpack the continuous solution operator S from the well-posedness hypothesis and choose S(d).

Every globally well-posed family has an admissible solution for every datum:

\operatorname{WellPosed}(P,\mathcal S) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall d,\ \exists u\in\mathcal S_d,\ \operatorname{realize}(u)\models P_d.
Unpack the uniqueness clause of WellPosed and apply it to u and v.

Two admissible solutions for the same datum are equal:

u,v\in\mathcal S_d,\quad \operatorname{realize}(u)\models P_d,\quad \operatorname{realize}(v)\models P_d \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=v.

Equip \mathcal D and X with topologies. Global Hadamard well-posedness for a data-dependent admissible class \mathcal S_d\subseteq X means that there is a solution operator

S:\mathcal D\longrightarrow X

with three precise properties:

\begin{aligned} &S(d)\in\mathcal S_d \text{ and }\operatorname{realize}(S(d))\models P_d &&\text{for every }d,\\ &u,v\in\mathcal S_d\text{ and }u,v\text{ solve }P_d \Longrightarrow u=v &&\text{for every }d,\\ &S:\mathcal D\to X\text{ is continuous}. && \end{aligned}

The realization map X\to(E\to F) keeps the topology and equality of the solution space separate from the raw field tested by PDEProblem. Thus X may be a Sobolev, Hölder, energy, quotient, or classical space. Equality in X must already encode the intended representative convention.

WellPosed is a single proposition. Its existential witness is the continuous solution operator; admissibility, the residual equations, and uniqueness are clauses of that proposition.

For affine initial data u(0,x)=a x+c, the characteristic construction gives u(t,x)=(a x+c)/(1+a t). The accompanying problem imposes the PDE on \{(t,x):0\leq t,\ 1+at\ne0\} and records the initial trace. When a<0 this domain also contains the branch t>-1/a beyond the singular time.

Split the problem into its evolution equation and initial condition. On the specified domain, the denominator is nonzero, so the explicit time and space derivative formulas reduce u_t+u\,u_x to a rational expression whose two terms cancel. On the time-zero slice, direct simplification gives u(0,x)=ax+c.

For u(0,x)=ax+c, the explicit profile

u(t,x)=\frac{ax+c}{1+at}

satisfies u_t+u\,u_x=0 wherever t\geq0 and 1+at\ne0, and recovers the affine initial trace. The pre-shock part of this domain is t\geq0, 1+at>0: all forward time for a\geq0, and 0\leq t<-1/a for a<0.

Split the half-plane into the two constant regions and the fan u=x/t. The conservation law and every smooth entropy identity hold classically in each region. The profile is continuous across both fan boundaries, so integration by parts creates no jump measure there. Summing the three regional identities therefore gives the weak equation and the entropy inequality, in fact with equality inside the fan.

For u_L\leq u_R, the profile

u(t,x)=\begin{cases} u_L,& x<u_Lt,\\ x/t,& u_Lt\leq x<u_Rt,\\ u_R,& x\geq u_Rt \end{cases} \qquad(t>0)

is an entropy weak solution on the positive-time half-plane.

Rankine–Hugoniot gives the weak equation. Integration by parts on the two sides of the shock expresses the entropy integral as A\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(t,st)\,dt, where

A=q(u_L)-q(u_R)-s\bigl(\eta(u_L)-\eta(u_R)\bigr) =\int_{u_R}^{u_L}\eta'(v)(v-s)\,dv.

Since s is the midpoint, \int_{u_R}^{u_L}(v-s)\,dv=0. Subtracting \eta'(s) from the other factor leaves (\eta'(v)-\eta'(s))(v-s)\geq0, because the derivative of a convex function is monotone. Thus A\geq0, which gives the required sign for every nonnegative test.

Let u_R<u_L and set s=(u_L+u_R)/2. The two-state profile with jump along x=st is an entropy weak solution on all of spacetime. For every C^1 entropy pair (\eta,q) with convex \eta and q'(v)=v\eta'(v), it satisfies

\int_{\mathbb R^2}\bigl(\eta(u)\varphi_t+q(u)\varphi_x\bigr)\,dt\,dx\geq0 \qquad\bigl(0\leq\varphi\in C^1_c(\mathbb R^2)\bigr).

For the flux f(u)=u^2/2, the Rankine–Hugoniot quotient is \bigl(f(u_L)-f(u_R)\bigr)/(u_L-u_R)=(u_L+u_R)/2. Since u_R<u_L, their arithmetic mean lies strictly between them. Because the characteristic speed is f'(u)=u, these are exactly the two Lax inequalities.
For Burgers data with u_R<u_L, the speed (u_L+u_R)/2 satisfies the Rankine–Hugoniot relation and the Lax compressive shock inequalities.

Split on the order of the two states. The strict branch restricts the whole-space entropy shock to positive time; the other branch uses the entropy rarefaction and almost-everywhere invariance. For each fixed x\ne0, the profile equals the corresponding initial state once t>0 is small enough. Both the profile and the datum are bounded in absolute value by M=\max(|u_L|,|u_R|). Their measurable difference is therefore dominated by 2M on each bounded interval. Dominated convergence gives the strong L^1_{\mathrm{loc}} trace.

For every pair of constant left and right states, the explicit Burgers Riemann profile selects the shock branch when u_R<u_L and the rarefaction branch otherwise. It is an entropy weak solution for positive time and converges strongly in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}} to the discontinuous Riemann datum as t\downarrow0.

The profile is the scalar planar shock with left state u_L, right state u_R and speed (u_L+u_R)/2. For the flux f(u)=u^2/2 this speed satisfies f(u_R)-f(u_L)=\tfrac{u_R^2-u_L^2}{2}=\tfrac{u_L+u_R}{2}\,(u_R-u_L), which is the Rankine–Hugoniot relation for every pair of states, so the general planar-shock theorem applies.

For every pair of states u_L,u_R\in\mathbb R, the Burgers shock profile

u(t,x)=\begin{cases} u_L,& x<\tfrac{u_L+u_R}{2}\,t,\\ u_R,& x\ge\tfrac{u_L+u_R}{2}\,t \end{cases}

is a weak solution of u_t+(u^2/2)_x=0 on all of spacetime. No ordering of the states is required: the expansive profile with u_L<u_R is a weak solution as well.

When a^{11}\ne0, the negative determinant makes the characteristic quadratic have two distinct real slopes; the corresponding covectors are independent null directions. Polarization shows their mixed pairing cannot vanish, since two independent null vectors with zero pairing would make the whole quadratic form zero. When a^{11}=0, explicit coordinate covectors give the same conclusions.

Every hyperbolic symmetric principal part has real covectors \xi,\eta such that

Q_A(\xi)=Q_A(\eta)=0,\qquad M_A(\xi,\eta)\ne0,\qquad \det(\xi,\eta)\ne0.

Apply the full second-order composition formula to the characteristic map. The null-coordinate identities eliminate both pure characteristic terms. The sum-and-difference chain rule converts the mixed term into the difference of pure second derivatives and converts the two first derivatives into their sum and difference. The zeroth-order term is unchanged by composition.

For a C^2 characteristic map (\xi,\eta) and C^2 function W(z_1,z_2), set z_1=\xi+\eta, z_2=\xi-\eta. With M and L_0 as in the local chart theorem, the full operator satisfies the composition identity

L\bigl(W(\xi+\eta,\xi-\eta)\bigr) =2M(W_{z_1z_1}-W_{z_2z_2}) +(L_0\xi+L_0\eta)W_{z_1} +(L_0\xi-L_0\eta)W_{z_2}+cW.

The derivatives of W are evaluated in the new coordinates. Thus the mixed-to-wave change retains the drift and potential as well as the principal part.

A fixed linear shear provides a noncharacteristic initial line, including when the original a^{11} vanishes. The two characteristic ODEs construct C^2 first integrals with independent differentials. The inverse function theorem supplies the chart; shrinking its source keeps the mixed coefficient nonzero. The second-order chain rule gives the transformed principal terms and the additional drift L_0\xi,L_0\eta. Dividing by 2M gives the stated equivalence with the full equation.

Suppose the three principal coefficients are C^2 near x_0 and \det A(x_0)<0. There is a local coordinate map e:x\mapsto(\xi,\eta), with open source containing x_0, whose map and inverse are C^2. On its source,

Q_A(D\xi)=Q_A(D\eta)=0,\qquad M=M_A(D\xi,D\eta)\ne0.

For the full nondivergence-form operator

Lu=\sum_{i,j}a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j u+\sum_i b^i\partial_i u+cu,

put w=u\circ e^{-1}. At each source point where u is C^2, the equation Lu=f is equivalent to

w_{\xi\eta}+\frac{L_0\xi}{2M}w_\xi +\frac{L_0\eta}{2M}w_\eta+\frac{c}{2M}w=\frac{f}{2M}, \qquad L_0=\sum_{i,j}a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+\sum_i b^i\partial_i.

All coefficients on the right are evaluated at e^{-1}(\xi,\eta). The drift b and potential c are arbitrary functions; only the principal coefficients carry a regularity hypothesis.

For the symmetric principal matrix

A=\begin{pmatrix}a^{11}&a^{12}\\a^{12}&a^{22}\end{pmatrix},

hyperbolicity means \det A=a^{11}a^{22}-(a^{12})^2<0. The associated quadratic and polarized forms are

Q_A(\xi)=a^{11}\xi_1^2+2a^{12}\xi_1\xi_2+a^{22}\xi_2^2, \qquad M_A(\xi,\eta)=a^{11}\xi_1\eta_1+ a^{12}(\xi_1\eta_2+\xi_2\eta_1)+a^{22}\xi_2\eta_2.

The mixed form is the transformed off-diagonal matrix coefficient.

Set the new wave coordinates to z_1=y_1+y_2 and z_2=y_1-y_2, where y_1,y_2 are the characteristic variables. Expanding both second derivatives, the equal mixed partials cancel the cross terms and the surviving pure terms have opposite signs. Multiplication by the original mixed coefficient gives the displayed factor.

Let z(y)=(y_1+y_2,y_1-y_2) and assume w is C^2 near z(y). The chain rule and equality of mixed partials give

\partial_{y_1}\partial_{y_2}(w\circ z)(y) =w_{z_1z_1}(z(y))-w_{z_2z_2}(z(y)).

Multiplying by the mixed coefficient turns the remaining principal expression into

2b^{12}\bigl(w_{z_1z_1}-w_{z_2z_2}\bigr).

The nonzero factor 2b^{12} is kept; dividing by it gives the wave operator.

Genuine nonlinearity means D\lambda_k(u)\,r_k(u)\ne0 at every state. Linear degeneracy means the same directional derivative vanishes everywhere. Lean expresses the latter by saying that the speed is a Riemann invariant of its own characteristic field, so differentiability of the speed is part of the proposition.

A characteristic field selects functions \lambda_k(u)\in\mathbb R and r_k(u)\ne0 satisfying

Df(u)r_k(u)=\lambda_k(u)r_k(u).

Its autonomous ODE field is u'=r_k(u). Unlike strict hyperbolicity, this is data for one consistently selected family. Smooth dependence of the selected speed or vector field is a separate hypothesis.

At time zero the flow law makes every trajectory start at its input state, so the derivative in the state variable is the identity. Differentiating the trajectory in time at zero and using the characteristic ODE gives r_k(u). Local C^1 regularity makes these two blocks a strict derivative at zero, as a local wave family requires.

A global Mathlib flow whose trajectories solve a characteristic ODE and whose joint time-state map is locally C^1 yields a LocalWaveFamily. The flow laws provide the identity state block at zero time, and the ODE provides the right-eigenvector strength column. This is the analytic rarefaction-curve germ used by Evans. An elementary T_k family also splices in the admissible shock branch, or the contact branch in the linearly degenerate case.
Expand the flux residual, apply the chain rule, and integrate the spacetime divergence against a compactly supported test function. Boundary terms vanish because of compact support.
A C^1 pointwise solution with a C^1 flux satisfies Definition 7.186.

Write the shock speed as the secant slope of f over [u_R,u_L]. For a strictly convex function, the derivative at the left endpoint of an interval lies strictly below the secant slope, which lies strictly below the derivative at the right endpoint; with u_R<u_L this reads f'(u_R)<s<f'(u_L).
