For the equivalence, Rankine–Hugoniot with distinct states forces s to be the secant speed. In the expansive case u_L<u_R the same secant inequalities give f'(u_L)<s, which contradicts the Lax inequality s<f'(u_L).

Let f be strictly convex on \mathbb R and differentiable at the two states u_L and u_R. If u_R<u_L, the Rankine–Hugoniot speed s=s(u_L,u_R) satisfies the Lax shock inequalities

f'(u_R)<s<f'(u_L).

More generally, if u_R\ne u_L and s is any speed satisfying f(u_R)-f(u_L)=s\,(u_R-u_L), then the Lax inequalities hold for s if and only if u_R<u_L. For a strictly convex flux, a Rankine–Hugoniot jump is therefore Lax-admissible exactly when it is compressive.

The secant identity is the definition of the slope after exchanging the two endpoints. For the chord inequalities, write the shock speed as the slope of f over [u_R,u_L]. Strict convexity makes secant slopes strictly increasing in each endpoint, so the slope over the initial segment [u_R,k] lies strictly below the slope over the whole interval, which in turn lies strictly below the slope over the final segment [k,u_L].

For any flux f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R and states u_L,u_R, the Rankine–Hugoniot speed

s(u_L,u_R)=\frac{f(u_R)-f(u_L)}{u_R-u_L}

is the secant slope of f between the two states; both sides are the totalized value 0 when u_L=u_R. If f is strictly convex on \mathbb R, then for every intermediate state u_R<k<u_L,

\frac{f(k)-f(u_R)}{k-u_R}<s(u_L,u_R)<\frac{f(u_L)-f(k)}{u_L-k}.

These strict chord inequalities are the Oleinik form of admissibility for a compressive jump; no differentiability of f is assumed.

The classical residuals vanish in the two open regions. Integration by parts with the moving boundary reduces the weak residual to the Rankine–Hugoniot coefficient, which is zero. For an entropy pair (\eta,q) with q'=\eta'f', the same calculation gives

\int_{\mathbb R^2}\bigl(\eta(u)\varphi_t+q(u)\varphi_x\bigr)\,dt\,dx =\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(s'[\eta(u)]-[q(u)]\bigr) \varphi(t,s(t))\,dt.

The integral on the right uses the time parameter along the interface. Convexity of the flux between the downward traces, together with convexity of the entropy, makes its coefficient nonnegative. Thus every nonnegative compactly supported test gives the entropy inequality. Neither constant traces nor a straight interface is used.

Let f,s\in C^1(\mathbb R) and u_L,u_R\in C^1(\mathbb R^2). Assume u_L solves u_t+(f(u))_x=0 on x<s(t) and u_R solves it on x>s(t). Suppose at every interface point

s'(t)[u](t)=[f(u)](t),\qquad u_R(t,s(t))\le u_L(t,s(t)),

and f is convex on the interval between these two traces. Then the piecewise field is a weak solution and satisfies every C^1 convex entropy inequality on all of \mathbb R^2.

The scalar entropy predicate is stated for any flux f and uses f' in the compatibility relation; it is the standard notion when f is C^1, as in every theorem that uses it. An entropy pair consists of globally C^1 functions \eta,q satisfying q'=\eta'f'. A weak solution on the open domain U is an entropy weak solution when, for every such pair with \eta convex on \mathbb R, \eta(u) and q(u) are locally integrable on U and the integrated entropy inequality holds for every nonnegative C^1 test with compact support contained in U.

Along a characteristic of the family that transports \Phi_i(u), the slope y=\partial_x\Phi_i(u) satisfies y'\le-\kappa\,y^2 up to a positive factor that is bounded below uniformly, because the solution stays in a compact set of states determined by the compactly supported data. A negative initial value y(0) therefore reaches -\infty before time (\kappa|y(0)|)^{-1}, contradicting the continuity of the second jet on any longer slab.

Let f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2 be C^2 and strictly hyperbolic at every state, and let \Phi be a global diffeomorphism of the state plane whose components are Riemann invariants: D\Phi_i\,Df=\lambda_{1-i}\,D\Phi_i. Assume that the speed carried by each invariant increases strictly in that invariant. If g is continuous with compact support and (\Phi_i\circ g)'(x_0)<0 for some i and x_0, then there is no C^2 solution of u_t+f(u)_x=0 on t>0 with u(0,\cdot)=g whose derivatives up to order two extend continuously to t\ge0.

For a jump from u_L to u_R moving with speed s, the Rankine–Hugoniot relation is

f(u_R)-f(u_L)=s(u_R-u_L).

When u_L\ne u_R, this selects the secant speed s=(f(u_R)-f(u_L))/(u_R-u_L). The scalar Lax inequalities

f'(u_R)<s<f'(u_L)

encode compressive admissibility through the characteristic speeds on the two sides.

Test the entropy inequality for u with k=v(s,y) and the one for v with k=u(t,x), add, and integrate against a test function concentrating on the diagonal (t,x)=(s,y). This gives \partial_t|u-v|+\partial_x q(u,v)\le0 in the sense of distributions, with |q(u,v)|\le c|u-v|. Integrating over the trapezoid that shrinks at speed c and using the strong initial traces gives the inequality.

Let F be C^1 and let u and v be entropy solutions with initial traces u_0 and v_0, both bounded by M almost everywhere. If |F'|\le c on [-M,M], then for almost every T>0, with a null set depending on the interval [a,b],

\int_{a+cT}^{b-cT}|u(T,x)-v(T,x)|\,dx\le\int_a^b|u_0(x)-v_0(x)|\,dx.

The contraction with u_0=v_0 makes almost every slice vanish on every interval, hence almost everywhere in space, and Fubini gives the spacetime statement. For the second claim, the contraction is rerun from the left trace at a fixed time instead of from almost every time.

For a C^1 flux, two bounded entropy solutions with the same initial trace agree almost everywhere on t>0. If the chosen representatives attain their left traces in time, their time slices agree almost everywhere at every T>0, not only for almost every T.

The lower bound on F'' makes L finite, strictly convex and superlinear, so minimizers exist and move monotonically with x. A monotone function has countably many jumps, which gives the uniqueness of the footpoint and the differentiability of w in x off a countable set. The weak equation for u comes from the almost-everywhere Hamilton–Jacobi equation for w, integrated by parts against \varphi_x. The bound by \|g\|_{L^\infty} is inherited from the datum through the footpoint formula. For the slope estimate, monotonicity of the chosen footpoint gives (x+z-y^*(t,x+z))/t-(x-y^*(t,x))/t\le z/t. Uniform convexity makes (F')^{-1} increasing and 1/\theta-Lipschitz. If the first argument is smaller, the solution difference is nonpositive; otherwise that Lipschitz estimate gives z/(\theta t). This uses the minimizing selection itself, so no differentiability at a shock is needed.

Let F be C^2 with F''\ge\theta>0 and let g\in L^\infty. The minimum defining w(t,x) is attained, the footpoint can be chosen monotone in x and is unique outside a countable set of x for each t>0, and at almost every spatial point

u(t,x)=(F')^{-1}\Bigl(\frac{x-y^*(t,x)}{t}\Bigr)=\partial_xw(t,x).

The function u is a weak initial-value solution with datum g, and |u|\le\|g\|_{L^\infty} almost everywhere. The actual selected representative also satisfies the sharp one-sided bound

u(t,x+z)-u(t,x)\le\frac{z}{\theta t} \qquad(t>0,\ x\in\mathbb R,\ z\ge0).

This includes points with nonunique minimizing footpoints. In particular it satisfies the weaker Oleinik bound C(1+1/t)z of the definition, with C=1/\theta.

The speed is constant along the characteristic integral curve by linear degeneracy; call the common value s. Along that curve the chain rule and the eigenvector equation give \frac d{d\tau}f(\gamma(\tau))=s\,\gamma'(\tau). Integrating between the two parameter values yields f(u_R)-f(u_L)=s(u_R-u_L), while constancy gives s=\lambda_k(u_L)=\lambda_k(u_R). These are precisely the contact conditions.

If the flux is globally C^1, any two states on a C^1 integral curve of a differentiable, linearly degenerate characteristic speed form a contact discontinuity. Integral curves use Mathlib's IsIntegralCurve, whose HasDerivAt formulation includes differentiability.

Apply the chain rule to \lambda_k\circ\gamma. Its derivative is D\lambda_k(\gamma(s))\,\gamma'(s), which becomes D\lambda_k(\gamma(s))\,r_k(\gamma(s))=0 by the integral-curve equation and linear degeneracy. A differentiable real-valued function with zero derivative on the interval is constant.

If D\lambda_k(u)r_k(u)=0 and \gamma'(s)=r_k(\gamma(s)), then

\lambda_k(\gamma(s))=\lambda_k(\gamma(t)) \qquad\text{for all }s,t.

Thus the characteristic speed of a linearly degenerate field is constant along each global integral curve of its right eigenvector field.

Local shock curves and characteristic integral curves supply an elementary wave family. The wave-strength theorem gives the strengths for nearby u_R and keeps the intermediate states inside the construction neighborhoods. The construction also supplies bounded, measurable, self-similar weak waves with those outer states in separated speed windows. Their finite gluing preserves the weak equation. Uniform boundedness and finite propagation give the strong local L^1 initial trace, which supplies the initial face in the weak initial-value identity.

Let f\in C^2(\mathbb R^m;\mathbb R^m) be strictly hyperbolic at every state, and let each characteristic family be genuinely nonlinear or linearly degenerate. For every u_L there are \delta>0 and bounds K,M\ge0 such that each u_R with \|u_R-u_L\|<\delta has intermediate states u_L=u_0,u_1,\ldots,u_m=u_R. Each successive pair admits an elementary connection: a k-rarefaction, a k-Lax shock, a k-contact, or equal states. There are also bounded, measurable, self-similar weak waves w_k with these outer states in separated, ordered speed windows in [-M,M]. Their finite gluing u=u_L+\sum_k(w_k-u_{k-1}) is a bounded, measurable, self-similar weak solution of u_t+f(u)_x=0 in t>0 that attains the Riemann datum in the weak initial-value sense and strongly in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}} as t\downarrow0. It equals u_L for x<-Mt and u_R for x\ge Mt.

IsElementaryConnection is a predicate on the endpoint states alone, so the elementary connections and the weak waves w_k are separate conclusions that share their outer states.

The derivative of \Phi at zero has the characteristic vectors r_1(u_L),\ldots,r_m(u_L) as its columns. Because these vectors form a basis, that strict derivative is invertible. The inverse function theorem for strict derivatives makes \Phi a local homeomorphism, giving existence and uniqueness of the nearby wave-strength vector.

Let

\Phi(t_1,\ldots,t_m;u_L) =T_m(t_m,\cdot)\circ\cdots\circ T_1(t_1,\cdot)(u_L).

For a left state in the family's state domain, if r_1(u_L),\ldots,r_m(u_L) form a basis, then the inverse function theorem gives open neighborhoods U of 0 and V of u_L such that every u_R\in V has a unique t\in U with \Phi(t;u_L)=u_R. This is the analytic parametrization step of Evans's argument; the elementary curves and the self-similar weak solution come from the wave family.

Write t=s^2. For large s, the solution vanishes outside the two fronts F'(0)t-\sqrt{pF''(0)t} and F'(0)t+\sqrt{qF''(0)t}, up to a bounded distance. On an interior interval of length O(s) the footpoint stays in the bounded support and the slope differs from the linear profile (x/t-F'(0))/F''(0) by O(s^{-2}), using a third-order expansion of the flux at 0. Two strips of bounded width near the fronts, where both functions are O(s^{-1}), contribute the leading error O(s^{-1}). For bounded s the bound follows from |u|\le\|g\|_\infty and the finite propagation of the support.

Let F be C^3 with F''\ge\theta>0 and F(0)=0, and let g\in L^\infty vanish almost everywhere outside a bounded interval, with both lobe masses p and q positive. Then there is a constant C such that, for the Lax–Oleinik solution u,

\int_{\mathbb R}|u(t,x)-N(t,x)|\,dx\le\frac{C}{\sqrt t}\qquad(t>0).

A function u on spacetime has Oleinik bound C\ge0 if

u(t,x+z)-u(t,x)\le C\Bigl(1+\frac1t\Bigr)z

for almost every (t,x,z) with t>0 and z>0.

Each solution has a Lipschitz potential w with w_x=u weakly, and the weak equation makes w a solution of w_t+F(w_x)=0 almost everywhere with initial value \int_0^xg. The Oleinik bound says that w(t,\cdot) is semiconcave for t>0. Uniqueness for semiconcave Hamilton–Jacobi solutions identifies the two potentials, and uniqueness of weak derivatives then identifies u and v almost everywhere. The one-sided bound is the key input.
Let F be C^2 and convex. If u and v are weak initial-value solutions with the same datum g, both essentially bounded on t>0, and each has some Oleinik bound, then u=v almost everywhere on t>0.

A local wave family on a state domain supplies transformations T_k(t_k,u) with a strict Fréchet derivative at zero strength at each domain state: the strength column is r_k(u) and the state block is the identity. No C^1 regularity near zero strength is required. Their ordered composition starts at the left state and applies one transformation for each characteristic family. An elementary family uses admissible shocks, rarefactions, or contacts for these transformations.

The forward implication is the chain rule applied to the two signed acoustic invariants. Conversely, adding the two diagonal equations recovers w_t-p'(v)v_x=0. Subtracting them and dividing by twice the positive sound speed recovers v_t-w_x=0.

Let the stress p be globally C^1. At a point where p'(v)>0, a field differentiable there solves the p-system if and only if both acoustic Riemann invariants satisfy their diagonal transport equations

\partial_t R_k-\lambda_k\partial_x R_k=0.

The sign is determined by the flux convention F(v,w)=(-w,-p(v)). For a classical solution, an invariant is constant along any characteristic with tangent (1,-\lambda_k) on an open connected time interval, provided the curve stays in the solution's domain and p'(v)\ge0 along it.

Split on the family and on the sign of the strength. On a shock branch, p'>0 makes the stress difference quotient positive, so the Hugoniot endpoint satisfies Rankine–Hugoniot and the planar shock is a weak solution on all of spacetime; restrict it to t>0. On a rarefaction branch, p''>0 makes the sound speed increasing in the strain, which orders the two edge speeds of the fan. Inside the wedge the self-similar middle state is C^1 and solves the system pointwise, because its tangent is a right eigenvector of the flux Jacobian with eigenvalue x/t; on each edge it agrees continuously with the adjacent constant state, so integrating by parts region by region produces no interface terms.

Let the stress law p be C^2 on \mathbb R with p'>0 and p''>0 everywhere. For every family k\in\{0,1\}, every left state u_L=(v_L,w_L) and every strength \sigma\in\mathbb R, the physical elementary wave W_k(\sigma;u_L), which is a rarefaction fan or a planar Hugoniot shock according to the sign of \sigma, is a weak solution of the p-system

v_t-w_x=0,\qquad w_t-p(v)_x=0

on the open forward half-space \{t>0\}.

Write \mathrm{fan}_k(\sigma;u_L) for the rarefaction fan and \mathrm{shock}(u_L,u_R;s) for the planar profile equal to u_L on x<st and to u_R on x\ge st. The physical elementary wave of family k with left state u_L=(v_L,w_L) and strength \sigma is

W_k(\sigma;u_L)=\begin{cases} \mathrm{fan}_0(\sigma;u_L),& k=0,\ \sigma\le0,\\ \mathrm{shock}\bigl(u_L,H_0(v_L+\sigma;u_L);s_0(v_L,v_L+\sigma)\bigr),& k=0,\ \sigma>0,\\ \mathrm{shock}\bigl(u_L,H_1(v_L+\sigma;u_L);s_1(v_L,v_L+\sigma)\bigr),& k=1,\ \sigma<0,\\ \mathrm{fan}_1(\sigma;u_L),& k=1,\ \sigma\ge0. \end{cases}

In every case the strain increment across the wave is \sigma; the right state is \gamma_k(\sigma;u_L) on the rarefaction branches and H_k(v_L+\sigma;u_L) on the shock branches. The definition places no hypothesis on p. For a C^2 stress with p'>0 and p''>0, the rarefaction branch is used where the edge speeds of the fan are ordered and the shock branch where the Hugoniot jump is a Lax k-shock; family-zero waves then propagate with negative speeds and family-one waves with positive speeds.
If p and P are globally C^1, P'=p, and p'>0, the mechanical energy and energy flux form a compatible convex entropy pair for the p-system.

For the p-system with stress law p, a left state u_L=(v_L,w_L) and a prescribed right strain v_R, let

q(v_L,v_R)=\begin{cases} \dfrac{p(v_R)-p(v_L)}{v_R-v_L},& v_R\ne v_L,\\ p'(v_L),& v_R=v_L \end{cases}

be the differentiable difference quotient of the stress. The signed shock speeds of the two families are

s_0(v_L,v_R)=-\sqrt{q(v_L,v_R)},\qquad s_1(v_L,v_R)=\sqrt{q(v_L,v_R)},

so that zero jump returns the characteristic speeds \mp\sqrt{p'(v_L)} rather than the artificial value 0. The Hugoniot endpoint of family k is

H_k(v_R;u_L)=\bigl(v_R,\;w_L-s_k(v_L,v_R)\,(v_R-v_L)\bigr).

Whenever q(v_L,v_R)\ge0, which is automatic when p'>0, the states u_L and H_k(v_R;u_L) satisfy the vector Rankine–Hugoniot relation with speed s_k(v_L,v_R). If moreover p is C^2 with p'>0 and p''>0, the jump is a Lax k-shock, \lambda_k(u_R)<s_k<\lambda_k(u_L), on the physical half of each branch: v_L<v_R for family 0 and v_R<v_L for family 1.

The characteristic polynomial of the flux Jacobian is \lambda^2-p'(v). Positivity of p'(v) gives the two distinct real roots \lambda=\pm\sqrt{p'(v)}. Solving the two corresponding linear systems produces nonzero eigenvectors with different eigenvalues, hence a basis of the two-dimensional state space.
Where p'(v)>0, the p-system flux Jacobian has the distinct characteristic speeds -\sqrt{p'(v)} and \sqrt{p'(v)}, with an explicit right eigenbasis.

The two local elementary-wave curves have the characteristic eigenvectors as their zero-strength tangents. Strict hyperbolicity makes those tangents a basis, so the inverse function theorem gives unique small strengths joining the left state to every nearby right state. Concatenating the corresponding shock or rarefaction profiles yields a self-similar weak solution. Rankine–Hugoniot handles jumps, convex mechanical entropy gives the admissible sign, and the shrinking width of the wave fan proves local L^1 convergence to the Riemann datum as t\downarrow0.

Assume p is C^2, p'>0, and p''>0, and let a C^1 potential P satisfy P'=p. For every left state there is an open neighborhood containing it such that each right state in that neighborhood admits an explicit two-wave p-system solution. The solution is weak on positive time, converges strongly in local L^1 to the Riemann datum, and satisfies the mechanical entropy inequality on the forward half-space.

Let c=\sqrt{p'} be the sound speed, A(v)=\int_0^v c(x)\,dx, and let \lambda_0=-c and \lambda_1=c be the characteristic speeds as functions of the strain. The kth characteristic curve through u_L=(v_L,w_L) at strength \sigma is

\gamma_k(\sigma;u_L)=\bigl(v_L+\sigma,\;w_L\pm(A(v_L+\sigma)-A(v_L))\bigr),

with the sign + for k=0 and - for k=1, so that the Riemann invariant w-A(v) of family 0, respectively w+A(v) of family 1, is constant along it. For t>0 and ordered edge speeds \lambda_k(v_L)\le\lambda_k(v_L+\sigma), the rarefaction fan of family k with left state u_L and strength \sigma has the spacetime profile

u(t,x)=\begin{cases} u_L,& x<\lambda_k(v_L)\,t,\\ R_k(x/t),& \lambda_k(v_L)\,t\le x<\lambda_k(v_L+\sigma)\,t,\\ \gamma_k(\sigma;u_L),& x\ge\lambda_k(v_L+\sigma)\,t. \end{cases}

For a C^2 stress with p'>0 and p''>0 and ordered edge speeds \lambda_k(v_L)\le\lambda_k(v_L+\sigma), the middle state R_k(\xi) is the point of the characteristic curve whose strain v solves \lambda_k(v)=\xi, so the fan is the self-similar rarefaction wave joining u_L to \gamma_k(\sigma;u_L). Lean extends R_k outside the fan interval by its endpoint tangent lines to obtain a global C^1 middle map; on the wedge this extension agrees with R_k, so it affects no value of an ordered fan. The definition is total in \sigma; for p''>0 the ordering holds when \sigma\le0 in family 0 and when \sigma\ge0 in family 1.

The fundamental theorem of calculus gives A'(v)=c(v). Consequently the gradients of w-A(v) and w+A(v) are (-c(v),1) and (c(v),1). Their products with the corresponding right eigenvectors (1,c(v)) and (1,-c(v)) vanish. Thus each function is a Riemann invariant, and the general constancy theorem applies along the associated integral curves.

For a globally C^1 stress law with p'(v)>0, set c(v)=\sqrt{p'(v)} and A(v)=\int_{\mathrm{base}}^v c(x)\,dx. With the p-system flux F(v,w)=(-w,-p(v)), the family with speed -c and right eigenvector (1,c) has invariant w-A(v), while the family with speed c and right eigenvector (1,-c) has invariant w+A(v). Each is constant along every global Mathlib integral curve of its field.

This is the p-system case of Evans's general two-equation Riemann-invariant calculation, distinct from the barotropic-gas invariants that follow it there. The hypotheses are global because CharacteristicField is defined on the whole state space.

The one-dimensional elasticity p-system has strain–velocity state (v,w) and flux F(v,w)=(-w,-p(v)), where p is the stress law. Its mechanical energy and energy flux are \eta(v,w)=w^2/2+P(v) and q(v,w)=-p(v)w.

The profile and its flux composition take only two values, so both are locally integrable. For a compactly supported C^1 test \varphi, the weak integral splits into the contribution of the constant state u_R over all of spacetime, which vanishes because the integral of each partial derivative of \varphi is zero, and the integral of the jump terms over the half-plane x<st. The divergence theorem on that half-plane turns the latter into the interface integral \int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(t,st)\,dt multiplied by the vector f(u_L)-f(u_R)-s\,(u_L-u_R). Rankine–Hugoniot makes this coefficient zero. For the converse, a nonnegative test function with positive interface integral forces the coefficient itself to vanish.

For states u_L,u_R\in\mathbb R^m and a speed s\in\mathbb R, the planar shock is the two-state profile

u(t,x)=\begin{cases}u_L,& x<st,\\ u_R,& x\ge st.\end{cases}

If the vector Rankine–Hugoniot relation f(u_R)-f(u_L)=s\,(u_R-u_L) holds, then u is a weak solution of u_t+(f(u))_x=0 on all of spacetime. The flux f\colon\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m is arbitrary: no continuity or differentiability is assumed. Conversely, if the planar shock is a weak solution on spacetime, then the Rankine–Hugoniot relation holds. The scalar case is recorded separately against the scalar weak formulation, with the same hypothesis and conclusion.

Apply the chain rule to R\circ\gamma. The integral-curve equation changes its derivative to DR(\gamma(s))\,r_k(\gamma(s)), and the Riemann-invariant condition makes this zero. The zero-derivative theorem then shows that the composition has the same value at every pair of parameters.

If \gamma'(s)=r_k(\gamma(s)) and DR\,r_k=0, then the chain rule gives

\frac d{ds}R(\gamma(s))=0, \qquad R(\gamma(s))=R(\gamma(t)).

Hence a Riemann invariant is constant along every Mathlib integral curve of its characteristic vector field.

A Riemann invariant R for the kth field is differentiable and satisfies

DR(u)\,r_k(u)=0

at every state.

Differentiate the footpoint identity in t and x. Solving the resulting linear equations for \xi_t and \xi_x gives the displayed fractions, with the nonzero Jacobian denominator permitting division. Applying the chain rule to u=u_0\circ\xi then factors the PDE residual through \xi_t+a(u)\xi_x=0.

Let a,u_0:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be differentiable on \mathbb R, and let \xi:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R satisfy the footpoint relation on an open set V. At each point of V where \xi is differentiable, the denominator is nonzero and implicit differentiation gives

\xi_t=-\frac{a(u_0(\xi))}{1+t a'(u_0(\xi))u_0'(\xi)},\qquad \xi_x=\frac{1}{1+t a'(u_0(\xi))u_0'(\xi)}.

Substitution gives u_t+a(u)u_x=0 at that point for u=u_0\circ\xi. The relation and differentiability are needed only near the point under consideration.

For the scalar equation u_t+a(u)u_x=0, a supplied characteristic footpoint \xi(t,x) on an open spacetime set V satisfies

x=\xi+t\,a(u_0(\xi)),\qquad u(t,x)=u_0(\xi(t,x)).

The Jacobian denominator is 1+t\,a'(u_0(\xi))u_0'(\xi).

If the denominator vanished at some nonnegative time t, then t would belong to the set whose infimum defines the shock time. Hence the shock time would be at most t, contradicting the strict pre-shock assumption. The nonvanishing denominator makes the derivative of (t,\xi)\mapsto(t,\xi+t\,a(u_0(\xi))) invertible. The inverse function theorem supplies a local inverse; its spatial component is the footpoint. For the global inverse, choose t<\tau<T_*. Positivity of the Jacobian at \tau implies the uniform bound X_t'(\xi)\ge(\tau-t)/\tau>0. The mean value theorem makes X_t strictly increasing with limits \pm\infty at the ends of the line, so the intermediate value theorem gives surjectivity. Injectivity makes every local inverse agree with the global inverse. The preceding residual identity verifies the PDE at positive time, and at time zero the footpoint relation reduces to \xi(0,x)=x.

Let a,u_0 be C^1 on \mathbb R. The formal shock time T_* is the infimum of nonnegative times at which the characteristic Jacobian vanishes somewhere; it is \infty if there are none. For every 0\leq t<T_* and label \xi_0, there is an open neighborhood V of (t,\xi_0+t\,a(u_0(\xi_0))) and a differentiable footpoint map on V whose value at that point is \xi_0. The resulting u=u_0\circ\xi satisfies u_t+a(u)u_x=0 on V and agrees with u_0 on V\cap\{t=0\}.

These local inverses agree with a global spatial inverse of X_t. Consequently u(t,x)=u_0(X_t^{-1}(x)) is a classical solution on the entire strip 0<t<T_*, is C^1 up to time zero from the right when T_*>0, and has u(0,x)=u_0(x) on the whole initial line. The strip may be empty, since an infimum of degeneracy times can be zero.

The shock branch uses the planar-shock theorem and strict convexity for the Lax inequalities. On the fan, G is Lipschitz with constant \theta^{-1}, which gives the slope bound z/(\theta t), and the profile is a classical solution of u_t+F'(u)u_x=0 joined continuously to the constant states. Uniqueness is the Oleinik theorem applied to the constructed profile and the competitor.

Let F be C^2 with F''\ge\theta>0, and let G=(F')^{-1}. For all states u_L,u_R, the profile equal to the Lax shock at the Rankine–Hugoniot speed when u_R<u_L, and to

u(t,x)=\begin{cases} u_L,& x<F'(u_L)t,\\ G(x/t),& F'(u_L)t\le x<F'(u_R)t,\\ u_R,& x\ge F'(u_R)t \end{cases}

when u_L\le u_R, is a weak initial-value solution and an entropy weak solution for t>0, with a strong L^1_{\mathrm{loc}} trace. It is invariant under the positive dilations (t,x)\mapsto(at,ax), bounded by \max(|u_L|,|u_R|), equal to u_L and u_R outside the cone |x|<\max(|F'(u_L)|,|F'(u_R)|)\,t, and satisfies u(t,x+z)-u(t,x)\le z/(\theta t) for positive times and nonnegative increments. Every bounded weak initial-value solution with the same data and some Oleinik bound equals it almost everywhere on positive time.

A classical solution transports u_0(\xi) along the characteristic of label \xi. Differentiating that identity gives u_x(t,X_t(\xi))X_t'(\xi)=u_0'(\xi). At a degeneracy, X_t'(\xi)=0 forces the left side to vanish, although the degeneracy identity forces u_0'(\xi)\ne0. A proposed continuation past the infimum encounters some degeneracy before its final time, giving the contradiction without choosing a minimizing label.

At an attained first degeneracy, the same derivative identity on the pre-shock strip gives the quotient u_0'(\xi)/(1+t\,a'(u_0(\xi))u_0'(\xi)). Its numerator is nonzero and its denominator tends to zero through positive values, proving divergence of the norm.

Let a,u_0\in C^1(\mathbb R). Any solution with the prescribed initial data that is C^1 at every point of the closed strip 0\le t\le T and satisfies u_t+a(u)u_x=0 there has T\le T_*. More generally, the constructed solution has no C^1 continuation from a slice 0<s<T_* to any T>T_*.

If T_*<\infty is attained at a label \xi, meaning 1+T_*a'(u_0(\xi))u_0'(\xi)=0, then

\left|u_x\bigl(t,\xi+t\,a(u_0(\xi))\bigr)\right| \longrightarrow\infty\qquad(t\uparrow T_*).

A degeneracy time t\ge0 has 1+t\,k(\xi)=0 for some label, so k(\xi)<0 and t=-1/k(\xi). Since m\le k(\xi)<0, this gives t\ge-1/m, and -1/m is a lower bound of the degeneracy times. Values of k approaching m from above give degeneracy times approaching -1/m from above, so no larger number is a lower bound. When k\ge0, the Jacobian is at least one at every nonnegative time and there is no degeneracy time.

If k(\xi)=a'(u_0(\xi))u_0'(\xi) has infimum m<0 over \xi\in\mathbb R, then

T_*=-\frac1m.

The infimum need not be attained. If k(\xi)\ge0 for every \xi, then T_*=\infty.

For \xi=x/t, direct differentiation gives \xi_t=-\xi/t and \xi_x=1/t. The chain rule therefore rewrites the quasilinear residual as t^{-1}\bigl(Df(w(\xi))-\xi I\bigr)w'(\xi), which vanishes by the profile eigenvector equation. The conservative residual agrees with the quasilinear one at the differentiability point.

At a point with t\ne0, suppose the profile is differentiable at \xi=x/t, the flux is differentiable at w(\xi), and Df(w(\xi))w'(\xi)=\xi w'(\xi). Then u(t,x)=w(x/t) solves the conservative system at that point. The centered-rarefaction construction builds the profile by inverting a characteristic speed and joins the fan to constant end states; for the p-system these steps are carried out in the rarefaction fan.

Differentiate u=w\circ\phi in time and space. The chain rule factors both derivatives through w'(\phi), and the eigenvector relation replaces Df(w(\phi))w'(\phi) by \lambda(\phi)w'(\phi). Factoring the common tangent vector leaves exactly \bigl(\phi_t+\lambda(\phi)\phi_x\bigr)w'(\phi).

At a spacetime point z, suppose \phi is differentiable at z and w is differentiable at \phi(z). If its tangent satisfies the eigenvector equation Df(w(\phi))w'(\phi)=\lambda(\phi)w'(\phi), the quasilinear residual of u=w(\phi) is (\phi_t+\lambda(\phi)\phi_x)w'(\phi), with all quantities evaluated at z. It also equals the conservative residual when f is differentiable at w(\phi(z)). The identity is pointwise; the phase and the characteristic curve are given.

The Jacobian is a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. The real spectral theorem supplies an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors and real eigenvalues. Reindexing this basis gives the characteristic speeds and spanning family required by hyperbolicity.

Every symmetric flux Jacobian is hyperbolic:

Df(u)^*=Df(u) \Longrightarrow \mathbb R^m=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\sigma(Df(u))} \ker(Df(u)-\lambda I).

Multiply the pointwise conservation law by a compactly supported scalar test function and integrate. Vector-valued integration by parts moves the time and space derivatives from u and f(u) onto the test function. Compact support removes every boundary term, leaving exactly the Bochner integral identity in the definition of a system weak solution.
As a regular special case, every globally C^1 pointwise system solution with globally C^1 flux is weak on the chosen open domain.

A k-Lax shock satisfies Rankine–Hugoniot, \lambda_k(u_R)<s<\lambda_k(u_L), and the neighboring-family conditions \lambda_j(u_L)<s for j<k and s<\lambda_j(u_R) for j>k. A k-contact discontinuity satisfies Rankine–Hugoniot and s=\lambda_k(u_L)=\lambda_k(u_R). A rarefaction connection follows the kth characteristic integral curve while its speed increases strictly along the entire oriented segment from u_L to u_R. The predicates contain only the displayed connection conditions.

The chain rule gives \partial_t\eta(u)=D\eta(u)u_t and \partial_xq(u)=Dq(u)u_x. Compatibility replaces Dq by D\eta\circ Df, so their sum is D\eta(u)\bigl(u_t+Df(u)u_x\bigr). The classical conservation law makes the vector in parentheses zero.
Every differentiable classical solution satisfies \partial_t\eta(u)+\partial_xq(u)=0 for each compatible system entropy pair.

Fix an open set U of spacetime, a state u with values in \mathbb R^m, and an entropy pair (\eta,q) compatible with the flux f. The state satisfies the entropy inequality for (\eta,q) on U when \eta(u) and q(u) are locally integrable on U and

0\le\int\bigl(\eta(u)\,\varphi_t+q(u)\,\varphi_x\bigr)\,dx\,dt

for every compactly supported C^1 test function \varphi\ge0 on U. This is the distributional form of \partial_t\eta(u)+\partial_xq(u)\le0. The state satisfies the entropy inequality when this holds for every convex entropy pair of f, and it is an entropy weak solution on U when it is in addition a weak solution there. No boundedness of u is assumed, and all three predicates are stable under restriction to smaller open sets and under changes of u on a null set.

The Lean definitions factor the conditions of an entropy pair: EntropyPair records scalar C^1 functions satisfying Dq=D\eta\circ Df, while ConvexEntropyPair adds convexity of \eta on the whole state space. Convex entropy inequalities need the second structure.

For a vector state u(t,x) and flux f, the conservative residual is u_t+(f(u))_x, while the quasilinear residual is u_t+Df(u)u_x. The Fréchet chain rule identifies the two forms at every point where both maps are differentiable.

A system is hyperbolic at u when f is differentiable there and

Df(u)r_k=\lambda_k r_k,\qquad \lambda_k\in\mathbb R,\qquad \operatorname{span}\{r_1,\ldots,r_m\}=\mathbb R^m.

Strict hyperbolicity additionally requires the speeds \lambda_k to be pairwise distinct. Symmetry means that the Fréchet Jacobian satisfies Df(u)^*=Df(u) for the Euclidean inner product.
The vector Rankine–Hugoniot relation is f(u_R)-f(u_L)=s(u_R-u_L). A nonzero jump determines at most one shock speed.

The local interior equation on an arbitrary open domain is the Bochner-valued identity \int(\phi_tu+\phi_xf(u))=0 against compactly supported scalar C^1 tests, assuming the state and flux are locally integrable. The interior definition has no initial term and no initial trace.

Multiply the viscous equation by a test function and integrate by parts twice in x; the viscous term becomes \varepsilon_i\int u_i\varphi_{xx}, which tends to zero by the uniform bound. Dominated convergence passes to the limit in the remaining terms. For a convex entropy pair, the chain rule gives \partial_t\eta(u_i)+\partial_xq(u_i)=\varepsilon_i\partial_{xx}\eta(u_i) -\varepsilon_iD^2\eta(u_i)(\partial_xu_i,\partial_xu_i), and the last term is nonpositive, so it can be dropped before passing to the limit.

Let f be C^1, let \varepsilon_i\ge0 tend to 0, and let each u_i be C^2 on t>0, continuous on t\ge0, and a classical solution of \partial_tu_i+\partial_xf(u_i)=\varepsilon_i\partial_{xx}u_i with |u_i|\le M almost everywhere. Suppose u_i(0,\cdot)=g for all i, or more generally u_i(0,\cdot)\to g in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}} for a locally integrable g. If u_i\to v almost everywhere on t>0, then v is almost everywhere measurable there, bounded by M, a weak initial-value solution with datum g, and satisfies the entropy inequality for every C^1 convex entropy pair.

Integrating once and using the end conditions at -\infty gives the first-order system v'=f(v)-f(q)-s(v-q); letting v\to u_R gives Rankine–Hugoniot. Near q every nonzero Rankine–Hugoniot jump lies, together with its speed, on one of m shock curves, one per family. For u_R on the k-th curve the two rest points q and u_R lie on a one-dimensional invariant graph of the first-order system, and the flow on it runs from q to u_R exactly when the shock is compressive. Genuine nonlinearity makes the derivative of the shock speed along the curve nonzero, which turns that orientation into the Lax inequality.

Let f be C^\infty on \mathbb R^m with m>0, strictly hyperbolic at every state, with every family genuinely nonlinear, and fix a state q. There are 0<\delta<\rho such that for every u_R\ne q with |u_R-q|<\delta and every speed s, a viscous profile from q to u_R with values in the ball of radius \rho exists if and only if (q,u_R,s) satisfies Rankine–Hugoniot and \lambda_k(u_R)<s<\lambda_k(q) for some k.

Differentiate the ordered composition with respect to the kth strength. Every other wave has zero strength, so its state derivative is the identity. The sole nonidentity factor is the strength derivative of T_k at zero, which is r_k(u_L). The chain rule therefore returns that vector as the kth derivative column.
At zero strengths, the kth column of the derivative of the ordered wave map is the kth right characteristic vector.

The shared forward-half-space weak initial-value formulation allows compactly supported scalar tests to meet t=0 and includes the boundary term. Its Bochner-valued identity covers both scalar laws and finite-dimensional systems; in Euclidean state spaces it is the coordinate-free form of the usual component equations. Restricting to tests supported away from t=0 recovers the interior weak equation. The complementary trace formulation combines that interior equation with strong convergence to a locally integrable datum u_0 in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R) as t\downarrow0. The scalar entropy version combines the trace with the positive-time entropy solution.

A weak solution of u_t + (f(u))_x=0 is defined on an open domain. Both u and f(u) are required to be locally integrable, and the equation is tested against compactly supported C^1 functions after moving derivatives onto the test function. The definition does not assume that u itself is differentiable.

Construct the common local characteristic family, shrink its parameter set so the compatibility condition holds everywhere, and apply uniqueness for the scalar ODE satisfied by the residual along each characteristic.

Retain the C^2 Hamiltonian and C^1 boundary-state hypotheses, and suppose the initial gradient is compatible with the boundary data throughout a neighborhood of the base parameter. Then there is a continuous family of characteristics that starts from the prescribed phase states, solves the full characteristic vector-field ODE, and satisfies

F(p(s),z(s),x(s))=0

at every point of the local flow.

Apply local existence with continuous dependence to the initial states q_0(y) near the base parameter, shrinking to one common time interval. The resulting flow composed with q_0 is jointly continuous, and its time derivative is the characteristic vector field; projecting to the three components gives Evans's equations.

Near any base parameter, a C^2 phase-space Hamiltonian and a C^1 boundary-state family q_0(y) give a family q(s,y), jointly continuous for short times, with

q(0,y)=q_0(y),\qquad \partial_sq(s,y)=\mathcal V_F(q(s,y)).

Projecting to components gives Evans's three equations for p, z, and x. The initial states need not be compatible.

Construct the local C^1 flow together with its state derivative. Compose the flow with i. The chain rule identifies the boundary derivative with the state derivative applied to Di(y); differentiating this expression in time gives the variational equation.

Let v be a globally C^1 vector field on a finite-dimensional real normed space, and let i be a locally C^1 initial map from a real normed parameter space. Near any parameter in its open domain, there is a jointly C^1 family \gamma(y,t) solving the ODE with \gamma(y,0)=i(y). Its boundary derivative B(y,t)=D_y\gamma(y,t) satisfies

\partial_t B(y,t)=Dv(\gamma(y,t))\circ B(y,t),\qquad B(y,0)=Di(y).

For characteristics, a globally C^2 Hamiltonian supplies the required C^1 vector field. Compatibility is not needed here; it enters when the PDE residual and the contact identity are propagated.

The C^2 Hamiltonian makes the characteristic vector field continuously differentiable and therefore locally Lipschitz. Picard–Lindelöf supplies a unique local integral curve through q_0, with the initial condition and ODE identities built into the resulting flow.

If the uncurried Hamiltonian is C^2, Picard–Lindelöf constructs, through every phase-space state q_0, a local curve satisfying

q(0)=q_0,\qquad q'(s)=\mathcal V_F(q(s)).

Differentiate X separately in characteristic time and in the boundary parameter. The characteristic ODE gives the time column D_pF, while the initial identity X(0,y)=x_0(y) gives the tangential columns Dx_0. Linearity of the total derivative combines them into the displayed map.

For a differentiable phase-space Hamiltonian and a C^1 characteristic family with the prescribed initial phase trace, in particular X(0,y)=x_0(y), the initial Jacobian is

D_{(s,y)}X(0,y_0)[\tau,\eta] =\tau\,D_pF(p_0,g(y_0),x_0(y_0)) +Dx_0(y_0)[\eta].

The right side is Evans's noncharacteristic linear map. The identity holds without the noncharacteristic condition, which is needed only for invertibility.

The initial-Jacobian identity identifies DX(0,y_0) with the noncharacteristic map. Since that map is invertible, the local inverse function theorem applies to the characteristic position map and produces the claimed coordinate neighborhoods and inverse.

For a differentiable phase-space Hamiltonian, a C^1 characteristic family with the prescribed initial trace and ODE has local inverse coordinates at a noncharacteristic basepoint, which the position map sends back to each nearby point:

\det D_{(s,y)}X(0,y_0)\ne0 \Longrightarrow (s,y)\longleftrightarrow x=X(s,y) \quad\text{locally}.

Applying this theorem to the continuous Picard–Lindelöf family requires the smooth-dependence input that supplies its C^1 family hypothesis.

For a phase-space state q=(p,z,x), the characteristic vector field is

\mathcal V_F(q)= \left(-D_xF(q)-F_z(q)p,\;D_pF(q)\mathbin{\cdot}p,\;D_pF(q)\right).

Thus an integral curve q(s) solves Evans's three equations (11) as one autonomous ODE. The field is defined on all of phase space; the PDE constraint and compatibility of the initial data are imposed separately.

Differentiate x(s), z(s)=u(x(s)), and p(s)=Du(x(s)) along a curve with velocity D_pF. The chain rule gives the equations for x and z; differentiating F(Du,u,x)=0 in the spatial directions and substituting the Hessian term gives the equation for p.

For a C^1 phase-space Hamiltonian, if a C^2 solution satisfies the equation on an open set, then at every parameter value where a characteristic lies in that set its position, gradient, and value satisfy Evans's characteristic ODE identities.

Each affine member has gradient a, so it solves the equation and the gradient component of the parameter-to-jet derivative is the identity. This proves complete-integral rank even when the Hessian of f is singular. At a point with invertible Hessian, the stationary-envelope theorem applies to x+\nabla f(a)=0 and constructs the claimed branch.

For f\in C^2(A) on an open parameter set, the family u(x,a)=a\cdot x+f(a) is a complete integral of

x\cdot Dv+f(Dv)=v.

At a_0\in A where D^2f(a_0) is invertible, it has a local stationary envelope near x_0=-\nabla f(a_0), with x+\nabla f(\phi(x))=0 and Dv(x)=\phi(x).

Evaluate the PDE at x_0(y_0) to obtain the residual equation. Then differentiate the trace identity u\circ x_0=g at y_0; the chain rule identifies its derivative with Du(x_0(y_0))\circ Dx_0(y_0), which is the tangential compatibility condition.

Suppose x_0 is differentiable at y_0, u is differentiable at x_0(y_0), the trace identity u(x_0(y))=g(y) holds near y_0, and the classical PDE holds at x_0(y_0). With p_0=Du(x_0(y_0)), the chain rule and the PDE give

F(p_0,g(y_0),x_0(y_0))=0,\qquad Dg(y_0)[\eta]=p_0\cdot Dx_0(y_0)[\eta].

The converse direction, solving for a compatible gradient field from boundary data, uses the implicit function theorem in Theorem 7.126.

For a parametrized initial surface x_0(y) and prescribed trace g(y), a candidate initial gradient p_0 is compatible at y_0 when

F(p_0,g(y_0),x_0(y_0))=0, \qquad Dg(y_0)[\eta]=p_0\mathbin{\cdot}Dx_0(y_0)[\eta]

for every tangent parameter \eta. This is the coordinate-free form of Evans's compatibility conditions (29)–(30).

In positive spatial dimension n, a complete integral is a jointly C^2 family u(x,a) on open spatial and parameter sets, with n parameters, whose members solve F(D_xu,u,x)=0 and whose parameter-to-jet derivative

D_a(u,D_xu):\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{n+1}

is injective at every point. This is rank n of the first jet; invertibility of D_a^2u is a separate condition, used by the envelope theorem.

Apply the chain rule to F(p(s),z(s),x(s)) and substitute the three characteristic equations. The D_xF, F_zp, and D_pF contributions cancel pairwise, so the derivative is zero and the residual is constant.

At a point where the phase-space Hamiltonian is differentiable, every differentiable characteristic triple q(s)=(p(s),z(s),x(s)) satisfies

\frac d{ds}F(p(s),z(s),x(s))=0.

The theorem is pointwise. If these hypotheses hold on an open interval containing zero, then F(q(s))=F(q(0)) there by the mean value theorem, so compatible initial data with F(q(0))=0 stay on the constraint hypersurface. For a continuously differentiable Hamiltonian, the interval form holds for every characteristic curve; see the automatic flow below.

Compatibility makes the contact defect zero at initial time. Its first-variation equation is a homogeneous scalar linear ODE with locally bounded coefficient, so uniqueness forces it to remain zero. Together with the characteristic-time identity, this identifies every derivative of z with pairing against p through the derivative of x.

For a regular characteristic flow satisfying the first-variation equation, the contact defect

\partial_y z-p\cdot\partial_y x

vanishes initially by compatibility and remains zero by uniqueness for its homogeneous linear ODE. Combining the tangential and characteristic-time directions proves that the differential of z is the pullback of the covector represented by p.

Compare the increment \Phi(t,q_0+h)-\Phi(t,q_0) with J(t,q_0)h. Taylor's formula turns the difference into an integral equation with a quadratic remainder. The local Lipschitz and derivative bounds control that remainder, and Grönwall's inequality makes it o(\lVert h\rVert), proving that J is the Fréchet derivative.

Let \Phi(t,q_0) be a local autonomous flow and let J solve

\partial_tJ(t,q_0)=Dv(\Phi(t,q_0))\circ J(t,q_0), \qquad J(0,q_0)=I.

Under explicit local Lipschitz control of \Phi, a bound on Dv, and a quadratic Taylor-remainder estimate, the theorem identifies

D_{q_0}\Phi(t,q_0)=J(t,q_0).

The proof treats positive and negative time by Grönwall estimates. Applying it to the automatic characteristic flow requires these quantitative hypotheses on one common neighborhood.

Solve one autonomous ODE on the product of the state space and the space of continuous linear operators, with vector field (q,J)\mapsto(v(q),Dv(q)\circ J). Local ODE theory gives a common family starting from (q_0,I), and projection yields the trajectory and variational equations.

For a C^2 autonomous vector field on a complete normed space, there is a common local time interval on which nearby initial states generate continuous trajectories together with continuous variational operators. The trajectories solve

q'=v(q),

and the operators start at the identity and solve

J'=Dv(q)\circ J.

The assumed initial derivative is a continuous linear equivalence, and the C^1 hypothesis supplies the neighborhood regularity. The Banach-space inverse function theorem therefore restricts X to mutually inverse maps between neighborhoods of (0,y_0) and X(0,y_0), giving the coordinate functions S and Y.

Let X(s,y) be the spatial characteristic map, C^1 near (0,y_0). If D_{(s,y)}X(0,y_0) is the noncharacteristic initial isomorphism, the inverse function theorem produces neighborhoods and a local inverse \Psi=(S,Y) satisfying

\Psi(X(s,y))=(s,y),\qquad X(S(x),Y(x))=x.

Thus boundary parameters and characteristic time give local spatial coordinates. The formal statement records only the second identity, near the image of the basepoint.

Choose a globally C^2 Hamiltonian G agreeing with F near the initial phase. Its value and derivatives there preserve compatibility and noncharacteristicity. For G, the implicit function theorem constructs a compatible C^1 momentum field through p_0. Construct the C^1 characteristic family and its first variation. Shrink the flow box so its positions lie in the ambient domain and G_z is bounded. Residual preservation and the variational equation give contact transport; the noncharacteristic map is the initial position derivative. The preceding theorem supplies inverse coordinates and the local C^2 solution, with base gradient p_0. Continuity of (Du,u,x) permits a smaller spatial neighborhood on which G(Du,u,x)=F(Du,u,x). Restrict the boundary neighborhood as well to retain the trace.

Assume F is C^2 near the initial phase (p_0,g(y_0),b(y_0)), the boundary parametrization b and values g are C^2 on an open parameter neighborhood of y_0, and the base momentum p_0 satisfies

F(p_0,g(y_0),b(y_0))=0,\qquad \langle p_0,Db(y_0)h\rangle=Dg(y_0)h.

Suppose the initial tangent/characteristic map at this state is invertible, and b(y_0) lies in the open ambient domain. Then some open spatial neighborhood within that domain carries a C^2 classical solution of F(Du,u,x)=0 with trace u(b(y))=g(y) near y_0 and Du(b(y_0))=p_0.

Invert the spatial characteristic map near the noncharacteristic basepoint and define u(x)=z(S(x),Y(x)). Contact preservation and the inverse-map identity give Du=p; residual preservation then yields F(Du,u,x)=0. Restricting to the initial surface recovers the prescribed trace. The momentum in inverse coordinates is C^1, so Du is C^1 and u is C^2.

For a C^1 phase-space Hamiltonian, given compatible boundary gradients, a noncharacteristic basepoint, and a regular characteristic flow, there are open neighborhoods of the boundary parameter and boundary point and a C^2 function u that satisfies

F(Du,u,x)=0

on the spatial neighborhood and has the prescribed boundary trace. Local invertibility, Du=p, and the PDE residual are all derived from noncharacteristicity and the characteristic and first-variation equations.

For a globally C^2 Hamiltonian, a C^1 characteristic family with the prescribed initial trace, compatible initial gradients, and a local bound on F_z determines a regular flow box, provided its boundary derivative satisfies the variational equation. The constructor derives the component equations and the contact evolution from these hypotheses.

A regular local flow box consists of C^1 maps (p,z,x)(s,y) satisfying

\dot x=D_pF,\qquad \dot z=D_pF\cdot p,\qquad \dot p=-D_xF-F_zp,

their prescribed initial traces, and the homogeneous first-variation equation for the contact defect C=\partial_yz-p\cdot\partial_yx. A uniform local bound on F_z records the coefficient control used by ODE uniqueness. The structure collects hypotheses; a constructor builds one from a C^1 characteristic family.

At a parametrized initial surface, the boundary-tangent directions together with the characteristic direction D_pF define an invertible linear map onto the ambient space. In coordinates this is Evans's determinant condition (36).

Apply the implicit function theorem to D_a u=0, using the actual parameter Hessian as its invertible derivative. This constructs the local C^1 selector and its local uniqueness. In the chain rule for v, stationarity cancels the parameter term. The remaining derivative D_xu(x,\phi(x)) is C^1, so v is C^2; substituting it into the family's PDE proves the envelope equation.

Let u(x,a) be a jointly C^2 family of classical solutions on open sets. At an interior base point (x_0,a_0), assume D_a u(x_0,a_0)=0 and that D_a^2u(x_0,a_0) is invertible. Then a neighborhood V of x_0 carries a C^1 selector \phi, with \phi(x_0)=a_0, taking values in the parameter domain and satisfying

D_a u(x,\phi(x))=0,\qquad v(x)=u(x,\phi(x)),\qquad Dv(x)=D_xu(x,\phi(x)).

The envelope v is C^2 and solves F(Dv,v,x)=0 on V. The stationary parameter is locally unique near the base point. The general result permits any finite number of parameters; complete integrals give a special case.

Starting from z, an admissible control a is an integrable velocity with integrable Lagrangian cost and terminal constraint

x=z+\int_0^t a(s)\,ds.

The autonomous value is

V(t,x)= \inf_{(z,a)\,\mathrm{admissible}} \left\{g(z)+\int_0^tL(a(s))\,ds\right\}.

Admissibility is a predicate on the initial state and the control.

Apply the general characteristic identities for F(Du,u,\cdot)=0 to this F. Since F is affine in p_0 with unit coefficient, the momentum gradient D_pF has time component 1 and spatial part D_pH, which gives \dot t=1 and \dot x=D_pH. The general equation \dot p=-D_{(t,x)}F-F_z\,p has F_z=0, and the spacetime gradient of F splits into the time derivative H_t and the spatial gradient D_xH. Finally \dot z=D_pF\cdot p=p_0+D_pH\cdot p_x, and the equation p_0=-H along the solution turns this into \dot z=D_pH\cdot p_x-H.

Let U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1} be open, let the phase function F(p,z,(t,x))=p_0+H(p_x,t,x) be C^1 in all of its arguments, and let u\in C^2(U) satisfy F(Du,u,(t,x))=0 on U, that is, u_t+H(D_xu,t,x)=0. Let \gamma\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{n+1} be differentiable at s with \gamma(s)\in U and

\dot\gamma(s)=D_pF\bigl(Du(\gamma(s)),u(\gamma(s)),\gamma(s)\bigr),

and assume that H is differentiable in its momentum argument and jointly differentiable in its time and space arguments at the point determined by \gamma(s). Write \gamma=(t,x), let p=Du\circ\gamma=(p_0,p_x) be the spacetime gradient along the curve, and let z=u\circ\gamma. Then at the parameter value s

\dot t=1,\qquad \dot x=D_pH(p_x,t,x),\qquad \dot p_0=-H_t(p_x,t,x),

\dot p_x=-D_xH(p_x,t,x),\qquad \dot z=D_pH(p_x,t,x)\cdot p_x-H(p_x,t,x).

These are Hamilton's equations for (x,p_x) with the curve parameter identified with time; the last identity is the classical \dot z=p\cdot\dot x-H.

At an interior point where a differentiable test function touches u from above, the difference u-\phi has a local maximum, so its derivative is zero and D\phi=Du. Substitution into the classical equation gives the subsolution inequality, in fact equality. A local minimum gives the same gradient identity and the supersolution inequality.
A differentiable pointwise solution of u_t+H(u_x,x)=0 on an open domain satisfies the corresponding domain-relative viscosity inequalities.

At every contact point where the test is differentiable, Fermat's theorem applied to u-\phi gives \phi_t=u_t and \phi_x=u_x. The classical equation therefore evaluates the test residual to zero, which implies the required inequality in either contact direction. Differentiability supplies continuity, and restricting the ambient local statement to the open domain gives the domain-relative viscosity solution.

A differentiable pointwise solution of u_t+H(u_x)=0 is a viscosity solution. If a test function \phi, differentiable at the contact point, touches u from above at (t_0,x_0), then

\phi_t(t_0,x_0)+H(\phi_x(t_0,x_0))\leq0;

touching from below gives the reverse inequality. At such a touching point, D\phi=Du, so both follow from the classical equation. On an open domain, the ambient-local inequalities induce the domain-relative continuous viscosity solution.

Replace each control value by its equal Hopf–Lax expression. Splitting the total time as s+(t-s) turns the right-hand side into the composition Q_{t-s}(Q_sg). The Hopf–Lax semigroup law identifies this composition with Q_tg, which is the original control value.

Under the same finite-conjugate and Lipschitz-data hypotheses, if 0<s<t, Bellman's principle holds:

V(t,x)=V_{t-s}\bigl(x;\,z\mapsto V(s,z)\bigr).

For an admissible control starting at z, the terminal constraint says that its mean velocity is (x-z)/t. Jensen's inequality bounds its integral cost below by tL((x-z)/t), so taking infima gives the Hopf–Lax lower bound. Conversely, every footpoint z defines the constant admissible control with that velocity and exactly that cost, giving the reverse bound.

For a finite Legendre transform, positive time, and Lipschitz initial data,

V(t,x)=(Q_tg)(x).

Jensen's inequality shows that every admissible control costs at least the constant control a(s)=(x-z)/t with the same displacement, while constant controls give the reverse bound.

Translating controls identifies u(x,t) with the forward value W(x,T-t). The contact arguments and the slab estimates make W a bounded uniformly continuous viscosity solution of W_t+H(D_xW,x)=0 with W(\cdot,0)=g, where H(p,x)=-\inf_v\{p\cdot f(x,v)+h(x,v)\}. Time reflection exchanges the two problems and reverses the inequalities. Uniqueness comes from the finite-dimensional comparison theorem for W, applied to the reflected competitor.

Let E be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and A a nonempty pseudometrizable control space, each with its Borel structure. Let f\colon E\times A\to E be continuous, bounded by M, and K-Lipschitz in x uniformly in v. Let h\colon E\times A\to\mathbb R be Borel measurable, bounded by C, and L-Lipschitz in x uniformly in v. Let g be bounded and Lipschitz, and let T>0. For 0\le t\le T put

u(x,t)=\inf_\alpha\left\{\int_t^T h(X(s),\alpha(s))\,ds+g(X(T))\right\},

the infimum over measurable controls on [t,T], where X is the response to \alpha starting from x at time t. Then u is bounded and uniformly continuous on E\times[0,T], u(x,T)=g(x), and u is a viscosity solution of

u_t+\inf_{v\in A}\{D_xu\cdot f(x,v)+h(x,v)\}=0\qquad(0<t<T)

for C^1 tests: if u-\varphi has a local maximum at a point of the open slab, then \varphi_t+\inf_v\{D_x\varphi\cdot f(x,v)+h(x,v)\}\ge0 there, and at a local minimum the reverse inequality holds. Every bounded uniformly continuous function on E\times[0,T] with terminal value g that satisfies the same two inequalities for C^\infty tests coincides with u on E\times[0,T].

For positive time, the control value equals the Hopf–Lax solution, so it inherits the interior viscosity inequalities and spacetime regularity. Define the closed-time value to be g at t=0; the Hopf–Lax initial trace proves continuity there. Bounded Lipschitz data and the established time and space estimates give bounded uniform continuity on each slab, so the subsolution, supersolution, and exact-trace components give the initial-value predicate above.

For a convex differentiable autonomous Hamiltonian with finite Legendre transform and bounded Lipschitz initial data, the closed-time control value satisfies

V_t+H(V_x)=0\quad(t>0),\qquad V(0,x)=g(x)

in the differentiable-test viscosity sense defined above. The theorem includes bounded uniform continuity on every closed time slab and gives the exact time-zero trace.

For a Hamiltonian H=H(p,t,x) on \mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n and a spacetime domain U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}, with time in coordinate zero, the Hamilton–Jacobi equation is the single-equation problem

\partial_tu+H(D_xu,t,x)=0\quad\text{on }U

with no side conditions; D_xu is the spatial gradient. In the fully nonlinear form F(Du,u,(t,x))=0 the same equation uses

F(p,z,(t,x))=p_0+H(p_x,t,x),

where p_0 is the time component of the spacetime gradient and p_x its spatial part; the value argument z does not enter. The autonomous equation u_t+H(Du,x)=0 is the special case of a time-independent Hamiltonian.

Let K be a Lipschitz constant for g. Test the supremum defining L at both slopes K+1 and -(K+1). These two bounds control the two tails: the action grows at least as (K+1)|x-y| minus a constant, while the datum can decrease by at most K|x-y|. Thus the integrand tends to +\infty as |y|\to\infty. Continuity gives a minimum on a large compact interval, and the coercive bound excludes every point outside it.

For a finite Legendre transform, positive time, and Lipschitz initial data, there exists a minimizing footpoint y_* with

(Q_tg)(x) =g(y_*)+tL\!\left(\frac{x-y_*}{t}\right).

The integrand is bounded below. The proof derives a linear coercive lower bound from the dual supremum, minimizes on a sufficiently large compact interval, and excludes every point outside that interval.

If t=0 or s=0, both sides agree because S_0 is the identity. For t,s>0, the Lipschitz datum makes all three Hopf–Lax infima bounded below, and the spatial Lipschitz estimate shows that Q_sg is again K-Lipschitz, so the positive-time semigroup identity applies. The restart form substitutes t=(t-s)+s.

For a finite Legendre transform and a K-Lipschitz datum g, the closed-time operators form a semigroup on the closed half-line: for t,s\ge0,

S_{t+s}g=S_t(S_sg).

Equivalently, the profile u(t,x)=(S_tg)(x) can be restarted from any intermediate time: if 0\le s\le t, then

u(t,x)=\bigl(S_{t-s}\,u(s,\cdot)\bigr)(x).

Unlike the positive-time semigroup law, no bounded-below hypotheses appear: the Lipschitz datum supplies them, and the time-zero cases reduce to S_0=\mathrm{id}.
At time zero both profiles reduce to the data, and the claims are the hypotheses. At positive time the profiles are the Hopf–Lax values, and the positive-time comparison theorem applies verbatim.

Let H have a finite Legendre transform, let g be K-Lipschitz, and let \tilde g be arbitrary. Write u_g for the closed-time Hopf–Lax profile of g. At every spacetime point z with z_0\ge0,

g\le\tilde g\ \text{pointwise}\ \Longrightarrow\ u_g(z)\le u_{\tilde g}(z), \qquad \left(\forall y,\ |g(y)-\tilde g(y)|\le C\right) \ \Longrightarrow\ |u_g(z)-u_{\tilde g}(z)|\le C.

Thus the evolution preserves order and is nonexpansive in the uniform distance on the closed forward half-plane, including the initial slice.

The closed-time Hopf–Lax evolution inserts the datum at time zero:

(S_tg)(x)= \begin{cases} g(x), & t=0,\\ (Q_tg)(x), & t\neq0. \end{cases}

Its spacetime form is u(z)=(S_{z_0}g)(z_1) on \mathbb R^2 with time in coordinate zero. This is Evans's candidate solution in §3.3.2, defined on \mathbb R\times[0,\infty) with u=g on \{t=0\}. The definitions are total; every theorem about them below carries the hypothesis t\ge0.

Apply local nonexpansiveness with distance bound zero. Agreement of the initial data on the propagation ball makes the required local supremum distance vanish, so the distance between the two Hopf–Lax values is zero and the values are equal.

Let L=H^* be finite, let g,\tilde g both be K-Lipschitz, and let t>0. Then

\left(g=\tilde g\ \text{on }\overline B(x,R_{H,K}(t))\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (Q_tg)(x)=(Q_t\tilde g)(x).

For t>0, the Hopf–Lax operator is

(Q_tg)(x)= \inf_{y\in\mathbb R} \left\{g(y)+tL\!\left(\frac{x-y}{t}\right)\right\}.

Thus the optimization variable is the initial footpoint y, and the Lagrangian is evaluated at the constant speed from y to x.

For the spatial estimate, let y_* be a minimizing footpoint for the value at x. Translating it by y-x gives a competitor for the value at y with the same Lagrangian term, so the difference of the two values is bounded by |g(y_*+y-x)-g(y_*)|\le K|x-y|; exchanging the roles of x and y gives the reverse bound. For the estimate against the datum, the stationary footpoint y=x gives (Q_tg)(x)\le g(x)+tL(0), while the Fenchel bound L(q)\ge K|q|-\max\{H(K),H(-K)\} together with the Lipschitz bound on g gives the matching lower bound. The time estimate restarts the evolution at time s through the semigroup law and applies the previous bound to the K-Lipschitz profile Q_sg; the spacetime estimate is the triangle inequality.

Let H have a finite Legendre transform L and let g be K-Lipschitz. Set

C_{H,K}=\max\bigl\{|L(0)|,\ |\max\{H(K),H(-K)\}|\bigr\}.

Then for all t,s>0 and x,y\in\mathbb R,

|(Q_tg)(x)-(Q_tg)(y)|\le K|x-y|,\qquad |(Q_tg)(x)-g(x)|\le C_{H,K}\,t,

|(Q_tg)(x)-(Q_sg)(x)|\le C_{H,K}|t-s|,\qquad |(Q_tg)(x)-(Q_sg)(y)|\le K|x-y|+C_{H,K}|t-s|.

Thus x\mapsto(Q_tg)(x) is K-Lipschitz with the constant of the datum, and the profile is Lipschitz in time with an explicit constant depending only on H and K. These are the estimates of Lemma 2 of Evans, §3.3.2.

Choose a minimizing footpoint for each datum. Localization places both footpoints in the common closed ball. Testing each Hopf–Lax infimum at the other datum's minimizer gives the two one-sided inequalities whose combination is the distance estimate.

Let L=H^* be finite, let g,\tilde g both be K-Lipschitz, and fix t>0 and x\in\mathbb R. If

|g(y)-\tilde g(y)|\leq C \qquad\text{whenever }|y-x|\leq R_{H,K}(t),

then |(Q_tg)(x)-(Q_t\tilde g)(x)|\leq C. Only values on this closed ball enter the comparison.

Lipschitz data give a coercive lower bound for the Hopf–Lax integrand, so the infimum for g is finite. If g\le\tilde g, every competitor value for \tilde g dominates the corresponding competitor value for g, which gives monotonicity. For the distance bound, the pointwise inequalities g\le\tilde g+C and \tilde g\le g+C transfer to the infima because adding a constant to the datum adds the same constant to the Hopf–Lax value; the two one-sided inequalities combine to the distance estimate.

For a finite Legendre transform, t>0, and a K-Lipschitz datum g, the Hopf–Lax operator preserves order and is nonexpansive in the uniform distance against an arbitrary second datum \tilde g:

g\le\tilde g\ \text{pointwise}\ \Longrightarrow\ Q_tg\le Q_t\tilde g, \qquad \left(\forall y,\ |g(y)-\tilde g(y)|\le C\right)\ \Longrightarrow\ |(Q_tg)(x)-(Q_t\tilde g)(x)|\le C .

Only the datum g is assumed Lipschitz, and in the first statement it is the smaller one. This hypothesis makes its Hopf–Lax infimum bounded below; the second datum needs no regularity of its own.

Jensen's inequality and the absolutely-continuous fundamental theorem bound every path action below by the pointwise Hopf–Lax integrand at its initial point. Constant-speed affine paths give the reverse inequality for every possible initial point. In finite dimension the Hamiltonian assumptions give a finite, continuous, convex, superlinear conjugate. Its superlinear growth dominates the possible linear decrease of g, making the footpoint cost coercive. A continuous coercive function on a finite-dimensional space attains its minimum, and the corresponding straight path has finite action and attains the path minimum as well.

In one dimension, for positive time, a finite Legendre transform, and Lipschitz initial data,

(Q_tg)(x)= \inf_{\substack{\gamma\in AC([0,t]),\ \gamma(t)=x\\L(\dot\gamma)\in L^1(0,t)}} \left\{ g(\gamma(0))+\int_0^tL(\dot\gamma(s))\,ds \right\}.

Thus the pointwise footpoint infimum equals Evans's variational infimum over finite-action absolutely continuous paths ending at x.

The path representation also holds on any finite-dimensional real inner-product space E. Assume H:E\to\mathbb R is convex and superlinear and g:E\to\mathbb R is Lipschitz. With the inner product identifying the dual space and L=H^*, for every t>0 and x\in E,

Q_tg(x)=\min_{y\in E}\left\{g(y)+tL\left(\frac{x-y}{t}\right)\right\} =\min_{\substack{\gamma\in AC([0,t];E),\ \gamma(t)=x\\ L(\dot\gamma)\in L^1(0,t)}} \left\{g(\gamma(0))+\int_0^t L(\dot\gamma(s))\,ds\right\}.

Both minima are attained: a minimizing footpoint y gives the minimizing path \gamma(s)=y+s(x-y)/t. The finite-dimensional statement uses the convex, superlinear Hamiltonian hypotheses; the subsequent one-dimensional comparison and viscosity theorems retain their own stated assumptions.

Let L=H^* be finite and let g be K-Lipschitz, with K\geq0. Set

C_H(K)=\max\{H(K+1),H(-(K+1))\},\qquad R_{H,K}(t)=\max\{0,\ t(C_H(K)+L(0))\}.

For t>0, every minimizing footpoint y_* for (Q_tg)(x) satisfies |x-y_*|\leq R_{H,K}(t). Such a minimizer exists. Indeed, the coercive lower bound is g(x)+|x-y|-tC_H(K), while the competitor y=x has cost g(x)+tL(0); comparison gives the radius.

Let y_* minimize the value at x. Use y_*+h and y_*-h as competitors for the values at x+h and x-h. Both competitors have the same displacement x-y_*, so their two Lagrangian terms cancel against twice the central one. What remains is precisely the assumed semiconcavity inequality for g at y_*.

If the initial datum is globally Lipschitz and satisfies

g(x+h)+g(x-h)-2g(x)\leq C h^2,

then for every t>0 its Hopf–Lax profile satisfies the same estimate:

(Q_tg)(x+h)+(Q_tg)(x-h)-2(Q_tg)(x)\leq C h^2.

A minimizer for the central point supplies translated competitors at the two neighboring points, and the common Lagrangian terms cancel.

The time-splitting inequality gives a lower bound for every two-segment cost; taking the two infima yields Q_{t+s}g(x)\leq Q_t(Q_sg)(x). Conversely, for each footpoint y, choose z=(sx+ty)/(t+s). Both segment velocities then equal (x-y)/(t+s), so the two-segment cost equals the direct cost. Testing the nested infima at z and y and then taking the infimum over y proves the reverse inequality.

Let L=H^* be finite and fix s,t>0 and x\in\mathbb R. Assume the sets of competitor costs defining Q_{t+s}g(x), Q_t(Q_sg)(x), and Q_sg(z) for every z\in\mathbb R are bounded below. Then

(Q_t(Q_sg))(x)=(Q_{t+s}g)(x).

This is the dynamic-programming semigroup identity for the autonomous Hamiltonian.

Lipschitz data provide lower bounds and attainment for the variational problem. Touching-test arguments establish the subsolution and supersolution inequalities first for the biconjugate Hamiltonian. Convex differentiability identifies the biconjugate with H; separate spacetime Lipschitz estimates give continuity and the one-sided initial trace.

For a convex differentiable Hamiltonian with finite Legendre transform, and for Lipschitz initial data, the Hopf–Lax profile is a continuous viscosity solution on t>0 and converges pointwise to the initial datum as t decreases to zero.

Fenchel's inequality gives H^{**}(p)\leq H(p). For the reverse inequality, convex differentiability supplies the supporting line H(r)\geq H(p)+H'(p)(r-p). Rearranging shows that the supremum defining H^*(H'(p)) equals pH'(p)-H(p). Testing the second conjugate at H'(p) therefore gives H^{**}(p)\geq H(p).

For a differentiable convex Hamiltonian with finite Legendre transform, H^{**}=H pointwise. No separate finiteness assumption on the biconjugate is required. The proof evaluates the first conjugate at H'(p) and combines the convex supporting-line inequality with the reverse Fenchel bound.

For each fixed p, the map q\mapsto pq-H(p) is affine. Its value at a convex combination is the same convex combination of its endpoint values; taking the supremum over p gives the convexity inequality. Finiteness on the open interval \mathbb R then invokes the standard theorem that a finite convex real function is continuous on the interior of its domain.

For 0\leq\theta\leq1,

L\bigl(\theta q_1+(1-\theta)q_2\bigr) \leq\theta L(q_1)+(1-\theta)L(q_2).

The finite Legendre transform is convex because it is a supremum of affine functions. In one dimension, finite convexity on all of \mathbb R also gives continuity L\in C(\mathbb R), which permits the Hopf–Lax integrand to attain its minimum after coercive localization.

The single-step velocity is the weighted average of the two segment velocities, with weights t/(t+s) and s/(t+s). Apply convexity of L to that average and multiply by t+s. The resulting right-hand side is exactly the sum of the two segment costs.

Let L=H^* be finite. For s,t>0 and any x,y,z\in\mathbb R,

(t+s)L\!\left(\frac{x-y}{t+s}\right) \leq sL\!\left(\frac{z-y}{s}\right) +tL\!\left(\frac{x-z}{t}\right).

Travel from y to z takes time s, and from z to x time t. The direct path costs no more than this two-segment path.

The one-dimensional Legendre–Fenchel transform is

L(q)=H^*(q)=\sup_{p\in\mathbb R}\bigl(pq-H(p)\bigr).

LegendreFinite H states that this defining supremum is bounded above for every q, so L\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R is well defined without introducing extended-real arithmetic into the interface.

The normalized quadratic Hamiltonian is

H(p)=\frac{p^2}{2}.

It is the model case of the one-dimensional theory: differentiable with H'(p)=p, and strongly convex on \mathbb R with constant one.

Completing the square gives pq-p^2/2=q^2/2-(p-q)^2/2. The right-hand side is at most q^2/2, which bounds the defining supremum and proves finiteness, and the choice p=q attains the bound. Substituting L=H into the Hopf–Lax integrand and simplifying t\,(x-y)^2/(2t^2) gives the Moreau cost.

The quadratic Hamiltonian has a finite Legendre transform and is self-dual:

L(q)=\sup_{p\in\mathbb R}\Bigl(pq-\frac{p^2}2\Bigr)=\frac{q^2}2=H(q).

Consequently, for every t\neq0 and every datum g, the Hopf–Lax value is the infimum of the Moreau cost

(Q_tg)(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R}\Bigl\{g(y)+\frac{(x-y)^2}{2t}\Bigr\}.

For t>0 this is the Moreau envelope of g with parameter t.

Unfold the three predicates. Their slab regularity and interior touching-test conditions agree componentwise. At time zero, the subsolution gives u(0,x)\leq g(x) and the supersolution gives the reverse inequality, so antisymmetry yields the exact trace. Conversely, equality with g immediately supplies both one-sided trace conditions.

The initial-value solution predicate is equivalent to the conjunction of the initial-value subsolution and supersolution predicates. Their initial conditions are respectively u(0,\cdot)\le g and g\le u(0,\cdot), so the conjunction recovers the exact trace.

For a one-dimensional spatially dependent Hamiltonian H(p,x) and initial datum g, the formal initial-value predicate requires boundedness and uniform continuity on every slab [0,T]\times\mathbb R, the domain-relative sub- and supersolution inequalities on t>0 for tests differentiable at the contact point, and the pointwise trace u(0,x)=g(x).

A continuous candidate is tested against differentiable functions touching it from above or below relative to an open spacetime domain. The resulting inequalities encode u_t+H(u_x)=0 without requiring derivatives of u. This is the domain-relative definition specialized to H=H(p).

Embed each formal compatibility value g_k into the common ambient energy space and pair adjacent values as displacement and velocity. The compatibility recurrence g_{k+2}=F_k(0)-Bg_k rearranges to the required initial acceleration equation. Coherence of the forcing representatives ensures that all levels use the same time-zero data rather than independent choices.

Compatible wave data determine the initial displacement g_k and velocity g_{k+1} of each differentiated problem, for 0\leq k\leq m. Adjacent levels satisfy the formal acceleration relation

g_{k+2}+Bg_k=F_k(0),\qquad 0\leq k<m.

The equality is interpreted in the dual energy space, using the pivot embedding for g_{k+2}. It is a compatibility identity for the initial data.

The data consist of a finite Sobolev time jet, initial displacement and velocity of matching spatial orders, and the formal initial derivatives

g_0=g,\qquad g_1=h,\qquad g_{k+2}=\partial_t^k f(0)-Bg_k.

Compatibility requires each g_k to lie in the spatial space prescribed for \partial_t^ku(0), to have the homogeneous Dirichlet trace when required, and to satisfy this recurrence. Compatibility thus fixes both the regularity budget and the boundary values of the formal derivatives.

Each assumed level estimate bounds one nonnegative summand almost everywhere. Intersect the finitely many full-measure sets so that all bounds hold simultaneously, then sum them pointwise. Monotonicity of the essential supremum transfers this finite pointwise sum to the left-hand side, and the assumed upper bound for the sum of level constants produces the single factor C multiplying the data budget.

Consider the decreasing Sobolev norm sum and the forcing and initial-data budget. If each differentiated level has an almost-everywhere quantitative energy or elliptic bound and the level constants sum to at most C, then

\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{t\in(t_0,t_1)} \sum_{k=0}^{m+1}\|\partial_t^k u(t)\|_{H^{m+1-k}} \leq C\left( \sum_{k=0}^{m}\|\partial_t^k f\|_{L^2_tH^{m-k}_x} +\|g\|_{H^{m+1}}+\|h\|_{H^m}\right).

Begin with the two highest time-derivative bounds. Strong induction descends through the Sobolev levels: at each step, the assumed recurrence controls the next spatial norm from the forcing at that level and the two already controlled higher time derivatives. This proves the recursive majorant M_k for every level. The finite assembly theorem then sums these almost-everywhere estimates into the stated essential-supremum bound.

Let M_k be the recursively defined majorant obtained from the two top differentiated energy bounds and an assumed two-step spatial recurrence, after factoring out the data budget B. The recurrence bounds the H^{k+2} entry \partial_t^{m-1-k}u(t) of the norm sum by the forcing, the H^k entry \partial_t^{m+1-k}u(t), and a shift term in the H^{k+1} entry \partial_t^{m-k}u(t). The resulting bound is

\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{t\in(t_0,t_1)} \sum_{k=0}^{m+1}\|\partial_t^ku(t)\|_{H^{m+1-k}} \leq \left(\sum_{k=0}^{m+1}M_k\right)B.

Here B is the forcing and initial-data budget in the preceding estimate. Both starting bounds and the recurrence are hypotheses, and the proof propagates them through the finite derivative hierarchy. The recurrence has a different shape from the higher-order lift, whose shift term falls on the level being solved for rather than on the neighbouring one.

Start with a representative of the highest weak time derivative. Descend through the jet, choosing at each level the Sobolev representative whose weak derivative is the representative already fixed one level above. The Sobolev time-derivative identities hold almost everywhere, and the canonical embeddings into the dual energy space preserve both those identities and the prescribed Bochner integrability.

A Sobolev time jet on a nontrivial interval admits coherent dual-valued representatives F_0,\ldots,F_m, all but the last absolutely continuous, such that

\partial_tF_k=F_{k+1}\quad\text{for almost every }t, \qquad 0\leq k<m.

Each representative agrees almost everywhere with the Dirichlet load of the matching jet entry, so later Galerkin systems use one compatible chain rather than unrelated representatives of the weak derivatives.

Full-operator Ritz orthogonality makes the projected initial jet satisfy the differentiated finite-dimensional equations. The uniform energy bounds take A as the coercive symmetric energy form. The mixed estimate on R absorbs the remainder in that energy estimate, at the cost of a larger exponential rate. Apply the common finite-chain compactness extraction to all differentiated Galerkin trajectories at once; weak convergence passes both the A and R terms to the limit and preserves every adjacent time-derivative identity.

Let the autonomous operator split as B=A+R, with A symmetric and coercive and with a possibly nonsymmetric remainder satisfying

|R(v,w)|\leq L_R\|v\|_V\|Jw\|_H.

In addition to compatible data, stable dense trial projections, and a uniform forcing budget, assume full-operator Ritz orthogonality:

(A+R)(q-P_kq,w)=0\qquad\text{for every }w\in S_k,

for each initial jet entry q used in the adjacent compatibility recurrence. Here P_k is the restriction of the stable pivot projection to V. This condition is separate from stability and density, and orthogonality for A alone does not imply it. Under these hypotheses, the theorem constructs a common finite chain of weak-wave limits for B, retaining every adjacent time-derivative identity.

Finite-dimensional differentiated trajectories are built first. Uniform energy bounds provide bounded families at every level. One common compactness extraction passes all equations and adjacent derivative identities to the limit, including the convergent projected initial values.

Compatible initial jets, stable dense trial spaces, Ritz orthogonality, coherent forcing, symmetric coercivity, and uniform forcing budgets produce weak-wave limits U_0,\ldots,U_m along one common filter, with

\partial_tU_k=U_{k+1},\qquad \partial_t^2U_k+BU_k=F_k \quad\text{for }0\leq k<m.
