The remainder estimate and Young's inequality give |R(v,v)|\leq \frac c2\|v\|_V^2+ \frac{L_R^2}{2c}\|Jv\|_H^2. Subtract this loss from the coercive lower bound for A(v,v) to obtain the displayed Gårding inequality. Adding the pivot-mass term therefore makes the shifted form coercive. Moving the same mass term to the load shows that an unshifted weak solution solves the shifted Lax–Milgram problem.

If the principal form is coercive and the lower-order remainder obeys the mixed V\times H bound, Young's inequality gives the exact Gårding loss

\frac c2\|v\|_V^2 \leq (A+R)(v,v)+\frac{L_R^2}{2c}\|Jv\|_H^2.

Adding this canonical pivot-mass shift makes the full, possibly nonsymmetric operator coercive, and identifies an unshifted weak solution with the shifted Lax–Milgram solution after correcting the load. This is an abstract Gelfand-triple analogue of the elliptic Gårding construction.

Rewrite the unshifted equation as the coercive shifted problem with corrected load f+\mu u. Lax–Milgram uniqueness identifies the given weak solution with the shifted solver. Apply the global divergence-form H^2 regularity operator to that load and use its norm bound; the triangle inequality yields the displayed dependence on \|f\|_{L^2} and |\mu|\|u\|_{L^2}.

Let n>0 and let the domain carry the operational C2BoundaryAtlas. Assume uniformly elliptic W^{1,\infty} principal coefficients with global C^1 representatives and bounded first- and zeroth-order coefficients. The Gårding-shifted homogeneous Dirichlet solver has a bounded L^2\to H^2 lift. Every unshifted weak solution u\in H^1_0(\Omega) with f\in L^2(\Omega) therefore has an H^2 representative satisfying

\|u\|_{H^2}\leq C\bigl(\|f\|_{L^2}+|\mu|\,\|u\|_{L^2}\bigr).

This supplies the order-two elliptic step in Evans's wave regularity argument, for a full operator that need not be symmetric.

As in the order-two case, shift the equation and correct the load by the pivot-mass term. The arbitrary-order elliptic bootstrap maps an H^k load to an H^{k+2} solution under the coefficient and boundary hypotheses. Uniqueness identifies this lift with the original weak solution, and boundedness of the solver gives the two-step norm estimate.

Retain the domain, uniform ellipticity, and homogeneous Dirichlet hypotheses of the order-two lift. At order k, assume principal coefficients in W^{k+1,\infty} with global C^{k+1} representatives, lower-order coefficients in W^{k,\infty}, and an operational boundary atlas whose charts are C^{k+2} and whose inverse charts are C^{k+1}. The shifted solver is then bounded from H^k to H^{k+2}. An unshifted weak solution with an already identified H^k representative receives an H^{k+2} lift, with a bound in terms of the H^k forcing and solution norms.

Test the Galerkin identity relating each trajectory to its time derivative against smooth compactly supported time functions. Weak convergence passes that distributional identity to the paired limits, identifying the latter as successive weak derivatives of one function. Then differentiate u_{tt}=\ell-Bu: autonomy gives u_{ttt}=\partial_t\ell-Bu_t in L^2(V^*). The almost-everywhere norm-bound sets are closed and convex in L^2, so their weak closedness preserves the uniform essential bounds.

For an autonomous operator, suppose the original limit is a weak wave, the forcing has a weak time derivative, and the original and differentiated Galerkin families have common weak limits with their exact derivative links. The theorem identifies u_t, u_{tt}, and a third weak time derivative. Uniform essential bounds on the differentiated families pass to the limit.

The compatibility data initialize all differentiated Galerkin systems. The finite common weak-wave chain supplies the time derivatives, and the assumed elliptic lift raises spatial order two derivatives at a time. Induction assembles the resulting representatives into one essentially bounded Sobolev time jet.

Under the explicit compatibility, stable-density, coercivity, Ritz, and elliptic-lifting hypotheses, and assuming the spatial operator is symmetric, there exists a weak wave with the prescribed initial data and an essentially bounded Sobolev time jet of order m+1 whose head agrees almost everywhere with the displacement and whose first time derivative is the velocity. For a nonsymmetric operator, the corresponding steps are the nonsymmetric Galerkin chain and the higher-order lift.

For almost every time, rewrite the wave equation as the elliptic problem Bu(t)=f(t)-u_{tt}(t). The global elliptic regularity solver supplies an H^2 representative of that spatial slice, and uniqueness identifies it with u(t). Measurability of the bounded solver assembles these slices into a Bochner representative, while the operator norm and the two essential L^2 bounds give the essential-supremum estimate.

Let n>0 and let the domain carry the operational C2BoundaryAtlas. Assume uniformly elliptic W^{1,\infty} principal coefficients with global C^1 representatives. For a time-L^2 trajectory in H^1_0(\Omega) satisfying the weak wave equation with spatial L^2 forcing and acceleration, essential bounds on those two spatial norms give an essentially bounded H^2 lift. The elliptic solver's operator norm gives the quantitative estimate.

The compatible strip solutions define one field for all forward times. Near any positive time, choose a fixed larger horizon. Compatibility makes the field agree on that neighborhood with the C^2 second insertion for this horizon. Near time zero, use the signed-time extension from the unit strip. These local representations prove global C^2 regularity; the nonlinear PDE is asserted for nonnegative time.

The Duhamel field has zero initial displacement and velocity, so subtracting it from H retains both assigned initial values. Continuity of u and u_t then gives the two joint traces. On every finite forward strip the field agrees with the bounded continuous fixed point, giving the stated horizon-dependent bound.

Let f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be C^1 and globally Lipschitz, and let g\in C^2(\mathbb R) and h\in C^1(\mathbb R) have bounded ranges. There is a field u\in C^2(\mathbb R^2) such that

u_{tt}-u_{xx}+f(u)=0\quad(t\ge0),\qquad u(0,x)=g(x),\qquad u_t(0,x)=h(x).

Both prescribed values are joint spacetime traces:

\lim_{(s,y)\to(0,x)}u(s,y)=g(x),\qquad \lim_{(s,y)\to(0,x)}u_t(s,y)=h(x).

For every finite T\ge0, the field is bounded on [0,T]\times\mathbb R; the bound may depend on T. No integrability, smallness, vanishing condition on f(0), or bound on the derivatives of g,h is assumed.

Write \Phi_T(w)=H-K(f\circ w). Its Lipschitz constant is at most LT^2/2, which need not be less than one. Repeated time integration gives the stronger estimate

\|\Phi_T^m(w)-\Phi_T^m(v)\|_\infty \le \frac{(LT^2)^m}{m!}\,\|w-v\|_\infty.

For each fixed T, the coefficient tends to zero as m\to\infty. Some iterate therefore contracts, giving a unique fixed point of \Phi_T on that whole strip. There is no small-time restriction on T. The value at time t uses source values only between 0 and t, so restriction to a shorter strip still solves its integral equation. Uniqueness identifies the restricted solution.

For bounded continuous g,h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R, a globally L-Lipschitz f, and every finite T\ge0, there is a unique bounded continuous solution u_T of u_T=H-K(f\circ u_T) on [0,T]\times\mathbb R. If 0\le S\le T, restricting u_T to [0,S]\times\mathbb R gives u_S.

For the quadratic auxiliary potential z\mapsto z^2/2, coercivity bounds the sum of the three squared difference terms by twice the augmented energy at time t. Compose this estimate with exponential stability of that energy between a and t.
The exponential estimate controls the integral of the squared velocity difference, spatial-gradient difference, and field difference by 2E_{u-v}(a)\exp((1+K)|t-a|).

Baire category supplies a time interval with common compact displacement support. Since V' is locally Lipschitz, finite propagation transports that support across each finite forward slab. The local energy balance can then be integrated on one fixed compact spatial region. A smooth extension across the initial face identifies the initial energy with the right differential; the answer is independent of the extension.

Let n>0, V\in C^2(\mathbb R), and V(0)=0. Suppose u is C^2 on the closed forward half-space, satisfies u_{tt}-\Delta u+V'(u)=0 at positive times, and u(t,\cdot) has compact support for every t\ge0. Then

E_+(t)=E_+(0)\qquad(t\ge0).

No common spatial support, sign condition on V, or assumption about negative-time values is required.

Let w=u-v and consider the quadratic cone energy

E(t)=\frac12\int_{B(c,T-t)}\bigl(w_t^2+|D_xw|^2+w^2\bigr)\,dx,

the semilinear cone energy of w for the potential z^2/2. By the shrinking-ball transport theorem its derivative is the lateral cone flux plus the volume term \int w_t\,(w_{tt}-\Delta w+w)\,dx. Cauchy–Schwarz makes the lateral flux nonpositive, and subtracting the two equations gives w_{tt}-\Delta w=-(f(u)-f(v)), so the Lipschitz bound controls the volume term by (1+K)E(t). Grönwall's inequality yields E(t)\le E(a)e^{(1+K)(t-a)}, and equal Cauchy data give E(a)=0. Hence the classical cone energy of w vanishes on [a,T), which forces w=0 throughout the closed cone by the vanishing argument of the linear theory. The open-cone version applies the closed-cone statement to a slightly smaller cone through each interior point.

Let n\ge1, let f be globally K-Lipschitz, and let u,v\in C^2(\mathbb R^{n+1}). Fix a center c\in\mathbb R^n and times a,T, and suppose both fields satisfy

w_{tt}-\Delta w+f(w)=0\quad\text{for } a\le t<T,\ |x-c|<T-t,

that is, inside the open backward cone with vertex (T,c). If u(a,\cdot)=v(a,\cdot) and u_t(a,\cdot)=v_t(a,\cdot) on the closed base ball \overline B(c,T-a), then

u(t,x)=v(t,x)\quad\text{whenever } a\le t\le T,\ |x-c|\le T-t .

With data agreeing only on the open base ball B(c,T-a), the conclusion holds on the open cone a\le t<T, |x-c|<T-t. No sign condition on f is needed, and the only regularity hypothesis is that both fields are globally C^2; this localizes the global uniqueness theorem above.

In one dimension, characteristic transport bounds the first derivatives locally uniformly in time. Separate compact slices make the endpoint flux vanish at each time, and dominated convergence removes the endpoints of a finite rectangular energy balance. Local constancy then gives conservation on the connected forward time interval.

In two dimensions, the equation supplies uniform smallness of the potential at spatial infinity on each finite slab. Integrating the energy and momentum balances leaves an annular stress term. The annulus area grows quadratically in its radius, while the cutoff's second derivatives decay quadratically. Their factors cancel, so the small potential tail makes the remaining term vanish.

Let V\in C^1(\mathbb R) and V(0)=0. Suppose u_{tt}-\Delta u+V'(u)=0 at positive times and u(t,\cdot) has compact support for each t\ge0. If n=1 and u is C^3 on the closed forward half-space, or n=2 and u is C^4 there, then

E_+(t)=E_+(0)\qquad(t\ge0).

There is no sign or growth condition on V.

Subtract the equations. Lipschitz continuity bounds the nonlinear residual in the difference-energy identity and gives |E'(t)|\leq(1+K)E(t). A two-sided Grönwall argument yields the estimate for arbitrary time order.

If f is globally K-Lipschitz and u,v solve w_{tt}-\Delta w+f(w)=0, assume both fields are globally C^2, every augmented difference-energy slice is integrable, and its time derivative has an integrable dominator valid almost everywhere in space throughout a common time neighborhood of each time. Assume also that each fixed-time difference-energy flux component has compact support. Then the augmented difference energy satisfies

E_{u-v}(t)\leq E_{u-v}(a) \exp\bigl((1+K)|t-a|\bigr).

Here E_{u-v} includes the auxiliary coercive term \frac12|u-v|^2, which is unrelated to any primitive of f.

The proof is the energy argument for finite propagation (Evans, 2010, p. 661).

Monotonicity of cone energy. Define e(t)=\int_{B(c,T-t)}(\frac12 u_t^2+\frac12|\nabla u|^2+V(u))\,dx on the shrinking ball B(c,T-t). By the transport theorem (proved above), e'(t) equals the lateral cone flux. The flux integrand is u_t\nabla u\cdot\nu-(\frac12 u_t^2+\frac12|\nabla u|^2+V(u)). By Cauchy–Schwarz,

u_t\nabla u\cdot\nu \leq |u_t||\nabla u| \leq \frac12 u_t^2+\frac12|\nabla u|^2.

Since V(u)\geq 0 (with V(0)=0), the full integrand is nonpositive. Therefore e'(t)\leq 0.

Zero initial energy. The zero data on the base ball give e(t_0)=0 (using V(0)=0 for the potential term). Combined with monotonicity, e(t)=0 for all t\in[t_0,T).

Vanishing of the solution. Zero kinetic-gradient energy forces u_t=0 and \nabla u=0 almost everywhere in each shrinking ball. The connected-component argument (integrating zero velocity along vertical segments from the initial surface) gives u\equiv 0 in the open cone. With closed-base data, continuity extends the conclusion to the closed cone boundary. The formal proof takes a more general route: it adds a multiple of u^2 to the cone energy, which allows any V with V(z)\ge -Cz^2 near zero, and applies Grönwall; for V\ge0 the bound holds with C=0.

In positive spatial dimension, suppose V is C^1, nonnegative, and V(0)=0. If a globally C^2 classical solution of u_{tt}-\Delta u+V'(u)=0 has zero displacement and velocity on the base ball, then it vanishes in the corresponding open backward cone. This is Evans's theorem. For the closed-cone theorem, require the data to vanish on the closed base ball. The conclusion then includes the lateral boundary and vertex.

Nonnegativity of V makes every term of the energy density nonnegative. Each individual integral is therefore bounded by their sum. Conservation replaces that sum at time t by E(t_0), giving the reference-time bounds.

If in addition V\ge0, then the total energy and each of its normalized kinetic, spatial-gradient, and potential contributions are nonnegative, and each contribution is bounded by E(t). Under the conservation hypotheses, the same quantities at any later time are bounded by the initial energy E(t_0).

We follow Evans (2010, pp. 659–660).

Differentiation under the integral. The local domination hypothesis justifies applying the Leibniz rule to E(t)=\int e(x,t)\,dx where e=\frac12(u_t^2+|\nabla u|^2)+V(u). This gives E'(t)=\int\partial_t e(x,t)\,dx.

Local balance to flux divergence. The local energy identity (proved above) shows that \partial_t e=\nabla\cdot(u_t\nabla u) whenever the semilinear wave equation holds. The chain-rule derivative of V(u) is V'(u)u_t, and this cancels with the corresponding term in u_t(u_{tt}-\Delta u+V'(u))=0.

Integration by parts. The spatial integral of \nabla\cdot(u_t\nabla u) equals the boundary flux by Gauss's theorem. Compact support of each u_tu_{x_i} makes this boundary flux vanish. Therefore E'(t)=0.

The conservation identity E(t)=E(t_0) then follows from the one-dimensional mean-value theorem: a differentiable function with zero derivative on an interval is constant.

Let V be C^1 and u be a globally C^2 solution of u_{tt}-\Delta u+V'(u)=0. Assume every energy slice is integrable, the time derivative of the density admits an integrable local dominator near every time, and each fixed-time spatial flux component u_tu_{x_i} has compact support. Then

E'(t)=0,\qquad E(t)=E(t_0)

for all real t,t_0. No sign condition on V is required for conservation. The domination hypothesis justifies differentiation under the spatial integral, while compact support makes every integrated flux derivative vanish.

At time t, the total semilinear-wave energy is

E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n} \left(\frac12|u_t|^2+\frac12|D_xu|^2+V(u)\right)(x,t)\,dx.

The Bochner integral of a nonintegrable density is zero. Each conservation theorem must therefore assume or derive integrability before interpreting this expression as physical energy.
The classical kinetic-gradient identity gives u_t(u_{tt}-\Delta u). The chain rule differentiates the potential energy as V'(u)u_t.

For a C^1 potential and a C^2 field, the local energy-balance defect equals

u_t\bigl(u_{tt}-\Delta u+V'(u)\bigr).

Consequently every classical semilinear wave has zero local energy defect.

Start with the mild evolution in H^5(\mathbb R^3)\times H^4(\mathbb R^3). Smooth composition is locally Lipschitz there. Sobolev embedding recovers a classical field, and persistence at higher orders makes it smooth for smooth compact data. Classical uniqueness identifies competing solutions with this trajectory, so its maximal lifetime is also maximal among the stated classical competitors.

If displacement were bounded on a terminal strip, the tame composition estimate would bound the source by an affine function of the Sobolev state norm on that strip. Grönwall would then bound the full state and allow continuation past T_*, contradicting maximality.

Let f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R) with f(0)=0, and let g,h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3). There are a lifespan T_*\in(0,\infty] and a field smooth on [0,T_*)\times\mathbb R^3 satisfying

u_{tt}-\Delta u+f(u)=0\quad(0<t<T_*),\qquad u(0,x)=g(x),\qquad \partial_t^+u(0,x)=h(x).

Every competing solution with these data that is C^2 for 0<t<T and C^1 up to t=0 has T\le T_*. If T_*<\infty, then

\forall a<T_*\;\forall B\in\mathbb R\;\exists t\in[\max(0,a),T_*)\; \exists x\in\mathbb R^3,\qquad |u(t,x)|>B.

Thus the displacement is unbounded on every terminal time strip.

Energy conservation keeps the negative sign in either time direction. The positive virial forcing makes the quadratic momentum strictly positive after a forward shift and strictly negative after a backward shift when its value at t_0 does not already have the required sign. The corresponding Riccati estimate then supplies a finite endpoint, contradicting global continuation in that direction.

For a globally C^2 spacetime field, under the same equation, compact-support, integrability and differentiation hypotheses on the relevant time half-line, negative energy implies both

\neg\bigl(\text{a solution exists for every }t\geq t_0\bigr), \qquad \neg\bigl(\text{a solution exists for every }t\leq t_0\bigr).

Both theorems derive E(t)=E(t_0)<0 from these hypotheses before applying the concavity obstruction in the forward and backward time directions.

Argue by contradiction. If both the mass coefficient and the nonlinear coupling were nonnegative, every term in the odd-power potential would be nonnegative. The spatial energy would then be nonnegative, contradicting the assumed negative energy.

For the odd-power potential V(z)=\frac{m^2}{2}z^2+\frac{\beta}{2k+2}z^{2k+2}, if m^2\geq0 and

E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n} \left(\frac12|u_t|^2+\frac12|\nabla u|^2+V(u)\right)\,dx<0,

then \beta<0.

Keep I(t)=\frac12\int u^2\,dx and P(t)=I'(t)=\int uu_t\,dx. The preceding virial estimate with \Lambda=2k+2 gives I''(t)\ge (k+2)\int|u_t|^2\,dx+k\int|\nabla u|^2\,dx+2(k+1)|E_0|, where E_0=E(t_0)=E(t)<0. Energy conservation follows from the stated integrability, domination and flux hypotheses.

The virial and Cauchy–Schwarz estimates imply that the positive ratio y=P/I satisfies y'\geq (k/2)y^2. Hence (1/y)'\leq-k/2. Integrating from t_0 and using y(t_0)>0 forces

t-t_0 < \frac{2}{k\,y(t_0)} = \frac{2I(t_0)}{kP(t_0)}.

The half-open endpoint theorem converts this strict interior inequality into the displayed non-strict upper bound for T.

Let I(t) be the spatial quadratic mass and P(t)=I'(t) its quadratic momentum. For a nonnegative mass coefficient m^2, k>0, and t_0<T, negative initial energy and P(t_0)>0 force the half-open classical lifespan [t_0,T) to satisfy

T\leq t_0+ \left(\frac{k}{2}\frac{P(t_0)}{I(t_0)}\right)^{-1}.

The hypotheses include the compact support and dominated differentiation needed for the mass, momentum, and energy identities.

Differentiating under the integral gives I'=P and P'=\int u_t^2+u\,u_{tt}\,dx. Using the equation, integrating by parts on the compactly supported slice, and applying the growth condition,

P'\ \ge\ \int u_t^2\,dx-\int|D_xu|^2\,dx-\Lambda\int V(u)\,dx \ =\ \Bigl(1+\frac\Lambda2\Bigr)\int u_t^2\,dx +\Bigl(\frac\Lambda2-1\Bigr)\int|D_xu|^2\,dx-\Lambda E(t_0),

so P'\ge(1+\Lambda/2)\int u_t^2\,dx because E(t_0)<0 and \Lambda>2. Negative conserved energy with V(0)=0 also forces I>0 on the slab. Cauchy–Schwarz, P^2\le2I\int u_t^2\,dx, then gives the concavity inequality I\,P'\ge\frac{\Lambda+2}{4}P^2, that is, (P/I)'\ge\frac{\Lambda-2}{4}(P/I)^2. The scalar Riccati comparison shows that the positive ratio P/I cannot remain finite beyond the displayed horizon, so a solution on a closed slab ends strictly before it, and a half-open lifespan ends no later than it.

Let V\in C^1(\mathbb R) with V(0)=0 satisfy the growth condition

z\,V'(z)\le\Lambda\,V(z)\quad\text{for all }z,\qquad \Lambda>2,

and let I(t)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^n}u^2\,dx and P(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u\,u_t\,dx be the spatial quadratic mass and momentum. Suppose that on the half-open slab [t_0,T), t_0<T, the field u is C^2 on a time neighborhood of every slice, solves u_{tt}-\Delta u+V'(u)=0, has compactly supported slices, admits the integrable local dominators needed to differentiate I and P under the integral, and has conserved energy E(t)=E(t_0). If

E(t_0)<0\qquad\text{and}\qquad P(t_0)>0,

then

T\le t_0+\left(\frac{\Lambda-2}{4}\,\frac{P(t_0)}{I(t_0)}\right)^{-1}.

If the same hypotheses hold on the closed slab [t_0,T] with t_0\le T, the inequality is strict. Energy conservation enters as a hypothesis; the odd-power specialization below derives it from the conservation theorem.

The potential V of the nonlinearity f satisfies \operatorname{deriv}V=f. Thus the semilinear wave operator is

u_{tt}-\Delta u+V'(u).

The corresponding energy density is \frac12(u_t^2+|D_xu|^2)+V(u).

Adding a suitable multiple of u^2 to the cone energy makes it nonnegative on the attained value range. The potential's local lower bound controls this modification near zero; continuity controls it away from zero. Grönwall then propagates zero Cauchy data across backward cones, in both time directions. Baire category gives a time near which all slices vanish outside one ball, so the Cauchy data there have common compact support, and finite propagation carries it across each finite slab. The resulting common support allows the ordinary energy balance to be integrated.

Let n>0, V\in C^1(\mathbb R), and V(0)=0. Assume that for some real C, V(z)\ge-Cz^2 throughout a neighborhood of zero. If u is C^2 on the closed forward half-space, solves u_{tt}-\Delta u+V'(u)=0 at positive times, and has compact displacement support separately at each t\ge0, then

E_+(t)=E_+(0)\qquad(t\ge0).

Reynolds transport differentiates the energy on the shrinking ball and produces the swept-boundary term. Integrating the local balance converts the spatial divergence into a sphere flux by Gauss's theorem. On a solution the volume residual vanishes, and separating the potential gives the displayed lateral flux.

For n>0, a C^1 potential, a globally C^2 field, and t<T, the derivative of the total energy on the shrinking ball B(c,T-t) is the sum of its local volume defect and lateral cone flux. If the equation holds throughout that ball, the volume defect vanishes and only the lateral flux

u_tD_xu\cdot\nu- \left(\frac12(u_t^2+|D_xu|^2)+V(u)\right)

remains. Its sphere integral equals the classical lateral flux minus the potential energy swept out by the shrinking boundary. Both identities follow from the Reynolds transport and Gauss formulas on balls.

Equal Cauchy data make the augmented difference energy zero at the reference time. Exponential stability keeps it zero on every time slice, and coercivity then forces the pointwise field difference to vanish.

Let u and v solve w_{tt}-\Delta w+f(w)=0 for the same globally Lipschitz f. If

u(t_0,\cdot)=v(t_0,\cdot),\qquad u_t(t_0,\cdot)=v_t(t_0,\cdot),

then u(t,x)=v(t,x) everywhere, under the analytic integrability and flux hypotheses used by the energy argument.

The coercive form \int(uw+\nabla u\cdot\nabla w) first constructs the linear wave evolution for 1-\Delta through Lax–Milgram and Hille–Yosida. The Lipschitz source u-f(u) cancels the added mass. Iterated Picard estimates construct its Duhamel trajectory for all forward times. Dense-generator observations give the integrated equations for arbitrary energy data. Conversely, linear weak uniqueness identifies every energy PDE solution with that mild trajectory, so fixed-point uniqueness applies to the PDE class itself. Time integration by parts gives the displayed scalar identity and its initial velocity term.

Let f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be globally Lipschitz with f(0)=0. For every dimension and every (u_0,v_0)\in H^1(\mathbb R^n)\times L^2(\mathbb R^n), there is a continuous forward energy trajectory (u,v) attaining both data strongly and satisfying

u(t)-u_0=\int_0^t v(s)\,ds,\qquad v(t)-v_0=\int_0^t\bigl(\Delta u(s)-f(u(s))\bigr)\,ds

for every t\ge0, in L^2 and the H^1 dual respectively. It is unique among forward energy-continuous trajectories satisfying these integrated PDE equations with the same data.

On every interval [0,b] with b>0, the trajectory has the Bochner weak-wave formulation. Take any spatial H^1 test w and time test \tau with an everywhere-defined derivative on [0,b], \tau,\tau'\in L^2(0,b), and \tau(b)=0. Its scalar weak equation is

-\int_0^b (v,w)_{L^2}\tau'\,dt +\int_0^b\bigl((\nabla u,\nabla w)_{L^2}+(f(u),w)_{L^2}\bigr)\tau\,dt =(v_0,w)_{L^2}\tau(0).

The gradient pairings use the actual Sobolev weak derivatives. No smallness, compact support, or classical regularity of the data is assumed.

Combine the exact energy derivative with the production bound to obtain E'(t)\leq\varepsilon+(1+C)E(t). The initial bound E(a)\leq\delta and continuity of E put this in Mathlib's right-derivative Grönwall form, whose explicit solution is the stated bound.

On a closed time interval, assume continuous total energy, the exact-balance and production-bound hypotheses at each earlier time, F(t)\leq\varepsilon, and the initial energy is at most \delta. Mathlib's Grönwall inequality then gives

E(t)\leq\operatorname{gronwallBound} (\delta,1+C,\varepsilon,t-a).

The dominated-differentiation hypothesis moves the time derivative through the spatial integral. Integrate the local balance over space; each compactly supported flux divergence has zero integral, leaving only forcing and the variable-coefficient production term.

Under explicit dominated-differentiation hypotheses, pointwise differentiability and the system equation, and compactly supported C^1 spatial flux slices, the spatial energy is differentiable and

E'(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\left( \langle f,u\rangle+\frac12\sum_j \langle(\partial_jB_j)u,u\rangle\right)\,dx.

A system is hyperbolic at (t,x) when, for every real covector \xi, the symbol has a real eigenbasis:

B(t,x;\xi)r_k=\lambda_k r_k,\qquad \lambda_k\in\mathbb R,\qquad \operatorname{span}\{r_1,\ldots,r_m\}=\mathbb R^m.

It is hyperbolic when this holds throughout the PDE domain. Strict hyperbolicity additionally requires \lambda_i\ne\lambda_j for i\ne j whenever \xi\ne0.

Cauchy–Schwarz and Young's inequality bound \langle f,u\rangle by one half of the forcing and solution squares. Operator norm bounds control each coefficient-derivative term by its norm times |u|^2. Summing the pointwise inequalities and integrating gives the claim.

If C almost everywhere bounds \sum_j\lVert\partial_jB_j\rVert, the integrated production satisfies

\int_{\mathbb R^n}\mathrm{production}\,dx \leq F(t)+(1+C)E(t),

where F(t)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^n}|f(t,x)|^2\,dx. The production, the forcing energy, and the solution energy are assumed integrable on the slice.

Pair the system equation with u. Symmetry rewrites \langle B_j u_{x_j},u\rangle as one half of the derivative of \langle B_ju,u\rangle, minus the derivative-of-coefficient correction. The time term is one half of \partial_t|u|^2, giving the local balance.

This is the pointwise form of the integration-by-parts energy calculation on Evans pp. 426-427. At a point where the coefficients are symmetric, the field and coefficient maps are differentiable, and the system equation holds, the identity keeps the variable-coefficient correction \frac12\sum_j\langle(\partial_jB_j)u,u\rangle. The domain-wide form supplies pointwise symmetry from a symmetric system.
Apply the pointwise substitution theorem at every profile parameter to obtain the homogeneous PDE. Evaluating the phase at t=0 removes the -\omega t term and gives the claimed initial trace.
If the vector profile is differentiable and its eigenvalue condition holds for every profile parameter, the plane wave solves the initial-value problem and has trace \psi(\langle\xi,x\rangle) at t=0.

The chain rule gives u_t=-\omega\psi' and u_{x_j}=\xi_j\psi'. Substitution into the constant-coefficient operator produces (B(\xi)-\omega I)\psi', whose vanishing is exactly the displayed eigenvalue relation.

For a homogeneous constant-coefficient system, the vector-profile wave

u(t,x)=\psi(-\omega t+\langle\xi,x\rangle)

solves the equation at a differentiability point exactly when B(\xi)\psi'=\omega\psi' there.

For a system

u_t+\sum_{j=1}^n B_j(x,t)u_{x_j}=f(x,t),

the principal symbol at the covector \xi is B(x,t;\xi)=\sum_j\xi_jB_j(x,t).

By linearity, the eigenvalue hypothesis gives the eigenvalue condition for the vector profile at every phase, whatever the value of \phi', so the vector-profile initial-value theorem gives the PDE and the trace.

If B(\xi)v=\omega v and \phi is differentiable, then

u(t,x)=\phi\bigl(-\omega t+\langle\xi,x\rangle\bigr)v

solves the homogeneous constant-coefficient initial-value problem and has the exact trace u(0,x)=\phi(\langle\xi,x\rangle)v.
For \psi(s)=\phi(s)v, differentiation gives \psi'(s)=\phi'(s)v. The vector-profile condition factors as \phi'(s)(B(\xi)v-\omega v)=0, so it holds precisely when either factor vanishes.
For \psi(s)=\phi(s)v the equation holds exactly when \phi'=0 at the point or the polarization satisfies B(\xi)v=\omega v. The latter relation gives a solution for every differentiable scalar profile.

For nonzero covectors, discard the pairwise-distinctness condition from the strict hyperbolicity data and retain its real eigenbasis. At the zero covector the symbol is the zero operator, for which the standard basis is an eigenbasis with eigenvalue zero.

Pointwise and domain-wide strict hyperbolicity imply the corresponding hyperbolicity predicates:

\operatorname{StrictHyp}(B)\Longrightarrow\operatorname{Hyp}(B).

Real linear combinations of self-adjoint coefficient operators are self-adjoint, so every principal symbol is self-adjoint. The finite-dimensional spectral theorem supplies an orthonormal basis of real eigenvectors, exactly the pointwise hyperbolicity condition.

If B_j(t,x)^*=B_j(t,x) for every spatial direction, then

B(t,x;\xi)^* =\left(\sum_j\xi_jB_j(t,x)\right)^* =\sum_j\xi_jB_j(t,x) =B(t,x;\xi).

Every symmetric first-order system is therefore hyperbolic.
A symmetric system has a self-adjoint coefficient operator B_j(x,t) in every spatial direction at every point of its PDE domain.

The affine characteristic has derivative (1,b). The chain rule evaluates Du on this direction, which is the transport operator by its coordinate identity. Substituting s=0 and s=t gives the two endpoints.

Along \gamma_{t,x}(s)=(s,x+(s-t)b), a differentiable profile obeys

\frac d{ds}u(\gamma_{t,x}(s)) =\partial_tu(\gamma_{t,x}(s)) +b\cdot\nabla_xu(\gamma_{t,x}(s)) =(L_bu)(\gamma_{t,x}(s)).

The endpoint identities \gamma_{t,x}(0)=(0,x-tb) and \gamma_{t,x}(t)=(t,x) are part of the statement.
The proof differentiates the affine foot map, applies the chain rule to g(x-tb), and cancels the time derivative against the spatial advection.
For differentiable initial data, translation along x-tb solves the homogeneous specialization of Definition 7.3, including its initial trace.
The characteristic through (t,x) is s\mapsto(s,x+(s-t)b). It joins the initial foot (0,x-tb) to (t,x) and has constant spacetime velocity (1,b).

First write the formula in the adapted coordinates (t,\xi)=(t,x-tb): g(\xi)+\int_0^t f(s,\xi+sb)\,ds. Since f is C^1, the integrand and its derivative with respect to \xi are continuous. On a compact neighborhood of the parameter and time segment, this derivative is uniformly bounded, so the parametric integral rule proves spacetime differentiability. Adding differentiable g and composing with the linear coordinate map preserves it. Restricted to a characteristic, the formula has derivative equal to the source by the fundamental theorem of calculus. The characteristic chain rule then identifies that derivative with the transport operator, and setting t=0 gives the assigned initial value.

For differentiable g and a C^1 source, the explicit formula is differentiable, has initial trace g, and satisfies the forced transport equation. When the source is only continuous, a variant takes differentiability of the formula as a hypothesis and reaches the same conclusion.
The source-parametric initial-value problem consists of u_t+b\cdot\nabla_xu=f on t>0 and u(0,x)=g(x). Homogeneous transport is the specialization f=0.

Decompose the spacetime direction (1,b) into its time basis vector and spatial coordinate directions. Linearity of the Fréchet derivative gives the time partial plus the weighted spatial partials; in the scalar case the finite sum is the Euclidean inner product with the gradient.

The abstract directional derivative equals the familiar coordinate operator \partial_t u + \sum_{i=1}^n b_i\,\partial_{x_i}u. The first identity is vector-valued; the second identifies the scalar spatial sum with b\cdot\nabla_xu.

For a constant spatial velocity b, the transport operator is the Fréchet derivative in spacetime direction (1,b). Its codomain is an arbitrary real normed space, so the same declaration applies to scalar unknowns and systems.

Unfold the initial-value predicate. Its two fields are precisely the positive-time residual equation and the assigned initial value, so projection proves one direction and pairing the two clauses constructs the converse.
The initial-value problem is equivalent to two clauses: the transport residual on positive time and the assigned value on t=0.

Ambient differentiability of u along the closed characteristic segment gives continuity of its pullback on [0,t]. On (0,t), the chain rule and the residual equation give derivative f(\gamma_{t,x}(s)). Its interval integrability permits the fundamental theorem of calculus; the endpoint identities and assigned initial value then give the formula.

Let u satisfy the transport residual and initial-value clauses, and let t\geq0. Assume u is Fréchet differentiable in spacetime at \gamma_{t,x}(s) for every s\in[0,t], including the endpoints, and s\mapsto f(\gamma_{t,x}(s)) is interval integrable on [0,t]. Then u(t,x)=g(x-tb)+\int_0^t f(s,x+(s-t)b)\,ds. The continuous-source variant obtains these hypotheses from global Fréchet differentiability of u and continuity of f.

The explicit spacetime function is

\mathcal S_{b,f,g}(t,x) =g(x-tb)+\int_0^t f\bigl(s,x+(s-t)b\bigr)\,ds.

Pulling \mathcal S_{b,f,g} back to a characteristic gives the initial value plus the accumulated source, while the coordinate theorem separates the footpoint x-tb from time.

At positive-time points, differentiability of the fields justifies applying the Fréchet derivative to their linear combination. Evaluation at the initial surface respects the same combination, giving the corresponding sources and assigned values. Subtracting equal data gives the homogeneous zero-trace problem. The zero and negation identities also hold without differentiability.

Fix b and assume u and v are Fréchet differentiable at every spacetime point with t>0. The residual is linear on positive time, and initial evaluation respects the same combination:

L_b(\alpha u+\beta v)=\alpha L_bu+\beta L_bv,\qquad (\alpha u+\beta v)(0,\cdot)=\alpha g_u+\beta g_v.

Consequently zero, addition, scalar multiplication, negation, subtraction, and arbitrary binary linear combinations preserve the corresponding source and assigned initial data. In particular, two sufficiently differentiable solutions with the same source and assigned value have a difference w=u-v satisfying L_bw=0 and w(0,\cdot)=0.

The representation theorem identifies every solution with the explicit formula determined by b, f, and g. Two solutions with the same data are therefore both equal to that formula and hence equal to each other.

Every globally differentiable solution with continuous source satisfies, for t\geq0,

u(t,x)=\mathcal S_{b,f,g}(t,x) =g(x-tb)+\int_0^t f\bigl(s,x+(s-t)b\bigr)\,ds.

Consequently, if u and v have the same b, f, and g, then u(t,x)=v(t,x) throughout the nonnegative-time domain.

The two translated displacement values are the endpoints of [x-t,x+t], and the velocity term integrates only over that interval. Agreement of both data there makes all three terms agree; vanishing data is the special case compared with zero.

At nonnegative time, d'Alembert's value at (x,t) depends only on the two initial data restricted to [x-t,x+t]. No differentiability assumptions are needed because this is a theorem about the representation formula itself.
For a point outside the enlarged interval, the entire backward characteristic interval misses the support of both initial data. Both translated endpoint terms and the integral term therefore vanish.
If both one-dimensional initial data are supported in [-R,R], then at nonnegative time t the support of d'Alembert's formula is contained in [-R-t,R+t].

For initial displacement g and velocity h, the one-dimensional d'Alembert field is

u(t,x)=\frac{g(x+t)+g(x-t)}2 +\frac12\int_{x-t}^{x+t}h(y)\,dy.

The spacetime form uses coordinate zero for t and coordinate one for x, matching the residual-and-assigned-data problem.
Differentiate the two translated copies of g and the interval integral of h, then check the wave residual, the displacement trace, and the velocity trace in turn.

For g of class C^2 and h of class C^1, d'Alembert's one-dimensional field is globally C^2, satisfies the residual and assigned Cauchy equalities in Definition 7.19, and converges jointly in spacetime to the prescribed displacement and velocity at the initial surface. Both initial limits allow approach from either time direction.

The difference w=u-v solves the homogeneous equation with zero lateral, displacement, and velocity data. The wave equation cancels the time derivative of the cylinder energy \int_\Omega(w_t^2+\lvert Dw\rvert^2), the boundary term vanishing because w=0 on the lateral boundary. The energy starts at zero, so w_t and Dw vanish, and the zero initial value gives w=0 on the closed cylinder.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open and bounded with C^1 graph boundary, and let a<b. Let u and v be C^2 up to the boundary of \Omega\times(a,b), continuous on its closure, and solve u_{tt}-\Delta u=f there with the same forcing f. If u=v on \partial\Omega\times[a,b], and u(a,\cdot)=v(a,\cdot) and u_t(a^+,\cdot)=v_t(a^+,\cdot) on \Omega, then u=v on \overline\Omega\times[a,b].

Apply finite propagation to the difference of the two waves. Linearity gives the homogeneous wave equation, and equality of the two initial traces makes the displacement and velocity of the difference vanish on the base ball.

Let n\ge1 and R>0. Let u and v be C^2 and solve the wave equation in the cone t_0\le t<t_0+R, \lVert x-x_0\rVert<R-(t-t_0). If u(t_0,\cdot)=v(t_0,\cdot) and u_t(t_0,\cdot)=v_t(t_0,\cdot) on \overline B_R(x_0), then

u(t,x)=v(t,x) \quad\text{for}\quad \ t_0\leq t\leq t_0+R,\qquad \lVert x-x_0\rVert\leq R-(t-t_0).

This is the closed-cone domain-of-dependence statement.

In dimension one, integrate the retarded d'Alembert formula. In higher dimensions, write n=2k+2 or n=2k+3; in either case m=k+2 and use the corresponding mean formula. For nonnegative time, the witness has the form

u(t,x)=\int_0^t W_s(t-s,x)\,ds,

where W_s is the corresponding homogeneous wave with displacement zero and velocity f(s,\cdot). Clipping the forcing index to \max(0,s) extends the construction to signed times. The retarded integral regularity and equation theorems give joint C^2 regularity and the forced residual. The collapsed integral and its first derivative give zero Cauchy data; continuity of the field and its time derivative gives the two joint traces.

Let n\geq1, put m=\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1, and let f:\mathbb R^{n+1}\to\mathbb R be C^m within the closed forward halfspace \{(t,x):t\geq0\}. Then there exists u\in C^2(\mathbb R^{n+1}) satisfying

u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=f\quad(t>0),\qquad u(0,x)=u_t(0,x)=0.

For every x\in\mathbb R^n, both initial traces hold jointly in space and time:

\lim_{(s,y)\to(0,x)}u(s,y)=0,\qquad \lim_{(s,y)\to(0,x)}u_t(s,y)=0.

The C^2 field is defined on all signed times. The forcing regularity assumption is only within the forward halfspace; no support or growth condition is imposed.

For a spacetime field u on \mathbb R^{n+1}, the classical wave-energy density, the spatial energy-flux components, and the local energy-balance residual are

e(u)=\frac12\bigl(u_t^2+|D_xu|^2\bigr),\qquad F_i(u)=u_t\,\partial_{x_i}u\quad(1\le i\le n),

R(u)=\partial_te(u)-\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_{x_i}F_i(u).

Here D_xu collects the spatial partial derivatives. The density is nonnegative, and the residual is the pointwise defect in the conservation law \partial_te-\operatorname{div}_x(u_tD_xu)=0.

Differentiate the fixed-sphere average twice in time and replace u_{tt} by \Delta u. The radial Laplacian identity for spherical means turns the average of \Delta u into \partial_{rr}M+(n-1)r^{-1}\partial_rM.

Let n>0, let u\in C^2(\mathbb R^{n+1}) satisfy u_{tt}-\Delta u=0, and let r>0. Then its spherical mean satisfies the Euler–Poisson–Darboux equation

\partial_{tt}M_u(t,x,r) =\partial_{rr}M_u(t,x,r) +\frac{n-1}{r}\,\partial_rM_u(t,x,r).

Apply the odd-dimensional construction to the lifted data. Independence of the extra coordinate holds before differentiation, so the extra Laplacian term vanishes. Sphere projection proves integrability of the weighted ball kernel and gives the ratio (2m+1)!!/(2m+2)!!. Equality of the profiles on the open positive-radius interval passes to their radial derivatives. Restriction of the signed-time field preserves regularity and both traces. Uniqueness follows from the energy domain-of-dependence theorem.

For n=2m+2, g\in C^{m+3}(\mathbb R^n) and h\in C^{m+2}(\mathbb R^n), set, for r>0,

Q_m[f,x](r)=\left(\frac1r\frac d{dr}\right)^m \left(\frac{r^{2m+2}}{|B_r(x)|}\int_{B_r(x)} \frac{f(y)}{\sqrt{r^2-\lVert y-x\rVert^2}}\,dy\right).

The field constructed by descent is jointly C^2 on all signed times and, for t>0, equals

u(t,x)=\frac{\partial_rQ_m[g,x](t)+Q_m[h,x](t)}{(2m+2)!!}.

It satisfies the wave equation at positive times, the assigned initial position and velocity, and both joint Cauchy traces. The statement includes m=0, hence the planar formula, without support or growth hypotheses. Every globally C^2 field with the same positive-time wave equation and assigned Cauchy data agrees with the constructed field at nonnegative times.

The wave equation kills the volume residual in Theorem 7.37. The lateral flux is nonpositive, so the nonnegative shrinking-cone energy cannot increase from its zero initial value. Vanishing energy yields vanishing time and spatial derivatives in the cone, and the initial trace fixes the remaining constant.

Let n\ge1 and R>0. Let u be C^2 and solve the wave equation in the cone t_0\le t<t_0+R, \lVert x-x_0\rVert<R-(t-t_0). If u(t_0,\cdot)=u_t(t_0,\cdot)=0 on \overline B_R(x_0), then

u(t,x)=0 \quad\text{whenever}\quad t_0\leq t\leq t_0+R,\qquad \lVert x-x_0\rVert\leq R-(t-t_0).

Thus zero Cauchy data on the base ball force vanishing throughout the corresponding closed backward cone.

For each positive start time the moving-ball identity makes the cone energy nonincreasing, and the C^1 regularity up to the initial slice makes that energy tend to zero as the start time decreases to zero. So the energy vanishes on every positive slice, u_t vanishes inside the cone, and integrating along vertical segments from the zero initial value gives u=0. Continuity extends this to the closed cone.

Let n\ge1 and T>0. Let u be C^2 on \{t>0\} and C^1 on \{t\ge0\}, and let u solve the wave equation for 0<t<T, \lVert x-x_0\rVert<T-t. If u(0,x)=0 and the right time derivative u_t(0^+,x) vanishes for \lVert x-x_0\rVert<T, then u(t,x)=0 for 0\le t\le T and \lVert x-x_0\rVert\le T-t, including the lateral boundary and the vertex.

For t>0, the three-dimensional Kirchhoff expression is defined by

u(t,x)=\frac{1}{4\pi t^2}\int_{\partial B_t(x)} \bigl(g(y)+t\,h(y)+Dg(y)\cdot(y-x)\bigr)\,dS(y),

while the two-dimensional Poisson expression integrates g(y)+t\,h(y)+Dg(y)\cdot(y-x) over B_t(x) with kernel (2\pi t\sqrt{t^2-\lVert x-y\rVert^2})^{-1}. Evans treats these constructions in §2.4.1.

The residual-and-assigned-data problem records u_{tt}-\Delta u=0 at positive times, initial displacement g, and initial velocity h. It is stated in n spatial dimensions with time in coordinate zero. Lean's derivative operations are total, so the problem by itself implies neither C^2 regularity nor convergence to the initial data.

If t>\lVert x\rVert+R, every point on the integration sphere lies strictly outside \overline B_R(0) by the reverse triangle inequality. Both data vanish there, and g vanishes on a neighborhood of each such point, so its spatial gradient is zero there as well. Every term of the Kirchhoff integrand therefore vanishes.

If R\geq0 and \operatorname{supp}g\cup\operatorname{supp}h\subseteq\overline B_R(0), then at a fixed point x the three-dimensional Kirchhoff expression obeys

u(t,x)=0\qquad\text{whenever }t>\lVert x\rVert+R.

This conclusion uses only the support geometry of the formula, with no regularity of the data. For C^3 displacement and C^2 velocity, the Kirchhoff solution theorem identifies it with a classical wave having both joint initial traces.

In three dimensions the radius times the spherical mean solves the wave equation. Differentiate the displacement potential once in time and add the velocity potential. Its signed-radius regularity justifies the second spacetime derivatives and identifies both values at zero. For the planar formula, lift the data constantly in a third coordinate and descend the Kirchhoff solution. Independence of that coordinate removes its second spatial derivative. The sphere-to-disk identity gives Poisson's kernel, and joint continuity gives the stated traces.

Let g\in C^3(\mathbb R^n) and h\in C^2(\mathbb R^n), with n=3 for Kirchhoff and n=2 for Poisson. The signed-time formula defines a jointly C^2 spacetime field, satisfies u_{tt}-\Delta u=0 for t>0, and has u(0,x)=g(x) and u_t(0,x)=h(x). Moreover,

u(t,y)\longrightarrow g(x),\qquad u_t(t,y)\longrightarrow h(x) \quad\text{as }(t,y)\longrightarrow(0,x).

These are joint traces, including approach through positive times. Neither compact support nor a growth bound on the data is required.

Differentiate the density with the product rule, \partial_te=u_tu_{tt}+\sum_iu_{x_i}\,\partial_tu_{x_i}, and each flux component, \partial_{x_i}(u_tu_{x_i})=u_{x_i}\,\partial_{x_i}u_t+u_tu_{x_ix_i}. Since u is C^2 at p, the mixed partial derivatives commute, \partial_tu_{x_i}=\partial_{x_i}u_t, so the cross terms cancel in the difference and what remains is u_t\,(u_{tt}-\sum_iu_{x_ix_i}).

If u is C^2 at a spacetime point p, then at p

\partial_te(u)-\operatorname{div}_x\bigl(u_tD_xu\bigr) =u_t\,\bigl(u_{tt}-\Delta u\bigr).

In particular a field that is C^2 at p with \Box u(p)=0 has zero local energy residual there. This is the pointwise computation behind Evans's energy proofs of uniqueness and of the domain of dependence; it involves no integration.

Differentiate the integral over the shrinking ball with Reynolds transport: the moving boundary contributes minus the energy density. By the definition of the energy-balance residual, the density derivative is that residual plus a spatial divergence. Gauss's theorem converts that divergence to the remaining lateral flux.

Let n\geq1, u\in C^2(\mathbb R^{n+1}), and fix a center x_0 and terminal time T. At every t<T, the derivative of the energy on B_{T-t}(x_0) is the integral of the local energy-balance residual over that ball plus the surface integral of u_tD_xu\cdot\nu-e.

Write the odd space dimension as n=2m+3 and set

P_m[f,x](r)= \left(\frac1r\frac d{dr}\right)^m \left(r^{2m+1}\frac1{|S^{n-1}|} \int_{S^{n-1}}f(x+r\omega)\,dS(\omega)\right).

For positive time, Evans's representation is

\mathcal E_m[g,h](x,t) =\frac{\partial_rP_m[g,x](t)+P_m[h,x](t)}{(2m+1)!!}.

The Lean radial transform is a total function, including at r=0.

Euler–Poisson–Darboux and the radial intertwining identity reduce the transformed spherical profile to a one-dimensional wave. Joint regularity justifies commuting the radial transform with time differentiation and controls its specified values and derivatives at the center. The assigned Cauchy data identify the transformed initial profiles, one-dimensional uniqueness gives d'Alembert's solution, and the center derivative recovers u(t,x) with normalization (2m+1)!!.

Let n=2m+3, fix x\in\mathbb R^n, and let u\in C^2(\mathbb R^{n+1}) solve the wave Cauchy problem with displacement g and velocity h. For each positive time, assume its spherical mean is C^{m+2} on the whole signed-radius line. Assume also P_m[g,x]\in C^2(\mathbb R) and P_m[h,x]\in C^1(\mathbb R). For every 0\leq k\leq m, require the specified totalized function

(q,r)\longmapsto \left(\frac1r\frac d{dr}\right)^k \left(r^{2m+1}M_u(q,x,r)\right)

to be C^3 on all of \mathbb R^2, including the axis r=0. Then for every t>0,

u(t,x)=\mathcal E_m[g,h](x,t).

These hypotheses are the removable-singularity input for the radial reduction; the reduced wave equation and the representation identity are proved from them. When g\in C^{m+3} and h\in C^{m+2}, the solution theorem removes them: every C^2 solution then equals \mathcal E_m[g,h].

Integral formulas for the weighted radial derivatives extend the potential smoothly across zero. Their finite-order bounds give a C^3 displacement potential and a C^2 velocity potential. The radial identity proves the wave equation; taking one time derivative of the displacement potential produces the formula with normalization (2m+1)!!. Its values and first time derivative at zero identify the traces. The energy domain-of-dependence theorem gives uniqueness among globally C^2 fields with the same Cauchy data.

For n=2m+3, g\in C^{m+3}(\mathbb R^n) and h\in C^{m+2}(\mathbb R^n), the constructed field is jointly C^2 on all signed times and equals \mathcal E_m[g,h] at positive times. It solves u_{tt}-\Delta u=0 there, has the assigned displacement and velocity at zero, and both u and u_t converge jointly to those data at every point of the initial surface. There are no support or growth assumptions. Every globally C^2 field satisfying the same positive-time wave equation and assigned Cauchy data agrees with this field at all nonnegative times, and so equals \mathcal E_m[g,h] at positive times with no hypothesis on its spherical means.

On \mathbb R^{n+1} with time in coordinate zero, the wave operator is the coordinate expression

\Box u=\partial_0\partial_0u-\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_i\partial_iu =u_{tt}-\Delta u,

built from total partial derivatives, so classical use requires C^2 hypotheses that are stated separately. The homogeneous and nonhomogeneous wave equations on a domain U are the single-equation problems \Box u=0 and \Box u=f on U with no side conditions, and each bundled problem is equivalent to the pointwise residual identity on U.
For t>0, substitute |t|=t and discard the zero-radius branch. The defining disk integral and its coefficient then have exactly the stated positive-time form.
At positive time, the total two-dimensional definition reduces to Evans's ordinary disk-integral formula with coefficient 1/(2\pi t).

For a spacetime field u in n spatial dimensions, its signed-radius spherical mean about x is

M_u(t,x,r)=\frac1{|S^{n-1}|} \int_{S^{n-1}}u(t,x+r\omega)\,dS(\omega).

The signed-radius convention makes M_u even in r; in positive dimension its value at r=0 is u(t,x).

Under the local C^2 hypotheses the first partial derivatives of the sum are differentiable, so the sum rule for partial derivatives applies twice and gives the second-order identity coordinate by coordinate. The total Fréchet derivative commutes with scalar multiplication without any hypothesis. The problem-level statements combine these operator identities with the residual identities of the two witnesses.

The wave operator is linear. If u and v are C^2 at a point, then at that point

\Box(u+v)=\Box u+\Box v,\qquad \Box(u-v)=\Box u-\Box v,

and \Box(cu)=c\,\Box u holds for every constant c with no regularity hypothesis. Consequently, if u,v\in C^2(\mathbb R^{n+1}) satisfy \Box u=f and \Box v=g on U, then for all constants c_1,c_2

\Box(c_1u+c_2v)=c_1f+c_2g\quad\text{on }U,

two witnesses with the same source have a difference solving the homogeneous equation on U, and homogeneous residual witnesses are closed under linear combinations. The conclusions are pointwise residual identities.

The weak equation is tested against a backward time primitive. Integration by parts exposes the endpoint pivot norm and the principal energy. Coercivity controls the primitive, while the coefficient derivative and lower-order form are estimated by their stated quadratic bounds.

For a<b and a terminal time \sigma\in[a,b], set W_\sigma(t)=\int_t^\sigma u(r)\,dr. Let a homogeneous weak wave have zero initial displacement and velocity at a. Assume its principal form A is symmetric, coercive with constant c>0, and absolutely continuous in time, with coefficient derivative bound L_A and pivot-to-energy lower-order bound L_R\geq0. Under the scalar integrability hypotheses for the backward-energy identity, it satisfies

\frac12\|u(\sigma)\|_H^2+\frac c2\|W_\sigma(a)\|_V^2 \leq \frac{L_A}{2}\int_a^\sigma\|W_\sigma(t)\|_V^2\,dt +\frac{L_R}{2}\int_a^\sigma \bigl(\|u(t)\|_H^2+\|W_\sigma(t)\|_V^2\bigr)\,dt.

Here u(\sigma) denotes the continuous pivot-space displacement representative. Zero initial data remove the initial boundary terms.

We follow Evans (2010, pp. 405–406) in the abstract Gelfand-triple setting.

Uniform bounds. The assumed energy bounds give \|u_m\|_{L^\infty(V)}+\|u_m'\|_{L^\infty(H)}\leq C, and the accelerations are assumed bounded, \|u_m''\|_{L^2(V^*)}\leq C, both independent of the trial dimension m.

Weak compactness. The spaces L^2(a,b;V), L^2(a,b;H), and L^2(a,b;V^*) are reflexive Banach spaces. The uniform bounds place the Galerkin family in a bounded ball of their product. Reflexive weak compactness, applied simultaneously to the three coordinates, gives weak limits u\in L^2(V), v\in L^2(H), a\in L^2(V^*).

Passing the equation to the limit. Bounded linear time-test functionals pass both integrated identities to the limit, retaining their fixed initial boundary terms. The projected spatial limit theorem Theorem 7.71 supplies the ambient equation by weak–strong testing. Together these give the weak-wave predicate.

Essential supremum bounds. The set of L^2(V) functions satisfying \|u(t)\|_V\leq C almost everywhere is norm-closed and convex, hence weakly closed in L^2(V). The displacement limit belongs to that same set. The identical argument in L^2(H) preserves the velocity bound.

Assume a bounded projected Galerkin family with stable trial projections converging to the identity. Every approximation must have the same exact initial displacement q_0 and velocity p_0 in its integrated boundary identities. Then it has a weak-wave limit with these data. Uniform almost-everywhere energy bounds pass to the limit as L^\infty(V) and L^\infty(H) bounds for displacement and velocity.

Apply the finite-interval continuous-representative theorem to the integrated displacement equation, with the pivot velocity embedded into V^* as its weak time derivative. This gives a continuous pivot-space representative agreeing almost everywhere with Ju. The initial boundary term identifies its value at the lower endpoint with Jq_0.

Every weak-wave displacement has a strongly continuous representative in the pivot space on the closed time interval, agreeing almost everywhere with the embedded L^2(V) representative and taking the prescribed initial value.

The second-order equation is rewritten as a first-order affine system for displacement and velocity. Finite-dimensional Carathéodory existence applies, and projection to the two state components recovers the two almost-everywhere equations and initial values.

On each finite-dimensional trial space, a bounded strongly measurable stiffness operator and an integrable dual forcing produce a global Carathéodory solution of the second-order Galerkin coefficient system on the chosen finite interval.

The backward estimate and Grönwall argument give vanishing on the first short interval. The zero displacement and velocity traces at its right endpoint restart the same argument on the next interval. Finite induction covers the whole interval.

Let a=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_N=b cover the time interval, with each \tau_{j+1}-\tau_j short enough to absorb the right-hand side in Theorem 7.75. Then a homogeneous zero-data weak wave has

u(t)=0\qquad\text{for every }t\in[a,b]

for its continuous pivot-space displacement representative.

The projected dual residual is the forcing minus the stiffness applied to the Galerkin displacement. Boundedness of the stiffness, stability of the trial projection, and the displacement and forcing norms control this residual in L^2(V^*), with constants independent of dimension. Evaluating the projection against a test gives the projected spatial equation.

Uniform energy stability of the trial projection yields a dimension-independent L^2(V^*) acceleration bound. The corresponding almost-everywhere spatial equation evaluates the stiffness and forcing on the projected ambient test.

For the acceleration realization, assume additionally that the ODE forcing is represented in L^2(a,b;V^*) and that B is strongly measurable almost everywhere and essentially bounded. Under these hypotheses, a finite-dimensional Galerkin trajectory is realized canonically as a displacement in L^2(a,b;V), a velocity in L^2(a,b;H), and an acceleration in L^2(a,b;V^*). The acceleration is the residual projected through a stable trial projection, since the finite system tests only against its own trial space. This projected residual agrees almost everywhere with the coefficient acceleration embedded in V^*.

Pair the coefficient equations with an ambient test and integrate by parts against \tau. The final-time term vanishes because \tau(b)=0; the initial terms are the pairings with Jq_m and Jp_m. Almost-everywhere agreement of the canonical Bochner realizations gives the displayed identities.

Write J:V\to H for the inclusion, and let q_m,p_m\in S_m be the finite-level initial displacement and velocity. The Galerkin displacement u_m, pivot velocity v_m, and dual acceleration a_m satisfy, for every w\in V and time test \tau with \tau(b)=0,

-\int_a^b (Ju_m,Jw)_H\tau' =\int_a^b(v_m,Jw)_H\tau+(Jq_m,Jw)_H\tau(a),

-\int_a^b(v_m,Jw)_H\tau' =\int_a^b\langle a_m,w\rangle\tau+(Jp_m,Jw)_H\tau(a).

Pass the time integrals through weak convergence. Strong convergence of q_m and p_m gives convergence of both initial boundary pairings against each fixed test. The projected spatial limit theorem Theorem 7.71 supplies the remaining ambient equation under the same measurable, essentially bounded coefficient hypothesis.

Suppose the projected Galerkin families have common weak limits, a uniform displacement bound, and stable trial projections converging to the identity. Their initial data may vary with the approximation index, provided q_m\to q_0 strongly in V and p_m\to p_0 strongly in H. Then the limits form a weak wave with initial data q_0,p_0.

The common weak limits are hypotheses; weak compactness extracts them from bounded families.

The residuals \ell-Bu_m converge weakly in L^2(V^*). Uniform projection stability lifts P_mw\to w to strong convergence on L^2(V) tests. Pairing the bounded weak residuals with those strongly convergent tests identifies the acceleration limit with \ell-Bu.

The projected spatial equations pass to the full ambient equation when the displacements and accelerations have common weak limits, the displacement family is uniformly bounded, and the stable trial projections converge strongly to the identity on V. The coefficient field is measurable and essentially bounded.

a(t)+B(t)u(t)=\ell(t)\quad\text{for almost every }t.

Fix a finite interval a<b and forcing \ell\in L^2(a,b;V^*). A weak wave consists of displacement in L^2(V), velocity in L^2(H), and acceleration in L^2(V^*). Integrated time-derivative identities carry the initial traces, and the spatial equation u_{tt}+B(t)u=\ell holds almost everywhere in V^*.

Subtract the two weak formulations. Linearity cancels the common forcing and initial traces, so the difference is a homogeneous zero-data weak wave. Applying homogeneous uniqueness to its displacement, velocity, and acceleration gives equality of the corresponding components.

Suppose every homogeneous zero-data weak wave satisfies (w,w_t,w_{tt})=(0,0,0). If u_1 and u_2 have the same operator, forcing, displacement trace, and velocity trace, then their difference is such a homogeneous solution, hence

u_1=u_2,\qquad (u_1)_t=(u_2)_t,\qquad (u_1)_{tt}=(u_2)_{tt}.

Subtract the two waves, construct a sufficiently fine uniform finite partition, apply the backward-energy estimate on each cell, restart from the zero endpoint traces, and identify the vanishing continuous representative with all three Bochner classes.

In the real Hilbert Gelfand-triple setting, write J:V\hookrightarrow H for the inclusion and assume B=A+R on [a,b]. Require A to be absolutely continuous in operator norm, with A'(t)=\dot A(t) for almost every t\in(a,b]. Both \dot A and R must be almost everywhere strongly measurable as operator-valued maps. For every t\in[a,b], assume A(t) is symmetric and, for all v,w\in V,

\kappa\|v\|_V^2\leq A(t)(v,v),\qquad |\dot A(t)(v,v)|\leq L_A\|v\|_V^2,\qquad |R(t)(v,w)|\leq L_R\|Jv\|_H\|w\|_V,

where \kappa>0 and L_A,L_R\geq0. Two weak waves for this operator with equal forcing and initial traces then satisfy

u_1=u_2\ \text{in }L^2(a,b;V),\qquad v_1=v_2\ \text{in }L^2(a,b;H),\qquad a_1=a_2\ \text{in }L^2(a,b;V^*).

The scalar integrability conditions inside the backward-energy identity are derived from the L^2 trajectories, the coefficient bounds, and the weak equation.

Bounded linear maps pass the displacement identity and the time-test velocity identity to the limit. Bounded operator-valued multiplication passes B(t)u_m weakly, and uniqueness of weak limits identifies the limiting acceleration equation.

With fixed forcing and common exact initial data, the weak-wave predicate is closed under a common weak limit in L^2(V)\times L^2(H)\times L^2(V^*), assuming the operator field is measurable and essentially bounded.

The exponential decreases with x, so the exact correction is bounded by its value at \delta, divided by the positive normalization. Subtracting the unnormalized layer from the exact correction leaves De^{-bL/\varepsilon}(e^{-bx/\varepsilon}-1)/(1-e^{-bL/\varepsilon}). On [0,L], the absolute value of the parenthesized term is at most one. These bounds tend to zero independently of position on the stated sets. The fixed nonzero endpoint discrepancy rules out uniform outer convergence. Finally substitute x=\varepsilon y; the left exponential becomes e^{-by}, while the right-end tail vanishes and v(\varepsilon y)\to v(0). Letting y\to\infty proves matching.

Under the same assumptions, for every fixed \delta>0 and x\in[\delta,L],

|u_\varepsilon(x)-v(x)| \le \frac{|D|e^{-b\delta/\varepsilon}}{1-e^{-bL/\varepsilon}}.

Thus u_\varepsilon\to v uniformly away from the left endpoint as \varepsilon\downarrow0. If D\ne0, uniform convergence to v on [0,L] fails: the error at zero is always |D|. The composite approximation w_\varepsilon(x)=v(x)+De^{-bx/\varepsilon} instead satisfies, throughout [0,L],

|u_\varepsilon(x)-w_\varepsilon(x)| \le\frac{|D|e^{-bL/\varepsilon}}{1-e^{-bL/\varepsilon}},

and this remainder tends uniformly to zero. At each fixed stretched coordinate y, u_\varepsilon(\varepsilon y)\to v(0)+De^{-by}. For y\ge0 this is the physical left layer, whose limit as y\to\infty matches v(0).

Positive b,L,\varepsilon make the denominator strictly positive. At zero the normalized exponential correction is one; at L it is zero. The two endpoint conditions follow. Differentiate the constructed function twice. The exponential terms in \varepsilon u_\varepsilon''+bu_\varepsilon' cancel, leaving bv'=f.

Let \varepsilon,b,L>0 and A,B,f\in\mathbb R. Define the outer solution and its left boundary mismatch by

v(x)=B+\frac fb(x-L),\qquad D=A-v(0).

The smooth function

u_\varepsilon(x)=v(x)+D\, \frac{e^{-bx/\varepsilon}-e^{-bL/\varepsilon}} {1-e^{-bL/\varepsilon}}

satisfies the actual differential equation \varepsilon u_\varepsilon''+bu_\varepsilon'=f, with u_\varepsilon(0)=A and u_\varepsilon(L)=B. The reduced function satisfies bv'=f and v(L)=B.

For real b>0, substitute y=\sqrt b\,x in the standard Gaussian integral \int_{\mathbb R}e^{-y^2}\,dy=\sqrt\pi. For complex \beta with positive real part, the damped Gaussian is absolutely integrable and the standard complex Gaussian theorem evaluates it using the principal square root.

The exact real and damped complex Gaussian integrals provide the normalization identities

\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-b x^2}\,dx=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{b}} \quad(b>0), \qquad \int_{\mathbb R}e^{-\beta x^2}\,dx =\left(\frac{\pi}{\beta}\right)^{1/2} \quad(\operatorname{Re}\beta>0).

Both are Mathlib theorems, used by the model Laplace and stationary-phase calculations.

An interior minimum has zero first derivative. The C^2 Taylor estimate and positivity of H give \phi(x)-\phi(x_0)\ge c_0|x-x_0|^2 near x_0, for some c_0>0. Outside a smaller ball, compactness and strict minimality give a positive gap above \phi(x_0). Since K is bounded, this gap extends the quadratic lower bound to all of K, with a possibly smaller constant c>0.

Substitute x=x_0+\varepsilon z. For fixed z, the rescaled domain eventually contains z because x_0 is interior, and Taylor's theorem gives (\phi(x_0+\varepsilon z)-\phi(x_0))/\varepsilon^2\to H[z,z]/2. The amplitude is bounded on K, so the rescaled integrand, extended by zero, is dominated by M e^{-c|z|^2}. Dominated convergence leaves a(x_0)\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-H[z,z]/2}\,dz. Orthogonal diagonalization evaluates this integral as (2\pi)^{n/2}/\sqrt{\det H}. Setting \varepsilon=\lambda^{-1/2} gives the large-parameter forms.

For the compact-amplitude version, adjoin a small closed ball about x_0 to the support and apply the compact-domain theorem. Explicit stationarity and Hessian positivity make x_0 a strict minimum on that ball. The integral outside the support is zero.

Let K\subseteq\mathbb R^n be compact and x_0\in\operatorname{int}K. Suppose \phi is continuous on K, is C^2 near x_0, and \phi(x)>\phi(x_0) for every x\in K\setminus\{x_0\}. Let H=D^2\phi(x_0) be its actual Hessian and assume H[v,v]>0 for every nonzero v. For an amplitude a:\mathbb R^n\to E continuous on K, with E a real Banach space,

\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\varepsilon^{-n} \int_K e^{-(\phi(x)-\phi(x_0))/\varepsilon^2}a(x)\,dx =\frac{(2\pi)^{n/2}}{\sqrt{\det H}}\,a(x_0).

Equivalently, the two large-parameter normalizations have the same limit:

\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\lambda^{n/2} \int_K e^{-\lambda(\phi(x)-\phi(x_0))}a(x)\,dx = \lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\lambda^{n/2}e^{\lambda\phi(x_0)} \int_K e^{-\lambda\phi(x)}a(x)\,dx =\frac{(2\pi)^{n/2}}{\sqrt{\det H}}\,a(x_0).

Stationarity at the interior minimum, symmetry of the Hessian, and the quadratic lower bound used in the proof are derived from these hypotheses. The result includes n=0, where the empty determinant and the Gaussian factor are one.

There is also a whole-space version for continuous compactly supported a:\mathbb R^n\to E. In that version, assume C^2 regularity near x_0, D\phi(x_0)=0, positive Hessian, continuity of \phi on the topological support of a, and \phi(x)>\phi(x_0) on that support away from x_0. The same exponentially normalized limit holds with \int_{\mathbb R^n}. The minimum need not belong to the support. In either version, a(x_0)=0 is allowed and gives a zero limit.

Pull the constant amplitude outside the integral and substitute y=\sqrt\lambda\,x. The Jacobian contributes \lambda^{-1/2}, while the Gaussian integral contributes \sqrt\pi. Multiplication by the normalizing factor \sqrt\lambda leaves exactly \sqrt\pi\,c.

For every positive parameter \lambda, the normalized constant-amplitude Gaussian integral is exactly \sqrt\pi c:

\sqrt{\lambda}\int_{\mathbb R}c\,e^{-\lambda x^2}\,dx =\sqrt{\pi}\,c.

The variable-phase Laplace limit uses this Gaussian normalization after rescaling about the minimum.

After y=\varepsilon x, Taylor's theorem gives \phi(\varepsilon x)/\varepsilon^2\to\phi''(0)x^2/2 for each fixed x, and continuity gives a(\varepsilon x)\to a(0). If \|a\|\le M, the norm of the rescaled integrand is bounded by M e^{-\delta x^2}, independently of positive \varepsilon. This Gaussian is integrable. Dominated convergence passes the pointwise limit through the Bochner integral, and the real Gaussian formula evaluates the resulting integral. Thus the local Taylor coefficient and the global tail bound supply different parts of the argument.

Let \phi\in C^2(\mathbb R) satisfy \phi(0)=\phi'(0)=0 and the global lower bound \phi(y)\ge\delta y^2 for some \delta>0. Let a:\mathbb R\to E be bounded and continuous, where E is a real Banach space. Then

\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\varepsilon^{-1} \int_{\mathbb R}e^{-\phi(y)/\varepsilon^2}a(y)\,dy =\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{\phi''(0)/2}}\,a(0).

The coefficient uses the actual second derivative of the phase. On a compact integration set, the Euclidean version derives the required lower bound from a strict minimum and a positive Hessian, in every finite dimension.

Write e^{i\omega t}=(i\omega)^{-1}(e^{i\omega t})' and integrate by parts. The two boundary terms have total norm at most 2M/|\omega|. The remaining integral is bounded by |\omega|^{-1}\int_{\min(a,b)}^{\max(a,b)}\|f'(t)\|\,dt, which is at most |b-a|M'/|\omega|. Adding the estimates proves the displayed bound.

For a nonlinear phase, use (e^{i\omega\phi})'=i\omega\phi'e^{i\omega\phi} and transfer the derivative to g=f/\phi'. The quotient rule gives g'=f'/\phi'-\phi''f/(\phi')^2, hence \|g\|\le M/\delta and \|g'\|\le M'/\delta+KM/\delta^2. The same integration-by-parts estimate now proves the explicit bound.

For every-order decay, repeat the operation f\mapsto(f/\phi')'. Global smoothness and nonvanishing make every transferred amplitude smooth. Division and differentiation preserve support inside the interval, so every boundary term vanishes. Each integration by parts gains |\omega|^{-1}; a compact-interval integral bound at the last step supplies C_k.

In Euclidean space the corresponding transfer is

Tf=\sum_j\partial_j\left( \frac{\partial_j\phi}{|\nabla\phi|^2}f\right).

On the support of f, nonstationarity makes the denominator nonzero. Off that closed support the product is locally zero, even where the phase is critical. Thus each normalized product is smooth everywhere, and taking its divergence preserves smoothness and keeps its support inside the original compact set. Coordinate integration by parts gives

i\omega\int e^{i\omega\phi}f=-\int e^{i\omega\phi}Tf.

The compact support removes boundary terms and justifies the finite sum of integrals. Iterate this identity: each step gains |\omega|^{-1}, and the final amplitude's L^1 norm bounds the remaining integral. This constructs the decay constants from the amplitude.

Let \omega\ne0 and let f take values in a complex Banach space. If \|f(t)\|\le M and \|f'(t)\|\le M' on the unordered closed interval with endpoints a,b, integration by parts gives the explicit estimate

\left\|\int_a^b e^{i\omega t}f(t)\,dt\right\| \le \frac{2M+|b-a|M'}{|\omega|}.

The theorem assumes pointwise differentiability on the unordered closed interval and interval integrability of the derivative.

More generally, let \phi be a real phase with two pointwise derivatives on that closed interval, with \phi'' continuous there. If f' is continuous there and

|\phi'|\ge\delta>0,\quad |\phi''|\le K,\quad \|f\|\le M,\quad \|f'\|\le M',

then the nonlinear-phase bound is

\left\|\int_a^b e^{i\omega\phi(t)}f(t)\,dt\right\| \le \frac{2M/\delta+|b-a|(M'/\delta+KM/\delta^2)}{|\omega|}.

The two endpoints contribute 2M/\delta; the amplitude need not vanish there. For every-order decay, assume instead that \phi and f are globally smooth, \phi' is nowhere zero on \mathbb R, and the topological support of f lies inside (a,b). For each k\in\mathbb N there is C_k\ge0, independent of nonzero \omega, such that

\left\|\int_a^b e^{i\omega\phi(t)}f(t)\,dt\right\| \le C_k|\omega|^{-k}.

The whole-space theorem extends rapid decay to every n\in\mathbb N: let \phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R be smooth, let f:\mathbb R^n\to E be smooth and compactly supported, with E a complex Banach space, and assume d\phi(x)\ne0 on the topological support of f. For each k\in\mathbb N there is C_k\ge0 such that

\left\|\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{i\omega\phi(x)}f(x)\,dx\right\| \le C_k|\omega|^{-k}\qquad(\omega\ne0).

Critical points of \phi outside the support of f are allowed.

Substitute y=(N+1)x; the left side becomes (N+1)^{-1}\int_0^{N+1}a(y)\,dy. The periodic-cell identity evaluates the last integral as (N+1)\int_0^1a, and cancellation of the positive integer factor proves the claim.

For a one-periodic interval-integrable function, positive-integer rescaling preserves the average over one cell:

\int_0^1a((N+1)x)\,dx=\int_0^1a(x)\,dx \qquad(N\in\mathbb N).

This is an exact identity used in the elementary algebra of periodic homogenization.

Partition [0,N] into the unit intervals [k,k+1]. Translation by the integer k and one-periodicity give integrability on each cell and identify its integral with \int_0^1a. Additivity of the interval integral then gives N identical summands.

The integral of a locally integrable periodic function over an integer number of cells is that integer times its one-cell integral. If a(x+1)=a(x) and a is integrable on [0,1], then

\int_0^N a(x)\,dx=N\int_0^1a(x)\,dx \qquad(N\in\mathbb N).

Use the antiderivative e^{i\omega t}/(i\omega). The interval integral is (e^{i\omega b}-e^{i\omega a})/(i\omega). Both endpoint exponentials have norm one, so the triangle inequality bounds the numerator by two and gives 2/|\omega|.

For every nonzero real frequency, the complex phase e^{i\omega t} has interval integral bounded by 2/|\omega|, independently of the interval length. The estimate is the elementary nonstationary cancellation mechanism behind more elaborate high-frequency arguments.

An integrating factor constructs the classical solutions and the homogeneous correction with both traces. The reduced function satisfies av'=f and v''=(f/a)' in the interior. Therefore r_\varepsilon=u_\varepsilon-v-DH_\varepsilon has zero boundary values and solves \varepsilon r_\varepsilon''+ar_\varepsilon'=-\varepsilon v''. The affine barriers \pm\varepsilon M(L-x)/\alpha bound this remainder by scalar comparison.

Freezing the coefficient produces the residual b(b-a(x))e^{-bx/\varepsilon}/\varepsilon. The variation bound and exponential decay control it by a multiple of e^{-\mu x/\varepsilon}. Adding and subtracting C\varepsilon e^{-\mu x/\varepsilon}+e^{-bL/\varepsilon} from e^{-bx/\varepsilon} gives comparison barriers for H_\varepsilon. The constant tail supplies the right boundary inequality. Adding the two error bounds proves the composite estimate, and e^{-bL/\varepsilon}\le\varepsilon/(bL) gives its uniform linear bound.

Let L,\alpha>0, let a,f be C^1 on an open neighborhood of [0,L], and assume a(x)\ge\alpha throughout that interval. For arbitrary real boundary values A,B, the construction supplies a family of classical solutions, for every \varepsilon>0, with

\varepsilon u_\varepsilon''+a(x)u_\varepsilon'=f(x),\qquad u_\varepsilon(0)=A,\quad u_\varepsilon(L)=B.

The solutions have C^2 extensions and satisfy the equation on the closed interval. Define

v(x)=B-\int_x^L\frac{f(s)}{a(s)}\,ds,\qquad D=A-v(0),\qquad b=a(0),\qquad \mu=\alpha/2.

The construction, not the statement, fixes constants M,K\ge0, independent of \varepsilon, with |(f/a)'|\le M and |a(x)-a(0)|\le Kx on [0,L], and it puts C=bK/\mu^3. The constructed homogeneous correction H_\varepsilon satisfies \varepsilon H_\varepsilon''+aH_\varepsilon'=0, H_\varepsilon(0)=1, H_\varepsilon(L)=0, and 0\le H_\varepsilon(x)\le e^{-\alpha x/\varepsilon}. For x\in[0,L],

|u_\varepsilon(x)-v(x)-D H_\varepsilon(x)| \le\frac{\varepsilon M(L-x)}{\alpha}, \qquad |H_\varepsilon(x)-e^{-bx/\varepsilon}| \le C\varepsilon e^{-\mu x/\varepsilon}+e^{-bL/\varepsilon}.

Consequently the frozen composite w_\varepsilon(x)=v(x)+De^{-bx/\varepsilon} obeys

\begin{aligned} |u_\varepsilon(x)-w_\varepsilon(x)| &\le\frac{\varepsilon M(L-x)}{\alpha} +|D|\left(C\varepsilon e^{-\mu x/\varepsilon}+e^{-bL/\varepsilon}\right)\\ &\le\varepsilon\left(\frac{ML}{\alpha} +|D|\left(C+\frac{1}{bL}\right)\right). \end{aligned}

The finite-interval tail e^{-bL/\varepsilon} is present even when K=0: at x=L, the difference between H_\varepsilon and the frozen exponential is exactly e^{-bL/\varepsilon}.

The outer error is bounded by |D|e^{-\alpha x/\varepsilon}+\varepsilon M(L-x)/\alpha. On [\delta,L], both terms tend to zero uniformly; when D=0, the same bound works on the whole interval. When D\ne0, the error at zero is always |D|, which rules out uniform outer convergence. The remainder estimates already hold uniformly up to both endpoints. For fixed y\ge0, the point \varepsilon y eventually lies in [0,L]. Evaluate the composite estimate there and use v(\varepsilon y)\to v(0). The frozen exponential becomes e^{-by}; positivity of b gives matching as y\to\infty.

For the constructed family, u_\varepsilon\to v uniformly on every [\delta,L] with \delta>0, as \varepsilon\downarrow0. Convergence is uniform on [0,L] exactly when D=0. Both the exact-correction remainder u_\varepsilon-v-DH_\varepsilon and the frozen composite remainder u_\varepsilon-w_\varepsilon tend uniformly to zero on [0,L].

At each fixed physical stretched coordinate y\ge0,

u_\varepsilon(\varepsilon y)\longrightarrow v(0)+De^{-by}.

This inner profile tends to v(0) as y\to\infty and is nonconstant if D\ne0.

The exact residual equivalence gives a_\varepsilon(z)E(p_\varepsilon)(z) =\varepsilon^2\Box a_\varepsilon(z). Finite sums and products preserve the stated limits, so a_0 E(p_0)(z)=0. Cancelling the nonzero number a_0 gives the conclusion. The scaled amplitude residual is a hypothesis in this argument; the full wave residual is zero because the family solves the PDE.

Fix a spacetime point z. Let a_\varepsilon,p_\varepsilon be real families which are C^2 near z and satisfy the actual equation \Box(a_\varepsilon e^{ip_\varepsilon/\varepsilon})(z)=0 for all sufficiently small positive \varepsilon. Suppose, as \varepsilon\downarrow0,
