a_\varepsilon(z)\longrightarrow a_0\ne0,\qquad \partial_jp_\varepsilon(z)\longrightarrow\partial_jp_0(z) \quad(0\le j\le n),\qquad \varepsilon^2\Box a_\varepsilon(z)\longrightarrow0,

where p_0 is differentiable at z. Then the limiting phase satisfies the squared eikonal equation

(\partial_tp_0(z))^2=|\nabla_xp_0(z)|^2.

The result is pointwise and chooses no sign for \partial_tp_0.

For any time or space coordinate j, the product and chain rules give

\partial_j^2(ae^{ip/\varepsilon}) =e^{ip/\varepsilon} \left(\partial_j^2a+ \frac{i}{\varepsilon}(a\,\partial_j^2p+2\partial_jp\,\partial_ja) -\frac{a}{\varepsilon^2}(\partial_jp)^2\right).

Subtract the spatial terms from the time term. Multiplication by \varepsilon^2 removes the negative powers, and taking real and imaginary parts after cancelling the exponential gives the equivalence. The derivatives here are those of the displayed ansatz.

Suppose a,p are C^2 near the point of evaluation and \varepsilon\ne0. Define the eikonal defect and transport expression by

E(p)=p_t^2-|\nabla_xp|^2,\qquad T(a,p)=a\Box p+2(p_ta_t-\nabla_xp\cdot\nabla_xa).

The actual complex wave residual is

\Box U_\varepsilon =e^{ip/\varepsilon} \left(\Box a+\frac{i}{\varepsilon}T(a,p) -\frac{a}{\varepsilon^2}E(p)\right).

Equivalently, \varepsilon^2\Box U_\varepsilon =e^{ip/\varepsilon}(\varepsilon^2\Box a-aE(p)+i\varepsilon T(a,p)). Since the exponential never vanishes and the two coefficients are real,

\Box U_\varepsilon=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad aE(p)=\varepsilon^2\Box a \quad\hbox{and}\quad T(a,p)=0.

The equivalence holds whether or not a vanishes.

Set L=\|u_0\|_\infty/(2\nu). The primitive bound gives 0<P(y)\le e^{L|y|}. Normalize it by e^{Ly}+e^{-Ly} to obtain a positive bounded continuous amplitude. Evolve this amplitude by the heat kernel and apply the two opposite exponential tilts. Their sum is a positive smooth heat solution; the Gaussian tilt identities prove both the displayed integral formula and integrability. The domain theorem now gives the Burgers PDE.

Continuity of u_0 gives P'=-u_0P/(2\nu). The normalized amplitude also has a bounded continuous derivative, so its heat evolution and spatial derivative extend continuously to time zero. Undoing the tilts yields the joint traces v\to P(x_0) and v_x\to P'(x_0). Since P(x_0)>0, the quotient tends to -2\nu P'(x_0)/P(x_0)=u_0(x_0).

For \nu>0 and bounded continuous u_0, the potential is

v(t,x)=\int_{\mathbb R} \frac{e^{-(x-y)^2/(4\nu t)}}{\sqrt{4\pi\nu t}}\,P(y)\,dy, \qquad t>0.

The integrand is integrable, and v is positive and smooth at positive time. Its Cole–Hopf transform u=-2\nu v_x/v is a classical, jointly C^2 solution of u_t+u u_x=\nu u_{xx} there. At every x_0\in\mathbb R,

\lim_{\substack{(t,x)\to(0,x_0)\\t>0}}u(t,x)=u_0(x_0).

The integral is formalized on the standard one-dimensional Euclidean space.

The analytic hypotheses justify the quotient rules and commutation of mixed partials. Differentiating the heat equation supplies the spatial derivative identity, after which the jet-level polynomial and rational cancellation closes the viscous Burgers residual.

On an arbitrary open spacetime domain, if v\in C^3, v\neq0, and

v_t=\nu v_{xx},

then u=-2\nu v_x/v satisfies

u_t+u\,u_x=\nu u_{xx}.

For v=e^{t+x}, both v_t and v_{xx} equal v, so v solves the unit heat equation and is everywhere positive. Also v_x=v, hence the Cole–Hopf quotient is -2v/v=-2. All derivatives of this constant vanish, so its Burgers residual is zero.

For the heat solution v(t,x)=e^{t+x} and unit viscosity, the Cole–Hopf transform is the constant velocity u=-2, which solves viscous Burgers on all spacetime. Positivity of the exponential discharges the denominator condition, while symbolic differentiation verifies the closed-form transform identity.

Differentiate u=-2\nu v_x/v formally in t and twice in x, put all terms over a common power of v, and substitute v_t=\nu v_{xx} together with v_{xt}=\nu v_{xxx}. The numerator then cancels term by term, leaving zero. No analytic hypothesis enters at this level.

The algebraic jet identity isolates the exact cancellation: the heat equation and its spatial derivative imply that the quotient-rule jets of the Cole–Hopf transform satisfy

u_t+u\,u_x-\nu u_{xx}=0.

Differentiate the two exponential summands separately; each solves the unit heat equation, so their sum does as well and is strictly positive. Substituting v_x=e^{t+x}-e^{t-x} into -2v_x/v gives the displayed velocity. Multiply numerator and denominator by e^{x-t} to obtain -2+4/(1+e^{2x}). Direct differentiation of this stationary expression, followed by clearing its positive denominator, reduces the Burgers residual to a polynomial identity that normalizes to zero.

The positive heat profile

v(t,x)=e^{t+x}+e^{t-x}

has zero heat residual, and its ordinary Cole–Hopf transform agrees pointwise with

-2\,\frac{e^{t+x}-e^{t-x}}{e^{t+x}+e^{t-x}}.

The algebraically equivalent stationary velocity -2+4/(1+e^{2x}) has zero unit-viscosity Burgers residual everywhere. Positivity of the exponential denominators discharges the quotient side conditions. In this stationary example, nonlinear advection and viscosity balance each other while the time derivative vanishes.

For a heat profile v, the Cole–Hopf transform is

u=-2\nu\,\frac{v_x}{v}.

Division in Lean is total, so the theorems about the transform assume separately that v is nonzero on the domain under consideration.

Run the direct method in the affine class of the given admissible map. The constraint set is weakly sequentially closed by the weak continuity of the determinant, and the energy is weakly lower semicontinuous because it is convex in Du. A bounded minimizing sequence in the constraint set has a weak limit that stays in it.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n\ge1, be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary, let q>n, and let L(x,s,P) be C^1, convex in P, with \alpha|P|^q-\beta\le L(x,s,P) for some \alpha>0. If g\in W^{1,q}(\Omega;\mathbb R^n) has \det Dg=1 almost everywhere, the extended energy \int_\Omega L(x,u,Du)\,dx attains its minimum among maps u\in g+W^{1,q}_0 with \det Du=1 almost everywhere. When L=L(x,P) does not depend on the value, the same holds in the class of maps with trace \gamma and \det Du=1, for every boundary datum \gamma for which that class is nonempty; if one admissible map has finite energy, the minimizer's density is integrable and its energy is finite.

For existence, an energy-bounded minimizing sequence has bounded gradients. Poincaré's inequality controls the zero-boundary differences from g, so weak compactness gives an H^1 limit with the same boundary values. Rellich compactness gives strong L^2 convergence, preserving unit length almost everywhere, and weak lower semicontinuity gives minimality. This existence argument itself needs only a bounded open domain of positive dimension.

For the equation, the projected variations are admissible competitors, so the energy along them has a minimum at t=0 and its derivative there vanishes. The previous theorem computes that derivative. An essentially bounded test field has an almost-everywhere bound M, which is all the variation theorem asks for, and the graph boundary supplies the Sobolev extension that the composition with G needs.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^{n+1} be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary, and let g\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m). Assume the class

\mathcal A_g=\{W\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m): |W|=1\text{ a.e.},\ W-g\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\}

is nonempty. Then the Dirichlet energy attains its minimum on \mathcal A_g. Every such minimizer U satisfies

\int_\Omega DU:DV\,dx=\int_\Omega|DU|^2\,U\cdot V\,dx \qquad\text{for every }V\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\cap L^\infty.

This is the weak form of the harmonic map equation -\Delta U=|DU|^2U. Nonemptiness of \mathcal A_g is a hypothesis.
The implicit function argument gives coefficients (a,b)\ne(0,0) with aJ'(u)+bF'(u)=0. If b were zero then a\ne0 and J'(u)=0, which is excluded. Take \lambda=-a/b.

Let E be a real Banach space and F,J:E\to\mathbb R strictly differentiable at u, with J'(u)\ne0. If u is a local extremum of F on the level set \{v:J(v)=J(u)\}, then F'(u)=\lambda J'(u) for some \lambda\in\mathbb R.

The graph boundary supplies the extension and trace infrastructure. The classical obstacle defines an H^2 field whose Sobolev trace agrees with its boundary values, so the boundary sign becomes the sign condition needed by the obstacle regularity theorem. The constrained variational inequality and its reaction estimate then give the H^2 lift and 0\le r\le(-\Delta\psi-f)^+. Complementarity sets the reaction to zero off contact. On contact, the Sobolev derivatives of U-\psi vanish almost everywhere on its zero set, giving equality of the Laplacians.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n>0, be bounded and open with C^2 graph boundary. Let f\in L^2(\Omega) and let the obstacle \psi be C^2 up to the boundary, continuous on \overline\Omega, and nonpositive on \partial\Omega. If u\in H^1_0(\Omega) minimizes J among fields above \psi, then u has an H^2 representative U. Its reaction obeys

0\le r=-\Delta U-f\le(-\Delta\psi-f)^+,\qquad r(U-\psi)=0 \quad\text{a.e. in }\Omega.

On the contact set U=\psi, one has \Delta U=\Delta\psi almost everywhere; on U>\psi, one has -\Delta U=f almost everywhere.

The graph-domain hypotheses supply the Sobolev extension operator and inward partition used for composition and preservation of the boundary values. The smooth compactly supported cutoff has bounded derivative and Lipschitz DG. Since |U|=1, the chain rule gives D(G(U+tV))=DG(U+tV)\,(DU+tDV), and at t=0 the derivative of the normalization z\mapsto z/|z| at a unit vector is the projection I-z\otimes z. Differentiating |U|^2=1 gives (DU)^TU=0, which turns the projected term into -|DU|^2U\cdot V. Differentiation under the integral sign is justified by an integrable bound built from the Lipschitz bound on DG.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^{n+1} be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary. Choose a smooth compactly supported map G:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m agreeing with z/|z| on \tfrac12\le|z|\le2. Let U\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m) have |U|=1 almost everywhere and let V\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m) be bounded by M. For |t|M<\tfrac12 the projected variation G(U+tV) has unit length almost everywhere, and if V\in H^1_0 it has the boundary values of U. The Dirichlet energy E(W)=\tfrac12\int_\Omega|DW|^2 of the projected variation is differentiable at t=0 with derivative

\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}E\bigl(G(U+tV)\bigr) =\int_\Omega\Bigl(DU:DV-|DU|^2\,U\cdot V\Bigr)\,dx.

The sublevel through x_0 is weakly closed by lower semicontinuity, weakly compact by boundedness, and nonempty because it contains x_0. The functional therefore attains a minimum there. That minimum is at most J(x_0), while every point outside the sublevel has larger energy, so the constrained minimum is global.

A weakly lower-semicontinuous real functional on a complete real Hilbert space attains a global minimum if the sublevel through some supplied x_0\in H is norm bounded:

\{x\in H:J(x)\leq J(x_0)\} \quad\text{is norm bounded}.

Then there is u\in H such that J(u)\leq J(v) for every v\in H. This is the compactness-plus-liminf core of the direct method.
Coercivity makes the sublevel through the origin norm bounded. Apply the bounded-sublevel direct-method theorem to that nonempty sublevel.

If J:H\to\mathbb R is weakly lower semicontinuous and coercive,

\lVert x\rVert\longrightarrow\infty \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J(x)\longrightarrow\infty,

then J has a global minimizer.
Convexity and norm lower semicontinuity give weak lower semicontinuity. The coercive direct method theorem then supplies a minimizer.

A convex functional on a complete real Hilbert space has a global minimizer if it is lower semicontinuous in norm and coercive:

\exists u\in H,\qquad J(u)=\inf_{v\in H}J(v).

For every real a, the sublevel \{x:J(x)\leq a\} is convex because J is convex and norm closed because J is norm lower semicontinuous. A norm-closed convex set is weakly closed by Hahn–Banach separation. Thus every sublevel is weakly closed, which is equivalent to lower semicontinuity of J in the weak topology.

Every convex real functional on a real normed space that is lower semicontinuous in norm is lower semicontinuous for the weak topology:

x_\alpha\rightharpoonup x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J(x)\leq\liminf_\alpha J(x_\alpha).

This is the functional-analytic step behind Evans's integral-functional argument.

Strict convexity supplies convexity, so the argument with closed convex sublevel sets gives weak lower semicontinuity. The weak direct method gives existence, and strict convexity identifies any two global minimizers.

Strict convexity upgrades the direct-method conclusion to a unique global minimizer:

\exists!\,u\in H,\qquad \forall v\in H,\ J(u)\leq J(v).

For almost every x, the canonical base representative of (1-t)u+tv equals (1-t)u(x)+tv(x). Pointwise convexity of G(x,-) therefore bounds the integrand by the corresponding affine combination. Integrability permits monotonicity and linearity of the integral, producing the convexity inequality for \Phi.

Almost-everywhere pointwise convexity of G(x,-) and integrability of every admissible density imply convexity of the integral potential on H^1_0(\Omega):

\Phi((1-t)u+tv)\leq(1-t)\Phi(u)+t\Phi(v) \qquad(0\leq t\leq1).

This requires convexity in the zeroth-order variable. The gradient-convexity criterion for weak lower semicontinuity permits nonconvex dependence on that variable, under its separate regularity, growth, and convergence hypotheses.

For a spatial set \Omega and a scalar density G(x,s), the induced potential on H^1_0(\Omega) is

\Phi(u)=\int_\Omega G(x,u(x))\,dx,

using the canonical L^2 representative of the base coordinate. The definition allows explicit spatial dependence.

Subtract the represented Dirichlet weak equations and test with u_1-u_2. The Dirichlet form contributes at least c\|u_1-u_2\|_{H^1_0}^2, and pointwise monotonicity makes the Nemytskii term nonnegative after integration. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the forcing term by \|f_1-f_2\|_2\|u_1-u_2\|_{H^1_0}; cancellation gives the result.

If the represented Nemytskii nonlinearity is pointwise monotone almost everywhere, two semilinear Dirichlet solutions satisfy

\lVert u_1-u_2\rVert_{H^1_0} \leq \frac{\lVert f_1-f_2\rVert_{L^2}}{c},

where c is any positive coercivity modulus for the Dirichlet form. This estimate uses only the two weak equations and monotonicity; the solutions need not be supplied by the variational construction.

The load functional of N(u) pairs N(u) with the base coordinate of v in L^2, and the product of two square-integrable functions is integrable. Replacing N(u) by its almost-everywhere representative g(x,u(x)) changes neither the integrand almost everywhere nor the integral, which gives the pairing identity and the integrability of the Nemytskii integrand for every test field. Substituting the pairing identity into the weak formulation turns it into the strong-dual equation and back.

Suppose N:H^1_0(\Omega)\to L^2(\Omega) represents the nonlinearity, in the sense that for every u the function N(u) agrees almost everywhere on \Omega with x\mapsto g(x,u(x)). Then for all u,v\in H^1_0(\Omega) the load functional of N(u) is the Nemytskii integral,

\langle N(u),v\rangle_{L^2}=\int_\Omega g(x,u(x))\,v(x)\,dx,

and u is a weak solution of the semilinear Dirichlet problem with forcing f if and only if

B(u,v)+\langle N(u),v\rangle_{L^2}=\langle f,v\rangle_{L^2} \qquad(v\in H^1_0(\Omega)),

where B is the Dirichlet form. This is the abstract strong-dual equation used by the monotonicity, fixed-point, and variational arguments; on this side the integrability clause of the weak formulation is automatic.

Split a=a_+-a_-. The nonnegative terms a_+u^2 and bu^{2k+2} preserve convexity and monotonicity. The negative quadratic part costs at most a_-\|u\|_2^2; the supplied Dirichlet coercivity estimate absorbs it because a_-<c. The modified Helmholtz form therefore retains a positive coercivity modulus. The same direct-method and first-variation argument then gives the unique weak solution.

The same conclusion holds for a signed linear coefficient a when its negative part is strictly smaller than a supplied Dirichlet coercivity modulus. The higher-power coefficient remains nonnegative. The condition is measured against the chosen modulus and is only sufficient.

Use the potential density G(s)=\frac a2s^2+\frac b{2k+2}s^{2k+2}. Nonnegativity of a and b makes G convex, and its derivative is g(s)=as+bs^{2k+1}. The assumed Sobolev integrability justifies the integral and Fréchet derivative formula. Applying variational Dirichlet well-posedness gives existence, while strict coercivity of the gradient term and monotonicity of g give uniqueness.

On a bounded spatial set \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n with n>0, for k\in\mathbb N, nonnegative coefficients a,b, and f\in L^2(\Omega), the direct method gives a unique weak Dirichlet solution of

-\Delta u + a u + b u^{2k+1}=f.

The theorem states explicitly the integrability and Fréchet-derivative hypotheses for the odd-power potential and assumes that a supplied L^2-valued Nemytskii map agrees almost everywhere with a u+b u^{2k+1}. These are the assumptions that depend on the dimension and the available Sobolev embedding.

For a spatial set \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n, a nonlinearity g:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R, and forcing f\in L^2(\Omega), a field u\in H^1_0(\Omega) is a weak solution of the semilinear Dirichlet problem -\Delta u+g(x,u)=f in \Omega when for every test field v\in H^1_0(\Omega) the Nemytskii integrand x\mapsto g(x,u(x))\,v(x) is integrable and

\sum_{i=1}^n\int_\Omega\partial_iu\,\partial_iv\,dx +\int_\Omega g(x,u(x))\,v(x)\,dx =\int_\Omega f\,v\,dx.

The homogeneous Dirichlet condition is encoded by membership in H^1_0(\Omega), the closure in the graph-space norm of smooth functions compactly supported in \Omega. For open \Omega, this is the usual H^1_0 space, and the boundary condition is not a pointwise statement.

Here u(x) and v(x) are the canonical L^2 representatives of the base coordinates, and every integral uses the restricted domain measure of \Omega. Integrability is part of the definition because the Bochner integral is totalized: without it the identity could hold vacuously for a nonintegrable integrand. The nonlinear Poisson equation -\Delta u=h(u) is the autonomous case g(x,u)=-h(u) with zero forcing.

Pointwise convexity and integrability make the integral potential convex. Poincaré coercivity gives the Dirichlet form a positive ellipticity modulus. The abstract strongly convex variational theorem then supplies a unique minimizer, and its first variation is the displayed weak equation.

On a bounded spatial set in positive dimension, an integrable convex potential whose Fréchet derivative is represented by an L^2 Nemytskii map yields, for every f\in L^2(\Omega), a unique u\in H^1_0(\Omega) satisfying

\sum_i\int_\Omega\partial_i u\,\partial_i v\,dx +\int_\Omega g(x,u)v\,dx =\int_\Omega fv\,dx \qquad(v\in H^1_0(\Omega)),

the weak form of -\Delta u+g(x,u)=f. No Lipschitz smallness condition is used. The set \Omega need not be open or measurable: all integrals use its restricted domain measure.

Fix a smooth compactly supported variation v in \Omega. Compactness of \overline\Omega bounds both v and Dv, so u+tv lies in the minimizing neighborhood for sufficiently small |t|. The function t\mapsto J(u+tv) therefore has derivative zero at zero. The continuous second jet supplies the bounds needed to differentiate under the integral. Integration by parts transfers the derivatives of v to the flux, with no boundary term. The fundamental lemma makes each Euler–Lagrange component zero almost everywhere; its continuity upgrades this to every interior point.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n>0, be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary, and let u\in C^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^m). Assume L is jointly C^2 for x\in\Omega, with its values and its first two derivatives extending continuously to x\in\overline\Omega. Suppose some \varepsilon>0 satisfies

J(u)\le J(u+v)

for every globally C^2 perturbation v that vanishes on \partial\Omega and obeys \|v(x)\|+\|Dv(x)\|<\varepsilon on \overline\Omega. The Jacobian norm here is the elementwise supremum norm. Then at every x\in\Omega and for every component k,

-\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_i \left(L_{P_{ki}}(Du,u,x)\right)+L_{z_k}(Du,u,x)=0.

The minimizer is assumed to be C^2, and the equation is a necessary condition for it.

For a competitor in the same affine class, w-u is an admissible variation. The weak equation makes the integral on the right zero, giving the extended-energy comparison. An infinite-energy competitor is immediate; a finite-energy competitor also forces the solution's energy to be finite. This converse needs integrability of the tested derivative, but no power growth or coercivity, and it includes p=\infty with the supported-closure boundary class. Joint convexity matters here: the earlier existence argument only required convexity in the gradient.

Let 1\le p\le\infty. Retain the measurable density and shift with F(x,z)+b(x)\ge0 almost everywhere for every state, and the same affine variation class. Write Ju=(u,\nabla u) for a member u of that class. Assume F(x,s,\xi) is jointly convex in (s,\xi) almost everywhere and has its actual derivative at Ju. Suppose the tested derivative is integrable and has integral zero for every admissible variation. Then u minimizes the shifted extended energy in that affine class. This follows from the tangent-plane inequality:

F(x,Jw)-F(x,Ju)\geq dF(x,Ju)[Jw-Ju].

Mathlib proves this for a local minimum, which every global minimum supplies. Its proof moves away from the minimizer along a fixed direction. Near a local minimum the difference quotients of the energy are nonnegative, and they converge to the first variation applied to that direction, so this value is nonnegative. The same bound for the opposite direction makes it zero. Since the direction was arbitrary, the first variation is the zero continuous linear map.

At an unconstrained global minimizer of a Fréchet-differentiable real functional,

u\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}J \quad\Longrightarrow\quad DJ(u)=0\in H^*.

This is the Banach-space form of Evans's directional first-variation calculation. Variations that preserve boundary values need a constrained version, such as the mixed-density first-variation theorem.

Because every admissible \varphi is supported in U, the integral over U equals the integral over \mathbb R^n, so the hypothesis says that f integrates to zero against every smooth compactly supported function with support in the open set U. Mathlib's theorem for such functions then applies: smooth cutoffs supported in U approximate indicator functions of compact subsets of U, dominated convergence passes the vanishing integrals to those indicators, and a locally integrable function whose integral over every compact subset of U vanishes is zero almost everywhere on U.

Let U\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open and let f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R be locally integrable on U for Lebesgue measure. If

\int_U f\,\varphi\,dx=0

for every smooth compactly supported \varphi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R whose support lies in U, then f vanishes almost everywhere on U:

f(x)=0\qquad\text{for almost every }x\in U.

Only the behavior of f inside U matters: each test function vanishes near the boundary and outside the domain. This is the localization step of Evans's Euler–Lagrange derivation in §8.1.2, which passes from the vanishing first variation to the almost-everywhere equation.

At parameter zero, D\Phi_0(x)=I. The inverse function theorem constructs a jointly C^2 induced field satisfying the graph identity. Differentiating that identity at fixed spatial coordinates gives the field variation \eta-Du\,X. Differentiating the finite density invariance also gives the volume term L\operatorname{div}X. The product and chain rules assemble these terms into the divergence of the displayed current, plus the Euler–Lagrange residual paired with the field variation. That residual vanishes at x, leaving conservation of the current.

Fix x. Assume u is C^2 at x, L is jointly C^2 at (Du(x),u(x),x), and the maps (t,y)\mapsto\Phi_t(y) and (t,y,z)\mapsto\Psi_t(y,z) are jointly C^2 at (0,x) and (0,x,u(x)), respectively. Near x, suppose \Phi_0(y)=y and \Psi_0(y,u(y))=u(y). For the locally induced field U_t, assume that for all sufficiently small t,

L(DU_t(\Phi_t(x)),\Psi_t(x,u(x)),\Phi_t(x))\det D\Phi_t(x) =L(Du(x),u(x),x).

If u satisfies the Euler–Lagrange system at x, define X(y)=\partial_t\Phi_t(y)|_{t=0} and \eta(y)=\partial_t\Psi_t(y,u(y))|_{t=0}. Then the current

J_i=\sum_k L_{P_{ki}}(Du,u,y)\bigl(\eta-Du\,X\bigr)_k +L(Du,u,y)X_i

satisfies \operatorname{div}J(x)=0. All hypotheses are local at the specified points; a global inverse or a transformation group is not required.

A common Hölder bound controls the line derivative for -1\leq t\leq1. The mean value theorem gives integrability of the shifted density along u+tv from its integrability at u. The nearby extended integrals can therefore be compared as real integrals and differentiated at t=0; minimality makes that derivative zero. This uses no separate upper growth bound on the density and does not require b itself to be integrable.

Let 1\leq p<\infty and let q be its Hölder conjugate. The theorem takes the full derivative dF(x,z) in the product state z=(s,\xi), with \|dF(x,z)\|\leq h(x)+C\|z\|^{p-1} and h\in L^q. Differentiability and the bound hold for every state outside a fixed null set. The density and the evaluated derivative (x,z,w)\mapsto dF(x,z)[w] are jointly measurable.

Suppose u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega) minimizes the nonnegative extended integral of F(x,u,\nabla u)+b(x) in the prescribed affine class and has finite energy. Here b is measurable and F(x,z)+b(x)\geq0 for every state outside a fixed null set. For every variation v in the supported smooth-core closure, the first-variation integrand dF(x,(u,\nabla u))[(v,\nabla v)] is integrable and has integral zero. On open sets this variation space is W^{1,p}_0(\Omega).

This necessary condition includes p=1,\ q=\infty, starting from a given finite minimum. The existence theorem uses p>1.

To see the differential equation inside this identity, write A=\partial_sF and D=\nabla_\xi F. Assume joint measurability and, almost everywhere in x, joint continuity of these partial derivatives in (s,\xi). Suppose they satisfy the conjugate growth bound with |A|+\|D\| in place of \|dF\|. Mathlib's product differentiation theorem assembles the full derivative:

dF(x,s,\xi)[r,z]=A(x,s,\xi)r+\langle D(x,s,\xi),z\rangle.

Substituting this expression into the first variation gives

\int_\Omega \left(A(x,u,\nabla u)v+ \langle D(x,u,\nabla u),\nabla v\rangle\right)\,dx=0.

This is the weak equation -\operatorname{div}D+A=0. The integral is finite for every admissible variation; no derivative of the integral functional is assumed.

The finite family of value-gradient pairs is in L^p. Apply the same dominated integral-differentiation argument to this product state. Every line u+tv remains in the componentwise affine class, so minimality makes the derivative vanish.

Under the same measurability, differentiability, shifted lower bound, finite-energy minimum, and finite-exponent growth hypotheses, collect the component states in Ju(x)=((u_k(x),\nabla u_k(x)))_k and allow F(x,Ju) to couple them. A shared minimum theorem gives \int_\Omega dF(x,Ju)[Jv]\,dx=0 for every vector variation in the zero-boundary class. The growth bound uses the maximum norm on the finite family of states.
Use linearity of the Fourier transform to distribute over the finite sum, apply the iterated-derivative multiplier theorem term by term, and factor out the common transformed function.

An arbitrary finite one-dimensional constant-coefficient differential operator on Schwartz functions is diagonalized by the Fourier transform: the same finite coefficient polynomial is evaluated at the symbol 2\pi i\xi.
Under Mathlib's Fourier convention, the one-dimensional derivative symbol is 2\pi i\xi.

The Fourier transform of an integrable datum is bounded. Multiplication by the positive-time Gaussian therefore produces an integrable frequency profile. Fourier pairing and the Gaussian transform identify its inverse as \int G_t(x-y)g(y)\,dy. The proved heat-kernel construction then supplies joint smoothness, the analytic heat equation, and the joint initial trace. At exactly zero time the multiplier is one, so ordinary Fourier inversion uses the additional integrability of \widehat g. Schwartz decay supplies that assumption in the final corollary.

Let n\in\mathbb N and let g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R be bounded, continuous, and integrable. For t>0, the inverse Fourier formula

u(x,t)=\mathcal F^{-1} \bigl(e^{-4\pi^2t|\xi|^2}\widehat g(\xi)\bigr)(x)

is real, jointly smooth, and satisfies u_t=\Delta u. As (t,x)\to(0,x_0) from positive times, u(x,t)\to g(x_0). The evolved Fourier data are integrable at positive time even when \widehat g\notin L^1.

If \widehat g\in L^1 as well, the same formula at t=0 equals g pointwise and satisfies the full pointwise heat Cauchy predicate. Real Schwartz data satisfy all these hypotheses.

Both operators are scalar Fourier multipliers on the common domain. Their symbols 2\pi i\xi and -i\operatorname{sign}(\xi) commute pointwise, and the Hilbert symbol, of norm at most one, preserves square integrability of the derivative multiplier.

Let D be the partial linear operator on complex L^2(\mathbb R) whose natural Fourier domain consists of functions satisfying

(2\pi i\xi)\widehat f(\xi)\in L^2(\mathbb R).

The Hilbert transform preserves this domain, and every f in it satisfies D(Hf)=H(Df).

Both kernels are inverse Fourier transforms of integrable functions in L^2. The Poisson kernel \varepsilon/(\pi(\varepsilon^2+x^2)) is that of e^{-2\pi\varepsilon|\xi|}: split at \xi=0, the integral is a sum of two decaying exponentials. The conjugate kernel x/(\pi(\varepsilon^2+x^2)) is that of the damped symbol -i\operatorname{sign}(\xi)e^{-2\pi\varepsilon|\xi|}. These integrals agree almost everywhere with the L^2 inverse transform, and on the Fourier side H multiplies by -i\operatorname{sign}(\xi), so the two kernels form a Hilbert pair. Multiplying both by \pi removes the normalization. The rotation is H(Hf)=-f.

Real functions \omega,v on \mathbb R form a Hilbert pair when \omega agrees almost everywhere with some f\in L^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb C) and v with Hf. For every \varepsilon>0,

H\Big[\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon^2+x^2}\Big]=\frac{x}{\varepsilon^2+x^2}.

The Poisson kernel is the inverse Fourier transform of the Abel weight, \mathcal F^{-1}\big[e^{-2\pi\varepsilon|\xi|}\big](x)=\varepsilon/(\pi(\varepsilon^2+x^2)). Since H^2=-I, a Hilbert pair (\omega,v) gives the pair (v,-\omega).

Away from the null singleton \{0\}, the multiplier has norm one and its square is -1. Transfer those pointwise identities to L^2, conjugate by the unitary Fourier transform, and combine preservation of the inner product with H^2=-I to obtain skew-adjointness.

For every f,g\in L^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb C), the transform is an isometry, squares to minus the identity, and is skew-adjoint:

\|Hf\|_2=\|f\|_2,\qquad H(Hf)=-f,\qquad \langle Hf,g\rangle=-\langle f,Hg\rangle.

On complex L^2(\mathbb R), the Hilbert transform is the Fourier multiplier

\widehat{Hf}(\xi)=-i\,\operatorname{sign}(\xi)\widehat f(\xi),

with the symbol assigned the harmless value zero at \xi=0. The operator is this multiplier conjugated by Mathlib's unitary L^2 Fourier transform.
Induct on n, applying Mathlib's Fourier rule for one Fréchet derivative at the successor step and combining the two multipliers; then restrict to the line.

Let n be a nonnegative integer and let f map the line into a complex normed space. Assume it is n times continuously differentiable, with f and those derivatives integrable. Then the transform turns the derivative of that order into multiplication by (2\pi i\xi)^n.

Apply Plancherel to \Delta f, rewrite its Fourier transform using Mathlib's multidimensional Laplacian multiplier theorem, take the squared norm of the scalar multiple, and normalize the real absolute values using positivity of \pi and nonnegativity of the Euclidean norm.

For a Schwartz map f:\mathbb R^n\to H into a complex Hilbert space, Mathlib's Fourier convention gives the exact Plancherel identity

\int_{\mathbb R^n}\!\lVert\Delta f(x)\rVert^2\,dx =(2\pi)^4\int_{\mathbb R^n}\! \lVert\xi\rVert^4\lVert\widehat f(\xi)\rVert^2\,d\xi.

The fourth power of 2\pi is forced by squaring the Laplacian multiplier -(2\pi)^2\lVert\xi\rVert^2.

Linearity sends -u''+\lambda u to -\widehat{u''}+\lambda\widehat u. The second-derivative multiplier is (2\pi i\xi)^2=-(2\pi\xi)^2; the leading minus sign therefore changes it to (2\pi\xi)^2. Factoring \widehat u yields the shifted symbol ((2\pi\xi)^2+\lambda)\widehat u.

On Schwartz functions, Fourier transformation diagonalizes -\partial_{xx}+\lambda: the transformed operator is pointwise multiplication by its shifted elliptic symbol. This shifted resolvent specializes Evans's constant-coefficient transform method.

Take absolute values in the resolvent formula. The denominator is real and satisfies (2\pi\xi)^2+\lambda\geq\lambda>0, so its reciprocal is at most 1/\lambda. Multiplying by |\widehat f(\xi)| gives the pointwise estimate.

Let \lambda>0. Every Schwartz solution of -u''+\lambda u=f with Schwartz f satisfies, at every frequency \xi, the estimate

|\widehat u(\xi)|\le \frac{|\widehat f(\xi)|}{\lambda}.

Apply the shifted-multiplier identity at the chosen frequency. Since \lambda>0 and (2\pi\xi)^2\geq0, the symbol is strictly positive, so division gives the displayed formula. Multiplying by the symbol recovers the transformed equation at that frequency.

For Schwartz functions u,f and \lambda>0, fix a frequency \xi. The transformed equation \widehat{(-\partial_{xx}+\lambda)u}(\xi)=\widehat f(\xi) is equivalent to

\widehat u(\xi)= \frac{\widehat f(\xi)}{(2\pi\xi)^2+\lambda}.

The Fourier symbol of the one-dimensional shifted elliptic operator -\partial_{xx}+\lambda is

(2\pi\xi)^2+\lambda.

The factor 2\pi comes from Mathlib's normalization.

Fourier inversion sends the cosine mode to (g(x+t)+g(x-t))/2. Express the sinc mode as an integral of phases over [-1,1]; integrability justifies Fubini, and inversion gives \frac12\int_{x-t}^{x+t}h(y)\,dy. Thus the full formula, including the velocity contribution, equals d'Alembert's solution. Its established regularity, wave equation, assigned data, and joint derivative trace transfer through this identity.

Let the real displacement g\in C^2(\mathbb R) and velocity h\in C^1(\mathbb R) be integrable, with both Fourier transforms integrable. Then

u(x,t)=\mathcal F^{-1}\! \left(\cos(2\pi\xi t)\widehat g(\xi) +t\,\operatorname{sinc}(2\pi\xi t)\widehat h(\xi)\right)(x)

is real and jointly C^2 at every real time, and satisfies u_{tt}-u_{xx}=0, u(x,0)=g(x), and u_t(x,0)=h(x). The field and its actual time derivative also have the corresponding joint space-time initial traces. Here \operatorname{sinc}(z)=\sin z/z with value one at zero, so the zero-frequency velocity multiplier is t. Real Schwartz data give the stated Cauchy solution without extra integrability assumptions.

The cosine and sinc modes solve v_{tt}=-\omega^2v. On each bounded time interval, their values and first two time derivatives are bounded by polynomials in \|\xi\| times |\widehat g|+|\widehat h|. Mathlib's Schwartz Fourier transform supplies integrable bounds for all these moments.

Apply the parameter integral theorem twice, the second time to an integral with values in continuous linear maps. This gives the joint Hessian. Its time-time entry and the sum of its spatial diagonal entries agree because \omega^2=4\pi^2\|\xi\|^2. Taking real parts preserves that identity. At time zero, the cosine multiplier is one and the sinc multiplier vanishes; their time derivatives are zero and one. Fourier inversion therefore recovers g and h, and joint continuity of the field and its first derivative gives the two traces.

Let g,h\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R). Set \omega(\xi)=2\pi\|\xi\| and define

u(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}\mathcal F^{-1}\! \left(\cos(\omega(\xi)t)\widehat g(\xi) +t\,\operatorname{sinc}(\omega(\xi)t)\widehat h(\xi)\right)(x).

Then u is jointly C^2 on all of \mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n and

u_{tt}-\Delta u=0,\qquad u(x,0)=g(x),\qquad u_t(x,0)=h(x).

Both initial values are also joint limits as (t,x)\to(0,x_0). The real part in the definition gives a real field directly. The formula includes \xi=0, where the velocity multiplier is t, and every finite spatial dimension, including n=0.
Translation by f preserves the cobounded filter, and squaring a nonnegative quantity tending to infinity again tends to infinity.

The energy is coercive:

\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}\longrightarrow\infty \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J_f(u)\longrightarrow\infty.
Take square roots in the identity J_f(u_i)=\lVert u_i-f\rVert^2; conversely, continuity of the energy sends strong convergence to convergence of energy values.

For any filter-indexed family (u_i),

J_f(u_i)\longrightarrow0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u_i\longrightarrow f\ \text{strongly in }L^2.

For prescribed Hilbert-valued data f\in L^2(\mu;H), the quadratic fidelity functional is the integral

J_f(u)=\int \lVert u(x)-f(x)\rVert_H^2\,d\mu(x).

It is a concrete model of the coercive convex energies used by the direct method.
Mathlib's L² inner-product formula identifies the integral of the pointwise squared norm with the Hilbert norm squared.

The integral is exactly the square of the L^2 distance:

J_f(u)=\lVert u-f\rVert_{L^2(\mu;H)}^2.
Subtracting the strong-convexity correction ‖u‖² from ‖u-f‖² leaves an affine functional of u, which is convex.

The map u\mapsto J_f(u) is 2-strongly convex in Mathlib's normalization:

J_f((1-t)u+tv) \leq (1-t)J_f(u)+tJ_f(v)-t(1-t)\lVert u-v\rVert_{L^2}^2

for 0\leq t\leq1. It is therefore strictly convex; the numerical modulus is specific to the squared-distance model.
Weak lower semicontinuity and coercivity give existence, and strict convexity gives uniqueness. Since J_f(f)=0 and the energy is nonnegative, the unique minimizer is f.

When the coefficient Hilbert space is complete, the direct method gives a unique global minimizer, characterized by

\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{u\in L^2(\mu;H)}J_f(u)=\{f\}.

This is the quadratic case of Evans's existence and uniqueness pattern.
The squared-distance formula gives strong continuity, while strong convexity gives convexity. The theorem on closed convex sublevel sets then gives weak lower semicontinuity.

The quadratic integral is lower semicontinuous for the weak L^2 topology:

u_\alpha\rightharpoonup u \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J_f(u)\leq\liminf_\alpha J_f(u_\alpha).

The chain rule verifies the transport PDE for g(t-x). Causality gives g(-x)=0 when x\ge0, and setting x=0 gives the boundary signal. Translating the time integral yields the delay factor e^{-sx}. The initial-term rule transforms u_t to sU, and differentiating the exponential profile gives U_x=-sU. For each fixed nonnegative x, the delayed signal remains smooth, compactly supported, and causal. Apply vertical inversion to it to obtain the displayed reconstruction.

Let g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C be globally smooth, compactly supported, and zero at nonpositive times. The field u(t,x)=g(t-x) solves u_t+u_x=0 on x\ge0, has zero initial data there, and satisfies u(t,0)=g(t). Its time transform is U(s,x)=e^{-sx}Lg(s), with \partial_xU=-sU. For every real a, t>0, and x\ge0, the actual field is reconstructed by the absolutely convergent integral

u(t,x)=e^{at}\int_{\mathbb R} e^{2\pi i\xi t}e^{-(a+2\pi i\xi)x}Lg(a+2\pi i\xi)\,d\xi.

Integrate (e^{-st}f(t))'=e^{-st}f'(t)-s e^{-st}f(t). The boundary value at infinity is zero, while the lower endpoint, using the right-hand trace at zero, contributes -f(0). The improper fundamental theorem of calculus and the two integrability hypotheses justify this calculation.

For complex-valued f, the operational rule is

L(f')(s)=sLf(s)-f(0).

The general theorem assumes right continuity at zero, pointwise differentiability at positive times, integrability of e^{-st}f(t) and e^{-st}f'(t) on the positive half-line, and e^{-st}f(t)\to0 at infinity. A globally C^1, compactly supported function satisfies these conditions for every complex s.

Rewrite the half-line transform on a+2\pi i\xi as the Fourier transform of the damped causal extension. At a positive continuity point, Fourier inversion recovers e^{-at}f(t), and multiplication by e^{at} gives the formula. A smooth compactly supported causal function remains smooth and compactly supported after damping. Its Schwartz Fourier transform is integrable, which proves convergence rather than leaving it as an assumption in that case.

For a complex Banach-valued function f, write Lf(s)=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt. Fix a\in\mathbb R. If the damped causal extension \mathbf1_{(0,\infty)}(t)e^{-at}f(t) and the vertical trace \xi\mapsto Lf(a+2\pi i\xi) are integrable, then at every t>0 where f is continuous,

f(t)=e^{at}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{2\pi i\xi t}Lf(a+2\pi i\xi)\,d\xi.

For globally smooth, compactly supported f vanishing at nonpositive times, both integrability conditions are derived for every real a. The inversion integral converges absolutely.

The Euler–Lagrange expression at a point depends only on the second jet of the map there, and every second jet is realized by a polynomial map, which is smooth. This passes the null property from smooth maps to C^2 maps. For the action, extend u and v across the boundary to C^2 maps on the whole space, using reflection in the graph charts, and consider w_t=(1-t)u+tv. The first-variation identity writes \frac{d}{dt}\int_\Omega L(Dw_t,w_t,x)\,dx as the integral of the Euler–Lagrange expression of w_t against v-u, plus a boundary term that vanishes because v-u=0 on \partial\Omega. The Euler–Lagrange expression is zero, so the action is constant in t.

Let L be a null Lagrangian on an open set \Omega with C^2 joint dependence on its arguments. Then every C^2 map on \Omega also satisfies its Euler–Lagrange system. If \Omega is bounded with C^2 graph boundary and L has a continuous second jet, then two maps that are C^2 up to the boundary, continuous on \overline\Omega, and equal on \partial\Omega have the same action

\int_\Omega L(Du,u,x)\,dx=\int_\Omega L(Dv,v,x)\,dx.

The derivative of \det in the entry (k,i) is the cofactor (\operatorname{cof}P)_{ki}, at singular matrices as well, and the density does not depend on z. The Euler–Lagrange expression is therefore -\sum_i\partial_i(\operatorname{cof}Du)_{ki}, and the rows of the cofactor matrix of a C^2 map are divergence free. This is the Piola identity. Each cofactor is a sum of products of first derivatives, and after differentiation the mixed second derivatives cancel in pairs.

In every dimension n, the Euler–Lagrange expression of the determinant vanishes at every point where u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n is C^2. In particular the determinant is a null Lagrangian on every open set.

A density L:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is a null Lagrangian on \Omega if every smooth map u on \Omega satisfies the Euler–Lagrange system, with classical derivatives, at every point of \Omega. The determinant density is L(P,z,x)=\det P on square matrices.

Lift each map to the pair (Du_k,\det Du_k), with values in \mathbb R^{n\times n+1}. Weak convergence of the determinants, from W^{1,q} to L^{q/n}, makes the lifted sequence converge weakly. The mixed convex lower semicontinuity theorem for integrands convex in a weakly converging variable and continuous in a strongly converging one then applies, with the values u_k converging strongly by compact embedding.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n\ge1, be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary, and let q>n be real. Let F(x,s,P,d) be C^1 on \Omega\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^{n\times n}\times\mathbb R, convex in (P,d) for each x\in\Omega and s, and bounded below by -\beta on the graph d=\det P. If u_k\rightharpoonup u weakly in W^{1,q}(\Omega;\mathbb R^n), then

\int_\Omega F(x,u,Du,\det Du)\,dx \le\liminf_{k\to\infty}\int_\Omega F(x,u_k,Du_k,\det Du_k)\,dx.

A nonempty trace class is the affine class g+W^{1,q}_0 of any of its members. If every competitor has infinite energy, any member minimizes. Otherwise the coercivity bound makes a minimizing sequence bounded in W^{1,q}, reflexivity extracts a weakly convergent subsequence, the affine class is weakly closed, and lower semicontinuity shows that the limit minimizes.

Under the hypotheses of the lower semicontinuity theorem, suppose also that \alpha|P|^q-\beta\le F(x,s,P,\det P) with \alpha>0 and \beta of either sign. For every boundary datum \gamma whose trace class

A=\{u\in W^{1,q}(\Omega;\mathbb R^n): u=\gamma\text{ on }\partial\Omega\text{ in the trace sense}\}

is nonempty, the extended energy \int_\Omega F(x,u,Du,\det Du)\,dx attains its minimum on A. The same holds for an affine class g+W^{1,q}_0. If some member of A has finite energy, the minimizer's density is integrable and its energy is an ordinary real integral.

Subtract g(x) from the unknown. Analyticity of g and its spatial derivatives makes the transformed coefficients analytic and reduces the initial trace to zero. A majorant bounds the recursively constructed formal solution and gives a positive convergence radius. Compatibility of power series with products, substitution, and differentiation proves the PDE for the sum. Restoring g gives the original equation and trace. To include explicit time dependence, adjoin a clock component with derivative one and zero initial value; analytic uniqueness identifies it with t.

Let d,m\in\mathbb N. Suppose g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^m is analytic near 0, and every coefficient B_{jik}(t,z,x) and c_i(t,z,x) is analytic near (0,g(0),0). There are r>0 and an analytic field u on the coordinate ball \|(t,x)\|_\infty<r such that

\partial_tu_i(t,x)=\sum_{j=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m B_{jik}(t,u(t,x),x)\,\partial_{x_j}u_k(t,x)+c_i(t,u(t,x),x), \qquad u(0,x)=g(x).

The initial equality holds for every \|x\|_\infty<r. The dimensions may be zero. The time-independent coefficient version is stated separately at the center (g(0),0).

Construct an analytic level chart and interpolate the individual normal data to an analytic function. These constructions determine the lower jet, so a compatible extension of the data need not be given. The nonzero principal symbol lets the transformed equation solve for its highest transverse derivative. Reduction to analytic evolution gives a local solution, which is pulled back through the chart. Tangential differentiation of equal normal data recovers the full lower jet, and analytic uniqueness gives germ equality.

Let n,m\ge1, let p\in\Omega with \Omega open, and suppose \varphi is analytic near p, \varphi(p)=0, and \nabla\varphi(p)\ne0. Let g_0,\ldots,g_{m-1} be analytic near p; their restrictions to \Gamma=\{\varphi=0\} are the prescribed data. Use the unit normal \nu=\nabla\varphi/|\nabla\varphi|. Consider the scalar equation

\sum_{|\alpha|=m}a_\alpha(x,J_{<m}u(x))\,\partial^\alpha u(x) =b(x,J_{<m}u(x)).

Here J_{<m}u records all derivatives below order m. Let q_0 be the lower jet at p determined by the prescribed data. Assume the coefficient germs are analytic at (p,q_0) and \sum_{|\alpha|=m}a_\alpha(p,q_0)\nu(p)^\alpha\ne0. Then some ball B(p,r)\subseteq\Omega, r>0, carries an analytic solution of the equation with D_\nu^j u=g_j on \Gamma\cap B(p,r) for every j<m. Two analytic solution germs with the same normal data agree near p.

After subtracting the initial function, the recurrence determines every Taylor coefficient of either solution. Analytic functions with the same Taylor series agree near their center. Adjoining the clock reduces the explicitly time-dependent case to the same argument.

Under the same analytic coefficient and data hypotheses, two fields analytic near (0,0) that satisfy the equation there and have initial trace g near 0 agree on a neighborhood of (0,0). This is uniqueness of analytic germs at (0,0), and the neighborhood depends on the two solutions.

The scalar nonzero derivative gives the invertible partial derivative required by Mathlib's implicit-function theorem. Apply it to the composite at order k. Its graph preserves the level F(0,x_0,g(x_0),p_0), which is zero by the base equation, and passes through the prescribed point.

Assume F(0,x_0,g(x_0),p_0)=0, the derivative in p is nonzero there, and the composite (x,p)\mapsto F(0,x,g(x),p) has positive regularity order k at (x_0,p_0). Then an open neighborhood of x_0 carries a graph p=p(x) with

F(0,x,g(x),p(x))=0

throughout that neighborhood, p(x_0)=p_0, and the same regularity order at x_0. The theorem covers finite, smooth, and analytic orders. Choosing Mathlib's analytic order \omega gives the analytic initial graph.

An equation F(t,x,z,p)=0 is noncharacteristic in p at (t_0,x_0,z_0,p_0) when

p\longmapsto F(t_0,x_0,z_0,p)\ \text{is differentiable at }p_0, \qquad \partial_pF(t_0,x_0,z_0,p_0)\neq0.

This is the scalar implicit-function condition for the flat surface \{t=0\}.

The affine map (t,x)\mapsto x+ct is analytic, so composition with analytic g is jointly analytic. The chain rule gives u_t=c\,g'(x+ct) and u_x=g'(x+ct), hence u_t-cu_x=0. At t=0, the translated argument is x, so the initial trace is exactly g.

For analytic one-dimensional initial data, the translated profile

u(t,x)=g(x+ct)

is jointly analytic and satisfies

u_t-cu_x=0,\qquad u(0,x)=g(x).

Analyticity is preserved by composition with the affine characteristic map. The ordinary transport formula supplies the coordinate residual, with the velocity sign chosen to match u_t-v\cdot\nabla u=0.

For any n\in\mathbb N, a constant velocity v\in\mathbb R^n, and initial datum g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R real-analytic at every point, the translated profile

u(t,x)=g(x+t v)

is jointly analytic, has initial trace g, and satisfies u_t-v\mathbin{\cdot}\nabla u=0 on all of spacetime.

For the one-dimensional Cauchy problem u_t-cu_x=0, u(0,x)=g(x), the translated profile is u(t,x)=g(x+ct). The solution predicate records differentiability of each time and space slice, the pointwise identity u(0,x)=g(x), and vanishing of the residual for all t,x\in\mathbb R. The slice hypotheses make the residual a sum of true partial derivatives.
The forward direction is the local first-variation condition. Conversely, the Dirichlet principle makes every weak solution a global minimizer, hence a local minimizer.

For u\in H^1_0(\Omega),

u\text{ is a local minimizer of }J \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sum_i\int_\Omega\partial_i u\,\partial_i v\,dx =\int_\Omega fv\,dx \quad(v\in H^1_0(\Omega)).
Evaluate the Hessian as the Dirichlet form and use its diagonal identity in terms of the squared L^2 norms of the weak derivatives.

The diagonal Dirichlet Hessian is

D^2J(u)[v,v] =\sum_{i=1}^n\lVert\partial_i v\rVert_{L^2(\Omega)}^2,

expressed through the canonical weak-derivative maps.
Specialize the quadratic Hessian formula to the symmetric Dirichlet form and the continuous load induced by the forcing term.

For the Poisson Dirichlet energy on H^1_0(\Omega),

D^2J(u)[v,w] =\sum_{i=1}^n\int_\Omega \partial_i v\,\partial_i w\,dx.

Restrict the functional to the affine line t\mapsto u+tv. The restriction has a local minimum at zero, so its second derivative is nonnegative there; the chain rule identifies that derivative with D²F(u)[v,v].

If a C^2 real-valued functional on a real normed space has a local minimum at u, then

D^2F(u)[v,v]\geq0\qquad\text{for every }v.
Mathlib's symmetry theorem for second Fréchet derivatives supplies symmetry, and diagonal nonnegativity supplies the remaining positive-semidefinite condition.

The bilinear form underlying the Hessian at a local minimum is symmetric and positive semidefinite:

D^2F(u)[v,w]=D^2F(u)[w,v],\qquad D^2F(u)[v,v]\geq0\qquad(v,w\in E).

Differentiate J(u+tv) twice under the integral using the continuous second jet. The scalar second-derivative test gives the integral inequality. Next fix a smooth cutoff g supported in \Omega and use the pair v_s(y)=g(y)a\sin(\lambda\xi(y)) and v_c(y)=g(y)a\cos(\lambda\xi(y)). Adding their second variations cancels the mixed oscillatory terms and gives A+\lambda^2 B\ge0 for every real \lambda, where

B=\int_\Omega g^2 D^2_{PP}L(Du,u,y)[a\otimes\xi,a\otimes\xi]\,dy.

Hence B\ge0. If the continuous rank-one Hessian were negative at an interior point, a nonzero cutoff in a neighborhood where it stays negative would give B<0. This local contradiction proves the pointwise condition.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be bounded and open and u\in C^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^m). Assume L(P,z,x) is jointly C^2 for x\in\Omega, with its values and first two derivatives extending continuously to x\in\overline\Omega. If t\mapsto J(u+tv) has a local minimum at zero for a globally C^2 variation v, then

\delta^2J(u)[v,v]=\int_\Omega D^2L(Du,u,x)[(Dv,v,0),(Dv,v,0)]\,dx\ge0.

If this local-minimum condition holds for every smooth compactly supported vector variation in \Omega, then at every x\in\Omega,

D^2_{PP}L(Du(x),u(x),x)[a\otimes\xi,a\otimes\xi]\ge0 \qquad(a\in\mathbb R^m,\ \xi\in(\mathbb R^n)^*).

The domain needs no boundary regularity. The pointwise condition tests the matrix Hessian on rank-one directions only, and it is necessary for a minimum but not sufficient.
Fermat's theorem makes the derivative vanish at a local minimum. Substituting the derivative formula and evaluating the zero functional gives the weak equation.

Every unconstrained local minimizer satisfies the weak Euler equation

B(u,v)=\ell(v)\qquad\text{for every test direction }v.
Expand both bilinear arguments and the linear load, use symmetry on the two mixed terms, and collect coefficients.

For a symmetric bounded bilinear form B and continuous load \ell, the energy

J(u)=\frac12B(u,u)-\ell(u)

satisfies the exact expansion

J(u+v)=J(u)+B(u,v)-\ell(v)+\frac12B(v,v).
Mathlib's bilinear derivative rule differentiates B(u,u). Symmetry combines the two resulting terms, while the load differentiates to itself.

The Fréchet derivative of the quadratic energy at u is

DJ(u)[v]=B(u,v)-\ell(v),

or equivalently DJ(u)=B(u,-)-\ell as a continuous linear functional.
Identify the Hessian of the quadratic energy with B, then apply the abstract diagonal nonnegativity theorem at the local minimum.

At a local minimum, the second variation obeys the necessary condition

B(v,v)=D^2J(u)[v,v]\geq0 \qquad\text{for every }v.
The first-variation map is the affine map u\mapsto B(u,\mathbin\cdot)-\ell; its derivative is therefore the continuous linear map B.

The second Fréchet derivative of the quadratic energy is independent of the base point:

D^2J(u)[v,w]=B(v,w).
The coercivity estimate bounds the Lax–Milgram solution operator by c^{-1}. The inequality K < c therefore implies that its composition with the nonlinear load is a strict contraction.

An explicit ellipticity estimate

c\lVert v\rVert^2\leq B(v,v)\qquad(c>0)

gives \lVert S_B\rVert\leq c^{-1} and reduces the contraction condition to the transparent smallness hypothesis K<c. The threshold comes from the Lax–Milgram operator bound.

Lax–Milgram supplies the bounded solution operator S_B. For two fields, linearity of S_B and Lipschitz continuity of N give \|T(u)-T(v)\|\leq\|S_B\|K\|u-v\|. The assumed product is below one, so T is a strict contraction on the complete Hilbert space. Banach's fixed point theorem gives a unique u=T(u), and expanding that identity yields the semilinear weak equation.

A coercive variational operator plus a globally Lipschitz nonlinear dual load has a unique solution when the norm of the Lax–Milgram solution operator times the Lipschitz constant is strictly less than one. If S_B:H^*\to H is the linear solution operator and N:H\to H^* has Lipschitz constant K, then the Picard map

T(u)=S_B(\ell-N(u)),\qquad \operatorname{Lip}(T)\leq\lVert S_B\rVert K<1,

has a unique fixed point.

Let \Phi be a convex functional on a real Hilbert space H with Fréchet derivative D\Phi(u) at every point. For \lambda\geq0 and x\in H, the convex-gradient resolvent J_\lambda x is the unique u\in H with

\langle u,v\rangle+\lambda\,D\Phi(u)[v]=\langle x,v\rangle \qquad(v\in H),

that is, J_\lambda x+\lambda\nabla\Phi(J_\lambda x)=x. For \lambda>0 the Yosida approximation of the gradient is

A_\lambda x=\lambda^{-1}\bigl(x-J_\lambda x\bigr).

Existence and uniqueness of J_\lambda x come from the variational theorem applied to the inner-product form and the potential \lambda\Phi.

Since g(0)=0, composition by g maps L^2(\Omega) to itself with Lipschitz constant K. The base-coordinate map from H^1_0 to L^2 and the map sending h\in L^2 to the load v\mapsto\int_\Omega hv both have norm at most one. Thus the nonlinear load has Lipschitz constant at most K, and K<c gives existence and uniqueness by the abstract contraction theorem.

Let f\in L^2(\Omega) and suppose the Dirichlet form on H^1_0(\Omega) satisfies B(v,v)\geq c\|v\|_{H^1}^2 for every v, with c>0. Let g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R satisfy g(0)=0 and |g(a)-g(b)|\leq K|a-b| for all a,b, where 0\leq K<c. Then there is a unique u\in H^1_0(\Omega) satisfying

B(u,v)+\int_\Omega g(u)v\,dx=\int_\Omega fv\,dx \qquad(v\in H^1_0(\Omega))

The norm is the full H^1 graph norm, so the coercivity hypothesis includes control of the L^2 coordinate. This theorem gives a small-Lipschitz Banach-contraction regime.

Differentiate the three summands of J separately. The derivative of the linear load is \ell. Bilinearity gives the derivative of \frac12B(u,u) in direction v as \frac12(B(v,u)+B(u,v)); symmetry reduces this to B(u,v). Adding the given derivative of \Phi and subtracting the load proves the formula.

If \Phi has Fréchet derivative D\Phi(u) at u, symmetry of B gives

DJ(u)[v]=B(u,v)+D\Phi(u)[v]-\ell(v).

The proof assembles three ingredients. First, coercivity: the quadratic term satisfies \frac12 B(u,u)\geq\frac{c}{2}\|u\|^2, the potential is bounded below by -(a\|u\|+b), and the load contributes at most \|\ell\|\|u\|. For large norms these linear terms are absorbed, giving J(u)\geq\frac{c}{4}\|u\|^2-C, confirming that J(u)\to+\infty as \|u\|\to\infty. Second, strong convexity: for 0<t<1,

J((1-t)u+tv)\leq(1-t)J(u)+tJ(v)-\frac{c}{2}t(1-t)\|u-v\|^2,

which follows from the quadratic identity for B and convexity of \Phi. Third, lower semicontinuity: the quadratic and load terms are continuous, while lower semicontinuity of \Phi is assumed. Convexity then upgrades this strong lower semicontinuity to weak lower semicontinuity through closed convex sublevel sets. The coercive direct method gives existence; the strict convexity inequality shows any two minimizers coincide.

If B(u,u)\geq c\lVert u\rVert^2 for c>0, \Phi is convex and lower semicontinuous, and for some a\geq0 and b\in\mathbb R

\Phi(u)\geq-\bigl(a\lVert u\rVert+b\bigr),

then J is coercive and strongly convex. Hence

\exists!\,u\in H,\qquad J(u)=\inf_{v\in H}J(v).

The hypotheses are abstract sufficient conditions.

For \lambda\geq0, a symmetric nonnegative form B, and a differentiable convex potential \Phi, the semilinear-energy resolvent J_\lambda x is the unique field satisfying

\langle J_\lambda x,v\rangle+ \lambda\bigl(B(J_\lambda x,v)+D\Phi(J_\lambda x)[v]\bigr) =\langle x,v\rangle

for every test vector v.

For a symmetric elliptic form B, nonlinear potential \Phi, and load \ell, the energy is

J(u)=\frac12B(u,u)+\Phi(u)-\ell(u).
Differentiate the energy at the minimizer, apply the vanishing first-variation theorem, and evaluate the resulting zero continuous linear functional on an arbitrary test vector.

Every differentiable global minimizer satisfies the weak semilinear equation

B(u,v)+D\Phi(u)[v]=\ell(v) \qquad\text{for every }v\in H.

The Lean theorem assumes the full Fréchet derivative as data.

Convexity of \Phi implies monotonicity of its Fréchet derivative. For any u_1,u_2\in H, convexity gives

\Phi(u_2)\geq\Phi(u_1)+D\Phi(u_1)[u_2-u_1], \qquad \Phi(u_1)\geq\Phi(u_2)+D\Phi(u_2)[u_1-u_2].

Adding these two inequalities yields (D\Phi(u_1)-D\Phi(u_2))[u_1-u_2]\geq 0, which is precisely monotonicity of the map u\mapsto D\Phi(u). With this monotonicity established, the abstract monotone stability theorem applies directly to the two Euler–Lagrange equations. Setting \ell_1=\ell_2 gives \|u_1-u_2\|\leq 0, hence uniqueness.

For a differentiable convex potential and a bilinear form with coercivity modulus c>0, weak solutions with loads \ell_1 and \ell_2 satisfy

\lVert u_1-u_2\rVert \leq \frac{\lVert \ell_1-\ell_2\rVert}{c}.

Continuity turns each assumed iterative limit into a fixed point. The order-interval iteration theorem compares every fixed point with every lower or upper iterate, and closedness of the order passes those inequalities to the limit. The fixed-point equation is then rewritten as the semilinear weak equation.

Let the ambient ordered Hilbert space have closed order relation, let the linear form be bounded and coercive, and let N:V\to V^* be continuous. Assume \underline u\leq\overline u and that the semilinear Picard map is monotone and preserves [\underline u,\overline u]. If the iterates from the lower endpoint converge, their limit is the least weak solution in the interval. If the iterates from the upper endpoint converge, their limit is the greatest weak solution there.

Convergence of the iterates is a hypothesis, since order monotonicity gives no compactness or strong convergence in the ambient Hilbert space.

Coercivity of B and semimonotonicity of N make A(u)=B(u,\cdot)+N(u) strongly monotone with modulus m=c-L>0, that is m\lVert u-w\rVert^2\leq(A(u)-A(w))[u-w]. Injectivity follows as in the monotone stability estimate. For surjectivity, identify H^* with H through the Riesz map and, for a target b, consider the forward step F_\tau(u)=u-\tau\bigl(A(u)-b\bigr). Expanding the square and using strong monotonicity together with the Lipschitz constant K of A gives \lVert F_\tau(u)-F_\tau(w)\rVert^2\leq(1-2\tau m+\tau^2K^2)\lVert u-w\rVert^2, so F_\tau is a contraction for small \tau>0. Its Banach fixed point satisfies A(u)=b. The unique-solvability form restates bijectivity load by load.

Let H be a real Hilbert space, B a bounded bilinear form with c\lVert z\rVert^2\leq B(z,z) for all z, and N:H\to H^* globally Lipschitz. Suppose N is semimonotone with loss L<c:

-L\lVert u-w\rVert^2\leq\bigl(N(u)-N(w)\bigr)[u-w]\qquad(u,w\in H).

Then the semilinear operator u\mapsto B(u,\cdot)+N(u) is a bijection of H onto H^*; equivalently, for every \ell\in H^*,

\exists!\,u\in H,\qquad B(u,v)+N(u)[v]=\ell(v)\quad(v\in H).

Monotone N with c>0 is the case L=0. The Lipschitz constant of N may be arbitrarily large. The proof is a forward-step contraction in Hilbert space rather than an application of the Browder–Minty theorem.

Subtract the two weak equations evaluated at the same test vector v:

B(u_1-u_2,v)+(N(u_1)-N(u_2))[v]=(\ell_1-\ell_2)[v].

Choose v=u_1-u_2. On the left, coercivity gives B(u_1-u_2,u_1-u_2)\geq c\|u_1-u_2\|^2, and monotonicity of N gives (N(u_1)-N(u_2))[u_1-u_2]\geq 0. Together:

c\|u_1-u_2\|^2\leq(\ell_1-\ell_2)[u_1-u_2] \leq\|\ell_1-\ell_2\|_{H^*}\|u_1-u_2\|.

If u_1=u_2 the estimate is trivial. Otherwise divide both sides by \|u_1-u_2\|>0 and then by c>0 to obtain the stated bound.

For a coercive bilinear form and a nonlinear dual-valued map that is monotone between two candidate states, subtracting their weak equations gives

\lVert u_1-u_2\rVert \leq \frac{\lVert \ell_1-\ell_2\rVert}{c}.

The estimate takes the two weak equations as hypotheses and uses no existence theorem or variational construction.

Compare the envelope at x and y using J_\lambda y and J_\lambda x as opposite competitors. Expanding the quadratic penalties and using monotonicity bounds the first-order remainder by \|y-x\|^2/(2\lambda). Dividing by \|y-x\| proves differentiability with gradient A_\lambda x, without differentiating the minimizing map. For convergence, choosing x as a competitor gives e_\lambda\Phi(x)\leq\Phi(x), while convexity gives the quantitative reverse bound \Phi(x)\leq e_\lambda\Phi(x)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\nabla\Phi(x)\|^2. The two bounds squeeze the envelope to \Phi(x) as \lambda\downarrow0.

For \lambda>0, the Moreau envelope is differentiable with gradient equal to the Yosida approximation,

\nabla e_\lambda\Phi(x)=A_\lambda x =\lambda^{-1}(x-J_\lambda x),

and it converges pointwise to the original functional:

e_\lambda\Phi(x)\longrightarrow\Phi(x) \qquad(\lambda\downarrow0).

The map u\mapsto\ell-N(u) is K-Lipschitz into H^*, and the bounded linear operator S_B multiplies Lipschitz constants by at most \lVert S_B\rVert, so T is q-Lipschitz; the hypothesis q<1 makes it a contraction. If T(u)=u, then u is the Lax–Milgram solution for the load \ell-N(u), so B(u,v)=\ell(v)-N(u)[v] for every v. Conversely, that identity says u is a weak solution for the load \ell-N(u), and uniqueness of Lax–Milgram solutions gives T(u)=u. The Picard solution is the fixed point of the contraction, so it satisfies the weak equation.

If N is Lipschitz with constant K and q=\lVert S_B\rVert K<1, then the Picard map is a contraction with constant q:

\lVert T(u)-T(w)\rVert\leq q\,\lVert u-w\rVert\qquad(u,w\in H).

A field u is a fixed point of T if and only if it solves the semilinear weak equation

B(u,v)+N(u)[v]=\ell(v)\qquad(v\in H),

and in particular the Picard solution satisfies this equation for every test field v.

Let B be a bounded coercive bilinear form on a real Hilbert space H, let N:H\to H^* be a nonlinear load, and let \ell\in H^*. Writing S_B:H^*\to H for the Lax–Milgram solution operator of B, the Picard map freezes the nonlinearity and solves the remaining linear problem:

T(u)=S_B\bigl(\ell-N(u)\bigr), \qquad\text{so that}\qquad B(T(u),v)=\ell(v)-N(u)[v]\quad(v\in H).

When N is Lipschitz with constant K and \lVert S_B\rVert K<1, the Picard solution is the fixed point of T supplied by Banach's theorem. The contraction hypothesis is an explicit argument of the Picard solution.

For a functional \Phi:H\to\mathbb R, a parameter \lambda, and a base point x, the proximal energy is

E_\lambda(x;u)=\Phi(u)+\frac{\lVert x-u\rVert^2}{2\lambda}.

When \Phi is convex and differentiable and \lambda>0, the Moreau envelope of \Phi is the proximal energy evaluated at the resolvent,

e_\lambda\Phi(x)=E_\lambda(x;J_\lambda x) =\Phi(J_\lambda x)+\frac{\lVert x-J_\lambda x\rVert^2}{2\lambda}.

The Lean definition uses this evaluated form; the proximal minimization theorem shows that it is the minimum value of E_\lambda(x;\cdot) over H.

With c>0 and \lambda>0, the resolvent estimate has contraction factor q=(1+\lambda c)^{-1}<1. Banach's theorem gives a unique fixed point and convergence of every resolvent iterate to it. Substituting J_\lambda u=u in the resolvent equation cancels the identity terms and shows B(u,v)+D\Phi(u)[v]=0 for every v; conversely every such zero is fixed.
For a positive coercivity modulus and positive step size, iterating the semilinear-energy resolvent from any initial field converges to the unique zero of u\mapsto B u+D\Phi(u).

Write J=J_\lambda x. Convexity gives the supporting-hyperplane bound D\Phi(J)[u-J]\leq\Phi(u)-\Phi(J), while the resolvent equation tested with u-J identifies \langle x-J,u-J\rangle with \lambda\,D\Phi(J)[u-J]. Expanding \lVert x-u\rVert^2=\lVert x-J\rVert^2-2\langle x-J,u-J\rangle+\lVert u-J\rVert^2 and inserting these two facts yields the three-point inequality. Dropping its nonnegative middle term shows that J is a minimizer. If u is any minimizer, comparing with J in the three-point inequality forces \lVert u-J\rVert^2/(2\lambda)\leq0, hence u=J.

Let \Phi be convex on H with Fréchet derivative D\Phi(u) at every u, and let \lambda>0. For every x\in H the resolvent satisfies the strong three-point inequality

E_\lambda(x;J_\lambda x)+\frac{\lVert u-J_\lambda x\rVert^2}{2\lambda} \leq E_\lambda(x;u)\qquad(u\in H).

Consequently J_\lambda x minimizes E_\lambda(x;\cdot), and the proximal energy has exactly one global minimizer:

\exists!\,u\in H,\qquad E_\lambda(x;u)\leq E_\lambda(x;v)\quad(v\in H).

Subtract the two resolvent equations and test with J_\lambda x-J_\lambda y. The identity term gives the squared norm, coercivity of B gives \lambda c times that squared norm, and monotonicity of D\Phi gives a nonnegative contribution. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the right side by \|x-y\|\|J_\lambda x-J_\lambda y\|; cancellation yields the factor (1+\lambda c)^{-1}.

If B(u,u)\geq c\lVert u\rVert^2 with c\geq0 and \lambda\geq0, then

\lVert J_\lambda x-J_\lambda y\rVert \leq\frac{\lVert x-y\rVert}{1+\lambda c}.

Positive c and \lambda make the resolvent a strict contraction.

Choose a direct-method minimizer and apply the first-variation bridge. Convexity makes the potential derivative monotone, so the load-stability estimate with equal loads proves uniqueness among all weak solutions.

For a bounded symmetric form B with coercivity modulus c>0, and under the global differentiability and convexity assumptions on the potential, the variational route produces

\exists!\,u\in H,\qquad B(u,v)+D\Phi(u)[v]=\ell(v)\quad(v\in H).

Each Yosida value lies in the subdifferential at its resolvent point. Writing A_\lambda=\lambda^{-1}(I-J_\lambda), monotonicity of the subdifferential at those two points rearranges to \langle A_\lambda x-A_\lambda y,x-y\rangle \geq\lambda\|A_\lambda x-A_\lambda y\|^2. This is \lambda-cocoercivity. Monotonicity follows at once, and Cauchy–Schwarz gives the 1/\lambda Lipschitz bound.

For \lambda>0 and a differentiable convex functional, its Yosida approximation A_\lambda=\lambda^{-1}(I-J_\lambda) is \lambda-cocoercive. In particular, the approximation is monotone and has global Lipschitz constant 1/\lambda.

Set a=(n+1)\pi. Differentiating x\mapsto\sin(ax) twice with the chain rule gives -a^2\sin(ax), which is -\lambda_nw_n(x). The traces follow from \sin0=0 and \sin((n+1)\pi)=0. Evaluating at x=1/(2(n+1)) gives \sin(\pi/2)=1\neq0, so the mode is nontrivial.

Each sine mode is a nontrivial Dirichlet eigenfunction on the unit interval: for every x\in\mathbb R,

w_n''(x)=-\lambda_n\,w_n(x),

together with the endpoint traces w_n(0)=w_n(1)=0 and w_n\not\equiv0.

For n\in\mathbb N, the nth unit-interval Dirichlet sine mode and its eigenvalue are

w_n(x)=\sin\bigl((n+1)\pi x\bigr),\qquad \lambda_n=\bigl((n+1)\pi\bigr)^2.

Indexing starts at zero, so every mode has a positive frequency. These are the one-dimensional instance of the Dirichlet eigenfunctions -\Delta w=\lambda w in U, w=0 on \partial U, in which Evans's separation of variables expands the solution.

The sine eigenfunction and exponential time factor satisfy the two separated ordinary differential equations. The product calculation gives the heat residual, while direct evaluation gives the two boundary traces and initial trace. The product of a sine and an exponential is smooth, hence jointly C^2.

For every positive Dirichlet sine frequency on the unit interval, the mode

u_n(t,x)=\sin((n+1)\pi x) \exp\!\left(-((n+1)\pi)^2t\right)

is jointly C^2 and satisfies u_t-u_{xx}=0, u_n(t,0)=u_n(t,1)=0, and u_n(0,x)=\sin((n+1)\pi x).
The constant-multiple rule gives u_t=XT' and u_{xx}=X''T. Substituting T'=-\lambda T and X''=-\lambda X makes both expressions equal to -\lambda XT, so their difference is zero.

If

X''=-\lambda X,\qquad T'=-\lambda T,

then u(t,x)=X(x)T(t) satisfies

u_t-u_{xx}=0.

The verified differentiator computes u_t=-e^{-t}\sin x and u_{xx}=-e^{-t}\sin x; normalization therefore proves the symbolic residual is zero. The analytic bridge proves that these symbolic derivatives equal the corresponding Euclidean partial derivatives everywhere, so the ordinary heat residual also vanishes.

The explicit mode

u(t,x)=e^{-t}\sin x

has zero analytic heat residual on all of one-dimensional spacetime.

The sine factors solve oscillator equations with the same eigenvalue. The product calculation supplies the wave residual, and the boundary and initial conditions follow from sine identities and a derivative at time zero. The product of two sines is smooth, hence jointly C^2.

The interval mode

u_n(t,x)=\sin((n+1)\pi x)\sin((n+1)\pi t)

is jointly C^2 and satisfies u_{tt}-u_{xx}=0, homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, u_n(0,x)=0, and \partial_tu_n(0,x)=(n+1)\pi\sin((n+1)\pi x). It is a concrete wave analogue of the separated boundary-value calculations in Evans §4.1.
Differentiate the product twice in each variable: u_{tt}=XT'' and u_{xx}=X''T. The two oscillator equations identify both with -\lambda XT, hence u_{tt}-u_{xx}=0.

If

X''=-\lambda X,\qquad T''=-\lambda T,

then u(t,x)=X(x)T(t) satisfies u_{tt}-u_{xx}=0. For positive \lambda the time factor oscillates, where the heat time factor decays.

For fixed t with L(t)\neq0, the centered dilation x\mapsto L(t)(x-x_0) is onto V, so the supremum of \lVert F(L(t)(x-x_0))\rVert over x equals the supremum of \lVert F(y)\rVert over y, and the amplitude factors out of the norm and then out of the supremum. For the sampled growth statement, follow the moving point x(t)=x_0+L(t)^{-1}y, where the ansatz equals A(t)F(y); divergence of its norm forces divergence of the supremum. For the backward field, the amplitude (T-t)^{-\alpha} is positive for t<T and tends to +\infty as t\uparrow T when \alpha>0, so \lVert A(t)F(y)\rVert=(T-t)^{-\alpha}\lVert F(y)\rVert diverges at any coordinate with F(y)\neq0. A global profile bound \lVert F(y)\rVert\le C gives S_u(t)\le\operatorname{ofReal}((T-t)^{-\alpha}C)<+\infty for each t<T, which supplies the finite-slice condition.

Let u(x,t)=A(t)\,F\bigl(L(t)(x-x_0)\bigr) be a scaled profile ansatz on a real vector space V with values in a normed space E. At every time with L(t)\neq0, the extended spatial supremum of u is the amplitude times that of the profile,

S_u(t)=\operatorname{ofReal}|A(t)| \cdot\sup_{y\in V}\operatorname{ofReal}\lVert F(y)\rVert,

including the case of an unbounded profile. In that case both sides are +\infty when A(t)\neq0, and both are zero when A(t)=0. If along a filter of times L(t)\neq0 eventually and \lVert A(t)F(y)\rVert\to+\infty at one fixed similarity coordinate y, then S_u(t)\to+\infty along that filter. In particular, the backward self-similar field u(x,t)=(T-t)^{-\alpha}F\bigl((T-t)^{-\beta}(x-x_0)\bigr) with \alpha>0 and a profile taking at least one nonzero value satisfies

S_u(t)\longrightarrow+\infty\qquad(t\uparrow T),

with no boundedness assumption on the profile. If the profile is bounded, then the spatial supremum is also finite for every t<T, so the field satisfies SpatialSupNormBlowsUpAt at T. The spatial exponent \beta is unrestricted: it moves the sampled point but not the amplitude. The first two statements need only a norm and a compatible real scaling on E; the backward-field statements take E to be a real normed space.

Set s=T-t>0. Then s^{-\alpha}\to+\infty as s\downarrow0 for \alpha>0. Differentiating s^{-\alpha}F(s^{-\beta}(x-x_0)) uses s'=-1: the two minus signs turn the amplitude contribution positive, and the similarity-coordinate derivative contributes \beta y\cdot\nabla F. Both terms contain the common factor s^{-\alpha-1}.

For t<T, the backward scale (T-t)^{-\alpha} is positive, and it diverges as t\uparrow T when \alpha>0. If the profile is differentiable at y=(T-t)^{-\beta}(x-x_0), differentiating the backward self-similar field produces the common factor (T-t)^{-\alpha-1} and the scaling generator \alpha F+\beta y\cdot\nabla F. This is the kinematic identity used before a model-specific profile equation is imposed.

The potential u^m is C^1 across the edge and its actual gradient is \nabla(u^m)=-(\beta/t)xu. Under x=t^\beta y, the identity \alpha=n\beta cancels the Jacobian against the amplitude. The test pairing becomes \int F_C(y)\psi(t,t^\beta y)\,dy. Differentiate on this fixed compact profile domain and use the flux identity to obtain the weak PDE, including its time endpoints. No classical derivative of the density at the edge is required.

The mass scales as M(C)=C^{1/(m-1)+n/2}M(1), with 0<M(1)<\infty, so choosing C=(M/M(1))^{1/(1/(m-1)+n/2)} gives mass M. Finally t^\beta y\to0; the integrable bound F_C(y)\|\varphi\|_\infty permits dominated convergence and gives the initial trace.

Let m>1 and M>0. There is an explicit C>0 such that

u(t,x)=t^{-\alpha}F_C(t^{-\beta}x),\qquad t>0,\ x\in\mathbb R^n,

has mass M at every positive time and solves the weak porous-medium equation through its free boundary. For every 0<a\le b and every C^1 spacetime test \psi,

\int_a^b\int_{\mathbb R^n} \bigl(u\psi_t-\nabla(u^m)\cdot\nabla\psi\bigr)\,dx\,dt =\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(b,x)\psi(b,x)\,dx -\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(a,x)\psi(a,x)\,dx.

For every bounded continuous \varphi,

\lim_{t\downarrow0}\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(t,x)\varphi(x)\,dx=M\varphi(0).

This is the prescribed Dirac initial trace M\delta_0 of the explicit solution.

On t>0, differentiate u=x/t to obtain u_t=-x/t^2 and \partial_x(u^2/2)=\partial_x(x^2/(2t^2))=x/t^2. The verified symbolic calculation proves these terms cancel pointwise. Integrating the zero residual over any subdomain of positive spacetime gives zero.

For every subdomain of positive spacetime, the conservation-law residual

u_t+\partial_x\!\left(\frac{u^2}{2}\right)

of the smooth rarefaction interior integrates to zero. The theorem combines the ordinary similarity statement with a CAS-checked pointwise residual.
Choose amplitude exponent \alpha=0, spatial exponent \beta=1, center x_0=0, and profile F(\xi)=\xi. The forward ansatz becomes F(t^{-1}x)=x/t whenever t>0, exactly the rarefaction interior.

On positive time, the smooth interior Burgers rarefaction

u(t,x)=\frac{x}{t}

is the similarity profile F(x/t) with F(\xi)=\xi. The positive-time domain is explicit because the profile is singular at t=0.

Differentiate the scalar amplitude and the space-time composition separately. The derivative of (L(\tau)x,t(\tau)) is (L'(\tau)x,t'(\tau)); applying the Fréchet chain rule and then the product rule gives the displayed formula. At fixed time, differentiating x\mapsto A f(Lx,t) in the direction a x gives A\,Df[L(a x)], which is A L\,Df[a x] by linearity.

Assume the three scale functions are differentiable at \tau and f is jointly differentiable at (L(\tau)x,t(\tau)). The time derivative splits into amplitude, physical-time, and moving-coordinate terms:

\partial_\tau\widetilde f =A'f+A\bigl(t'\partial_t f+Df[L'x]\bigr).

The companion spatial theorem states that advection by a x contributes A L\,Df[a x]. These two identities are the chain rules behind the dynamically rescaled Boussinesq equations.

For time-dependent amplitude A(\tau), spatial scale L(\tau), physical time t(\tau), and a field f, the dynamic pullback is

\widetilde f(x,\tau)=A(\tau)f(L(\tau)x,t(\tau)).

The construction is purely kinematic: no PDE and no law for the three scale functions enters.

Differentiate the amplitude t^\alpha and the similarity coordinate y(t)=t^{-\beta}(x-x_0) separately. The power rule gives (t^\alpha)'=\alpha t^{\alpha-1} and y'=-\beta t^{-1}y. The product and Fréchet chain rules then give \alpha t^{\alpha-1}F(y)-\beta t^{\alpha-1}DF(y)y, which is the stated generator formula.
