The time derivative of a scaled profile splits into the derivative of its amplitude and the derivative of its moving similarity coordinate. In particular, for positive time the forward ansatz satisfies the generator identity

\frac{d}{dt}\left[t^\alpha F\!\left(t^{-\beta}(x-x_0)\right)\right] =t^{\alpha-1}\left(\alpha F(y)-\beta DF(y)y\right), \qquad y=t^{-\beta}(x-x_0).

The theorem is vector-valued and assumes differentiability only at the similarity point used in the calculation.

Insert ax and a^2t into \Gamma_n(x,t)=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}\exp(-\|x\|^2/(4t)). The quotient in the exponent is unchanged because both \|ax\|^2 and the time denominator gain a^2. Positivity of a lets the prefactor simplify as (a^2)^{-n/2}=a^{-n}, yielding the stated scaling law.

For a>0 and t>0, the Euclidean heat kernel obeys the exact parabolic scaling law

\Gamma_n(ax,a^2t)=a^{-n}\Gamma_n(x,t).

Positivity excludes the totalized nonpositive-time branch and removes every ambiguity in the real powers.

Put U(z)=A\operatorname{sech}^2(kz). Direct differentiation gives U''=4k^2U-(6k^2/A)U^2. With A=3c/a and k=\sqrt{c/b}/2, the identities c=4bk^2 and aA=12bk^2 give bU''-cU+(a/2)U^2=0. Differentiate this identity once and apply the traveling-wave chain rule to obtain the KdV residual. Positivity of b,c makes k>0, so decay of the hyperbolic secant gives localization.

For a\ne0, b>0, c>0, and x_0\in\mathbb R, the smooth field

u(t,x)=\frac{3c}{a}\operatorname{sech}^2 \left(\frac{\sqrt{c/b}}{2}(x-ct-x_0)\right)

solves u_t+a u u_x+b u_{xxx}=0 at every spacetime point. Its profile tends to zero at both spatial infinities. The center value is 3c/a, positive when a>0. Thus the coefficient convention matters: a=b=1 gives center value 3c, whereas a=6, b=1 gives c/2.

The forward self-similar ansatz is

u(t,x)=t^\alpha f\!\left(t^{-\beta}(x-x_0)\right).

The function is total in Lean; analytic theorems state domains such as t>0 explicitly.

At fixed time, the map x\mapsto y=L(t)(x-x_0) has derivative L(t)I. The Euclidean chain rule therefore contributes one factor of L(t) to each first spatial derivative and leaves the scalar amplitude A(t) unchanged. For the Laplacian, translation commutes with each partial derivative and the dilation contributes L(t)^2, for any profile; the divergence identity is the same coordinate calculation componentwise.

Centered dilation contributes one spatial-scale factor to a gradient or divergence and two factors to a Laplacian. Thus a scalar ansatz with amplitude A(t) and spatial scale L(t) obeys

\nabla_x u=A(t)L(t)\nabla F(y),\qquad \Delta_x u=A(t)L(t)^2\Delta F(y).

The gradient identity requires differentiability of F at y; the divergence identity requires differentiability of each vector-field component there. The Laplacian identity holds without assuming F\in C^2(\mathbb R^n). No time regularity of A or L is needed for these fixed-time identities.
Apply the chain rule to u(t,x)=f(x-ct). It gives u_t=-c f'(x-ct) and u_x=f'(x-ct). Therefore u_t+c u_x=(-c+c)f'(x-ct)=0.
Every differentiable traveling-wave profile satisfies the one-dimensional transport equation u_t+c u_x=0.

The traveling-wave construction sends a profile f and speed c to

u(t,x)=f(x-ct).

The canonical representatives of (1-t)u+tv agree almost everywhere with the same affine combination of the representatives of u and v, both in the base coordinate and every weak-derivative coordinate. Apply pointwise convexity of F(x,-,-) to these jets for almost every x, then integrate the resulting inequality. Linearity of the integral gives the stated convex combination of energies.

Almost-everywhere compatibility of canonical Sobolev representatives with affine combinations, pointwise joint convexity in (z,p), and integrability of every admissible density imply

J_F((1-t)u+tv)\leq(1-t)J_F(u)+tJ_F(v) \qquad(0\leq t\leq1).

Joint convexity is a clean sufficient condition for this theorem.

Given a density F(x,z,p), the functional is the integral

J_F(u)=\int_\Omega F(x,u(x),Du(x))\,dx.

For the unconstrained Hilbert result, the Sobolev integral theorem supplies weak lower semicontinuity, and the coercive direct method attains the infimum.

For the affine result, write each competitor as g+w with w\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega). The gradient lower bound and Poincaré control the W^{1,p} norm of corrections in the sublevel below the finite competitor. Reflexivity and separability give a weakly convergent subsequence of a minimizing sequence in this closed Sobolev subspace. Compactness of its base coordinate gives strong L^p convergence of the values; adding the fixed field g preserves that convergence. The gradients remain bounded and converge weakly along the same subsequence. Apply the preceding sequential inequality with a=-b. The limit stays in the affine class and its energy is no larger than the infimum approached by the sequence, hence it minimizes. Comparison with the finite competitor makes its energy finite.

Pointwise convexity, density integrability, strong lower semicontinuity, and coercivity give

\exists u\in H^1(\Omega),\qquad J_F(u)=\inf_{v\in H^1(\Omega)}J_F(v).

This first conclusion is unconstrained. The mixed-energy result works in a prescribed affine class. Let n\geq1, let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be bounded and measurable, and let 1<p<\infty. Assume the measurability, value-continuity, and gradient convexity and differentiability hypotheses of the sequential lower-semicontinuity theorem, with Lebesgue measure restricted to \Omega. Suppose that b:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is measurable and that, for some c>0, almost every x satisfies

F(x,s,z)\geq c|z|^p-b(x)\qquad\text{for every }s\in\mathbb R,\ z\in\mathbb R^n.

For g\in W^{1,p}(\Omega), set \mathcal A=g+W^{1,p}_0(\Omega) and define

J_b^+(u)=\int_\Omega\bigl(F(x,u(x),\nabla u(x))+b(x)\bigr)\,dx \in[0,\infty].

If one v_0\in\mathcal A has J_b^+(v_0)<\infty, there is a u\in\mathcal A such that

J_b^+(u)<\infty,\qquad J_b^+(u)\leq J_b^+(v)\quad\text{for every }v\in\mathcal A.

The lower bound is uniform in the value s. It makes the shifted density nonnegative, so the energy is a nonnegative Lebesgue integral even when some competitors have infinite energy. No upper growth bound is required. If b is integrable, this also minimizes the original extended energy after subtracting the finite constant \int_\Omega b. On measurable sets, W^{1,p}_0 means the supported smooth-core closure; on open sets it is the usual zero-boundary space. No boundary atlas is assumed.

For the Hilbert-space criterion, pointwise convexity and integrability give convexity of the integral functional. Closed convex sublevel sets then upgrade strong lower semicontinuity to weak lower semicontinuity.

For the sequential result, first choose indices tending to infinity along which the energies tend to their liminf. Strong convergence of the values allows a further selection converging almost everywhere. Convexity in z gives a supporting affine function at the limiting gradient. Restrict to measurable sets on which these supporting densities and fields are uniformly bounded. Continuity in s and dominated convergence give strong L^{p'} convergence of the restricted fields, where p'=p/(p-1)<\infty. Pairing them with the bounded, weakly convergent gradients passes the affine inequality to the limit. Fatou's lemma removes the restriction to those sets. The proof never requires a global integrable bound on the supporting field.

Suppose F(x,-,-) is jointly convex for almost every x, every admissible density F(x,u(x),Du(x)) is integrable, and the resulting functional is lower semicontinuous in the strong H^1 topology. Then

u_\alpha\rightharpoonup u\ \text{in }H^1(\Omega) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J_F(u)\leq\liminf_\alpha J_F(u_\alpha).

This Hilbert-space criterion takes strong lower semicontinuity as an input. A second result derives sequential lower semicontinuity from convexity in the gradient variable, using strong convergence of the values.

On a finite measure space, let 1<p<\infty and write the density as F(x,s,z), with s\in\mathbb R and z\in\mathbb R^n. Assume that F, its gradient derivative D=\partial_zF, and a spatial lower bound a(x) are measurable in their indicated variables. For almost every x, assume that F(x,s,z) and D(x,s,z) are continuous in s for each fixed z, that F(x,s,\cdot) is convex and differentiable for every s, and that F(x,s,z)\geq a(x) for all s,z.

If v_j\to v strongly in L^p, while z_j\rightharpoonup z weakly in L^p with \sup_j\|z_j\|_p<\infty, then

\int \bigl(F(x,v,z)-a(x)\bigr)\,d\mu \leq\liminf_j\int \bigl(F(x,v_j,z_j)-a(x)\bigr)\,d\mu.

These are nonnegative Lebesgue integrals with values in [0,\infty]. There is no upper growth bound on F or D, and a need only be measurable. An integrable a makes this a finite constant shift of the original energy. The Lean theorem also permits the values to converge strongly in a different L^r space, 1\leq r\leq\infty.

For a scalar field u\in H^1(\Omega), the first-order Sobolev jet bundles its canonical L^2 representative and all canonical first weak derivatives:

j^1u(x)=(u(x),Du(x))\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n.

Its values are the arguments of Evans's Lagrangian.

The concrete integral equals the squared H^1 distance to g. Its weak lower semicontinuity and coercivity give a minimizer by the direct method; comparison with g forces the squared distance to vanish and hence proves uniqueness.

For the concrete energy

J_g(u)=\int_\Omega\left( |u-g|^2+\sum_i|\partial_i u-\partial_i g|^2 \right)\,dx =\lVert u-g\rVert_{H^1(\Omega)}^2,

the library proves integrability, identifies the energy with squared H^1 distance, proves coercivity and weak lower semicontinuity, and obtains the prescribed field g as the unique global minimizer. This elementary quadratic model runs through the whole direct-method chain.

Mathlib defines a Hilbert basis by its coefficient map, a linear isometric equivalence onto the square-summable sequences; it sends u to the sequence of its coefficients. Such a sequence is the sum, in the sequence norm, of its single-entry pieces. The inverse isometry is continuous and maps each piece to the coefficient times the basis vector in H, so the expansion converges to u.

For any Hilbert basis (e_i) and any vector u, the Fourier coefficients \langle e_i,u\rangle reconstruct u: the net of finite sums \sum_i\langle e_i,u\rangle e_i converges to u in the Hilbert norm. This is Mathlib's basis theorem behind Evans's eigenfunction-series method.

Mathlib's coefficient map is a linear isometry onto the square-summable sequences, and the coefficient of each index is the inner product with that basis vector. The squared norm of a square-summable sequence is the sum of the squared norms of its entries. Applying this to the coefficient sequence and using that the isometry preserves norms yields Parseval's identity.

The squared Hilbert norm is exactly the sum of the squared norms of the Hilbert-basis coefficients:

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \left\lVert\langle e_n,u\rangle\right\rVert^2 =\lVert u\rVert^2.

The basis expansion gives convergence of the net over all finite index sets. The initial segments \{0,\dots,N-1\} eventually contain every fixed finite set. Restricting the convergent net to these initial segments gives \sum_{n<N}\langle e_n,u\rangle e_n\to u in norm.

For a basis indexed by the natural numbers, the conventional first-N partial sums converge in norm:

\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\langle e_n,u\rangle e_n \longrightarrow u.
Multiply the exact omitted tail by the monotone weight at index N, compare it termwise with the weighted tail, and divide by the strictly positive quantity (N+1)^q.
For q\in\mathbb N, if the coefficient energy weighted by (n+1)^q is summable, then the first-N squared truncation error is bounded by that weighted energy divided by (N+1)^q.

Split the series of squared coefficient norms after its first N terms; the tail is indexed by k+N. Orthonormality makes the squared truncation error equal to the squared norm minus the retained squared coefficients, and Parseval identifies the squared norm with the full series. Hence, with k\in\mathbb N, the error equals the tail, which is the displayed formula.

The squared error of the first-N approximation is exactly the sum of the squared omitted coefficients:

\left\lVert u-\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\langle e_n,u\rangle e_n \right\rVert^2 =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left\lVert\langle e_{k+N},u\rangle\right\rVert^2.

This is the quantitative identity behind spectral truncation and Galerkin approximation estimates.

For a finite family of functions B_j:X\to\Bbbk and matching points x_i\in X, indexed by the same finite type, the collocation matrix is

A_{ij}=B_j(x_i).

If \Bbbk is a field and \det A\ne0, the family (B_j) is linearly independent as \Bbbk-valued functions: a vanishing combination evaluated at the points gives a vanishing product with A, and invertibility forces the coefficients to vanish.

The degree-zero B-spline with index i is the indicator of the half-open knot cell [t_i,t_{i+1}), and the recursion

N_{i,p+1}(x) =\frac{x-t_i}{t_{i+p+1}-t_i}\,N_{i,p}(x) +\frac{t_{i+p+2}-x}{t_{i+p+2}-t_{i+1}}\,N_{i+1,p}(x)

defines the higher degrees, with the convention that a quotient with zero denominator equals zero. That convention is Lean's totalized division, and it is exactly the standard treatment of repeated knots. A finite family selects the indices 0\le i<m of a fixed degree.

All statements are proved by induction on the degree. At degree zero they are properties of the indicator of a half-open cell. In the recursion, a nonzero value requires one of the two child B-splines to be nonzero, and the child supports [t_i,t_{i+p+1}) and [t_{i+1},t_{i+p+2}) lie inside [t_i,t_{i+p+2}). On those supports both blending weights are nonnegative, giving nonnegativity. For strict positivity, away from a repeated knot block one of the two children is positive by induction and its weight is positive; when the point coincides with an entire block of equal knots, the left-clamped identity N=1 resolves the right-continuous convention.

For every nondecreasing knot sequence, degree p, and index i,

N_{i,p}(x)\ne0\ \Longrightarrow\ x\in[t_i,t_{i+p+1}), \qquad N_{i,p}\ge0,

so the B-spline vanishes for x<t_i and for x\ge t_{i+p+1}. Moreover it is strictly positive on the open interior of its canonical support,

t_i<x<t_{i+p+1}\ \Longrightarrow\ N_{i,p}(x)>0,

including when interior knots are repeated.

A knot sequence is a nondecreasing map

t:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R,\qquad i\le j\ \Longrightarrow\ t_i\le t_j,

bundled as an order homomorphism. Repeated knots are allowed, and a finite knot vector is represented by repeating its final knot with the desired endpoint multiplicity.

For a square matrix A over a linearly ordered commutative ring with strictly ordered multiplication, a positive LDU certificate consists of matrices L, U and pivots d_i>0 with

A=L\,\operatorname{diag}(d)\,U,

where L is lower triangular with unit diagonal and U is upper triangular with unit diagonal. The certificate stores no determinant assertion; a validated backend supplies the factors, and Lean checks the product, the triangular structure, the unit diagonals, and the positivity of every pivot.

The determinant is multiplicative, the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries, which are all one, and the determinant of the diagonal factor is the product of the pivots, a product of strictly positive elements. The collocation criterion converts nonvanishing of the determinant into linear independence.

A valid positive LDU certificate for A proves

\det A>0,

hence \det A\ne0. When A is the collocation matrix of a finite family of functions at matching points over a linearly ordered field, the family is therefore linearly independent.

A family of sample points x_0<x_1<\dots<x_{m-1} satisfies the Schoenberg–Whitney condition for the degree-p B-splines N_{0,p},\dots,N_{m-1,p} when it is strictly increasing and

t_i<x_i<t_{i+p+1}\qquad(0\le i<m).

Each sample point then lies in the open interior of the canonical support of its own B-spline, so every diagonal entry N_{i,p}(x_i) of the collocation matrix is strictly positive, including at repeated interior knots.

Insert p+1 copies of each sample point so that its tracked refined support begins with p+1 equal knots and ends strictly to their right. Boehm's knot-insertion formula expresses every coarse B-spline as a nonnegative combination of two adjacent refined B-splines, so each insertion factors the coarse collocation matrix as the refined collocation matrix times a bidiagonal matrix with nonnegative entries, and such matrices are totally nonnegative on ordered minors. At a fully clamped knot the refined B-splines evaluate as a Kronecker delta, so after all insertions the refined collocation rows selected by the sample points form an identity minor. The rectangular Cauchy–Binet formula writes the coarse determinant as a sum of products of ordered minors, all nonnegative; tracking one strictly positive ordered minor through every insertion, which the interlacing inequalities guarantee, makes the sum strictly positive. Nonsingularity and the collocation criterion then give linear independence.

If the points x_0<\dots<x_{m-1} satisfy the Schoenberg–Whitney condition for an arbitrary nondecreasing knot sequence, repeated knots included, then

\det\bigl[N_{j,p}(x_i)\bigr]_{0\le i,j<m}>0.

In particular the collocation matrix is nonsingular and the B-splines N_{0,p},\dots,N_{m-1,p} are linearly independent real functions.

Interior locality identifies the clamped extension's derivatives with those of the polynomial. Weak integration by parts then proves the candidate's Poisson identity against every H^1_0 test. The containing unit-width slab gives Dirichlet coercivity 1/2; the explicit Sobolev estimate gives \|v\|_{L^4}\leq12\|v\|_{H^1} because the cube has volume one. Nonnegativity of P preserves coercivity under linearization.

The quadratic residual has dual norm at most 1/4096. With identity reconstruction and radius r=1/512, CEGA checks

\frac1{4096}+144\left(\frac1{512}\right)^2 =\frac{13}{16384}\leq\frac{16}{16384}=\frac12\cdot\frac1{512}.

Compactness of the zero-boundary L^4 inclusion supplies the fixed point. This validates a concrete instance of the cube model in Hou et al. (2025), §3.1.

There is u\in H^1_0(\Omega) satisfying

\|u-P\|_{H^1}\leq\frac1{512}.

For every v\in H^1_0(\Omega),

\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+\int_\Omega u^2v=\int_\Omega fv.

The forcing is the fixed linear Poisson forcing above. The construction proves the weak Poisson identity, the candidate range, the domain volume, the embedding bound and coercivity before applying validated existence.

Expand the interpolation tail and the complete solve residual. The two terms K\Psi S cancel, leaving A+A\Phi S. The operator norm of B-L_0 is at most \delta+\eta; evaluating this difference on u and then pairing with u costs at most (\delta+\eta)\lVert u\rVert^2. Subtract this bound from the coercivity estimate for L_0.

For bounded weak-form operators and coordinate maps,

\begin{aligned} B&=L_0+K(I-\Psi S)\\ &\quad +(A\Phi+K\Psi)S\\ &=A(I+\Phi S). \end{aligned}

If L_0[u,u]\ge c_0\lVert u\rVert^2, the interpolation tail K(I-\Psi S) has norm at most \delta, and the residual after applying the coordinate map, (A\Phi+K\Psi)S, has norm at most \eta, then

B[u,u]\ge(c_0-\delta-\eta)\lVert u\rVert^2.

The identities hold for any coordinate space; finite dimension is needed by a numerical construction, rather than by this algebraic transfer.

The classical boundary-value theorem places the polynomial candidate in H^1_0. CAS proves its first and second derivatives; integration by parts identifies its linear Poisson load. CEGA certifies the polynomial range and the radius budget. The quantitative embedding, coercivity, and residual estimates then supply every hypothesis of the validated existence theorem.

There is u\in H^1_0(0,1) such that

\lVert u-p\rVert_{H^1}\le\frac1{16}.

For every v\in H^1_0(0,1),

\int_0^1u'v'+\int_0^1u^2v=\int_0^1v.

The nonlinear pairing is integrable for every test. This is a complete interval certificate using the validation argument of Hou–Wang–Yang Hou et al. (2025), §3.1; their example uses the three-dimensional cube. The next application treats that domain directly.

Rellich compactness makes the image of the closed energy ball compact in L^4. Hölder's inequality bounds the quadratic load and its difference there. The reconstruction bound gives continuity of the iteration in this weaker topology, so Schauder supplies a fixed point. The exact linear factorization and quadratic expansion recover the original weak equation after reconstruction.

Let \Omega be bounded and open in dimension 1\le n\le3, and let p\in H^1_0(\Omega), f\in L^2(\Omega). Assume the linear reconstruction, coercivity, embedding, and residual bounds above, together with \lVert eRu\rVert_{L^4}\le\gamma\lVert eu\rVert_{L^4} for some finite \gamma, where e:H^1_0\to L^4 is the canonical inclusion. If r\ge0 and the radius budget holds, there is a weak solution u with

\lVert u-p\rVert_{H^1_0}\le gr.

For every v\in H^1_0(\Omega),

\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+\int_\Omega u^2v=\int_\Omega fv.

The nonlinear pairing is integrable for every test. Existence is asserted; uniqueness and convergence of the iteration are not conclusions of this theorem.

The proof is by induction on m. For m=0 it is the H^2 theorem for the full operator: u\in L^2(H^2) and u_t\in L^2(L^2).

For the step from m to m+1, let v be the weak solution with forcing f_t and initial value g_1=f(a)-Lg. The data of v satisfy the hypotheses at order m, with the compatibility conditions shifted by one, so the induction hypothesis gives v its derivatives. The primitive g+\int_a^tv\,ds solves the original problem, so uniqueness of weak solutions identifies it with u, and v=u_t. At almost every time the equation then reads Lu(t)=f(t)-u_t(t), whose right side lies in H^{2m+2}, and the elliptic estimate of every order lifts u(t) to H^{2m+4}. The norms combine into the stated bound, with the trace constant for f(a) and the operator norm of L entering C.

The induction works with weak solutions only. After the base case no Galerkin approximation is differentiated: the order-m theorem is applied to the data (f_t,g_1) directly, and the identification v=u_t comes from uniqueness.

Fix m\geq0. There is a constant C>0, depending on m, \Omega, [a,b] and the coefficients, with the following property. Let

\partial_t^kf\in L^2(a,b;H^{2m-2k}(\Omega))\qquad(0\leq k\leq m),

where each derivative is the weak time derivative of the previous one, let g\in H^{2m+1}(\Omega), and suppose that g_0,\dots,g_m all lie in H_0^1(\Omega). Then every weak solution u of u_t+Lu=f in \Omega\times(a,b) with u=0 on the lateral boundary and u(a)=g satisfies

\partial_t^ku\in L^2(a,b;H^{2m+2-2k}(\Omega))\qquad(0\leq k\leq m+1),

again with each derivative the weak time derivative of the previous one, and

\sum_{k=0}^{m+1}\bigl\|\partial_t^ku\bigr\|_{L^2(H^{2m+2-2k})} \leq C\Bigl(\|g\|_{H^{2m+1}}+\sum_{k=0}^m\bigl\|\partial_t^kf\bigr\|_{L^2(H^{2m-2k})}\Bigr).

The compact inclusion produces canonical finite-dimensional spectral trial spaces. Their pivot projections converge uniformly on the compact image of the energy unit ball, hence their Bochner lifts make the spatial tails uniformly small on every L^2(a,b;V)-bounded family.

At one fixed trial dimension, the Lions–Magenes pairing identity expresses the projected trajectory increment as the interval integral of the mass-inverted restricted dual derivative. The derivative bound gives a common one-half Hölder modulus, while the quantitative time-Sobolev estimate gives a common pivot bound. Finite-dimensional Arzelà–Ascoli therefore makes the projected family precompact. A finite-net argument combines that compact projected family with the uniform spatial tail and yields compact closure in L^2(a,b;H).

Let V,H be real Hilbert spaces with a Gelfand triple V\hookrightarrow H\hookrightarrow V^* whose inclusion J:V\to H is compact. Equip each trajectory u_j and its dual time derivative \partial_tu_j with a Lions–Magenes continuous pivot evolution. Suppose

\sup_j\|u_j\|_{L^2(a,b;V)}<\infty, \qquad \sup_j\|\partial_tu_j\|_{L^2(a,b;V^*)}<\infty

on a finite interval (a,b) with a<b. Then the family Ju_j has compact closure in L^2(a,b;H).

The integrated dual derivative gives the pairing identity (\tilde u(t)-\tilde u(s),Jv)_H=\int_s^t\langle g(r),v\rangle\,dr, and Cauchy–Schwarz in time bounds the interval integral of an L^2 function by |t-s|^{1/2} times its L^2 norm. For the projection, the increment P\tilde u(t)-P\tilde u(s) is the Bochner integral of the mass-inverted restricted dual derivative, and the same estimate applies. The pivot bound and Cauchy–Schwarz bound the curves uniformly, so they take values in a compact ball of the finite-dimensional target; the common modulus gives equicontinuity, and Arzelà–Ascoli yields compact closure.

Let V\hookrightarrow H be a Gelfand triple with inclusion J, let a\le b, and let (u_j,g_j) be a family with u_j\in L^2(a,b;V) and g_j\in L^2(a,b;V^*), each equipped with a Lions–Magenes continuous pivot representative \tilde u_j:[a,b]\to H whose integrated dual derivative is g_j. For a fixed test vector v\in V and all s,t\in[a,b],

\bigl|(\tilde u_j(t),Jv)_H-(\tilde u_j(s),Jv)_H\bigr| \le|t-s|^{1/2}\,\bigl\lVert\langle g_j(\cdot),v\rangle\bigr\rVert_{L^2(a,b)}.

If \lVert\tilde u_j(t)\rVert_H\le U for all j and t\in[a,b], and \lVert\langle g_j(\cdot),v\rangle\rVert_{L^2(a,b)}\le D for all j, then the scalar coefficient curves t\mapsto(\tilde u_j(t),Jv)_H, regarded as bounded continuous functions on [a,b], have compact closure in the uniform norm.

For a finite-dimensional trial space S\subseteq V with a stable trial projection P, the projected curves satisfy the analogous modulus

\lVert P\tilde u_j(t)-P\tilde u_j(s)\rVert \le|t-s|^{1/2}\,\lVert M_S^{-1}g_j|_S\rVert_{L^2(a,b;S)},

where M_S^{-1}g|_S is the pivot-mass-inverted restriction of the dual derivative to S, and under uniform bounds U and D on the two quantities the family t\mapsto P\tilde u_j(t) has compact closure in C([a,b];S). The underlying abstract step is that a uniformly bounded family of continuous curves into a proper normed space with a common modulus \lVert f(t)-f(s)\rVert\le C|t-s|^{1/2} is relatively compact in the uniform norm.

Construct the autonomous weak solution with the improved pivot-valued time derivative, rewrite the equation at almost every time as an elliptic problem, and apply the Bochner-valued spatial H^2 lift to f-u_t.

For autonomous symmetric uniformly elliptic principal coefficients in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega) with global C^1 representatives, on a domain carrying the twice differentiable boundary atlas, forcing in L^2(a,b;L^2(\Omega)), and initial data in H_0^1(\Omega), there exist

u\in L^\infty(a,b;H_0^1(\Omega)),\qquad u_t\in L^2(a,b;L^2(\Omega)),\qquad U_2\in L^2(a,b;H^2(\Omega)).

The theorem simultaneously returns the integrated weak equation, the almost-everywhere pivot-valued residual, the identification of U_2 with u, and quantitative bounds for both u_t and U_2. The abstract Galerkin theorem also records the explicit almost-everywhere energy-space norm bound used to obtain the L^\infty membership.

The difference w=u-v satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 6.47 with zero lateral values, so it suffices to treat w. Its energy E is continuous on [a,b], nonnegative, has E''\geq0, satisfies (E')^2\leq EE'', and E(b)=0. For \varepsilon>0 the function \log(E+\varepsilon) is convex, because (E+\varepsilon)E''-(E')^2\geq EE''-(E')^2\geq0. Convexity on [a,b] gives

E(t)+\varepsilon\leq(E(a)+\varepsilon)^{(b-t)/(b-a)}(E(b)+\varepsilon)^{(t-a)/(b-a)},

and letting \varepsilon\to0 gives E(t)=0 for a<t<b. Continuity of w then gives w=0 on each slice and on the closure.

The regularization by \varepsilon avoids a case analysis on the set where E>0, and it is where the sign condition E''\geq0 is used. The statement holds on any interval [a,b] and for every bounded open \Omega with C^1 graph boundary.

Let a<b, and let u and v solve u_t-\Delta u=0=v_t-\Delta v in \Omega\times(a,b). If u=v on \partial\Omega\times[a,b] and u(\cdot,b)=v(\cdot,b) in \Omega, then u=v on \overline\Omega\times[a,b]. In particular a solution with zero lateral values that vanishes at time b vanishes on the whole closed cylinder.

Split the difference as

B(u_j,v_j)-B(u,v) =B(u_j-u,v_j)+B(u,v_j-v).

The Bochner Hölder estimate bounds its L^r norm by

\|B\|\,\|u_j-u\|_{L^p}\|v_j\|_{L^q} +\|B\|\,\|u\|_{L^p}\|v_j-v\|_{L^q}.

Both terms tend to zero. Formally, the Hölder operation is itself a continuous bilinear map between the three Bochner spaces, so the result is also an immediate continuity argument. The quadratic L^2 statement is the specialization p=q=2, r=1, and v_j=u_j.

Let B:E\times F\to G be a continuous bilinear map, and suppose p,q,r\geq1 satisfy

\frac1p+\frac1q=\frac1r.

If u_j\to u in L^p(\mu;E) and v_j\to v in L^q(\mu;F), then

B(u_j,v_j)\longrightarrow B(u,v) \qquad\text{strongly in }L^r(\mu;G).

In particular, taking p=q=2 and r=1, strong L^2 convergence implies B(u_j,u_j)\to B(u,u) strongly in L^1. This passes quadratic terms to the limit once compactness gives strong L^2 convergence.

By the scalar-multiplication norm identity, the norm of the product is \lVert A(t)\rVert\lVert v(t)\rVert. Eventually this is bounded below by c\lVert A(t)\rVert. Multiplication by the positive constant c preserves convergence to +\infty, so the product norm also diverges.

Let E be a seminormed module over a normed field \mathbb K. If \lVert A(t)\rVert\to+\infty as t\uparrow T and a profile family v(t)\in E satisfies

c\le \lVert v(t)\rVert

eventually for some c>0, then A(t)v(t) blows up in the norm of E. This is the quotient-friendly route for Sobolev and L^p profiles: once a dilation or pullback has been defined on the function space itself, the argument needs only a lower norm bound and never chooses a pointwise representative.

Suppose \lVert u-v\rVert\leq C eventually. To force \lVert v(t)\rVert above a threshold R, first force \lVert u(t)\rVert above R+C. The triangle inequality \lVert u\rVert\leq\lVert u-v\rVert+\lVert v\rVert then gives the desired bound. The reverse implication is the same argument after using \lVert v-u\rVert=\lVert u-v\rVert.
If \lVert u(t)-v(t)\rVert is eventually bounded as t\uparrow T, then u blows up at T if and only if v does. Thus an eventually bounded remainder neither creates nor removes norm blow-up.

For continuation, extend u to \bar u by the value x at b. On (a,b) the derivative f(u(t)) tends to f(x), so \bar u has left derivative f(x) at b. Since f is C^1 at x, the Picard–Lindelöf theorem supplies a local solution w with w(b)=x on (b-\varepsilon,b+\varepsilon). Define v=\bar u for t\le b and v=w for t\ge b. Away from b the curve v locally coincides with a solution; at b its left and right derivatives are both f(x), so v is differentiable there with the correct derivative. In the Cauchy form, completeness produces the limit x.

For the obstruction, a left-continuous extension v would give u(t)=v(t)\to v(T) as t\uparrow T, hence \lVert u(t)\rVert\to\lVert v(T)\rVert<\infty, contradicting divergence of the norm.

Let E be a complete real normed space, f:E\to E, a<b, and let u:\mathbb R\to E be an integral curve of the autonomous equation

u'(t)=f(u(t))\qquad(a<t<b).

If u(t)\to x as t\uparrow b and f is C^1 at x, then there are c>b and v:\mathbb R\to E with v=u on (a,b) and v'(t)=f(v(t)) for all t\in(a,c). The same conclusion holds when u is Cauchy as t\uparrow b and f is C^1 at every point, and, without completeness, when a local solution through (b,x) on some (b-\varepsilon,b+\varepsilon) is supplied and f is merely continuous at x.

Conversely, in any normed group, if \lVert u(t)\rVert\to+\infty as t\uparrow T, then no v:\mathbb R\to E with v(t)=u(t) for all t<T is continuous within (-\infty,T] at T. The same holds along any nontrivial clock \sigma\to T^- for which \lVert u(\sigma(s))\rVert\to+\infty, and more basically a trajectory whose norm tends to infinity along a nontrivial filter converges to no point.

The obstruction half is the no-extension theorem for norm blow-up stated without the blow-up predicate, together with its reparametrized and raw-filter variants.

For a field u : X\to\mathbb R\to E, the pointwise spatial supremum is the extended nonnegative real

S_u(t)=\sup_{x\in X}\operatorname{ofReal}\lVert u(x,t)\rVert \in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\cup\{+\infty\}.

In Lean this is ⨆ x, ENNReal.ofReal ‖u x t‖. An unbounded spatial slice therefore has value +\infty. The limit S_u(t)\to+\infty alone does not identify a blow-up time: the stationary field u(x,t)=x on \mathbb R has S_u(t)=+\infty at every time.

SpatialSupNormBlowsUpAt u T requires both this limit as t\uparrow T and finite spatial slices for all t<T sufficiently close to T. The finite bound may depend on t; no uniform bound in time is imposed. General divergence statements use Tendsto (spatialSupNorm u) directly, so they also apply to fields with unbounded slices.

This is a pointwise supremum: changing one value of u can change S_u. Sobolev and L^p trajectories use norm divergence at the finite horizon in their own normed state space, for example through the scalar-amplitude blow-up criterion.
Unfold norm blow-up and composition. A linear isometry satisfies \lVert Lu\rVert=\lVert u\rVert pointwise, so the two convergence statements are identical.

A linear isometric embedding preserves and reflects norm blow-up. This lets a trajectory move between isometric models of a Sobolev or L^p space without choosing representatives or reproving its asymptotic norm behavior.

A continuous extension v would converge to the finite value v(T) from within (-\infty,T]. Restrict this convergence to times below T and use the pointwise agreement v=u there. This gives a finite left limit for u, contradicting norm blow-up.

A trajectory whose norm blows up at T has no left-continuous extension through T. More precisely, there is no function continuous within (-\infty,T] at T that agrees with the trajectory for every t<T.

A trajectory u : \mathbb R\to E in a type equipped with a norm blows up at T when

\lVert u(t)\rVert\longrightarrow+\infty\qquad\text{as }t\uparrow T.

This is an equation-independent predicate. It can be applied to scalar observables, Banach-space solution trajectories, and Sobolev- or L^p-valued evolutions.

For each t before the horizon \tau, restrict the hypotheses to the compact interval [t_0,t] and apply the reciprocal estimate. Its right-hand side is exactly a(\tau-t), and positivity permits inversion, giving (a(\tau-t))^{-1}\leq y(t). The lower bound tends to +\infty as t\uparrow\tau, so order comparison proves divergence of y and hence norm blow-up.

Under a>0 and y(t_0)>0, the same differential inequality implies

y(t)\longrightarrow+\infty \qquad\text{as}\qquad t\uparrow \tau=t_0+\frac{1}{a\,y(t_0)}.

The hypotheses require continuity only on the half-open interval before the horizon, so Lean's total value y(\tau) plays no role in the norm-divergence conclusion.

If T<t_0, the claim is immediate because the Riccati horizon lies strictly after t_0. Otherwise suppose the horizon \tau belonged to [t_0,T]. Applying the reciprocal estimate at \tau makes its right-hand side zero, while positivity of y(\tau) makes 1/y(\tau)>0, a contradiction.

If a>0 and the stated inequalities hold on [t_0,T], then its right endpoint satisfies

T<t_0+\frac{1}{a\,y(t_0)}.

This is the scalar comparison mechanism in Kaplan-type eigenfunction and moment arguments; see Kaplan (1963, DOI 10.1002/cpa.3160160307) and Quittner–Souplet (2019, DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-18222-9).

The differential inequality first shows that y is nondecreasing, hence it stays positive after t_0. The reciprocal is therefore differentiable in the interior, with \left(\frac1y\right)'=-\frac{y'}{y^2}\leq-a. Apply the mean-value inequality to 1/y on [t_0,t] and rearrange the result.

Let y(t_0)>0 and a\ge0. If y is continuous on [t_0,T], differentiable in its interior, and

a\,y(t)^2\le y'(t),

then positivity propagates and

\frac{1}{y(t)} \le \frac{1}{y(t_0)}-a(t-t_0).

No separate positivity hypothesis is needed away from t_0: monotonicity supplies it.

Evans obtains the related inequality \eta'\ge -\lambda_1\eta+\eta^2 for a weighted PDE observable and removes the linear term by an exponential change of variables. The Lean theorem is the autonomous quadratic comparison step of that argument.

Rewrite the solution as 1/(a(T-t)). As t\uparrow T, the positive quantity T-t tends to zero from the right, so its reciprocal tends to +\infty; multiplication by 1/a>0 preserves that limit. Positivity of the trajectory identifies order divergence with norm divergence.
If a>0 and y_0>0, then y(t) tends to +\infty as t approaches T from below. The corollary states this as NormBlowsUpAt (Riccati.solution a y₀ t₀) (Riccati.horizon a y₀ t₀).

The denominator factors as 1-a y_0(t-t_0)=a y_0(T-t). Positivity of a y_0 and the inequality t<T make both factors nonzero. The quotient rule can therefore be applied to the explicit formula, and a ring calculation reduces the derivative to a y(t)^2.
If a y_0>0 and t<T, the explicit formula satisfies y'=a y^2 at t.

Substitute the definition of T and factor the original denominator as a y_0(T-t). Since a y_0\ne0, also y_0\ne0; cancelling this factor from the numerator and denominator yields 1/(a(T-t)). Lean's total division makes the resulting identity valid even at t=T.

Whenever a y_0\ne0, the solution has the reciprocal-distance form

y(t)=\frac{1}{a(T-t)}.

This algebraic identity is total in t; its analytic use is on the pre-blow-up interval.

For y'=a y^2 with initial value y(t_0)=y_0, the explicit candidate is

y(t)=\frac{y_0}{1-a y_0(t-t_0)}, \qquad T=t_0+\frac{1}{a y_0}.

The formula is total as a Lean function, including at its pole. Analytic statements therefore work on t<T under a y_0>0.

Evans notes the scalar model y'=y^2 before beginning the weighted eigenfunction argument. The theorem carries a coefficient a, an arbitrary initial time, and the horizon formula.

For every time t, the sampled quantity \operatorname{ofReal}\lVert u(x(t),t)\rVert is one term in the supremum defining S_u(t). The sampled norm tends to +\infty, hence so does its ENNReal.ofReal image. Monotonicity of convergence to the top element then transfers the limit to S_u. Together with the supplied finite-slice condition, this proves divergence of the spatial supremum norm.

If the norm along a possibly time-dependent spatial sample x(t) tends to +\infty, then the extended pointwise spatial supremum also tends to +\infty. This limit transfer holds along any filter of times. For the left limit at T, the single-point blow-up criterion also takes eventual finiteness of the slices and concludes finite-time blow-up.

A pointwise profile f : X \to E, amplitude exponent \alpha, spatial exponent \beta, center x_0, and time T determine

u(x,t)=(T-t)^{-\alpha} f\!\left((T-t)^{-\beta}(x-x_0)\right).

The pointwise construction is polymorphic in the spatial and value types: scalar, vector-valued, complex-valued, and system profiles can share it when the required real scaling operations exist. This is a pointwise profile construction; it assumes no differentiability until an equation-specific theorem requires it.

An L^p or Sobolev profile is instead an almost-everywhere equivalence class. Its similarity theory needs dilation pullbacks on that quotient and a weak form of the reduced equation, instead of pointwise composition. Once the quotient-level pullback is available, the scalar-amplitude blow-up criterion supplies the abstract amplitude-times-profile step.

First bound the absolute value of the Bochner integral by the integral of the absolute value and rewrite that integral as a nonnegative extended integral. Almost everywhere, nonnegativity of w and the definition of S_u(t) give |w(x)u(x,t)|\leq w(x)S_u(t). Monotonicity of the nonnegative Lebesgue integral permits this pointwise bound, after which the constant S_u(t) is pulled outside. Integrability and nonnegativity of w identify the remaining extended integral with \operatorname{ofReal}\int_X w\,d\mu.

If w is almost everywhere nonnegative and integrable, and x\mapsto w(x)u(x,t) is integrable, then

\operatorname{ofReal}\left|\mathcal M_w[u](t)\right| \le S_u(t)\operatorname{ofReal}\!\left(\int_X w\,d\mu\right).

Because S_u(t) takes values in the extended nonnegative reals, this estimate also covers unbounded slices without an auxiliary boundedness hypothesis. The weight need not have mass one.

Divide the weighted-moment estimate by the positive finite mass m=\int_Xw\,d\mu. The resulting quantity \operatorname{ofReal}|\mathcal M_w[u](t)|/m tends to +\infty and is eventually bounded above by S_u(t). The order characterization of convergence to the top element therefore proves divergence of the extended spatial supremum.

If the nonnegative integrable weight has positive mass, the weighted field is integrable eventually, and |\mathcal M_w[u](t)|\to+\infty as t\uparrow T, then the extended pointwise spatial supremum tends to +\infty.

The theorem works along any filter of times and needs no spatial slice bound. A PDE-specific theorem supplies divergence of the chosen moment; eventual finiteness of the slices is the additional condition needed to conclude divergence of the spatial supremum norm.

For a scalar field u, measure \mu, and spatial weight w, define

\mathcal M_w[u](t)=\int_X w(x)u(x,t)\,d\mu(x).

The spatial type and measure are arbitrary. Euclidean geometry enters only through a model-specific choice of weight. Mathlib's Bochner integral is totalized, so the weighted spatial moment is defined even for a nonintegrable integrand, where the integral is set to zero. Every theorem that reads this expression as a moment therefore assumes integrability.

Mathlib's lifted map agrees almost everywhere with pointwise composition. Extensionality of Bochner classes therefore identifies its kernel with pointwise almost-everywhere vanishing. Each lifted kernel is weakly closed, arbitrary intersections of those kernels remain weakly closed, and closed sets contain the weak limits of eventually constrained nets. Intersecting with an already weakly compact bounded set then preserves compactness.

Let A_j:E\to F be any family of continuous linear spatial constraints. For a Bochner trajectory u\in L^2(\mu;E), the conditions

A_j(u(t))=0\quad\text{for each }j,\text{ almost everywhere in }t

are exactly the kernel conditions

(A_j)_{L^2}u=0

for the continuously lifted maps (A_j)_{L^2}:L^2(\mu;E)\to L^2(\mu;F). Consequently, constrained trajectories form a weakly closed subset of L^2(\mu;E), the constraints survive weak L^2 limits, and imposing them on any weakly compact bounded family preserves weak compactness.

This single result covers every side condition represented by continuous linear maps, including divergence-free, zero-mean, trace, and conservation constraints once the corresponding spatial operator has been constructed.
For a field written with separate spatial and time arguments, the classical heat operator is u_t-\Delta u. The heat maximum, comparison, and uniqueness statements use this operator directly.

Under these hypotheses, pair the pointwise weak equation with a scalar time test and integrate. Integration by parts changes \int (u'(t),v)_H\tau(t)\,dt into -\int(u(t),v)_H\tau'(t)\,dt plus endpoint terms. A test vanishing at both ends removes both terms; a test vanishing only at the final endpoint leaves (u(a),v)_H\tau(a). Almost-everywhere replacement of u does not change any Bochner integral, giving the completed-space identity.

Suppose the Hilbert-space weak evolution has the stated time derivative throughout the interval. For the chosen spatial and scalar time tests, assume the derivative pairing (u',v)_H, the scalar test derivative, and B(t)u(t)[v]\tau(t) are interval-integrable. Integration by parts then gives the distributional time-test identity. Tests vanishing only at the final endpoint retain the initial boundary term. Replacing the trajectory by an almost-everywhere equal Bochner L^2 representative gives the identity used by the Hilbert integrated weak formulation.

The two solutions have the same heat residual and the same parabolic boundary data. Comparison first gives u\leq v; exchanging the two solutions gives v\leq u. Pointwise antisymmetry of the real order then gives u=v on the whole closed cylinder.

Let \Omega be nonempty and open with compact closure, and T>0. Under the regularity hypotheses of Theorem 6.38, two classical heat solutions with equal residual on \Omega\times(0,T] and equal parabolic boundary data agree throughout the closed cylinder:

Hu=Hv\ \text{ on }\Omega\times(0,T],\qquad u=v\ \text{ on }\partial_pQ \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=v\ \text{ on }\overline Q.
For an open spatial domain \Omega and T>0, the closed spacetime cylinder is \overline\Omega\times[0,T].

First descend \ell to the Hilbert quotient E/\ker T. Closedness of the range identifies this quotient continuously and linearly with \operatorname{range}T. Fréchet–Riesz representation on that closed subspace produces p. Testing against every Tx gives the representation formula. If two range-valued multipliers represent \ell, their difference is both in the range and orthogonal to the range, hence is zero. The adjoint identity is the same representation formula rewritten using the defining property of T^*.

Let E,F be real Hilbert spaces and let T:E\to F be continuous linear with closed range. If \ell\in E^* vanishes on \ker T, then \ell factors continuously through \operatorname{range}T. Moreover, there is a unique p\in\operatorname{range}T such that

\ell(x)=\langle p,Tx\rangle_F\qquad(x\in E).

Equivalently, p solves the adjoint equation

T^*p=R_E^{-1}\ell,

where R_E:E\to E^* is the Fréchet–Riesz equivalence.

This is the equation-independent Lagrange-multiplier step behind weak pressure recovery. When T is a divergence operator with closed range, \ker T is the divergence-free test space and p is the pressure.

Set w=u-v. Linearity of the heat operator gives w_t-\Delta w\leq0, and the boundary assumption gives w\leq0 on the parabolic boundary. The weak maximum principle therefore yields w\leq0 on the closed cylinder, which is exactly u\leq v.

If u_t-\Delta u\leq v_t-\Delta v on \Omega\times(0,T] and u\leq v on the parabolic boundary, with the classical regularity required by the maximum principle, then u\leq v on the entire closed cylinder.

Write the coefficient equation as c_m'=M_mc_m+f_m. Define its velocity directly by v_m=M_mc_m+f_m. Absolute continuity of c_m and f_m makes v_m absolutely continuous, and differentiation gives v_m'=M_mv_m+f_m' almost everywhere. Its initial value is M_mc_m(a)+f_m(a). Thus the original right-hand side itself supplies the differentiated trajectory and agrees almost everywhere with c_m'. The L^2(V^*) load-derivative hypothesis gives the required finite-dimensional L^2 bounds. Applying the pivot inclusion identifies the resulting Bochner classes: J\widetilde u_m=\partial_t(Ju_m).

For an autonomous form and an absolutely continuous load whose derivative belongs to L^2(a,b;V^*), every finite-dimensional Galerkin approximation canonically produces an L^2-forced approximation of the differentiated equation. Its state is the original coefficient derivative almost everywhere, and the Bochner identity

J\widetilde u_m=\partial_t(Ju_m)

is proved rather than supplied as a hypothesis.

The energy predicate records a weak time derivative in L^2(a,b;H^{-1}(\Omega)), a continuous L^2(\Omega) representative with the prescribed initial value, the almost-everywhere residual identity u_t=\ell+\Delta u, and the coercive integral estimate on every prefix.
Apply the abstract Galerkin theorem to the Dirichlet form. Poincaré coercivity gives the uniform energy bound, while Lions–Magenes supplies the continuous L^2 representative and the initial trace.

Let a<b be finite real endpoints and let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be bounded and open, with n>0. Every \ell\in L^2(a,b;H^{-1}(\Omega)) and u_0\in L^2(\Omega) determine a unique weak solution u\in L^2(a,b;H_0^1(\Omega)).

The conclusion also supplies u_t\in L^2(a,b;H^{-1}(\Omega)), a representative in C([a,b];L^2(\Omega)) with value u_0 at the initial time, the residual identity u_t=\ell+\Delta u, and the coercive energy estimate on every time prefix.

For an open set \Omega, we specialize the Gelfand triple to

H_0^1(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Omega)\hookrightarrow H^{-1}(\Omega)

and use the Dirichlet form

B(u,v)=\sum_{i=1}^n\int_\Omega D_i u\,D_i v.

Thus the abstract evolution equation is exactly the variational form of u_t-\Delta u=\ell with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary data.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open. The weak Dirichlet Laplacian A is the partially defined operator on L^2(\Omega) with Ax=f exactly when x is the class of some u\in H_0^1(\Omega) with \Delta u=f weakly, that is, \sum_i\int_\Omega D_iu\,D_iv=-\int_\Omega fv for every v\in H_0^1(\Omega). Its domain is dense in L^2(\Omega). For every \lambda>0 the operator \lambda-A is onto, with inverse (\lambda-A)^{-1}f given by the weak solution of the modified Helmholtz problem \lambda u-\Delta u=f in H_0^1(\Omega), and

\|(\lambda-A)^{-1}f\|_{L^2}\leq\frac1\lambda\|f\|_{L^2}.

The resolvent bound comes from testing the modified Helmholtz equation with its own solution: \lambda\|u\|^2+\|\nabla u\|^2=\int_\Omega fu\leq\|f\|\,\|u\|, so \lambda\|u\|\leq\|f\|. A densely defined operator all of whose positive shifts are onto with inverse norm at most 1/\lambda generates a contraction semigroup, and the generator of the semigroup that the Hille–Yosida construction returns is the operator it started from, not an extension of it. The construction is carried out once for any coercive form on a Gelfand triple, and the Dirichlet case applies it to the form B(u,v) shifted by the pivot inner product, which is coercive on H_0^1(\Omega) with no Poincaré inequality. This is why no boundedness of \Omega is needed, in contrast with Theorem 6.111.

The generator of the Dirichlet heat semigroup is exactly the weak Dirichlet Laplacian A, with equal domains. In particular A is closed, and g lies in the generator domain if and only if g is the class of some u\in H_0^1(\Omega) whose distributional Laplacian lies in L^2(\Omega).

On the generator domain the orbit is differentiable with derivative AS(t)g=S(t)Ag, and it stays in the domain. Membership in the domain provides the H_0^1 function u(t) with \Delta u(t)=AS(t)g, which is the weak equation after substituting the derivative. For continuity in H_0^1, the Dirichlet energy of a difference is a pivot pairing: \|\nabla(u(t)-u(s))\|^2=-\int_\Omega(Au(t)-Au(s))(u(t)-u(s)), and both factors are continuous in L^2.

Let g lie in the domain of the weak Dirichlet Laplacian. Then S(t)g stays in that domain, and the orbit is continuously differentiable in L^2(\Omega) for t>0. It has a representative u:\mathbb R\to H_0^1(\Omega) that is continuous in the H_0^1 norm, equals the H_0^1 function of g at t=0, and has L^2 class S(t)g. For every t>0 its strong L^2 derivative is S(t)Ag, and

\int_\Omega u_t\,v\,dx+\sum_{i=1}^n\int_\Omega D_iu\,D_iv\,dx=0 \qquad\text{for all }v\in H_0^1(\Omega).

In particular \Delta u(t)=u_t(t) holds distributionally.

The Dirichlet heat semigroup on an open set \Omega is the strongly continuous semigroup (S(t))_{t\geq0} on L^2(\Omega) produced by the Hille–Yosida theorem from the resolvents of Definition 6.112. Each S(t) is a contraction, \|S(t)g\|_{L^2}\leq\|g\|_{L^2}, and S(t)h\to g in L^2(\Omega) as (t,h)\to(0,g): every L^2 datum is attained, continuously in the datum.

The weak solution is an L^2(a,b;H_0^1(\Omega)) Bochner class satisfying the integrated time-tested identity with forcing in L^2(a,b;H^{-1}(\Omega)) and initial datum in L^2(\Omega). The definition is the direct specialization of the strengthened integrated-solution structure, including a nonempty interval and integrability of every tested term; no pointwise representative of the forcing is chosen.

Shift the Gårding form by its lower-order mass constant, apply the abstract nonautonomous Galerkin theorem, undo the exponential shift, and use Lions–Magenes for the continuous pivot representative and endpoint control.

On a finite interval a<b and a bounded open set \Omega, assume uniform ellipticity of the principal part and uniform bounds on the lower-order terms throughout [a,b]. Assume the induced form is a.e. strongly measurable as a map into \mathcal L(H_0^1(\Omega),H^{-1}(\Omega)) with its operator norm, and uniformly bounded in that norm on [a,b]. Then every L^2(a,b;H^{-1}(\Omega)) forcing and L^2(\Omega) initial datum have a unique weak solution.

The result includes a continuous L^2 representative, weak time derivative, the variational residual equation, and the Gårding energy inequality with its lower-order mass term.

The nonautonomous form is an operator-valued extension of

u_t-\partial_i(a^{ij}(t)\partial_j u)+b^i(t)\partial_i u+c(t)u=f

through the principal, first-order, and zeroth-order terms

B(t;u,v)=\sum_{i,j}(A_{ij}(t)D_j u,D_i v)_{L^2}+\sum_i(b_i(t)D_i u,v)_{L^2}+(c(t)u,v)_{L^2}.

The coefficient data are bounded operators on the spatial L^2 space. Pointwise L^\infty coefficients give multiplication operators, and nonlocal bounded coefficient operators are allowed as well.

The endpoint estimate consists of the weak H^{-1} time derivative, continuous L^2 representative, initial trace, residual equation, and Gårding energy inequality

\frac12\lVert u(t)\rVert_{L^2}^2+ \frac\theta2\int_a^t\lVert u\rVert_{H_0^1}^2 \le \frac12\lVert u_0\rVert_{L^2}^2+ \frac1{2\theta}\int_a^t\lVert f\rVert_{H^{-1}}^2+ \gamma\int_a^t\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2.

The last term is left for Grönwall, since the unshifted form need not be coercive.

One inclusion is elliptic boundary regularity: if u\in H_0^1 solves Lu=f weakly with f\in L^2, then u\in H^2. For the other, an H^2\cap H_0^1 function can be integrated by parts against every v\in H_0^1 using the weak Leibniz rule for a^{ij}D_iu, which identifies its form with the pairing against the strong expression Lu. The coefficient classes in L^\infty and W^{1,\infty} are computed from the given functions, so no extension of the coefficients is assumed.

Let \Omega be bounded and open with a C^2 graph boundary, n\geq1. Let a^{ij} be C^1 up to the boundary with \sum a^{ij}(x)\xi_i\xi_j\geq\alpha|\xi|^2 for x\in\Omega, and let b^i, c be continuous up to the boundary. Then the semigroup of Theorem 6.120 for these coefficients satisfies \|S(t)\|\leq e^{\gamma t}, its generator domain is exactly H^2(\Omega)\cap H_0^1(\Omega), and on that domain the generator acts as -L computed with strong second derivatives.

The Gårding inequality makes B+\gamma(\cdot,\cdot)_{L^2} coercive on H_0^1(\Omega), so the form construction behind Theorem 6.114 gives a contraction semigroup S_\gamma generated by -(L+\gamma). Then S(t)=e^{\gamma t}S_\gamma(t) has generator -L, with the same domain. The first-order term makes B nonsymmetric, which the Hille–Yosida argument does not need: coercivity alone bounds the resolvents.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open, let a^{ij},b^i,c\in L^\infty(\Omega), and let (a^{ij}) be uniformly elliptic with constant \alpha>0. Write Lu=-\sum_{i,j}D_j(a^{ij}D_iu)+\sum_ib^iD_iu+cu with its Dirichlet form B. With the explicit Gårding shift \gamma\geq0 computed from \alpha, \sum_i\|b^i\|_\infty and \|c\|_\infty, the form satisfies \frac\alpha2\|u\|_{H_0^1}^2\leq B(u,u)+\gamma\|u\|_{L^2}^2, and there is a strongly continuous semigroup S(t) on L^2(\Omega) with

\|S(t)\|\leq e^{\gamma t}\qquad(t\geq0).

Its generator is -L with the weak Dirichlet domain: S has generator value f at x exactly when x is the class of some u\in H_0^1(\Omega) with B(u,v)=-\int_\Omega fv for all v\in H_0^1(\Omega).

The time-dependent divergence-form weak solution is the same integrated Gelfand-triple notion, specialized to the form B(t). For a<b, the state u is a Bochner L^2(a,b;H_0^1(\Omega)) class, the tested form and forcing terms are integrable, and the initial datum enters through the boundary term in time integration by parts.

Under the form-measurability and boundedness hypotheses of Theorem 6.119, this class has a continuous L^2 representative U. For t\in[a,b], it satisfies

(U(t),v)_H-(u_0,v)_H +\int_a^t B(s;u(s),v)\,ds =\int_a^t\ell(s)(v)\,ds \qquad(v\in H_0^1(\Omega)).

The integrals use the energy-space Bochner representative u; the endpoint value U(t) belongs to the continuous pivot representative. The Dirichlet and divergence-form problems share this one weak-solution predicate.

Apply the homogeneous heat equation to every interior source slice, integrate that identity over source time, and use the supplied Leibniz and derivative-interchange identities. The two integrated Laplacians cancel, leaving exactly the moving-endpoint contribution f(x,t).

At a fixed positive-time point, the following hypotheses justify the differentiation of Duhamel's integral: assume continuity and boundedness of each interior source slice, the moving-boundary Leibniz formula with endpoint term f(x,t), and passage of both pure spatial derivatives through the source-time integral, together with interval integrability of the resulting second derivatives. Then

\partial_tu-\Delta_xu=f.

The dominated-differentiation theorem assumes that, on a spatial neighbourhood, the slice evolutions are measurable and integrable in source time, and they and their first coordinate derivatives are spatially differentiable for almost every source time. Measurable derivative covectors with locally uniform, integrable norm bounds then justify spatial interchange and give integrability of the resulting second derivatives. For globally C^2, compactly supported sources, Theorem 6.27 verifies these hypotheses and the moving-endpoint calculation.
Combine the residual and trace theorem with the separately established joint spacetime differentiability of the compactly supported Duhamel integral.

Under the same global C^2 and compact-support assumptions, the Duhamel formula gives a SatisfiesPDEProblem witness for the forced heat residual and assigned zero initial value. The uniform trace as t\downarrow0 is part of Theorem 6.27.

Write S(r) for heat evolution. For each r>0, the parameterized convolution theorem gives the joint Fréchet derivative of (t,x)\mapsto [S(r)f(t-r)](x). Compact support bounds its operator norm uniformly in heat age, so dominated differentiation applies first on a fixed age interval. Continuity at the moving upper endpoint then permits the moving-interval rule, which adds the covector (h_t,h_x)\mapsto [S(t)f(0)](x)h_t. This proves joint differentiability for t>0 without differentiating the zero-age kernel.
For a globally C^2, compactly supported spacetime source, the Duhamel integral is jointly Fréchet differentiable in observation time and space at every positive-time point.

Use the source-time representation u(t)=\int_0^t S(t-s)f(s)\,ds, where S(r) is heat evolution and S(0) is the identity. The source-time Leibniz theorem gives endpoint term f(t); the homogeneous heat equation identifies the interior derivative with the integrated spatial Laplacian. Spatial interchange then gives u_t-\Delta u=f. Compact support supplies the required bounds. In particular, \|u(t)\|_\infty\le t\|f\|_\infty gives the uniform initial trace, and the formula has exact value zero at t=0.

If f is globally C^2 and compactly supported in spacetime, Duhamel's formula satisfies

\partial_tu-\Delta_xu=f

at every positive time, has exact value u(x,0)=0, and converges uniformly in space to zero as t\downarrow0.

For a spacetime source f and t>0, define

u(x,t)=\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma_n(x-y,t-s)f(y,s)\,dy\,ds.

The Lean function is zero for t\leq0. For 0<s<t, the inner integral is the heat evolution of the source slice f(\cdot,s) at age t-s. Replacing it by the totalized initial-value solution changes only an endpoint of the time integral. Recovery of the zero initial trace as a limit uses the compact-support estimates of Theorem 6.27.

Substitute the heat age r=t-s, so the integrand is the heat evolution at age r of the source slice at time t-r. For fixed positive age, the initial-value convolution theorem permits source-time and spatial differentiation under the spatial integral. Compact spacetime support bounds all source derivatives on one compact set; convolution with the positive unit-mass kernel transfers those bounds uniformly. These estimates provide the domination needed near both the moving endpoint and positive heat ages.

After the substitution from source time to heat age, observation-time differentiation can be transferred to the source rather than applied to the kernel at age zero. For a globally C^2, compactly supported source, the source-time derivative and both spatial derivatives commute with fixed-age heat evolution, and compact support supplies a uniform bound on the pure second spatial derivatives. These lemmas provide the domination and endpoint control used in the classical Duhamel calculation.

Differentiate under the integral and replace u_t by \Delta u. Green's first identity with the zero boundary values turns 2\int_\Omega u\,\Delta u into -2\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2. For the second identity, the time derivative of |\nabla u|^2 is 2\nabla u\cdot\nabla u_t, and integrating by parts gives -2\int_\Omega\Delta u\,u_t, which is -2\int_\Omega u_t^2 by the equation. The boundary term vanishes because u_t=0 on the lateral boundary, which follows from u=0 there for all times. The proof commutes the mixed second derivatives of u; it never differentiates \Delta u in time, so C^2 regularity is enough.

Let u solve u_t-\Delta u=0 in \Omega\times(a,b) and vanish on \partial\Omega\times[a,b]. Then for every t\in(a,b),

\frac{d}{dt}\int_\Omega u^2\,dx=-2\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,dx, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,dx=-2\int_\Omega u_t^2\,dx.
By the first energy identity, E'=2\int_\Omega u\,u_t. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives (E')^2\leq4\int_\Omega u^2\int_\Omega u_t^2, and the right side is E\,E'' by the second identity.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 6.47, write E(t)=\int_\Omega u^2\,dx. Then E'(t)=-2\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2 and E''(t)=4\int_\Omega u_t^2 satisfy

\Bigl(-2\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,dx\Bigr)^2 \leq\int_\Omega u^2\,dx\cdot4\int_\Omega u_t^2\,dx, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad (E')^2\leq E\,E''.

For a scalar field u(x,t) on a real normed space, finitely many direction fields \sigma_k(x,t), and a drift b(x,t), define

Pu=u_t-\sum_k D_x^2u[\sigma_k,\sigma_k]+D_xu[b].

The potential variant is P_cu=Pu+c(x,t)u(x,t). The definitions impose no sign condition on c; Theorem 6.34 assumes c\geq0.

Writing \sigma_{ki} for coordinate i of direction \sigma_k, the principal matrix has entries A_{ij}=\sum_k\sigma_{ki}\sigma_{kj}. Every symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix has such a factorization. The theorems use only this semidefinite sign.

For \varepsilon>0, the perturbation u_\varepsilon=u-\varepsilon t satisfies Pu_\varepsilon<0 and retains the boundary upper bound. If its maximum on the compact cylinder exceeded M, a maximizer would lie in \Omega\times(0,T]. There the spatial gradient vanishes and every directional second derivative is nonpositive. The time derivative is nonnegative, including at t=T, where comparison with earlier times gives the same sign. Thus Pu_\varepsilon\geq0, a contradiction. Let \varepsilon\downarrow0 to recover the bound for u.

Let \Omega be nonempty and open with compact closure, and let T>0. Assume u is continuous on the closed cylinder. At every (x,t)\in\Omega\times(0,T], assume its spatial slice is C^2 at x, its time slice is differentiable at t, and Pu\leq0. If u\leq M on the parabolic boundary, then u\leq M throughout the closed cylinder.

The time derivative is required at T even at spatial interior points, where terminal boundary data are not prescribed. It is the two-sided derivative on the real line, not a one-sided derivative within [0,T]. The potential variants use the same hypotheses; the heat versions ask for less at the terminal face.

A Galerkin approximation consists of a finite-dimensional trajectory, its coefficient derivative, and the restricted weak equation

(u_m'(t),v)_H+B(t;u_m(t),v)=\ell(t)(v) \qquad(v\in V_m).

For a coercivity constant C>0 and a load bound M\geq0, it also records the dimension-independent estimate

\frac12\|u_m(t)\|_H^2 +\frac C2\int_a^t\|u_m(s)\|_V^2\,ds \leq \frac12\|u_m(a)\|_H^2 +\frac{M^2}{2C}(t-a).

For continuous, uniformly coercive time-dependent forms and continuous bounded loads on a compact time interval, Lean constructs one approximation in every trial space; the finite ODE partitions are chosen internally.

For a Banach space S, an affine Carathéodory solution of u'=A(t)u+f(t) is absolutely continuous, has the prescribed initial value, and satisfies the equation almost everywhere. A strongly measurable operator coefficient uniformly bounded on [a,b] and an integrable forcing produce a unique trajectory on the whole finite interval. The proof uses a contracting Picard iterate, so no short-time or smallness hypothesis is needed.

Apply differential Grönwall with coefficient -\alpha and forcing \beta. The explicit bound is a convex combination of e(a) and the equilibrium level \beta/\alpha, with weights e^{-\alpha(t-a)} and 1-e^{-\alpha(t-a)}. Both endpoints of this combination are at most R.

Let e be a differentiable scalar energy on [a,b]. If

e'(t)+\alpha e(t)\leq\beta,\qquad \alpha>0,

then

e(t)\leq e(a)e^{-\alpha(t-a)} +\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\bigl(1-e^{-\alpha(t-a)}\bigr).

Consequently, every level R satisfying e(a)\leq R and \beta\leq\alpha R is invariant: e(t)\leq R throughout the interval. This is the abstract damping step that turns a coercive energy calculation into a bounded region for finite-dimensional continuation.

Choose the first local solution from the prescribed initial state. At each cell endpoint, the pointwise invariant places its terminal value in the next allowable set. Start the next solution there, glue adjacent trajectories at their common value, and induct over the finite partition.

Fix an initial state u_0\in K(a) and a finite uniform time partition of [a,b]. Suppose a nonlinear finite-dimensional Galerkin vector field has a local solution on each cell from every state in K at that cell's initial time, and each such solution remains in K(t) throughout the cell. Those solutions glue to a trajectory on the whole interval with u(a)=u_0, remaining in the same moving family.

Taking

K(t)=\{x:\mathcal E(t,x)\leq B(t,x)\}

gives the energy-envelope form. The theorem is independent of the equation.
For a continuous inclusion J:V\to H of Hilbert spaces, its Gram operator is J^*J:V\to V. Its spectral subspaces take the place of an eigenbasis chosen in advance.

The adjoint identity gives (J^*Ju,v)_V=(Ju,Jv)_H, which is symmetric in u,v and nonnegative when v=u. If J is compact, composition with the bounded adjoint J^* keeps J^*J compact. If J^*Ju=0, pairing with u gives \|Ju\|_H^2=0; injectivity of J then forces u=0.

The identity

(J^*Ju,v)_V=(Ju,Jv)_H

makes the Gram operator positive and symmetric. If J is compact, then J^*J is compact; if J is injective, then J^*J is injective.

On every bounded open domain, compactness of H^1_0(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Omega) specializes the abstract spectral construction to a stable trial system dense in both the energy and pivot spaces. This provides the finite-dimensional approximation data required by the weak parabolic existence theorem.

Restriction to S produces a bounded form on the complete space S and a continuous S^*-valued forcing. Riesz representation on S converts the restricted weak equation into the affine linear equation u'=R_S\ell(t)-A_Su, which the variation-of-constants formula solves globally, or on any closed interval on which \ell is continuous. The energy inequality is the coercive smooth energy estimate tested with u(t), using that restriction does not increase norms. The derivative bound follows from the Riesz isometry, the contractivity of restriction, and the operator bound \lVert A_Su\rVert\le\lVert B\rVert\lVert u\rVert.

Let V be a real inner product space, S\subseteq V a complete subspace (for instance any finite-dimensional trial space), B:V\to V^* a bounded bilinear form, and \ell:\mathbb R\to V^* continuous. For every t_0\in\mathbb R and u_0\in S there is a trajectory u:\mathbb R\to S with u(t_0)=u_0 which is differentiable at every time and solves the restricted weak equation

(u'(t),w)_V+B(u(t),w)=\ell(t)(w)\qquad(w\in S,\ t\in\mathbb R),

its derivative being the Riesz-reduced vector field u'(t)=R_S\ell(t)-A_Su(t) of the restricted data. If \ell is merely continuous on [a,b] and t_0\in[a,b], the same conclusion holds for t\in[a,b], and it also gives the interval-level weak evolution predicate. If moreover \lVert\ell(t)\rVert_{V^*}\le M on [a,b] and B(w,w)\ge C\lVert w\rVert_V^2 for all w\in V with C>0, the trajectory started at u(a)=u_0 satisfies, for t\in[a,b],

\tfrac12\lVert u(t)\rVert_V^2 \le\tfrac12\lVert u_0\rVert_V^2+\frac{M^2}{2C}(t-a), \qquad \lVert u'(t)\rVert_V\le M+\lVert B\rVert\,\lVert u(t)\rVert_V.

These are Evans's Galerkin approximations in the special case where the mass form is the energy inner product itself, H=V. No smallness or time-step restriction is needed because the restricted system is affine linear.

Restrict the form, pivot mass pairing, and forcing to the finite-dimensional trial space. Strong measurability and uniform bounds pass to the resulting matrix coefficients, so the Carathéodory theorem gives an absolutely continuous coefficient trajectory satisfying the projected equation almost everywhere. Testing that equation with the trajectory, using coercivity, and applying Young's inequality gives the dimension-independent energy estimate. The coefficient derivative then belongs to L^2 by the finite-dimensional equation and the uniform coefficient bounds.

Restricting a strongly measurable bounded form and forcing to a finite-dimensional trial space gives a Carathéodory pivot-mass system. Under strict coercivity, its solution supplies an almost-everywhere Galerkin approximation with an L^2 coefficient derivative, the projected weak equation, and an energy estimate whose constants are independent of the trial dimension. It replaces the C^1 Galerkin curve when the coefficients are only measurable in time.

The pivot inner product restricts to a nondegenerate bilinear form on S, giving a map S\to S^*. Its Riesz representative is the mass operator M_S:S\to S, a continuous linear equivalence on a finite-dimensional trial space. Applying M_S^{-1} to the Riesz representative of the restricted residual gives the ODE on S. This is the basis-free analogue of multiplying a Galerkin matrix equation by the inverse mass matrix; for an L^2-orthonormal basis that mass matrix is the identity.

The trilinear bound gives \|N(u,u)-N(w,w)\|\lesssim(\|u\|+\|w\|)\|u-w\|, which yields local Lipschitz continuity of the mass-inverted vector field on bounded balls. The stated time-continuity hypotheses give its continuity along continuous state paths. Apply Picard–Lindelöf on one cell. Testing the projected equation with its state removes the skew term and gives the pivot-energy envelope. Finite dimensional norm equivalence converts this into a uniform coefficient bound. Choose a partition fine enough for the same unit Picard radius on every cell, preserve the energy envelope locally, and glue the solutions.

Let V\hookrightarrow H\hookrightarrow V^* be a Gelfand triple and S\subseteq V a finite-dimensional trial space. Consider

(u'(t),v)_H+A(t;u(t),v)+N(t;u(t),u(t),v)=\ell(t)(v), \qquad v\in S.

Assume A and \ell are continuous in time on [a,b], and that t\mapsto N(t;w,w,\cdot) is continuous as a dual-valued map for every fixed w\in V. The latter condition does not require operator-norm continuity of the full trilinear form.

Restricting the dual residual to S, applying Riesz representation, and inverting the pivot mass operator produces a quadratic ODE on S. Under uniform bounds on A, N, and \ell, Picard–Lindelöf gives a solution from u_0\in S on every interval short enough in terms of those bounds and \|u_0\|.

Assume in addition that A(t;v,v)\geq C\|v\|_V^2 with C>0, that N is skew in its last two arguments, and that M\geq0 bounds \|\ell(t)\|_{V^*} on [a,b]. Then every u_0\in S starts a classical Galerkin trajectory on all of [a,b], with continuous derivative, satisfying the projected equation at every time and

\frac12\|u(t)\|_H^2 \leq \frac12\|u_0\|_H^2+\frac{M^2}{2C}(t-a) \qquad(t\in[a,b]).

The integrated estimate of the skew energy theorem then also holds for this trajectory. The theorem is abstract in N; a fluid application supplies the domain, the divergence-free constraint, and the convection form.

For a finite-dimensional trial subspace S\subseteq V, dual forcing and the bilinear form are restricted to tests in S. These restriction maps preserve the linear operations used by the evolution equation and satisfy the expected norm bounds.

Evaluate the projected equation at the state. Skew-symmetry gives N(t;u_m,u_m,u_m)=0, leaving precisely the state-tested linear energy identity. Apply the pivot estimate and the integrated coercive estimate. Subtracting two weak equations and expanding the quadratic term gives the stated difference identity.

Consider the projected quadratic weak equation

(u_m'(t),v)_H+A(t;u_m(t),v) +N(t;u_m(t),u_m(t),v)=\ell(t)(v).

If N(t;x,y,z) is skew in its last two arguments, testing with v=u_m(t) removes the nonlinear term. For the integrated estimate, assume the trajectory has the prescribed derivative within [a,b], that A and \ell are continuous there, and that C>0, M\geq0 satisfy A(t;v,v)\geq C\|v\|_V^2 and \|\ell(t)\|_{V^*}\leq M for all t\in[a,b] and v\in V. Then, for every t\in[a,b], the trajectory satisfies the same estimate as the linear Galerkin equation:

\frac12\|u_m(t)\|_H^2 +\frac C2\int_a^t\|u_m(s)\|_V^2\,ds \leq \frac12\|u_m(a)\|_H^2+\frac{M^2}{2C}(t-a).

Two solutions of the quadratic weak equation also satisfy an exact difference energy identity, used for stability and uniqueness.

The compact self-adjoint spectral theorem decomposes the orthogonal complement of the kernel into finite-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces, with possible eigenvalues accumulating only at zero. Injectivity makes the kernel trivial. For a fixed threshold, only finitely many eigenvalues have magnitude at least 1/(m+1), so the corresponding sum is finite-dimensional. As the threshold decreases, every nonzero eigenspace eventually appears; completeness of the spectral decomposition makes the increasing union dense.

For an injective compact symmetric operator, sum all eigenspaces whose eigenvalues have magnitude at least 1/(m+1). Each threshold space is finite-dimensional, the spaces increase with m, and their union is dense in the energy space. Taking whole eigenspaces makes the construction independent of a basis within each repeated eigenspace: the spectral subspaces themselves determine the trial spaces.

The energy-orthogonal projection onto each Gram spectral threshold space is also orthogonal after inclusion into the pivot space. It therefore defines a Galerkin trial projection P_m with

\|P_m v\|_V\leq\|v\|_V \qquad\text{and}\qquad (J(v-P_m v),Jw)_H=0 \quad(w\in V_m).

Thus its energy stability constant is exactly one.

A stable trial system is a sequence of finite-dimensional spaces dense in both V and H, together with pivot-compatible projections uniformly bounded in the energy norm. The nested spans of one basis orthogonal in both H^1_0(U) and L^2(U) form such a system.

Reflexivity of the Bochner L^2 spaces makes the bounded families weakly relatively compact. Extract a weak state limit along an ultrafilter refining the index filter. For each fixed v\in V, use the projected test P_m v in the integrated Galerkin identity. Strong convergence P_m v\to v, the uniform state bound, and weak–strong pairing pass the time, form, and forcing terms to the limit. Strong convergence of the initial projections gives the prescribed initial boundary term. Since v was arbitrary, the limiting identity holds for every energy-space test. If a derivative family is also extracted, refine the same filter before taking that limit.

Uniform L^2(a,b;V) bounds for the states and L^2(a,b;V^*) bounds for their derivatives have a common weakly convergent ultrafilter refinement. Strong convergence of the trial projections and the weak–strong pairing rule then justify passage to the limit in the time-tested Galerkin identity. When state and derivative limits are both taken, they must be taken along a common refinement to identify one evolution.

Apply the Galerkin existence theorem to obtain the unique integrated weak solution. For continuous bounded forcing, the residual \ell-B(\cdot)u is an L^2(V^*) weak derivative. Lions–Magenes gives the continuous pivot representative and its initial trace, and the exact energy identity combined with coercivity and Young's inequality gives the prefix estimate. Uniqueness identifies this enriched solution with the one already constructed.

For continuous bounded forcing, the Galerkin theorem returns the unique integrated weak solution together with its continuous pivot representative, weak L^2(a,b;V^*) time derivative, initial trace, and the coercive energy estimate on every prefix [a,t].

First take a bounded continuous forcing. Construct the finite-dimensional trajectories, extract a weak state limit using the uniform energy bound, and pass the projected time-tested equations to the limit. To reach a prescribed L^2(V^*) forcing, approximate it by bounded continuous loads. The C^{-1} continuous-dependence estimate makes their solutions Cauchy in L^2(V), and strong-limit closure gives the integrated equation for the prescribed load. The uniqueness theorem identifies the solution.

Let a<b. For a continuous, uniformly bounded, and uniformly coercive time-dependent form, stable finite-dimensional trial projections dense in both V and H produce a unique integrated weak solution for every forcing in L^2(a,b;V^*) and every initial datum in H.

The theorem contains both stages of Evans's Galerkin argument: solve the finite-dimensional ODEs for regular forcing, then use uniform energy bounds, weak compactness, and density to pass to arbitrary Bochner L^2 forcing.

Test the weak equation with the solution, identify the derivative term with one half of the derivative of \lVert Ju\rVert_H^2, use coercivity on the form term, and absorb the forcing by Young's inequality. The uniform forcing bound and the mean-value inequality give the stated estimate.

Let a\le b and let u satisfy the pointwise weak equation on [a,b]. Suppose Ju is differentiable within the interval at every time, with derivative d_H(t) representing the supplied dual vector d(t). Assume throughout [a,b] that B(t)(u(t),u(t))\ge C\lVert u(t)\rVert_V^2 with C>0, and \lVert\ell(t)\rVert_{V^*}\le M with M\ge0. Then

\frac12\lVert Ju(t)\rVert_H^2\le \frac12\lVert Ju(a)\rVert_H^2+ \frac{M^2}{2C}(t-a)\qquad(t\in[a,b]).

The integrated L^2(a,b;V) estimate is a separate conclusion, proved for Galerkin approximations and for integrated weak solutions.
Subtract the equations, apply the pivot energy identity to the difference, and use injectivity of the dense inclusion after its pivot norm is forced to vanish.

Let a\le b.
