Suppose two pointwise weak evolutions have the same forcing and initial datum, their included trajectories are differentiable at every time of [a,b], and those derivatives represent the supplied dual vectors. If B(t)(z,z)\ge0 for every z\in V and t\in[a,b], the trajectories agree throughout the interval.

A Gelfand triple begins with a continuous injective map J:V\to H having dense range. The pivot inner product then defines the canonical maps

H\longrightarrow V^*,\qquad h\longmapsto \bigl(v\mapsto (h,Jv)_H\bigr),

and V\to V^* by composition with J. The Lean structure stores exactly the embedding data. Completeness and reflexivity are hypotheses of the theorems that need them. The concrete Sobolev triple H_0^1\hookrightarrow L^2\hookrightarrow H^{-1} is an instance.

For B(t):V\to V^*, forcing \ell(t)\in V^*, trajectory u(t)\in V, and supplied dual vector d(t)\in V^*, the pointwise weak equation is

\langle d(t),v\rangle+\langle B(t)u(t),v\rangle =\langle \ell(t),v\rangle\qquad(v\in V).

For a supplied pivot-space vector d_H(t), the separate predicate the pivot derivative condition records d(t)=J^*d_H(t). Identifying d_H(t) with the actual derivative of Ju is a separate hypothesis of the smooth energy and uniqueness theorems.

The scalar test identity for each v\in V is exactly the distributional derivative relation for the V^*-valued trajectory J^*Ju. If g_1 and g_2 both satisfy it, their difference pairs to zero against every spatial test vector and every compactly supported time test. Uniqueness of Banach-valued weak derivatives gives g_1=g_2 almost everywhere, hence the same Bochner L^2(V^*) class.

The Gelfand test identity induces the ordinary local Banach-valued weak derivative relation for the V^*-valued trajectory J^*Ju. Completeness of V and separation by continuous linear functionals then imply that two L^2(a,b;V^*) weak derivatives of the same trajectory are equal as Bochner classes. Thus the derivative appearing in the weak evolution equation is determined by the trajectory.

For Bochner classes u\in L^2(a,b;V) and g\in L^2(a,b;V^*), the statement that g=u_t is encoded by

\int_a^b g(t)[v]\,\tau(t)\,dt =-\int_a^b (Ju(t),Jv)_H\,\tau'(t)\,dt

for every v\in V and every admissible endpoint-vanishing time test \tau. Both sides are unchanged when either Bochner representative is modified on a null set. The definition involves no pointwise time derivative or endpoint trace; continuous representatives and endpoint traces come from the Lions–Magenes theorem.

The Hessian bounds make the extended gradient energy proper, convex, and lower semicontinuous on L^2. Its subdifferential domain is exactly H^2\cap H^1_0 under the boundary hypotheses, so u_0 is admissible for the global weak subgradient-flow construction. That construction provides the continuous trajectory, bounded weak time derivative, and domain membership at every nonnegative time. The first-variation identity identifies -g(t) as the subgradient precisely when the displayed spatial test equation holds, which supplies the PDE and the boundary condition.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n>0, be bounded and open with C^2 graph boundary. Suppose L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is C^2 and there are constants \theta>0 and C\ge0 such that

\theta|v|^2\le D^2L(p)[v,v],\qquad \|D^2L(p)\|\le C \qquad(p,v\in\mathbb R^n).

For every u_0\in H^2(\Omega)\cap H^1_0(\Omega) there is a global continuous L^2 trajectory u with u(0)=u_0, a distributional time derivative g\in L^\infty((0,\infty);L^2(\Omega)), and u(t)\in H^2(\Omega)\cap H^1_0(\Omega) at every t\ge0. At almost every positive time, for every v\in H^1_0(\Omega),

\langle g(t),v\rangle_{L^2} +\int_\Omega DL(Du(t))\cdot Dv\,dx=0.

This is the weak Dirichlet equation u_t=\operatorname{div}DL(Du) with a continuous initial trace.

The proof uses the contact-set method of Krylov and Safonov, in the form presented by Imbert and Silvestre. Suppose a supersolution is small at some point at a later time. Slide a family of paraboloids up from below until they first touch the graph at earlier times. At each contact point the spatial Hessian of the solution is bounded below by that of the paraboloid. The supersolution inequality then bounds the Jacobian of the contact map, using only ellipticity and bounds on the trace and the drift. The change of variables formula turns this into a lower bound on the measure of the set where the solution was small earlier. An expanding barrier and an iteration of this growth step give a measure estimate on nested cylinders. The upper side comes from propagating almost-maximal values forward to later balls. Together they give the comparison on small cylinders, and a finite covering of \overline V gives the constant. A potential of either sign is absorbed by adding one spatial variable z and multiplying by an exponential in z. The potential then becomes a drift in z. The contact argument needs a jointly C^2 gradient. The classical hypotheses stated here are reached by averaging forward in time and letting the width tend to zero.

The coefficients are only assumed continuous.

Let U be open, and let V be connected with compact closure \overline V\subseteq U. Let 0<s<t\leq T. Let a, b, c be continuous on U\times(0,T], with a symmetric and uniformly elliptic; c may have either sign. Then there is C>0 with the following property. Let u\geq0 be continuous on U\times(0,T]. Suppose u has continuous spatial first and second derivatives and a continuous time derivative on U\times(0,T), and Lu=0 there. Then

u(x,s)\leq C\,u(y,t)\quad(x,y\in\overline V),\qquad \sup_V u(\cdot,s)\leq C\inf_V u(\cdot,t).

Parabolically scale the domain to the unit heat ball and differentiate the weighted integral with respect to the scale. On each backward-time slice, Watson's transport identity converts that derivative into a spatial flux. The boundary flux and both singular endpoint contributions vanish. Fubini and the fundamental theorem of calculus therefore make the weighted integral constant in scale, and its zero-scale value is 4u(x,t). Scaling back contributes the factor r^n.

Let n>0, r>0, and let u\in C^2(\mathbb R^{n+1}) satisfy u_t-\Delta u=0 on E(x,t;r). Then

u(x,t)=\frac1{4r^n} \int_{E(x,t;r)} u(y,s)\frac{\lVert x-y\rVert^2}{(t-s)^2}\,dy\,ds.

The Lean statement assumes only continuous first derivatives, continuous second spatial derivatives, and caloricity on the displayed heat ball.

For a pole (x,t) and radius parameter r>0, the backward heat ball is

E(x,t;r)= \left\{(y,s): \Gamma_n(x-y,t-s)>r^{-n}\right\},

and Watson's mean-value weight is

W_{x,t}(y,s)=\frac{\lVert x-y\rVert^2}{(t-s)^2}.

Every point of a positive-radius heat ball lies strictly before its pole in time, so the denominator is nonzero on the integration domain.

Unfold the bundled initial-value problem. Satisfaction consists of exactly two fields: satisfaction of the positive-time heat problem and satisfaction of the time-zero initial condition. Apply the heat-problem characterization to the first field and unfold the second to obtain the conjunction. Conversely, the two conjuncts construct those two fields and hence the bundled IVP witness.

Each bundled problem is equivalent to the conjunction of its heat-operator identity at positive times and its assigned time-zero value:

u\models\operatorname{HeatResidualAssigned}(f,g) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bigl(\forall t>0,\ \forall x,\ Hu(t,x)=f(t,x)\bigr) \ \land\ \bigl(\forall x,\ u(0,x)=g(x)\bigr).
Use heat-operator linearity on positive time and ordinary pointwise linearity on the time-zero hyperplane. The bundled Cauchy-problem constructor then joins the two clauses.

Superposition also preserves the Cauchy data. If u and v have source terms f,g and initial values u_0,v_0, then au+bv has source af+bg and initial value au_0+bv_0. The theorem family includes the homogeneous and forced equations, with addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication, and general real linear combinations.

The homogeneous and forced residual problems combine the positive-time equation with an assigned value on the time-zero hyperplane:

Hu=0\ \text{or}\ f\quad(t>0),\qquad u(0,x)=g(x).

The second clause is an equality on the time-zero slice. Continuity up to time zero and convergence of a representation formula to g are separate analytic conclusions, proved for the kernel and Duhamel solutions.

Work on the time ball |s-t|<t/2. There the coefficient \lVert z\rVert^2/(4s^2)-n/(2s) is bounded by \lVert z\rVert^2/t^2+n/t, and the Gaussian \Gamma_n(z,s) is bounded by a constant depending on t times \exp(-\lVert z\rVert^2/(6t)). Their product is therefore dominated by a polynomial in \lVert z\rVert times the slower Gaussian \exp(-\lVert z\rVert^2/(12t)), which is integrable, and multiplying by the global bound M for g keeps it integrable. The dominated differentiation theorem for parameter-dependent integrals then moves the time derivative of the Gaussian inside the integral.

Let g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R be continuous with |g(y)|\le M for every y, fix x\in\mathbb R^n, and let t>0. Then the heat-kernel convolution

s\longmapsto\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma_n(x-y,s)\,g(y)\,dy

is differentiable at s=t, with derivative

\int_{\mathbb R^n} \left(\frac{\lVert x-y\rVert^2}{4t^2}-\frac{n}{2t}\right) \Gamma_n(x-y,t)\,g(y)\,dy.

The integrand is the pointwise time derivative of the Gaussian multiplied by the datum, so this is the first "differentiate under the integral sign" step of Evans's heat initial-value theorem. The statement concerns the convolution integral itself; the totalized initial-value formula agrees with it near every positive time, which is how Theorem 6.17 inherits this derivative.

Differentiate the Gaussian time factor and exponential factor, compute each spatial second derivative, and sum the diagonal Hessian entries. Both sides reduce to (\lVert x\rVert^2/(4t^2)-n/(2t))\Gamma_n(x,t).

At every positive time, the Gaussian satisfies the homogeneous heat equation pointwise:

\partial_t\Gamma_n(x,t)-\Delta_x\Gamma_n(x,t)=0.

The identity holds in every finite spatial dimension n.
Apply Mathlib's Gaussian integral with coefficient 1/(4t). The spatial integral of the exponential is (4\pi t)^{n/2}; multiplying by the prefactor (4\pi t)^{-n/2} gives one.

For every t>0, the heat kernel has unit spatial mass:

\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma_n(x,t)\,dx=1.

This is the normalization needed for preservation of constants and for the approximate-identity argument.

For x \in \mathbb R^n and t>0, the heat kernel is

\Gamma_n(x,t)=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert x\rVert^2}{4t}\right).

The Lean function is total: it is defined to be zero when t \leq 0. The differential identities for it assume t>0.

Expand H=\partial_t-\Delta_x. For a sum, apply the pointwise sum rules to the time derivative and to the Laplacian of the fixed-time spatial slices, then collect terms. For a scalar multiple, pull the constant through both operators and distribute it across the difference.

Suppose u and v are differentiable at z=(t,x) and their fixed-time spatial slices are C^2 at x. Then the heat operator preserves their sum at z. It also commutes with multiplication by a real constant:

H(u+v)=Hu+Hv,\qquad H(cu)=c\,Hu.

The scalar identity holds without regularity assumptions on u, using the total derivative operators. These two calculus lemmas supply the superposition results for the homogeneous, forced, and initial-value problems.

With coordinate zero reserved for time, the classical heat operator on \mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n is

Hu=\partial_tu-\Delta_xu.

HeatEquation.heatOperator is an ordinary function on Euclidean spacetime. It computes the time-coordinate partial derivative and the Laplacian of the fixed-time spatial slice. Like Mathlib's Fréchet derivative, it is defined for every u, and the analytic theorems state the regularity they need.

By the weak minimum principle u\geq0 on the closed cylinder. If u(x,t)=0 for some x\in U and t>0, then (x,t) is an interior minimum, and the strong principle makes u identically zero on \overline U\times[0,t]. This contradicts u(y,0)>0.

Let U be open and connected with compact closure. Let u be a classical supersolution, u_t-\Delta u\geq0 on U\times(0,T), with u\geq0 on the parabolic boundary and u(y,0)>0 for some y\in\overline U. Then u(x,t)>0 for every x\in U and 0<t\leq T.

Unfold satisfaction of the bundled PDEProblem. Its equation field is defined pointwise as Hu(z)=f(z) on the stored domain U, so a witness of satisfaction immediately projects to the displayed identity. Conversely, the pointwise identity fills the sole equation field of the problem witness. The homogeneous statement is the specialization f=0.

Satisfaction of either bundled problem is equivalent to its pointwise heat operator identity:

u\models\operatorname{Heat}(f,U) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall z\in U,\ H u(z)=f(z),

with f=0 for the homogeneous problem. The forward and reverse directions are also exposed as projection and constructor theorems.

On a spacetime set U, the homogeneous and forced residual problems are

Hu=0\quad\text{and}\quad Hu=f\qquad\text{on }U.

They are represented by PDEProblem values so that explicit formulas and symbolic calculations can target the same ordinary Lean proposition. The problem values contain only equations and domains; differentiability, existence, uniqueness, and boundary regularity belong to separate theorems.
The heat operator equals the matrix operator with coefficients (I,0,0), identically in u. The identity matrix is symmetric with ellipticity constant one, and constant coefficients are continuous.

Let U be open and connected, and let u be continuous on \overline U\times[0,T], with C^2 spatial slices and differentiable time slices on U\times(0,T). If u_t-\Delta u\leq0 and u attains its maximum over the closed cylinder at an interior point (x_0,t_0) with 0<t_0\leq T, then u is constant on \overline U\times[0,t_0]. The same holds for a minimum of a supersolution.
Apply the pointwise linearity of the heat operator and then substitute the residual equations for the two solutions. The homogeneous results are the zero-forcing specializations.

Constant functions solve the homogeneous equation. Under the regularity assumptions of Theorem 6.2 at every point of U, sums, differences, and real linear combinations of homogeneous solutions are again solutions. More generally, if H u=f and H v=g, then H(au+bv)=af+bg. Multiplication of a solution by a constant needs no additional regularity.

Differentiate the variation-of-constants formula. The derivative of the operator exponential contributes -A_Bu(t), while the Banach-valued fundamental theorem of calculus contributes the endpoint value R\ell(t). At t=t_0, the exponential is the identity and the integral vanishes, so the initial value is u_0. The Riesz equivalence then converts the affine ODE back into the pointwise weak equation on the chosen interval.

For a time-independent bounded form and continuous dual forcing, the variation-of-constants formula produces a global classical solution of the Riesz-reduced affine equation

u'(t)=R\ell(t)-A_Bu(t),\qquad u(t_0)=u_0,

namely

u(t)=e^{-(t-t_0)A_B} \left(u_0+\int_{t_0}^t e^{(s-t_0)A_B}R\ell(s)\,ds\right).

A closed-interval theorem gives the same trajectory with its pointwise weak equation.

Riesz representation gives vectors R\ell(t) and A_Bu(t) satisfying (R\ell(t),v)_V=\ell(t)(v) and (A_Bu(t),v)_V=B(t)(u(t),v) for every v. Substituting these into the weak equation shows that (u'(t)-R\ell(t)+A_Bu(t),v)_V=0 for all v. Nondegeneracy of the inner product gives the vector ODE, and pairing that ODE with arbitrary v gives the converse.

On a complete real Hilbert space, Riesz representation converts the smooth weak equation into the ordinary differential equation

u'(t)=R\ell(t)-A_Bu(t),

where R\ell is the Riesz vector of the functional and A_B is the bounded operator represented by the bilinear form. This is the Riesz step of the Galerkin argument (Evans §7.1.2); the theorem is valid on any complete Hilbert space.

Use the Galerkin velocity as test vector. Symmetry and time independence of A identify A(u_m,u_m') with \frac12\frac d{dt}A(u_m,u_m). The equation therefore controls \|Ju_m'\|_H^2 plus this exact principal-energy derivative. Bound the lower-order term by L\|u_m\|_V\|Ju_m'\|_H and the forcing term by \|f\|_H\|Ju_m'\|_H, absorb both velocity factors with Young's inequality, and integrate. The earlier energy estimate controls the remaining L^2(V) term uniformly in the trial dimension.

Suppose B(t)=A+R(t), where A:V\to V^* is bounded, autonomous, and symmetric, and the remainder satisfies

|R(t)(u,v)|\leq L\lVert u\rVert_V\lVert Jv\rVert_H.

For a supplied Galerkin trajectory u_m with pivot forcing f\in L^2(a,b;H), every t\in[a,b] satisfies

\frac12 A(u_m(t),u_m(t)) +\frac12\int_a^t\|Ju_m'(s)\|_H^2\,ds \leq \frac12 A(u_m(a),u_m(a)) +\int_a^t\bigl(\|f(s)\|_H^2+L^2\|u_m(s)\|_V^2\bigr)\,ds.

The constants are independent of the trial dimension. When the principal form is nonnegative, uniform bounds for the initial energy and the remaining L^2(V) term give the velocity estimate. The existence theorem Theorem 6.124 uses the stronger assumption of principal coercivity.

The proof has four steps.

Step 1: Differentiated energy. The forcing hypothesis f\in H^1(a,b;L^2(\Omega)) implies f_t\in L^2(a,b;L^2(\Omega)). The Ritz-compatible initial data give a differentiated Galerkin family whose energy estimate bounds \|u_t\|_{L^\infty(L^2)} and \|\nabla u_t\|_{L^2(L^2)} by the initial compatibility residual and \|f_t\|_{L^2(L^2)}.

Step 2: Derivative identification. The paired compactness theorem extracts a common weak limit for both the original and differentiated Galerkin families. The finite-dimensional identity J\widetilde u_m=\partial_t(Ju_m) passes to the limit, proving that the differentiated weak solution is the time derivative of the original rather than an independently selected function.

Step 3: Second time derivative. From the weak equation J^*u_t+Au=J^*f (almost everywhere in time), differentiate in time: u_{tt}=J^*f_t-Au_t. Since A:V\to V^* is bounded and u_t\in L^2(V), this gives u_{tt}\in L^2(V^*)=L^2(H^{-1}).

Step 4: Spatial bootstrap. At almost every time, u_t(t)\in L^2 and the equation gives -\nabla\cdot(A\nabla u(t))=f(t)-u_t(t)\in L^2. The elliptic H^2 theorem uses the operational C^2 atlas and the W^{1,\infty} coefficients with global C^1 representatives. It lifts u(t) to H^2(\Omega). The differentiated energy estimate bounds u_t in L^\infty(L^2), and the time-Sobolev representative bounds f in the same space. Their difference is therefore essentially bounded in L^2; applying the bounded elliptic solution operator gives u\in L^\infty(H^2) (Evans, 2010, §7.1.3).

Retain the operational domain and autonomous symmetric uniformly elliptic W^{1,\infty} coefficient hypotheses, including the global C^1 representatives. For initial data in H^2(\Omega)\cap H_0^1(\Omega) and forcing in H^1(a,b;L^2(\Omega)), the paired Ritz–Galerkin construction identifies the differentiated trajectory with the weak time derivative of the original trajectory. Combining the differentiated energy and elliptic estimates gives

u\in L^\infty(a,b;H^2(\Omega)),

u_t\in L^\infty(a,b;L^2(\Omega)) \cap L^2(a,b;H_0^1(\Omega)),

and

u_{tt}\in L^2(a,b;H^{-1}(\Omega)).

The assumed time-Sobolev regularity f\in H^1(a,b;L^2(\Omega)) supplies its own L^\infty(a,b;L^2(\Omega)) bound through the closed-interval Lions–Magenes representative; no separate pointwise forcing bound is an input. More precisely, the constructed representative satisfies

\|f(t)\|_{L^2}\leq \left( \frac{\|f\|_{L^2_tL^2_x}^2}{b-a} +2\|f\|_{L^2_tL^2_x}\|f_t\|_{L^2_tL^2_x} \right)^{1/2}

on the closed interval, and the original Bochner trajectory satisfies the same estimate almost everywhere.

The estimate theorem records data-dependent bounds for the L^\infty_tL^2_x, L^2_tH_0^1, L^2_tH^{-1}_x, and L^\infty_tH^2_x components displayed, including the quantitative bound for u_{tt}. The estimates control the second time derivative in H^{-1}(\Omega).

First construct Galerkin families for bounded continuous pivot loads. The principal-energy calculation bounds their velocities in L^2(H); for time-dependent A, the additional coefficient is N/2. Pass to a common weak limit and identify the pivot velocity with the weak derivative of the state. Finally, approximate an arbitrary Bochner load by bounded continuous loads. The estimates depend only on their L^2(H) norms, and full-form coercivity controls the differences, so both state and velocity pass through the forcing-completion argument.

Let B(t)=A(t)+R(t) be strongly measurable almost everywhere and uniformly bounded in operator norm on [a,b]. Assume A is absolutely continuous in operator norm, A(t) is symmetric for every t\in[a,b], and its supplied almost-everywhere derivative is bounded by N\geq0. For one C>0, require both

C\|w\|_V^2\leq A(t)(w,w),\qquad C\|w\|_V^2\leq B(t)(w,w),

for every t\in[a,b] and w\in V. Suppose also, for all such times and every u,v\in V,

|R(t)(u,v)|\leq L\lVert u\rVert_V\lVert Jv\rVert_H.

With trial spaces that approximate every vector of V and pivot projections uniformly bounded in V, every f\in L^2(a,b;H) and u_0\in V admit an integrated weak solution whose time derivative is represented by u_t\in L^2(a,b;H). Almost everywhere,

J^*u_t+A(t)u+R(t)u=J^*f.

The theorem records quantitative L^2(H) derivative and L^\infty(V) state bounds. Here J^*:H\to V^* is the pivot embedding. The autonomous case takes A'(t)=0 and N=0.

Continuity gives a ball on which the datum has a uniform positive lower bound. At a fixed positive time the Gaussian has a positive lower bound on that ball, so the convolution has a strictly positive contribution there; the remaining integrand is nonnegative.

If the initial datum is continuous and bounded, is nonnegative everywhere, and is strictly positive at some point, then

g\geq0,\quad g(x_0)>0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (\Gamma_n(\cdot,t)*g)(x)>0 \quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n,\ t>0.

Thus the heat-kernel evolution is immediately positive at every spatial point, even when the initial positivity is localized.

Work in a positive-time neighbourhood bounded away from zero. Derivatives of the Gaussian are bounded there by a polynomial times a slower Gaussian, which is integrable and remains an admissible majorant after multiplication by the global bound for g. Apply the parameter-dependent integral theorems for the time derivative, spatial derivative, and Hessian slots, and sum the diagonal Hessian slots to obtain the Laplacian formula.

Let g be continuous and globally bounded. At every positive-time point, the heat-kernel convolution is differentiable in time and Fréchet differentiable in space, with both derivatives obtained by differentiating the Gaussian beneath the integral. It is jointly differentiable in (t,x), every first spatial coordinate derivative is itself spatially differentiable, and the spatial Laplacian may be moved through the convolution integral.

These are dominated-differentiation theorems with explicit integrable Gaussian majorants. They give the first- and second-order regularity that the classical heat residual needs. Joint C^\infty smoothness on the positive-time half-space is the joint smoothness theorem.
For constant data, pull the constant through the convolution and use unit mass. For bounded data, dominate the absolute value of the integrand by M\Gamma_n, integrate, and again use unit mass.

The whole-space heat evolution preserves constant data. More generally, if g is continuous and |g(y)|\le M for every y, then

\left|\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma_n(x-y,t)g(y)\,dy\right|\le M \qquad (t>0).

The totalized Lean formula satisfies the same estimate for t\le0 by its definition. This is the L^\infty-contraction estimate for the explicit heat-kernel evolution, stated pointwise.
Differentiate beneath the integral using Gaussian derivative majorants, then integrate the pointwise heat-kernel identity against the bounded datum.

If g is continuous and bounded, then its heat-kernel evolution satisfies

\partial_tu(x,t)-\Delta_xu(x,t)=0

for every x and every t>0. The assumptions justify differentiating under the spatial integral.
Combine the positive-time differentiability and residual theorems with the locally uniform initial-trace theorem.

For bounded continuous initial data, the convolution formula simultaneously satisfies

u(x,t)=(\Gamma_n(\cdot,t)*g)(x),\qquad \partial_tu-\Delta u=0\quad(t>0),\qquad u(\,\cdot\,,t)\longrightarrow g

locally uniformly as t\downarrow0. The conclusion is bundled as a pointwise-solution structure containing the required derivative hypotheses, the residual equation, the assigned value at zero, and the locally uniform trace.
Use unit mass to subtract g(x_0) inside the convolution. Split into a near region controlled by continuity and a far Gaussian tail controlled by boundedness.

For bounded continuous g, fix x_0 and \varepsilon>0. Then there is \delta>0 such that, for every x and t,

\lVert x-x_0\rVert<\delta,\quad 0<t<\delta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |u(x,t)-g(x_0)|<\varepsilon.

For initial data g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R and t>0, define

u(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma_n(x-y,t)g(y)\,dy.

The total Lean function returns g(x) for t\leq0.

Subtract the two integrated equations. The difference is an integrated weak solution with initial datum u_{01}-u_{02} and forcing \ell_1-\ell_2. Apply the Lions–Magenes energy identity, use the Gårding lower bound on the form, and estimate the dual forcing by Young's inequality. The stated estimate retains the lower-order pivot integral; a further Grönwall step can bound it. With common initial data and strict coercivity, integration and cancellation give \|u_1-u_2\|_{L^2(V)}\leq C^{-1}\|\ell_1-\ell_2\|_{L^2(V^*)}.

Consider two solutions for the same strongly measurable, essentially uniformly bounded form on [a,b], where a<b. Assume the Gårding inequality with \theta>0. Subtracting their integrated equations gives the Gårding energy inequality for the continuous pivot-space difference, with both the difference of initial data and the difference of L^2(V^*) forcings visible. In the strictly coercive case C>0, a common initial datum gives the operator estimate

\lVert u_1-u_2\rVert_{L^2(a,b;V)} \le C^{-1}\lVert\ell_1-\ell_2\rVert_{L^2(a,b;V^*)}.

The zero-data specialization gives uniqueness, and the quantitative continuous-dependence form completes the Galerkin solution operator from regular to arbitrary L^2 loads.

A pivot-space trajectory u_H:\mathbb R\to H has integrated dual derivative g:\mathbb R\to V^* on [a,b] when g is Bochner integrable there and

J^*u_H(t)=J^*u_H(a)+\int_a^t g(s)\,ds \qquad(t\in[a,b]).

This is endpoint-inclusive data in V^*. Differentiability of u_H as an H-valued map would require the stronger assumption that g is represented by an integrable pivot-space velocity.

The defining identity writes J^*u_H(t) as a fixed vector plus the indefinite Bochner integral of g, which is continuous. Subtract the identities at s and t, then evaluate the resulting V^* equality on v to obtain the pairing formula. For s\le t, taking the dual norm and applying the Bochner integral norm estimate gives the final bound.

The integrated identity makes J^*u_H continuous as a V^*-valued map and gives, for every v\in V and s,t\in[a,b],

(u_H(t),Jv)_H-(u_H(s),Jv)_H =\int_s^t g(r)[v]\,dr.

For s\le t it also gives

\lVert J^*u_H(t)-J^*u_H(s)\rVert_{V^*} \le\int_s^t\lVert g(r)\rVert_{V^*}\,dr.

These are spatially weak forms of the fundamental theorem of calculus; strong continuity in H is the extra content of Lions–Magenes.

Recover the weak time derivative and Lions–Magenes representative from the integrated identity, identify the initial endpoint, and combine the exact pivot energy identity with coercivity and Young's inequality.

Let a<b, let B be strongly measurable and essentially uniformly bounded, and let \ell be continuous on [a,b]. Assume C>0, M\geq0, B(t)(v,v)\geq C\|v\|_V^2, and \|\ell(t)\|_{V^*}\leq M for every t\in[a,b] and v\in V. Every integrated weak solution admits a continuous pivot representative with the prescribed initial value and, for every t\in[a,b],

\frac12\lVert u_H(t)\rVert_H^2+ \frac C2\int_a^t\lVert u(s)\rVert_V^2\,ds \le \frac12\lVert u_0\rVert_H^2+ \frac{M^2}{2C}(t-a).

This is the final-solution counterpart of Evans's uniform Galerkin estimate. The theorem also reconstructs an L^2(a,b;V^*) weak derivative; endpoint values refer to the returned continuous representative.

Apply the Lions–Magenes identity to the difference, discard the nonnegative energy term, and use integral Grönwall on the squared pivot norm. Almost everywhere equality of included representatives then gives equality in L^2(a,b;V) by injectivity of J.

Let a<b and let B be strongly measurable and essentially uniformly bounded. Assume, for all t\in[a,b] and v\in V,

\theta\lVert v\rVert_V^2\le B(t)(v,v)+\gamma\lVert Jv\rVert_H^2

with \theta\ge0 and \gamma\in\mathbb R. Two integrated weak solutions with the same forcing and initial datum are equal as L^2(a,b;V) classes. This follows Evans's lower-order uniqueness argument; the unshifted form need not be nonnegative.

Uniform boundedness of B(t) sends u\in L^2(V) to B(\cdot)u\in L^2(V^*), so g=\ell-B(\cdot)u is a valid Bochner class. Move the form term in the integrated equation to the right; the remaining identity is exactly the Gelfand weak-derivative test formula for g. Lions–Magenes supplies the continuous pivot representative. Comparing the initial boundary term in the integrated identity with its fundamental theorem formula forces the left trace to equal u_0.

If B(t):V\to V^* is strongly measurable and essentially uniformly bounded, the time-tested integrated equation identifies the residual

g(t)=\ell(t)-B(t)u(t)

as an element of L^2(a,b;V^*) and proves that it is the Gelfand weak time derivative of u. Consequently g+B(\cdot)u=\ell almost everywhere. For a<b, the same theorem chain returns a continuous pivot representative with left endpoint exactly u_0; the trace equality comes from the initial-endpoint test.

Let a<b. In one Hilbert space V, the integrated formulation uses its inner product for both the time term and initial datum. More generally, let V\hookrightarrow H\hookrightarrow V^* be a Gelfand triple, let B(t):V\to V^* be induced by a time-dependent bilinear form, and fix u_0\in H and \ell\in L^2(a,b;V^*). A Gelfand integrated weak solution is a Bochner class u\in L^2(a,b;V) for which the tested spatial-form and forcing terms are integrable and the following identity holds:

-\int_a^b (u(t),v)_H\,\tau'(t)\,dt+\int_a^b B(t)u(t)[v]\,\tau(t)\,dt =\int_a^b \ell(t)[v]\,\tau(t)\,dt+(u_0,v)_H\,\tau(a)

This is required for every v\in V and every scalar function \tau:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R differentiable at each point of [a,b], with \tau,\tau'\in L^2(a,b) and \tau(b)=0. The forcing pairing is integrable by Hölder under the stated L^2 assumption; the definition records integrability of both tested terms explicitly. Both versions are invariant under almost-everywhere changes of the forcing or trajectory.

Fix (x_0,t_0) and a cutoff \chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega) equal to 1 near x_0. Restart the clock at a=t_0/2. The product \chi u solves the heat equation with forcing R, which involves \nabla\chi and \Delta\chi and is therefore supported away from x_0. Duhamel's principle represents \chi u on [a,T] as the Gaussian convolution of \chi u(\cdot,a) at age t-a plus the integral in time of the Gaussian convolutions of R(\cdot,s) at age t-s. The first term is smooth because its age is bounded away from zero near t_0. In the second term, the kernel is evaluated only at spatial offsets bounded away from zero, where \Gamma_n(x,t) extended by 0 for t\leq0 is smooth. Hence the second term is smooth in (x,t) near (x_0,t_0), also when t_0=T.

As in Evans, the proof localizes with a cutoff, writes the result as a heat-kernel integral, and integrates by parts to remove \nabla u. It keeps the terminal time: the extension is smooth on an open set around (x_0,T), while u itself is only asserted smooth within \Omega\times(0,T]. No mixed derivative and no second time derivative are assumed.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be open and T>0. Suppose u is continuous on \Omega\times(0,T], has continuous first and second spatial derivatives there and a continuous time derivative taken within (0,T], and solves u_t-\Delta u=0 on \Omega\times(0,T]. Then u is C^\infty on \Omega\times(0,T]. Near every point of this set, including points with t=T, u agrees with a function that is C^\infty on an open neighborhood of the point.

Apply the general backward self-similar blow-up theorem with amplitude exponent 1 and spatial exponent \beta_j. A moving spatial sample keeps the similarity coordinate at a point where Q is nonzero, so its norm is a fixed positive constant times (T-t)^{-1}. The global profile bound also bounds each spatial slice by a finite multiple of this amplitude for t<T.

A bounded density profile that is nonzero at one point makes the abnormal density ansatz blow up in spatial supremum norm at T: its slices are finite and their supremum diverges because the amplitude is (T-t)^{-1}. Without boundedness, the extended supremum still diverges.

The exact substitution theorem factors the physical residual as -(T-t)^{-2} times the abnormal profile residual. Under the diffusion-free aggregation equation, every term in that profile residual cancels except -(T-t)^{\delta_j}\Delta Q. Multiplying the two negative factors gives the displayed diffusion error.

Suppose Q,\Phi\in C^2, t<T, and the pair satisfies the diffusion-free aggregation profile equation at the displayed similarity coordinate. Exact substitution into the density equation leaves

\mathcal R_u(x,t) =(T-t)^{-2}(T-t)^{\delta_j} \Delta Q\!\left((T-t)^{-\beta_j}(x-x_0)\right).

The identity separates the singular physical prefactor from the lower-order profile error.
The mode assumption gives \delta_j=\frac13-\frac1j>0. The base T-t tends to zero as t\uparrow T, and continuity of r\mapsto r^{\delta_j} at zero for a positive exponent sends this limit to zero.

For every j\ge4,

(T-t)^{\delta_j}\longrightarrow0\qquad\text{as }t\uparrow T.

So diffusion is asymptotically lower order in similarity variables; at each pre-singular time the coefficient is positive.

At a fixed pre-singular time, positivity of the physical prefactor and inverse dilation reduce global vanishing of the physical residual to global vanishing of the profile residual. The aggregation equation rewrites that profile residual as a nonzero positive power of T-t times -\Delta Q(y). It therefore vanishes at every profile point exactly when \Delta Q does.

Suppose Q,\Phi\in C^2 and the diffusion-free aggregation profile equation holds at every profile point. At any fixed t<T, the uncorrected abnormal ansatz has zero density residual at every spatial point if and only if

\Delta Q(y)=0\qquad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb R^3.

This is an exact no-go theorem for nonharmonic leading profiles. It concerns the density equation; the elliptic potential equation is a separate condition.

At x=x_0, the centered dilation is zero. Combine (T-t)^{-2} with (T-t)^{1-2\beta_j} to obtain (T-t)^{-(1+2\beta_j)}. The mode bound implies 1+2\beta_j>0, so this power tends to +\infty; multiplication by the positive constant |\Delta Q(0)| preserves the limit.

Assume j\ge4, the profiles are C^2, the diffusion-free aggregation profile equation holds everywhere, and \Delta Q(0)\ne0. At the similarity center, the exact residual identity reduces to

\left|\mathcal R_u(x_0,t)\right| = (T-t)^{-(1+2\beta_j)}|\Delta Q(0)|.

Since 1+2\beta_j>0, this physical residual tends to +\infty as t\uparrow T, while the rescaled diffusion coefficient tends to zero.

For modes j\ge4, the Liu–Wang–Zhou abnormal scaling uses

\beta_j=\frac13+\frac{1}{2j}, \qquad \delta_j=1-2\beta_j=\frac13-\frac1j>0.

The exponent lies strictly between 1/3 and the parabolic value 1/2. Consequently diffusion enters the rescaled density equation with the lower-order coefficient (T-t)^{\delta_j}.

The scaling follows Liu et al. (2025), Theorem 1.1 and equations (1.8), (1.12), and (1.13), with \mu=0. The Lean development treats the leading ansatz, the exponent arithmetic, and the residual identities.

Unfold the physical density residual. Substitute the flux-divergence formula and the time-derivative formula; each has the same factor (T-t)^{-2}. Distributing that factor leaves exactly the definition of \mathcal R_Q[Q,\Psi].

The density residual identity for the parabolic ansatz combines the time-derivative and flux formulas for C^2 profiles and t<T into the full density residual factorization

\mathcal R_u[u_Q,\Phi_\Psi](x,t) =(T-t)^{-2}\mathcal R_Q[Q,\Psi](y),

where \mathcal R_u=\operatorname{div}(\nabla u-u\nabla\Phi)-\partial_t u. Consequently, vanishing profile residuals imply both pointwise Keller–Segel equations before T.

The density gradient scales by (T-t)^{-1}(T-t)^{-1/2}, and the potential gradient by (T-t)^{-1/2}. Hence both terms in the flux share the first factor. Taking one more divergence contributes another (T-t)^{-1/2}. The identity ((T-t)^{-1/2})^2=(T-t)^{-1} then combines the factors into (T-t)^{-2}.

The flux divergence identity for the parabolic ansatz states that if both profiles are C^2 and t<T, then the conservative flux satisfies

\operatorname{div}_x \left(\nabla_x u_Q-u_Q\nabla_x\Phi_\Psi\right)(x,t) =(T-t)^{-2} \operatorname{div}_y\left(\nabla Q-Q\nabla\Psi\right)(y).

Choose a physical sample whose similarity coordinate is the point where Q is nonzero. Along this sample the profile value is fixed, while the amplitude (T-t)^{-1} tends to +\infty. The general backward self-similar blow-up theorem transfers this sampled divergence to the extended spatial supremum. A global bound |Q(y)|\le C bounds each slice by the finite value (T-t)^{-1}C for t<T.

If the density profile is bounded and nonzero at one point, then its parabolic density ansatz has finite spatial slices and blows up in the pointwise spatial supremum at T. One nonzero value suffices for divergence of the extended supremum; boundedness supplies the finite-slice condition. The theorem uses only the similarity scaling of the density.

For t<T, write

y=(T-t)^{-1/2}(x-x_0),\qquad u_Q(x,t)=(T-t)^{-1}Q(y),\qquad \Phi_\Psi(x,t)=\Psi(y).

The reduced residuals are

\mathcal R_\Phi[Q,\Psi]=-\Delta\Psi-Q,\qquad \mathcal R_Q[Q,\Psi] =\operatorname{div}(\nabla Q-Q\nabla\Psi) -Q-\frac12 y\mathbin{\cdot}\nabla Q.

The two equations are represented by separate residual functions, defined in every finite dimension without regularity or sign assumptions.

Generic regularity lemmas for scaled profiles give joint C^1 regularity of the density, joint continuity of the potential, and C^2 regularity of every spatial slice. Positivity of the amplitude transfers Q\geq0 to the physical density. Finally, the two residual factorizations turn the assumed profile equations into the density and potential equations at every t<T.

If both profile residuals vanish, the density profile is nonnegative, and both profiles are C^2, then the parabolic ansatz is a nonnegative pointwise classical solution on (-\infty,T). The density is jointly C^1, the potential is jointly continuous, and both have C^2 spatial slices.

The Laplacian of the scaled potential contributes the square of the spatial dilation factor. Before T, the identity ((T-t)^{-1/2})^2=(T-t)^{-1} makes this factor equal to the density amplitude. Expanding the potential residual and collecting the common factor gives the stated profile residual.

The potential residual identity for the parabolic ansatz states that, whether or not \Psi is C^2, for every t<T,

\mathcal R_\Phi[u_Q,\Phi_\Psi](x,t) =(T-t)^{-1}\mathcal R_\Phi[Q,\Psi](y).

The forward direction of each equivalence evaluates the physical residual at x=x_0+s^{-1}y, where s=(T-t)^{-1/2}. The scale is positive, and the centered dilation sends this x back to y. The residual factorization then has a nonzero scalar factor, so the profile residual must vanish. The reverse direction substitutes the vanishing profile residual directly into the same factorization.

At every fixed time t<T, the similarity substitution loses no spatial information. Positivity of the scale and inverse dilation give the two exact equivalences

\begin{aligned} \mathcal R_\Phi[u_Q,\Phi_\Psi](\mathbin{\cdot},t)=0 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathcal R_\Phi[Q,\Psi]=0,\\ \mathcal R_u[u_Q,\Phi_\Psi](\mathbin{\cdot},t)=0 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathcal R_Q[Q,\Psi]=0. \end{aligned}

Each physical equation is also equivalent pointwise to its reduced equation at the corresponding similarity coordinate. The elliptic direction requires \Psi\in C^2; the density direction requires Q,\Psi\in C^2.

On an open time set I, classical parabolic–elliptic Keller–Segel solutions use the sign convention

u_t=\operatorname{div}(\nabla u-u\nabla\Phi),\qquad -\Delta\Phi=u.

The density is nonnegative and jointly C^1 in spacetime, the potential is jointly continuous, and both have C^2 spatial slices; joint C^{2,1} regularity is not required. The elliptic equation alone determines \Phi only up to a harmonic component, and the definition imposes neither a Newtonian-potential normalization nor decay at spatial infinity.

Apply the general differentiation formula for a backward self-similar ansatz with amplitude exponent 1 and spatial exponent 1/2. The derivative of the amplitude gives Q(y), while differentiation of the moving coordinate gives \frac12 y\mathbin{\cdot}\nabla Q(y). Both terms carry the common factor (T-t)^{-2}.

The density time-derivative identity for the parabolic ansatz states that if Q is C^1 and t<T, then the density time derivative is exactly

\partial_t u_Q(x,t) =(T-t)^{-2}\left(Q(y)+\frac12 y\mathbin{\cdot}\nabla Q(y)\right).

Rewrite the assumed derivative as the constant -\gamma(M). The lower and upper mean-value inequalities on the convex interval [0,T] then bound I(t)-I(0) from both sides by -\gamma(M)t. The two bounds coincide, which gives the affine identity.

If I is continuous on [0,T], differentiable on (0,T), and satisfies the virial identity there, then

I(t)=I(0)-\gamma(M)t\qquad(0\le t\le T).

Mass conservation rewrites the differentiated density-level virial identity as the scalar identity with the fixed mass M. Integrability of the quadratic moment and pointwise nonnegativity at T imply I_u(T)\geq0 by monotonicity of the integral. The scalar endpoint theorem then yields the displayed bound.

For a density u : \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\to\mathbb R, define its mass and second moment directly by

M_u(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}u(x,t)\,dx, \qquad I_u(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}|x|^2u(x,t)\,dx.

These are totalized Bochner integrals. The theorem assumes T\geq0 and a finite quadratic moment on every slice in [0,T]; the nonzero conserved mass certifies integrability of the density slices. If u(\cdot,T) is pointwise nonnegative, M_u(t)=M>8\pi, and I_u has the required continuity, differentiability, and virial identity, then

T\le \frac{I_u(0)}{M^2/(2\pi)-4M}.

Mass conservation and the differentiated virial law are hypotheses.

For mass M>8\pi, define

\gamma(M)=\frac{M^2}{2\pi}-4M>0, \qquad T_{\mathrm{vir}}=\frac{I(0)}{\gamma(M)}.

For the whole-space system with sensitivity one and the normalized Newtonian potential, the classical second-moment identity is I'(t)=-\gamma(M) (Blanchet–Dolbeault–Perthame, Electron. J. Differential Equations 2006(44), Theorem 1.1 and equation (2.3)).

The pointwise Keller–Segel solution predicate does not fix this normalization: adding a harmonic function to \Phi preserves -\Delta\Phi=u but can change the drift. A PDE derivation of the sharp virial law therefore also needs the Newtonian normalization or equivalent decay, finite moments, mass conservation, differentiation under the integral, and justified integration by parts. The theorems take the resulting scalar derivative identity as a hypothesis.

Supercritical mass makes \gamma(M) positive. If the endpoint lay strictly beyond I(0)/\gamma(M), the affine formula at T would give I(T)=I(0)-\gamma(M)T<0. This contradicts the assumed nonnegativity of the endpoint moment.

Suppose T\geq0, the second moment is continuous on [0,T], differentiable on (0,T), and satisfies the virial identity there. If M>8\pi and the second moment is nonnegative at T, then

T\le T_{\mathrm{vir}}.

The endpoint T is any time up to which the hypotheses hold. Jäger–Luckhaus, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 329 (1992), DOI 10.1090/S0002-9947-1992-1046835-6, is the historical background for radial explosion arguments; the whole-space identity is the one of Blanchet–Dolbeault–Perthame.

For global data, mollify u and g in time; on a finite interval use the reflected cutoff extensions. For the smooth approximants, the Hilbert chain rule gives \frac d{dt}\|Ju_\varepsilon\|_H^2 =2\langle g_\varepsilon,u_\varepsilon\rangle. Integrate from s to t. The selected sequence converges in H at each endpoint, while strong L^2(V) convergence of u_\varepsilon and strong L^2(V^*) convergence of g_\varepsilon pass the duality integrals to the limit. This gives the endpoint identity. Hölder makes r\mapsto g(r)[u(r)] integrable, so the squared norm is an indefinite integral of an L^1 function and is absolutely continuous.

For the continuous pivot representative u_H, the squared norm is absolutely continuous and obeys, for all s,t\in[a,b],

\lVert u_H(t)\rVert_H^2-\lVert u_H(s)\rVert_H^2 =2\int_s^t g(r)[u(r)]\,dr.

For u,g square integrable on \mathbb R and satisfying the weak derivative identity there, the companion theorem gives the corresponding identity for Ju at two continuity points of u. The finite-interval evolution instead uses the canonical H representative and needs no such pointwise assumptions.

The Gelfand weak derivative gives the distributional derivative of the dual-valued trajectory through the weak time-derivative condition. Apply the global theorem to interior cutoff extensions. Their continuous pivot representatives agree on overlaps because each equals Ju almost everywhere, so they glue on (a,b). Reflect the state and dual derivative compatibly, then choose a cutoff equal to one near [a,b]. The global theorem for this extension supplies both endpoint traces, and its integrated derivative and energy identities restrict to the closed interval.

Under the same Hilbert-space hypotheses, for a<b, an L^2(a,b;V) trajectory with an L^2(a,b;V^*) Gelfand weak derivative first has a canonical continuous pivot representative on (a,b). Reflected cutoff extensions at both endpoints then produce a representative in C([a,b];H) without assuming pre-existing traces. The returned structure records almost-everywhere agreement with Ju, the integrated V^* derivative identity, and the exact energy identity for all endpoints in [a,b].

Regularize both u and its dual derivative in time, prove the energy identity for the smooth approximants, obtain a pointwise pivot-space limit, and strengthen it to a continuous representative using the integral energy formula.

For a Gelfand inclusion between real Hilbert spaces V and H, if u\in L^2(\mathbb R;V) has weak derivative u'\in L^2(\mathbb R;V^*), then the pivot-space class has a continuous representative u_H:\mathbb R\to H. It agrees almost everywhere with the dense inclusion of u, has integrated dual derivative u' on every finite interval, and satisfies

\lVert u_H(b)\rVert_H^2-\lVert u_H(a)\rVert_H^2 =2\int_a^b \langle u'(t),u(t)\rangle_{V^*,V}\,dt.

This is the abstract theorem used by Evans to infer u\in C([0,T];L^2(U)) before interpreting the initial condition in the parabolic weak problem.

By translation and parabolic scaling, it suffices to treat the unit cylinder ending at (0,0). There fixed cutoffs in space and time, equal to 1 near the half cylinder, localize u. The cutoff residual contains \nabla u; integrating by parts in space moves those derivatives onto a single smooth compactly supported kernel that agrees with the Gaussian on the support of the residual. The representation then expresses u near the half cylinder as an integral of u alone against that kernel and its derivatives, and differentiating under the integral bounds D_x^kD_t^lu by a constant times \int|u|. The constant depends only on the kernel, hence only on n, k and l. Scaling back produces the factor r^{-(k+2l+n+2)}. This is Evans's proof, with the fixed kernel as the representation formula.

For all n,k,l\geq0 there is a constant C=C_{n,k,l}>0 with the following property. Let u satisfy the hypotheses of Theorem 6.50 on \Omega\times(0,T], and let r>0 with C(x,t;r)\subset\Omega\times(0,T]. Then u is integrable on C(x,t;r), the norm of the mixed derivative D_x^kD_t^lu attains its maximum on C(x,t;r/2), and

\max_{C(x,t;r/2)}\bigl\|D_x^kD_t^lu\bigr\| \leq\frac{C}{r^{k+2l+n+2}}\int_{C(x,t;r)}|u|\,dy\,ds.

The derivatives are taken within \Omega\times(0,T], so the cylinder may touch the terminal time, and the norm is the operator norm of the k-linear spatial derivative.

For a matrix field a(x,t), a drift b(x,t), and a potential c(x,t),

Lu=u_t-\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}(x,t)\,\partial_i\partial_ju+Du\cdot b+c\,u.

When a_{ij}=\sum_k\sigma_{ki}\sigma_{kj} and the spatial slice is C^2 at the point, this agrees with the factored operator.

The same perturbation u_\varepsilon=u-\varepsilon t produces the additional term -c\varepsilon t, which has the favorable sign because c,\varepsilon,t\geq0. At a positive maximum the zeroth-order term is also nonnegative.

If c\geq0, M\geq0, Pu+cu\leq0, and u\leq M on the parabolic boundary, then u\leq M throughout the closed cylinder. Taking M to be the maximum of the positive part of the boundary data gives Evans's Theorem 9(i).

Set w(t)=e^{-\gamma(t-a)}u(t). The shifted form B_\gamma(t)(v,z)=B(t)(v,z)+\gamma(Jv,Jz)_H is coercive, and the shifted forcing is e^{-\gamma(t-a)}\ell(t). For bounded continuous loads, solve the measurable finite-dimensional Carathéodory systems and pass their integrated equations to a weak state limit. Complete this coercive solution operator to arbitrary L^2 loads using the continuous-dependence estimate, and apply it to the shifted forcing. Multiplication by e^{\gamma(t-a)} returns a solution of the original equation. The residual theorem and Lions–Magenes give the weak derivative, continuous pivot trace, and prefix energy estimate; Gårding uniqueness follows from the homogeneous difference equation and integral Gronwall.

Let a<b and let B(t):V\to V^* be strongly measurable and uniformly bounded on [a,b]. Assume the Gårding inequality

\theta\lVert v\rVert_V^2\le B(t)(v,v)+\gamma\lVert Jv\rVert_H^2,\qquad \theta>0.

Given stable finite-dimensional projections dense in both V and H, every forcing in L^2(a,b;V^*) and every initial datum in H determine a unique integrated weak solution. The full theorem additionally returns its L^2 weak derivative, the almost-everywhere identity u'=\ell-B(\cdot)u, a continuous pivot representative with the prescribed left trace, and the Gårding energy estimate on every prefix [a,t].
Apply the maximum principle with potential to -u and the nonnegative upper bound -M, then negate the resulting inequality.

If c\geq0, M\leq0, Pu+cu\geq0, and u\geq M on the parabolic boundary, then u\geq M throughout the closed cylinder. This is the dual minimum statement in Evans's Theorem 9(ii), with the sign restriction on M required by the nonnegative zeroth-order coefficient.

Choose y_0 with Q(y_0)\ne0 and sample the field at x(t)=x_0+\lambda(t)y_0. There the profile argument is exactly y_0, so the absolute value is \lambda(t)^{-2/(p-1)}|Q(y_0)|. Since p>1 and \lambda(t)\to0^+, this quantity tends to +\infty and is bounded above by the spatial supremum. If |Q(y)|\le C everywhere, the same formula bounds the whole slice by the finite number \lambda(t)^{-2/(p-1)}C whenever \lambda(t)>0. Positivity holds eventually by the scale-limit hypothesis.

If p>1, the profile is nonzero somewhere, and \lambda(t)\to0 through positive values as t\uparrow T, then the extended pointwise spatial supremum of the ansatz tends to +\infty. No global boundedness assumption on the profile is needed for this limit. If the profile is bounded, every slice has finite supremum and the ansatz satisfies divergence of the spatial supremum norm.

By the global criterion, a moving stationary profile with \Lambda Q\not\equiv0 is not a nonlinear-heat solution, and correction terms are needed.

At x=x_0 the similarity variable is zero, so \Lambda Q(0)=\frac{2}{p-1}Q(0). This quantity is nonzero because p\ne1 and Q(0)>0; hence the scaling-generator branch of the pointwise criterion is impossible, and \lambda'(t)=0.

Suppose p\ne1, Q is a C^2 stationary profile with Q(0)>0, and the scale is positive and differentiable at t. If the pure concentration ansatz has zero residual at the spatial center x=x_0, then

\lambda'(t)=0.

This gives a local obstruction without imposing a global nonvanishing condition on the scaling generator.

Differentiate the ansatz through the similarity coordinate. Each spatial derivative contributes one factor of \lambda^{-1}, while the time derivative contributes the scale-velocity term \lambda\lambda'\Lambda Q. The nonlinear power has the same prefactor as the Laplacian because \frac{2p}{p-1}=\frac{2}{p-1}+2. Collecting these terms gives the stated stationary residual plus modulation defect.

Suppose p\ne1, Q is C^2 and nonnegative at y=\lambda(t)^{-1}(x-x_0), and the scale is positive and differentiable at t. Write

\Lambda Q(y)=\frac{2}{p-1}Q(y)+y\mathbin{\cdot}\nabla Q(y).

The full parabolic residual has the exact factorization

\mathcal R_p[u](x,t) =\lambda(t)^{-\left(\frac{2}{p-1}+2\right)} \left( \mathcal R_{\mathrm{stat}}[Q](y) +\lambda(t)\lambda'(t)\Lambda Q(y) \right).

Thus the formal identity separates the stationary elliptic error from the modulation defect.

If \lambda'(t)=0, the pointwise criterion settles every spatial point. Otherwise it forces \Lambda Q to vanish at every similarity coordinate. Every y\in\mathbb R^n occurs by choosing x=x_0+\lambda(t)y, because the positive scale is invertible. Conversely, either global alternative implies the pointwise disjunction for each x.

Let p\ne1, let Q be a globally nonnegative C^2 stationary profile, and let the scale be positive and differentiable at a fixed time. The residual vanishes at every spatial point at that time exactly when

\lambda'(t)=0 \quad\text{or}\quad \Lambda Q(y)=0\ \text{for every }y\in\mathbb R^n.

Thus a moving scale, \lambda'(t)\ne0, forces the scaling generator to vanish on the whole profile.

Substitute the stationary profile equation \mathcal R_{\mathrm{stat}}[Q]=0 into the exact factorization. The elliptic term disappears, leaving only the scale derivative multiplied by the scaling generator.

Under the same regularity, sign, exponent, and scale assumptions, a stationary elliptic profile has vanishing profile residual, and the remaining parabolic error is exactly

\lambda(t)^{-\left(\frac{2}{p-1}+2\right)} \lambda(t)\lambda'(t)\Lambda Q(y).

This specialization exposes the additional modulation condition required for the concentration ansatz to solve the evolution equation.

Positivity of \lambda(t) makes the common power of \lambda(t) nonzero. The residual therefore vanishes exactly when \lambda(t)\lambda'(t)\Lambda Q(y)=0. Removing the second nonzero scale factor and splitting the remaining product yields the two alternatives.

Let p\ne1, let Q be a C^2 stationary elliptic profile that is nonnegative at the relevant similarity coordinate, and let the scale be positive and differentiable at t. The pure concentration ansatz has zero residual at (x,t) if and only if

\lambda'(t)=0\quad\text{or}\quad \Lambda Q(y)=0.

Apply center rigidity at every point of I to obtain \lambda'=0 throughout the interval. Since an open connected subset of \mathbb R is an interval, the mean-value theorem applied between any two of its points shows that their scale values agree.

Let p\ne1, let Q be a C^2 stationary profile with Q(0)>0, and let I be an open, preconnected time set. If the scale is positive and differentiable on I and the center residual vanishes for every t\in I, then

\lambda(s)=\lambda(t)\qquad\text{for all }s,t\in I.

For every p>1 and finite time T, define the spatially constant field

u(x,t)=\big((p-1)(T-t)\big)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}, \qquad t<T.

This is the spatially homogeneous solution of the scalar equation u_t=u^p, viewed as a function on \mathbb R^n. It comes with a complete PDE and norm-divergence proof.

This whole-space example isolates the spatially homogeneous ODE blow-up mechanism. Its slices are nonzero constants, so it satisfies no homogeneous Dirichlet condition and, in positive dimension, does not lie in L^2(\mathbb R^n).

The spatial supremum is at least the value at any fixed point and, because the field is constant, equals that value. As t\uparrow T, the positive base (p-1)(T-t) tends to zero. The exponent -1/(p-1) is negative, so the power tends to +\infty. Passing through ENNReal.ofReal preserves this divergence. The displayed supremum identity supplies finiteness at every preceding time.

The theorem uses the pointwise value at any spatial sample to prove blow-up. The companion identity for every t<T is

S_u(t) =\operatorname{ofReal}\!\left( \big((p-1)(T-t)\big)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}} \right),

which is finite for every t<T and tends to +\infty as t\uparrow T. Thus the field satisfies divergence of the spatial supremum norm at T for every p>1.

Let a=1/(p-1) and s=(p-1)(T-t)>0. The field is independent of x, so every spatial derivative and hence \Delta u vanishes. The real-power chain rule gives u_t=s^{-a-1} after the factor p-1 cancels a; since ap=a+1, this equals u^p. Positivity of s also gives positivity and the required smoothness on t<T.

The constant-profile solution theorem for the nonlinear heat equation states that on \mathbb R^n\times(-\infty,T), the field is a nonnegative classical solution of

u_t=\Delta u+u^p.

The equation field of the classical-solution proof is the constant-profile equation theorem, proved without the Type I profile theory. The formal theorem also checks joint spacetime C^1 regularity, C^2 regularity of every spatial slice, and positivity on the entire pre-singular cylinder.

Choose the explicitly defined constant field. The equation theorem supplies its nonnegative pointwise classical-solution structure on the full pre-singular cylinder, and the divergence theorem supplies spatial supremum-norm blow-up at T. Combining those two facts for the same witness proves the existential statement.

For every p>1 and finite T, there exists a nonnegative pointwise classical whole-space solution on t<T whose spatial supremum norm blows up at T. The witness is the spatially constant field ((p-1)(T-t))^{-1/(p-1)}.

The minimum principle makes u nonnegative. Testing the equation against w, the diffusion term becomes -\lambda\eta, and Jensen's inequality for the probability weight w gives \int_\Omega w\,u^2\ge\eta^2, so \eta'\ge\eta^2-\lambda\eta. Since no boundary derivative of u is available, the formal proof tests against compactly supported convex truncations of w and absorbs their error into a slightly larger damping \lambda+\delta. For v=1/\eta the inequality reads v'\le\lambda v-1, and comparison with the solution of v'=\lambda v-1 keeps v positive only while 1-e^{-\lambda t}<\lambda/\eta_0. Letting \delta\to0 gives 1-e^{-\lambda T}\le\lambda/\eta_0, which is the bound.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be nonempty, bounded and open. Let w\ge0 be C^2 in \Omega, continuous on \overline\Omega and zero on \partial\Omega, with -\Delta w=\lambda w in \Omega, \lambda>0 and \int_\Omega w=1. Let g\ge0 on \Omega with

\eta_0=\int_\Omega w\,g>\lambda.

Suppose u is C^2 in (0,T)\times\Omega, continuous on [0,T]\times\overline\Omega, solves u_t-\Delta u=u^2 in (0,T)\times\Omega, vanishes on (0,T)\times\partial\Omega and equals g at t=0. Then

T\le\frac1\lambda\log\frac{\eta_0}{\eta_0-\lambda}.

In particular there is no such solution for every T>0. No derivative of u or w on the boundary and no regularity of the boundary are used.

The first Dirichlet eigenfunction gives a positive probability weight. Lions–Magenes regularity supplies the continuous L^2 representative of the weak solution, and pairing its integrated derivative with w gives an absolutely continuous moment M(t)=\int_\Omega w u(t), with M(a)=M_0. The weak eigen-equation identifies diffusion as \lambda M. The reaction identity and weighted Jensen inequality then give, almost everywhere,

M'(t)+\lambda M(t)=\int_\Omega wF(u(t)) \ge F(M(t))\ge c M(t)^p.

For z(t)=e^{\lambda(t-a)}M(t), the coefficient in the power inequality is bounded below by c e^{-\lambda(b-a)(p-1)}. Absolute continuity justifies integrating the negative-power derivative. Positivity and finiteness at b force the strict opposite of the displayed threshold, a contradiction.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n>0, be nonempty, bounded, connected, and open, and let a<b. The domain admits a positive first Dirichlet eigenweight w\in H^1_0(\Omega) with eigenvalue \lambda>0 and \int_\Omega w=1. Suppose F, not necessarily differentiable, is convex on the nonnegative half-line, with

F(s)\ge c s^p\quad(s\ge0),\qquad c>0,\quad p>1.

For initial datum u_a\in L^2(\Omega), set M_0=\int_\Omega w u_a. If M_0>0 and

M_0^{1-p}\le (p-1)c\,e^{-\lambda(b-a)(p-1)}(b-a),

there is no nonnegative weak energy solution of u_t-\Delta u=F(u) on [a,b] with zero Dirichlet boundary data and initial datum u_a.

Precisely, the excluded class has u\in L^2((a,b);H^1_0(\Omega)) and a dual forcing \ell\in L^2((a,b);H^{-1}(\Omega)) satisfying the integrated weak heat equation with that initial trace. For almost every time, u\ge0 almost everywhere in space, and for every v\in H^1_0(\Omega), vF(u) is integrable and \ell(v)=\int_\Omega vF(u). The threshold is a sufficient condition for nonexistence on the prescribed interval [a,b].

The derivative and the divergence of u_* are those of the constant field at any spatial point. For the converse, u stays at least u_0, since its right derivative u_0^p is positive wherever it equals u_0. Then u^{1-p} has right derivative 1-p on [0,T), so u(t)^{1-p}=u_0^{1-p}-(p-1)t. The left side is positive on [0,T], which is T<T_p(u_0), and solving for u gives u_*.

Let p>1 and u_0>0, and set

T_p(u_0)=\frac{u_0^{1-p}}{p-1},\qquad u_*(t)=\big((p-1)(T_p(u_0)-t)\big)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}.

Then u_*(0)=u_0, u_*'=u_*^p for t<T_p(u_0), and |u_*(t)|\to\infty as t\uparrow T_p(u_0). Conversely, let T\ge0 and let u be continuous on [0,T] with u(0)=u_0 and right derivative u(t)^p at every t\in[0,T). Then T<T_p(u_0) and u=u_* on [0,T]. For p=2, T_2(u_0)=1/u_0 and u_*(t)=1/(u_0^{-1}-t).

For a positive scale \lambda(t), the concentration ansatz is

u(x,t)=\lambda(t)^{-2/(p-1)} Q\!\left(\lambda(t)^{-1}(x-x_0)\right).

Its stationary elliptic residual is

\mathcal R_{\mathrm{stat}}[Q](y)=\Delta Q(y)+Q(y)^p,

and the stationary profile equation says exactly that this residual vanishes pointwise.

The exponent is invariant under the nonlinear-heat equation scaling. Whether that scaling is critical for a particular Sobolev or Lebesgue norm also depends on the dimension and exponent, hence the name "scaling-invariant" rather than "critical".

Type II blow-up constructions with this leading profile, such as the modulation analyses of Schweyer (arXiv:1201.2907v2) and of Collot (2017), add correction terms and prove the asymptotic law of the scale. The residual and rigidity identities here concern the pure profile.

For a real exponent p and an open time set I, this structure records a nonnegative classical solution of

u_t=\Delta u+u^p

on \mathbb R^n\times I. Its regularity scope is joint spacetime C^1 for u together with C^2 regularity of each spatial slice. Time differentiability is derived from the joint C^1 field; joint C^{2,1} regularity is not required. The equation is imposed only at times in I, so a solution on t<T says nothing at T.

The factorization writes the full residual as the profile residual multiplied by (T-t)^{-(1/(p-1)+1)}. For t<T, this prefactor is strictly positive and hence nonzero. Therefore the product vanishes exactly when the profile residual at the corresponding similarity point vanishes. Applying this pointwise to the Type I profile equation hypothesis proves the equation everywhere.

Under the factorization hypotheses, the full parabolic residual vanishes at x\in\mathbb R^n and t<T if and only if the reduced profile residual vanishes at the corresponding similarity coordinate. Consequently, the ansatz of a nonnegative C^2 profile with p\ne1 and zero Type I profile residual everywhere satisfies

u_t=\Delta u+u^p

pointwise throughout the pre-singular cylinder.

Write s=T-t, \alpha=1/(p-1), and y=s^{-1/2}(x-x_0). The backward similarity chain rules give u_t=s^{-\alpha-1}(\alpha f+\frac12y\cdot\nabla f) and \Delta u=s^{-\alpha-1}\Delta f, because two spatial scale factors produce s^{-1}. Nonnegativity permits u^p=s^{-\alpha p}f^p, and \alpha p=\alpha+1. Factoring s^{-\alpha-1} leaves the stated profile residual.

Suppose t<T, p\ne1, and the profile is C^2 and nonnegative at the displayed similarity coordinate. Then the exact residual identity is

\mathcal R_p[u](x,t) =(T-t)^{-\left(\frac{1}{p-1}+1\right)} \mathcal R_{\mathrm{prof}}[f]\! \left((T-t)^{-1/2}(x-x_0)\right).

The two balance laws are visible in the formal proof: 2\beta=1 aligns the Laplacian scale and \alpha p=\alpha+1 aligns the reaction scale. Profile nonnegativity is used only to split the real power of the amplitude-profile product.

For the Type I ansatz

u(x,t)=(T-t)^{-1/(p-1)} f\!\left(\frac{x-x_0}{\sqrt{T-t}}\right),

The reduced elliptic residual is

\Delta f-\frac12 y\cdot\nabla f-\frac{1}{p-1}f+f^p=0,

and the Type I profile equation says exactly that this residual vanishes pointwise. This is the standard Type I reduction used by Giga–Kohn, Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 38 (1985), DOI 10.1002/cpa.3160380304; the Lean statements are the exact substitution identities.

On t<T, the amplitude and similarity scale are smooth and positive. Composition with the C^2 profile gives joint C^1 regularity and C^2 regularity of each spatial slice; profile nonnegativity and the positive amplitude give u\geq0. The Type I profile equation and the zero-residual equivalence supply u_t=\Delta u+u^p at every point. These fields assemble the classical-solution structure. The converse evaluates the same nonzero factorization.

If the Type I profile residual vanishes everywhere, then under the same regularity and sign assumptions, with p>1, the ansatz is a nonnegative pointwise classical solution on (-\infty,T). For a bounded profile with a nonzero value, the Type I blow-up theorem separately gives finite spatial slices and supremum-norm blow-up at T.

Under the same regularity and sign hypotheses, the companion theorem on the profile-solution equivalence also proves the converse: a Type I ansatz is a pointwise classical solution on the full pre-singular interval exactly when its profile residual vanishes.

Apply the coercive energy estimate directly to each supplied differentiated family, using the L^2(V^*) norm of its load. Extract common weak limits for the original state, its pivot velocity, and the differentiated state. Testing their Bochner identity with bounded linear functionals identifies the two limits for the first derivative. Passing the differentiated weak equation to the limit gives u_{tt}=\dot\ell-Bu_t; boundedness of B:V\to V^* puts this residual in L^2(V^*).

For a bounded autonomous coercive form B, suppose the original and differentiated Galerkin families are supplied with initial pivot data converging in H and uniformly bounded there, a uniform L^2(H) velocity bound, and the Bochner identity J\widetilde u_m=\partial_t(Ju_m). Assume the supplied original family also carries its common integrated Galerkin energy bound. Both dual-valued loads \ell,\dot\ell must lie in L^2(a,b;V^*).

One common weak compactness filter identifies the differentiated state with the time derivative of the original limit and gives

u_{tt}=\dot\ell-Bu_t\in L^2(a,b;V^*).

For a pivot load with f_t\in L^2(a,b;H), take \dot\ell=J^*f_t. The second derivative is dual-valued, while the identified first derivative belongs to L^2(a,b;V).
The parabolic boundary consists of the initial face \overline\Omega\times\{0\} and the lateral boundary \partial\Omega\times[0,T]. The terminal face \Omega\times\{T\} is excluded.

A pointwise solution of the forced heat Cauchy problem has the time and spatial differentiability needed to interpret every derivative in the equation, satisfies the forced residual at positive time, takes the assigned value at time zero, and converges locally uniformly to that datum as time decreases to zero.

The abstract theorem, the Lipschitz-reaction existence theorem, applies to any Gårding form on a Gelfand triple. Given a trajectory w, solve the linear problem with forcing f(w) by the Galerkin theorem. This defines a map w\mapsto u whose fixed points are the solutions. Replace the unknown by e^{-\eta(t-a)}u: the rescaled reaction has the same Lipschitz constant, because the exponential factors cancel in its difference estimate, while the linear part gains the coercive term \eta\|u\|^2. For \eta large the map is a contraction on the whole interval [a,b], and the Banach fixed point theorem gives existence and uniqueness in the integrated formulation. The Gelfand evolution theorem then supplies the derivative in L^2(a,b;H^{-1}) and the continuous representative.

The exponential weight makes the contraction global on [a,b], with no restarting. The value f(0) may be nonzero, since a constant offset is square integrable on a finite interval, and no boundary regularity of \Omega is used.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be bounded and open, a<b, m\geq0, and let f:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m be globally Lipschitz. For every g\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^m) the system u_t-\Delta u=f(u) with zero boundary values has a unique weak solution u\in L^2(a,b;H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)): it has a weak time derivative u_t\in L^2(a,b;H^{-1}), a representative continuous from [a,b] into L^2 with value g at t=a, and for almost every t

\langle u_t,v\rangle+\int_\Omega\nabla u:\nabla v\,dx =\int_\Omega f(u)\cdot v\,dx\qquad\text{for all }v\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m).

Two such solutions with the same initial value have the same class, the same derivative, and equal continuous representatives on [a,b]. For g\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m) the same conclusions hold with initial value g.

Lax–Milgram defines the Ritz projection R_mg by B(R_mg,v_m)=B(g,v_m) for every trial vector. Evaluate the original right-hand side at the initial time with u_m(a)=R_mg. The Ritz identity replaces the form term by B(g,v_m), and compatibility leaves (J\widetilde u_m(a),Jv_m)_H=(h_{\mathrm{init}},Jv_m)_H. This is precisely the characterizing equation for the pivot-orthogonal projection of h_{\mathrm{init}} onto JV_m.

For each finite-dimensional trial space, Lax–Milgram constructs the Ritz projection for a bounded autonomous coercive form B. It satisfies Galerkin orthogonality B(g-R_mg,v_m)=0, Céa's estimate, and convergence along an approximating family of trial spaces. Symmetry is not needed for these statements.

Suppose a vector h_{\mathrm{init}}\in H represents the initial residual:

\ell(a)(v)=(h_{\mathrm{init}},Jv)_H+B(g,v)\qquad(v\in V).

With u_m(a)=R_mg, the initial value of the differentiated trajectory is the pivot projection of that vector:

J\widetilde u_m(a)=P_m^Hh_{\mathrm{init}}.

Here P_m^H denotes the orthogonal projection in H onto JV_m.

Initialize each original Galerkin trajectory with the Ritz projection of g. Ritz compatibility turns the assumed initial residual into a uniformly controlled pivot projection, which is valid initial data for the differentiated Galerkin system. Apply the paired L^2 theorem to these two families. Its common limit identifies the pivot derivative of Ju with Ju_t and passes the differentiated equation to u_{tt}=\dot\ell-Bu_t.

For a bounded autonomous coercive form B, take an absolutely continuous load with L^2(V^*) derivative and a pivot-valued initial compatibility residual as in Theorem 6.126. Initialize the supplied original Galerkin family, with its common integrated energy bound, by Ritz projections of g and assume its uniform L^2(H) velocity bound. The Ritz variational identity converts the compatibility condition at the initial time into the exact pivot projection of the initial velocity. The paired L^2 compactness theorem then constructs the original solution and its differentiated trajectory on one common limit, with

Ju_t=\partial_t(Ju),\qquad u_{tt}=\dot\ell-Bu_t\in L^2(a,b;V^*).

In the pivot-forcing specialization, \dot\ell=J^*f_t with f_t\in L^2(a,b;H) supplies the differentiated load bound. Its pointwise size need not be bounded.

The Galerkin theorem supplies a weak solution u, and smooth data satisfy the hypotheses of Theorem 6.134 at every order. For fixed orders s and d, the jets place u,\dots,\partial_t^du in one common space L^2(a,b;H^s(\Omega)) with weak time derivatives between consecutive entries. A function whose time derivatives up to order d lie in L^2(H^s) with s large has a representative that is C^k in space and time up to the boundary. The representatives for different choices agree, which gives a single U. It satisfies the equation, the initial condition and the lateral condition pointwise, because it agrees with the weak solution almost everywhere and all three sides are continuous.

For uniqueness, a classical solution with data (f,g) is also a weak solution with these data. Weak solutions are unique by the energy estimate with the Gårding shift, so every classical solution agrees with u almost everywhere, which gives item 6, and by continuity two classical solutions agree on the closed cylinder, end times included.

Under the standing hypotheses on \Omega and L, there are constants C_m>0, m\geq0, chosen before the data, with the following property. Let f be C^k up to the boundary of \Omega\times(a,b) for every k, let g be C^r up to the boundary of \Omega for every r and continuous on \overline\Omega, and suppose that every g_k vanishes on \partial\Omega. Then there is a function U with these properties.

  1. U is continuous on \overline\Omega\times[a,b] and C^k up to the boundary of \Omega\times(a,b) for every k. It satisfies U_t+LU=f in \Omega\times(a,b), U(\cdot,a)=g on \overline\Omega, and U=0 on \partial\Omega\times[a,b].

  2. For every m, the Sobolev norms of its time derivatives obey the bound of Theorem 6.134 with constant C_m.

  3. \partial_t^kU(\cdot,a)=g_k on \overline\Omega for every k.

  4. If f is continuous on the closed cylinder, the equation holds on \Omega\times[a,b], end times included.

  5. Every other function with the properties in item 1 equals U on \overline\Omega\times[a,b].

  6. Every weak solution with data (f,g) agrees with U almost everywhere.

Set the test vector equal to u(t). The Hilbert-space chain rule identifies (u'(t),u(t))_V with \frac12\frac d{dt}\|u(t)\|_V^2, giving the exact identity. Coercivity bounds the form term below, while duality and Young's inequality bound \ell(t)(u(t)) by a multiple of \|\ell(t)\|_{V^*}^2 plus half the coercive energy. The uniform forcing bound gives E'(t)\le M^2/(2C) for E(t)=\tfrac12\lVert u(t)\rVert_V^2. The mean-value inequality then gives the finite-interval estimate.

For a differentiable trajectory satisfying the smooth weak equation, testing by u(t) gives

\frac{d}{dt}\frac12\lVert u(t)\rVert_V^2 =\ell(t)(u(t))-B(t)(u(t),u(t)).

Under B(t)(u(t),u(t))\ge C\lVert u(t)\rVert_V^2 with C>0, duality and Young's inequality give the coercive differential inequality.

On [a,b] with a\le b, assume the equation and coercivity hold at every time and the specified derivative exists within the interval at every time. If \lVert\ell(t)\rVert_{V^*}\le M throughout [a,b], with M\ge0, then

\frac12\lVert u(t)\rVert_V^2\le \frac12\lVert u(a)\rVert_V^2+\frac{M^2}{2C}(t-a) \qquad(t\in[a,b]).

The same calculation reappears in the pivot norm for Galerkin trajectories. The finite-interval bound controls the energy at each time and carries no integrated coercive term.

In a real Hilbert energy space V, the pointwise predicate takes a state u(t)\in V and a supplied vector d(t)\in V and records

(d(t),v)_V+B(t)(u(t),v)=\ell(t)(v)\qquad(v\in V).

The interval predicate imposes this identity at every time in a chosen set. The energy and uniqueness theorems separately assume that d(t) is the strong time derivative of u. This is the Hilbert-space precursor of the Gelfand-triple and integrated formulations, in which the derivative u'(t) lies in V^*.

The difference w=u-v satisfies the homogeneous equation with derivative u'-v' and w(a)=0. Testing it with w(t) gives (w'(t),w(t))_V=-B(t)(w(t),w(t))\le0, so the energy E(t)=\tfrac12\lVert w(t)\rVert_V^2, whose one-sided derivative within [a,b] is exactly (w'(t),w(t))_V, is nonincreasing on the interval. Since E(a)=0 and E\ge0, the energy vanishes identically and so does w.

Let V be a real inner product space, let a\le b, and let B(t):V\to V^* be bounded bilinear forms with

B(t)(w,w)\ge0\qquad(w\in V,\ t\in[a,b]).

Suppose u,v:\mathbb R\to V are differentiable within [a,b] at every t\in[a,b], with derivatives u'(t) and v'(t), and that both satisfy the smooth weak equation with the same forcing \ell(t)\in V^*:

(u'(t),w)_V+B(t)(u(t),w)=\ell(t)(w) \qquad(w\in V,\ t\in[a,b]).

If u(a)=v(a), then u(t)=v(t) for every t\in[a,b]. A time-independent form is the case B(t)=B. The homogeneous kernel statement says that a solution with \ell=0 and u(a)=0 vanishes on [a,b]; it needs nonnegativity only along the trajectory.

This is Evans's uniqueness argument for weak solutions, for the smooth Hilbert-space model with a strong time derivative. The case with a lower-order term controlled by a Gårding inequality is the integrated Gårding-uniqueness theorem.

Apply the bounded elliptic H^2 solution operator to the measurable residual f-u_t. Its H^1 restriction agrees almost everywhere with the weak solution by elliptic uniqueness, and the operator norm gives the integrated estimate.

Retain the domain and coefficient hypotheses of the slice theorem. If u\in L^2(a,b;H^1_0(\Omega)), the weak evolution identity holds almost everywhere, and f,u_t\in L^2(a,b;L^2(\Omega)), there is a canonical Bochner lift

U_2\in L^2(a,b;H^2(\Omega))

whose canonical restriction to H^1(\Omega) agrees almost everywhere with u. It satisfies the integrated elliptic estimate

\lVert U_2\rVert_{L^2_tH^2_x}\leq \lVert \mathcal{S}_{H^2}\rVert\lVert f-u_t\rVert_{L^2_tL^2_x},

where \mathcal{S}_{H^2} is the bounded global elliptic solution operator.

The improved Galerkin estimate bounds both the essential supremum of the principal energy and \|u_t\|_{L^2(H)} solely by the initial energy, \|f\|_{L^2(H)}, and the form constants M,C. The elliptic solution operator applied to f-u_t gives \|u\|_{L^2(H^2)}\leq \|\mathcal S_{H^2}\|(\|f\|_{L^2(H)}+\|u_t\|_{L^2(H)}). Substituting the first data-only estimate into this inequality removes every solution quantity from the right-hand sides.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 6.131, let M\geq0 bound the form and let C>0 be a coercivity constant. Set

Q=M\|u_0\|_V^2+2\|f\|_{L^2_tH}^2.

The constructed solution and its H^2 lift satisfy

\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{t\in(a,b)}\|u(t)\|_V\leq\sqrt{Q/C}, \qquad \|u_t\|_{L^2_tH}\leq\sqrt Q,

\|U_2\|_{L^2_tH^2_x} \leq\|\mathcal S_{H^2}\|\bigl(\|f\|_{L^2_tH}+\sqrt Q\bigr).
