These are data-only bounds for the principal-part problem. Once the domain, coefficients, and interval are fixed, their right-hand sides contain only the initial datum and forcing.

Move the pivot time-derivative term to the forcing side of the weak equation. The resulting identity is exactly the elliptic Dirichlet weak problem with right-hand side f(t)-u_t(t)\in L^2(\Omega). Apply the global H^2 regularity theorem for the operational C^2 atlas and the coefficient hypotheses of the statement. That theorem returns an H^2 element whose order-zero representative agrees almost everywhere with the original H^1_0 time slice.

At a time where u(t)\in H_0^1(\Omega), f(t),u_t(t)\in L^2(\Omega), and the weak residual identity holds, rewrite the parabolic equation as

-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u(t))=f(t)-u_t(t).

On a domain equipped with a twice differentiable boundary atlas, assume the principal coefficients belong to W^{1,\infty}(\Omega) and have global C^1 representatives that are uniformly elliptic on \Omega. Elliptic regularity then gives an H^2(\Omega) representative with the same spatial value class as the time slice. The atlas is a hypothesis. For a bounded open set with C^2 graph boundary, the graph-boundary atlas construction provides one.

Put M=u(x_0,t_0) and v=M-u\geq0. The sign conditions ensure that v is a supersolution. The argument proves that positivity of v moves forward in time. If v(y,s)>0, a small cubic bump centred at y lies below v at time s. Moved along a segment and damped exponentially in time, the bump remains a subsolution: uniform ellipticity and bounds on the continuous coefficients over a compact piece of the cylinder fix the damping rate. Comparison on the moving ball then keeps v>0 at the end of the segment. Any two points of the connected set U are joined by a finite chain of overlapping balls inside U. So if v(y,s)>0 for some s<t_0, then v(x_0,t_0)>0, which is false. Hence v=0 on U\times(0,t_0), and continuity extends this to \overline U\times[0,t_0].

The proof uses only comparison with explicit barriers. It needs neither boundedness of U nor derivatives of the coefficients. It also uses derivatives only strictly before T, so a maximum at t_0=T is covered.

Let U be open and connected. Let a, b, c be continuous on U\times(0,T], with a symmetric and \sum a_{ij}\xi_i\xi_j\geq\theta|\xi|^2 for some \theta>0. Let u be continuous on \overline U\times[0,T], with C^2 spatial slices and differentiable time slices on U\times(0,T). Suppose Lu\leq0 there and u attains its maximum over the closed cylinder at (x_0,t_0) with x_0\in U and 0<t_0\leq T. If c=0, or if c\geq0 and u(x_0,t_0)\geq0, then u\equiv u(x_0,t_0) on \overline U\times[0,t_0]. The minimum versions hold for Lu\geq0, with u(x_0,t_0)\leq0 in the case c\geq0.

Apply Banach-valued mollifier theory to the functions on \mathbb R, using local integrability for smoothness and global L^p membership for norm convergence. Applications on a finite interval require a compatible extension or cutoff before this global derivative identity applies. To identify the derivative, test the convolution against a continuous linear functional, move the scalar derivative from the mollifier onto the weak derivative by the distributional identity, and use separation of points in the Banach space. This yields (\rho_\varepsilon*f)'=\rho_\varepsilon*g.

For \varepsilon>0, convolution in time with the normalized one-dimensional mollifier sends a locally integrable Banach-valued function on \mathbb R to a smooth trajectory. If f\in L^p(\mathbb R;X) for 1\le p<\infty, the regularizations converge to f in that Bochner L^p norm along every positive sequence \varepsilon\to0. If g is the weak time derivative of f on all of \mathbb R, then

\frac{d}{dt}(\rho_\varepsilon*f)(t) =(\rho_\varepsilon*g)(t).

This approximation identity is the mechanism behind the Lions–Magenes energy identity.

For Hilbert-valued data u,u' in L^2(a,b;H), the explicit one-dimensional time-Sobolev bound is

\left(\frac{\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2}{b-a} +2\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}\lVert du\rVert_{L^2}\right)^{1/2}.

Choose an interior time at which the squared norm equals its interval average. The exact Hilbert-space energy identity controls the change from that time to an arbitrary endpoint, and the L^2 Hölder inequality bounds the resulting dual pairing integral.

If du is the weak time derivative of u on a nontrivial finite interval, then the Lions–Magenes representative for the identity Gelfand triple is continuous on the closed interval and satisfies

\|\widetilde u(t)\|_H \leq \left( \frac{\|u\|_{L^2(a,b;H)}^2}{b-a} +2\|u\|_{L^2(a,b;H)}\|du\|_{L^2(a,b;H)} \right)^{1/2}

for every t\in[a,b]. The original Bochner trajectory satisfies the same estimate almost everywhere.

For a Gelfand inclusion J:V\hookrightarrow H, a trajectory u\in L^2(a,b;V), and a dual weak derivative g\in L^2(a,b;V^*), define

C_{J,a,b}(u,g)= \left( \frac{\|J\|^2\|u\|_{L^2(V)}^2}{b-a} +2\|u\|_{L^2(V)}\|g\|_{L^2(V^*)} \right)^{1/2}.

Choose a time where the squared pivot norm equals its interval average. The inclusion operator bounds that average by \|J\|^2\|u\|_{L^2(V)}^2/(b-a). Apply the exact energy identity between that time and t, then use the duality estimate and L^2 Hölder to bound the pairing integral by \|u\|_{L^2(V)}\|g\|_{L^2(V^*)}.

On a nontrivial interval a<b, every Lions–Magenes representative satisfies

\|\widetilde u(t)\|_H\le C_{J,a,b}(u,g) \qquad(t\in[a,b]).

Consequently, uniform L^2(a,b;V) and L^2(a,b;V^*) bounds give a uniform pivot-space bound without an additional L^\infty(a,b;H) hypothesis.

Skew-symmetry with w=v gives b(u,v,v)=-b(u,v,v), hence the value is zero over \mathbb R. Substituting this identity removes the cubic term from the tested evolution equation. For the difference formula, write u=v+d with d=u-v, expand by trilinearity, and cancel the terms b(v,d,d) and b(d,d,d). The product bound applied to b(d,v,d) gives the quantitative estimate.

Let b:V\times V\times V\to\mathbb R be a continuous trilinear form that is skew in its last two arguments:

b(u,v,w)=-b(u,w,v).

Then b(u,v,v)=0, and in particular b(u,u,u)=0. Thus a nonlinear evolution equation tested against its state has the same energy balance as its linear coercive part. The same cancellation gives the difference identity

b(u,u,u-v)-b(v,v,u-v)=b(u-v,v,u-v).

If |b(x,y,z)|\leq C\|x\|\|y\|\|z\|, the right-hand side is bounded by C\|u-v\|^2\|v\|. This is the abstract algebra behind convective energy cancellation and many weak-uniqueness estimates. The same product bound shows that the dual-valued quadratic map u\mapsto b(u,u,\cdot) is Lipschitz on bounded subsets of V.

The functionals b(u_j,v_j,\cdot) converge strongly in G^* by continuity of the first two slots. Split

b(u_j,v_j,w_j)-b(u,v,w) =\bigl(b(u_j,v_j,\cdot)-b(u,v,\cdot)\bigr)(w_j) +b(u,v,w_j-w).

Uniform boundedness of w_j sends the first term to zero, while weak convergence tested against the fixed functional b(u,v,\cdot) sends the second term to zero.

Let b:E\times F\times G\to\mathbb R be a continuous trilinear form. Suppose

u_j\to u,\qquad v_j\to v,\qquad w_j\rightharpoonup w,

with the first two convergences strong and the weakly convergent family w_j uniformly bounded. Then

b(u_j,v_j,w_j)\longrightarrow b(u,v,w).

In particular, strong convergence of u_j and bounded weak convergence of w_j identify the quadratic expression b(u_j,u_j,w_j). This is the abstract strong–strong–weak passage used after compactness has supplied the strong factors.

The trace and determinant of A give homogeneous asymptotic stability. For a spatial mode with \mu=k^2, the determinant becomes d_1d_2\mu^2-w\mu+(ad-bc). The strict inequalities make this quadratic negative for some \mu>0, so the mode matrix has a positive real eigenvalue \lambda and a nonzero eigenvector with nonzero first component. Multiplying that eigenvector by a sufficiently small scalar gives any requested initial uniform bound, while e^{\lambda t} forces growth at the origin. Setting the interval length to \pi/k makes the sine factors in both boundary derivatives vanish.

Suppose d_1,d_2>0 and, writing w=ad_2+dd_1,

a+d<0,\qquad ad-bc>0,\qquad w>0,\qquad w^2>4d_1d_2(ad-bc).

Then the homogeneous ODE is asymptotically stable, but the linear PDE on the line admits arbitrarily small uniformly bounded initial perturbations whose first component at the origin grows without bound in magnitude. The constructed solutions are cosine modes e^{\lambda t}\cos(kx)q with k,\lambda>0. There is also an explicitly chosen interval [0,\pi/k] on which these solutions have zero Neumann derivatives at both endpoints and spatially nonconstant initial data.

The interval length is determined by the unstable frequency, and the instability is that of the linear system.

At a spatial maximum \Delta u\leq0, while at a positive-time maximum on [0,s] one has u_t\geq0. The perturbation u_\varepsilon=u-\varepsilon t reduces the non-strict case to this strict contradiction on each cylinder \overline\Omega\times[0,s] with s<T, where the hypotheses hold up to the top face. Every point of \Omega\times(0,T) lies in such a cylinder, and the closed cylinder is the closure of this open slab, so continuity gives the bound everywhere.

Let \Omega be nonempty and open with compact closure, T>0, and u continuous on the closed cylinder. Suppose that at every (x,t)\in\Omega\times(0,T) the spatial slice is C^2, the time slice is differentiable, and u_t-\Delta u\leq0. If u\leq M on the parabolic boundary, then u\leq M throughout the closed cylinder.

Set w=-u. Then w_t-\Delta w=-(u_t-\Delta u)\leq0, while the boundary hypothesis u\geq M becomes w\leq-M. The weak maximum principle gives w\leq-M throughout the cylinder, which is equivalent to u\geq M.

For the heat operator, if u_t-\Delta u\geq0 on \Omega\times(0,T) and u\geq M on the parabolic boundary, then u\geq M on the closed cylinder. Unlike the potential case, no sign condition on M is needed.

Test the two weak convergences against u and v. Cauchy–Schwarz and Young's inequality give

2\bigl(a\langle u,u_j\rangle+b\langle v,v_j\rangle\bigr) \leq a\|u\|^2+b\|v\|^2+a\|u_j\|^2+b\|v_j\|^2.

The assumed bound controls the last two terms. Passing to the scalar limit and subtracting one copy of the limiting energy proves the claim. Zero weights are allowed, so the statement also contains the usual one-component weak lower-semicontinuity bound.

Let u_j\rightharpoonup u in a real Hilbert space H and v_j\rightharpoonup v in a real Hilbert space V. For nonnegative weights a,b, if

a\|u_j\|_H^2+b\|v_j\|_V^2\leq C

eventually, then

a\|u\|_H^2+b\|v\|_V^2\leq C.

Thus a Galerkin bound coupling a kinetic component with a dissipation component passes intact to simultaneous weak limits. Either component may instead represent any Hilbert-valued state, derivative, gradient, flux, or auxiliary variable.

Use the pointwise Riesz map to rewrite each integral as the real L^2 inner product of the Riesz representative of g_j with u_j. The generic weak–strong inner-product theorem then passes to the limit: the fixed-test term follows from weak convergence, and the varying-test error is controlled by the uniform norm bound times \|u_j-u\|_{L^2}.

Let W be a real Hilbert space. Suppose g_j\rightharpoonup g weakly in L^2(\mu;W^*), the Riesz representatives of g_j are uniformly bounded, and u_j\to u strongly in L^2(\mu;W). Then

\int \langle g_j(t),u_j(t)\rangle\,d\mu(t) \longrightarrow \int \langle g(t),u(t)\rangle\,d\mu(t).

The explicit bound is retained in the formal statement because it is valid for arbitrary filters; ordinary weakly convergent sequences supply that bound automatically.

Only the upper bound needs work, and the extended-real formulation makes the case of initial data unbounded above trivial. So fix M with u(\cdot,0)\leq M. On a short time interval, of length fixed by a, compare u on a large ball with M plus a small multiple of the growing Gaussian (T_1-t)^{-n/2}\exp\bigl(|x-y|^2/4(T_1-t)\bigr). This barrier solves the heat equation, and on the sphere |x-y|=r it outgrows Ae^{a|x|^2} once r is large. The weak maximum principle on the ball gives u(y,t)\leq M plus the small multiple, and letting the multiple tend to zero gives u(y,t)\leq M. The short intervals are then concatenated up to T. The equality with the positive-time supremum uses continuity at t=0.

Let T>0 and a\geq0. Let u be continuous on \mathbb R^n\times[0,T], with C^2 spatial slices and differentiable time slices on \mathbb R^n\times(0,T), and suppose u_t-\Delta u=0 there. If u(x,t)\leq Ae^{a|x|^2} for 0<t<T, then

\sup_{\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]}u=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}u(x,0),

with suprema in the extended reals. The same equality holds with [0,T] replaced by (0,T].

The difference w=u-v solves the homogeneous equation, vanishes at t=0, and satisfies |w|\leq(A_1+A_2)e^{\max(a_1,a_2)|x|^2}. The maximum principle applied to w and to -w gives \sup w\leq0 and \sup(-w)\leq0.

Let u and v satisfy the regularity hypotheses of Theorem 6.40 and solve the same forced equation u_t-\Delta u=f=v_t-\Delta v on \mathbb R^n\times(0,T). If |u|\leq A_1e^{a_1|x|^2} and |v|\leq A_2e^{a_2|x|^2} for 0<t<T, and u(\cdot,0)=v(\cdot,0), then u=v on \mathbb R^n\times[0,T].

Mathlib transports the inner product from L^2 along toLp. Injectivity follows by applying the inverse Bessel potential. The norm identity is therefore immediate from the transported inner product structure.

The Sobolev norm is exactly the norm of the Bessel representative:

\lVert u\rVert_{H^s} =\left\lVert(1-(2\pi)^{-2}\Delta)^{s/2}u\right\rVert_{L^2} =\lVert\operatorname{toLp}(u)\rVert_{L^2}.

For s\in\mathbb R, the order-s Bessel symbol is

J_s(\xi)=(1+\lVert\xi\rVert^2)^{s/2}.

The implementation is complex-valued because the Fourier theory of tempered distributions is complex-linear, although J_s(\xi) itself is a positive real number. The identities

J_s(\xi)J_{t-s}(\xi)=J_t(\xi), \qquad J_s(-\xi)=J_s(\xi)

are the algebraic facts behind the nested scale and the preservation of real-valuedness.

Use Theorem 4.50 to obtain a global Sobolev function, apply the density upgrade of Theorem 4.104, and restrict the resulting L^{p^*} representative to \Omega. Almost-everywhere agreement of the extension with the original base row transfers MemLp back to the domain.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be an operational bounded C^1 domain, let n>0, and let 1\leq p<n. Every representative in W^{1,p}(\Omega) belongs to L^{p^*}(\Omega).

The graph-space endpoint is written with higherOrderExponent n 1 p; the exponent algebra identifies it with p^*. Because the atlas is bounded, the restricted volume measure is finite, and Mathlib's exponent monotonicity also gives MemLp at every extended nonnegative exponent r\leq p^*. No lower bound on r is needed for that raw predicate, although 1\leq r is needed to interpret the target as a Banach L^r space.

Apply Theorem 4.45 to the bounded first-order operator from Theorem 4.50. Use the resulting representative-level extension in the abstract extension-domain approximation and graph-space density theorems.

Let n>0, let 1\leq p<\infty, and suppose \Omega carries the operational bounded C^1 atlas. Then restrictions to \Omega of globally smooth compactly supported functions are dense in W^{1,p}(\Omega).

The approximants converge in L^p together with their first weak derivatives, hence in the norm of the completed first-order graph space.

The conclusion excludes p=\infty, even though the extension operator itself exists there, because compactly supported smooth functions are not generally dense in the L^\infty-based Sobolev norm. Under the C^1 hypothesis the density theorem is first order.

These approximants are restrictions of functions in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n) and may be nonzero on the boundary; the closure of C_c^\infty(\Omega) is the zero-trace space.
The operational atlas supplies a finite-measure open domain and the canonical extension operator. Apply Theorem 4.193.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be a bounded operational C^1 domain, let 1\leq p<\infty, and let U\in W^{1,p}(\Omega). For every ordered interval a\leq b, the pointwise clamp defines a completed operation

T_{a,b}:W^{1,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\Omega)

without requiring 0\in[a,b]. Its base coordinate is T_{a,b}(U) and

\partial_i(T_{a,b}U) =\mathbf 1_{\{a<U<b\}}\,\partial_iU \quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega.

Equivalently, before using the level-set theorem, the weak derivative is (\operatorname{sign}(U-a)-\operatorname{sign}(U-b))\partial_iU/2.

Choose a smooth compactly supported cutoff in V that equals one on \overline\Omega, and postcompose the extension operator with multiplication by this cutoff. Agreement on \Omega is unchanged, while the cutoff support gives the almost-everywhere indicator identity.

Let V\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open and suppose \overline\Omega\subseteq V. The first-order bounded extension can be chosen so that its base coordinate satisfies

\mathbf 1_V(E_Vu)=E_Vu \qquad\text{almost everywhere on }\mathbb R^n

for every u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega).

This is the generic support localization of Definition 4.44 applied to Theorem 4.50.

Construct a continuous linear interior piece and one continuous linear boundary piece for each chart. Sum this finite family. Almost everywhere on \Omega, each piece has base coordinate equal to its partition cutoff times the original base function. The cutoff sum is one, so the assembled base coordinate agrees with the input.

Let n>0, let 1\leq p\leq\infty, and suppose \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n carries a Boundary.C1ExtensionAtlas. Then there is a bounded linear extension

E:W^{1,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)

whose base coordinate agrees almost everywhere with the input on \Omega. The construction has one interior contribution and finitely many boundary contributions. An interior cutoff allows zero extension away from the boundary. For each boundary piece, compose the localized function with the inverse chart, extend across the half-space boundary by reflection, localize in the chart target, and compose with the chart to return to physical coordinates. The partition identity proves agreement on \Omega; boundedness of the component maps and their finite sum proves continuity.

The theorem is first order. Bounded extension in W^{k,p} for k>1 requires stronger chart regularity and higher-order composition estimates; weighted reflection constructs such an extension on every bounded open set with local C^k graph boundary.

The linked Lean operator includes the endpoint p=\infty, under the operational atlas assumptions.

The chart component is the half-space fractional trace of Theorem 4.264 composed with the ith flattening operator. Its physical representative is the localized flat trace, which is the compatibility condition, so the tuple lies in the closed subspace. The norm identity is the product norm, and the kernel statement follows from injectivity of the boundary-value map.

The lifting sums, over the charts, the whole-space Fourier lifting of v_i, restricted to the half-space and transported back to \Omega by the prepared chart operator. The boundary cutoffs sum to one on \partial\Omega, so the traces of the pieces add up to g. The bound on L is explicit: each piece costs at most \|P_i\|\,\|J\|\,\pi^{-1/2}\|v_i\|, where P_i is the prepared chart operator and J the half-space H^1 graph identification.

On an operational C^1 domain there is a bounded linear map

\operatorname{Tr}^{1/2}:H^1(\Omega)\to\text{(chartwise half-order boundary space)}

whose surface component is the trace \operatorname{Tr}u and whose ith chart component is the flat fractional trace of the flattened ith piece of u. Its norm is given by

\|\operatorname{Tr}^{1/2}u\|^2 =\|\operatorname{Tr}u\|_{L^2(\partial\Omega)}^2 +\sum_{i=1}^N\|\operatorname{Tr}^{1/2}_iu\|_{H^{1/2}}^2,

and its kernel is \ker\operatorname{Tr}. A bounded lifting L with \operatorname{Tr}(Lg)=g makes \operatorname{Tr}^{1/2} surjective. So g\in L^2(\partial\Omega) is the trace of an H^1(\Omega) function if and only if every localized chart coordinate \Lambda_ig lies in H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^m).

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+1} carry an operational C^1 atlas with N boundary charts. The chartwise half-order boundary space is the closed subspace of the Hilbert product

L^2(\partial\Omega,d\sigma)\times\prod_{i=1}^NH^{1/2}(\mathbb R^m;\mathbb R)

of tuples (g,v_1,\dots,v_N) in which each v_i represents \Lambda_ig. Its norm satisfies

\|(g,v)\|^2=\|g\|_{L^2(\partial\Omega)}^2+\sum_{i=1}^N\|v_i\|_{H^{1/2}}^2 .

The boundary-value map (g,v)\mapsto g is injective, and g lies in its range exactly when every \Lambda_ig lies in real H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^m).

The fractional trace has the same kernel as \operatorname{Tr}, so it descends to the quotient. The class of Lg is an inverse, because \operatorname{Tr}^{1/2}(Lg)=g by injectivity of the boundary-value map. The two bounds are the operator bound of \operatorname{Tr}^{1/2} on the minimal representative and the quotient norm of Lg.

For the change of atlas, the physical H^1 trace does not depend on the atlas (the case p=2 of Theorem 4.85). Tracing L_Ag with B therefore returns the surface function of g, and since surface values determine chart coordinates in either space, the two composites are mutually inverse.

The quotient H^1(\Omega)/\ker\operatorname{Tr} is isomorphic, as a Banach space, to the chartwise half-order boundary space, by an isomorphism that preserves surface values. The two norms are comparable:

\|\Phi q\|\le\|\operatorname{Tr}^{1/2}\|\,\|q\|, \qquad \|q\|\le\|L\|\,\|\Phi q\| .

For two operational atlases A and B of the same domain, the map \operatorname{Tr}^{1/2}_B\circ L_A is an isomorphism between their chartwise spaces. It preserves surface values, sends \operatorname{Tr}^{1/2}_Au to \operatorname{Tr}^{1/2}_Bu, composes along a third atlas, is inverted by exchanging A and B, and has norm at most \|\operatorname{Tr}^{1/2}_B\|\,\|L_A\|. In particular both atlases admit the same surface functions.

Define E_{\min} by applying the same representative map to the assembled trace T=\operatorname{Tr}. The quotient theorem gives, for every class q,

[E_{\min}q]=q,\qquad \operatorname{Tr}(E_{\min}q)=\iota(q),\qquad \|E_{\min}q\|_{H^1(\Omega)}=\|q\|_{\mathcal T^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)}.

This extension has least H^1(\Omega) norm among all functions with the same boundary value and is the unique such representative orthogonal to the zero-trace kernel.

The intrinsic Hilbert boundary space of an operational C^1 domain is

\mathcal T^{1/2}(\partial\Omega) :=H^1(\Omega)/\ker(\operatorname{Tr}).

It carries the quotient norm inherited from H^1(\Omega), and the induced boundary-value map

\mathcal T^{1/2}(\partial\Omega) \longrightarrow L^2(\partial\Omega,d\sigma)

is injective. Hence this quotient realizes precisely the range of the assembled trace inside boundary L^2. The Fourier chapter identifies it, with two-sided norm bounds, with a space of compatible chartwise H^{1/2} data, and shows that two atlases give equivalent chartwise spaces.

For a compactly supported smooth u both sides of the second statement are restrictions of continuous functions, and the first statement identifies them. Both sides are bounded linear in u, and smooth compactly supported functions are dense in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^{m+1}) by Theorem 4.22, so the identity extends. The last statement is a pointwise check that separates the points of the chart target where \psi_i vanishes.

Let p>1 be real.

  1. If the base function of u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega) has a C^1 representative f on \mathbb R^{m+1}, then \operatorname{Tr}_pu=f almost everywhere on \partial\Omega. No support condition on f is needed.

  2. For every u\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^{m+1}), the trace of T_iu is the flat trace of u on \{x_{m+1}=0\}, multiplied by an auxiliary cutoff \eta_i on the chart target and moved to \partial\Omega through the chart.

  3. The cutoff \eta_i fixes every localized datum \Lambda_ig, since \eta_i=1 on the chart image of the support of \psi_i.

Flattening sends the ith piece of u to W^{1,p} of the upper half-space, and Theorem 4.266 gives its trace in the Gagliardo space. The work is in identifying the base coordinate. The physical trace is assembled from the same partition pieces, so the flat trace of the flattened piece and the zero-extended chart coordinates of \operatorname{Tr}_pu agree almost everywhere. The comparison transports the flat surface measure through the chart, and it also has to cover the complement of the chart target, where both sides vanish.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+1} carry an operational C^1 atlas and let p>1 be real. For every chart i there is a bounded linear map

\operatorname{Tr}^{(i)}_p:W^{1,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow \operatorname{GagliardoSpace}(m,1-1/p,\mathbb R^m;p),

the flat fractional trace of the flattened ith piece of u, with norm at most the product of the norms of the flat trace and of the flattening operator. Its L^p coordinate is \Lambda_i\operatorname{Tr}_pu. The chart contribution of the physical trace is \psi_i\operatorname{Tr}_pu. In particular \Lambda_i\operatorname{Tr}_pu satisfies the Gagliardo condition of order 1-1/p for every u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega).

The mollified lifting has flat trace v by Theorem 4.267, and reflection does not change the trace on the flat boundary. The chart-transport identity then gives the trace of L_iv. When v represents \Lambda_ig, the cutoff \eta_i acts as the identity, and moving \Lambda_ig back through the chart returns \psi_ig.

Let p>1 be real. For each chart i the map

L_i=T_i\circ E\circ E_\mu: \operatorname{GagliardoSpace}(m,1-1/p,\mathbb R^m;p)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\Omega),

with E_\mu the standard mollified lifting and E extension by reflection, is bounded, with \|L_i\|\le\|T_i\|\,\|E\|\,\|E_\mu\|. The trace of L_iv is the chart image of \eta_i times v. If v represents \Lambda_ig for a surface datum g, then \operatorname{Tr}_p(L_iv)=\psi_ig. The full lifting is L(v_1,\dots,v_N)=\sum_iL_iv_i.

For an operational C^1 domain and 1\leq p<\infty, the intrinsic trace space is

\mathcal T_p(\partial\Omega) :=W^{1,p}(\Omega)/\ker(\operatorname{Tr}_p).

This Banach quotient maps continuously and injectively into L^p(\partial\Omega,d\sigma), with image exactly \operatorname{range}(\operatorname{Tr}_p). It is linearly equivalent to that algebraic range. For 1<p<\infty the range is characterized chartwise: g is a trace if and only if every localized chart coordinate of g lies in the Gagliardo space of order 1-1/p, and compatible chart data lift boundedly to W^{1,p}(\Omega). The range is thus identified as a set, together with a bounded lifting, rather than through a norm equivalence between \mathcal T_p(\partial\Omega) and a chartwise Gagliardo space.

Factor the trace through the quotient map and the injective boundary-value realization. A right inverse immediately gives the trace identity. Conversely, the trace identity becomes equality after applying the boundary realization, whose injectivity recovers the quotient identity.

A bounded linear map E:\mathcal T_p(\partial\Omega)\to W^{1,p}(\Omega) splits the quotient map if and only if

\operatorname{Tr}_p(Eq)=\iota(q)

for every intrinsic trace class q, where \iota is the injective boundary realization.

The finite and Hilbert operators agree on ambient smooth compactly supported functions after exponent transport. Density of that core in H^1(\Omega) upgrades the agreement to equality of continuous linear maps. Kernel compatibility follows from injectivity of the boundary exponent equivalence, and the generic kernel-quotient construction supplies the trace-space equivalence and its commuting boundary-value identity.

For every operational C^1 domain, the finite-exponent trace at p=2 commutes with the canonical identifications

J_\Omega:W^{1,2}(\Omega)\simeq H^1(\Omega), \qquad J_\partial:L^2(\partial\Omega)\simeq L^2(\partial\Omega):

J_\partial\operatorname{Tr}_2 =\operatorname{Tr}J_\Omega.

Consequently J_\Omega identifies the zero-trace kernels and induces a continuous linear equivalence

\mathcal T_2(\partial\Omega)\simeq \mathcal T^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)

compatible with quotient classes and their intrinsic boundary values.

Choose A=A_{\varepsilon/2}. Compactness of A places A(S) inside a compact set, hence inside finitely many balls of radius \varepsilon/2. Every x\in S is within \varepsilon/2 of Ax, so the same finite set of centers covers S by balls of radius \varepsilon.

Let E be a real normed space and let S\subseteq E be bounded. Suppose that for every \varepsilon>0 there is a compact continuous linear operator A_\varepsilon:E\to E satisfying

\sup_{x\in S}\|A_\varepsilon x-x\|<\varepsilon.

Then S is totally bounded.

Mollify f and its continuous weak gradient. Weak differentiation commutes with convolution, and the approximate identity converges locally uniformly for both quantities. Mathlib's uniform-limit theorem for derivatives then identifies the limiting Fréchet derivative. For an open domain, first multiply by a compactly supported cutoff equal to one near the chosen interior point.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open. Suppose f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R and its chosen weak coordinate derivatives g_i are continuous, with \partial_i f=g_i weakly on \Omega. Then at every x\in\Omega, f has the classical Fréchet derivative

Df(x)v=\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x)v_i.

The global theorem is the specialization \Omega=\mathbb R^n.

For \varepsilon>0, clamp the function to a small interval about zero:

T_\varepsilon(t)=\min\{\varepsilon,\max\{-\varepsilon,t\}\}.

Subtracting this clamp gives g_\varepsilon=f-T_\varepsilon\circ f. Its support lies in the compact superlevel set \{x:|f(x)|\ge\varepsilon\}\subseteq\Omega. Mollifying inside the positive collar between this support and the complement of \Omega therefore puts g_\varepsilon|_\Omega in H^1_0(\Omega).

As \varepsilon\to0, the removed clamp converges to zero in L^2. Its weak derivative is the derivative of U on \{|f|<\varepsilon\} and zero elsewhere. The derivative of U vanishes almost everywhere on \{f=0\} by the level-set theorem, so dominated convergence also sends the derivative error to zero. Thus g_\varepsilon\to U in H^1, and the closedness of H^1_0(\Omega) finishes the proof.

For the Lipschitz case, Rademacher's theorem supplies differentiability almost everywhere. The derivative is bounded by the Lipschitz constant and is compactly supported, so every derivative row belongs to L^p, including L^\infty. The weak derivative identity gives the global Sobolev element to which the zero-exterior criterion applies.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open and let U\in H^1(\mathbb R^n) have a continuous, compactly supported representative f. If f(x)=0 for every x\notin\Omega, then

U|_\Omega\in H^1_0(\Omega).

The boundary may have corners. The hypotheses concern a global Sobolev function and its representative; continuity alone does not supply its weak derivatives.

In particular, a globally Lipschitz, compactly supported function that vanishes outside \Omega gives an H^1_0(\Omega) element directly. Its weak coordinate derivatives agree almost everywhere with its classical partial derivatives, even if the function has corners. More generally, compact Lipschitz functions belong to every W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n) with 1\le p\le\infty.

Separate the selected coordinate from its complement by Mathlib's Fin.insertNthEquiv; the induced measurable equivalence preserves Euclidean volume. Approximate U in the completed graph norm by smooth compactly supported functions. Fubini gives a subsequence whose value slices and selected derivative slices converge in L^1(\mathbb R) for almost every y. Each smooth slice satisfies the classical fundamental theorem. The normalized line-representative closure theorem passes that identity to the limit, gives compact-interval absolute continuity, and identifies the classical derivative with the stored weak derivative almost everywhere.

Let U\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb R^{n+1}) and choose any coordinate i\in\{1,\ldots,n+1\}. For almost every complementary-coordinate point y\in\mathbb R^n, the slice of U on the line t\mapsto (y,t)_i has an explicit representative \widetilde U_{i,y} that is absolutely continuous on every compact interval. It agrees almost everywhere with the selected Sobolev value slice, and

\frac{d}{dt}\widetilde U_{i,y}(t) =(\partial_i U)(y,t)_i \quad\text{for almost every }t.

Thus every global W^{1,1} class is absolutely continuous on almost every line parallel to every coordinate axis.

The interval form of the theorem fixes [a,b] first, so its null set may depend on the interval. A single null set also serves every interval: for almost every y the derivative slice is integrable, and the line representative of an integrable derivative is absolutely continuous on every compact interval.

Mollify u and its weak derivatives on compact subsets, apply the classical chain rule to the smooth approximants, control pullback in Lp by local Jacobian bounds, and pass to the limit in the distributional identity.

Assume 1\leq p<\infty. Let E be an open partial homeomorphism of \mathbb R^n whose forward and inverse maps are C^1. If u\in L^p(E(\mathrm{source})) has chosen first weak derivatives d_j u\in L^p on the target, then u\circ E has the weak derivative

\partial_i(u\circ E)(x) =\sum_{j=1}^n (\partial_j u)(E(x))\,\partial_i E_j(x)

on the source.

For 0<p<n, the critical Sobolev exponent is

p^*=\frac{np}{n-p},\qquad \frac1{p^*}=\frac1p-\frac1n.

The Lean definition is totalized through Real.toNNReal, so it has a value even outside the analytic range. The formula for its real coercion requires n>0 and p<n; the reciprocal identity additionally requires p>0. Sobolev inequalities use the Banach range 1\leq p<n.

The operational atlas supplies the extension operator. In dimension one, its W^{1,1}(\mathbb R) extension has a bounded representative; restriction and finite measure give every finite L^q(\Omega) norm. For n\geq2, fix a finite q. If q\leq n, finite-measure monotonicity lowers the base L^n coordinate directly to L^q. If q>n, set s=nq/(n+q). Then 1\leq s<n and 1/q=1/s-1/n. A cutoff equal to one near the domain gives the global extension finite-measure support, lowering it from L^n to L^s, producing a global W^{1,s} field; the whole-space first-order Sobolev theorem places its base function in L^q on the domain.

Let n\geq1 and let \Omega carry the operational bounded C^1 extension atlas. Every W^{1,n}(\Omega) field belongs to L^q(\Omega) for every finite 1\leq q<\infty. When n=1, extension to \mathbb R and the bounded representative of a W^{1,1}(\mathbb R) function also give membership in L^\infty(\Omega).

Here q is an NNReal, so finiteness is built into its type. The linked theorem is a MemLp statement.

Use the operational atlas iteration directly for k-1 steps. Since kp=n, the exponent recurrence reaches n exactly while leaving one weak derivative, producing a W^{1,n} element whose base row agrees almost everywhere with u. The critical first-order theorem gives membership in every finite L^q, and almost-everywhere equality transfers that membership back to the original field.

On an operational bounded C^1 atlas domain, the extra order-k extension hypothesis can be removed. Iterating k-1 subcritical first-order steps produces a W^{1,n} representative with the same base function almost everywhere; the critical first-order theorem then gives

W^{k,p}(\Omega)\subset L^q(\Omega) \quad\text{for every finite }1\leq q<\infty

whenever n\geq1, k>0, 1\leq p, and kp=n. As in Evans, the endpoint q=\infty is excluded. The iteration defines a bounded operator on graph space with an explicit operator-norm bound.

If q\leq n, the supplied extension gives the critical L^n membership and finite-measure monotonicity lowers it to L^q. If q>n, set s=nq/(n+q), so 1\leq s<n and 1/q=1/s-1/n. The extension and the critical relation kp=n, with a cutoff, produce a global first-order W^{1,s} field localized near \Omega; the whole-space first-order Sobolev theorem then gives L^q membership. Almost-everywhere agreement on the domain identifies the extension with the original base field.

Let n\geq1, k>0, 1\leq p, and kp=n. Suppose \Omega is bounded and admits a bounded order-k extension operator; no atlas is assumed. Then every W^{k,p}(\Omega) field belongs to L^q(\Omega) for every finite 1\leq q<\infty. The closed graph theorem makes each inclusion a continuous linear map.

For the integrability assertion, the supplied extension gives L^n membership without any boundedness assumption on \Omega; boundedness then lowers that result to every extended exponent r\leq n; finally, the Sobolev-conjugate preimage argument reaches finite q>n.

Extend the domain element to a global W^{1,1} function, apply the global critical embedding, and restrict the bounded continuous representative to \Omega. The global representative theorem and the extension agreement combine to give almost-everywhere agreement with the original base coordinate; restriction, the global contraction and the extension norm give the bound.

If \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R carries the operational C^1 extension atlas, extension followed by the global critical embedding and restriction gives a bounded linear map

W^{1,1}(\Omega)\longrightarrow C^0_b(\Omega).

The output agrees almost everywhere with the original Sobolev base coordinate, and

\|\mathcal C_\Omega U\|_\infty \leq \|E_\Omega\|\,\|U\|_{W^{1,1}(\Omega)}.

For a compactly supported smooth function, integrate the derivative from a point outside the support to obtain \lVert u\rVert_\infty\leq\lVert u'\rVert_{L^1}. Smooth density and this uniform estimate produce a bounded continuous representative for every W^{1,1} element. Almost-everywhere agreement identifies it with the base coordinate, and uniqueness of continuous almost-everywhere representatives proves linearity. The same estimate makes the resulting map a contraction.

At the one-dimensional critical endpoint there is a bounded linear contraction

W^{1,1}(\mathbb R)\longrightarrow C^0_b(\mathbb R).

Its value agrees almost everywhere with the Sobolev base coordinate. The core estimate is \|u\|_\infty\leq\|u'\|_{L^1} for compactly supported smooth functions. Since the derivative coordinate is bounded by PDEAtlas's finite PiLp graph norm, the completed operator has norm at most one.

Let 1\le p\le\infty and let \psi be a smooth compactly supported function on \mathbb R^n. Multiplication by \psi, followed by finite-measure-support exponent restriction, defines a continuous linear map

T_\psi:W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)\longrightarrow W^{1,1}(\mathbb R^n).

Every coordinate of T_\psi U agrees almost everywhere with the corresponding coordinate of the localized W^{1,p} value \psi U. Writing M_\psi for the bounded cutoff operator and S=\operatorname{tsupp}\psi, one has

\|T_\psi U\|_{W^{1,1}} \le N_{n,1}^{\,1-1/p}\, |S|^{\,1-1/p}\, \|M_\psi\|\, \|U\|_{W^{1,p}},

and the same expression bounds \|T_\psi\|. Compactness of S supplies the finite-measure hypothesis. The localization step of the whole-space weak-calculus arguments is thus a bounded operator.
The proof first proves equality of the corresponding iterated derivatives of a smooth test function and then rewrites the integration-by-parts identity from Definition 4.1.

If two coordinate words are permutations of one another, a weak derivative witness for one word is also a witness for the other. This theorem does not require \Omega to be open: it follows because every smooth test function has commuting classical mixed derivatives, and a permutation preserves the sign (-1)^{|\alpha|}.

This is the formal reason the completed graph model can use commutative multi-indices rather than one coordinate for every ordered word. It does not assume that f itself has classical mixed derivatives.

For a derivative word \alpha with |\alpha|+r\leq m, coordinate extraction defines a bounded linear map

W^{m,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow W^{r,p}(\Omega), \qquad U\longmapsto D^\alpha U.

For the finite-product graph norms used by PDEAtlas this map is contractive: \|D^\alpha U\|_{W^{r,p}}\leq\|U\|_{W^{m,p}}. The target bundle contains the coordinates D^{\alpha+\beta}U for |\beta|\leq r; permutation invariance of weak derivatives makes the map independent of how the corresponding symmetric multi-index is listed.

At every non-isolated point of the fiber f^{-1}(\{c\}), the function is frequently equal to c, so Mathlib's derivative-of-a-frequently-constant theorem gives derivative zero. The remaining one-sided isolated points are countable in the second-countable real line and therefore null.

For every function f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R and every c\in\mathbb R,

f(x)=c\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{deriv}f(x)=0

for almost every x. No regularity assumption on f is needed: Mathlib's total derivative is zero at nondifferentiability points, while the exceptional isolated points of a level set form a countable set.

Apply the one-coordinate criterion separately to each i to obtain g_i\in L^2 and the weak-derivative identity for \partial_i u. Build the order-one graph-space family by assigning u to the empty derivative index and g_i to the singleton index [i]. There are no higher-order indices at order one. The base identity is inherited from the chosen L^2 class, and the coordinate weak-derivative identities prove membership in the closed Sobolev graph subspace.

Let u\in L^2(\mathbb R^n) and let h_m\to0 with every h_m\ne0. Assume that for each coordinate i there is a constant C_i such that

\|D_i^{h_m}u\|_2\le C_i \qquad\text{for every }m.

Then there exists U\in H^1(\mathbb R^n) whose bundled base coordinate is equal almost everywhere to u.

The constants may depend on the coordinate but not on m. The conclusion is existence of a bundled H^1 representative, with no bound on its full H^1 norm; coordinatewise derivative bounds come from the one-coordinate theorem.

This is the sequential global converse at p=2. For 1<p<\infty the local converse also keeps the gradient bound.

Translation by a is unitary on L^2, and its adjoint is translation by -a:

\langle\tau_a u,v\rangle=\langle u,\tau_{-a}v\rangle.

Expand h^{-1}(\tau_{h e_i}-I), move the translation to the second slot, and use (-h)e_i=-(h e_i). The scalar identity (-h)^{-1}=-h^{-1} gives the displayed minus sign.

For u,v\in L^2(\mathbb R^n) and h\ne0,

\left\langle D_i^h u,v\right\rangle_{L^2} =-\left\langle u,D_i^{-h}v\right\rangle_{L^2}.

The adjoint of the forward quotient is therefore the negative backward quotient. Using D_i^h on both sides would be a sign-and-translation error. The identity has no boundary term because it is proved on all of \mathbb R^n.

For compactly supported smooth functions, pointwise convergence follows from the one-dimensional derivative along x+t e_i. For all sufficiently small steps, the quotients are dominated by a bounded function supported in a fixed compact enlargement of the original support, so dominated L^p convergence applies.

For general Sobolev data, write

T_mU=D_i^{h_m}U_0,\qquad DU=U_i.

The sharp estimate implies \|T_m\|\le1 uniformly in m; hence the family (T_m) is equicontinuous. The set of U for which T_mU\to DU is closed. Since global smooth density places a dense subset in that closed set, it is the whole space. This closed-set argument avoids choosing a density approximation depending on m.

Under the same finite-exponent hypotheses, let h_m\to0 and assume every h_m\ne0. Then

D_i^{h_m}U_0\longrightarrow U_i \quad\hbox{strongly in }L^p(\mathbb R^n).

This is convergence in the norm topology of the bundled L^p space.

For a compactly supported smooth function f, the one-dimensional fundamental theorem of calculus along the coordinate segment gives

D_i^h f(x)=\int_0^1\partial_i f(x+t h e_i)\,dt.

Convexity of |\cdot|^p, Jensen's inequality in t, Tonelli–Fubini, and translation invariance of Lebesgue measure give

\|D_i^h f\|_p^p\le\|\partial_i f\|_p^p.

The endpoint p=1 is included; no reflexivity is used in the forward argument. Global smooth density supplies a sequence of compactly supported smooth graph-space elements converging to U. The set

\{V:\|D_i^hV_0\|_p\le\|V_i\|_p\}

is closed because both coordinates are continuous. Passing to the limit therefore preserves the sharp inequality without introducing a larger constant.

Let p\in[1,\infty] be an extended-real exponent satisfying p\ne\infty, let U\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n), and let h\ne0. For every coordinate i,

\|D_i^h U_0\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)} \le \|U_i\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}.

Here U_0 is the bundled base coordinate and U_i is its selected weak derivative in direction i. The constant is exactly one. In particular, the theorem is stronger than the coarser estimate \|D_i^hU_0\|_p\le\|U\|_{W^{1,p}}.

The exponent is not restricted syntactically to the form \operatorname{ofReal}(r). The theorem accepts any finite extended-real exponent carrying the standard 1\le p instance.

At the representative level, insert and subtract a(x+h e_i)u(x):

a(x+h e_i)u(x+h e_i)-a(x)u(x) =a(x+h e_i)\bigl(u(x+h e_i)-u(x)\bigr) +\bigl(a(x+h e_i)-a(x)\bigr)u(x).

The formal proof transports this algebra through almost-everywhere representatives of translation, subtraction, scalar multiplication, and the L^\infty action on L^2.

Let a\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n) and u\in L^2(\mathbb R^n). For every real step h, the exact product rule in L^2 is

D_i^h(a u) =(\tau_{h e_i}a)\,D_i^h u+(D_i^h a)\,u.

The coefficient multiplying the principal difference is translated. Replacing \tau_{h e_i}a by a would omit the commutator created by the forward difference convention. The theorem is an equality of bundled L^2 classes and is valid at h=0 because all operations are total.

Translation preserves null sets, so the almost-everywhere identity a=f remains valid after composition with x\mapsto x+h e_i. Hence the abstract quotient and the concrete quotient of f agree almost everywhere. Lipschitz continuity gives

|f(x+h e_i)-f(x)|\le C|h e_i|=C|h|,

and division by |h| yields the L^\infty bound.

Suppose an L^\infty coefficient class a has a representative f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R which is Lipschitz with constant C, and a=f almost everywhere. For every h\ne0,

\|D_i^h a\|_{L^\infty}\le C.

More precisely, the abstract L^\infty quotient is equal to the bundled class built directly from the Lipschitz representative.

Together with the exact Leibniz rule, this gives uniform control of the coefficient commutator term (D_i^h a)u in L^2.

Let 1\le p\le\infty. On the global L^p(\mathbb R^n) model, the coordinate difference quotient is the continuous linear map

\mathcal D_{i,h}^{(p)} = h^{-1}\bigl(\tau_{h e_i}-I\bigr),

where \tau_a u(x)=u(x+a). For every L^p class u, its representative satisfies

\bigl(\mathcal D_{i,h}^{(p)}u\bigr)(x) =h^{-1}\bigl(u(x+h e_i)-u(x)\bigr) \quad\text{for almost every }x.

Thus the bundled operator agrees almost everywhere with the pointwise formula, while remaining independent of the chosen representative. The operator is defined only on the whole-space model in this chapter because translation need not preserve a proper domain.

At h=0 the bundled map is also total, but no derivative meaning is assigned to that value. The elementary operator bound behaves like 2|h|^{-1} and is therefore useful only away from zero. The uniform estimate near zero comes from Sobolev regularity, not from boundedness of translation alone.

The Lipschitz constant bounds |\operatorname{deriv}F|, so multiplying by each weak derivative of U preserves its L^p integrability. The graph space constructor then has every row it needs. For finite measure, write F(U)=(F(U)-F(0))+F(0): the first term is controlled by |U|, and the second is an integrable constant.

Under the hypotheses above, if F\circ U\in L^p(\Omega), then F\circ U\in W^{1,p}(\Omega), with the displayed weak derivative. In particular, this holds for every Lipschitz F when \Omega has finite measure, including every bounded C^1 domain.

For positive dimension, an operational C^1 extension atlas on \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n contains:

  • proofs that \Omega is open and bounded;

  • a finite number N of boundary charts;

  • for each i:\operatorname{Fin}N, an open partial homeomorphism of \mathbb R^n;

  • globally defined C^1 representatives of the chart map and inverse map;

  • the local equivalence x\in\Omega\Longleftrightarrow\Phi_i(x)\in\mathbb R^n_+ on the chart source;

  • boundedness of each chart target;

  • one smooth compactly supported interior cutoff supported in \Omega;

  • finitely many smooth compactly supported boundary cutoffs, each supported in its chart source;

  • the pointwise partition identity

    \chi_{\mathrm{int}}(x)+\sum_{i=1}^N\chi_i(x)=1 \qquad(x\in\Omega).

The partial homeomorphism is required to be invertible only between its open source and target. The total functions used to represent it are globally C^1 because the weak chain rule and pullback theorems are stated for global maps.

The class contains the finite atlas and partition of unity that the proofs use. Every bounded open set with C^1 graph boundary admits these data.

The domain

\{x\in\mathbb R^1:-1<x_0<1\}

has a fully constructed operational atlas. The left chart is translation by +1; the right chart is reflection x\mapsto1-x. On suitable bounded open chart sources these maps flatten the two endpoints to the positive half-line. A finite smooth partition of unity on the closure supplies one interior and two boundary cutoffs.

The resulting c1ExtensionAtlas is installed as the typeclass instance domainC1ExtensionAtlas. Thus all the extension, density, trace, and compactness results formulated for an operational atlas can be instantiated on this concrete nonempty interval without adding geometric axioms.

Choose a global Sobolev extension U of u. Apply whole-space compact-support approximation to U. Monotonicity of eLpNorm under measure restriction transfers convergence to \Omega. Restrict each global weak derivative identity to the open domain, then replace the base function U by u using their almost-everywhere equality.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open, let k be a natural number, and let the extended nonnegative-real exponent satisfy

1\leq p,\qquad p\neq\infty.

Assume Representative.HasExtension n k p Ω. For every representative-level u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega), there is a sequence u_m:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R such that:

  • every u_m is smooth to all finite orders;

  • every u_m has compact support in \mathbb R^n;

  • the base functions converge on \Omega in eLpNorm;

  • for every derivative word \alpha:\operatorname{List}(\operatorname{Fin}n) with |\alpha|\leq k, there is an L^p(\Omega) function g_\alpha which is the weak \alpha-derivative of u, and D^\alpha u_m\to g_\alpha in eLpNorm on \Omega.

The conclusion is coordinatewise and representative-level.

The proof uses no uniform estimate for the extension. For the fixed input u, choose its global extension U, apply Theorem 4.21 to U, and restrict every convergence statement from Lebesgue measure on \mathbb R^n to Lebesgue measure restricted to \Omega. The global weak derivatives restrict to weak derivatives of u because U=u almost everywhere on \Omega.

The approximants are smooth on all of \mathbb R^n, which is why the extension hypothesis is needed. The finite-exponent condition comes from the whole-space compact-support approximation theorem.

Convert U to a representative, apply Theorem 4.46, and inspect one symmetric derivative coordinate at a time. Uniqueness of weak derivatives replaces the coordinatewise limiting representative by the coordinate stored in U. Finite-coordinate convergence then gives convergence in the graph norm.

Under the same openness, finite-exponent, and representative-extension hypotheses, every

U\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)

in the completed graph-space model is the norm limit of restrictions to \Omega of globally smooth compactly supported functions.

More precisely, the theorem returns concrete functions f_m, their ContDiff and compact-support proofs, and convergence of mkWkpSpaceOnOfContDiff f_m to U in the ordinary real-valued graph-space norm.

The graph space indexes derivatives by finite symmetric multi-indices, whereas the representative theorem is stated for derivative words. For each graph index, its canonical word has length at most k. Weak-derivative uniqueness identifies the representative theorem's limiting function with the derivative coordinate already stored in U. Coordinatewise convergence over the finite index type is then assembled into convergence for the finite PiLp norm.

The approximating global functions need not have support contained in \Omega. Their restrictions are the standard smooth-up-to-the-boundary approximants of an extension domain; density of C_c^\infty(\Omega) itself would impose a zero-boundary condition.

Apply the global truncation theorem to the centered clamp T_{a,b}-T_{a,b}(0) and the extension of U. Restrict to \Omega and restore T_{a,b}(0). The restoration lemma supplies the base and derivative coordinates, and extension-coordinate agreement replaces the global extension rows by the original local rows. The level-set theorem then turns the sign multiplier into the open-interval indicator.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be open, have finite measure, and be equipped with a bounded first-order extension operator. Let 1\leq p<\infty and U\in W^{1,p}(\Omega). For every ordered interval a\leq b, including intervals not containing zero, the completed truncation satisfies

T_{a,b}(U)\in W^{1,p}(\Omega), \qquad \partial_i(T_{a,b}U) =\mathbf 1_{\{a<U<b\}}\,\partial_iU

almost everywhere on \Omega. The sign-difference formula is also retained before the endpoint level sets are removed.

Send the input representative to the domain graph space. Apply the continuous linear extension and convert the result back to a global representative. Combine the extension operator's agree_ae field with the almost-everywhere base-coordinate identity for ofRepresentative.

Every bounded graph-space extension operator induces a representative-level extension.

Given u in the representative model, first store its weak derivatives in graph space by ofRepresentative, apply the bounded graph-space operator, and then forget the global derivative coordinates with toRepresentative. The operator's base-coordinate agreement and the model bridge show that the resulting global representative equals u almost everywhere on \Omega.

The converse would need linearity and norm control, which a representative-level extension does not carry.

A graph-space extension operator of order k is a continuous linear map

E:W^{k,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)

whose base coordinate agrees almost everywhere with the base coordinate of the input on \Omega. The structure stores:

  • toContinuousLinearMap, the bounded linear map between the completed graph spaces;

  • agree_ae, the almost-everywhere agreement statement for the base coordinate with respect to Lebesgue measure restricted to \Omega.

The proposition HasExtensionOperator is Nonempty applied to this structure: it asserts existence without selecting a canonical operator in theorem statements.

Agreement of the derivative coordinates is not stored separately. Both the output and input graph bundles certify that their stored coordinates are weak derivatives of their base coordinates, so restriction of the global weak-derivative identities, followed by uniqueness on the open domain, recovers derivative-coordinate agreement whenever it is required.

Absolute value is one-Lipschitz, fixes zero, and has Mathlib derivative \operatorname{deriv}|\cdot|=\operatorname{sign}, so the Lipschitz chain rule gives the displayed formula. Positive and negative parts are then the graph-space combinations (U+|U|)/2 and (|U|-U)/2. Applying the absolute-value rule again to the nonnegative function U^+ and invoking uniqueness of weak derivatives shows that \partial_iU=0 almost everywhere on \{U=0\}; the indicator formulas follow.

Let 1\leq p\leq\infty and U\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n). Then |U|, U^+, and U^- belong to W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n). For every coordinate i,

\partial_i |U| =\operatorname{sign}(U)\,\partial_i U \quad\text{almost everywhere}.

Every first weak derivative vanishes almost everywhere on the zero set \{U=0\}. Consequently, the positive and negative parts satisfy the sharp formulas

\partial_i U^+ =\mathbf 1_{\{U>0\}}\,\partial_i U, \qquad \partial_i U^- =-\mathbf 1_{\{U<0\}}\,\partial_i U

almost everywhere. Their completed graph-space base coordinates agree with \max(U,0) and \max(-U,0), respectively.

To transfer the zero-level Stampacchia theorem to \{U=c\}, compose U with a smooth one-Lipschitz probe that vanishes at both 0 and c and has nonzero derivative at c. The smooth Nemytskii theorem places the probe in W^{1,p}; its gradient vanishes on its zero set, forcing \partial_iU=0 on \{U=c\}.

For truncation, approximate the clamp by smooth zero-preserving one-Lipschitz maps. Their values converge pointwise to T_{a,b}, and their slopes converge to (\operatorname{sign}(U-a)-\operatorname{sign}(U-b))/2. Dominated L^p convergence and closedness of weak derivatives give the completed operation. The full level-set theorem removes the endpoint ambiguity and turns the sign coefficient into the displayed open-interval indicator.

Let 1\leq p<\infty, U\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n), and c\in\mathbb R. Every first weak derivative vanishes almost everywhere on the full level set \{U=c\}:

U(x)=c\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \partial_iU(x)=0 \quad\text{for almost every }x.

If a\leq0\leq b, interval truncation defines a completed operation

T_{a,b}:W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)

whose base coordinate is the pointwise clamp and whose derivatives satisfy

\partial_i(T_{a,b}U) =\mathbf 1_{\{a<U<b\}}\,\partial_iU \quad\text{almost everywhere}.

The condition 0\in[a,b] is necessary for a global operation on the infinite-measure domain: otherwise a truncated function can approach a nonzero constant at infinity and fail to belong to L^p.

Let k\in\mathbb N, let 1\le q\le p\le\infty, and assume the restricted domain measure of \Omega is finite. There is a continuous linear map

R_{p,q}^{(k)}:W^{k,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow W^{k,q}(\Omega)

that changes only the exponent attached to each derivative coordinate. For every symmetric multi-index \alpha of order at most k,

\bigl(R_{p,q}^{(k)}U\bigr)_\alpha = U_\alpha \quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega.

Set

\delta_{p,q}=\frac1q-\frac1p, \qquad N_{n,k}=\#\{\alpha:\lvert\alpha\rvert\le k\},

with 1/\infty=0, and write \mu_\Omega for Lebesgue measure restricted to \Omega. Specializing the common support in Definition 4.161 to the whole ambient space gives the quantitative estimate

\left\|R_{p,q}^{(k)}U\right\|_{W^{k,q}} \le N_{n,k}^{\delta_{p,q}}\, \mu_\Omega(\mathbb R^n)^{\delta_{p,q}}\, \|U\|_{W^{k,p}},

and the same expression bounds the operator norm. The volume factor is the standard finite-measure L^p\to L^q estimate on each weak-derivative coordinate; the N_{n,k} factor is inherited from the finite \ell^p\to\ell^q comparison for the graph-space coordinates.

The construction works at every order, and Rellich uses it directly. Exponent restriction is the identity when p=q, composes transitively across intermediate exponents, and commutes with forgetting higher Sobolev derivatives.

Let k\in\mathbb N, let 1\le q\le p\le\infty, and suppose every coordinate of U\in W^{k,p}(\Omega) vanishes almost everywhere outside one set S of finite restricted measure. The same coordinate representatives define an element R_{p,q,S}^{(k)}U\in W^{k,q}(\Omega). In particular,

Positivity and finiteness of the named constant give the finiteness equivalences.

For 1\leq n, 0<s<1, a unit vector e, and u\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C),

\iint_{\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n} \frac{\lvert u(x)-u(y)\rvert^2}{\lVert x-y\rVert^{n+2s}}\,dx\,dy =J_{n,s}(e) \int_{\mathbb R^n}\lVert\xi\rVert^{2s} \lvert\widehat u(\xi)\rvert^2\,d\xi.

The equality is in [0,\infty], so no finiteness assumption is hidden. For a real function whose complexification lies in L^2, the same formula holds for gagliardoSq, and MemGagliardo on the whole space is equivalent to finiteness of the homogeneous Fourier seminorm.

This is the normalization of Proposition 3.4 in Nezza et al. (2012) corresponding to Mathlib's 2\pi Fourier character.

For \xi,h\in\mathbb R^n, the Fourier-side increment kernel is

K_{n,s}(\xi,h) =\frac{\lvert e^{2\pi i\langle h,\xi\rangle}-1\rvert^2} {\lVert h\rVert^{n+2s}}, \qquad J_{n,s}(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}K_{n,s}(\xi,h)\,dh.

The extended-real quantities gagDouble and fourierSq are respectively the complex whole-space Gagliardo seminorm squared and the homogeneous Fourier seminorm squared. They are kept separate from the inhomogeneous Bessel norm.

By the Gagliardo-Fourier identity, the Gagliardo condition on \mathbb R^n is square integrability together with a finite homogeneous Fourier integral. For 0\leq s\leq2 the pointwise bounds \lVert\xi\rVert^s\leq(1+\lVert\xi\rVert^2)^{s/2}\leq1+\lVert\xi\rVert^s show that such an L^2 function has Bessel regularity of order s, and conversely. An L^2 function that agrees almost everywhere with a real function is real, so the element lies in the real subspace. For monotonicity, include H^t in H^s; the inclusion preserves the physical representative.

Let 0<s<1. A real function v on \mathbb R^n satisfies the Gagliardo condition on \mathbb R^n if and only if its complexification agrees almost everywhere with the physical L^2 representative of some u\in H^s(\mathbb R^n), and u can then be taken in H^s(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R). Consequently the condition is monotone in the order: for 0<s\leq t<1, a function satisfying it at order t satisfies it at order s.

The step from Fourier data to H^s holds for 0\leq s\leq2: an L^2 function F with \int\lVert\xi\rVert^{2s}\lvert\widehat F(\xi)\rvert^2\,d\xi<\infty is the physical representative of an element of H^s(\mathbb R^n).

This is the identification of Proposition 3.4 in Nezza et al. (2012), stated for raw functions.

The fold does not increase distances, so for n/p+s\geq0 the difference quotient of u\circ\phi at (x,y) is at most that of u at (\phi(x),\phi(y)). The fold carries Lebesgue measure on \mathbb R^n to twice Lebesgue measure on \mathbb R^n_+, because the boundary hyperplane is null and reflection preserves measure, and folding both variables carries the product measure to four times the product measure on \mathbb R^n_+\times\mathbb R^n_+. Changing variables gives the factors 2 and 4. Both are at most 4, so the graph norm grows by at most 4^{1/p}.

Let n\geq1 and let \phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n replace the last coordinate by its absolute value, so that u\circ\phi is the even reflection of a function u on the upper half-space \mathbb R^n_+. If u is real and almost everywhere strongly measurable on \mathbb R^n_+ and n/2+s\geq0, then

\int_{\mathbb R^n}|u\circ\phi|^2=2\int_{\mathbb R^n_+}|u|^2, \qquad [u\circ\phi]_{s,\mathbb R^n}^2\leq4\,[u]_{s,\mathbb R^n_+}^2.

For 1\leq p<\infty, n/p+s\geq0 and functions with values in a real normed space, even reflection is a bounded linear map from the Gagliardo space of exponent p on \mathbb R^n_+ to the one on \mathbb R^n, of norm at most 4^{1/p}, and restricting the reflection back to \mathbb R^n_+ gives the identity.

Suppose graph elements (u_k,D_su_k) converge in the product L^2 space. From u_k\to u in L^2(\Omega), choose a subsequence converging pointwise almost everywhere. From convergence of the second coordinates, choose a further subsequence converging pointwise almost everywhere on \Omega\times\Omega. Pulling the first convergence through both product projections shows that the pointwise limit of the difference quotients is Q_{s,u}. Uniqueness of limits identifies it with the second L^2 coordinate, so the graph is closed. A closed subspace of the Hilbert \ell^2 product is complete, and the norm and inner-product formulas are the product formulas. The graph relation gives injectivity and the raw-function characterization.

The operator D_s is closed for every real s and every set \Omega. Consequently GagliardoSpace is a complete real Hilbert space. Its two continuous coordinate maps satisfy

\lVert u\rVert_{\mathrm{Gag}}^2 =\lVert u\rVert_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 +\lVert D_su\rVert_{L^2(\Omega\times\Omega)}^2

and

\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathrm{Gag}} =\langle u,v\rangle_{L^2(\Omega)} +\langle D_su,D_sv\rangle_{L^2(\Omega\times\Omega)}.

The first coordinate is injective and its range is exactly \operatorname{dom}(D_s). A raw function satisfies MemGagliardo exactly when it agrees almost everywhere on \Omega with the first coordinate of an element of GagliardoSpace.

Near the origin, the Fourier character differs from one by at most a constant times \lvert\langle h,\xi\rangle\rvert; at infinity its norm is at most two. Radial power-integrability gives the two endpoint conditions. Dilation gives the factor \lVert\xi\rVert^{2s}, while invariance under linear isometries makes the remaining value constant on the unit sphere. Positivity comes from an open slab on which the character is not one.

Assume 1\leq n and 0<s<1. The kernel is integrable in h, J_{n,s}(\xi) is positive for \xi\neq0, and for every unit vector e,

J_{n,s}(\xi)=J_{n,s}(e)\,\lVert\xi\rVert^{2s}.

The constant is left as the integral J_{n,s}(e) at a unit vector.

A Schwartz function lies in H^s(\mathbb R^n), so its homogeneous Fourier integral is finite and the Gagliardo-Fourier identity makes its Gagliardo double integral finite. A smooth compactly supported function is a Schwartz function. For the last statement take a bump function equal to one near the origin and zero far from it. It is continuous and not constant, so its seminorm is positive.

Let 0<s<1. Every smooth compactly supported real function on \mathbb R^n, and every real function whose complexification is a Schwartz function, satisfies the Gagliardo condition on \mathbb R^n and has finite seminorm there. For n\geq1 some smooth compactly supported function that is not constant has positive and finite seminorm on \mathbb R^n.

A restriction class is realized in the Gagliardo space of \Omega by HsRestrictionSpace.toGagliardoCLM, which restricts to \Omega the whole-space Gagliardo element of its minimal extension; this gives the inclusion. On \mathbb R^n the reverse inclusion is the function-level identification after taking real parts. On \mathbb R^n_+ it is the even-reflection equivalence GagliardoSpace.halfSpaceEquivHsRestrictionSpace. The half-space member is a bump function centred at the origin. Its seminorm on \mathbb R^n_+ is positive by continuity and at most its seminorm on \mathbb R^n, which is finite.

Let 0<s<1. For every set \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n, the restriction to \Omega of a real function in H^s(\mathbb R^n) satisfies the Gagliardo condition on \Omega:

\operatorname{hsRestrictionSubmodule}(n,s,\Omega) \subseteq \operatorname{gagliardoSubmodule}(n,s,\Omega).

The two submodules are equal for \Omega=\mathbb R^n and, when n\geq1, for the upper half-space \mathbb R^n_+. For n\geq1 some function that is not constant lies in both on \mathbb R^n with positive and finite seminorm, and some function satisfies the Gagliardo condition on \mathbb R^n_+ with positive and finite seminorm there.

Restricted Lebesgue measure and its product measure are monotone under \Omega_1\subseteq\Omega_2. Mathlib's canonical restriction maps on L^2 are therefore contractions. Almost-everywhere equality of the first coordinates implies almost-everywhere equality of their difference quotients, so the restricted pair remains in the graph of D_s. Applying the two coordinate contraction estimates to the graph norm proves the norm bound. Identity, composition, and compatibility with ofFunction follow from equality of the first L^2 coordinates.

If \Omega_1\subseteq\Omega_2, restriction of representatives defines a continuous linear contraction

\rho_{\Omega_2,\Omega_1}: \operatorname{GagliardoSpace}(n,s,\Omega_2) \longrightarrow \operatorname{GagliardoSpace}(n,s,\Omega_1), \qquad \lVert\rho_{\Omega_2,\Omega_1}\rVert\leq 1.

Its first coordinate is the canonical restriction L^2(\Omega_2)\to L^2(\Omega_1), and its second coordinate is the canonical restriction L^2(\Omega_2\times\Omega_2)\to L^2(\Omega_1\times\Omega_1). Packaging a raw function by ofFunction commutes with this map. Restriction to the same domain is the identity, and restrictions compose along chains of domain inclusions.

For constants, and for functions vanishing on a measurable \Omega, the difference quotient is zero almost everywhere on \Omega\times\Omega. At s=-n/2, it reduces to u(x)-u(y). On a finite-measure product domain, the two pullbacks of an L^2(\Omega) function are in L^2, and their difference is in L^2; the converse is the base L^2 clause of the definition.

On a finite-measure domain, every constant belongs because its difference quotient vanishes. On a measurable domain \Omega, every function vanishing on \Omega also belongs, regardless of its values outside \Omega. At s=-n/2 the denominator exponent is zero and

\operatorname{MemGagliardo}(n,-n/2,\Omega,u) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\in L^2(\Omega)

for finite-measure \Omega. This concrete degeneracy is why the formal definition is named MemGagliardo, not unconditionally MemHs.

Mathlib's formula expressing an L^2 seminorm squared as a lintegral gives the first identity. The forward implication extracts finiteness from MemLp; the reverse implication combines the finite lintegral with the measurability inherited from the base L^2 function.

For every real s and every set \Omega, gagliardoSq is exactly the square of the raw extended L^2 seminorm eLpNorm' of Q_{s,u}. Consequently, MemGagliardo is equivalent to square integrability of u on \Omega together with finiteness of gagliardoSq.

No separate measurability assumption is needed: the L^2 hypothesis on u makes both coordinate pullbacks almost everywhere strongly measurable, and division by the measurable distance power preserves that property. Under this hypothesis, eLpNorm' agrees with eLpNorm for the difference quotient.

Monotonicity holds because the integrand is nonnegative and the restricted product measure grows with the set. If v(x)\neq v(y), continuity gives a radius \rho>0 such that both balls of radius \rho lie in \Omega and v(a)\neq v(b) for all a in the first ball and b in the second. The integrand is positive on the product of the two balls, which has positive measure.

For every real s, the seminorm is monotone in the set: [u]_{s,\Omega_1}^2\leq[u]_{s,\Omega_2}^2 when \Omega_1\subseteq\Omega_2. If \Omega is open and a continuous real function v takes different values at two points of \Omega, then

[v]_{s,\Omega}^2>0.

In particular a continuous real function on \mathbb R^n that is not constant has positive seminorm on \mathbb R^n.

The Gagliardo condition on \Omega is

u\in L^2(\Omega) \quad\text{and}\quad Q_{s,u}\in L^2(\Omega\times\Omega).

For 0<s<1, this is the usual Sobolev–Slobodeckij membership condition. The corresponding raw functions form gagliardoSubmodule. On almost-everywhere classes, the difference quotient is the partially defined linear operator

D_s:\operatorname{dom}(D_s)\subseteq L^2(\Omega) \longrightarrow L^2(\Omega\times\Omega),\qquad D_su=Q_{s,u}.

The completed intrinsic space GagliardoSpace is the graph of D_s inside the Hilbert product

L^2(\Omega)\mathbin{\oplus_2}L^2(\Omega\times\Omega).

The extended-real integral gagliardoSq records the square of the seminorm, while raw membership is phrased with MemLp so that measurability and closure under linear operations come from Mathlib's L^p API.

Choose scales \varepsilon_m\to0, mollify u, and multiply by smooth cutoffs \eta_m that equal one on expanding balls. Mollification controls the local smoothing error. The tails of every L^p weak derivative vanish outside large balls, while Leibniz terms involving derivatives of \eta_m carry inverse powers of the cutoff radius. These estimates give convergence of every derivative word and also make \eta_m(\rho_{\varepsilon_m}*u) compactly supported.

Assume 1\leq p<\infty. For every representative-level u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n), there is a sequence u_m\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n) such that

\|u_m-u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\longrightarrow0.

For each derivative word \alpha with |\alpha|\leq k, the theorem also chooses a function g_\alpha\in L^p(\mathbb R^n), proves that it is an \alphath weak derivative of u, and proves

\|D^\alpha u_m-g_\alpha\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)} \longrightarrow0.

In Lean the conclusions are eLpNorm → 0. Smoothness and compact support are separate predicates on each approximating function rather than membership in a bundled test-function type.

Convert the graph-space element to its selected representative and apply Theorem 4.21. For each symmetric derivative index, weak-derivative uniqueness on the open set \mathbb R^n identifies the chosen derivative from the representative theorem with the coordinate stored by the graph element. The finite PiLp index type then turns coordinatewise L^p convergence into convergence of the Sobolev graph norm.

For 1\leq p<\infty and arbitrary finite order k, the same construction gives convergence in the ordinary real norm of the Banach space W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n). Each approximant is built by mkWkpSpaceOnOfContDiff from a globally smooth compactly supported function and its classical derivative bundle:

\left\|\operatorname{mk}(u_m)-U\right\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)} \longrightarrow0.

This is sequential density in the graph model, stated with explicit approximants rather than as DenseRange or a closure equality.

The proof specializes Mathlib's finite-dimensional Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev theorem to Euclidean space and rewrites the exponent using Definition 4.103. For the coordinate endpoint bound, pull back along the canonical volume-preserving coordinate map and apply Mathlib's grid-lines inequality. The operator norm of the derivative on the maximum-norm coordinate space is bounded by the sum of the coordinate derivative norms. Integration and the endpoint root give the stated estimate.

To obtain the subcritical estimate, first bound the coordinate sum by n\lVert Du\rVert_{L^1}. Apply this scalar endpoint bound to \lVert u\rVert^\gamma, with \gamma=p(n-1)/(n-p), and use Hölder on its derivative. Cancelling the common power of \lVert u\rVert_{L^{p^*}} leaves the coefficient n\gamma. The lifting theorem accepts a supplied endpoint constant, so a better endpoint bound can be used without repeating the power argument.

Let u\in C_c^1(\mathbb R^n) and 1\leq p<n. The Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev estimate gives

\lVert u\rVert_{L^{p^*}}\le C_{n,p}\lVert Du\rVert_{L^p},

where C_{n,p} depends only on dimension and exponent. For p=1 and n\ge2, a coordinate version has the explicit bound

\lVert u\rVert_{L^{n/(n-1)}}\le \sum_{i=1}^n\lVert\partial_i u\rVert_{L^1}.

The coordinate endpoint holds for functions into any real normed space. For 1<p<n, the power argument gives an explicit sufficient constant for functions into a real inner product space:

\lVert u\rVert_{L^{p^*}}\le \frac{np(n-1)}{n-p}\lVert Du\rVert_{L^p}.

For example, n=3 and p=2 give \lVert u\rVert_{L^6}\le12\lVert Du\rVert_{L^2}. This bound is not claimed to be sharp; its value is available for a numerical residual budget. Passing from smooth functions to weak Sobolev representatives uses compactly supported smooth approximation.

For 1\leq p\leq\infty, the ambient coordinate bundle is

\mathcal A^{k,p}(\Omega) = \prod_{\substack{|\alpha|\leq k\\\text{mod permutation}}}^{\ell^p} L^p(\Omega).

In Lean this is the finite PiLp product WkpAmbientOn n k p Ω. If p<\infty, its norm is exactly

\|U\|_{\mathcal A^{k,p}} = \left(\sum_a \|U_a\|_{L^p}^{\,p}\right)^{1/p}.

At p=\infty it is the supremum, hence the maximum, of the finitely many coordinate norms:

\|U\|_{\mathcal A^{k,\infty}}=\max_a\|U_a\|_{L^\infty}.

Some texts instead sum the finitely many L^\infty coordinate norms. Those norms are equivalent, but every quantitative PDEAtlas estimate uses the PiLp maximum convention unless it explicitly states another norm.

For each symmetric derivative index a and each test function supported in \Omega, subtract the two sides of the weak-derivative identity. The result is a continuous linear functional on the finite PiLp bundle: its two terms are the L^p–L^q pairings with D^a\varphi and \varphi, where q is the Hölder conjugate of p. The graph submodule is the intersection of the zero sets of all these functionals, hence is closed. A closed subspace of the complete finite product of Lp spaces is complete.

For every set \Omega and every p\geq1, WkpSpaceOn n k p Ω is complete. Consequently it is a Banach space at both endpoints p=1 and p=\infty as well as in the reflexive range 1<p<\infty.

At p=2, the ambient PiLp product has the coordinatewise sum inner product, the graph submodule inherits that inner product, and completeness makes HkSpaceOn n k Ω = WkpSpaceOn n k 2 Ω a Hilbert space. Openness is needed to interpret the relation as the usual Sobolev space, not for the closed-subspace argument itself.

Project the finite derivative bundle along the canonical inclusion of multi-indices of order at most k into those of order at most m. This inclusion is injective, so monotonicity of the finite \ell^p sum, or of the finite supremum when p=\infty, gives contraction. The retained weak-derivative identities are unchanged. Transitivity, reflexivity, and commutation with domain restriction follow coordinatewise.

If k\le m, forgetting every represented derivative of order greater than k defines a continuous linear map

\pi_{m,k}:W^{m,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\Omega).

Every retained coordinate is literally the corresponding coordinate of the original derivative bundle, and forgetting coordinates is contractive:

\|\pi_{m,k}U\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)} \le \|U\|_{W^{m,p}(\Omega)}, \qquad \|\pi_{m,k}\|\le 1.

These maps satisfy \pi_{k,r}\circ\pi_{m,k}=\pi_{m,r} and \pi_{k,k}=\mathrm{id}. They also commute with restriction to measurable subdomains. The canonical first-derivative coordinate \partial_i is named uniformly at every positive ambient order and is preserved by these order casts.

Monotonicity of restricted Lebesgue measure gives the canonical contractive map on each derivative-coordinate L^p space. Restricting the test-function identity that defines a weak derivative shows that the coordinate family still satisfies IsWkpOn on the smaller domain. The coordinatewise map therefore restricts to the graph submodule. Monotonicity of the finite \ell^p sum, or of the finite supremum when p=\infty, gives contraction of the graph norm. Identity and composition follow from the corresponding laws for the coordinate L^p restrictions.

Let \Omega_1\subseteq\Omega_2, with \Omega_1 measurable. Coordinatewise restriction of the stored weak derivatives defines a bounded linear map

\rho_{\Omega_2,\Omega_1}: W^{k,p}(\Omega_2)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\Omega_1).

Every restricted coordinate agrees almost everywhere on \Omega_1 with the corresponding coordinate on \Omega_2. The map is contractive:

\|\rho_{\Omega_2,\Omega_1}U\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega_1)} \le \|U\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega_2)}, \qquad \|\rho_{\Omega_2,\Omega_1}\|\le 1.

Restriction to the same measurable domain is the identity. For \Omega_1\subseteq\Omega_2\subseteq\Omega_3, with both \Omega_1 and \Omega_2 measurable,

\rho_{\Omega_2,\Omega_1}\circ\rho_{\Omega_3,\Omega_2} =\rho_{\Omega_3,\Omega_1}.

Let 0 denote the empty multi-index. The predicate IsWkpOn U imposed on an ambient family U is
