\forall a,\qquad \operatorname{HasWeakDerivativeOn} (\Omega,\operatorname{toList}(a),U_0,U_a).

wkpSubmoduleOn is the real submodule cut out by these identities, and WkpSpaceOn is the same submodule used as a type, for every exponent. The assumption Fact (1 ≤ p) is not part of the type; where it is available, it gives the finite PiLp bundle its normed-space structure. Local integrability of every coordinate is a field of the weak-derivative relation itself.

Each coordinate is a Mathlib Lp value, so equality is already almost-everywhere equality. On an open domain, uniqueness identifies these coordinates with the usual distributional derivatives of the base coordinate. On an arbitrary set, the type still records the restricted-test relation, and the available tests may be too few to determine the derivative coordinates.

On a test function, restriction does not change either global norm because the function and its derivative are supported in \Omega. For a scalar function, the Euclidean norm of the gradient equals the operator norm of the Fréchet derivative. The weak gradient of the test-function inclusion agrees with this classical gradient almost everywhere.

Both norms are continuous on the completed space, so the inequality defines a closed set. Density of the test functions extends the bound with the same constant. The explicit critical coefficient is the case p=2 of Theorem 4.104.

Let n>2 and let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be measurable with finite volume. The inclusion from the supported-core closure H^1_0(\Omega) into L^{2n/(n-2)}(\Omega) has the explicit bound

\lVert u\rVert_{L^{2n/(n-2)}}\le \frac{2n(n-1)}{n-2}\lVert u\rVert_{H^1}.

Thus in three dimensions its operator norm is at most 12. The domain may have corners; openness and boundary regularity are not needed for this closure-space estimate. On an open domain the closure is the usual H^1_0(\Omega).

More generally, for C\geq0, a supplied bound \lVert\varphi\rVert_{L^q}\le C\lVert D\varphi\rVert_{L^2} for supported smooth test functions transfers to \lVert u\rVert_{L^q}\le C\lVert\nabla u\rVert_{L^2} throughout the supported finite-exponent range. The inclusion's operator norm is then at most C for the full H^1 norm.

Hölder lowers the target exponent with its explicit volume factor. For two supported exponents 2\leq q\leq r,

\lVert u\rVert_{L^q(\Omega)}\leq |\Omega|^{1/q-1/r}\lVert u\rVert_{L^r(\Omega)}.

In three dimensions, taking q=4 and r=6 therefore gives \lVert u\rVert_{L^4}\leq12|\Omega|^{1/12}\lVert u\rVert_{H^1}. For a unit-volume domain, including the unit cube, the coefficient is 12.

Let \iota:C_c^\infty(\Omega)\to H^1(\Omega) be the test-function map of Definition 4.11, where C_c^\infty(\Omega) denotes the smooth compactly supported functions with support inside \Omega. The zero-trace space is the closure of its range:

H^1_0(\Omega) :=\overline{\iota\bigl(C_c^\infty(\Omega)\bigr)}^{\,H^1(\Omega)} .

h10SubmoduleOn is this closed submodule of H1SpaceOn n Ω, and H10SpaceOn n Ω is the same submodule used as a normed type with the restricted H^1 norm. It is the case k=1, p=2 of the general supported-core closure wkp0SubmoduleOn. The linked closure interface records the defining facts used later:

  • every test function lies in H^1_0(\Omega), and so does every H^1(\Omega) limit of a sequence of test functions;

  • every u\in H^1_0(\Omega) lies in the closure of the test functions, and the canonical map C_c^\infty(\Omega)\to H^1_0(\Omega) has dense range;

  • if S\subseteq H^1(\Omega) is closed and contains \iota(C_c^\infty(\Omega)), then H^1_0(\Omega)\subseteq S.

The last item is the closure principle behind every estimate that is proved first on test functions and then extended to H^1_0. For open \Omega this is Evans's H^1_0(\Omega). No boundary regularity enters the definition.

For every n and every set \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n, the Hilbert Sobolev space used by the variational chapters is the order-one, exponent-two graph space:

H^1(\Omega):=W^{1,2}(\Omega), \qquad \|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2 =\|u_0\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\sum_{i=1}^n\|u_i\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 .

In Lean, H1SpaceOn n Ω is literally WkpSpaceOn n 1 2 Ω. An element is a bundle (u_0,u_1,\ldots,u_n) of L^2(\Omega) classes in which u_i is a weak derivative of u_0 in direction i on \Omega, and the norm is the \ell^2 sum of the coordinate norms. The space is complete, hence a Hilbert space, and H1Space n is the whole-space case \Omega=\mathbb R^n.

A smooth compactly supported \varphi whose support lies in \Omega determines the element (\varphi,\partial_1\varphi,\ldots,\partial_n\varphi) whose derivative coordinates are the classical derivatives; testFunctionToH1 is this map and testFunctionToH1Linear is its linear form. When \Omega is open this is Evans's H^1(\Omega). The definition itself imposes no regularity on \Omega; on a nonopen set it retains the restricted-test meaning of the weak-derivative relation.

Use the base and first derivative coordinates of U for words of length zero and one. For each canonical word [i,j], use g_{ij} and append the given weak derivative of \partial_iU to the stored weak derivative of U. The graph-space constructor supplies the bundled H^2 element. Its norm formula is the definition of the finite-product Hilbert norm after the coordinate identifications.

Let U\in H^1(\Omega) and suppose that for every ordered pair i,j an L^2 function g_{ij} is supplied with

\partial_j(\partial_iU)=g_{ij}

weakly on \Omega. Then these rows assemble into an H^2(\Omega) element with the same base function and the same stored first derivatives as U. Its squared norm is exactly the finite sum of the integrals of the selected order-zero, order-one, and canonical order-two rows.

No equation g_{ij}=g_{ji} is an input to this constructor. The symmetric derivative index stores one canonical ordering for each second-order row. On an arbitrary non-open set the redundant ordered representatives need not agree; on open domains they are identified separately by weak-derivative uniqueness.

Endpoint evaluation is first bounded by the H^1 norm on restrictions of global smooth compactly supported functions. Those restrictions have dense range in the half-line Sobolev space, so the bounded linear map extends uniquely by continuity. The extension theorem gives both agreement with literal evaluation on the dense core and the same norm-one estimate on the completion.

The completed half-line trace agrees with literal evaluation at zero on its smooth core and satisfies the unit operator estimate

|\operatorname{Tr}_0u|\leq\lVert u\rVert_{H^1(0,\infty)}.

On the positive half-line, completion of endpoint evaluation on globally smooth compactly supported functions gives a continuous linear map

\operatorname{Tr}_0:H^1(0,\infty)\longrightarrow\mathbb R.

This one-dimensional model is the normal-slice ingredient in the flat half-space trace theorem.

Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus to |f|^p on the positive half-line, using compact support to eliminate the endpoint at infinity. Mathlib's derivative rule for the real norm power expresses the result as an integral of p|f|^{p-1}|f'|. Young's inequality with conjugate exponents p/(p-1) and p bounds that integrand by (p-1)|f|^p+|f'|^p.

If 1\leq p<\infty and f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R is compactly supported and C^1, then

|f(0)|^p\leq (p-1)\int_0^\infty |f(t)|^p\,dt+ \int_0^\infty |f'(t)|^p\,dt.

This is the finite-exponent endpoint estimate used to construct the flat W^{1,p} trace.

Every compactly supported smooth function on the open half-line vanishes at the endpoint, so continuity of \operatorname{Tr}_0 shows that H^1_0(0,\infty) lies in its kernel. Conversely, if an H^1 function has zero endpoint trace, approximate it in H^1 by restrictions of globally smooth, compactly supported functions. Subtract each approximant's endpoint value times a fixed smooth bump with value one at zero. Trace continuity makes these corrections tend to zero in H^1. Each corrected function vanishes at zero but need not vanish near it. Multiply it by cutoffs that vanish on successively smaller neighborhoods of zero; its linear growth near the endpoint controls the cutoff derivative and gives convergence in H^1. Thus each corrected function belongs to H^1_0, and closedness gives the same conclusion for the original function.

For the positive half-line, the completed endpoint trace has exactly the closure-defined zero-trace Sobolev space as its kernel:

H^1_0(0,\infty)=\ker(\operatorname{Tr}_0).

The half-space and C^1 versions are proved at the end of the chapter by a different argument.

The trace is the composite of even reflection, the integer-order equivalence and T_1. Its physical value is \operatorname{Tr}_+u because the reflected function restricts back to u and the whole-space trace of a restriction is its half-space trace. The lifting is L_1 followed by restriction to the half-space. Injectivity of the physical representative on H^{1/2} turns the physical identity into the kernel identity.

There are bounded linear maps

\operatorname{Tr}^{1/2}:H^1(\mathbb R^{n+1}_+)\to H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R), \qquad E^{1/2}:H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R)\to H^1(\mathbb R^{n+1}_+)

such that the physical L^2 representative of \operatorname{Tr}^{1/2}u is \operatorname{Tr}_+u, and \operatorname{Tr}^{1/2}E^{1/2}=\mathrm{id}. So every element of real H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^n) is the trace of a half-space H^1 function, and \operatorname{Tr}^{1/2} has the same kernel as \operatorname{Tr}_+. On restrictions of whole-space functions, \operatorname{Tr}^{1/2} agrees with T_1. Both norm bounds are explicit products of the constants of the maps involved.

On [\varepsilon,R], integrate u^2 against the derivative of -1/x. The endpoint values remove the boundary terms and give

\int_\varepsilon^R\frac{u^2}{x^2} =2\int_\varepsilon^R\frac{u}{x}u'.

Cauchy–Schwarz implies X\leq2\sqrt X\sqrt Y, where X and Y are the quotient and derivative square integrals, hence X\leq4Y. Compact support inside the positive half-line supplies suitable endpoints and identifies these finite-interval integrals with the half-line integrals.

The one-dimensional p=2 Hardy argument starts from integration by parts on [\varepsilon,R], followed by Cauchy–Schwarz and passage to the half-line for C^1 functions with compact support contained in (0,\infty):

\int_0^\infty \frac{|u(x)|^2}{x^2}\,dx \le 4\int_0^\infty |u'(x)|^2\,dx.

This is the p=2 specialization of the finite-exponent inequality, stated separately because the iterated higher-order construction is built from the Hilbert-space quotient operators. It uses the same integration-by-parts mechanism as Hardy's inequality in Evans §5.8.4.

Flatten \psi_i\varphi through the i-th boundary chart. Its transported support lies strictly inside the upper half-space, so Theorem 4.136 applies directly to the transported C^1 compactly supported function and controls division by the flat height using its normal derivative.

On the relevant compact chart support, the atlas geometry supplies a constant comparing physical boundary distance with flattened height. A change-of-variables estimate contributes the inverse-Jacobian constant, and the chart-flattening continuous linear map bounds the transported normal derivative by the original W^{1,p}(\Omega) graph norm. The product of these three finite factors is a valid C_i.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n carry the operational C^1 boundary atlas used by the extension theory, and let \psi_i be one boundary partition function. For every p>1, there is a finite chart-dependent constant C_i such that every smooth compactly supported \varphi in \Omega satisfies

\left\| \frac{\psi_i\varphi} {\operatorname{dist}(\,\cdot\,,\partial\Omega)} \right\|_{L^p} \leq C_i\|\varphi\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}.

The comparison between flattened height and physical boundary distance is derived from the atlas, not assumed as an extra atlas field. The constant also absorbs the inverse Jacobian bound and the norm of the chart-flattening operator.

The smooth estimate gives a bounded linear quotient map on the dense compactly supported core. Extend that map continuously to the closure W^{1,p}_0(0,\infty). Agreement on test functions identifies the extension with literal division there, and closedness passes the derivative-only bound to every element of the completion.

For every p>1 and every u\in W^{1,p}_0(0,\infty),

\|Q_pu\|_{L^p(\mathbb R)} \leq \frac{p}{p-1}\,\|u'\|_{L^p(0,\infty)}.

The constant is the classical one inherited from the smooth Hardy inequality. The derivative on the right is the first weak-derivative coordinate of the bundled Sobolev element.

The atlas partition writes \varphi as one interior piece plus finitely many boundary pieces. The interior cutoff stays a positive distance from \partial\Omega, so division by boundary distance is bounded there. Each boundary piece is controlled by Theorem 4.139. The finite L^p triangle inequality and the partition identity combine those estimates into one domain constant.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n carry the bounded operational C^1 boundary atlas, and let p>1. There is a finite constant C_{\Omega,p} such that every \varphi\in C^\infty_c(\Omega) satisfies

\left\| \frac{\varphi} {\operatorname{dist}(\,\cdot\,,\partial\Omega)} \right\|_{L^p(\Omega)} \leq C_{\Omega,p}\|\varphi\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}.

By density the quotient extends to a bounded linear map from W^{1,p}_0(\Omega) to L^p(\Omega), agreeing almost everywhere with division of the Sobolev representative by boundary distance. Poincaré reduces the bound to the weak gradient alone.

The smooth estimate bounds the quotient map on the dense compactly supported core by the full W^{1,p} graph norm, so it has a unique continuous extension to W^{1,p}_0(\mathbb H^{n+1}). Agreement on test functions identifies the extension with literal division there. Passing to the closure preserves the sharper estimate involving only the normal derivative, which gives the displayed bound.

For every p>1 and u\in W^{1,p}_0(\mathbb H^{n+1}),

\|Q_{\mathbb H,p}u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^{n+1})} \leq \frac{p}{p-1} \|\partial_{n+1}u\|_{L^p(\mathbb H^{n+1})}.

The right side uses only the normal weak-derivative coordinate. Bounding it by the full gradient gives the standard upper-half-space Hardy inequality with the same constant. This theorem completes the flat model.

For p>1, division by the normal coordinate extends uniquely from C^\infty_c(\mathbb H^{n+1}) to a bounded linear operator

Q_{\mathbb H,p}: W^{1,p}_0(\mathbb H^{n+1}) \longrightarrow L^p(\mathbb R^{n+1}).

On the smooth core, Q_{\mathbb H,p}u is represented by x\mapsto u(x)/x_{n+1}. Since x_{n+1}=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\mathbb H^{n+1}) inside the half-space, this is the completed distance quotient. On a general Sobolev element it is the L^p equivalence class given by density. The Lean constructor takes 1<p as an explicit hypothesis.

Write x=(y,t) with y\in\mathbb R^n and t>0. For each fixed y, the normal slice t\mapsto u(y,t) has compact support in (0,\infty). Apply Theorem 4.135 to that slice. The derivative of the slice is \partial_{n+1}u(y,t). Integration over y and the tangential-normal change of variables preserve the same constant. Finally, \operatorname{dist}((y,t),\partial\mathbb H^{n+1})=t.

Let

\mathbb H^{n+1} =\{x\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:x_{n+1}>0\},

let p>1, and let u\in C^1_c(\mathbb H^{n+1}). Then

\int_{\mathbb H^{n+1}} \frac{|u(x)|^p} {\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\mathbb H^{n+1})^p}\,dx \leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p \int_{\mathbb H^{n+1}} |\partial_{n+1}u(x)|^p\,dx.

The distance to the boundary is exactly the positive normal coordinate. The right side therefore needs only the normal derivative; replacing it by the full gradient gives the customary weaker form.

Differentiate |u|^p, integrate it against x^{1-p}, and retain the right-endpoint contribution. For a,b\geq0 and c>0, scaled Young inequality gives

p\,a^{p-1}b \leq (p-1)c\,a^p+c^{-(p-1)}b^p.

Bound the signed mixed term by its absolute value. Then apply the inequality pointwise with a=|u(x)|/x, b=|u'(x)|, and c=(p-1)/p. After integration, the first term is absorbed into the left side, and c^{-p}=(p/(p-1))^p gives the displayed constant.

Let 0<\varepsilon<R, let p>1, and let u:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be C^1 with u(\varepsilon)=0. Then

\int_\varepsilon^R \frac{|u(x)|^p}{x^p}\,dx \leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p \int_\varepsilon^R |u'(x)|^p\,dx.

Only the left endpoint is fixed. The exact integration-by-parts identity is

(p-1)\int_\varepsilon^R\frac{|u(x)|^p}{x^p}\,dx + |u(R)|^pR^{1-p} = p\int_\varepsilon^R |u(x)|^{p-2}u(x)u'(x)x^{1-p}\,dx.

The right-endpoint term is nonnegative and may therefore be discarded when deriving the inequality; no condition u(R)=0 is needed.

For p>1, let W^{1,p}_0(0,\infty) denote the closure of smooth compactly supported functions in the positive half-line with respect to the bundled W^{1,p} graph norm. The Hardy quotient extends uniquely to a bounded linear operator

Q_p:W^{1,p}_0(0,\infty)\longrightarrow L^p(\mathbb R).

On the smooth core, Q_pu is represented by x\mapsto u(x)/x. On a general completed-space element, Q_pu is defined by continuity as an L^p equivalence class. The Lean constructor takes 1<p as an explicit hypothesis.

Compactness of the topological support produces 0<\varepsilon<R containing the supports of both u and u'. Consequently the two half-line integrals equal their restrictions to (\varepsilon,R]. Apply Theorem 4.134 on that interval; compact support supplies u(\varepsilon)=0.

Let p>1, and let u:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be C^1 with compact support contained in (0,\infty). Then

\int_0^\infty \frac{|u(x)|^p}{x^p}\,dx \leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p \int_0^\infty |u'(x)|^p\,dx.

The support condition keeps both integrands away from the singular endpoint and from infinity, so the half-line integrals coincide with finite-interval integrals.

Starting from the order-k+j graph-space element, apply the operational first-order extension and Sobolev embedding to each derivative row of order at most k+j-1. This consumes one derivative and changes p_\ell to p_{\ell+1} with 1/p_{\ell+1}=1/p_\ell-1/n. Iterating j times is valid because jp<n; the retained rows remain almost everywhere equal to the original weak derivatives. The resulting element therefore lies in W^{k,p_j}(\Omega) and has the same base function.

Let \Omega carry the operational bounded C^1 atlas, let u\in W^{k+j,p}(\Omega) with 1\leq p, and suppose jp<n. Repeated use of the concrete first-order extension theorem gives

W^{k+j,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow W^{k,p_j}(\Omega), \qquad \frac1{p_j}=\frac1p-\frac jn.

The target retains the original weak-derivative coordinates almost everywhere. Taking k=0 gives bounded-domain higher-order integrability without assuming an order-j extension operator.

This continuous linear map has norm at most the number of retained coordinates times an explicit recursive constant built from the first-order GNS constants, the extension norm, and the coordinate counts. On the whole space, by contrast, the bound of Theorem 4.110 is the operator norm itself.
Apply the operator-norm bound for Theorem 4.110 to EU, then apply the operator-norm bound for E, and reassociate the three nonnegative factors.

For a supplied bounded extension E:W^{k,p}(\Omega)\to W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n), the quantitative estimate is

\|I_{n,k,p}(EU)\|_{L^{p_k}(\mathbb R^n)} \leq \|I_{n,k,p}\|\,\|E\|\,\|U\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}.

Both constants are operator norms of continuous linear maps. The estimate measures the global extension; restriction to \Omega and almost-everywhere agreement give the corresponding estimate for the domain representative.

Apply the supplied bounded extension operator to obtain a global W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n) representative. The global higher-order embedding places that extension in L^q, and its almost-everywhere agreement with u transfers the result to \Omega. On a bounded domain, finite-measure monotonicity gives L^r membership for every r\leq q.

Let u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega), with 1\leq p and kp<n, and supply a bounded order-k extension operator that agrees with u almost everywhere on \Omega. Then u\in L^q(\Omega) for 1/q=1/p-k/n. If \Omega is bounded, finite-measure monotonicity also gives every usual target exponent 1\leq r\leq q; the Lean declaration in fact accepts any extended nonnegative exponent r\leq q.

Nothing else about \Omega is used; boundedness enters only for the lower target exponents, through finite measure.

Induct on k. At each step, apply the first-order Sobolev inequality to all weak derivatives of the current order, replacing the exponent p_j by its Sobolev conjugate p_{j+1}. The relation 1/p_{j+1}=1/p_j-1/n shows after k steps that 1/q=1/p-k/n. The strict inequality kp<n keeps every intermediate exponent finite, and the graph-space compatibility identifies the final base row with u.

If u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n), 1\leq p, and kp<n, then u\in L^q(\mathbb R^n) for the exponent in Definition 4.107. The proof iterates the first-order Sobolev inequality through compatible weak-derivative slices.

The reusable derivative-family form is more general. If U\in W^{m,p}(\mathbb R^n), a derivative word \alpha satisfies |\alpha|+r\leq m, and rp<n, then its chosen representative D^\alpha U belongs to L^{p_r}. Later arguments use this form when they need integrability of lower derivatives and not only of the base row.

For k p<n, the higher-order Sobolev exponent is

q=\frac{np}{n-kp}, \qquad \frac1q=\frac1p-\frac{k}{n}.

The analytic theorems carry the strict subcritical hypothesis explicitly. The definition itself is totalized through Real.toNNReal. Under n>0, p>0, and kp<n, the library proves both the closed formula and

\frac1{p_k}=\frac1p-\frac{k}{n}.

It also proves p_0=p, p\leq p_k, p^*(p_k)=p_{k+1} whenever one more step is subcritical, and p_{k-1}=n when kp=n and k>0.

The first-order product theorem supplies the base case. At each successor order, extraction by derivative words places the two factors and every first derivative in the previous Sobolev order; the Leibniz sums are formed there and then assembled into the next graph-space bundle. Weak-derivative uniqueness supplies both compatibility of the assembled rows and uniqueness of the product from its base coordinate.

Derivative-word extraction is contractive. If the order-k product is bounded by C_{n,k}, the undifferentiated product row has that bound and each of the n Leibniz rows has bound 2C_{n,k}\|A\|\|U\|. The quantitative successor-order assembly theorem therefore gives the displayed recurrence. Choose the unique product and prove linearity in each factor by comparing base coordinates. The recursive estimate then makes the linear maps bounded, first for a fixed coefficient and then as the bilinear operator M_k. Order restriction preserves the base coordinate, so uniqueness proves the naturality identity. Restricting to order one and invoking the first-order coordinate theorem gives the displayed first-row Leibniz formula.

On an open set and for every positive integer k, multiplication is a bounded bilinear map

M_k:W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)\longrightarrow \mathcal L\bigl(W^{k,2}(\Omega),W^{k,2}(\Omega)\bigr), \qquad M_k(A)(U)=AU.

Its base coordinate agrees almost everywhere with the pointwise product, and the actual graph norms satisfy an explicit recursive estimate. Set

C_{n,1}=2\sqrt{\#\mathcal I_{n,1}}, \qquad C_{n,k+1} = \sqrt{\#\mathcal I_{n,k+1}}\,(1+2n)\,C_{n,k} \quad(k\geq1).

Then

\|M_k(A)(U)\|_{W^{k,2}} \leq C_{n,k}\|A\|_{W^{k,\infty}}\|U\|_{W^{k,2}}, \qquad \|M_k(A)\|\leq C_{n,k}\|A\|_{W^{k,\infty}}, \qquad \|M_k\|\leq C_{n,k}.

This is stronger than the smooth-cutoff case but remains specific to an L^2 target factor. The displayed constant is elementary, not sharp.

The chosen products are coherent across Sobolev order. If 1\leq r\leq k, then

\pi_{k,r}\bigl(M_k(A)(U)\bigr) = M_r\bigl(\pi_{k,r}A\bigr)\bigl(\pi_{k,r}U\bigr).

At r=1 this agrees, by graph-space uniqueness, with the dedicated first-order multiplier. Consequently every first derivative coordinate of the higher-order operator satisfies

\partial_i(AU) =A\,\partial_iU+(\partial_iA)U \quad\text{almost everywhere}.

The existential closure theorem is used only to construct this canonical operator. Applications use M_k itself, so independently chosen product witnesses do not leak into elliptic regularity, localization, or pullback arguments.

Compose a with a globally smooth safe inverse agreeing with t^{-1} for t\geq\delta. On a bounded domain, every continuous classical derivative through order k is bounded and hence belongs to L^\infty. For the compact-perturbation variant, subtract the limiting constant: all nonzero derivatives retain compact support, while the zero-order row is a bounded compact perturbation of a constant. The classical-to-Sobolev constructor assembles these rows, and positivity identifies the base with the reciprocal almost everywhere.

Let a:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R be globally C^k and satisfy a\geq\delta>0 almost everywhere on \Omega.

  • If \Omega is bounded, then the selected reciprocal representative a^{-1} is the base coordinate of some W^{k,\infty}(\Omega) element.

  • On an arbitrary domain, the same conclusion holds if a equals a constant outside a compact set.

The theorem asserts existence of this element, without explicit bounds on its derivatives.

Induct on k. The successor step applies Theorem 4.104 at exponent p_k to u, applies the induction hypothesis to every first partial derivative, and uses compact-support stability under differentiation. The identity p^*(p_k)=p_{k+1} closes the exponent calculation.

Let u\in C_c^k(\mathbb R^n), 1\leq p, and kp<n. Then

\|u\|_{L^{p_k}} \leq C(n,k,p) \sum_{(i_1,\ldots,i_k)\in\{1,\ldots,n\}^k} \|\partial_{i_1}\cdots\partial_{i_k}u\|_{L^p}.

Lean implements the right-hand side recursively as higherDerivativeSum. It sums over ordered coordinate words. Consequently, a mixed derivative may occur more than once; this finite multiplicity is harmless and differs from a multi-index sum only by a dimension-and-order comparison constant. The constant higherOrderConstant is also recursive: each step multiplies the previous constant by Mathlib's first-order Sobolev constant at the current exponent.

The property that an order-\alpha derivative slice lies in the closed H^1_0 subspace is closed in W^{m,2}. Classical differentiation preserves compact support for every smooth core function, so density passes the property to the supported-core closure.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be any set, not necessarily open. If u\in W^{m,2}_0(\Omega) and |\alpha|<m, then the canonical first-order slice representing D^\alpha u belongs to H^1_0(\Omega). This is the closure form of the statement that all derivatives below top order have zero boundary values, and it is one direction of the characterization of W^{m,2}_0 by vanishing traces of derivatives.

For every finite order k, the supported-core space

W^{k,2}_0(\Omega) = \overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega)}^{\,W^{k,2}(\Omega)}

is defined as a closed submodule of the completed Sobolev graph space. This is Evans's closure definition on open domains. The Lean definition makes sense for arbitrary sets; trace characterizations need an open domain with regular boundary.

Apply the representative map to T=\operatorname{Tr}_+. This defines the canonical extension E_{\min}. For every class q\in\mathcal T^{1/2}(\mathbb R^n), the shared quotient theorem gives

[E_{\min}q]=q,\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_+(E_{\min}q)=\iota(q),\qquad \|E_{\min}q\|_{H^1}=\|q\|_{\mathcal T^{1/2}}.

Here the middle equality uses the injective L^2 realization of the quotient class. Moreover,

\|E_{\min}q\|_{H^1}\leq\|u\|_{H^1}

for every u with the same boundary value. It is the unique such representative orthogonal to \ker(\operatorname{Tr}_+).

Since \operatorname{Tr}^{1/2} and \operatorname{Tr}_+ have the same kernel, \operatorname{Tr}^{1/2} descends to the quotient; the lifting followed by the quotient map is its inverse. The forward bound applies the trace bound to the minimal representative, and the reverse bound uses E^{1/2}v as one representative of the class of v.

The range of \operatorname{Tr}_+ in L^2(\mathbb R^n) is exactly the set of physical representatives of real H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^n). The quotient \mathcal T^{1/2}(\mathbb R^n) of the trace chapter is isomorphic to H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R) by a continuous linear equivalence compatible with the two boundary realizations in L^2, and the quotient norm and the Bessel norm bound each other with explicit constants.

The natural Hilbert boundary space of the flat trace is the quotient

\mathcal T^{1/2}(\mathbb R^n) :=H^1(\mathbb R^{n+1}_+)/\ker(\operatorname{Tr}_+).

Its quotient norm is the least upper-half-space H^1 norm among all representatives of the same trace. The induced map

\mathcal T^{1/2}(\mathbb R^n)\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^n)

is injective. Consequently the quotient is canonically realized as the range of \operatorname{Tr}_+ equipped with its quotient norm. The Fourier chapter identifies this range, with equivalent norms, with H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^n), which justifies the notation.

The triangle and scalar laws combine the corresponding laws for bounded continuous functions with Mathlib's subadditivity and homogeneity of nnHolderNorm.

For completeness, let f_j be Cauchy in the displayed norm. The uniform parts are Cauchy in the Banach space of bounded continuous functions, so they converge uniformly to a bounded continuous function f. A tail of the sequence lies within distance one of a fixed term. Passing the pointwise difference estimate to the uniform limit shows that this term minus f is \gamma-Hölder, hence so is the limit. Repeating this with smaller tolerances makes f_j-f small in Hölder seminorm as well as uniformly, hence convergence in the full norm.

The real vector space HolderSpace.C0GammaOn Ω γ carries the norm

\|f\|_{C^{0,\gamma}(\Omega)} = \sup_{x\in\Omega}|f(x)| + [f]_{C^{0,\gamma}(\Omega)}.

Both summands are bounded by the full norm, and this norm makes the space complete. Hence C0GammaOn Ω γ is a real Banach space for every metric type \Omega.

Let \Omega be a metric type and let 0<\gamma\leq1. HolderSpace.C0GammaOn Ω γ consists of:

  1. a bounded continuous function f:\Omega\to\mathbb R; and

  2. evidence that f has a finite \gamma-Hölder constant.

The first item supplies the uniform norm and global boundedness. The second supplies quantitative regularity. Extensionality is pointwise: two elements are equal exactly when their values agree at every point of \Omega.

There is no almost-everywhere quotient. This is the target in which Morrey theory records the continuous representative selected from a Sobolev equivalence class.

HolderSpace.Exponent records the classical range 0<\gamma\leq 1 as a nonnegative real together with proofs of both inequalities. Keeping the range in the type prevents every analytic theorem from repeating the same side conditions.

The endpoint \gamma=1 is included and is available as the numeral 1; it is exactly the Lipschitz case. The exponent \gamma=0 is excluded, so every exponent of this type gives continuity and not only an oscillation bound.

There are canonical norm-at-most-one continuous linear maps

C^{0,\gamma}(\Omega)\longrightarrow C_b(\Omega), \qquad f\longmapsto f,

and, for every x\in\Omega,

\operatorname{ev}_x:C^{0,\gamma}(\Omega)\longrightarrow\mathbb R, \qquad f\longmapsto f(x).

The estimates are immediate from the uniform-norm term:

\|f\|_\infty\leq\|f\|_{C^{0,\gamma}}, \qquad |f(x)|\leq\|f\|_{C^{0,\gamma}}.

Later proofs use these maps to extract uniform or pointwise information from a Hölder-space element.

For metric spaces X,Y, a map f:X\to Y satisfies HolderWith C γ f when

d_Y(f(x),f(y))\leq C\,d_X(x,y)^\gamma \qquad\text{for every }x,y\in X.

MemHolder γ f means that such a finite nonnegative constant C exists. For a function satisfying this predicate, Mathlib's nnHolderNorm γ f is the least admissible nonnegative Hölder constant and is itself admissible. PDEAtlas uses this least constant as its Hölder seminorm.

If S\subseteq Z is a metric subspace, literal restriction defines a continuous linear contraction

C^{0,\gamma}(Z)\longrightarrow C^{0,\gamma}(S), \qquad f\longmapsto f|_S.

Restriction preserves every admissible Hölder constant, so neither the uniform norm nor the least Hölder seminorm can increase:

\|f|_S\|_{C^{0,\gamma}(S)} \leq \|f\|_{C^{0,\gamma}(Z)}.

No measurability or extension hypothesis is involved. This is ordinary pointwise restriction of continuous representatives, not the restriction operator on Sobolev equivalence classes.

For f\in C^{0,\gamma}(\Omega), the bundled seminorm is exactly

[f]_{C^{0,\gamma}(\Omega)} = \operatorname{nnHolderNorm}(\gamma,f).

This least constant is nonnegative and satisfies the pointwise estimate:

|f(x)-f(y)| \leq [f]_{C^{0,\gamma}(\Omega)}\,d(x,y)^\gamma.

Thus later estimates can bound the seminorm once and immediately recover the corresponding pointwise modulus of continuity.

In weighted Fourier coordinates, integration against a unit L^2 normal kernel is contractive; multiplying by \kappa_s gives the physical trace. The corresponding kernel lifting is isometric before multiplication by \kappa_s^{-1}. Fubini and the unit normalization give the right-inverse identity and the exact lifting norm. Agreement with pointwise restriction for Schwartz functions uses the Fourier slice identity. Both maps preserve Hermitian symmetry of the Fourier transform, so they restrict to the real subspaces.

Let s>1/2. There are bounded real-linear maps

T_s:H^s(\mathbb R^{n+1};\mathbb R)\to H^{s-1/2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R), \qquad L_s:H^{s-1/2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R)\to H^s(\mathbb R^{n+1};\mathbb R),

with \|T_su\|\leq\kappa_s\|u\|, \|L_sv\|=\kappa_s^{-1}\|v\| and T_sL_s=\mathrm{id}. In particular T_s is surjective. If u is represented by a Schwartz function f, the physical representative of T_su is y\mapsto\operatorname{Re}f(y,0) almost everywhere.

The linear equivalence upgrades to a continuous linear equivalence:

H^k(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R) \simeq_{\mathrm{top},\mathbb R} W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R).

The equivalence is topological, not isometric. Already at first order the Fourier convention gives the identity

\lVert u\rVert_{H^1}^2 =\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2 +(2\pi)^{-2}\sum_{j=1}^n\lVert\partial_j u\rVert_{L^2}^2,

whereas the graph norm aggregates derivative coordinates without the (2\pi)^{-2} factor.

Each coordinate of derivative length j\leq k is bounded by (2\pi)^j\lVert u\rVert_{H^k}, hence by (2\pi)^k\lVert u\rVert_{H^k}. The graph norm is the Euclidean \ell^2 norm of finitely many coordinates, so summing the common square bound contributes the square root of the number of derivative indices.

The forward graph-space map is bounded by

\lVert\operatorname{toWkpSpace}(u)\rVert_{W^{k,2}} \leq \sqrt{\#\operatorname{DerivIndex}(n,k)}\, (2\pi)^k\lVert u\rVert_{H^k}.

The implementation records the displayed constant as toWkpSpaceNormBound n k and packages the map as a continuous real-linear map.

For u\in H^k(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R), toWkpSpace forms the graph tuple

\bigl(D^\alpha u\bigr)_{\lvert\alpha\rvert\leq k} \in W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R).

The base coordinate is the physical L^2 representative of u; every other coordinate is a chosen L^2 representative of the corresponding weak derivative. The chosen weak-derivative identities place the tuple in the graph space. Uniqueness identifies each coordinate independently of the choice and proves linearity. On HsSpaceReal, the construction is bundled as the real-linear map toWkpSpaceLinear.

For every natural number k, the mutually inverse maps define a real-linear equivalence

H^k(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R) \simeq_{\mathbb R} W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R).

The Bessel-weight estimate controls the weighted Fourier transform by the Fourier transforms of the base coordinate and the n pure k-th derivatives. Plancherel converts those terms back to their L^2 norms, and each graph coordinate has norm at most \lVert U\rVert. Summing the base term and n derivative terms contributes the factor n+1.

For every natural order k and U\in W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R), the inverse satisfies

\lVert\operatorname{ofWkpSpace}(U)\rVert_{H^k} \leq 2^{k-1}(1+n^{k-1})(n+1) \lVert U\rVert_{W^{k,2}}.

The exponents use natural-number subtraction. Thus at k=0 the displayed constant evaluates to the valid but loose value 2(n+1). The separate order-zero theorem above is the sharp statement.

For U\in W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R), ofWkpSpace U is the tempered distribution induced by the complexification of the base L^2 coordinate. The weak derivatives stored in the remaining coordinates prove that this distribution belongs to Fourier H^k.

Starting from a graph tuple, extracting its base coordinate and then taking all weak derivatives recovers every coordinate by uniqueness of weak derivatives. Starting from a real Fourier-Sobolev element, its graph tuple has the same base physical representative, so rebuilding the induced tempered distribution recovers the original element.

The forward and reverse constructions are mutually inverse:

\operatorname{toWkpSpace}(\operatorname{ofWkpSpace}(U))=U, \qquad \operatorname{ofWkpSpace}(\operatorname{toWkpSpace}(u))=u.

Approximate the graph-space element by smooth compactly supported functions. For the approximants the identity is classical. Plancherel gives convergence of the transformed base and derivative coordinates in L^2. Embed them in tempered distributions, where multiplication by the polynomial symbol is continuous, and pass the identity to the limit there. Equality of the induced distributions then gives the almost-everywhere multiplier identity. An elementary power-mean estimate bounds (1+\lVert\xi\rVert^2)^{k/2} using 1 and the pure powers \lvert\xi_i\rvert^k.

For each coordinate direction i, the Fourier transform of the pure k-th derivative is almost everywhere

(2\pi i\xi_i)^k\widehat u(\xi).

Together with a pointwise domination of the Bessel weight by the base frequency and the pure coordinate powers, this yields the explicit factor

B_{n,k}=2^{k-1}\bigl(1+n^{k-1}\bigr)

for k\geq 1.
The forward bound specializes to constant one because there is only the base coordinate. The reverse map is a contraction at order zero, and the two maps are inverse, giving the opposite inequality.

At order zero, the forward conversion preserves the norm exactly:

\lVert\operatorname{toWkpSpace}(u)\rVert_{W^{0,2}} = \lVert u\rVert_{H^0}.

Global L^p convergence of the zero-extension mollifications restricts to K. Compactness of K inside the open set \Omega gives a positive collar. Eventually the scaled kernel lies within that collar, so the local commutation theorem identifies D^\alpha u_m on K with the mollification of the zero-extended weak derivative. Applying the approximate-identity theorem to that derivative completes the proof.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open, let u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega) in the representative model, and assume 1\leq p<\infty. For every compact set K\subseteq\Omega, there are globally smooth functions u_m:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R such that

\|u_m-u\|_{L^p(K)}\longrightarrow0,

and, for every derivative word \alpha of length at most k, there is a chosen weak derivative g_\alpha\in L^p(\Omega) for which

\|D^\alpha u_m-g_\alpha\|_{L^p(K)}\longrightarrow0.

The approximants are the mollifications of the zero extension \mathbf1_\Omega u at scales \varepsilon_m=1/(m+1). They need not have compact support or be supported in \Omega.

For every j\in\mathbb N, let W^{j,2}_0(0,\infty) be the closure of C^\infty_c(0,\infty) in the bundled W^{j,2} graph norm. Literal division by r^j on the smooth core extends uniquely to a bounded linear operator

Q_j: W^{j,2}_0(0,\infty)\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R).

For a test function \varphi,

Q_j\varphi = \left[r\mapsto\frac{\varphi(r)}{r^j}\right]_{L^2}.

Compact support strictly inside the positive half-line makes the displayed representative square-integrable. The preliminary estimate \|Q_j\varphi\|_2\leq2^j\|\varphi\|_{W^{j,2}} supplies the bounded extension. For a completed Sobolev element, Q_j u is defined by this extension.

First work on \varphi\in C^\infty_c(0,\infty). The weighted one-dimensional integration-by-parts estimate is iterated at derivative levels 0,\ldots,j. Compact support chooses one interval [\varepsilon,R]\subset(0,\infty) containing the supports of all those derivatives. The smooth-core chain gives exactly

\left(\prod_{\ell=1}^{j}(2\ell-1)^2\right) \int_0^\infty\frac{|\varphi(r)|^2}{r^{2j}}\,dr \leq 4^j\int_0^\infty|D^j\varphi(r)|^2\,dr.

The quotient-representative lemma identifies the first integral with \|Q_j\varphi\|_2^2, and the Sobolev-coordinate lemma identifies the second with the square of the top bundled derivative coordinate.

The full graph-norm estimate obtained from this core theorem defines Q_j on the closure. To retain the sharper exact inequality, use the dense range of the canonical map C^\infty_c(0,\infty)\to W^{j,2}_0(0,\infty). The set of completed elements satisfying the displayed inequality is closed because the quotient operator and the top-coordinate evaluation are continuous. Dense-range induction therefore passes the exact odd-weight product and the factor 4^j unchanged to every completed element. The completion step needs no boundary trace for an intermediate derivative.

For every j\in\mathbb N and every u\in W^{j,2}_0(0,\infty),

\left(\prod_{\ell=1}^{j}(2\ell-1)^2\right) \|Q_j u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R)}^2 \leq 4^j\|D^j u\|_{L^2(0,\infty)}^2.

Here D^j u is the top weak-derivative coordinate in the bundled W^{j,2} element. At j=0, the product is empty, Q_0 is division by r^0=1, and the statement is the identity estimate. At j=1, the odd product is 1 and the theorem becomes the usual constant-4 Hardy inequality.
If u_k lies in the set and converges weakly to u, then \det Du_k=\rho for every k and \det Du_k\rightharpoonup\det Du. Weak limits in L^{q/n} are unique, so \det Du=\rho.

Under the hypotheses of the previous theorem, for every \rho\in L^{q/n}(\Omega) the set

\{u\in W^{1,q}(\Omega;\mathbb R^n):\det Du=\rho\ \text{a.e.}\}

is sequentially closed for the weak topology of W^{1,q}(\Omega;\mathbb R^n).

In dimension one the determinant is the derivative itself, which is linear. Otherwise the bounded C^1 graph boundary yields an operational atlas, and the previous theorem applies with m=n and \sigma=\mathrm{id}. For the pair, the gradient component is the composition of the gradient with the inclusion L^q\subseteq L^{q/n} on a set of finite measure, a continuous linear map, so it converges weakly as well. A pair of weakly convergent components converges weakly in the product.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n, n\ge1, be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary, and let q>n be real. If u_k\rightharpoonup u weakly in W^{1,q}(\Omega;\mathbb R^n), then

\det Du_k\rightharpoonup\det Du\quad\text{weakly in }L^{q/n}(\Omega).

The pair (Du,\det Du), packed as one function with values in \mathbb R^{n\times n+1}, lies in L^{q/n}(\Omega;\mathbb R^{n\times n+1}), and (Du_k,\det Du_k)\rightharpoonup(Du,\det Du) weakly there.

For a C^2 map, \det A\,\varphi is the divergence of the flux with components u_k(\operatorname{adj}A)_{jk}\varphi, up to the term with \partial\varphi, because the cofactor rows are divergence free: the mixed second derivatives cancel in pairs. Integrating against a test function supported in the open set removes the boundary. For Sobolev maps, both sides of the second identity are continuous in U for the W^{1,p} norm, by Hölder's inequality and the continuity of minors. Smooth maps are dense in W^{1,p}(\Omega) on every open set, by the Meyers–Serrin argument built on Theorem 4.20, so the identity passes from smooth maps to all of W^{1,p}(\Omega)^{m+1}. No boundary regularity is used.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open.

  1. If u\in C^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^m), A is the selected square Jacobian (\partial_{\sigma(j)}u_i), k is a row index, and \varphi is a test function supported in \Omega, then

    \int_\Omega\det A\,\varphi\,dx =-\sum_j\int_\Omega u_k\,(\operatorname{adj}A)_{jk}\, \partial_{\sigma(j)}\varphi\,dx .

  2. Let m\ge1, p<\infty, and let the exponents satisfy \frac{m+1}{p}=\frac1p+\frac mp with p/m\ge1 and p/(m+1)\ge1. For U=(U_0,\dots,U_m)\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)^{m+1} and every test function \varphi,

    \int_\Omega M_\sigma(U)\,\varphi\,dx =-\sum_{j=0}^m(-1)^j\int_\Omega\partial_{\sigma(j)}\varphi\;U_0\; M_{\sigma\circ\delta_j}(U_1,\dots,U_m)\,dx,

    where \sigma\circ\delta_j omits the column \sigma(j).

Induction on m. A minor of degree one is a weak derivative, a continuous linear function of u, and continuous linear maps preserve weak convergence. For degree m+1, the divergence identity pairs U_0, which converges strongly in L^q, with minors of degree m, which converge weakly in L^{q/m} by induction. Each term of the identity therefore converges when tested against a fixed \varphi. Weakly convergent sequences are bounded, so the minors of degree m+1 are bounded in L^{q/(m+1)}. Since m+1<q, that exponent is larger than one and the space is reflexive. Every subsequence has a weakly convergent subsequence, the test functions identify its limit as M_\sigma(u), and so the whole sequence converges. On a C^1 domain a compact operator turns weak convergence into strong convergence; compactness at every finite exponent, including p\ge n, comes from compactness below n on the same bounded domain, as in Theorem 4.178.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open, let q be real, and let 0<m<q with q/m\ge1. Suppose u_k\rightharpoonup u weakly in W^{1,q}(\Omega)^m and each component converges strongly in L^q(\Omega). Then

M_\sigma(u_k)\rightharpoonup M_\sigma(u)\quad\text{weakly in }L^{q/m}(\Omega).

If n\ge2 and \Omega carries the operational C^1 atlas, the strong convergence is automatic: the map W^{1,p}(\Omega)\to L^p(\Omega) that forgets the derivatives is compact for every finite p\ge1, so weak convergence in W^{1,q}(\Omega)^m alone implies weak convergence of every minor of degree m<q.

The kernel is closed because T is continuous. Mathlib's orthogonal decomposition gives the quotient isometry and its inverse law, hence the class identity and norm equality. Applying \iota_T gives the value identity. Every representative has norm at least its quotient norm, which proves minimality. Uniqueness follows from the same orthogonal decomposition.

For every q\in Q_T,

[R_Tq]=q,\qquad TR_Tq=\iota_T(q),\qquad \|R_Tq\|_E=\|q\|_{Q_T}.

Moreover, R_Tq lies in (\ker T)^\perp and has no larger norm than any x with Tx=\iota_T(q). It is the unique such vector orthogonal to \ker T. The norm here is the quotient norm; it need not agree with the norm of the boundary value in F.

If E is a real Hilbert space, orthogonal decomposition identifies Q_T isometrically with (\ker T)^\perp. Composing that identification with the inclusion into E defines a continuous linear representative map R_T:Q_T\to E.

Two vectors have the same value under T precisely when their difference lies in \ker T. They therefore define the same quotient class. The formal proof uses Mathlib's quotient map and its kernel identity.
The map \iota_T is injective and satisfies \iota_T([x])=Tx. Thus quotient classes record exactly the distinct values of T.

For a continuous linear map T:E\to F between real normed spaces, set

Q_T:=E/\ker T.

Write [x] for the class of x. The quotient carries its quotient norm, and T induces a continuous linear map \iota_T:Q_T\to F, defined by \iota_T([x])=Tx.

Let \Omega be measurable. Suppose an L^\infty(\Omega) class F has a globally Lipschitz representative f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R and that F=f almost everywhere on \Omega. Then the representative and its Rademacher weak partial derivatives determine a canonical bundled element of W^{1,\infty}(\Omega) whose base coordinate is F.

The construction accepts the L^\infty class and the globally defined representative separately. This is useful for elliptic coefficients, where the variational object is an almost-everywhere class but coefficient regularity is stated for a concrete Lipschitz function.

The construction uses Rademacher's theorem to obtain almost-everywhere line derivatives of f; the global Lipschitz constant bounds every coordinate derivative in L^\infty. Restrict the weak derivative identities to the measurable domain, replace the base representative by the agreeing class F, and assemble the base and first derivative rows in graph space.

Rademacher's theorem makes F differentiable outside a null set. The one-dimensional null-preimage theorem proves that the derivative of an absolutely continuous inner curve vanishes almost everywhere above that exceptional set, so the classical Lipschitz chain rule holds almost everywhere on each coordinate-line representative from Theorem 4.186. The converse ACL theorem reconstructs the global W^{1,1} weak derivative by linewise integration by parts and coordinate Fubini. For general p, localize around an arbitrary test function by a smooth cutoff. The bounded operator from Definition 4.187 views the localized W^{1,p} element in W^{1,1} without changing its coordinates almost everywhere. Apply the W^{1,1} identity and transport it back through the cutoff. Lipschitz control and F(0)=0 give the required L^p bounds, including at p=\infty, and the graph-space constructor assembles the result.

Let n>0, let 1\leq p\leq\infty, let F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be Lipschitz with F(0)=0, and let U\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n). Then F\circ U belongs to W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n), and for every coordinate i,

\partial_i(F\circ U) =(\operatorname{deriv}F\circ U)\,\partial_iU \quad\text{almost everywhere}.

The completed graph-space element has base coordinate F\circ U and the displayed weak derivative coordinate. For finite p, preserving the whole global space requires F(0)=0: composing with the zero function otherwise produces a nonzero constant outside L^p(\mathbb R^n). At p=\infty, constants belong to L^\infty, so this obstruction disappears. The theorem uses the zero-preserving hypothesis uniformly across exponents.

Take h_m\to0 inside (0,\delta). Euclidean-valued L^p(V) is reflexive, so the bounded quotients have a weakly convergent refinement, whose limit has norm at most C. Pairing with compactly supported tests in V and moving the quotient onto the test identifies the coordinates of the limit as the weak derivatives of u.

Let 1<p<\infty, let V\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open, and let u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R lie in L^p(V). Suppose there are \delta>0 and C\ge0 with

\|D^hu\|_{L^p(V)}\le C \qquad\text{for every }0<|h|<\delta.

Then there is U\in W^{1,p}(V) whose base coordinate equals u almost everywhere on V and whose full gradient satisfies \|\nabla U\|_{L^p(V;\mathbb R^n)}\le C. The same holds when the bound is assumed only along one nonzero sequence h_m\to0.

Apply Hilbert weak compactness to

s_m=q\,D_i^{h_m}u

and let g be the weak ultrafilter limit. For a test function \varphi supported in V, self-adjointness of real L^\infty multiplication and the identity action of q give

\langle s_m,\varphi\rangle =\langle D_i^{h_m}u,q\varphi\rangle =\langle D_i^{h_m}u,\varphi\rangle.

Discrete integration by parts changes the last expression to -\langle u,D_i^{-h_m}\varphi\rangle. Strong convergence of the test-function quotients identifies the limit with -\langle u,\partial_i\varphi\rangle. Weak lower semicontinuity gives the norm bound.

Finally, both integrands vanish off V: the support of \varphi lies in V, and the support of \partial_i\varphi lies in the topological support of \varphi. Therefore the whole-space integral identity is exactly the weak-derivative identity over V.

Fix a coordinate i, an arbitrary set V\subseteq\mathbb R^n, u\in L^2(\mathbb R^n), and a multiplier q\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n). Let h_m\to0, with every h_m\ne0. Assume

\|q\,D_i^{h_m}u\|_2\le C \qquad\text{for every }m,

and assume that for every smooth compactly supported test function \varphi with \operatorname{tsupp}\varphi\subseteq V,

q\varphi=\varphi \quad\text{as an }L^2\text{ class}.

Then there exists g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n) with \|g\|_2\le C satisfying the integration-by-parts relation against every such test function. For open V, this says that g is the usual weak derivative \partial_i u. On an arbitrary set, the test class can be trivial and uniqueness need not hold.

The test relation is defined without a measurability or openness hypothesis on V. It uses integrals restricted to V; compact support of the test function and its derivative permits the global pairing identities to be restricted to that set.

The multiplier hypothesis is semantic and exact. A smooth cutoff equal to one pointwise on V satisfies it, but the theorem also accepts any bounded multiplier with the same action on supported test vectors. Conversely, membership of q in L^\infty alone is not enough.

Expand the squared norm of the bundled graph-space element as the finite sum of the squared L^2 norms of its base, gradient, and Hessian rows. The localized first- and second-order chain rules identify those rows with the displayed coordinate formulas. Apply the corresponding chart estimate to each row and sum the inequalities over the finite derivative index set.

The squared norm of the localized pullback is bounded by the finite sum of the explicit base-, gradient-, and Hessian-row chart constants:

\left\|\mathcal P^{(2)}_{E,K}U\right\|^2 \leq \sum_{a\in\mathcal I_{n,2}} C_a(E,K,U)^2.

Here \mathcal I_{n,2} indexes all derivative rows of order at most two. Keeping the finite sum explicit leaves every dimension-dependent coordinate multiplicity visible rather than hiding it in an unspecified constant. Each row constant has the form C_a(E,K,U)=c_a(E,K)\,\|U\|, built from the norm of the localized first-order pullback and the chart coefficient bounds, so the estimate is uniform and linear: \|\mathcal P^{(2)}_{E,K}U\|\leq C(E,K)\|U\| with C(E,K)^2=\sum_a c_a(E,K)^2.

The base, gradient, and Hessian chain-rule rows form one localized order-two graph-space element on the compact source patch. Because that patch need not be open, this object records the weak identities required by chart localization; open-domain uniqueness is not available to make it an intrinsic H^2 function on the patch.

The element is constructed for each U separately, with no continuous linear map between Sobolev spaces.

The first statement is the defining almost-everywhere property of MemLp.toLp. For the second, compare one symmetric coordinate at a time. The reconstructed base coordinate agrees almost everywhere with the original one. Transport the reconstructed weak-derivative identity across that equality, then use open-domain uniqueness to identify the reconstructed derivative with the original coordinate almost everywhere. Equality in Lp, followed by extensionality of the finite product and the graph subtype, gives exact equality.

The two round trips have the exact strengths forced by the models.

For every set \Omega, converting a SobolevSpaceOn value to graph space and reading the base coordinate back recovers the original function almost everywhere on \Omega.

If \Omega is open, converting a graph-space element to a representative and back is exactly the original graph-space element. Openness is needed: without it weak derivatives need not be unique, so different choices can yield different derivative coordinates.

toRepresentative reads the Lp representative of the base coordinate of a graph-space element and uses the derivative coordinates to certify every ordered derivative word. Each word is read through its symmetric index, and the permutation theorem carries the stored identity back to the word.

ofRepresentative goes in the other direction, for exponents at least one. It keeps the given base function, chooses one L^p weak-derivative representative for every symmetric index, and sends those functions to their Lp classes. This map is noncomputable because SobolevSpaceOn asserts the existence of derivatives rather than selecting canonical ones.

First approximate f in L^p by a continuous compactly supported function g. Mollification is an L^p contraction, while \rho_{\varepsilon_m}*g\to g follows from pointwise approximate-identity convergence, compact support, and dominated convergence. A three-term triangle estimate for

\rho_{\varepsilon_m}*f-f =\rho_{\varepsilon_m}*(f-g) +(\rho_{\varepsilon_m}*g-g)+(g-f)

then gives the result. The proof includes the endpoint p=1.

Let X be a complete real normed space with the required Borel measurable structure, let 1\leq p<\infty, and let f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n;X). For every positive sequence \varepsilon_m\to0,

\|\rho_{\varepsilon_m}*f-f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n;X)} \longrightarrow 0.

In Lean the conclusion is convergence to zero of the extended seminorm eLpNorm, whose values lie in \mathbb R_{\geq0}\cup\{\infty\}. The companion scalar theorem is obtained from this Banach-valued result by specializing X to \mathbb R.

Differentiate the convolution on its smooth-kernel side. For fixed x, use y\mapsto\rho_\varepsilon(x-y) as the test function in the weak-derivative identity. Iterated differentiation of x-y supplies the sign (-1)^{|\alpha|}, which cancels the sign in weak integration by parts. For a proper domain, the closed-ball hypothesis ensures that this translated kernel is an admissible test function supported inside \Omega.

Suppose \alpha is a nonempty derivative word and g is the \alphath weak derivative of a locally integrable scalar function f. On the whole space, every positive mollification scale satisfies the pointwise identity

D^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*f) =\rho_\varepsilon*g.

For the domain-local form, suppose g is the weak derivative of f on \Omega and the zero extension \mathbf1_\Omega f is locally integrable on \mathbb R^n. Extend both functions by zero, and choose R with \operatorname{tsupp}\rho\subseteq\overline B(0,R). At a point x, the same identity holds provided

\overline B(x,\varepsilon R)\subseteq\Omega.

The ball condition is the formal version of “stay away from the boundary.” Zero extension need not preserve weak derivatives across \partial\Omega, as the example of \mathbf1_{(0,1)} above shows.

A Mollifier n consists of a scalar kernel \rho:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R together with proofs that it is C^\infty, compactly supported, nonnegative, and normalized by

\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho(x)\,dx=1.

For positive \varepsilon, scaled μ ε is the usual kernel

\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(\varepsilon^{-1}x).

The definition sets this function to zero when \varepsilon\leq0; every analytic theorem below therefore carries a strict-positivity hypothesis on the scale. mollify μ ε f is convolution \rho_\varepsilon*f. Mathlib's normalized smooth bump supplies standardMollifier n, so applications need not construct a kernel by hand, while theorems retain an explicit mollifier parameter and hence do not depend on a particular choice.

Apply the bounded C^1 extension operator, use the global Morrey embedding, and restrict the resulting Hölder function to \Omega. Restriction does not increase the Hölder norm. The extension's almost-everywhere agreement on the domain, composed with the global representative theorem, identifies the restricted function with the original Sobolev base coordinate.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n carry the operational bounded C^1 extension atlas and let 0<n<p<\infty. Extension, the global Morrey map, and restriction define a bounded linear map

W^{1,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow C^{0,1-n/p}(\Omega).

Its output agrees almost everywhere on \Omega with the original Sobolev base coordinate. The quantitative theorem is

\|\mathcal M_\Omega U\|_{C^{0,1-n/p}} \leq C_{\mathrm{Morrey}}(n,p,q)\, \|E_\Omega\|\,\|U\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}.

Restriction has operator norm at most one, so the only domain-dependent factor is the norm of the selected C^1 extension operator.

Approximate a Sobolev element by compactly supported smooth functions. The smooth Morrey estimate makes their Hölder representatives Cauchy in the C^{0,1-n/p} norm, so completeness gives a Hölder limit, which is also their pointwise limit. A subsequence converges almost everywhere to the base coordinate, so the two agree. Continuous representatives that agree almost everywhere are equal, which proves additivity and homogeneity; the uniform smooth estimate then makes the map continuous.

Let 0<n<p<\infty. There is a bounded linear map

W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)\longrightarrow C^{0,1-n/p}(\mathbb R^n)

whose value agrees almost everywhere with the Sobolev base coordinate. Its operator norm has an explicit bound in the finite-coordinate Sobolev norm. This is the completed-space version of Morrey's inequality (Evans, 2010, §5.6.2, Theorems 4 and 5), a bounded operator between Banach spaces.

The full target norm is the sum of the uniform norm and the Hölder seminorm. Accordingly, the explicit constant has two analytic sources: the base L^p coordinate controls one value on each unit ball, while the first derivative coordinates control oscillation. The construction takes a real Hölder-conjugate exponent q together with the proof p.HolderConjugate q; hence this operator is the finite-p branch.

For each derivative word \alpha, the derivative-slice map sends W^{m,p} continuously into W^{1,p} whenever |\alpha|+1\leq m. Compose that map with the first-order domain Morrey embedding. Almost-everywhere agreement of derivative slices identifies the result with D^\alpha u.

Let 0<n<p<\infty and let \Omega carry the operational bounded C^1 extension atlas. For every derivative word \alpha with |\alpha|+1\leq m, there is a bounded linear map

W^{m,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow C^{0,1-n/p}(\Omega)

whose value represents D^\alpha u almost everywhere. There is also a global derivative-word operator on \mathbb R^n. Each coordinate has an explicit norm estimate, the product of the first-order Morrey constant, the extension norm in the domain case, and the first-order Sobolev norm of the extracted derivative-word slice of the input.

The Morrey exponent is

\gamma(n,p)=1-\frac{n}{p}.

Lean implements this as 1-n/p_{\mathrm{real}}, where ENNReal.toReal sends \infty to zero. Thus \gamma(n,\infty)=1. Totalized real division also makes \gamma(n,0)=1; the latter is a formal artifact and is not an analytic endpoint. In the analytic range 0<n<p\leq\infty, the exponent is strictly positive. The completed finite-exponent embeddings use 0<n<p<\infty.

For 0<n<p<\infty, every compactly supported global C^1 function defines an element of C^{0,1-n/p}(\mathbb R^n).

finiteMorreyHolderExponent carries the inequalities 0<1-n/p\leq1, while finiteMorreyHolderConstant is the explicit finite constant obtained from the multidimensional Morrey theorem. Compact support is not needed for the extended pointwise oscillation estimate; it is used here to obtain a bounded continuous function and to prove the coefficient finite.

Continuity of Du upgrades its almost-everywhere L^\infty bound to the pointwise estimate \lVert Du(z)\rVert\leq\lVert Du\rVert_{L^\infty} at every z. The convex mean-value inequality on the segment from x to y then gives the stated Lipschitz bound.

In every dimension, a global C^1 function whose Fréchet derivative has finite L^\infty norm is Lipschitz:

|u(y)-u(x)| \leq \|Du\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)}\,\|y-x\|.

The statement is for continuously differentiable scalar functions. The completed Morrey embedding uses finite p. Smooth functions are not norm-dense in W^{1,\infty}, so the completed p=\infty endpoint is proved separately, from a Lipschitz representative: every U\in W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb R^n) has one with Hölder-one norm at most (n+1)\|U\|. Higher-order domain embeddings likewise reconstruct Lipschitz representatives of the derivative coordinates.

Collecting the finitely many derivative indices of order at most k produces a continuous linear map into the completed finite-product Hölder jet. The coordinate agreement follows from the derivative representative's almost-everywhere agreement theorem.

Keep the same exponent and extension-atlas assumptions. For u\in W^{k+1,p}(\Omega), these maps form one bounded linear map into a finite Hölder product. Each coordinate agrees almost everywhere on \Omega with its weak derivative.

Compare each endpoint with the average of u on a ball of radius R=\lVert y-x\rVert. Line-segment integration in polar coordinates bounds each point-to-average difference by the gradient paired with the radial kernel \lVert z-a\rVert^{1-n} on an enlarged ball. Hölder's inequality separates the L^p gradient norm from the conjugate-power kernel integral. The exact polar-coordinate evaluation of that integral contributes R^{1-n/p}. The triangle inequality combines the estimates at x and y.

For 1\leq n<p<\infty and a global C^1 real-valued function,

|u(y)-u(x)| \leq C(n,p)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)} |y-x|^{1-n/p}.

The principal linked theorem is unconditional: it derives a Riesz-potential estimate from a point value to a ball average by integration along line segments in polar coordinates and then applies Hölder's inequality and the exact radial kernel integral. It is stated with extended norms, so it needs neither compact support nor a separate finiteness hypothesis. Its explicit constant includes enlarged-ball factors.

Two conditional factorized versions are also proved, useful when a different point-to-average estimate or kernel estimate is available. The finite real-valued corollary uses compact support only to prove finiteness of the global derivative seminorm.

Assume first that x\leq y. The fundamental theorem of calculus bounds |u(y)-u(x)| by the L^1 norm of u' on [x,y]. Hölder's inequality lowers this local norm from L^p to L^1, contributing the interval-length factor |y-x|^{1-1/p}. Restriction can only decrease the global L^p norm, and exchanging x and y handles the remaining order.

Let 1<p\leq\infty, let u:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be continuously differentiable, and suppose u' has finite L^p norm. Then

|u(y)-u(x)| \leq \|u'\|_{L^p}\,|y-x|^{1-1/p}.

No compact-support hypothesis occurs in the linked declaration. The theorem is scalar-valued, is the one-dimensional specialization of Morrey's line-segment estimate, and includes the p=\infty endpoint. The extended norm form needs no finiteness assumption; the real-valued form assumes that the derivative seminorm is finite. The same estimate is also stated with Mathlib's HolderWith and MemHolder predicates.

At an interior point, use the ordinary weak-to-classical theorem. At a boundary point, flatten the domain with an operational chart. The chart image is locally a convex upper half-ball. Continuity of the Morrey representative and its derivative field, together with Mathlib's derivative-extension theorem, identifies the limiting derivative on the closed half-ball. Transport this derivative back by composing with the chart and induct on the requested differentiability order.

Let \Omega carry the operational C^1 extension atlas. If u\in W^{k+1,p}(\Omega) with 0<n<p<\infty, then its selected Morrey representative is classically C^k within \overline\Omega. More generally, for u\in W^{m,p}(\Omega) and a derivative word \alpha with |\alpha|+r+1\leq m, the representative of D^\alpha u is ContDiffOn of order r on the closure.

The derivatives are taken within the closed set \overline\Omega; the theorem concerns the closure, not an open neighbourhood of it.

Almost-everywhere agreement transfers the graph-space weak-derivative certificate to each adjacent pair of continuous Morrey representatives. The general weak-to-classical bridge localizes near an interior point with a compactly supported cutoff, mollifies the function and its continuous weak gradient, and applies the locally uniform limit theorem for Fréchet derivatives. This identifies the first classical derivative. Induction on r, together with the corresponding statement for every appended coordinate direction, yields the ContDiffOn theorem.

The domain \Omega is open, since openness is part of the atlas. Adjacent Hölder representatives in the Morrey jet satisfy the weak-derivative relation. If |\alpha|+2\leq m, those adjacent representatives assemble pointwise into the ordinary Fréchet derivative of the representative of D^\alpha u.

More generally, if

|\alpha|+r+1\leq m,

then the representative of D^\alpha u is ContDiffOn of order r on \Omega. In particular, for u\in W^{k+1,p}(\Omega) with p>n, the selected representative of u is classically C^k in the interior, and its classical derivatives are the adjacent Morrey representatives.

The bounded quotient sequence has a weakly convergent ultrafilter refining the tail filter. Write g for its weak limit. For a test function \varphi, discrete integration by parts gives

\langle D_i^{h_m}u,\varphi\rangle =-\langle u,D_i^{-h_m}\varphi\rangle.

The left side converges to \langle g,\varphi\rangle by weak convergence. The backward quotients of the smooth test function converge strongly in L^2 to \partial_i\varphi, so the right side converges to -\langle u,\partial_i\varphi\rangle. This is exactly the weak-derivative identity. Weak lower semicontinuity of the norm yields \|g\|_2\le C.

No subsequence is selected: the compactness theorem returns an ultrafilter \mathcal U with \mathcal U\le\operatorname{atTop}. This is enough because every ordinary limit along \operatorname{atTop} also holds along \mathcal U.

Fix a coordinate i. Let u\in L^2(\mathbb R^n), let h_m\to0 with h_m\ne0, and suppose

\|D_i^{h_m}u\|_2\le C \qquad\text{for every }m.

Then there exists g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n) such that

\|g\|_2\le C

and g is the weak derivative \partial_i u on \mathbb R^n. The norm bound is part of the conclusion.

Away from a kink, apply the ordinary derivative chain rule. On each kink fiber, the level-set theorem makes the inner derivative vanish almost everywhere. The scalar maps are one-Lipschitz, so composition preserves interval absolute continuity; integrating the almost-everywhere derivative then gives the FTC identities.

Let \widetilde U be the selected representative of U\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb R) and let G be its weak derivative. Absolute value, positive and negative parts, and every interval truncation T_{a,b} with a\leq b are absolutely continuous on compact intervals. Their derivatives agree almost everywhere with the expected finite-kink formulas; in particular,

(|\widetilde U|)'=\operatorname{sign}(\widetilde U)\,G

and

(T_{a,b}\widetilde U)' =\frac{\operatorname{sign}(\widetilde U-a) -\operatorname{sign}(\widetilde U-b)}{2}\,G.

Each transformed representative satisfies the corresponding literal fundamental theorem of calculus.

First subtract F(0) so that the outer map fixes zero. Apply the whole-space chain rule to the cutoff extension described above. On the support of the test function, \psi=1 and \nabla\psi=0, so the weak identity is exactly the one for U. Outside that support both test pairings vanish. Restoring the constant F(0) does not change the derivative.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be open, let 1\leq p\leq\infty, and let F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be Lipschitz. For every U\in W^{1,p}(\Omega), the composition has weak derivative

\partial_i(F\circ U) =(\operatorname{deriv}F\circ U)\,\partial_iU.

No boundary regularity, finite-volume assumption, or condition on F(0) is needed for this local identity. The derivative belongs to L^p(\Omega).

The inclusion H^s\to H^0 preserves the underlying tempered distribution and is a contraction. At order zero the Bessel potential is the identity. Injectivity follows because two L^2 representatives inducing the same tempered distribution are equal.

For s\geq 0, toL2Fun has the three properties needed by the weak calculus:

  • its induced tempered distribution is exactly the original Sobolev element;

  • it is norm-decreasing, \lVert\operatorname{toL2Fun}(u)\rVert_2\leq\lVert u\rVert_{H^s};

  • it is injective.

Thus an element of nonnegative-order H^s can safely be treated as an L^2 function modulo almost-everywhere equality.

For s\geq 0, the physical L^2 representative is obtained by first including H^s into H^0 and then using the order-zero Bessel representative:

\operatorname{toL2Fun}:H^s(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C) \longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C).

This is different from toLp: the latter represents (1-(2\pi)^{-2}\Delta)^{s/2}u, whereas toL2Fun represents u itself.

Localize by a smooth cutoff supported in a relatively compact open neighborhood of the rectangle. For the resulting global data, mollification gives the classical identity on every line. Product-space L^1 convergence, Fubini, and an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence pass the derivative integrals to almost every transverse coordinate, while continuity controls the endpoint values.

Let U\subset\mathbb R^2 be open. Suppose F is continuous and has weak first-coordinate derivative H on U. If the compact rectangle [a,b]\times[c,d] lies in U, then for almost every s\in[c,d],

\int_a^b H(r,s)\,dr=F(b,s)-F(a,s).

The weak derivative supplies the local integrability needed on a compact neighborhood of the rectangle.

A bounded atlas domain has finite measure, so an H^1(\Omega) element lowers to W^{1,q}(\Omega) with the same coordinates for every q<2. The operational extension theorem and the first-order Sobolev inequality place its base representative in L^{q^*}(\Omega), and finite measure lowers this to every p\leq q^*. For U\in H^2(\Omega) and an index a of order at most one, apply this to the first-order derivative slice representing U_a, whose base coordinate is U_a almost everywhere. The weak-derivative identities of the assembled bundle are those of the order-one restriction \pi_{2,1}U. Linearity holds coordinatewise almost everywhere. Continuity comes from the closed graph theorem: convergence in either graph norm implies convergence in measure of every coordinate, and source and target coordinates agree almost everywhere, so the graph is sequentially closed.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2 carry the operational bounded C^1 extension atlas, and let 1\leq q<2 and 1\leq p\leq q^*=2q/(2-q). Since q\mapsto q^* maps [1,2) onto [2,\infty), every finite p\geq1 is admissible for a suitable q, while p=\infty is not.

For V\in H^1(\Omega) the base coordinate lies in L^p(\Omega), and for U\in H^2(\Omega)=W^{2,2}(\Omega) every coordinate of order at most one, namely U_0, U_1, and U_2, lies in L^p(\Omega). These coordinates assemble into an element of W^{1,p}(\Omega) with the same rows almost everywhere, and the assembly is a continuous linear map

J_p:H^2(\Omega)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\Omega), \qquad (J_pU)_a=U_a\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega\ \text{for }|a|\leq1, \qquad \|J_pU\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\leq\|J_p\|\,\|U\|_{H^2(\Omega)} .

This is the planar instance of the first-order embedding on bounded C^1 domains, applied to each derivative row of U; it reaches every finite exponent because p=2 is the critical exponent in dimension two. The bound is in terms of the operator norm \|J_p\|. The Lean operator takes the exponent data as arguments, and its values are determined by the rows of U.

Each branch is first proved for a test function \varphi supported in \Omega. For n>2, the Sobolev inequality for functions supported in a set of finite measure, at p=q=2, bounds \|\varphi\|_2 by C_{n,\Omega} times the sum of the partial-derivative norms. For n=2, the same inequality at p=1, q=2 gives \|\varphi\|_2\leq C_{1,2}(\Omega)\sum_i\|\partial_i\varphi\|_1, and Hölder on the bounded support gives \|\partial_i\varphi\|_1\leq|\Omega|^{1/2}\|\partial_i\varphi\|_2. For n=1, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \|\varphi\|_\infty\leq\|\varphi'\|_1, and two finite-measure comparisons give \|\varphi\|_2\leq|\Omega|^{1/2}\|\varphi\|_\infty and \|\varphi'\|_1\leq|\Omega|^{1/2}\|\varphi'\|_2.

In each case the set of u\in H^1(\Omega) satisfying the inequality is closed, because both sides are continuous in the graph norm, and it contains the test functions. The closure principle of Definition 4.12 extends the inequality to all of H^1_0(\Omega).

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be bounded; no measurability or regularity of \Omega is assumed. The three dimension branches of Theorem 4.131 are separate theorems with named constants. For every u\in H^1_0(\Omega),

\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \leq C\sum_{i=1}^n\|\partial_iu\|_{L^2(\Omega)},

where the constant is

  • C=C_{n,\Omega} when n>2: Mathlib's constant in the Sobolev inequality for C^1 functions supported in \Omega at the exponents p=q=2;

  • C=C_{1,2}(\Omega)\,|\Omega|^{1/2} when n=2, where C_{1,2}(\Omega) is the same Mathlib constant for the critical pair p=1, q=2;

  • C=|\Omega| when n=1.

Here |\Omega| is Lebesgue measure. The left side is the base coordinate of the bundled element and the right side sums its n first-derivative coordinates. For n>2 the estimate is the case q=p=2 of Evans's W^{1,p}_0 estimate on bounded open sets. The two low-dimensional branches are separate arguments, because p=2 is critical in dimension two and supercritical in dimension one.

On each coordinate line, the fundamental theorem of calculus bounds the function by the L^1 norm of its derivative. Two applications of Hölder on [a,b] give the factor \ell. Squaring and integrating over the remaining coordinates proves the smooth estimate by Fubini. The coordinate split preserves Euclidean volume.

Both coordinate norms are continuous on H^1, so density carries the same inequality to H^1_0. Squaring it and using \|\partial_i u\|_2^2\leq\|\nabla u\|_2^2 gives the displayed bound for \|u\|_{H^1}^2=\|u\|_2^2+\|\nabla u\|_2^2.

Let n\geq1 and suppose \Omega\subseteq\{x:a\leq x_i\leq b\}. With \ell=\max(b-a,0), every u\in H^1_0(\Omega) satisfies

\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\leq\ell\|\partial_i u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.

The full graph norm therefore obeys the explicit Dirichlet coercivity bound

\frac{\|u\|_{H^1}^2}{1+\ell^2}\leq \int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2.

In particular, a unit-width slab gives the constant 1/2, including for the three-dimensional unit cube. No smooth boundary or numerical approximation of a Sobolev constant is needed.

Since n>0, one of n=1, n=2, or n>2 holds. Choose the corresponding nonnegative constant from the explicit dimension branches. Each estimate holds for every u\in H^1_0(\Omega), so it supplies the required constant independently of u.

Let n>0 and let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be any bounded set. There is C\geq0 such that every u\in H^1_0(\Omega) satisfies

\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \leq C\sum_{i=1}^n\|\partial_i u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.

This is the zero-boundary form of the Poincaré inequality. By zero-trace closure, \Omega is only assumed bounded, with no measurability or boundary regularity. The norm on the left is the zeroth coordinate of the bundled H^1 graph element, and the terms on the right are its first weak-derivative coordinates.

For \delta>0, define the globally safe reciprocal

R_\delta(t)=\frac1{\max\{\delta,t\}}.

This map is bounded and globally Lipschitz. Hence, for every globally Lipschitz scalar field a:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R and every measurable domain \Omega, R_\delta\circ a has a canonical W^{1,\infty}(\Omega) element. Its base coordinate agrees almost everywhere on \Omega with R_\delta\circ a, which equals a^{-1} at every point where a\geq\delta.

This first-order construction is meant for uniformly elliptic coefficients, where the singular reciprocal is only needed on a\geq\delta.

The maximum map is one-Lipschitz and keeps its output above \delta; the identity |x^{-1}-y^{-1}|=|x-y|/|xy| therefore gives the explicit Lipschitz constant \delta^{-2}.
