Composition with the Lipschitz coefficient remains globally Lipschitz and bounded by \delta^{-1}. The preceding Lipschitz construction applies, and \max\{\delta,a\}=a on the positive region gives the reciprocal identity.

Apply the bounded extension operator H^1(\Omega)\to H^1(\mathbb R^n). Choose a smooth cutoff equal to one on \overline\Omega and supported in a ball B. Multiplication by the cutoff and restriction to B give a continuous map into H^1_0(B). Compose this map with the compact zero-extension theorem on B, then restrict the resulting global L^2 function back to \Omega. Extension agreement and the fact that the cutoff is one on \Omega identify this compact composite with the original base-coordinate map.

Let n>0 and let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n carry the operational bounded C^1 atlas. The base-coordinate map

H^1(\Omega)\longrightarrow L^2(\Omega)

is compact.

Choose a supported global extension inside a fixed ball. Its global base-coordinate map is compact by the preceding theorem. Restriction L^1(\mathbb R^n)\to L^1(\Omega) is continuous, and the extension agrees almost everywhere with the original function on \Omega. The resulting compact composite is therefore exactly the domain base-coordinate map.

Let n>0 and let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n carry the operational bounded C^1 atlas. Then the base-coordinate map

W^{1,1}(\Omega)\longrightarrow L^1(\Omega)

is compact. Stated through the general subcritical inclusion, the theorem acquires the additional condition 1<n, because that inclusion assumes the source exponent satisfies p<n.

From 1\le p<n one obtains 1<n, so the endpoint inclusion is available through the general inclusion. Its compactness was proved by supported extension, the global L^1 translation estimate, and finite-cell averaging. Apply the W^{1,1} reduction theorem to obtain the desired target exponent q.

Let 1\le p<n, let \Omega carry the operational bounded C^1 atlas, and let 1\le q<p^*. Then the canonical inclusion

W^{1,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow L^q(\Omega)

is compact.

This includes both endpoints p=1 and q=1.

Let 1\le p<n, let 1\le q\le p^*, and let \Omega carry the operational bounded C^1 atlas. The canonical inclusion is the continuous linear map

J_{p,q}:W^{1,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow L^q(\Omega)

that retains the order-zero coordinate and forgets the weak-derivative coordinates. If U is the Sobolev graph-space value and u is its chosen base representative, then

(J_{p,q}U)(x)=u(x) \quad\text{for almost every }x\in\Omega.

The target L^q class is built from the proved Sobolev membership u\in L^q. Continuity is then obtained from the closed graph theorem: source convergence gives convergence in measure through the L^p base coordinate, target convergence gives convergence in measure through L^q, and uniqueness of limits in measure identifies the graph limit. Thus later compactness theorems all concern the same concrete operator.

For a smooth compactly supported function \varphi, the fundamental theorem of calculus along t\mapsto x+th gives

|\varphi(x+h)-\varphi(x)| \le \|h\|\int_0^1 |\nabla\varphi(x+th)|\,dt.

Integrate in x, use translation invariance and Fubini, and bound the L^1 gradient by the graph norm. Global finite-exponent density approximates an arbitrary W^{1,1} value by smooth compactly supported functions. Continuity of translation and closedness of the inequality pass the estimate to the limit.

For U\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb R^n) and h\in\mathbb R^n,

\|U(\,\cdot+h)-U\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^n)} \le \|h\|\,\|U\|_{W^{1,1}(\mathbb R^n)}.

The squared cell-average error is bounded by the average of |\widetilde u(x)-\widetilde u(y)|^2 over pairs of points in the same cell. Write h=y-x. Such shifts lie in the box [-\delta,\delta]^n, where \|h\|^2\le n\delta^2. The translation estimate bounds the integrated defect by

(2\delta)^n n\delta^2\|u\|^2.

Dividing by the cell volume \delta^n gives 2^n n\delta^2\|u\|^2; taking square roots yields the stated estimate. Only finitely many cells are retained, so the range is spanned by finitely many cell indicators.

Let \Omega be measurable. Fix a grid width \delta>0 and a radius R. Assume the zero extension of u\in H^1_0(\Omega) vanishes almost everywhere outside the finite union of cells in the finite grid cover selected for the ball of radius R. Let A_{\delta,R} replace the function on each retained cell by its cell average. Then

\|A_{\delta,R}\widetilde u-\widetilde u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^n)} \le \sqrt{2^n n}\,\delta\,\|u\|_{H^1_0(\Omega)}.

For fixed \delta and R, the operator A_{\delta,R} has finite-dimensional range and is therefore compact.

Finite measure gives the continuous coordinate-preserving map W^{1,p}(\Omega)\to H^1(\Omega). Compose it with the compact H^1(\Omega)\to L^2(\Omega) base map. This proves compactness into L^2. Compactness into every L^q with 1\le q<p^* is the separate theorem proved below.

Let 2\le p<n and let \Omega carry the operational bounded C^1 atlas. Then the canonical inclusion

W^{1,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow L^2(\Omega)

is compact.
At q=2, the general inclusion operator agrees with the compact base-coordinate map. Apply strict-subcritical transfer with lower target s=2 and the critical H^1\to L^{2^*} bound.

Let n>2, let \Omega carry the operational bounded C^1 atlas, and let 1\le q<2^*. Then

H^1(\Omega)\longrightarrow L^q(\Omega)

is compact. The target endpoint q=1 is included.

Start with a sequence in the closure of the image of the Sobolev unit ball. Approximate it by actual images J_{p,q}U_m. Compactness of J_{p,s} gives a subsequence for which the base representatives converge in L^s, hence in measure. The critical inclusion J_{p,p^*} uniformly bounds the same representatives in L^{p^*}.

Because q<p^*, the critical bound makes the qth powers uniformly integrable. On the finite domain measure, tightness is automatic by choosing the whole space. Vitali convergence upgrades convergence in measure to convergence in L^q. The original closure sequence differs from the actual images by an error tending to zero, so the selected subsequence also converges. Thus the closure of the image of the unit ball is sequentially compact and hence compact.

Let \Omega carry the operational bounded C^1 atlas, let 1\le p<n, and choose exponents

1\le s\le p^*, \qquad 1\le q<p^*.

If

J_{p,s}:W^{1,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow L^s(\Omega)

is compact, then

J_{p,q}:W^{1,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow L^q(\Omega)

is compact. Taking s=p gives the base-exponent specialization.

The supported extension operator uniformly bounds the global W^{1,1} norm and places every base coordinate in one fixed ball. Finite grid-cell averages have finite-dimensional range. The global translation estimate bounds their approximation error by a constant times the grid width, uniformly on the source unit ball. The compact-approximation criterion gives total boundedness of the image and therefore compactness.

Let the operational C^1 extension of W^{1,1}(\Omega) be localized inside one ball. The map taking a Sobolev value to the global order-zero coordinate of this supported extension is compact into L^1(\mathbb R^n).

Every \tau_h is an isometry, so it suffices to check continuity on a dense class and use equicontinuity: for g close to u in L^p, \|\tau_hu-\tau_{h'}u\|_p\leq2\|u-g\|_p+\|\tau_hg-\tau_{h'}g\|_p. For p<\infty, bounded continuous functions with compact support are dense, and for such g the last term tends to zero as h\to h' by uniform continuity and bounded support. The formal proof invokes Mathlib's joint continuity of composition with a continuously varying measure-preserving map at finite exponent, applied to the continuous family h\mapsto(x\mapsto x+h) in the compact-open topology.

Let 1\leq p<\infty and u\in L^p(\mathbb R^n). The translation map

\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow L^p(\mathbb R^n), \qquad h\longmapsto\tau_hu,

is continuous. In particular, h\mapsto\|\tau_hu-u\|_{L^p} is continuous. In the L^2 grid argument, its square is therefore integrable on the compact box of within-cell shifts.

For 1\leq p\leq\infty and h\in\mathbb R^n, the map x\mapsto x+h preserves Lebesgue measure, so composition with it is a linear isometry of the whole-space coordinate L^p space of the graph model:

\tau_h:L^p(\mathbb R^n)\longrightarrow L^p(\mathbb R^n), \qquad (\tau_hu)(x)=u(x+h)\ \text{a.e.}, \qquad \|\tau_hu\|_{L^p}=\|u\|_{L^p} .

Translations form an additive action, \tau_0=\mathrm{id} and \tau_a\tau_b=\tau_{a+b}. Translating a product translates both the L^\infty coefficient and the field: \tau_h(a\,u)=(\tau_ha)(\tau_hu). The translation defect has the representative (\tau_hu-u)(x)=u(x+h)-u(x) almost everywhere. Translation defects of zero-extended H^1_0 functions and of W^{1,1} functions are the quantities estimated in the two Fréchet–Kolmogorov layers below.

The finite-measure restriction operator continuously lowers W^{1,p}(\Omega) to W^{1,1}(\Omega) without changing any derivative representative. Composing with the compact endpoint map gives compactness of W^{1,p}(\Omega)\to L^1(\Omega). Apply the strict-subcritical transfer theorem with lower target s=1.

Let \Omega carry the operational bounded C^1 atlas, and let 1\le p<n and 1\le q<p^*. If the endpoint inclusion

W^{1,1}(\Omega)\longrightarrow L^1(\Omega)

is compact, then

W^{1,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow L^q(\Omega)

is compact.

Boundedness of \Omega places the support of every zero-extended base coordinate in one fixed ball. Apply the grid estimate to the image of the closed unit ball. Its error tends to zero uniformly as \delta\downarrow0, while every grid-average operator is compact. The uniform compact approximation criterion makes the image totally bounded; completeness of L^2 then gives compact closure.

If \Omega is measurable and bounded, then zero extension followed by the base-coordinate projection is a compact operator

H^1_0(\Omega)\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^n).

For restrictions of global test functions, integrate the gradient along the line segment from x to x+h, then use Cauchy–Schwarz and translation invariance of Lebesgue measure. Test functions are dense in H^1_0(\Omega), zero extension is isometric, and the inequality defines a closed condition. Density therefore extends the smooth estimate to every zero-trace Sobolev value.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be measurable, let u\in H^1_0(\Omega), and write \widetilde u for its zero extension to \mathbb R^n. For every translation vector h,

\|\widetilde u(\,\cdot+h)-\widetilde u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^n)} \le \|h\|\,\|u\|_{H^1_0(\Omega)}.

The constant is exactly one relative to the graph norm used in the development. The estimate is uniform on every norm-bounded subset of H^1_0(\Omega).

Zero extension sends the unit ball of W^{1,p}_0(\Omega) to a bounded family in L^p(\mathbb R^n) supported in one fixed ball. Its translations satisfy a uniform bound \|\tau_h u-u\|_p\leq C\|h\|.

At p=1, the finite-grid criterion makes this family totally bounded. For p>1, apply the signed power u\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(u)|u|^p. Hölder's inequality gives the transformed family a uniform L^1 translation bound. The same grid criterion gives compact closure in L^1, and the continuous inverse signed power sends that compact set back into L^p. Thus the original zero-extended family has compact closure. Continuous restriction to \Omega proves compactness of the base-coordinate map. For p=2, the preceding Hilbert grid argument also proves this conclusion directly.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be measurable and bounded and let 1\leq p<\infty. The canonical base-coordinate map

W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)\longrightarrow L^p(\Omega)

is compact. Here W^{1,p}_0 is the closure of smooth functions compactly supported in \Omega, taken in the Sobolev graph norm. On open sets this gives the usual zero-boundary space. No boundary regularity is required, and the theorem has no lower bound on n; in particular it includes n=1. Taking p=2 recovers the H^1_0\to L^2 statement above.

For natural order k, exponent p, and domain \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n, the representative-level extension property is the existence of a map

\mathcal E_{\mathrm{rep}}: W_{\mathrm{rep}}^{k,p}(\Omega) \longrightarrow W_{\mathrm{rep}}^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)

such that

\mathcal E_{\mathrm{rep}}u=u \qquad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega

for every representative-level Sobolev function u.

Only the existence of \mathcal E_{\mathrm{rep}} and the almost-everywhere agreement of base functions are required; the map need not be linear or bounded, and its values outside \Omega are unconstrained.

The chosen global object is a global Sobolev representative. When \Omega is open, its weak derivatives restrict to \Omega, and almost-everywhere agreement of the base functions and uniqueness of weak derivatives identify them with the derivatives of u. This is the information used by the extension-and-restriction density theorems.

SobolevSpaceOn n k p Ω contains:

  • a concrete function u : \mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R;

  • a proof that u\in L^p(\Omega);

  • for every coordinate word \alpha with |\alpha|\leq k, a proof that some g_\alpha\in L^p(\Omega) satisfies HasWeakDerivativeOn Ω α u gα.

The derivative clause is existential: it records that derivative representatives exist but does not expose a canonical derivative-valued function. That is why it is convenient for hypotheses and pointwise formulas but not the primary normed-space model.

Equality of two SobolevSpaceOn values is literal equality of their toFun fields, not almost-everywhere equality. The base MemLp field is stated separately. On an open domain it can be recovered from the order-zero weak-derivative clause and uniqueness, but on an arbitrary set that uniqueness can fail. The type is meaningful for every extended nonnegative p; its standard Sobolev interpretation uses an open domain and 1\leq p\leq\infty.

Approximate U smoothly on the compact target set, apply the classical second-order chain rule, transport each derivative row through the chart, and use L^2 closedness of weak derivatives to identify the limit with the canonical graph-space rows of U. Finally restrict the compact-carrier identity to the open pullback patch.

Let E be a C^2 coordinate chart with C^1 inverse, let V be open, and suppose V\subseteq K\subseteq E.\mathrm{target} for a compact set K. For U\in H^2(E.\mathrm{target}), the first weak derivative on the open pullback E^{-1}(V) is the usual gradient chain-rule row, and the second weak derivative is the classical Hessian chain-rule row

\partial_{ik}(U\circ E) =\sum_{j,l}(\partial_{lj}U)\circ E\, \partial_iE_l\,\partial_kE_j +\sum_j(\partial_jU)\circ E\,\partial_{ik}E_j.

No smoothness of U is assumed. The compact set controls localization and L^2 estimates; the distributional identity itself is stated on an open domain.

The proof localizes the two weak coordinate derivatives near the compact family of rays, pulls them back through the smooth slope map, and applies the planar coordinate-line FTC. The weak coordinate chain rule identifies the pulled-back first derivative with g_r+s g_z, while cutoff removal recovers the original endpoint values.

Let \delta>0, let f be continuous on \mathbb R^2, and suppose that g_r,g_z are its weak coordinate derivatives on the region \{(r,z):\delta<r\}. Fix an interval [a,b] contained in \{r>\delta\} and a bounded interval of slopes. Then for almost every slope s in that interval,

\int_a^b \bigl(g_r(r,rs)+s g_z(r,rs)\bigr)\,dr = f(b,bs)-f(a,as).

Thus the weak derivative along the slope-chart ray r\mapsto(r,rs) is the expected chain-rule combination. The theorem concerns one fixed radial interval; its exceptional null set may depend on the chosen endpoints.

Use the graph-space representative of every weak derivative of U through order k. The weak Leibniz theorem applies because each derivative of \zeta appearing in a split is essentially bounded. For every derivative word \alpha, the resulting finite sum is therefore the weak derivative of \zeta U.

For U\in W^{k,p}(\Omega) and a smooth multiplier \zeta whose derivatives through order k are in L^\infty(\Omega), every derivative word of \zeta U of length at most k is represented by the corresponding weak Leibniz expansion.

First use Theorem 4.109 to define the algebraic linear inclusion into Mathlib's Lp space. If a source sequence converges in the graph-space norm, its base rows converge in L^p and hence in measure. If their images converge in L^{p_k}, they converge in measure to the target limit as well. Uniqueness of limits in measure identifies the two limits almost everywhere, proving that the graph is sequentially closed. The closed graph theorem for Banach spaces supplies continuity; the norm inequality is the standard continuous-linear-map operator bound.

Under the same subcritical hypotheses, with source and target exponents at least one, the global inclusion

I_{n,k,p}:W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)\longrightarrow L^{p_k}(\mathbb R^n)

is a continuous linear map. Therefore

\|I_{n,k,p}U\|_{L^{p_k}} \leq \|I_{n,k,p}\|\,\|U\|_{W^{k,p}}.

The constant is the operator norm of I_{n,k,p}, which is finite because the closed graph theorem makes the inclusion continuous.

For a derivative row of order at most m, use the corresponding row of U. For a new top-order row, write its canonical derivative word as i::\beta and use the \beta row of V_i. The hypothesis identifies the base of V_i with the stored first derivative of U. Compose the first-derivative identity with the weak-derivative identity for that row of V_i; the graph-space constructor then assembles the finite family.

Let m>0 and U\in W^{m,p}(\Omega). Suppose that for every coordinate i there is a bundled field V_i\in W^{m,p}(\Omega) whose base coordinate is exactly the stored first derivative \partial_iU. Then there exists W\in W^{m+1,p}(\Omega) whose base coordinate agrees almost everywhere with that of U.

For p=2, writing \mathcal I_{n,m+1} for the finite derivative index, the canonical assembly also satisfies

\|W\|_{W^{m+1,2}} \leq \sqrt{\#\mathcal I_{n,m+1}} \left(\|U\|_{W^{m,2}}+\sum_{i=1}^n\|V_i\|_{W^{m,2}}\right).

The order-m Sobolev control of every first derivative is a hypothesis, and the estimate bounds the assembled element in terms of it.

Prescribed support is data added to an extension operator. A supported operator over a set V consists of an extension operator together with

\mathbf 1_V\, (Eu)=Eu \qquad\text{almost everywhere on }\mathbb R^n

for the base coordinate of every input u. This indicator identity is independent of modifications on null sets and is equivalent to saying that the chosen base representative vanishes almost everywhere outside V.

At every Sobolev order k, including k=0 and p=\infty, any bounded extension operator can be localized when \Omega is measurable, \overline\Omega is compact, and V is an open neighborhood of \overline\Omega. Choose a smooth compactly supported cutoff \psi in V with \psi=1 on \overline\Omega, and define

E_Vu=\psi\,Eu.

Boundedness follows from boundedness of multiplication by \psi on W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n), agreement is preserved because the cutoff equals one on \Omega, and the cutoff support gives the indicator identity (Operator.withSupportIn).

The frontier of the open half-space is computed directly from the last coordinate. The inclusion \iota preserves distances, and an isometry pushes normalized Hausdorff measure of any dimension forward to the same Hausdorff measure restricted to its range; since \mathcal H^n on \mathbb R^n is Lebesgue measure and the range of \iota is the hyperplane, this is the pushforward identity. The integral formula is the change of variables along the closed measurable embedding \iota. A bounded set has bounded preimage under the isometry, hence finite Lebesgue measure.

Let \mathbb R^{n+1}_+=\{x:x_{n+1}>0\} and let \iota:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{n+1}, \iota(y)=(y,0), be the inclusion of the boundary hyperplane. Then \partial\mathbb R^{n+1}_+=\{x_{n+1}=0\}, \iota is an isometry onto this hyperplane, and

\sigma_{\mathbb R^{n+1}_+} =\mathcal H^{n}\restriction\{x_{n+1}=0\} =\iota_*\mathcal L^n,

the pushforward of Lebesgue measure \mathcal L^n on \mathbb R^n. Consequently, for every f:\mathbb R^{n+1}\to\mathbb R,

\int f\,d\sigma_{\mathbb R^{n+1}_+} =\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y,0)\,dy ,

as Bochner integrals, with no integrability hypothesis on f, and every bounded measurable subset of the hyperplane has finite surface measure.

For any set \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n, the intrinsic surface measure is the normalized codimension-one Euclidean Hausdorff measure restricted to the topological frontier:

\sigma_\Omega:=\mathcal H^{n-1}\restriction\partial\Omega .

The normalization is Mathlib's, for which \mathcal H^n on \mathbb R^n is Lebesgue measure, so on a flat hyperplane \sigma_\Omega is Lebesgue measure in tangential coordinates. The definition needs no regularity of \Omega; in dimension n=0 the codimension n-1 is truncated to 0 by natural subtraction, a case nothing uses. Every trace operator on an operational C^1 domain below takes values in L^2(\partial\Omega,d\sigma) or L^p(\partial\Omega,d\sigma) for this measure. The boundary-calculus chapter proves that it has finite total mass on bounded operational C^1 domains and compares it with the chart-assembled atlas measure.

The graph model does not retain every ordering of a mixed derivative. DerivIndex n k is the finite type

\coprod_{m=0}^{k}\operatorname{Sym}^m(\{1,\ldots,n\}),

implemented as a dependent pair of an order m\leq k and a symmetric power of Fin n. Thus D_1D_2u and D_2D_1u use the same coordinate.

DerivIndex.toList chooses an ordered representative only when a declaration such as HasWeakDerivativeOn needs a list. Conversely, derivIndexOfList α hα sends a word of length at most k to its symmetric index, and converting it back produces a permutation of \alpha, not necessarily the same list. The permutation theorem shows that this choice is analytically harmless.

For finite p, restrictions of ambient smooth compactly supported functions are dense in W^{1,p}(\Omega): extend with any one atlas, mollify in the whole space, and restrict. On that set T and \operatorname{Tr}_p both give literal restriction, by hypothesis and by classical agreement. The target is built from intrinsic surface measure, which involves no chart, so the two maps have the same codomain and agree everywhere by continuity. For two atlases, apply the first statement to the trace built from the first atlas, with the second atlas defining \operatorname{Tr}_p.

Let 1\leq p<\infty. A continuous linear map T:W^{1,p}(\Omega)\to L^p(\partial\Omega,d\sigma) that sends every restriction of an ambient smooth compactly supported function to its boundary values is the trace \operatorname{Tr}_p. In particular, two operational C^1 atlases on the same domain construct the same continuous linear trace. Both statements also hold for functions with values in a real Banach space.

Each flattened boundary piece satisfies the half-space trace estimate. The surface-measure pushforward bound transports that estimate to the physical boundary, and the triangle inequality sums over the finite chart cover.

The trace norm is bounded by a finite sum of atlas-dependent chart constants:

\|\operatorname{Tr}u\|_{L^2(\partial\Omega)} \leq \left(\sum_i C_i^{1/2}\|F_i\|\right)\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}.

Here F_i is the continuous linear flattening operator for the ith localized chart and C_i is its surface-measure distortion bound. Thus the map in Definition 4.75 is quantitatively continuous.

Localize the ambient smooth function by the finite boundary partition of unity. Flattening with a C^1 chart and a target cutoff gives a compactly supported C^1 function, so the compact-C^1 flat-trace agreement theorem identifies its boundary value. The chart's surface-measure pushforward bound transports this almost-everywhere identity back to the physical patch. Summing the partition pieces yields literal boundary restriction in L^2(\partial\Omega,d\sigma).

For a continuous representative, inward mollification gives smooth approximants converging both in W^{1,p} and pointwise on \overline\Omega. Their traces converge in boundary L^p, so a subsequence converges almost everywhere there. Smooth agreement identifies this limit with the representative's boundary restriction.

For every globally smooth compactly supported ambient function, the assembled trace agrees in boundary L^2 with literal restriction to \partial\Omega.

Agreement also holds beyond the smooth core. Let 1\leq p<\infty and let U\in W^{1,p}(\Omega) have a representative continuous on \overline\Omega. Then the finite-exponent trace \operatorname{Tr}_pU constructed below equals the boundary restriction of that representative \sigma-almost everywhere, and so does \operatorname{Tr}U when p=2. These statements assume an inward partition of unity, a finite family of cutoffs with a fixed inward direction on each patch. Such a partition exists on bounded open C^1 domains, and one version of the statement assumes only a bounded open set with C^1 graph boundary.

Localize by the finite boundary partition, flatten each piece, and apply the finite-exponent half-space trace estimate. The chart pushforward inequality transports the local trace back with factor C_i^{1/p}. On smooth input, the compact-C^1 agreement theorem identifies each contribution with \psi_i u on the physical boundary. Summing the partition gives literal restriction; summing the local norm estimates gives the stated bound.

The completed operator agrees with literal boundary restriction on every ambient smooth compactly supported function. It also satisfies

\|\operatorname{Tr}_p u\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)} \leq \left(\sum_i C_i^{1/p}p^{1/p}\|F_i\|\right) \|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)},

where F_i is the chart-flattening operator and C_i is the corresponding surface-measure distortion bound.

One inclusion is the previous theorem. For the other, a half-space function with zero trace is approximated by the zero extension, upward translation and mollification described above. On a C^1 domain, the partition of unity splits the function into an interior piece with compact support and boundary pieces; each boundary piece is flattened, approximated on the half-space, and returned through its chart.

Let 1\leq p<\infty, and let \Omega be the upper half-space or an operational C^1 domain. Then

\ker(\operatorname{Tr}_p)=W^{1,p}_0(\Omega),

and in particular \ker(\operatorname{Tr})=H^1_0(\Omega). The same holds for functions with values in a real Banach space.

For every real p\geq1 and every operational bounded C^1 domain \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+1}, the chart construction gives a continuous linear map

\operatorname{Tr}_p:W^{1,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega,d\sigma).

The source is the general completed Sobolev graph space, and the target uses intrinsic codimension-one Hausdorff measure on the frontier.

For an operational bounded C^1 domain \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+1}, the library constructs a continuous linear map

\operatorname{Tr}:H^1(\Omega)\longrightarrow L^2(\partial\Omega, d\sigma).

Here d\sigma is the intrinsic codimension-one Hausdorff measure restricted to the frontier; the charts enter the operator, not the measure. This is the exponent-two case of Evans's theorem. The C1ExtensionAtlas hypothesis supplies global chart extensions, cutoffs and a finite partition of unity. For a bounded open set with C^1 graph boundary, such an atlas exists. It also builds the global extension operator of the preceding chapter, but the trace is assembled directly from localized flattening maps and flat traces.

The operator is the finite sum over charts of localize, flatten, take the half-space trace, and transport back to surface measure. Each summand is bounded, which gives the bound. On a C^1 representative each summand is the restriction of \psi_if, and the cutoffs sum to one on the boundary; the cutoffs also supply the compact support the flat theorem needs. For naturality, both sides are continuous in U and agree on ambient smooth compactly supported functions by the classical formula, which are dense. Scalar compatibility is the same density argument, since the scalar identification preserves every Sobolev coordinate and the graph norm.

Let F be a real Banach space, 1\leq p<\infty, and \Omega an open set carrying an operational C^1 atlas. There is a continuous linear map

\operatorname{Tr}_p:W^{1,p}(\Omega;F)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega,d\sigma;F)

with the same chart-sum bound as the scalar trace. If the base coordinate of U agrees almost everywhere on \Omega with an ambient C^1 function f, then \operatorname{Tr}_pU=f|_{\partial\Omega}; f need not have compact support. For every bounded linear L:F\to G into a real Banach space,

\operatorname{Tr}_p(L\circ U)=L\circ\operatorname{Tr}_pU ,

and for F=\mathbb R the trace agrees with the scalar \operatorname{Tr}_p under the identification of the two graph spaces. The flat half-space trace has the same properties, with a compactly supported C^1 representative in the classical formula.

For a boundary difference g(x)-g(y) with r=|x-y|, pass through the points at height r above x and above y. The two vertical legs are controlled by Hardy's inequality in the normal variable, applied to the real function t\mapsto\|\partial_tu(\cdot,t)\|_F, and the horizontal leg at height r by a tangential translation estimate. Integrating against r^{-n-(1-1/p)p} gives the fractional energy bound for compactly supported C^1 functions, with a constant depending only on n and p. Compact smooth density, an almost everywhere convergent subsequence of boundary values, and Fatou's lemma for nonnegative integrands extend the bound to the Sobolev trace; Fatou keeps the constant. The lifting is the cutoff mollification of the scalar case with a Bochner integral in place of the real one. No approximation property of F is used.

Let F be a real Banach space and 1<p<\infty. The trace of W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^{n+1}_+;F) satisfies the Gagliardo condition of order 1-1/p with values in F, and defines a bounded linear map into \operatorname{GagliardoSpace}(n,1-1/p,\mathbb R^n;p;F) whose kernel is the kernel of the physical trace. For every mollifier the F-valued mollified lifting is a bounded right inverse, so this trace is surjective.

The same scalar kernel regularizes functions with values in a real normed space X by the Bochner convolution

(\rho_\varepsilon*f)(x) =\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho_\varepsilon(y)\,f(x-y)\,dy.

The scalar definition mollify is the specialization X=\mathbb R. Keeping the Banach-valued operation primitive makes the analytic core reusable for vector-valued Sobolev functions and for time regularization of evolution trajectories taking values in a space such as V or V^*.

The critical one-dimensional Morrey theorem supplies a bounded continuous representative. The weak fundamental theorem expresses its increments as the interval integral of the stored derivative. Since that derivative is in L^1, Mathlib's indefinite-integral theorem makes the primitive absolutely continuous, and Lebesgue differentiation identifies its derivative almost everywhere.

Every global U\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb R) has a selected bounded continuous representative \widetilde U that is absolutely continuous on every compact interval. If G is the stored weak derivative, then

\widetilde U'(x)=G(x)\quad\text{for almost every }x, \qquad \widetilde U(b)-\widetilde U(a)=\int_a^b G(t)\,dt.

Thus the graph-space weak derivative agrees almost everywhere with the classical derivative of the selected representative.

The weak Leibniz rule gives the derivative formula. Hölder multiplication L^\infty\cdot L^2\to L^2 and the triangle inequality give the displayed rowwise bound. Bounding every output coordinate by 2\|A\|_{W^{1,\infty}}\|U\|_{W^{1,2}} and summing their squares yields C_n. Assemble the coordinate formulas as a continuous linear map on the ambient finite L^2 product. The weak Leibniz identity shows that this map preserves the closed Sobolev graph subspace. Linearity in both factors and the quantitative estimate then make the construction the bounded bilinear map M.

Let \Omega be open, let A\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega), and let U\in W^{1,2}(\Omega). Multiplication is a bounded bilinear map

M:W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)\longrightarrow \mathcal L\bigl(W^{1,2}(\Omega),W^{1,2}(\Omega)\bigr), \qquad M(A)(U)=AU.

Write \mathcal I_{n,1} for the finite first-order derivative index and set

C_n=2\sqrt{\#\mathcal I_{n,1}}.

For the actual finite-product graph norms used by PDEAtlas,

\|M(A)(U)\|_{W^{1,2}} \leq C_n\|A\|_{W^{1,\infty}}\|U\|_{W^{1,2}}, \qquad \|M(A)\|\leq C_n\|A\|_{W^{1,\infty}}, \qquad \|M\|\leq C_n.

The explicit dimension-dependent constant is not sharp in general. The base coordinate represents the pointwise product Au. More precisely, if u has weak i-th derivative d_i u, then the i-th derivative row of M(A)(U) is

g_i=A\,d_i u+(\partial_iA)u, \qquad \|g_i\|_{L^2} \leq \|A\|_{L^\infty}\|d_i u\|_{L^2} +\|\partial_iA\|_{L^\infty}\|u\|_{L^2},

and \partial_i(Au)=g_i almost everywhere.
Subtract the two distributional identities and apply the fundamental lemma for locally integrable functions paired against all compactly supported smooth test functions.

On an open domain, two proposed derivative representatives satisfying the same weak-derivative identity for the same base function agree almost everywhere with respect to volume.restrict Ω. Concretely, if

\int_\Omega f\,D^\alpha\varphi =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega g_1\varphi =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega g_2\varphi \quad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega),

then g_1=g_2 almost everywhere on \Omega. This is Evans's primitive uniqueness result. No exponent and no global L^p hypothesis occur in the statement.

Let \Omega \subseteq \mathbb R^n, let \alpha be a word of coordinate indices, and let f,g : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R. The predicate HasWeakDerivativeOn Ω α f g is defined for an arbitrary set \Omega. It requires both functions to be locally integrable on \Omega with respect to ambient Lebesgue measure and requires

\int_\Omega f\,D^\alpha\varphi = (-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega g\,\varphi

for every globally smooth compactly supported test function \varphi whose closed support tsupport φ is contained in \Omega. Both integrals are Bochner integrals against the restricted measure volume.restrict Ω; compact support and local integrability make the pairings integrable.

Thus the declaration is an arbitrary-set restricted-test relation. When \Omega is open, these are exactly the usual C_c^\infty(\Omega) tests and the definition has Evans's distributional meaning. On a nonopen set, especially one with empty interior, the available tests can be too small to determine g. PDE-facing predicates such as weak Poisson and weak divergence solutions therefore carry an explicit IsOpen Ω field. The relation says nothing about pointwise differentiability of f.

For open domains, weak derivatives are unique almost everywhere under only the local-integrability hypotheses already present in the predicate.

Choose a smooth cutoff equal to one on the interval, extend the localized data by zero, and mollify. The classical FTC holds for every mollification. Pointwise convergence of the mollified continuous representative and L^1 convergence of the mollified weak derivative pass the identity to the limit.

Let U\subset\mathbb R be open, let f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be continuous, and suppose f,g\in L^1(U) with g a weak derivative of f on U. If the closed interval from a to b lies in U, then

\int_a^b g(t)\,dt=f(b)-f(a).

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n, 1\le p, m\ge1 with p/m\ge1, and \sigma:\{1,\dots,m\}\to\{1,\dots,n\}. For u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)^m the selected Jacobian (\partial_{\sigma(j)}u_i)_{i,j} is a matrix-valued L^p function, and its determinant M_\sigma(u) is an element of L^{p/m}(\Omega). It agrees almost everywhere with the determinant of the weak partial derivatives. If \Omega is open and the components of u have a common C^1 representative f, then M_\sigma(u) is the corresponding minor of the Jacobian matrix of f. For p<\infty the map u\mapsto M_\sigma(u) is continuous from W^{1,p}(\Omega)^m to L^{p/m}(\Omega), and it sends bounded sets to bounded sets. The case m=n, \sigma=\mathrm{id} is the Jacobian determinant \det Du\in L^{p/n}(\Omega).

The proof inducts over the derivative word. The first-order weak product rule is applied at each step, and the list of splits records repeated coordinates, including the multiplicities that become binomial or multinomial coefficients in conventional notation.

Let \zeta be smooth with every derivative used in the expansion belonging to L^\infty(\Omega). Let D_\beta be an L^p family compatible under successive first weak derivatives. Then, for every derivative word \alpha, the product \zeta D_{\varnothing} has weak derivative given by the full Leibniz expansion over all ways of distributing the entries of \alpha between the two factors.

By the last identity of Theorem 4.38, the left side is bounded by \int|u||u''|\Phi_{\mathrm{mid}}+\int|u||u'||\Phi_{\mathrm{mid}}'|. The weight comparisons turn these into A_0\|u\|_{\mathrm{prev}}\|u''\|_{\mathrm{next}} and A_1\|u\|_{\mathrm{prev}}\|u'\|_{\mathrm{mid}}. Young's inequality with parameters chosen from \eta and \theta and absorption of the \|u'\|_{\mathrm{mid}}^2 term into the left side give the constant.

Let u\in C^2(\mathbb R) have compact support, let the three weights be nonnegative and C^1, and suppose

|\Phi_{\mathrm{mid}}|\le A_0\sqrt{\Phi_{\mathrm{prev}}\Phi_{\mathrm{next}}},\qquad |\Phi_{\mathrm{mid}}'|\le A_1\sqrt{\Phi_{\mathrm{prev}}\Phi_{\mathrm{mid}}} .

Then for \eta>0 and 0<\theta<1

\int u'^2\Phi_{\mathrm{mid}}\le\eta\int u''^2\Phi_{\mathrm{next}} +\Bigl(\frac{A_0^2}{4(1-\theta)^2\eta}+\frac{A_1^2}{4\theta(1-\theta)}\Bigr) \int u^2\Phi_{\mathrm{prev}} .

For a finite family u_1,\dots,u_d the same estimate holds for the sums \bigl(\sum_i\|u_i'\|_{\mathrm{mid}}\bigr)^2 and their analogues, with A_0^2 and A_1^2 multiplied by d^2. There are versions on (0,\infty), and axial and radial row versions on the half plane in which compact support is replaced by the vanishing of the boundary products in the limit.

The lower bounds make the map from the completion to H^k(\mathbb R^n) continuous, as in Theorem 4.24. It sends the parity core into the closed parity subspace of H^k, so it sends the closure of the core there as well.

Let w_\alpha be the row weights on \mathbb R^n. The eligible test functions whose derivative rows have the parity of the previous theorem form a subspace of the smooth core, and its closure in the weighted completion is a complete space in which the core is dense. If every row measure is bounded below, dx\le D_\alpha\,w_\alpha\,dx, then each element of this closure, viewed as a function in H^k(\mathbb R^n), has every row in the prescribed eigenspace. The weights may grow or be singular.

On an open set a Sobolev function determines its weak derivatives, so positivity of w_0 makes the zeroth row, and hence the whole row tuple, determine the graph element. The lower measure comparison bounds each unweighted L^2 norm by a weighted one; the forgetful map is therefore bounded on the realized rows, lands in the closed graph subspace of W^{k,2}(\Omega), and extends to the closure. Its injectivity is injectivity of the forgetful map on row tuples. Closability is the same bound read on the graph of the derivative operator. With upper bounds as well, the weighted and unweighted norms are equivalent on realized rows, so the realized range is closed and equals its closure.

Let \Omega be open.

  1. If w_0>0 almost everywhere, the map from weighted-integrable graph elements into the completion is injective.

  2. If each row measure controls Lebesgue measure, dx\leq D_\alpha\,w_\alpha\,dx with D_\alpha<\infty, forgetting the weights gives a bounded injective map from the completion into W^{k,2}(\Omega). The weights may be unbounded.

  3. If w_\alpha\geq c_\alpha>0 almost everywhere, the weighted derivative operator, which sends the zeroth row to the full jet, is closable. When in addition w_0>0 almost everywhere, every element of the completion is the value of the closed operator at its zeroth row, an L^2(w_0) function.

  4. If c_\alpha\leq w_\alpha\leq C_\alpha with 0<c_\alpha and C_\alpha<\infty, the completion is exactly the set of realized rows of W^{k,2}(\Omega).

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n, k\in\mathbb N, and assign a density w_\alpha\geq0 to every derivative index |\alpha|\leq k. The weighted row space is the Hilbert direct sum \bigoplus_{|\alpha|\leq k}L^2(\Omega,w_\alpha\,dx). A graph element u\in W^{k,2}(\Omega) whose derivatives have finite weighted energy maps linearly to its rows (\partial^\alpha u)_\alpha. The completed weighted space is the closure of the image of this map. It is a real Hilbert space for arbitrary nonnegative densities, the realized graph elements are dense in it, and

\|U\|^2=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq k}\int_\Omega|U_\alpha|^2w_\alpha\,dx .

Let u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega) and let w\ge0 be a density. The row \partial^\alpha u lies in L^p_w when it is p-integrable for the measure w\,dx, and u has all its rows in L^p_w when this holds for every |\alpha|\le k. Both conditions are monotone in the density: if w'\le Cw then a row in L^p_w is in L^p_{w'}.

For anisotropic problems each coordinate direction gets a cost c_i\in\mathbb N, and a derivative index gets the degree \sum_i c_i\alpha_i. The anisotropic family of budget b consists of the indices of degree at most b. It grows with the budget and shrinks when the costs grow, and with all costs equal to one it is the usual family |\alpha|\le b. An anisotropic weighted condition asks for L^p_w membership of the rows in that family only.

The energy is an integral against the sum of the row powers, so the first statement is log-convexity of the integral in the density followed by the q-th root. The certificate statements then multiply the endpoint bounds.

For a finite family A of derivative indices, q>0 and a density w, let

G_w(u)=\Bigl(\sum_{\alpha\in A}\int|\partial^\alpha u|^q\,w\Bigr)^{1/q}.

For 0\le\theta\le1, G_{w_0^{1-\theta}w_1^\theta}(u)\le G_{w_0}(u)^{1-\theta}G_{w_1}(u)^\theta. A certificate is a stored upper bound for such a gauge. Certificates for w_0 and w_1 combine into one for every geometric mean w_0^{1-\theta}w_1^\theta. This holds for arbitrary families, for the full Sobolev family and for anisotropic families, and for bounds that hold eventually along a filter.

Support in (\varepsilon,R) forces u(\varepsilon)=u(R)=0 and makes each half-line integrand vanish outside (\varepsilon,R), so both sides equal the corresponding finite-interval integrals and Theorem 4.144 applies. The derivative version is the same statement for u=f^{(m)}, whose derivative is f^{(m+1)}. The chain is an induction on j: the step at weight s=j+1 trades one factor x^{-2} against one derivative and multiplies the constant by (2j+1)^2 on the left and by 4 on the right, and the induction hypothesis at level m+1 handles the remaining j steps. For compactly supported f with support in (0,\infty), compactness yields one interval [\varepsilon,R]\subset(0,\infty) containing the support, and every derivative is supported inside the support of f.

Let 0<\varepsilon<R and s>1/2. If u is C^1 and u (hence also u') is supported in (\varepsilon,R), then

(2s-1)^2\int_0^\infty u(x)^2\,x^{-2s}\,dx \leq 4\int_0^\infty u'(x)^2\,x^{2-2s}\,dx .

The same estimate holds with u replaced by the m-th derivative of a C^{m+1} function f whose derivative of order m (hence also of order m+1) is supported in (\varepsilon,R). Iterating it j times with the weight exponents s=j,j-1,\ldots,1 gives the explicit chain: if f\in C^{m+j} and f^{(m+l)} is supported in (\varepsilon,R) for every l\leq j, then

\Bigl(\prod_{l=1}^{j}(2l-1)^2\Bigr) \int_0^\infty f^{(m)}(x)^2\,x^{-2j}\,dx \leq 4^j\int_0^\infty f^{(m+j)}(x)^2\,dx .

Finally, the chain holds for every C^{m+j} function with compact support contained in (0,\infty), with no explicit interval. The support hypotheses are what allow the half-line integrals to be replaced by finite-interval integrals, and no decay or endpoint trace is needed. At j=0 the product is empty and the chain reduces to an equality.

Integrate u^2 against the derivative of x^{1-2s}, namely (1-2s)x^{-2s}, by parts on [\varepsilon,R]. The endpoint zeros remove the boundary terms and give the identity. Write X and Y for the two weighted integrals and apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the right side of the identity, so that (2s-1)X\leq2\sqrt X\sqrt Y. If X=0 the inequality is trivial; otherwise divide by \sqrt X and square, using 2s-1>0.

Let 0<\varepsilon<R, let s>1/2, and let u:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be C^1 with u(\varepsilon)=u(R)=0. Then

(2s-1)^2\int_\varepsilon^R u(x)^2\,x^{-2s}\,dx \leq 4\int_\varepsilon^R u'(x)^2\,x^{2-2s}\,dx .

The underlying identity needs only C^1 regularity and the two endpoint zeros, with no restriction on s:

(2s-1)\int_\varepsilon^R u(x)^2\,x^{-2s}\,dx =2\int_\varepsilon^R \bigl(u(x)\,x^{-s}\bigr)\bigl(u'(x)\,x^{1-s}\bigr)\,dx .

At s=1 this is the finite-interval step of the classical core. The inequality is stated multiplied out, without dividing by (2s-1)^2, so that it can be iterated across weight exponents without case splits. This is the power-weighted Hardy inequality of Hardy, Littlewood, and Pólya.

The first inequality is the log-convexity of Theorem 4.27 applied to the densities F and r^{2k}F with \theta=j/k. Young's inequality a^{\theta}b^{1-\theta}\le\theta\chi a+(1-\theta)\chi^{-\theta/(1-\theta)}b, with \chi chosen to make the top coefficient \eta, gives the additive form and the constant K. The symbol bounds follow from the binomial expansion of (\xi_r^2+\xi_z^2)^m.

Let r,F\ge0 be measurable on a measure space and 0<j<k integers. Then

\int r^{2j}F\le\Bigl(\int r^{2k}F\Bigr)^{j/k}\Bigl(\int F\Bigr)^{1-j/k},

as an inequality in [0,\infty]. If both integrals on the right are finite, then for every \eta>0

\Bigl(\int r^{2j}F\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\eta\Bigl(\int r^{2k}F\Bigr)^{1/2} +K(j,k,\eta)\Bigl(\int F\Bigr)^{1/2},\qquad K(j,k,\eta)=\frac{k-j}{k}\Bigl(\frac{j}{k\eta}\Bigr)^{j/(k-j)} .

Taking r=|\xi| and F=|\hat f(\xi)|^2 on \mathbb R^2 gives the Fourier form. In the plane the aggregate symbol \sum_{q=0}^m\xi_r^{2q}\xi_z^{2(m-q)} of all mixed derivatives of order m lies between 2^{-m}|\xi|^{2m} and |\xi|^{2m}.

A matrix with nonnegative entries preserves componentwise inequalities, so applying Q^{-1} to both sides and using Q^{-1}Qy=y gives the first bound. The second uses \sqrt{a+b}\le\sqrt a+\sqrt b. Whether the inverse of a given recursion matrix is nonnegative is data supplied with the certificate.

Let Q be a square matrix with a left inverse Q^{-1} whose entries are nonnegative, and let b_0,b_1\ge0 be vectors. If

(Qy)_i\le b_{0,i}\,y_0+b_{1,i}\,y_1\quad\text{for all }i,

then y_j\le(Q^{-1}b_0)_j\,y_0+(Q^{-1}b_1)_j\,y_1. Applied to the squares of nonnegative gauges g_j with endpoint values L,H\ge0 it gives

g_j\le\sqrt{(Q^{-1}b_0)_j}\,L+\sqrt{(Q^{-1}b_1)_j}\,H .

The nearest-neighbour recursion g_j^2\le\beta_jg_{j-1}^2+\phi_jg_{j+1}^2 has the tridiagonal matrix with 1 on the diagonal, -\phi_j above it and -\beta_j below it, with sources in the first and last rows.
Monotonicity of the integral reduces the first statement to Hölder's inequality with exponents 1/(1-\theta) and 1/\theta. The second is the first with F_j=|\partial^\alpha u|^qw_j.

Let 0\leq\theta\leq1 and let F_0,F_1,F_\theta\geq0 with F_\theta\leq F_0^{1-\theta}F_1^\theta almost everywhere. Then

\int F_\theta\leq\Bigl(\int F_0\Bigr)^{1-\theta}\Bigl(\int F_1\Bigr)^\theta .

Consequently the energy \int|\partial^\alpha u|^qw_\theta of a Sobolev graph coordinate against the geometric density w_\theta=w_0^{1-\theta}w_1^\theta is at most the product of the endpoint energies raised to the powers 1-\theta and \theta.

The first part is the chain rule for f\circ\sigma_i, whose derivative in x_i carries a sign and whose other derivatives do not, iterated along the index. For the second, each row condition says that two continuous maps into L^p agree, the row itself and c(-1)^{\alpha_i} times its reflection, so it cuts out a closed subspace, and the intersection of closed subspaces is closed. The parity of each row is imposed as a separate condition. For Sobolev functions on the whole space the parity of u already forces the parity of the weak derivatives, but that implication is not used.

Say that f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is a reflection eigenfunction with eigenvalue c in the direction i if f\circ\sigma_i=cf; the cases c=1 and c=-1 are even and odd functions.

  1. If f\in C^k(\mathbb R^n) has eigenvalue c, then \partial_if has eigenvalue -c, \partial_jf has eigenvalue c for j\ne i, and in general \partial^\alpha f has eigenvalue c(-1)^{\alpha_i} for |\alpha|\le k.

  2. The map u\mapsto u\circ\sigma_i is a linear isometry of L^p(\mathbb R^n). The set of u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n) whose row \partial^\alpha u lies in the c(-1)^{\alpha_i} eigenspace of this isometry, for every \alpha, is a closed subspace. For c=\pm1 it is the even or odd Sobolev space.

  3. Intersecting with the rows in L^2_{w_\alpha} gives the weighted even and odd subspaces of H^k(\mathbb R^n).

The row with no r derivative is interpolated in z, and each row with a>0 is interpolated in r against its predecessor of order n that has one fewer r derivative. These are the axial and radial cases of Theorem 4.39. The successor identities identify the derivatives without commuting mixed partials. Summing over the n+2 rows gives the factor d=n+2.

Suppose the rows of f of order n, whose line derivatives give orders n+1, n+2, are C^2 along the lines they are differentiated on and compactly supported there, that every row of order n vanishes on the axis r=0, that the three weights satisfy the hypotheses of the previous theorem in both the r and the z direction, and that the relevant weighted squares and cross terms are integrable on the half plane. Then for \eta>0 and 0<\theta<1

X_{n+1}(f)^2\le\eta\,X_{n+2}(f)^2+K\,X_n(f)^2,

with K the one-step constant for d=n+2. A second version drops compact support and the axis condition. It asks instead for C^2 regularity on r>0, weighted L^2 membership of the rows, and vanishing limits of the boundary products.

Away from the axis the reflection is a composition with r\mapsto-r, so its derivatives are those of f with a sign (-1)^q. On the axis the one-sided derivatives agree exactly when the odd-order radial derivatives vanish, which is the gluing hypothesis. The axis has measure zero, so the integral identity needs only the off-axis formula and the symmetry of the integrand under r\mapsto-r. The identity does not by itself give Sobolev membership.

Let Ef(r,z)=f(|r|,z) be the even reflection and Of the odd one.

  1. If F\in C^1(\mathbb R^2) and \partial_rF=0 on the axis, then EF is C^1. The same condition gives C^2 when F\in C^2. The odd reflection of F is C^1 when F vanishes on the axis, and C^2 when in addition \partial_r^2F vanishes there.

  2. If A\in C^2(\mathbb R^2) vanishes on the axis and its derivatives up to order two are in L^2 of the half plane, its odd reflection agrees almost everywhere, up to swapping the coordinates, with an element of W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^2).

  3. If the radial derivatives of \partial_z^\ell f exist along each line and the odd-order ones vanish on the axis, then \partial_r^{2m}\partial_z^\ell Ef=E(\partial_r^{2m}\partial_z^\ell f) and \partial_r^{2m+1}\partial_z^\ell Ef=O(\partial_r^{2m+1}\partial_z^\ell f).

  4. For all q,\ell and any f,\Phi,

    \int\!\!\int(\partial_r^q\partial_z^\ell Ef)^2\,E\Phi =2\int\!\!\int_{r>0}(\partial_r^q\partial_z^\ell f)^2\,\Phi,

    as an identity of iterated integrals, and the same holds for the odd reflection.

Integrability is derived first: on H the lower bound gives f^2\leq f^2w/c, and the reflection is measure preserving, so the two halves each contribute at most \frac1c\int_Hf^2w. The even-density statement applies this to \sqrt f with weight one.

Let H=\{x:x_i\geq0\}, let w\geq c>0 almost everywhere on H, and let \int_Hf^2w<\infty. For either sign \sigma=\pm1, the reflection Rf(x)=f(x) on H and Rf(x)=\sigma f(x^*) off H, where x^* flips the sign of x_i, belongs to L^2(\mathbb R^n) and

\int_{\mathbb R^n}(Rf)^2\,dx\leq\frac2c\int_Hf^2w\,dx .

A continuous nonnegative density even in x_i and integrable on H is integrable on \mathbb R^n, with at most twice the half-space integral.

The completion is a closed subspace of the finite product of the weighted L^2 spaces with the product topology. Row limits give a limit in the product, and a closed set contains the limits of its sequences.

A map into the weighted completion is continuous if and only if each of its rows is continuous into its weighted L^2 space. If a family U_j in the completion has rows converging to limits R_\alpha, then there is U in the completion with rows R_\alpha and U_j\to U. No comparison between the row measures is needed.

Forgetting a weight costs at most D^{1/2} in each row. On the whole space, Fourier interpolation bounds every intermediate unweighted row by the base row and the pure top rows. Each row outside s has a bounded weight, so its weighted norm is at most C^{1/2} times its unweighted norm. Adding the rows and applying Cauchy–Schwarz to the finite sum gives the inequality. An injective bounded operator with a bound from below has closed range, and it is a linear homeomorphism onto that range.

Let k\ge1 and let w_\alpha be row weights on \mathbb R^n with a common lower bound, dx\le D\,w_\alpha\,dx for all \alpha. Let s be a set of rows that contains the base row and the pure top rows \partial_i^k, and assume the rows outside s have bounded weights, w_\alpha\,dx\le C\,dx for \alpha\notin s. Then there is B>0 with

\|U\|^2\le B\sum_{\alpha\in s}\|U_\alpha\|_{L^2_{w_\alpha}}^2

for every U in the weighted completion. Consequently the projection onto the rows in s is injective with closed range, and the completion is linearly homeomorphic to that range, a Hilbert space whose squared norm is exactly the selected energy.

The first part follows from the operator bound for the change of weights and Theorem 4.22. The second is an \varepsilon/3 argument: U is close to V, the test functions are eventually close to V in the q-norm by the first part, and the distance comparison converts that into closeness in the w-norm.

Let v_\alpha be bounded row weights, v_\alpha\le B_\alpha, and let q_\alpha\le C_\alpha v_\alpha.

  1. Distances measured with the weights q are at most a constant times distances measured with v, and every element of H^k(\mathbb R^n) is a limit of test functions in the q-weighted row norm.

  2. Suppose that for every realizable U and every \varepsilon>0 there is such a pair (v,q), a function V within \varepsilon/3 of U in the w-norm, and test functions converging to V in the v-norm whose w-distance to V eventually exceeds their q-distance by at most \varepsilon/3. Then the smooth core is dense in the w-completion.

Because q=v=0 and V=U are allowed, the hypothesis of the second part is equivalent to plain approximation of every realizable U by test functions in the w-norm. The theorem fixes the shape of a density proof; the approximation itself has to be supplied for each singular weight.

With finite upper bounds the weighted norm of a row is at most a constant times its L^2 norm. Realized graph elements are dense in the completion by definition, and each of them is approximated in W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n) by smooth compactly supported functions, by Theorem 4.22. The upper bound carries that approximation into the weighted norm.
Let w_\alpha\leq C_\alpha<\infty almost everywhere on \mathbb R^n. Then the test functions whose rows have finite weighted energy are dense in the completed weighted space.

Each identity is the fundamental theorem of calculus for a product, (Pf^2)'=wf^2+2Pfg, (G\Phi f^2)', or (uu'\Phi)', integrated with the boundary terms removed by the stated limits, compact support, or the zero value at the origin.

1. Let a<b, P'=w and f'=g on (a,b), with wf^2 and Pfg integrable and Pf^2\to0 at both ends. Then

    \int_a^bw\,f^2=-2\int_a^bP\,f\,g .

    The same holds on (0,\infty). If |P|\le|AB|, Young's inequality bounds the right side by the energies of Af and Bg.

  2. For G,\Phi,f\in C^1, f compactly supported with f(0)=0,

    \int_0^\infty(-Gf')\,f\,\Phi\,dr=\frac12\int_0^\infty f^2\,(G\Phi)'\,dr,

    and if |(G\Phi)'|\le C\Phi on (0,\infty) the left side is at most \frac C2\int_0^\infty f^2\Phi. The analogous identity and bound hold on \mathbb R and on \mathbb R^2 for the transport field (-G_r,-G_z).

  3. For u\in C^2 with compact support and \Phi\in C^1, \int u'^2\Phi=-\int u\,u''\,\Phi-\int u\,u'\,\Phi'.

Write vw\Phi=(v\Phi^{1/2})(w\Phi^{1/2}), bound each factor, and use Hölder's inequality for the integrability of V_iW_i. The null set does not depend on t, which is the order of quantifiers that dominated differentiation in time asks for.

Let \iota be finite, \Phi_i\ge0 almost everywhere, and W_i,V_i\in L^2(\mu). Suppose that outside a single null set, for every parameter t\in S and every i,

|w_i(t,x)|\,\Phi_i(x)^{1/2}\le|W_i(x)|,\qquad |v_i(t,x)|\,\Phi_i(x)^{1/2}\le|V_i(x)| .

Then \sum_i|V_iW_i| is integrable, and outside a null set, for all t\in S, \bigl|\sum_iv_i(t,x)\,w_i(t,x)\,\Phi_i(x)\bigr|\le\sum_i|V_i(x)W_i(x)|.

The zero-extension translation-defect estimate gives

\|\tau_a\widetilde u-\widetilde u\|_2 \le |a|\,\|u\|_{H_0^1(\Omega)}.

Take a=h e_i, use |h e_i|=|h|, and divide by |h|. The nonzero-step hypothesis is used exactly in cancelling this factor.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be measurable, let u\in H_0^1(\Omega), and extend u by zero to all of \mathbb R^n. For every coordinate i and every h\ne0,

\|D_i^h\widetilde u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^n)} \le \|u\|_{H_0^1(\Omega)}.

The statement concerns the base coordinate of the global Sobolev zero extension. It avoids extending an arbitrary H^1(\Omega) function by zero: without the zero-trace hypothesis such an extension may acquire a boundary distribution and need not belong to H^1(\mathbb R^n).

For a test function supported in \Omega, the zero extension of the bundle is the bundle of the same smooth function on \mathbb R^n, so the whole-space identities hold literally. The set of u\in H^1(\Omega) whose extended bundle lies in the closed whole-space graph submodule is the preimage of a closed set under a continuous linear map, hence closed, and it contains the test functions; the closure principle for H^1_0 gives the first claim. Indicator extension preserves each coordinate's L^2 norm, and the graph norm is the \ell^2 sum of coordinate norms, which gives the isometry and injectivity. The coordinate formula is the almost-everywhere description of L^2 zero extension. For open \Omega, restricting \mathbf 1_\Omega u_a to \Omega recovers u_a almost everywhere, and an H^1(\Omega) element on an open set is determined by its base coordinate through uniqueness of weak derivatives.

Let \Omega be measurable, let u\in H^1_0(\Omega), and write \widetilde u=E_0u. The coordinatewise zero extension of u satisfies every whole-space weak-derivative identity, so \widetilde u\in H^1(\mathbb R^n), and its coordinates are

\widetilde u_0=\mathbf 1_\Omega u_0, \qquad \widetilde u_i=\mathbf 1_\Omega u_i \quad\text{almost everywhere on }\mathbb R^n ,

so the weak derivatives of the extension are the zero extensions of the weak derivatives. Moreover:

  • \|\widetilde u\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}, and E_0 is injective;

  • for a test function \varphi supported in \Omega, E_0\varphi is \varphi itself regarded as an element of H^1(\mathbb R^n);

  • if \Omega is open, restriction back to \Omega is a left inverse: \rho_{\mathbb R^n,\Omega}\circ E_0 is the inclusion H^1_0(\Omega)\to H^1(\Omega).

Let V and \Omega be open subsets of \mathbb R^n. Restricting the whole-space zero extension of Definition 4.90 to \Omega gives a continuous linear map H^1_0(V)\to H^1(\Omega). When V\subseteq\Omega, its values lie in the zero-trace subspace, and the resulting map

E_{V,\Omega}:H^1_0(V)\longrightarrow H^1_0(\Omega), \qquad \|E_{V,\Omega}u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}=\|u\|_{H^1(V)},

is a linear isometry, hence injective, with restriction as a left inverse: \rho_{\Omega,V}\circ E_{V,\Omega} is the inclusion H^1_0(V)\to H^1(V). The construction is functorial: E_{\Omega,\Omega} is the identity, and E_{V,\Omega}\circ E_{U,V}=E_{U,\Omega} for open U\subseteq V\subseteq\Omega. This is the operator behind localization arguments that regard a function supported in a subdomain as a zero-trace function on the whole domain.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be measurable. Extending each coordinate of an H^1(\Omega) bundle by zero outside \Omega is a continuous linear map of coordinate bundles, (u_a)_a\mapsto(\mathbf 1_\Omega u_a)_a. On the zero-trace subspace it lands in whole-space H^1, giving a continuous linear map and a linear isometry

E_0:H^1_0(\Omega)\longrightarrow H^1(\mathbb R^n), \qquad \|E_0u\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)} .

Measurability of \Omega is the only hypothesis; no openness or boundary regularity is required. The zero extension of an arbitrary H^1(\Omega) function is not in H^1(\mathbb R^n) in general, because a jump across \partial\Omega creates a boundary measure; the theorem below shows that the closure definition of H^1_0 rules this out.

Literal boundary restriction vanishes for every compactly supported smooth function on the open domain. The trace is continuous, and those functions have dense image in the closure defining W^{1,p}_0, so the identity extends to the whole supported-core completion.

For every real p\geq1,

W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)\subseteq\ker(\operatorname{Tr}_p).

Here W^{1,p}_0 is the closure of compactly supported smooth functions in the same finite-exponent graph space used by the trace.
Smooth compactly supported test functions have vanishing classical boundary values. Continuity of the trace passes this identity to their H^1 closure, which is the definition of H^1_0.
Every element of the closure-defined subspace H^1_0(\Omega) has zero trace: H^1_0(\Omega)\subseteq\ker(\operatorname{Tr}). The reverse inclusion is the kernel characterization below.

Adaptive two-point Gauss–Legendre search uses the same subdivision policy with the corresponding sharp Peano-kernel certificate at each accepted leaf.

Its successful-result contract is likewise

\operatorname{gaussLegendreTwoRule.fourthOrder.search}(\ldots) =\operatorname{some}(R) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left|\int_a^b f-R.\mathrm{tree}.\mathrm{value}\right|\leq\tau.

The quadrature tree's soundness theorem bounds the root error by the sum of its leaf budgets. The dependent result type stores a proof that this accumulated budget is at most \tau; transitivity gives the displayed estimate.

A successful adaptive result contains a quadrature tree together with a proof that the sum of its leaf errors is at most the root tolerance. Projecting this result gives the ordinary interval-integral estimate for the tree's accumulated value.

For R:\mathrm{WithErrorAtMost}(f,a,b,\tau), the public theorem is

\left\|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx -R.\mathrm{tree}.\mathrm{value}\right\|\leq\tau.

The generic depth-bounded search takes a proved local panel builder and interval integrability on every nondegenerate panel in the domain. It accepts a panel when its certificate meets the local tolerance, even at depth zero. Otherwise it bisects and gives each child half the budget if depth remains; with no depth left, it returns none. This generic definition compares real error bounds; the rational-budget interface supplies exact rational stopping comparisons.

Every successful search satisfies

\operatorname{search}(d,a,b,\tau)=\operatorname{some}(R) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left\|\int_a^b f-R.\mathrm{tree}.\mathrm{value}\right\|\leq\tau.

Induct on the binary tree. A leaf is exactly its stored local certificate. At a branch, interval-integral additivity splits the root integral across the two adjacent children; apply the two inductive estimates and the triangle inequality. Their values and budgets add, giving the recursively stored root certificate.

A QuadratureTree records a rule-independent binary subdivision. Each leaf contains an ordinary local quadrature certificate and integrability evidence; adjacent children compose by interval-integral additivity. The root therefore certifies the sum of all leaf values with the sum of their error budgets. An adaptive tactic or external checker may choose the tree; soundness does not depend on that choice.

If \mathcal L(T) is the set of leaves, then the root certificate states

\left\|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx -\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L(T)}Q_\ell\right\| \leq\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L(T)}E_\ell.

For two complete trees, choose the one whose stored error budget is smaller; its existing soundness theorem supplies the integral estimate. For leafwise refinement, use structural induction on the original tree. At each leaf retain the original certificate or a proved-better replacement, and at each branch add the two inductive error inequalities.

Competing subdivision trees for the same interval can be compared by their proved error budgets. The selector returns a tree with the minimum budget. More generally, a dependent leaf-refinement rule may propose a replacement tree at every accepted leaf; retaining the better local alternative is proved never to increase the accumulated root error. Candidate generation is untrusted.

For two root trees T_1,T_2,

\left\|\int_a^b f -\operatorname{select}(T_1,T_2).\mathrm{value}\right\| \leq\min\!\left(E(T_1),E(T_2)\right),

and leafwise improvement satisfies E(\operatorname{improve}(T))\leq E(T).

Adaptive Simpson search instantiates the generic engine with sharp local Simpson certificates built from panelwise fourth-derivative bounds.

Every successful result therefore proves

\operatorname{simpsonRule.fourthOrder.search}(\ldots)=\operatorname{some}(R) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left|\int_a^b f-R.\mathrm{tree}.\mathrm{value}\right|\leq\tau,

with each accepted leaf justified by the fourth-order Simpson bound.

Every accepted leaf is produced from a derivative enclosure and the Taylor remainder theorem, hence carries a local model certificate. Recursive subdivision assembles these leaves with the model-tree soundness theorem. The successful search result also stores that the maximum leaf error is at most \eta; composing the two facts proves the root-domain approximation.

ExprAdaptiveTaylor.panelOfRange is the analytic handoff from a proved derivative enclosure to a real Taylor model with an exact-rational error bound. Both it and the adaptive constructor adaptiveToTolerance? are noncomputable. The latter constructs a leaf of the requested order on each panel from the exact-rational enclosure of its remainder derivative. It retries rejected leaves on half-panels until the model tree meets the requested tolerance \eta or the finite search budget is exhausted. If the optional search returns a result with piecewise model P, Lean proves

\forall x\in[a,b],\qquad \left|\operatorname{eval}(e,x)-P(x)\right|\leq\eta.

Failure returns none, and success carries an ordinary ApproxOn theorem.

Expand symbolic advection as a finite coordinate sum and apply Theorem 10.18 to each derivative term. The analytic operator is Du(x)[b(x)]; expanding b(x) in the Euclidean basis identifies it with that sum.

If the advected scalar expression is valid at the evaluation point, checked symbolic advection evaluates directly to our analytic advectiveDerivative. The componentwise convection and source-subtracted transport residual theorems use the same bridge, so later proofs need not depend on the reflected evaluator's coordinate-sum representation: \operatorname{Adv}(b^\sharp,u^\sharp)(x) =\sum_i b_i^\sharp(x)\,\partial_i u^\sharp(x).

Induct on the reflected expression, using the affine semantic theorem for each accepted constructor. Recover one unit noise per input coordinate from the boxed point, prove its magnitude is at most one, and rewrite the recentered coordinates back to the original point. The model-range theorem then supplies the ordinary enclosure.

The affine compiler accepts rational constants, variables, addition, subtraction, negation, multiplication, and natural powers. If it returns a model for an expression on a rational box, every point of that box evaluates inside the model's reported range.

Each input interval is recentered as c_i+r_i\varepsilon_i. For any boxed point, the recovered noise lies in [-1,1] and recenters to the original point. On unsupported expression constructors the compiler fails.

Write x=A+r and y=B+s. Expand xy=AB+As+Br+rs, separate the constant-linear part of AB, and enclose the discarded quadratic term using \varepsilon_i^2\in[0,1] on the diagonal and \varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j\in[-1,1] off the diagonal. The existing rational interval addition and multiplication theorems enclose the remaining three terms.

Suppose affine models M_A and M_B represent x and y at a common noise assignment satisfying |\varepsilon_i|\leq1. The checked product model represents xy at the same assignment.

Its affine part retains the constant and linear terms. Its interval remainder contains the quadratic noise product, the two affine-remainder cross terms, and the product of the old remainders.

An affine model consists of an exact rational affine form A(\varepsilon) and a rational interval R for the terms not retained in that form. It represents a real value x when

x-A(\varepsilon)\in R.

The reported range is the interval sum of the affine range and R. The noise variables are shared between occurrences of the same input coordinate, so the model retains dependencies that ordinary interval substitution would forget.

An approximation certificate stores two functions, an explicit domain and uniform error budget, and a proof of the corresponding norm bound. Exact equality is the zero-error special case. The budget is stored as a real number.

Its theorem-facing field is exactly

\operatorname{ApproxOn}(f,g,s,\varepsilon) \;:\!\Longleftrightarrow\; \forall x\in s,\quad \lVert f(x)-g(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon.

Approximation certificates compose by adding error budgets, pass through Lipschitz maps, and recover exact equality when the final budget is zero.

The three principal rules are

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{ApproxOn}(f,g,s,\varepsilon_1) \land\operatorname{ApproxOn}(g,h,s,\varepsilon_2) &\Longrightarrow \operatorname{ApproxOn}(f,h,s,\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2),\\ \operatorname{ApproxOn}(f,g,s,\varepsilon) \land L\geq0 \land\left(\forall u,v,\ \lVert\phi(u)-\phi(v)\rVert\leq L\lVert u-v\rVert\right) &\Longrightarrow \operatorname{ApproxOn}(\phi\circ f,\phi\circ g,s,L\varepsilon),\\ \operatorname{ApproxOn}(f,g,s,0) &\Longrightarrow f= g\quad\text{on }s. \end{aligned}

For finite square matrices, an approximate-inverse candidate stores a target matrix A, a proposed inverse B, and a nonnegative residual bound \eta. The proposal contains no proof. Certification requires

\lVert I-BA\rVert\leq\eta<1

in Mathlib's Euclidean matrix operator norm.

Expression evaluation commutes with matrix multiplication, so the generated symbolic matrix denotes the actual residual I-B(x)A(x). Interval soundness bounds each residual entry. Summing endpoint absolute maxima bounds every row, and taking the finite maximum gives the advertised q. The checked row-sum Neumann theorem then proves invertibility pointwise.

Let A(x) and the proposed inverse B(x) be square matrices of reflected real expressions. A constant rational matrix is one possible choice of B. The compiler forms I-B(x)A(x), evaluates every entry through one checked interval context, replaces each interval by its exact endpoint absolute maximum, and computes the largest rational row sum q.

If every entry compiles and q<1, then for every parameter point x in the context domain the real matrix A(x) is invertible. Failure of any entry or of the strict comparison returns none.

The strict residual bound makes I-(I-BA)=BA a unit by Mathlib's Neumann theorem. Direct finiteness of the square matrix algebra then implies that both factors B and A are units. Mapping the matrix unit into continuous linear maps gives bijectivity. Finally, A^{-1}-B=(I-BA)A^{-1} and norm submultiplicativity give the error bound.

Every certified approximate inverse proves that A is a unit and that its Euclidean continuous linear operator is bijective. It also gives the a posteriori estimate

\lVert A^{-1}-B\rVert \leq \eta\,\lVert A^{-1}\rVert.

The proposed inverse need not equal A^{-1}.

Sum the checked entry bounds along each row and use Mathlib's formula for the matrix infinity norm as the maximum absolute row sum. The strict row-sum bound allows the same Neumann argument for BA; direct finiteness again projects invertibility to A.

An alternative checker accepts exact rational upper bounds u_{ij} for the absolute values of the entries of I-BA. If every row sum of these bounds is at most \eta<1, then the matrix infinity norm of the residual is below one and A is invertible.

This route matches the output of entrywise interval evaluation. Its conclusion is algebraic invertibility, so later Euclidean arguments do not need to identify the infinity norm with the Euclidean operator norm.

FloatLib's pointwise arctangent bound transports the small-argument series bounds through the arctangent identities, using a certified Machin enclosure for \pi/4. Monotonicity then combines the lower bound at the left endpoint with the upper bound at the right endpoint.
For every rational panel, atanRange contains the real arctangent throughout that panel. It uses FloatLib's atanBounds with parameter 16, and no sign restriction on the input panel is needed.

Use the checked monic decomposition to rewrite a hypothetical root equation. If |x| were at least the computed coefficient bound, the leading term would strictly dominate the sum of all lower-degree terms, contradicting that their sum is zero. Hence every root lies inside (-B,B).

A checked rational Cauchy certificate gives an explicit outer interval containing every real root. Its exact monic decomposition is verified before the resulting coefficient bound is used.

For its derived rational bound B,

p(x)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |x|<B.

The box is convex, so the segment from the midpoint m to x stays in it; apply the mean value theorem to t\mapsto f(m+t(x-m)) on [0,1], whose derivative is the Fréchet derivative of f applied to x-m, that is the sum of the partial derivatives weighted by the coordinate offsets, to obtain the intermediate point c. Interval soundness of the midpoint evaluation, of each partial-derivative enclosure at c, and of the products with I_i-m_i then places f(x) in the assembled box. For the face reduction, a one-signed partial derivative makes t\mapsto f(x+t e_i) monotone on the segment across the box, so f(x) lies between the values at the two faces, hence in the hull of their enclosures.

For a rational box B=I_1\times\cdots\times I_n with midpoint m and a function differentiable on the box, the mean value theorem in centered form gives

f(x)=f(m)+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\partial_i f(c)\,(x_i-m_i) \qquad\text{for some }c\text{ on the segment from }m\text{ to }x,

so that f(B)\subseteq f(m)+\sum_i \partial_i f(B)\,(I_i-m_i); a coordinate whose panel is a single point contributes nothing. For a symbolic expression, the checked route first certifies analytic validity throughout the box. It encloses the midpoint value and the symbolic partial derivatives, then adds the interval products with I_i-m_i. In one dimension, if J_0 encloses f(m) and D encloses f' on I, the result is J_0+D(I-m), with width \mathrm{width}(J_0)+2\,\mathrm{radius}(I)\max(|\inf D|,|\sup D|). This can improve the natural extension without a fixed derivative sign; the midpoint error and derivative magnitude determine the gain. The companion monotonicity route works coordinatewise on the same boxes: when a partial derivative \partial_i f keeps one sign on B, every value of f lies in the hull of the enclosures of f on the two faces x_i=\min I_i and x_i=\max I_i, and one planner level nests up to n such face reductions. On [1,2]^2, direct interval substitution in xy-x gives [1,4]-[1,2]=[-1,3]. As a hand calculation, the factorization x(y-1) makes the exact range [0,2] visible; likewise, xyz-xy=xy(z-1) has exact range [0,4] on [1,2]^3. Previews rank candidate routes by width, endpoint magnitude, and route length, after any correlated hyperbolic enclosure; the selected route must still construct its certificate, with fallback on failure.

If the domain is nonempty, choose one point in it. Soundness bounds a norm, which is nonnegative, by the stored budget; hence the budget is nonnegative by transitivity. If no point exists, the alternative s=\varnothing holds.

An approximation or residual certificate has a nonnegative error budget unless its certified domain is empty. Equivalently, a negative budget can never be used to establish a nonvacuous estimate.

For either certificate family,

0\leq c.\mathrm{eps}\quad\lor\quad s=\varnothing.

At a point of the smaller domain, the subset hypothesis places that point in the original domain, where the stored semantic theorem already applies. Every certificate family uses this same set-theoretic argument.

Approximation, residual, upper-bound, enclosure, and model-approximation certificates may be restricted from a domain s to any subset t ⊆ s. The resulting theorem is the original sound field composed with the subset proof; no backend computation is repeated.

For every semantic predicate P, the restriction step is simply

t\subseteq s,\qquad \bigl(\forall x\in s,\ P(x)\bigr) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall x\in t,\ P(x).

The Taylor compiler constructs the derivatives of orders zero through n+1 under one checked validity certificate. It fails when the panel crosses an unsupported branch boundary or when rational canonicalization cannot prove its generated side conditions. Each compiled derivative reuses its canonical derivative object and adds only the panel orientation and analytic-validity route. A successful result exposes every derivative through this same checked interface.

Instantiate the uniform composite construction with the sharp two-point Gauss–Legendre certificate and denominator 4320. Summing the panel certificates gives the global error, while the generic flattening theorem retains the exact ordered nodes and weights.

For N>0 equal two-point Gauss–Legendre panels and the same root-local smoothness and panelwise derivative-bound hypotheses, the composite certificate has error C(b-a)^5/(4320N^4). Its ordered term list retains the two exact irrational nodes on every panel and is proved equal to the analytic composite value.

Instantiate the generic composite theorem with the sharp one-panel Simpson certificate and denominator 2880. The common fourth-derivative bound dominates every panel certificate, and the generic error calculation gives the displayed N^{-4} estimate.

For N>0 equal Simpson panels, an integrand that is C^4 on [a,b], and certified panelwise fourth within-derivative bounds at most C, summing the sharp local certificates gives \lVert\int_a^b f-S_N(f)\rVert\le C(b-a)^5/(2880N^4). Each panel consists of the usual two half-subintervals.
