Unfold the uniform composite rule panel by panel. On each panel the three listed weighted terms are definitionally the transported Simpson value. Induction over the panel list shows that flattening and then taking the weighted sum equals the sum of the analytic panel values.

The composite rule has a canonical flattened list of ordered weighted terms. Its exact-real weighted sum is proved equal to the analytic composite Simpson value. Verified rational, interval, or floating-point evaluators can therefore evaluate the same term list.

For the canonical panel-major list T_N(f,a,b),

\operatorname{weightedSum}\!\left(T_N(f,a,b)\right) =S_N(f;[a,b]).

The canonical term list fixes the nodes and accumulation order; this equality certifies its exact-real value. Equality of sums alone would not fix an order.

Finite-model approximations compose through the canonical ApproxCert calculus after projecting a ModelApproxCert to its stored certificate. If f and g are approximated on S by p and q with errors \varepsilon and \delta, respectively, then the additive rules prove

\begin{aligned} f+g&\sim_{\varepsilon+\delta}p+q,& f-g&\sim_{\varepsilon+\delta}p-q,& -f&\sim_{\varepsilon}-p. \end{aligned}

For real-valued functions, checked bounds |f(x)|\leq A and |q(x)|\leq B give the nonlinear rule

fg\sim_{A\delta+B\varepsilon}pq\qquad\text{on }S.

Here u\sim_\eta v abbreviates \forall x\in S,\ \lVert u(x)-v(x)\rVert\leq\eta. The rules act on the underlying ApproxCert; model-order metadata can be reattached afterwards.

An IteratedDerivativeBounderOn n f s produces a BoundCert for \lVert f^{(n)}\rVert on every requested nondegenerate compact interval contained in s. The specialized interface stores only the scalar panel bound and its direct proof for Mathlib's iteratedDerivWithin; its generic BoundCert is a derived projection. Constructors accept a panelwise Lean estimate, CEGA derivative enclosures, or any sound RealIntervalBackend. Smoothness is a separate analytic hypothesis; an enclosure of a formal derivative says nothing about differentiability of the original function.

The direct constructor encloses the structurally normalized symbolic derivative. A second constructor accepts an explicitly proved rewrite before range evaluation. In both cases the resulting certificate bounds Mathlib's analytic iterated derivative.

For every accepted panel, the produced bound B(a,b) satisfies

\forall x\in[a,b],\qquad \left\|\operatorname{iteratedDerivWithin} n\,f\,[a,b]\,x\right\|\leq B(a,b).

The rational interval with the endpoints of I contains x, so the CEGA soundness theorem places f(x) in F(I), and outward rounding only enlarges F(I). The global ranges follow from -1\le\sin x\le 1, 0<e^x, 0\le\sqrt x, \lvert\arctan x\rvert<\pi/2\le 2 and the corresponding bounds for \arcsin, \arccos, \cosh and \tanh. Mathlib's inclusion tactic composes these one-step facts along the expression tree.

Mathlib's dyadic_interval tactic evaluates a real proposition over intervals with dyadic endpoints and checks the outcome in the kernel. The cega_real family adds CEGA's ranges to it: quotients, natural powers, \pi, the exponential, the logarithm, the square root, the trigonometric and inverse trigonometric functions, and the hyperbolic functions. A bounded dyadic interval I has rational endpoints, so it passes unchanged to a CEGA range F, and the rational interval F(I) is rounded outward to the grid 2^{-p}, where p is the tactic's prec parameter. If x\in I, then f(x) lies in the rounded interval. An unbounded argument, and a reciprocal or logarithm whose argument interval contains zero, give a range that holds for every real input: [-1,1] for sine and cosine, [0,\infty) for the exponential and the square root, and the whole line otherwise. The Taylor order of the exponential family and the series length of the logarithm are at least p/2, and the square root keeps at least p+4 binary digits. The \pi bracket and the trigonometric and inverse-trigonometric series use fixed parameters; increasing p refines their outward rounding but does not refine those underlying rational ranges.

Bare cega runs this evaluation with p=32 on a goal without free variables that its carrier and box routes do not prove, such as a conjunction, a disjunction, a negation, an interval membership or an equality of real constants.

Translate the candidate quotient and remainder into the sparse normal form and normalize P-DQ-R. Acceptance means this difference has zero normal form. Normalization soundness gives the polynomial identity over the rationals, which is then transported to Mathlib's polynomial representation.

An exact quotient-and-remainder candidate is accepted only after sparse polynomial normalization proves the corresponding identity. The checked identity is then projected to Mathlib's Polynomial ℚ.

Every accepted certificate proves the polynomial identity

P=DQ+R

in Polynomial ℚ, including the exact quotient and remainder supplied by the candidate.

FloatLib's pointwise exponential bound encloses the exponential of the reduced argument; repeated squaring transports that bound through \exp q=(\exp(q/2^s))^{2^s}, and monotonicity covers the panel. Attaching the order proof and translating containment back to MemReal preserves the resulting inequalities.

For every rational panel I and every requested order, expRangeWith contains \exp x whenever x\in I. The implementation passes \max(\mathrm{order},1) to FloatLib's expBounds, and the automatic expRange uses degree 8. Positive, negative, and zero-crossing input panels all satisfy the same theorem.

The expression compiler maps every constructor of the verified real expression language to an arbitrary-order multivariate formal jet. Arithmetic nodes use formal power-series algebra. A unary elementary function is lifted by finite formal composition with coefficients computed from normalized symbolic derivatives of the corresponding one-variable primitive.

Under sufficient differentiability and Taylor-remainder hypotheses, this is the familiar finite composition formula

\sum_{k=0}^{N}\frac{g^{(k)}(f(x))}{k!} \bigl(f(x+h)-f(x)\bigr)^k.

Compilation is algebraically total, but analytic claims retain the original ValidAt conditions. In particular, division requires a nonzero denominator, the real logarithm requires a nonzero argument, and the classical square-root rule requires a positive argument.

Before interval compilation, an intrinsic syntax check rejects malformed rational literals whose denominator is zero. Division, logarithm, and square root remain ordinary real expressions with pointwise analytic validity conditions; this check handles only malformed syntax, so it cannot be bypassed by evaluating over an empty domain.

The nontrivial recursive clauses are

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{WF}(\operatorname{rat}(m,d))&\Longleftrightarrow d\neq0,\\ \operatorname{WF}(e_1\mathbin\circ e_2) &\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{WF}(e_1)\land\operatorname{WF}(e_2),\\ \operatorname{WF}(\operatorname{op}(e)) &\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{WF}(e). \end{aligned}

Here \circ ranges over binary syntax constructors and \operatorname{op} over unary constructors; branch-domain proofs are deliberately separate.

The core expression type is an inductive syntax tree indexed by its variable type. It contains rational constants, arithmetic operations, natural powers, real powers with an arbitrary real exponent (Mathlib's Real.rpow), trigonometric functions, exponential and logarithmic functions, square roots, and the inverse tangent, sine, and cosine. Evaluation uses Lean's total real functions. A separate validity predicate records sufficient conditions for their analytic rules: a nonzero denominator or logarithm argument, a positive square-root argument or power base, and an inverse sine or cosine argument different from \pm1. These conditions are needed by the calculus bridges; an equality about total values need not require them.

Schematically, the reflected language and its semantics are

e ::= q\mid x_i\mid \pi\mid \mathrm e \mid -e\mid e_1\mathbin\circ e_2\mid e^n\mid e_1^{\,e_2} \mid \sin e\mid\cos e\mid\arctan e\mid\arcsin e\mid\arccos e \mid\exp e\mid\log e\mid\sqrt e, \qquad \operatorname{eval}: \operatorname{Expr}(\iota)\to(\iota\to\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R.

Here \circ\in\{+,-,\times,/\}, the exponent n of e^n is a natural number while e_2 in e_1^{\,e_2} is an arbitrary expression, and rational literals with zero denominator are rejected by the well-formedness layer.

Successful interval evaluation first supplies a two-sided enclosure for every point of the input box. The enclosure query returns it directly; the upper-bound and absolute-bound queries project elementary consequences of its endpoints; and the midpoint query rewrites membership in the interval as a distance bound from its center. Each projection preserves the evaluator's quantification over the whole domain.

The public query layer accepts an arbitrary finite rational box and reports failure unless it can produce a proof. One successful enclosure supplies four theorems: the two-sided range, an ordinary upper bound, a bound for the magnitude, and uniform approximation by the rational center with the rational radius as error. Each theorem connects the executable query result to an ordinary semantic proposition. Route steps remain diagnostic metadata.

Writing B=\prod_i[a_i,b_i] and [\ell,h] for the certified interval of a successful enclosure of e on B, the four contracts are

\begin{aligned} &\forall x\in B,\quad \ell\leq e(x)\leq h,\\ &\forall x\in B,\quad e(x)\leq h,\\ &\forall x\in B,\quad |e(x)|\leq\max(|\ell|,|h|),\\ &\forall x\in B,\quad \left|e(x)-\tfrac{\ell+h}{2}\right|\leq\tfrac{h-\ell}{2}. \end{aligned}

For index i and batch size b>0, Euclidean division writes i=b\lfloor i/b\rfloor+(i\bmod b). The remainder lies in its batch, including the shorter final batch. Apply that batch's check and then the analytic soundness theorem. The empty domain needs no checks.

For any positive batch size, consecutive truncated batches cover every index of a finite domain. A sound checker therefore supplies all finite hypotheses of an analytic theorem, independently of the chosen batch size.

For a Euclidean scalar function f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R, the proposition that a formal jet J represents f to first order at x records

\begin{aligned} &f\text{ is differentiable throughout a neighborhood of }x,\\ &J_0=f(x),\\ &J_{e_i}=\partial_i f(x)\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n). \end{aligned}

The function, point, and jet are parameters of the proposition. Only the value and the first coefficients are constrained.

The planner chooses a positive panel count whose formula is below \tau. Build the corresponding composite Simpson or Gauss–Legendre certificate from the supplied smoothness and derivative bounds, then compose its analytic error estimate with the planner inequality.

Given root-interval smoothness and certified panelwise fourth-derivative bounds, the planned Simpson and two-point Gauss–Legendre constructors return ordinary QuadratureCerts whose semantic error is at most the user's positive tolerance. The public conclusion refers only to the integral, computed rule value, and tolerance; panel selection remains an internal construction.

For either planned fourth-order rule Q_{N(\tau)},

\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-Q_{N(\tau)}(f)\right| \leq\tau.

For the planar logarithmic expression, Theorem 10.23 transports the checked CAS residual to the analytic Laplacian. The Newtonian core instead reuses the general radial-Laplacian identity: the coefficient k(k+2-n) vanishes at k=1, n=3. Its value bridge identifies the reflected expression with the inverse norm; constant scaling gives the normalized fundamental solution.

The linked value bridges identify the logarithmic planar expression with the normalized two-dimensional fundamental solution and the three-dimensional fundamental solution with a constant multiple of the Newtonian core. The symbolic profiles are checked to be harmonic away from the pole, with domain hypotheses kept explicit.

For the Poisson-normalized kernels

\Phi_2(x)=-\frac1{2\pi}\log\|x\|, \qquad \Phi_3(x)=\frac1{4\pi\|x\|},

the linked theorems prove

x\neq0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Delta\Phi_2(x)=0 \quad\text{and}\quad \Delta\Phi_3(x)=0.

Apply the same executable fourth-order planner with denominator 4320, the error constant of the composite two-point Gauss–Legendre theorem: its panel count N satisfies C(b-a)^5/(4320N^4)\leq\tau in exact rational arithmetic.

Substituting the two-point Gauss–Legendre denominator D=4320 gives the corresponding executable panel count, whose composite error bound C(b-a)^5/(4320N^4) is at most the requested rational tolerance.

Use cubic exactness to express the rule error through the fourth-order Peano kernel. The exact two Gauss nodes make the boundary terms vanish, and the kernel is nonnegative with mass (b-a)^5/4320. The uniform fourth-derivative bound therefore yields the claimed certificate.

For an ordered interval [a,b], a C^4 scalar integrand, and a bound C on its fourth within-derivative, the two-point Gauss–Legendre Peano kernel is nonnegative and has mass (b-a)^5/4320. Consequently \lVert\int_a^b f-G_2(f)\rVert\le C(b-a)^5/4320, with the irrational nodes treated exactly; the estimate is returned as a QuadratureCert.

Each valid bracket contains a unique root, and the ordering of the brackets orders the roots. A monic polynomial of degree n with n distinct roots is the product of the corresponding linear factors. The vanishing moments, extended linearly to every q of degree below n, make the nodal polynomial orthogonal to lower degrees; the Gaussian exactness and weight positivity arguments then apply without change.

Let p be a sparse rational polynomial and let n valid root brackets for p be ordered, each strictly to the left of the next. The bracketed roots are strictly increasing and lie in their brackets. If p is monic of degree n over \mathbb R, its nodal polynomial on these roots is p itself. If moreover the brackets lie inside (-1,1) and the rational moments \int_{-1}^1p(x)x^k\,dx vanish for k<n, the roots are the nodes of a Gaussian rule for the unit weight on [-1,1], with the interpolatory weights.

Exactness through degree 2n-1 is a finite list of moment identities, each checked by normal-form arithmetic using (\sqrt{3/5})^2=\tfrac35 or the squares of the four-point radicals. Positivity of the weights and the ordering of the nodes are inequalities between radicals. The characterization theorem then identifies each nodal polynomial with the monic Legendre polynomial, and for n=2 it pins down the nodes, whose weights are then fixed by exactness.

The normalized three- and four-point Gauss–Legendre rules, written in radicals, are exact through degrees five and seven. Transported to [-1,1], the midpoint rule, the two-point rule, and these two rules are Gaussian rules for the unit weight, and the nodal polynomial of the n-point rule is the monic Legendre polynomial of degree n, defined as the monic orthogonal polynomial of that weight, for n=1,2,3,4. For n=2 and any a<b, every Gaussian rule for the unit weight on [a,b] has the transported two-point nodes and weights and the same value as the two-point QuadratureRule.

The Lagrange basis polynomial at a node is the nodal polynomial divided by x-r_i and by the nodal weight, which equals p'(r_i) for a simple root. The division by x-r is carried out monomial by monomial through (x^k-r^k)/(x-r)=\sum_{j<k}x^jr^{k-1-j}, and integrating the result term by term gives \tilde p. The bracket's direction fixes the sign of p' on it, so dividing the numerator enclosure by the derivative enclosure is sound.

If the nodal polynomial of a family of nodes is p and r_i is a root, the interpolatory weight at r_i is \tilde p(r_i)/p'(r_i), where \tilde p is the rational polynomial integratedQuotient p with \tilde p(r)=\int_{-1}^1p(x)/(x-r)\,dx. For a valid bracket the rational interval weightInterval p bracket contains this quotient at the bracketed root, and each Christoffel number of the certified rule lies in the interval computed from its own bracket.

The nodal polynomial times any q of degree below n has degree below 2n and vanishes at every node, so its integral is its rule value, zero. Uniqueness of the monic orthogonal polynomial identifies the nodal polynomial. For the weights, apply exactness to \ell_i, which has degree n-1 and takes the value 1 at x_i and 0 at the other nodes.

For every Gaussian rule with n nodes for a continuous weight that is strictly positive on [a,b], the nodal polynomial \prod_i(x-x_i) is the monic orthogonal polynomial p_n of w, and the weight at x_i is the interpolatory weight \int_a^b\ell_i\,w, the Christoffel number. A Gaussian rule is therefore unique up to the order of its nodes.
The rules are positive with nodes in [a,b] and are exact to degree 2(n+1)-1, which tends to infinity. Apply the Pólya–Steklov theorem.

Let w be continuous on [[a,b]] with a\le b, and for each n let Q_n be a Gaussian rule with n+1 nodes for w. Then Q_n(f)\to\int_a^b f\,w for every f continuous on [a,b]. In particular the rules of the existence theorem converge whenever w is strictly positive and a<b.

The positive-time assumption supplies the nonzero and positivity conditions needed when differentiating the Gaussian factor. The heat-kernel calculation then identifies its time derivative with its spatial Laplacian. Rewriting the heat residual by that identity gives zero at every point of the stated domain, which is the SatisfiesPDEProblem conclusion.

The two-dimensional Gaussian heat kernel satisfies the analytic heat equation on a domain where time is positive. The theorem statement uses the ordinary heat-equation predicate defined in the parabolic API. Its proof comes from the analytic heat-kernel theorem; the CAS computation of the same identity in spacetime coordinates is the symbolic Gaussian bridge.

For every \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3,

\left(\forall p\in\Omega,\ 0<\operatorname{time}(p)\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{SatisfiesPDEProblem} (\operatorname{heatEquation}(\Omega),\Phi).

Write \xi=(x,y) and r^2=x^2+y^2. Differentiating the prefactor 1/(4\pi t) and the exponential gives

\begin{aligned} \Phi_t&=\left(\frac{r^2}{4t^2}-\frac1t\right)\Phi,\\ \Phi_{xx}&=\left(\frac{x^2}{4t^2}-\frac1{2t}\right)\Phi,\qquad \Phi_{yy}=\left(\frac{y^2}{4t^2}-\frac1{2t}\right)\Phi. \end{aligned}

Adding the two spatial derivatives recovers the time derivative. The CAS checks this cancellation. The assumption t>0 discharges its time denominators and the validity conditions needed to interpret both rounds of differentiation; \pi\ne0 handles the constant denominator. The residual bridge then gives the displayed equation for the coordinate partial derivatives.

Positive time also selects the branch on which this formula agrees with the analytic heat kernel, whose definition is zero for t\le0. At the spatial origin the positive-time value is 1/(4\pi t), which grows without bound as t\downarrow0. Thus substituting the definition's value at time zero cannot establish an initial-trace theorem.

The symbolically represented planar Gaussian ansatz, interpreted as an ordinary spacetime function, has zero heat residual in spacetime coordinates at positive time, and the CAS proves it. With

\Phi(t,x,y)=\frac{\exp\!\left(-(x^2+y^2)/(4t)\right)}{4\pi t},

the linked Lean theorem states

t>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \partial_t\Phi-\partial_x^2\Phi-\partial_y^2\Phi=0

at (t,x,y). The slice-Laplacian identity turns this into the residual predicate \operatorname{SatisfiesPDEProblem}(\operatorname{heatEquation}(\{t>0\}),\Phi). For the analytic kernel that predicate is the Gaussian heat theorem; for the symbolic expression the Lean module derives it in an example.

Take the nodes to be the roots of p_n. The interpolatory rule on n distinct nodes reproduces every polynomial of degree below n. For \deg p<2n, divide by the monic nodal polynomial: the quotient term is annihilated by the rule, because the nodal polynomial vanishes at the nodes, and by the integral, by orthogonality; the remainder has degree below n. For the weights, apply exactness to \ell_i^2, which has degree 2n-2: the rule returns w_i, and the integral \int_a^b\ell_i^2w is positive.

Let w be continuous on [[a,b]] and strictly positive on [a,b], a<b, and let n\ge1. There are n distinct nodes in (a,b) whose interpolatory weights w_i=\int_a^b\ell_i\,w are all strictly positive and for which

\sum_{i<n}w_i\,p(x_i)=\int_a^b p(x)\,w(x)\,dx\qquad\text{whenever }\deg p<2n.

As a NodalRule, the rule is positive, has its nodes in [a,b], and is exact to degree 2n-1.

Fix x away from the nodes and choose c so that G=f-H-c\,\omega^2 vanishes at x. Then G has double zeros at the n nodes and a simple zero at x, 2n+1 zeros counted with multiplicity. A generalized Rolle theorem, proved for a chain of functions each the derivative of the previous one on the open interval, gives a zero \eta_x of G^{(2n)}. Since H^{(2n)}=0 and (\omega^2)^{(2n)}=(2n)!, this is the pointwise remainder. Multiply by w and integrate. The continuous function f^{(2n)} takes values between its minimum and maximum on [a,b], so the integral of (f-H)w lies between those extremes times \int\omega^2w, and the intermediate value theorem produces \xi. Finally \omega=p_n by the characterization.

Let w be continuous on [[a,b]] and strictly positive on [a,b], a<b, let Q be a Gaussian rule with n\ge1 nodes, and let f\in C^{2n} on [a,b]. There is \xi\in[a,b] with

\int_a^b f(x)\,w(x)\,dx-Q(f) =\frac{f^{(2n)}(\xi)}{(2n)!}\int_a^b \omega(x)^2\,w(x)\,dx,

where \omega=\prod_i(x-x_i) is the nodal polynomial, equal to p_n by the characterization. Here f^{(2n)} is the iterated derivative within [a,b], so smoothness is needed only on the closed interval. If |f^{(2n)}|\le M on [a,b], the error is at most M/(2n)!\,\int_a^bp_n^2w.

A Gaussian rule with n nodes for the weight w on [a,b] is a structure GaussianRule a b w hw n, where hw records that w is continuous on [[a,b]]. It holds nodes x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}, weights w_0,\dots,w_{n-1}, and four facts: the nodes are pairwise distinct, they lie in the open interval (a,b), the weights are strictly positive, and

\sum_{i<n}w_i\,p(x_i)=\int_a^b p(x)\,w(x)\,dx\qquad\text{whenever }\deg p<2n.

Its value on a function f is \sum_iw_if(x_i). For n=0 the rule is empty and the exactness field says nothing, so the theorems about Gaussian rules assume n>0.

For a<b, a weight that is strictly positive on [a,b], and n>0, gaussianRule is the Gaussian rule of the existence theorem, with nodes at the roots of p_n and interpolatory weights. Every Gaussian rule with n>0 is a positive NodalRule exact to degree 2n-1. Exactness on the constant 1 makes its weights add up to \int_a^b w, so each weight is at most \int_a^b w.

The finite polynomial is the sum of the within-derivative coefficients through order n, so its evaluation agrees term by term with Mathlib's Taylor evaluation and its degree is at most n. Mathlib's mean-remainder theorem, together with the supplied next-derivative bound, gives the uniform error, which is the sound field of the approximation certificate.

For an ordinary scalar function on an ordered closed interval, we build the actual order-n Taylor polynomial from within-derivatives, prove that its evaluation is Mathlib's Taylor evaluation, and prove that its degree is at most n. Assuming C^{n+1} regularity on that interval, a bound C on the norm of the (n+1)-st within-derivative produces an ApproxCert with uniform error C(b-a)^{n+1}/n!, the conservative remainder supplied by Mathlib's mean-remainder theorem.

The isolation certificates combine square-free reduction, a Sturm subdivision, transport back to the original zero set, and a checked rational Cauchy outer bound. GlobalPolynomialIsolationCertificate.valid checks every stage, and the noncomputable toGlobalRootAtlas projection then yields a global atlas covering every distinct real root; a nonzero constant has an empty atlas. SymLean checks these certificates when a caller supplies them and has no generator for them.

The final global contract is

p(x)=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists R\in\mathcal A.\mathrm{rootRegions},\ x\in R,

with each root-bearing region carrying a unique-root theorem.

For a differentiable objective f:E\to\mathbb R on a real Hilbert space, the gradient-descent map is

x^+=x-\eta\,\nabla f(x).

In Euclidean coordinates, the Adam-style map first sets g=\nabla f(x) and computes

\begin{aligned} m^+&=\beta_1m+(1-\beta_1)g,\\ v^+&=\beta_2v+(1-\beta_2)(g\odot g),\\ x_i^+&=x_i-\eta\,\frac{m_i^+}{\sqrt{v_i^+}+\varepsilon}. \end{aligned}

Both are total update functions defined from the analytic gradient. An analytic use of the Adam-style map must separately prove the sign and nonvanishing facts it needs for \sqrt{v_i^+}+\varepsilon.

For substitutions, the proportionality checker validates its proposed factor with Theorem 10.3. Polynomial, rational, substitution, and integration-by-parts passes only propose candidates. The integration checker validates the symbolic derivative identity with Theorem 10.3. Under the certificate's requirements, Theorem 10.18 turns it into an analytic derivative along \gamma. The interval-wide requirements also make the evaluated integrand continuous there, so the fundamental theorem gives the endpoint difference.

The integration entry point accepts a candidate F only after checking that \operatorname{diff}_iF-f normalizes to zero. Its certificate records requirements for the primitive, the integrand, and the conditional cancellations used in that check.

Fix a coordinate line \gamma(s)=x+s e_i. At each point where those requirements hold, the evaluated primitive has derivative f^\sharp(\gamma(s)). If they hold for every s\in[\min(a,b),\max(a,b)], then

\int_a^b f^\sharp(\gamma(s))\,ds =F^\sharp(\gamma(b))-F^\sharp(\gamma(a)).

The interval hypothesis is Set.uIcc a b in Lean. It includes both endpoints and every point between them, regardless of their order. Validity of the integrand supplies continuity and hence interval integrability; validity of the primitive supplies the derivative needed by the fundamental theorem of calculus. Every search method uses this same certificate. At the reflected API, IntegrationCheck.certifyCandidate? takes the coordinate, original integrand, and proposed primitive explicitly, so it can check a candidate without running primitive search. The ordinary interval tactic uses this boundary for a supplied function or a common function reconstructed from the requested endpoint difference. It reflects the integrand and candidate over one parameter table, so each coefficient has the same meaning in both expressions. Checking a candidate against its own derivative would not establish the requested integral.

Integrate the pointwise difference and apply the norm bound for an interval integral. Uniform approximation bounds the integrand norm by \varepsilon, while the integral of that constant over the oriented interval contributes |b-a|. A final triangle inequality adds this model error to the existing quadrature error.

If both functions are interval integrable, uniform approximation on [[a,b]] transports through interval integration with error \varepsilon |b-a|. Consequently a quadrature certificate for a finite or symbolic model becomes a certificate for the original integrand, with model and quadrature errors added explicitly.

A real interval implementation supplies lower and upper endpoints, a membership predicate, and proofs that membership implies the corresponding real inequalities. Exact rational intervals are the registered instance; a verified finite-precision representation with the same two proofs feeds the same enclosure theorems.

Every backend instance must establish

x\in_{\!B} I \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{lo}(I)\leq x\leq\operatorname{hi}(I).

The representation of I and the implementation of membership are otherwise abstract. For the rational backend, CEGA's endpoint inequalities are equivalent to FloatLib's real containment predicate. Attaching hle preserves that predicate and gives refinement and quadrature an ordered interval with a nonnegative radius.

Apply the backend membership theorem pointwise to obtain the real lower and upper inequalities. If those endpoints lie in [-\varepsilon,\varepsilon], transitivity gives -\varepsilon\leq f(x)\leq\varepsilon, which is equivalent to the required absolute residual bound.
Backend membership yields ordinary real enclosures. If the interval lies inside [-\varepsilon,\varepsilon], the same bridge yields a certified residual bound.

FloatLib proves containment by induction on its expression tree: leaves use the environment and constant contracts, and each operation uses the backend's soundness theorem on the inductive enclosures. Compose this result with the CAS translation's real-denotation equality. The rational callback route uses the same inductive argument with its checked denominator and unary facts. Failed operations propagate none, so every successful branch retains its containment proof.

Successful evaluation by a sound FloatLib backend encloses every real value of the expression on the input panel. The semantic translation identifies that value with the original CAS expression when the coordinate environments agree and every real-power base is positive.

For an environment enclosure \rho(i)\in_{\!B}\operatorname{env}(i), successful evaluation satisfies

\operatorname{evalInterval}(\operatorname{env},e) =\operatorname{some}(J) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(e,\rho)\in_{\!B}J.

The admissible numerical domains depend on the provider. FloatLib's generic backends require positive logarithm panels and nonnegative square-root panels. CEGA's rational callback route also treats strictly negative logarithm panels through \log(-x)=\log x, the singleton zero through \log0=0, and negative square-root inputs through \sqrt x=0. A nontrivial panel touching zero has no finite logarithm range. Division requires exclusion of zero; unsupported or failed operations return none.

The rational callback evaluator has the same enclosure conclusion once its division and unary-range callbacks prove their semantic contracts. A checked denominator entry stores a positive rational lower bound \delta, its direct theorem \delta\leq|\operatorname{eval}(d,\rho)| on the chart, and route provenance.

An interval jet assigns a rational interval to each formal multivariate coefficient. Encloses F J means that every coefficient through the declared order lies in its interval:

\deg\alpha\le N \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J_\alpha\in F_\alpha.

The interval operations are explicit rather than typeclass ring operations. This is necessary because interval multiplication is sound but not distributive.

The mean value theorem expresses a root relative to the interval midpoint. The derivative enclosure and its sign select a valid reciprocal interval, so interval arithmetic places the root in the proposed Newton image. Endpoint signs give existence by the intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity gives uniqueness. Disjointness contradicts image membership and therefore proves root exclusion.

A checked interval-Newton step for a rational univariate polynomial uses a nondegenerate input interval and a sign-definite interval enclosure of the derivative. It checks the proposed image against the exact Newton image computed from the midpoint. Every input root lies in that image.

For the checked Newton image N(I), the localization contract is

x\in I\ \land\ p(x)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\in N(I).

If endpoint signs bracket a root, derivative nonvanishing gives exactly one root in the input interval. If the checked image is disjoint from the input, the input interval contains no root:

N(I)\cap I=\varnothing \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall x\in I,\ p(x)\ne0.

Both conclusions are local to the stated interval.

The interval product bound follows from FloatLib's multiplication theorem. To see why the four corners suffice, fix the sign of y. Multiplication by y is then monotone or antitone, so xy lies between ay and by. Each of these is a fixed factor times a value between c and d, hence lies between the two corner products with that factor. Both bounds are therefore between the minimum and the maximum of the four corners.

FloatLib computes interval multiplication as the exact four-corner product. For rational panels I=[a,b] and J=[c,d] the product panel has endpoints \min(ac,ad,bc,bd) and \max(ac,ad,bc,bd), which is sharp for independent factors in every sign configuration; on x\in[-1,2], y\in[2,3] it gives [-3,6] where a symmetric magnitude bound gives [-6,6].

x\in I\ \land\ y\in J \quad\Longrightarrow\quad xy\in I\cdot J.

Write the enclosure as center c and radius r. Interval membership gives |f(x)-c|\leq r uniformly, so integration stability compares f with the constant function c. The constant integral is (b-a)c, and its transported error is r|b-a|.

If the scalar integrand is interval integrable and one backend interval contains every value on [[a,b]], its midpoint defines a constant integral model and its radius gives the uniform pointwise error. The resulting certificate has value (b-a)c and error r|b-a|, with no endpoint-order assumption and no backend-specific integration theorem. Exact rational ranges, directed floating-point ranges, Taylor enclosures, and adaptive local ranges therefore share the same analytic bridge.

Induct on the derivative order. The base case is evaluation itself. At the successor step, apply the one-step symbolic derivative bridge to the current derived expression and use the induction hypothesis to identify the analytic within-derivative already constructed. The validity assumptions propagate to every intermediate expression.

On a set with UniqueDiffOn ℝ s, assume validity of the intermediate symbolic derivatives at levels k<n. The order-n checked derivative then denotes Mathlib's iteratedDerivWithin. This includes every nondegenerate closed interval contained in the validity domain. The linked regularity theorem uses the sufficient stronger assumption of validity through level n inclusive to prove ContDiffOn ℝ n: it establishes continuity of the final derivative by proving that derivative differentiable.

If e^{[n]} is the expression obtained by n checked symbolic derivatives, then on every admissible panel [a,b] and every x\in[a,b],

\operatorname{iteratedDerivWithin} n\,(\lambda y,\operatorname{eval}(e,y))\,[a,b]\,x =\operatorname{eval}\!\left(e^{[n]},x\right).

For a real map F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n, a ball-form Krawczyk proposal stores a center x_0, nonnegative radius r, real approximate-inverse matrix B, and nonnegative contraction bound q. Certification requires an actual Fréchet Jacobian J(x) on the closed ball together with

\lVert I-BJ(x)\rVert_2\leq q<1, \qquad \lVert BF(x_0)\rVert_2+qr\leq r.

For a fixed rational matrix B, the interval layer encloses the entries of J(x) and compiles those bounds to I-BJ(x). Its Frobenius checker computes the sum of squared endpoint absolute bounds in exact nonnegative-rational arithmetic. The certificate is stated for a closed Euclidean ball rather than for the rectangular boxes of the classical Krawczyk operator.

The map T(x)=x-BF(x) has derivative I-BJ(x), hence is q-Lipschitz on the convex ball. The self-map inequality sends that ball into itself, so Banach's fixed-point theorem gives a unique fixed point. At the center, the same strict residual estimate proves BJ(x_0) and then B invertible by the Neumann argument. Thus T(x)=x implies BF(x)=0 and hence F(x)=0. Conversely every zero is a fixed point, which transfers fixed-point uniqueness to zero uniqueness.

Every certified ball-form Krawczyk proposal proves

\exists!x\in\overline B(x_0,r),\qquad F(x)=0.

Uniqueness is local to the certified ball. The proof derives the invertibility of B from the contraction bound.

The certificate-projection route of cega searches the local context and target for a recognized checked certificate. It first tries the certificate's semantic theorem exactly, then permits a proved domain restriction, a larger error budget, or a wider enclosure when those changes match the goal. Any new real inequalities are discharged separately by ordinary arithmetic. The tactic succeeds only after Lean confirms that the constructed proof has the user's target type.

For an approximation certificate, the representative projection is

t\subseteq s,\quad c.\mathrm{eps}\leq\varepsilon \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall x\in t,\qquad \lVert c.\mathrm{lhs}(x)-c.\mathrm{rhs}(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon.

Residual, bound, enclosure, model, and quadrature goals use the analogous typed projection; cega never changes the proposition being proved.

FloatLib's sine and cosine bounds include the error introduced by period reduction. If m is the midpoint, r the panel radius, and [a,b] contains f(m), the one-Lipschitz estimate gives f(x)\in[a-r,b+r] for every panel member. For each accepted branch test, monotonicity and symmetry justify endpoint bounds from the same FloatLib point enclosures; a proved sign permits clamping at zero. Each intersection contains the exact function value, so the final interval retains the containment theorem.

For every rational panel, the sine and cosine ranges contain all real function values on it. The base ranges are FloatLib's degree-32 bounds; CEGA intersects them with endpoint or sign bounds when the panel satisfies a proved principal-branch condition.

The positive lower endpoint establishes the domain condition. The two logarithm series and their geometric tails bound \log(1+t)-\log(1-t); binary scaling and, for inputs below one, reciprocation restore the original argument. Monotonicity lifts the point bounds to the whole positive panel.

For every rational panel I=[\ell,h] with 0<\ell, logRangeWith contains \log x whenever x\in I. It calls FloatLib's logBounds? with degree 2\max(\mathrm{terms},1). The positivity proof ensures that the upstream optional routine succeeds. The default request is 10, hence FloatLib degree 20.

A model-approximation certificate records an original function, a reference function, model-order metadata, an error budget, and the proved uniform error estimate. Writing its source as f, its model as p, its domain as S, and its error as \varepsilon, the trusted field is

\forall x\in S,\qquad \lVert f(x)-p(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon.

The stored order does not occur in this proposition; it is metadata. A supplied model need not be a Taylor polynomial or have a finite-dimensional representation, and such structure requires a separate construction.

Induct on the model tree. A leaf uses its local model certificate. At a split, membership in the root interval places the point in one child panel; apply the corresponding inductive estimate and weaken its leaf error to the maximum of the two child errors. The adaptive conclusion follows by transitivity with E_\tau\leq\eta.

RationalModelTree joins local approximation certificates along exact rational split points; the leaf models need not be polynomials. If P_\tau is the piecewise model selected by a tree \tau and E_\tau is the maximum of its leaf errors after replacing each by \max(0,E_\ell), structural induction proves

\forall x\in[a,b],\qquad |f(x)-P_\tau(x)|\leq E_\tau.

For an adaptive result with E_\tau\leq\eta, the exported theorem replaces E_\tau by the requested tolerance \eta.

Follow the same endpoint comparison used by the piecewise model evaluator to select a leaf. Structural induction shows that erasing payloads does not change this branch choice or the selected local model. The payload tree therefore evaluates to the certified leaf model, while the erased tree supplies its approximation bound.

A payload tree may retain derivative enclosures, centers, or backend data at each leaf while erasing to the underlying model tree. For x\in[a,b], let \ell_x be the selected leaf and p_{\ell_x} its certified local model. Selection satisfies the exact identity

P_\tau(x)=p_{\ell_x}(x),

while erasure supplies |f(x)-P_\tau(x)|\leq E_\tau. Payloads leave the approximation semantics unchanged.

A polynomial of degree below m coincides with its Lagrange interpolant on the m nodes, and the rule applied to it is the integral of that interpolant against w. The Newton–Cotes nodes are distinct because the spacing (b-a)/(n-1) is nonzero. For two nodes the Lagrange basis polynomials are linear and each integrates to (b-a)/2.

Let w be continuous on [[a,b]] and let x_0,\dots,x_{m-1} be m\ge1 distinct nodes. The interpolatory rule with weights w_i=\int_a^b\ell_i\,w is exact to degree m-1. For n\ge2 and a\ne b, the closed Newton–Cotes rule on the nodes a+i(b-a)/(n-1), i=0,\dots,n-1, is exact to degree n-1 for the unit weight; its nodes lie in [a,b] when a\le b, and for n=2 its value is \frac{b-a}2\bigl(f(a)+f(b)\bigr).

Both sides of the exactness identity are linear in the integrand, so a polynomial written in the monomial basis reduces to its monomials. The continuity of w supplies the integrability that splitting the integral needs. For transport, substitute x=c+(t-a)(d-c)/(b-a): the change of variables formula turns \int_c^d f\,v into (d-c)/(b-a) times an integral over [a,b], and composing a polynomial with an affine map does not raise its degree.

For a weight continuous on [[a,b]], a nodal rule is exact to degree d exactly when it integrates the monomials 1,x,\dots,x^d. Exactness moves with the rule under the affine map sending a,b to c,d: if Q is exact to degree n on [a,b] for the pulled-back weight, the transported rule, with nodes mapped and weights scaled by (d-c)/(b-a), is exact to degree n on [c,d] for the original weight. A normalized rule with the moments through degree d is exact to degree d on every interval for the unit weight, and a normalized rule with nonnegative weights is positive on every ordered interval.

A nodal rule consists of a size m, nodes x_0,\dots,x_{m-1}\in\mathbb R, and weights w_0,\dots,w_{m-1}\in\mathbb R. It is exact to degree d for the weight w on a..b when

\sum_{i<m} w_i\,p(x_i)=\int_a^b p(x)\,w(x)\,dx \qquad\text{for every real polynomial }p\text{ with }\deg p\le d.

It is positive when every w_i\ge0, and its nodes lie in s when every x_i\in s. A normalized QuadratureRule becomes a nodal rule on [a,b] with nodes a+t_i(b-a) and weights (b-a)w_i.

The normalizer is accompanied by an invariant equating evaluation of each intermediate form with evaluation of the input. Specializing that invariant to a returned literal zero identifies the original value with the evaluation of zero, hence with zero in every environment.

If the executable normalizer reduces an expression to literal zero, evaluating the original expression in any real environment gives zero. The computation therefore proposes a normal form, while this theorem is the kernel-checked semantic justification.

\operatorname{normalize}(e)=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall\rho,\ \operatorname{eval}(e,\rho)=0.

A normalized quadrature rule is an ordered list of exact-real weights and nodes in [0,1]. The order remains explicit for verified finite-precision evaluation. Generic definitions transport the rule affinely to any oriented interval, while moment identities characterize exactness independently of a particular numerical backend.

The residual certificate bounds the defect between the proposed velocity and the vector field. Apply the approximate-trajectory Grönwall estimate to this defect and the initial discrepancy, then use monotonicity of the exponential bound to replace its time-dependent right-hand side by its value at the final time. This produces the uniform approximation certificate.

An ODETrajectoryCert stores an ordinary Lean curve, its proposed velocity, continuity on [a,b], a proof that the velocity is its right derivative on [a,b), membership in the state region, and one backend-independent residual bound for u'(t)-F(t,u(t)). Mathlib's approximate-trajectory Grönwall theorem compares two such trajectories. The pointwise estimate is converted to a uniform ApproxCert by evaluating the monotone Grönwall bound at the right endpoint. No ordering hypothesis is needed: if the left endpoint is below the right one, residual soundness there makes both budgets nonnegative, and otherwise the claim is immediate.

As an example, the affine Euler curve 1+t is compared with the exact trajectory \exp t for u'=u on [0,1]. Its residual is -t, hence has norm at most one, and the generated uniform error is \exp(1)-1. An exact CAS proof or a FloatLib enclosure may supply the residual bound. The ODE stability theorem consumes that real bound and gives the same final ApproxOn statement.

Let L:\mathbb R[X]\to\mathbb R be linear with L(q^2)>0 for every q\ne0. The monic orthogonal polynomial p_n of L is monic of degree n and satisfies L(p_nq)=0 for every q with \deg q<n. It is unique: any monic polynomial of degree n with this property equals p_n. For a weight w continuous on [[a,b]] and strictly positive on [a,b], a<b, the functional p\mapsto\int_a^b p\,w is positive on nonzero squares, and its orthogonal polynomials are the ones used for Gaussian quadrature.

The divisor statement is the sign argument for \int_a^b q\,r^2w. An irreducible real factor of degree two has no real root, so it cannot divide p, and p splits. If q^2 divides p with q nonconstant, write p=q^2r; then L((qr)^2)=L(p\,r)=0, contradicting positivity, so p is squarefree. A root at the endpoint a would give p=(x-a)r with \int_a^b(x-a)\,r^2w=0, but (x-a)w is a weight that is positive on the interior; the endpoint b is symmetric. A monic squarefree polynomial that splits is the product of x-x_i over its distinct roots.

Let w be continuous on [[a,b]] and strictly positive on [a,b], a<b, and let p\ne0 be orthogonal against w to every polynomial of lower degree. Then every nonconstant divisor of p has a root in [a,b], p is squarefree and splits over \mathbb R, and every root of p lies in the open interval (a,b). Consequently the monic orthogonal polynomial p_n has exactly n distinct real roots, all in (a,b), and they can be listed as x_0,\dots,x_{n-1} so that the nodal polynomial \prod_i(x-x_i) equals p_n.

A verified panel evaluator, checked variable boxes, and a proof of successful evaluation define a total range provider for one symbolic expression. The provider stores the returned backend interval together with its direct enclosure theorem.

For every a<b with [a,b]\subseteq s, its total contract is

\forall x\in[a,b],\qquad \operatorname{eval}(e,x)\in\operatorname{result}(a,b).

The ceiling gives N\ge(B/\varepsilon)^{1/m}, and raising both sides to the power m gives N^m\ge B/\varepsilon. The composite budget is B/N^m, and certificate soundness bounds the actual error by the budget.

Let m\ne0, D>0, a\le b, C\ge0 and \varepsilon>0, put B=C(b-a)^{m+1}/D, and let N=\max(1,\lceil(B/\varepsilon)^{1/m}\rceil). Then B/N^m\le\varepsilon. Consequently, for a panel rule of order m, an integrand in C^m[a,b], a<b, and a derivative bounder whose bound on every subinterval is at most C, the composite certificate on the planned mesh has error budget at most \varepsilon, and its value is within \varepsilon of \int_a^bf.

A panel rule of order m is a normalized rule Q with a positive constant D and a proof that, on every ordered interval [a,b], every f\in C^m[a,b] with \|f^{(m)}\|\le M there satisfies \|\int_a^b f-Q(f)\|\le M(b-a)^{m+1}/D. Its composite certificate on N>0 equal panels, given a panelwise derivative bounder with common bound C, has error budget C(b-a)^{m+1}/(DN^m). Simpson's rule and the two-point Gauss–Legendre rule are panel rules of order four.

Structural induction on the expression constructs its Fréchet derivative using the analytic sum, product, quotient, power, and elementary chain rules. The validity hypotheses discharge each rule's domain conditions. Evaluating the resulting continuous linear map on e_i gives exactly the evaluated symbolic derivative, hence the stated coordinate identity.

At every point satisfying the generated validity conditions, symbolic differentiation in coordinate i agrees with our analytic Euclidean partial derivative: (\operatorname{diff}_i e)^\sharp(x)=\partial_i(e^\sharp)(x).

Fix a point in the global domain and use the cover property to choose a patch containing it. The local certificate on that patch proves the desired predicate at the point. Since the argument is independent of the selected patch, it assembles the local soundness fields into the global theorem.

Patch covers assemble local approximation or residual proofs into a global theorem on the covered domain. The atlas layer, used near singularities or across piecewise regimes, rests on this theorem.

The shared logical contract is

\left(\forall x\in s,\ \exists i,\ x\in s_i\right) \land \left(\forall i,\ \forall x\in s_i,\ P(x)\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall x\in s,\ P(x).

For approximation and residual atlases, P(x) is the corresponding stored norm bound.

Normalize each reflected residual, rewrite its differentiated components using Theorem 10.20, and identify the transport term with Theorem 10.21. The remaining sums and products evaluate definitionally.

For momentum component i, assume ValidAt at x for u_i and p. The Navier–Stokes bridge also assumes validity of every first symbolic partial of u_i; the conservation bridge assumes validity of every flux component. These give the stationary Euler and Navier–Stokes momentum residuals and the divergence-form conservation residual. Incompressibility is a separate equation. The undifferentiated viscosity and source terms need no validity hypotheses for these identities. Componentwise, the Euler bridge gives R_i^{E}(x)=\sum_j u_j(x)\partial_j u_i(x)+\partial_i p(x)-f_i(x), while the Navier–Stokes bridge adds -\nu(x)\Delta u_i(x) and the conservation bridge gives R^{C}(x)=\sum_i\partial_i F_i(x)-f(x).

Here u_t=4, u_{xx}=2, and u_{yy}=2, so the checked residual is 4-2-2=0. Polynomial evaluation and its derivatives are valid everywhere; the coordinate and fixed-time slice bridges therefore apply on all spacetime.

The polynomial profile

u(t,x,y)=x^2+y^2+4t

has zero residual for the ordinary two-dimensional heat-equation problem on all spacetime; the linked SatisfiesPDEProblem theorem is exactly that residual property.

Termwise evaluation encloses each monomial with interval multiplication and natural powers and combines the terms with interval addition. The basic interval operations preserve membership, so induction over the sparse term list shows that the real polynomial value lies between the computed rational endpoints. For the centred form, write p(x)=\sum_k c_k(x-m)^k with the exact shifted coefficients c_k, where m is the midpoint and r the radius of the panel. Since |x-m|\le r, an even power (x-m)^k lies in [0,r^k] and an odd one in [-r^k,r^k], so every term lies in a rational interval and their sum encloses p(x). The enclosure returns one of these two sound intervals.

Exact interval evaluation encloses the value of a sparse rational polynomial at every real point of a rational panel. The root checks first try the centred form, the exact Taylor shift of the polynomial to the midpoint of the panel bounded term by term over its radius, and use termwise evaluation when the centred interval does not exclude zero. This theorem is the semantic basis for both root exclusion and derivative-sign checks.

x\in[a,b] \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p(x)\in\operatorname{enclosure}(p,[a,b]).

Expand a polynomial of degree at most d in the monomial basis. Linearity of both integration and the weighted rule reduces exactness to each monomial, where it is exactly the assumed moment identity. Affine substitution transports the normalized-interval result to any oriented interval.

If a normalized rule has the exact moments through degree d, it exactly integrates every real polynomial of degree at most d. Affine transport preserves this conclusion on arbitrary oriented intervals. Both the three-node Simpson rule and the two-point Gauss–Legendre rule have the exact moments through degree three, hence exactly integrate every cubic and generate zero-error QuadratureCerts.

Exactness on constants makes the weights of Q_n sum to \int_a^b w. If a polynomial p of degree at most d_n is within \delta of f on [a,b], positivity bounds |Q_n(f)-Q_n(p)| by \delta\int_a^b w, and |\int_a^b (p-f)w| is at most \delta\int_a^b|w|. Since Q_n(p) is the integral of p w, the error on f is at most \delta(\int_a^b w+\int_a^b|w|), a bound independent of n. The Weierstrass theorem supplies p for every \delta>0, and d_n\to\infty makes p admissible for all large n.

Let w be continuous on [a,b] and let Q_n be rules with nonnegative weights and nodes in [a,b], where Q_n integrates every polynomial of degree at most d_n exactly against w and d_n\to\infty. Then Q_n(f)\to\int_a^b f\,w for every f continuous on [a,b]. This is the theorem of Pólya and Steklov. The same statement holds for normalized rules with nonnegative weights transported to [a,b].

A Precision value bundles three requests for FloatLib-backed elementary ranges and a depth for checked box refinement:

(\mathrm{expOrder},\ \mathrm{sqrtDigits},\ \mathrm{logTerms},\ \mathrm{depth}) \quad\text{with defaults}\quad(8,\ 12,\ 10,\ 2).

expOrder supplies FloatLib's exponential degree after promotion of zero to one. sqrtDigits sets the binary grid for the denominator-scaled square-root bounds. logTerms maps to FloatLib degree 2\max(\mathrm{logTerms},1). The sine, cosine, and arctangent adapters use their own fixed parameters. The configuration group (prec := n) sets the first three fields to n; (depth := n) sets the subdivision depth. An omitted policy uses the defaults.

The policy is planner data. Every range theorem holds for all parameter values, so changing the policy preserves soundness while affecting cost and potential sharpness. The final width also depends on input variation, dependence between subexpressions, and period uncertainty, any of which can dominate the error.

Finite search returns a key only together with evidence that the family's acceptance predicate holds for that key. The policy theorem converts this evidence into the requested tolerance bound, and the candidate's stored quadrature soundness identifies the quantity being bounded. A failed search has no conclusion to prove.

A candidate family associates mesh, rule, or arithmetic-schedule keys with ordinary quadrature certificates and an executable Boolean acceptance test. The policy proves that every accepted result meets the requested tolerance. Finite search returns the first accepted key together with that theorem, or none if every candidate fails.

If finite search returns an accepted key k, its projection proves

\left\|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx -\operatorname{candidate}(k).\mathrm{value}\right\|\leq\tau.

A quadrature certificate stores a proposed value of a Bochner interval integral, an explicit error budget, and a proof of the corresponding norm estimate. The certificate is indexed by the ordinary Lean integrand and endpoints, so no symbolic expression type appears in theorem statements.

Its trusted field is

q.\mathrm{sound}:\qquad \left\|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-q.\mathrm{value}\right\| \leq q.\mathrm{error}.

Insert and subtract the exact certificate value Q. The triangle inequality bounds the new integral error by the original quadrature error plus \lVert Q-\widehat Q\rVert; applying the two stored bounds yields E+\delta.

An independently certified numerical value may replace the exact-real quadrature value. Its roundoff bound is added to the analytic quadrature error by the triangle inequality. The theorem is the common interface for a verified exact, interval, or floating-point implementation: a backend must prove the displayed norm bound before its computed value enters the quadrature certificate.

Concretely, if Q is the value stored in a certificate with error E and \widehat Q is a computed replacement satisfying \lVert Q-\widehat Q\rVert\leq\delta, then

\left\lVert\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-\widehat Q\right\rVert \leq E+\delta.

At every node, the sample difference is at most \varepsilon. Apply the triangle inequality to the weighted sum, bound each term by |w_j|\varepsilon, and sum to obtain V\varepsilon on the normalized interval. Affine transport contributes the factor |b-a|.

If two scalar integrands differ uniformly by \varepsilon on [[a,b]], their values under a normalized rule differ by at most |b-a|\,V\varepsilon, where V is the sum of the absolute rule weights. This estimate lets a rule that is exact on a nearby model be evaluated on the original integrand while accounting separately for integral-model error and sample-value perturbation.

The quadrature specialization stores accepted local QuadratureCerts in the same backend-independent tree used by real-valued adaptive search. Local interval-integrability evidence justifies composing adjacent panel integrals. Both an over-budget root and a missing root candidate may therefore be recovered by proved child certificates, while a failed finite search returns none.

On success it returns exactly the root theorem

\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx -R.\mathrm{tree}.\mathrm{value}\right|\leq(\tau:\mathbb R),

where a, b, and \tau are the input rationals cast to reals.

The generic rational adaptive kernel keeps endpoints, midpoints, and local tolerances exact. A rejected or unavailable parent candidate is bisected at its rational midpoint; accepted children are combined only through the client's proved error-subadditivity theorem.

The dependent result type records the invariant

\operatorname{searchPartial}(\ldots,\tau)=\operatorname{some}(R) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{error}(R.\mathrm{result})\leq(\tau:\mathbb R).

The candidate's proof bounds its semantic real error by the cast of its exact rational budget. Boolean acceptance is precisely the decidable rational comparison of that budget with \tau. Casting this comparison to the reals and composing the inequalities proves the result.

A rational-budget candidate contains a client result, an exact rational upper bound for its semantic error, and a proof relating the two. When decidable rational comparison accepts the candidate, its real error is at most the requested rational tolerance.

Precisely,

\operatorname{accepted}(c,\tau)=\mathrm{true} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{error}(c.\mathrm{cert})\leq(\tau:\mathbb R).

Polynomial gcd cancellation proposes the reduced rational expression, but the exact normalizer proves the cross-multiplied identity. Checked interval facts then show that every cancelled denominator is nonzero throughout the panel. Substituting those side facts into the conditional normalization theorem gives the pointwise equality used by the derivative bounder.

The rational route proposes a polynomial-gcd cancellation, checks its semantic equality through the exact normalizer, and turns generated denominator conditions into interval obligations. Exact rational hulls cover arbitrary real panels, and checked zero exclusion or an absolute lower bound discharges the nonzero conditions on the whole declared domain.

Writing the checked route as \operatorname{route}(d)=(r,S), its semantic boundary is the conditional identity

\operatorname{SideHolds}(\rho,S) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(d,\rho)=\operatorname{eval}(r,\rho).

The interval phase proves the premise uniformly on the panel.

Mathlib's Nat.lt_pow_nthRoot_add_one says that one more than the integer fourth root of \lceil B/\tau\rceil has fourth power above it, so the chosen natural's fourth power is at least the exact rational ratio. Rearranging with \tau>0 gives the same tolerance estimate as the real planner.

For exact rational error data, the executable planner rounds B/\mathrm{tolerance} upward and takes one more than the integer fourth root of the result (Mathlib's Nat.nthRoot 4). The resulting positive natural panel count satisfies the same fourth-order inequality without evaluating a noncomputable real root.

Prove the rational evaluator correct by structural induction on the algebraic expression, rejecting precisely the division cases with zero denominator. Apply that equality at each rational quadrature node. Casting commutes with the finite products and sum, so the compiled ordered table has the same real weighted value as the analytic rule.

The rational algebraic fragment of the shared expression language has a fail-closed exact evaluator. Every successful result is proved equal to the existing real expression semantics. A quadrature rule with rational weights and nodes can therefore sample a symbolic integrand exactly, preserve the ordered rule schedule, and cast term-for-term to the existing transported QuadratureRule. Transcendental nodes, malformed literals, and sampled zero denominators are rejected. Optional finite-precision backends consume the exact table through the same interval and weighted-sum interfaces.

At the expression boundary,

\operatorname{evalRat?}(e,\rho)=\operatorname{some}(q) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(e,\rho_{\mathbb R})=(q:\mathbb R).

For a successfully compiled rule, casting every rational term preserves the analytic schedule and value:

\operatorname{cast}\!\left(\sum_j w_j e(x_j)\right) =\sum_j (w_j:\mathbb R)\, \operatorname{eval}(e,(x_j:\mathbb R)).

Map every rational source node and weight by the affine panel formula and cast the result to the reals. Field identities show term by term that the cast node and weight equal those of the analytic transported rule. Mapping this equality over panels and flattening proves equality of both schedules and values.

Every normalized exact-rational rule compiles uniformly to N > 0 panels by mapping a source term (w,\xi) on panel k to (w/N,(k+\xi)/N). The cast rule is proved equal term-for-term to the canonical analytic uniform-composite list. This preserves both the exact-real value and the panel-major accumulation schedule used by verified numerical backends.

If B<0 the bound holds for every N. Otherwise the ceiling construction gives N\geq(B/\tau)^{1/4} and N\geq1. Positivity permits raising the first inequality to the fourth power, yielding N^4\geq B/\tau. Rearranging with \tau>0 proves B/N^4\leq\tau.

Let B=C(b-a)^5/D. For a positive tolerance, choosing N=\max(1,\lceil(B/\mathrm{tolerance})^{1/4}\rceil) proves B/N^4\leq\mathrm{tolerance}. This is the case m=4 of the planner for an error model B/N^m of any order m>0, and it is the rule-independent planner behind every fourth-order uniform composite rule.

Each local rewrite uses the corresponding identity for real powers, square roots, or exponentials under its recorded positivity conditions. The bottom-up traversal retains every condition from the rewrites it applies. Induction over the traversal composes the local evaluation equalities into the equality for the whole tree; when the expression contains no power atom the pass returns it unchanged.

The side-conditioned pipeline contains a pass for the algebra of real powers and of the exponential, which it treats as the power of \mathrm e. Inside a product or quotient all powers of one base collect into a single power, nested powers flatten, powers of products distribute, exponents are put into a polynomial normal form, and a literal exponent is read back as a natural power, a reciprocal, or a square root. Each rewrite that Mathlib states for a positive base records the positivity of that base as a condition unless the base is structurally positive (a positive numeral, \pi, \mathrm e, an exponential, or a product of these); rewrites valid for the total Real.rpow, and the exponential identities, record nothing.

Writing (e',S) for the output of the pass on e,

\operatorname{SideHolds}(\rho,S) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(e',\rho)=\operatorname{eval}(e,\rho).

Structural induction on the expression. Constants and coordinate projections are smooth; sums, products, and negations preserve ContDiffAt; quotients, logarithms, square roots, real powers, and the inverse sine and cosine are smooth at every point satisfying the validity clause of their constructor, by Mathlib's ContDiffAt lemmas for the elementary functions and the field operations; the remaining elementary functions are smooth everywhere. The derivative bridge also gives differentiability, and the set and global forms quantify these pointwise statements over their domain.

The validity predicate that justifies one symbolic derivative also certifies regularity of every order. At a point where ValidAt holds, evaluation of a reflected expression is C^m for every smoothness order m, the analytic order included, because each constructor is interpreted by an elementary function that Mathlib proves smooth of every order away from its singularities; the On and global forms assume validity at every point of the set or the space. The theorems are stated for the two conventions of the theorem-facing tactics, functions on \mathbb R^n and functions on \mathbb R with frozen parameters, and they are what cas applies to a DifferentiableAt, Differentiable, ContDiffAt, ContDiffOn, or ContDiff goal:

\operatorname{ValidAt}(x,e) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^\sharp\text{ is }C^m\text{ at }x \qquad\text{for every }m\in\{0,1,2,\ldots,\infty,\omega\}.

Rewrite the analytic residual as the evaluation of the lowered residual, using the analytic side conditions. ClosedResidualVanishesAt is exactly the assertion that this evaluation is zero, so it finishes the proof. A side-aware normalizer is one way to supply that vanishing proof after its denominator and branch conditions have been discharged.

In positive dimension, lower a differential equation against a closed-form ansatz to a symbolic residual. If that residual evaluates to zero at the point and its analytic side conditions hold there, then R_{\mathrm{closed}}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ R_{\mathrm{analytic}}(u^\sharp,x)=0.

A pointwise residual energy is the square of a LinearPDE's totalized residual expression. A sampled loss sums these energies over a finite list of points. Interpreting this objective as a classical PDE loss requires a separate regularity proof for the candidate field. Given a parameterized model \theta \mapsto u_\theta, its objective is the ordinary composition \theta \mapsto \operatorname{sampledLoss}(u_\theta).

The checked derivative bridge computes the four coordinate derivatives of (-y,x) as 0,-1,1,0. Each symmetric-gradient entry therefore vanishes, so the sum of their squares is pointwise zero. Integral congruence gives the result on every set.

For the planar rigid rotation u(x,y)=(-y,x), every entry of the symmetric gradient vanishes. Consequently its small-strain energy density integrates to zero on every domain. The public theorem is an ordinary integral identity; the symbolic engine is used only to calculate the coordinate derivatives and close the pointwise algebra.

Take a root in the covered domain and choose an atlas panel containing it. A root-free panel is impossible because its certificate excludes zero. Consequently the chosen panel is one of the root regions, which proves the covering conclusion. The global version first uses the outer bound to place the root in the covered domain.

A root atlas combines root-free and uniquely rooted panels with a proved cover. Every real root in the outer domain therefore belongs to one of the atlas's isolated root regions.

If \mathcal A is an atlas over D, its projection is

x\in D\land p(x)=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists R\in\mathcal A.\mathrm{rootRegions},\ x\in R.

For a global atlas the premise x\in D is removed by its outer-root bound.
Sound interval evaluation places every p(x) in the computed range. The Boolean root-free test proves that zero is outside that range. Therefore no enclosed value can equal zero.

If checked interval evaluation excludes zero, the polynomial is nonzero throughout the panel. The result can be used directly as a side condition for an ordinary real-expression theorem.

\operatorname{rootFree}(p,[a,b])=\mathrm{true} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall x\in[a,b],\ p(x)\neq0.

Two integrations by parts write each error as \int_a^bK(t)f''(t)\,dt. For the trapezoid rule the kernel is (t-a)(b-t)/2\ge0, of mass (b-a)^3/12. For the midpoint rule it is (t-a)^2/2 on the left half and (b-t)^2/2 on the right, of mass (b-a)^3/24. Bound f'' by C.

On an ordered interval, for f\in C^2[a,b] with \|f''\|\le C there,

\left\|\int_a^bf-\frac{b-a}2\bigl(f(a)+f(b)\bigr)\right\| \le\frac{C(b-a)^3}{12},\qquad \left\|\int_a^bf-(b-a)f\!\left(\tfrac{a+b}2\right)\right\| \le\frac{C(b-a)^3}{24}.

Both rules are exact through degree one, and they are panel rules of order two with D=12 and D=24.

For each splittable coordinate x_i, the planner encloses the symbolic partial derivative and assigns the exact rational score

(b_i-a_i)\max\{|L_i|,|U_i|\}, \qquad \operatorname{eval}(\operatorname{diff}_i e,X)\subseteq[L_i,U_i].

This is an enclosure of the formal derivative expression. Its identification with an analytic partial derivative requires the separate validity hypotheses. The largest positive score selects the coordinate; if no score is positive, the widest coordinate with an unenclosed derivative is chosen. The ranking is a heuristic, and soundness comes from the checked interval enclosures used by the adaptive search.

Every checked symbolic transformation is recorded by one route type. A SideClaimRoute stores the source and target expressions, the list of expressions that must not vanish, and a proof that the target and source evaluate equally wherever that list holds; a positivity requirement is encoded as the nonvanishing of a square root. An unconditional transformation is the same object with an empty list of assumptions.

For a route with source l, target r, and assumption list S,

\operatorname{SideHolds}(\rho,S) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(r,\rho)=\operatorname{eval}(l,\rho), \qquad S=[\,]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall\rho,\ \operatorname{eval}(r,\rho)=\operatorname{eval}(l,\rho).

Side-aware constructors consume a checked equality route together with proofs of every emitted nonzero condition. The rational specialization may cancel polynomial factors, but its simplified derivative enters the bounder only through that conditional semantic equality.

The constructor composes

\left(\forall x\in[a,b],\operatorname{SideHolds}(x,S)\right) \land \left(\forall x\in[a,b],|\operatorname{eval}(r,x)|\leq B\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall x\in[a,b],\|f^{(n)}(x)\|\leq B.

The side-aware route proves evaluation preservation conditionally on every emitted nonzero or branch requirement. Once SideHolds supplies those requirements, the route's final zero expression evaluates to zero, so the original expression does as well.

Rational cancellation and other conditional rewrites return the nonzero conditions they require. Under those conditions, reduction to zero again implies equality of the original real expression.

If normalization returns a zero expression together with side conditions S, then

\operatorname{normalizeWithSide}(e)=(0,S) \land\operatorname{SideHolds}(\rho,S) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(e,\rho)=0.

Apply the rational fourth-order planner with denominator 2880, the error constant B=C(b-a)^5/2880 of the composite Simpson theorem: its panel count N satisfies B/N^4\leq\tau in exact rational arithmetic.

Substituting the sharp Simpson denominator D=2880 into the executable rational planner produces a panel count whose composite error bound C(b-a)^5/(2880N^4) is at most the requested rational tolerance.

Represent the Simpson error as the integral of the fourth derivative against its Peano kernel, whose two polynomial pieces live on [a,(a+b)/2] and [(a+b)/2,b]; four integrations by parts produce it, and cubic exactness cancels all boundary polynomial terms. The kernel has fixed sign and exact mass (b-a)^5/2880. Bounding the fourth derivative by C gives the stated norm estimate.

For an ordered interval [a,b], a C^4 scalar integrand, and a bound C on its fourth within-derivative, the Peano-kernel argument gives the classical one-panel Simpson estimate \lVert\int_a^b f-S(f)\rVert\le C(b-a)^5/2880, returned as a QuadratureCert.

FloatLib proves both containment and the width bound for its integer-root enclosure. Since d>0, division by d preserves the endpoint order, and \sqrt{qd^2}=d\sqrt q gives the desired point enclosure. For negative arguments, Mathlib's square root is zero. Apply monotonicity of this total function to the two endpoint certificates to enclose the full panel.

For every rational panel and every binary precision s, sqrtRangeInterval contains Mathlib's total real square root throughout the panel. At a nonnegative endpoint q=n/d in lowest terms, the point enclosure has width at most 1/(d2^s) and is exact when its lower endpoint squares to q. Negative endpoints map to zero. The default precision is 12 binary digits.

The checked division identities certify the gcd decomposition used by the square-free reduction. They show that removing repeated factors preserves exactly the zero set. Coprimality of the reduced polynomial and its derivative then rules out a point where both vanish, so every remaining root is simple.

A radical certificate proves that a proposed square-free reduction has exactly the same real zero set as the original polynomial and has nonzero derivative at every root. The executable Yun-style generator returns only a certificate that passes the independent check of two divisibility identities and a Bézout identity.

Writing the checked radical as r,

\forall x\in\mathbb R,\qquad p(x)=0\Longleftrightarrow r(x)=0, \qquad r(x)=0\Longrightarrow r'(x)\neq0.

A signed Euclidean chain is proposed outside the checker and accepted only when the independent structural checker SturmCertificate.valid accepts every initial, recurrence, degree, and terminal condition. SymLean has no chain generator: a caller supplies the chain.

\mathrm{valid}(p, C)=\mathrm{true} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad C\text{ is a validated Sturm certificate for }p.

The independent checker verifies the first two entries and every signed quotient-remainder identity using exact polynomial normalization. At the terminal entry it checks a zero formal derivative and a nonzero value at zero. The mean value theorem makes that polynomial constant, hence nowhere zero. Collecting these checked equalities yields the defining Sturm-chain conditions.

An accepted Sturm certificate begins with the requested polynomial and its formal derivative, satisfies every signed Euclidean recurrence exactly, and ends in a polynomial that is nonzero on the real line. These are structural facts about the checked chain, before any root-counting theorem is applied.

For a chain S_0,\ldots,S_m, validation establishes

S_0=p,\qquad S_1=p',\qquad S_{i-1}=Q_iS_i-S_{i+1},\qquad \forall x\in\mathbb R,\ S_m(x)\neq0.

Apply the Sturm count theorem at every node. A node of count zero is root-free; a node of count one contains a root and cannot contain two distinct roots. For a split node, additivity of root counts over its adjacent children preserves the parent's exact count. Structural induction over the accepted subdivision tree therefore produces the root atlas.

Sturm counts certify unique-root intervals and exact root counts for a checked subdivision tree. An accepted finite subdivision therefore projects to the same root-atlas interface used by interval and monotonicity certificates.

For each accepted node N with interval I_N,

N.\mathrm{rootCount} =\#\{x\in I_N^\circ\mid p(x)=0\},

and every leaf with count one projects to an \exists!\,x\in I_N,\ p(x)=0 certificate.

Along an interval containing no endpoint root, sign variation is locally constant except when crossing a root of p. The signed Euclidean recurrence shows that noninitial chain entries cannot create a net jump, while each distinct root of p decreases the variation by one. Summing the jumps from a to b gives the root count.

For an accepted chain and ordered rational endpoints that are not roots, the drop in endpoint sign variations equals the number of distinct real roots in the intervening open interval. This is the analytic Sturm theorem that gives the executable variation count its mathematical meaning.

V(a)-V(b) =\#\{x\in(a,b)\mid p(x)=0\}.

Subtract the two finite power series term by term and apply the triangle inequality. Each coefficient difference is at most \delta_k, while |x-a|^k\leq(b-a)^k on the ordered interval. Summing these bounds gives the displayed perturbation estimate.

Suppose the stored coefficient c_k is within \delta_k\geq0 of the exact Taylor coefficient c_k^\ast for 0\leq k\leq n. For the stored jet q_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}c_k(x-a)^k, the coefficient bounds imply

\forall x\in[a,b],\qquad \left|T^{[a,b]}_{n,a}f(x)-q_n(x)\right| \leq\sum_{k=0}^{n}\delta_k(b-a)^k.

This estimate contains coefficient uncertainty only.

FloatLib identifies its rational Taylor sum and error radius with their real counterparts, then applies Mathlib's Real.exp_bound with d+1 terms. The hypothesis |q|\leq1 gives the bound |\exp q-T_n(q)|\leq R_n(q). Its contains_expSmall theorem expresses that absolute-error estimate as interval containment. CEGA reuses the upstream kernel through its exponential range adapter.

For every rational q with |q|\leq1 and every degree d, FloatLib's expSmall q d encloses \exp q. With n=d+1, the polynomial T_n(q) has absolute error at most R_n(q), so the real exponential lies between the exact rational endpoints T_n(q)-R_n(q) and T_n(q)+R_n(q).

Insert the exact Taylor polynomial between f and the stored jet q_n. The Taylor remainder theorem bounds the first difference, and the coefficient perturbation theorem bounds the second. The triangle inequality adds these two independent budgets, producing the certificate's soundness field.

The combined certificate converts derivative enclosures into coefficient centers c_k, coefficient radii \delta_k, and a bound C on the (n+1)-st within derivative. For q_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}c_k(x-a)^k, its soundness theorem is

\forall x\in[a,b],\qquad |f(x)-q_n(x)| \leq C\frac{(b-a)^{n+1}}{n!} +\sum_{k=0}^{n}\delta_k(b-a)^k.

The same proposition is exported as an ordinary ModelApproxCert. Runtime roundoff in evaluating q_n is a separate error.

Expand the finite real jet as its coefficient sum and substitute the definition c_k=D^k_{[a,b]}f(a)/k!. The resulting finite sum is exactly the definition of Mathlib's scalar Taylor evaluation, so the two functions agree for every x.

Let c_k=(k!)^{-1}D^k_{[a,b]}f(a) be the exact within-derivative coefficient. For every real x, evaluating the finite power-basis jet gives exactly Mathlib's scalar Taylor polynomial:

\sum_{k=0}^{n}c_k(x-a)^k =T^{[a,b]}_{n,a}f(x).

Thus the finite coefficient sum and the analytic object used by the remainder theorem have the same real semantics.

For a multi-index \alpha:\iota\to_0\mathbb N, an order-N jet is a formal coefficient family J_\alpha. When a separate semantic theorem identifies these coefficients with derivatives, the normalization convention is

J_\alpha(f,x)=\frac{D^\alpha f(x)}{\alpha!}.

Formal products use ordinary power-series convolution:

(JK)_\alpha =\sum_{\beta+\gamma=\alpha}J_\beta K_\gamma.
